### [1] [Simulator-Grounded Large Language Models for Industrial Causal Reasoning: Tool-Use, Structured Injection, and Plant-Portable Retrieval for Wastewater Treatment Decision Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05151)
*Gary Simethy,Daniel Ortiz Arroyo,Petar Durdevic*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Compares three methods for grounding a frozen LLM in a wastewater simulator to answer causal and counterfactual questions. A live simulator oracle achieves near-perfect accuracy, while a lightweight Decoupled Recall-Reasoning (DRR) retriever (110M params, ~17s training) offers strong performance and cross-plant transferability, outperforming retrieval-augmented baselines and static parameter injection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wastewater operators need causal answers grounded in their specific plant's dynamics (interactions, propagation speed), not in generic pretraining text. Existing LLMs lack this operational grounding, and no prior work has systematically compared tool-use, parameter injection, and retrieval-based approaches for industrial causal QA using a single simulator.

Method: Three grounding methods are compared using a frozen Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model paired with the CCSS-IX wastewater simulator: (1) a live simulator oracle, (2) structured parameter injection, and (3) a Decoupled Recall-Reasoning (DRR) retriever (110M parameters, trained per plant in ~17s). Evaluation uses a 198-question causal benchmark, a 60-question counterfactual benchmark, and out-of-domain replication on ARC with OpenBookQA.

Result: On the 198-question causal benchmark: Method 1 reaches 99.5%, Method 2 reaches 79%, Method 3 reaches 75.8%, versus a retrieval-augmented baseline at 48%. DRR transfers cross-plant at 88% (Method 2's static table fails to transfer). On counterfactuals, DRR outperforms Method 2 by +16.3 pp (95% CI [+7.1, +26.4]), with 100% on timescale/operating-regime categories. On ARC, DRR achieves 79% vs. Llama-3.1-8B (76%) and full-injection (74%), a +3 pp out-of-domain replication.

Conclusion: The three methods form a "deployment ladder" trading off accuracy, latency, and transferability. The lightweight DRR retriever offers a practical middle ground: near-oracle cross-plant transfer, strong counterfactual handling, and out-of-domain generalization, establishing the first systematic single-simulator comparison of these grounding paradigms for industrial causal QA.

Abstract: Wastewater operators need answers grounded in how their plant's variables interact and how fast effects propagate, not in generic pretraining text, when asking causal questions such as "why is N2O rising?" or "what happens if I cut aeration by 20%?". We compare three concrete ways to ground a frozen Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model in an architecturally interpretable wastewater simulator (CCSS-IX): a live simulator oracle (Method 1), structured parameter injection (Method 2), and a Decoupled Recall-Reasoning (DRR) retriever (Method 3). On a 198-question causal benchmark the three reach 99.5%, 79%, and 75.8%, forming a deployment ladder above the strongest retrieval-augmented baseline at 48%. The DRR retriever has 110M parameters and trains per plant in ~17 seconds; after cross-plant transfer to a biologically distinct plant it still reaches 88%, while Method 2's static table cannot transfer. On a 60-question counterfactual benchmark only Method 3 handles queries about what happens after an intervention: +16.3 pp over Method 2, paired 95% CI [+7.1, +26.4] pp, with 100% on the timescale and operating-regime categories. On the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC) with an OpenBookQA fact corpus, the same selective-retrieval mechanism reaches 79% versus unconstrained Llama-3.1-8B 76% and full-injection 74%, a +3 pp out-of-domain replication that argues against a result specific to wastewater treatment. We provide the first single-simulator comparison of live tool-use, static parameter injection, and learned numerical-parameter retrieval for industrial causal question answering.

</details>


### [2] [Mean-Field Dynamics of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05152)
*Hao Ai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a mean-field framework that models LLM chain-of-thought reasoning as a guided clue-discovery process on a graph, deriving an ODE for the fraction of discovered clues, with empirical validation using surprisal-based clue identification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing theoretical explanations of LLM reasoning either oversimplify model architecture or rely on analogies to physical systems. The authors seek a principled framework that captures statistical regularities in LLM reasoning without such simplifications, to deepen understanding and guide optimization.

Method: LLM reasoning is formalized as a guided discovery process traversing a clue graph. Using mean-field approximation, the authors derive a one-dimensional ordinary differential equation (ODE) governing the fraction of clues discovered over reasoning steps. Clue tokens are empirically identified via normalized surprisal of a student LLM on teacher LLM outputs. Statistical regularities are extracted by averaging over many chain-of-thought reasoning traces.

Result: The statistical regularities observed are reproducible within the same dataset and can be accurately fitted by solving the derived theoretical ODE, validating the proposed framework.

Conclusion: The mean-field ODE framework successfully captures and predicts the dynamics of clue discovery during LLM chain-of-thought reasoning, offering a theoretically grounded tool for analyzing and potentially optimizing LLM reasoning behavior.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with chain-of-thought reasoning have been widely applied in recent years, and theoretical explanations of their behavior may help deepen our understanding and guide model optimization. In this study, we introduce a framework that seeks statistical regularities and theoretical interpretations in LLM reasoning without simplifying the model architecture or making analogies to existing physical systems. We formulate LLM reasoning as a guided discovery process on a clue graph, and derive a one-dimensional ordinary differential equation for the fraction of discovered clues using the mean-field approximation. Experimentally, clue tokens are identified using the normalized surprisal of a student LLM on the outputs of a teacher LLM, and statistical regularities are obtained by averaging over many reasoning chains of thought. Our experiments show that the resulting statistical regularities are reproducible within the same dataset and can be fitted by the solving the proposed theoretical equation.

</details>


### [3] [Universal Pathologies, Conditional Consequences: A Triple-Robustness Analysis of RAG for Multi-Hop Traceability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05153)
*Meftun Akarsu,Burak Ozdemir*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A systematic triple-robustness study (varying embedder, corpus, and judge) demonstrates that GraphRAG's over-citation problem is architecturally universal, but its faithfulness consequences are corpus-conditional. The authors also expose single-judge LLM evaluation fragility and propose a learned router for hop classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior reports that GraphRAG underperforms vector RAG on citation precision have been anecdotal and corpus-bound. The authors seek to characterize *where* and *why* this occurs through a controlled, multi-axis robustness framework, arguing that triple-robustness should be the minimum bar for trustworthy RAG architecture claims.

Method: Triple-robustness analysis holding retrieval architecture fixed while varying three orthogonal axes: (1) embedder (local e5-small vs. Azure text-embedding-3-small), (2) corpus (DO-178C typed-edge requirements vs. Wikipedia paragraph chains via MuSiQue), and (3) judge (paired GPT-5.4 vs. GPT-4.1). The study runs 4,440 main-matrix experiments, 600 cross-corpus runs, and 1,200 paired faithfulness judgments. Four claims (C1-C4) are tested, including hop-conditional winner analysis, over-citation quantification, single-judge reliability (self-kappa), and a learned router for hop classification.

Result: (C2a) Over-citation is architecturally universal: GraphRAG emits 11–15 IDs per answer with citation precision 0.12–0.23 and retrieval recall 0.68–0.87 across all settings. (C2b) Faithfulness consequences are corpus-conditional: on DO-178C, faithfulness drops from 74% to 40% across hops; on Wikipedia chains, it rises from 42% to 58% because over-cited paragraphs remain topically supporting. (C1) Stratum-conditional winners are corpus-conditional but embedder-robust. (C3) Single-judge LLM faithfulness is fragile: GPT-5.4 self-kappa across embedders is only 0.137, with verdict changes on 41% of items. (C4) A learned router using dense embeddings achieves macro-F1 of 0.86 on hop classification.

Conclusion: Triple-robustness analysis reveals that GraphRAG's citation behavior is governed by architectural invariants (universal over-citation) modulated by corpus-conditional faithfulness effects. The fragility of single-judge LLM evaluation and the success of a dense-embedding router suggest both methodological and practical paths forward. The authors advocate triple-robustness as a minimum standard for credible RAG architecture comparisons.

Abstract: GraphRAG underperforms vector RAG on citation precision in many reports, but where and why have remained corpus-bound. We present a triple-robustness analysis that holds the retrieval architecture fixed and varies three orthogonal axes embedder (local e5-small -> Azure text-embedding-3-small), corpus (DO-178C typed-edge requirements -> Wikipedia paragraph chains via MuSiQue), and judge (paired GPT-5.4 x GPT-4.1) across 4,440 main-matrix runs, 600 cross-corpus runs, and 1,200 paired faithfulness judgments. (C2a) Over-citation is architecturally universal: GraphRAG emits 11-15 IDs per answer at citation precision 0.12-0.23 and retrieval recall 0.68-0.87 across all three settings. (C2b) Its faithfulness consequence is corpus-conditional: in typed-edge DO-178C, GraphRAG faithfulness collapses 74%->40% across hops; on Wikipedia chains the same pipeline rises 42%->58% because over-cited paragraphs remain topically supporting. (C1) Stratum-conditional winners are corpus-conditional but embedder-robust: vanilla wins 2-hop on DO-178C, GraphRAG wins 2-hop on MuSiQue, identical under either embedder. (C3) Single-judge LLM faithfulness is fragile to retrieval state: same-judge self-kappa across embedders is 0.137 for GPT-5.4 (verdict change on 41% of items). A learned router on dense embeddings alone reaches macro-F1 0.86 on hop classification (C4). We argue triple-robustness is the minimum bar for trustworthy RAG architecture claims.

</details>


### [4] [RIG-RoPE: Relation- and Instance-Gated Rotary Positional Encoding with Duration-Aware Temporal Coordinates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05154)
*Donggen Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RIG-RoPE introduces instance-gated spatial rotations and duration-aware temporal coordinates to fix two flaws in M-RoPE: cross-modal/inter-instance spatial interference and equal-step temporal counters across modalities of vastly different information density.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: M-RoPE's static multidimensional position assignment causes two problems in interleaved multimodal contexts: (1) height/width rotations applied to token pairs lacking well-defined geometric spatial displacement produce cross-modal and inter-instance spatial interference; (2) treating temporal coordinates as equal-step counters ignores the differing information density of text, images, and video.

Method: RIG-RoPE augments each token with a modality indicator, a visual instance identifier, and a scalar information-duration coordinate. H/W rotations are enabled only for query-key pairs from the same visual instance; otherwise unknown spatial displacement is marginalized. Temporal rotations use interpolated cumulative block durations — text tokens consume unit duration, images use a dimension-aware logarithmic spatial scale, and videos apply a logarithmic temporal extension over effective frames. The method adds no learned parameters and operates in tiled attention kernels with constant per-token metadata overhead. Theoretical support includes a gauge-invariance argument against cross-instance spatial rotation, an impossibility result for static IDs under shared H/W subspaces, and a duration-consistency argument against equal-step multimodal time.

Result: This is a preliminary report that establishes the formulation and validation path without claiming empirical superiority. No experimental results are reported.

Conclusion: RIG-RoPE provides a theoretically grounded reformulation of multidimensional RoPE for interleaved multimodal contexts, addressing two identified limitations of M-RoPE through instance-gated spatial rotations and duration-aware temporal coordinates. Empirical validation remains future work.

Abstract: Rotary positional encoding (RoPE) is a core component of modern language models and has been extended to multimodal LLMs through multidimensional variants such as multimodal RoPE (M-RoPE), which split positional channels into temporal, height, and width subspaces. This report identifies two limitations of static multidimensional position assignment in interleaved multimodal contexts. First, height/width rotations may be applied to token pairs whose spatial displacement is not a well-defined geometric object, producing cross-modal and inter-instance spatial interference. Second, temporal coordinates are often treated as equal-step counters, so a text token, an image block, and a video segment can advance the temporal phase by comparable amounts despite different information density.
  We propose RIG-RoPE, a relation- and instance-gated RoPE mechanism with duration-aware temporal coordinates. RIG-RoPE augments each token with a modality indicator, a visual instance identifier, and a scalar information-duration coordinate. It enables H/W rotations only for query-key pairs from the same visual instance; otherwise the unknown spatial displacement is marginalized rather than set to zero. Temporal rotations use interpolated cumulative block durations: text tokens consume unit duration, images use a dimension-aware logarithmic spatial scale, and videos further apply a logarithmic temporal extension over effective frames. We provide a gauge-invariance argument for avoiding ordinary cross-instance spatial rotation, an impossibility result for static IDs under shared H/W subspaces, and a duration-consistency argument against equal-step multimodal time. RIG-RoPE adds no learned parameters and can be implemented inside tiled attention kernels with constant additional metadata per token. This preliminary report establishes the formulation and validation path without claiming empirical superiority.

</details>


### [5] [Beyond Sentiment: Comparing Traditional NLP and LLM-Based Multi-Dimensional Analysis for Political News Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05155)
*Maryam Fooladi,Federico Bottino*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RoBERTa-based sentiment analysis fails to capture political discourse nuance, classifying 70% of articles as neutral ("neutral collapse"), whereas an LLM-based multi-dimensional framing analysis reveals bias direction, sensationalism, emotional appeal, and political framing — better aligning with social sciences and humanities research needs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional sentiment analysis models are insufficient for political discourse analysis because they only capture polarity, ignoring the rhetorical, ideological, and framing dimensions essential to social sciences and humanities (SSH) research.

Method: Comparative study applying both RoBERTa-based sentiment analysis and an LLM-based multi-dimensional framing analysis platform to a corpus of 50 political news articles from 17 international media outlets.

Result: RoBERTa exhibits "neutral collapse" — 70% of articles classified as neutral, with 23% of those having negative probability scores above 0.30. The LLM-based approach successfully captures political bias direction/intensity, sensationalism, emotional appeal, and political framing.

Conclusion: Traditional sentiment analysis alone is insufficient for political media analysis. LLM-based multi-dimensional framing frameworks provide a more epistemologically adequate computational lens for SSH research.

Abstract: Traditional sentiment analysis (SA) models, while effective for polarity classification, provide limited insight into the rhetorical, ideological, and framing dimensions of political discourse -- dimensions that are central to research in the social sciences and humanities (SSH). In this paper, we present a comparative study of RoBERTa-based sentiment analysis and an LLM-based multi-dimensional framing analysis platform applied to a corpus of 50 political news articles from 17 international media outlets. The results reveal a critical limitation we term neutral collapse: RoBERTa classifies 70% of articles as neutral, effectively flattening substantively rich political content into an analytically uninformative category. We find that 23% of neutral-classified articles exhibit negative probability scores above 0.30. By contrast, the LLM-based approach captures political bias direction and intensity, sensationalism, emotional appeal, and political framing -- yielding multi-dimensional analytical outputs aligned with SSH epistemologies. We argue that for political media analysis, traditional SA alone is insufficient, and that LLM-based multi-dimensional frameworks offer a more epistemologically adequate computational lens for SSH research needs.

</details>


### [6] [Scaffold-Mediated Post-Training: Co-Evolving Model Parameters and Procedural Scaffold Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05156)
*Fei Ding,Yongkang Zhang,Runhao Liu,Yuhao Liao,Zijian Zeng,Huiming Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes "Skill Training," a scaffold-mediated post-training paradigm where procedural scaffolds are organized into an evolvable graph that co-evolves with model parameters through discovery, distillation, and dynamic recompilation. On FeatureBench, discovered skills improve pass rate by 8.1pp, and after distillation, the model retains 85.2% of performance without external scaffolds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current post-training optimizes only model parameters, while inference-time procedural scaffolds are designed independently. This disconnect prevents models from automatically acquiring and internalizing complex strategies that scaffolds can provide.

Method: Scaffold-mediated post-training (Skill Training): procedural scaffolds are structured as an evolvable graph that co-evolves with model parameters. The process involves three stages: (1) discovery of effective skills/scaffolds, (2) distillation of scaffold behaviors into model parameters, and (3) dynamic recompilation to update the scaffold graph based on evolving model capabilities.

Result: On FeatureBench, automatically discovered skills improve the passed rate by 8.1 percentage points. After progressive distillation, the model achieves a 27.7% passed rate without any external scaffold, corresponding to a distillation retention rate of 85.2% (post-distillation / with-skill passed rate). This significantly outperforms standard SFT on the same data.

Conclusion: Scaffold-mediated post-training enables models to both leverage scaffolds at inference time and internalize scaffold-derived strategies into their parameters. The paradigm bridges the gap between parameter optimization and procedural scaffolding, enabling automatic acquisition and retention of complex reasoning strategies.

Abstract: Post-training of large language models optimizes only parameters, while inference-time procedural scaffolds are typically designed independently of parameter training. This disconnect makes it difficult to automatically acquire and internalize complex strategies. We propose scaffold-mediated post-training: procedural scaffolds are organized into an evolvable graph structure that co-evolves with model parameters through discovery, distillation, and dynamic recompilation. We instantiate this paradigm as Skill Training. On FeatureBench, automatically discovered skills improve the passed rate by 8.1pp, and after progressive distillation the model still achieves a 27.7% passed rate without any external scaffold (distillation retention rate 85.2%, defined as post-distillation / with-skill passed rate), significantly outperforming standard SFT on the same data.

</details>


### [7] [Large Language Models Threaten Double-blind Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05157)
*Bulambo Mwendelwa Gloire,Prasenjit Mitra*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs can infer authors from anonymized paper titles and abstracts with alarming accuracy, undermining the effectiveness of double-blind peer review by exploiting latent conceptual signatures in problem framing and research focus — even when explicit stylistic and bibliographic cues are removed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Double-blind peer review relies on the assumption that anonymized manuscripts do not reveal author identity. Prior work showed authorship can be recovered via citation networks or stylistic markers, but this paper investigates whether large language models pose a fundamentally new threat by leveraging semantic and conceptual patterns alone.

Method: The authors test LLM-based authorship inference using only titles and abstracts from papers published after the models' training cutoff dates. Candidate pools consist of five domain experts. They systematically exclude stylistic and bibliographic cues to isolate whether stable patterns in problem framing and research focus — termed "latent conceptual signatures" — are sufficient for author identification.

Result: LLMs collapse anonymity more efficiently than humans, concentrating belief onto a small subset of plausible authors from the candidate pool. The vulnerability persists even after removing stylistic and bibliographic cues, demonstrating that conceptual framing alone carries an authorial fingerprint.

Conclusion: Double-blind review is vulnerable to automated semantic inference via LLMs. This necessitates rethinking how anonymity and fairness are preserved in an AI-augmented research ecosystem, as the assumption that anonymized text conceals authorship is increasingly untenable.

Abstract: Double blind peer review serves as the scientific community primary defense against status and affiliation bias. Its effectiveness rests on the assumption that anonymized manuscripts convey scientific merit without revealing their authors. While authorship can often be recovered using citation networks or stylistic markers, we show that this assumption is increasingly fragile in the presence of large language models (LLMs). Using only titles and abstracts from papers published after model training, we find that LLMs collapse anonymity more efficiently than humans, with belief concentrating onto a small subset of plausible authors drawn from pools of five domain expert candidates. This vulnerability persists even when stylistic and bibliographic cues are excluded, indicating that stable patterns in problem framing and research focus function as latent conceptual signatures of authorship. Together, these findings indicate that double blind review is vulnerable to automated semantic inference, necessitating a revaluation of how anonymity and fairness are maintained in an AI augmented research ecosystem.

</details>


### [8] [Safe Evolution with Circuit Anchors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05158)
*Yan Liu,Jie Fu,Tsung-Yi Ho*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies that current LLM self-evolution algorithms optimize purely for capability without safety constraints, leading to "misevolved" models that are powerful but dangerous. Inspired by biological developmental constraints (e.g., Hox genes), the authors propose Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE), which uses mechanistic interpretability to identify a small safety circuit (<2% of features) and constrains it during evolution, preserving safety while allowing other features to adapt. CAE outperforms reward-based constraints across 3 model families and 2 evolution algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current self-evolution algorithms for LLMs optimize solely for capability under the implicit assumption that safety is preserved. The authors demonstrate this assumption is dangerously wrong: models can "misevolve" into highly capable yet unsafe entities. Nature solves an analogous problem through developmental constraints (e.g., Hox genes anchoring body plans while peripheral genes adapt), but no similar constrained evolution mechanism exists for LLMs.

Method: The proposed method, Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE), operates in two stages: (1) Using mechanistic interpretability, the authors identify a "safety circuit" — a small set of features (<2% of the model) that causally mediate safety behaviors. (2) During self-evolution, this safety circuit is anchored by constraining it within a small displacement bound, while the remaining ~98% of features evolve freely. This mirrors biological evolvability with constraint: preserving essential functions while adapting peripheral ones.

Result: Experiments across 3 model families and 2 evolution algorithms show that CAE achieves superior safety preservation with minimal capability loss compared to explicit reward-based constraints. The approach is more effective and efficient at preventing models from becoming capable but dangerous systems.

Conclusion: Just as developmental constraints prevent biological evolution from producing nonviable organisms, circuit anchoring prevents model self-evolution from producing capable but dangerous systems. The work establishes a biologically-inspired paradigm for safe model evolution, demonstrating that mechanistic interpretability can provide principled, efficient safety constraints without sacrificing capability.

Abstract: In biological evolution, unconstrained mutation can lead to catastrophic outcomes: organisms may evolve enhanced capabilities while losing essential functions for survival. Nature's solution is \textit{developmental constraints}, where core regulatory genes remain anchored while peripheral genes adapt freely. We observe that current self-evolution algorithms for large language models lack analogous constraints. They optimize purely for capability, implicitly assuming safety will be preserved. Our experiments reveal this assumption to be dangerously wrong: models can \textit{misevolve} into powerful yet dangerous entities. Inspired by how Hox genes anchor body structure across $500$ million years of evolution, we propose \textbf{Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE)}. Using mechanistic interpretability, we identify a tiny \textit{safety circuit}, comprising less than $2$\% of model features, that causally mediates safety behaviors. We anchor this circuit during evolution, constraining it within a small displacement bound while allowing the remaining features to evolve freely. This mirrors the biological principle of \textit{evolvability with constraint}: preserving what is essential while adapting what is peripheral. Experiments across $3$ model families and two evolution algorithms demonstrate that CAE achieves superior safety preservation with minimal capability loss, substantially outperforming explicit reward-based constraints in both effectiveness and efficiency. Just as developmental constraints prevent biological evolution from producing nonviable organisms, circuit anchoring prevents model evolution from producing capable but dangerous systems.

</details>


### [9] [SemiAdapt-Instruct: Extensible Instruction Tuning via Latent Domain-Specialised Adapters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05161)
*Josh McGiff,Salma Mekaoui,Robert Shanahan,Nikola S. Nikolov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SemiAdapt-Instruct is a modular framework that discovers latent instruction domains, trains per-domain LoRA adapters in parallel with parameter-free routing, and enables extensible updates to LLMs by training only a single new adapter for new domains—outperforming full fine-tuning while matching single LoRA performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Instruction-tuned LLMs face a practical challenge: deployment environments evolve with new domains, but extending a fine-tuned model's capabilities typically requires costly full retraining. Existing monolithic approaches lack extensibility for incremental domain additions.

Method: SemiAdapt-Instruct employs a three-stage modular framework: (1) unsupervised discovery of latent instruction domains from heterogeneous data, (2) parallel training of per-domain LoRA adapters, and (3) parameter-free routing to dispatch inputs to the appropriate adapter. New domains are incorporated by training only a single new adapter without modifying existing components.

Result: SemiAdapt-Instruct outperforms full model fine-tuning across all configurations on both ROUGE-L and LLM-as-a-judge metrics. It matches single LoRA fine-tuning performance while providing extensibility that monolithic approaches lack. Updating a single adapter with new domain data surpasses all monolithic baselines. Independent discovery methods converge on identical specialisation-friendly domains.

Conclusion: Decomposing heterogeneous instruction data into latent domains enables extensible NLP systems where evolving domains require only targeted single-adapter updates, eliminating the need for full model retraining.

Abstract: Instruction-tuned LLMs are deployed into environments where domains evolve, yet extending a fine-tuned model's capabilities without full retraining remains an unsolved practical challenge. We present SemiAdapt-Instruct, a modular framework that discovers latent instruction domains, trains per-domain LoRA adapters in parallel, and performs parameter-free routing, incorporating new domains via single-adapter training without modifying existing components. SemiAdapt-Instruct outperforms full model fine-tuning across all configurations on both ROUGE-L and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, while matching single LoRA fine-tuning and delivering extensibility that monolithic approaches cannot provide. We empirically demonstrate this extensibility by showing that updating a single adapter with new domain data outperforms all monolithic baselines. Our study also finds that independent discovery methods converge on the same specialisation-friendly domains. These findings demonstrate that decomposing heterogeneous instruction data into latent domains enables extensible NLP systems where evolving domains require only targeted single-adapter updates, eliminating the need for full model retraining.

</details>


### [10] [PoolBench: A Benchmark for Pooling Strategies in Concept Representation Evaluation for Decoder-Only LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05162)
*Ayushi Agarwal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PoolBench isolates pooling as an experimental variable in decoder-only concept representation, showing W4_hierarchical significantly outperforms the default P1_last_token (AUROC 0.7799 vs 0.7640). Strong detection does not imply strong steering, and construction method matters more than pooling choice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pooling is a critical yet under-examined design choice in decoder-only concept representation. Reported gains are confounded by simultaneous changes in dataset, layer, construction method, and pooling rule, preventing principled comparisons. No shared protocol exists.

Method: PoolBench: a benchmark with 17 concepts, 19 pooling strategies, 3 open-weight decoder-only models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B), evaluated on 37,693 real-text passages. Three diagnostic axes: D1 (linear separability/AUROC), D2 (steered concept prevalence/SCP), and D3 (output-level disentanglement). Uses Friedman+Nemenyi for statistical testing.

Result: W4_hierarchical achieves a cross-model mean AUROC of 0.7799 vs. P1_last_token at 0.7640 (statistically significant, p=2.0e-36). Rankings are stable across layers (Spearman rho=0.961–0.990). Construction method choice (DiffMean vs. REPE, delta AUROC 0.15) has larger effect than pooling (delta AUROC 0.016). Strong detection (D1) does not imply strong steering (D2/D3).

Conclusion: Pooling choice matters but is secondary to construction method. W4_hierarchical is the recommended strategy. A fundamental representational limit exists between detection and steering. PoolBench provides a reusable protocol for future pooling research.

Abstract: Pooling is a consequential but under-examined design choice in decoder-only concept representation work: practitioners must collapse token-level hidden states into a passage-level vector, yet no shared protocol exists for comparing this choice across concepts, models, and tasks. Reported gains are confounded by simultaneous changes in dataset, layer, construction method, and pooling rule, making principled decisions impossible. We introduce PoolBench, a benchmark that isolates pooling as the experimental variable under a fixed evaluation protocol. PoolBench covers 17 concepts, 19 pooling strategies, and 3 open-weight decoder-only models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B), evaluated on a single audited corpus of 37,693 real-text passages. The primary axis is linear separability (D1/AUROC); steered concept prevalence (D2/SCP) and output-level disentanglement (D3) serve as diagnostic axes. The primary finding is decisive: W4_hierarchical reaches a cross-model mean AUROC of 0.7799, while the widely adopted P1_last_token baseline reaches only 0.7640 and is statistically significantly worse (Friedman+Nemenyi, p = 2.0e-36; 77 significant pairs among 18 effective strategies). Rankings are stable across layers (rho = 0.961--0.990). A key negative result: strong detection does not imply strong steering -- D2 and D3 are substantially weaker than D1 for most concepts, indicating a fundamental representational limit rather than a pooling failure. On mid-difficulty concepts, W4_hierarchical outperforms P1_last_token by 0.042--0.113 AUROC; construction method choice (DiffMean vs. REPE) has a larger effect (delta AUROC 0.15) than pooling (delta AUROC 0.016), establishing the correct practical hierarchy. We release the corpus, pre-extracted activations, scorer models, steering vectors, and evaluation code as a reusable protocol for pooling research.

</details>


### [11] [Where Privacy Risk Lives in English-Source Multilingual RAG: A Stage-Decomposed Audit Across Five Query Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05163)
*Yanhang Li,Zhichao Fan,Zexin Zhuang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper challenges the assumption that non-English queries make multilingual RAG systems more vulnerable to PII leakage. Using a synthetic-PII corpus and an all-Qwen2.5-7B pipeline, English showed the highest leak rate under output-only filtering. An input judge reduced leaks but left residual leaks on Arabic and Swahili. Oracle document attachment blocked 15/17 residual cases, framed as a mechanism diagnostic rather than a deployable defence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test the common assumption that switching to non-English languages increases the attack surface for extracting personally identifiable information (PII) from multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems.

Method: An English-source synthetic-PII corpus is queried across five languages. A two-stage defence pipeline is evaluated: (1) an LLM input judge and (2) a regex output filter. All components — translator, judge, back-translator, and generator — are Qwen2.5-7B. Output-only filtering and judge-augmented conditions are compared. An ablation with back-translated queries and an oracle document-attachment diagnostic (gold corpus document fed to the input judge) are also conducted, with an n=17 residual corner analysed.

Result: Under output-only filtering, English exhibits the highest unstructured-PII leak rate; only English vs. Swahili separates cleanly under document-level bootstrap intervals. Adding the input judge leaves residual leaks on Arabic and Swahili; back-translating queries does not close the gap. Attaching the gold corpus document to the input judge blocks 15 of 17 residual cells.

Conclusion: The findings are pipeline-conditional and do not establish a causal ranking of language-inherent risk. The oracle document-attachment result serves as a mechanism diagnostic, not a deployable defence, since it relies on oracle retrieval, measures only adversarial queries, and omits benign-query false-positive rates and answer-utility costs. Priority follow-up work includes replication with independent machine translation, a non-Qwen judge, and a native-speaker query set.

Abstract: A common assumption holds that switching to a non-English language makes a multilingual RAG system easier to attack for personal information. We test this on an English-source synthetic-PII corpus with five query languages and a two-stage defence (LLM input judge + regex output filter), in a pipeline whose translator, judge, back-translator, and generator are all Qwen2.5-7B -- so every finding below is pipeline-conditional, not a causal ranking of language-inherent risk. Under output-only filtering, English has the highest observed unstructured-PII leak rate; only English-vs-Swahili separates cleanly under document-level bootstrap intervals. Once the input judge is added, residual leaks remain on Arabic and Swahili, and back-translating the query does not close the gap (an ablation we report but cannot use as a causal diagnostic, since the back-translator is also Qwen). On a separate n=17 multilingual-prompted-judge residual corner, attaching the gold corpus document to the input judge blocks 15/17 residual cells. We frame this last result as a mechanism diagnostic, not a deployable defence: it uses oracle retrieval, BLOCK/ALLOW rates are measured on adversarial queries only, and we measure no benign-query false-positive rate and no answer-utility cost. The supplementary material contains code, corpora, queries, and per-trial JSONLs; the priority follow-up is an independent-MT plus non-Qwen-judge replication with a native-speaker query set, scoped in the Limitations section.

</details>


### [12] [Cross-Architecture Steering Transfer in Language Models: A Systematic Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05164)
*Ayushi Agarwal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Independently trained LLMs develop shared internal representations that enable cross-model steering transfer, but only above a scale threshold (~1.7B parameters). Below this, alignment and functional transfer degrade sharply, demonstrating that geometric similarity has actionable behavioural consequences conditionally tied to representational capacity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior work has documented geometric similarity (shared representational structure) across independently trained LLMs — the "Platonic Representation Hypothesis" — no study had tested whether this similarity enables functional cross-model control. The authors aim to bridge this gap by systematically evaluating whether concept-direction vectors from one model can steer another's behaviour.

Method: The authors studied five open-weight LLMs spanning 0.8B–8B parameters across two architectural lineages. They trained one Sparse Autoencoder per model on 15 semantic domains, extracting concept directions. Alignment was tested across all 20 directed model pairs using Pearson correlation and Procrustes cosine similarity. Cross-model steering was evaluated by transferring vectors (B3-TI) and measuring win rates against same-model baselines, including a single universal vector tested across models without per-model supervision.

Result: A discontinuity emerged near 1.7B parameters: at ≥1.7B, 47–49% of cross-model feature pairs validated (Pearson r ≥ 0.60, Procrustes cosines 0.895–0.956), while alignment collapsed below 0.8B. Cross-model steering achieved a 71.0% win rate vs. 68.0% for same-model vectors. A universal vector reached 67.3% across 4 of 5 models without per-model tuning. Transfer failed for sub-1.7B models and one instability-prone model.

Conclusion: Shared geometry in LLMs is functionally exploitable for cross-model behavioural control, but only above a critical parameter scale (~1.7B). This provides the first functional complement to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and highlights that mechanistic interpretability tools validated at large scale may not transfer to smaller models without revalidation.

Abstract: Independently trained large language models may develop shared internal representations of semantic concepts despite architectural differences -- but whether this geometric similarity has functional consequences for cross-model behavioural control remains untested. We present the first systematic evaluation of cross-model steering transfer and show that shared LLM geometry is functionally exploitable, conditionally: concept directions from one model can steer a different independently trained model when sufficient representational capacity exists. We study five open-weight models spanning three parameter scales (0.8B--8B) and two architectural lineages, training one Sparse Autoencoder per model across 15 semantic domains and testing alignment across all 20 directed model pairs. We observe a suggestive discontinuity near 1.7B parameters: at >= 1.7B scale, 47--49% of cross-model feature pairs validate (Pearson r >= 0.60, Procrustes cosines 0.895--0.956), while alignment degrades sharply below 0.8B. Cross-model steering vectors (B3-TI) achieve a 71.0% win rate across 15 supervised concepts versus 68.0% for same-model native vectors; a single universal vector achieves 67.3% in 4 of 5 models without any per-model supervision. Transfer degrades for models below 1.7B and for one model with generation instability, confirming that functional exploitability requires sufficient representational capacity. Our findings underscore the importance of scale thresholds in mechanistic interpretability: tools validated at 7B scale may not transfer to smaller models without revalidation. We provide the first functional complement to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis -- geometric convergence across independently trained LLMs supports cross-model behavioural control without fine-tuning, under the identified scale conditions.

</details>


### [13] [A Study of ASR Adaptation and Representation Dimensionality Reduction in Persian Speech Emotion Recognition Using Whisper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05165)
*Ali Shendabadi,Parnia Izadirad,Mostafa Salehi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes an efficient SER framework for Persian using Whisper encoder embeddings reduced via PCA and aggregated with attention pooling, finding that PCA consistently improves performance while ASR fine-tuning yields only modest gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Limited labeled data makes SER challenging for low-resource languages like Persian. The authors aim to efficiently leverage large pretrained models (Whisper) without incurring heavy computational costs, and to understand whether language-specific ASR adaptation transfers beneficially to emotion recognition.

Method: Frame-level embeddings from the Whisper encoder are extracted, then dimensionality-reduced via PCA (eliminating learned projection layers). An attention-based pooling mechanism aggregates these reduced representations, which are classified by a lightweight prediction head. The authors also fine-tune Whisper on Persian ASR before downstream SER evaluation on the ShEMO dataset under a speaker-independent protocol.

Result: PCA-based dimensionality reduction consistently improves emotion recognition accuracy while reducing training latency and memory usage. ASR fine-tuning provides only modest gains for SER, indicating limited transfer from language adaptation to emotion representations under the tested conditions.

Conclusion: Efficient use of large pretrained speech models for low-resource SER is feasible with simple dimensionality reduction (PCA) and lightweight aggregation. Language-specific ASR fine-tuning does not substantially benefit emotion recognition, suggesting that emotion-related and language-related representations are not strongly aligned in Whisper.

Abstract: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) in low-resource languages remains a challenging problem due to limited labeled data. In this work, we study the use of Whisper for Persian SER with a particular focus on representation dimensionality reduction and language-specific model adaptation. We propose a SER framework in which frame-level embeddings extracted from the Whisper encoder are reduced in dimensionality using PCA, eliminating the need for learned projection layers and substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters. The reduced representations are aggregated using an attention-based pooling mechanism and classified with a lightweight prediction head. In addition, we investigate whether fine-tuning Whisper on a Persian automatic speech recognition (ASR) task improves downstream SER performance. Experiments conducted on the ShEMO dataset under a speaker-independent evaluation protocol show that PCA-based dimensionality reduction consistently improves emotion recognition performance while reducing training latency and memory usage. ASR fine-tuning yields only modest gains for SER, suggesting limited transfer from language adaptation to emotion-related representations under the evaluated conditions. These findings provide practical insights into the efficient use of large pretrained speech models for emotion recognition in low-resource languages.

</details>


### [14] [Conditional Cognitive Biases in LLMs: How Biased User Turns Modulate In-Context Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05166)
*Sachini Weerasekara,Sagar Kamarthi,Jacqueline Isaacs*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper evaluates how cognitive biases emerge in instruction-tuned LLMs under multi-turn conversations. Using a novel 3-condition experimental framework and 24,300 validated prompts (covering a 9×9 bias interaction matrix), the study finds that biased conversational context increases bias expression in 6 of 8 frontier LLMs, driven by two competing dynamics: exposure amplification vs. alignment-related suppression triggered by explicit bias cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on LLM bias largely focuses on single-turn, zero-shot evaluations — an unrealistic setting given that real-world human-AI interaction is multi-turn and conversational. The authors aim to understand whether and how exposure to biased user turns in a dialogue shapes downstream bias expression, and to disentangle the mere presence of biased context from its semantic content.

Method: The authors propose a three-condition experimental framework: (1) a zero-shot baseline, (2) exposure to a biased user turn, and (3) a control isolating semantic content from the conversational framing. They construct a benchmark of 24,300 jury-validated user prompts spanning an exhaustive 9×9 target-human bias interaction matrix (81 cells). Eight frontier instruction-tuned LLMs are evaluated on bias expression across these conditions.

Result: Biased conversational context systematically increases bias expression over zero-shot baselines in 6 of 8 models. Two competing dynamics are identified: (a) conversational exposure to biased reasoning amplifies downstream bias tendencies, and (b) explicitly stated bias cues often trigger alignment-related suppression, reducing overt bias expression. The net effect depends on the interplay between these mechanisms.

Conclusion: Multi-turn interaction is a critical but underexplored variable in LLM bias evaluation. The findings reveal that contextual bias can both amplify and suppress model bias depending on how it is presented, underscoring the complexity of behavioral adaptation in aligned models. The authors release their framework, code, and dataset to facilitate further research.

Abstract: We present an evaluation of cognitive bias expression in state-of-the-art instruction-tuned LLMs under realistic multi-turn interaction settings. Our work introduces a novel three-condition experimental framework that disentangles the effect of exposure to a biased user turn from the effect of the turn's semantic content, alongside a benchmark of 24,300 jury-validated user prompts spanning all 81 cells of a 9x9 target-human bias interaction matrix. Across eight frontier LLMs, we find that biased conversational context systematically increases bias expression relative to zero-shot baselines in 6 of 8 models. We identify two competing behavioral dynamics underlying this effect: conversational exposure to biased reasoning generally amplifies downstream bias tendencies, while explicitly stated bias cues often trigger alignment-related suppression behaviors that reduce overt bias expression. We release our framework, codebase, and dataset to support future research on context-conditioned cognitive biases and behavioral adaptation in LLMs.

</details>


### [15] [CNM-BERT: A Drop-In Structural Embedding for Chinese Characters via Ideographic Description Sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05167)
*Thomas Sing-wing Wu,Liqian Yan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CNM augments BERT with explicit Chinese character structure via tree-encoded IDS sequences, yielding large gains on rare/OOV characters (+9.8 structure accuracy) and consistent downstream improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BERT treats Chinese characters as atomic tokens, ignoring their compositional orthographic structure (radicals, components). This forces models to rely solely on contextual co-occurrence, leading to poor representations for rare and out-of-vocabulary characters, which are prevalent in Chinese NLP.

Method: CNM first parses Ideographic Description Sequences (IDS) into tree structures representing character composition. A recursive Tree-MLP then encodes these trees into structural embeddings. These embeddings are fused into BERT's token representations via a lightweight injection mechanism, without modifying the backbone Transformer parameters or architecture.

Result: On the Wu et al. (2025) structural-probing benchmark, CNM-BERT outperforms ChineseBERT by +9.8 Structure accuracy and +7.7 Radical F1 on long-tail and OOV characters. Consistent gains are also observed on CLUE, MRC, and NER tasks at both base and large model scales.

Conclusion: Explicit injection of compositional orthographic structure into Transformer encoders yields both robust OOV character understanding and tangible downstream performance improvements, validating that discrete structural knowledge complements distributional pretraining for Chinese NLP.

Abstract: Token-based encoders like BERT treat Chinese characters as atomic identifiers, ignoring their recursive orthographic structure. Consequently, models rely on contextual co-occurrence, degrading performance on rare and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) characters. We propose the Compositional Network Model (CNM), a lightweight augmentation that injects discrete compositional structure into Transformer encoders. CNM parses Ideographic Description Sequences (IDS) into trees, encodes them via a recursive Tree-MLP, and fuses the structural embeddings into BERT without modifying the backbone. Evaluated on the Wu et al. (2025) structural-probing benchmark, CNM-BERT outperforms the strongest baseline (ChineseBERT) on long-tail and OOV characters by +9.8 Structure accuracy and +7.7 Radical F1. Furthermore, CNM-BERT achieves consistent gains across CLUE, MRC, and NER tasks at both base and large scales, demonstrating that explicit structural injection delivers both robust OOV understanding and tangible downstream value.

</details>


### [16] [ConWriter: Transition-Constrained Stateful Long-Form Story Generation with Lightweight Neuro-Symbolic Consistency Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05169)
*Jindong Li,Yang Yang,Zihao Liu,Yutao Yue,Menglin Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ConWriter is a training-free framework for long-form story generation that maintains narrative consistency by writing incrementally at the scene level, using static requirements, dynamic memory, symbolic state reasoning, and uncertainty-aware risk signals to detect and repair errors before they propagate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prompting-based long story generation methods suffer from accumulating temporal, factual, character, commonsense, and stylistic errors as stories grow longer, because they lack mechanisms to monitor and enforce narrative consistency during generation.

Method: ConWriter generates stories incrementally at the scene level. It employs four components: (1) static story requirements that define unchanging narrative constraints, (2) dynamic narrative memory that tracks evolving story states, (3) symbolic state reasoning to check whether new scenes satisfy required narrative transitions, and (4) uncertainty-aware risk signals that prioritize validation and trigger localized repair when inconsistencies are detected, preventing error propagation to later scenes.

Result: Evaluated on ConStory-Bench across four tasks (continuation, generation, expansion, completion) at 3k, 6k, and 12k target lengths, using Qwen3.5-Plus, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5 series models. Experiments followed the official ConStory-Bench protocol, though specific performance metrics are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: Treating long-story generation as a stateful, incremental process with consistency checks and targeted repairs — rather than a single free-form decoding pass — enables better narrative coherence and prevents local errors from cascading into later scenes.

Abstract: Long-form story generation requires models to preserve narrative consistency across extended contexts, yet existing prompting-based methods often accumulate temporal, factual, character, commonsense, and stylistic errors as the story grows. We propose ConWriter, a training-free framework for consistency-aware long story generation. ConWriter writes stories incrementally at the scene level, guided by static story requirements, dynamic narrative memory, symbolic state reasoning, and uncertainty-aware risk signals. Rather than treating long-story generation as a single free-form decoding process, ConWriter maintains evolving story states, checks whether new scenes satisfy required narrative transitions, and uses uncertainty-aware risk signals to prioritize validation and localized repair. This enables consistency control during generation, before local errors propagate into later scenes. We evaluate ConWriter on ConStory-Bench, covering four long-story tasks: continuation, generation, expansion, and completion. Due to the high cost of long-form generation and evaluation, we use the first five cases from each task and test 3k, 6k, and 12k target lengths across Qwen3.5-Plus, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5 series. Experiments follow the official ConStory-Bench evaluation protocol.

</details>


### [17] [DREAM: LLM-based Dynamic Role-playing via Event-Aware Memory Graph](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05170)
*Zhihao Xiao,Mengting Li,Xintao Wang,Linfeng Li,Limin Shui,Mengqi Ji,Borui Cai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DREAM introduces a structured memory framework for role-playing agents that organizes character experiences into temporally ordered, causally linked event graphs, enabling dynamic dual-granularity character profiles. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks, including a newly proposed Temporal Causal Memory benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing role-playing agents rely on static character descriptions and unstructured memory, which limits their ability to maintain long-term narrative coherence, temporal consistency, and causally grounded behavioral reasoning — capabilities essential for accurate character simulation beyond mere stylistic imitation.

Method: DREAM transforms unstructured literary text into an Event-aware Memory Graph (EMG) that organizes experiences into temporally ordered and causally linked event structures, inspired by the Activating Event-Belief-Consequence (ABC) cognitive model. This graph enables construction of dual-granularity character profiles capturing both stable personality traits and event-driven behavioral evolution. The authors also introduce the Temporal Causal Memory (TCM) benchmark for evaluating temporal consistency and long-range causal narrative coherence.

Result: DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance across three benchmarks: CoSER, LIFECHOICE, and the newly proposed TCM, outperforming multiple strong baselines.

Conclusion: Structured memory representations, specifically event-aware memory graphs grounded in cognitive models, are effective for enhancing both the interpretability and consistency of role-playing agents, addressing key limitations of unstructured memory approaches.

Abstract: Role-playing agents (RPAs) have emerged as a key application of large language models, enabling immersive and high-fidelity character simulation. Accurate role-playing of established characters requires not only stylistic imitation but also temporally consistent and causally grounded behavioral reasoning. However, existing RPAs primarily rely on static character descriptions and unstructured memory, limiting their ability to maintain long-term narrative and personality coherence. We introduce DREAM, a structured memory framework for role-playing agents inspired by the Activating Event-Belief-Consequence (ABC) cognitive model. DREAM transforms unstructured literary text into an Event-aware Memory Graph (EMG) that organizes character experiences into temporally ordered and causally linked event graph. This representation enables the construction of dynamic, dual-granularity character profiles that capture both stable personality traits and event-driven behavioral evolution. We further propose the Temporal Causal Memory (TCM) benchmark to evaluate temporal consistency and long-range causal narrative coherence. DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance across CoSER, LIFECHOICE, and TCM, outperforming multiple strong baselines. Our approach demonstrates the effectiveness of structured memory in enhancing the interpretability and consistency of role-playing agents.

</details>


### [18] [Position: It's Time to Optimize LLMs for Self-Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05188)
*Itamar Pres,Belinda Z. Li,Laura Ruis,Zifan Carl Guo,Keya Hu,Mehul Damani,Isha Puri,Ekdeep Singh Lubana,Jacob Andreas*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper argues that many persistent LM failures (sycophancy, poor logical generalization, confident errors) stem from evaluating behavior on isolated input-output pairs rather than across relationships between responses. It proposes self-consistency as a unifying framework, showing that diverse improvement techniques are special cases of consistency optimization, and outlines a vision for generally consistent LMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LM training and evaluation pipelines assume behavior can be specified independently per single-output pair. This misses critical failure modes—sycophancy, incomplete logical reasoning, and hallucination—that only become detectable when examining relationships across multiple inputs and outputs. The authors argue a paradigm shift toward consistency-based thinking is needed.

Method: This is a position paper. The authors (1) identify a common modeling flaw across LM pipelines, (2) demonstrate that existing techniques (adversarial robustness, factuality, etc.) reduce to special cases of a unified "consistency optimization" procedure with standard optimization tools, and (3) propose new model properties achievable through consistency objectives, sketching a research agenda for generally consistent LMs.

Result: The paper provides a conceptual synthesis rather than empirical results. It reveals that disparate LM improvement methods share a common structure as consistency optimization, and identifies new properties (e.g., transitive preference consistency, counterfactual invariance) that could be targeted through this lens.

Conclusion: Pursuing self-consistency as a core design principle would enable LMs with more robust reasoning, reduced sycophancy, and better-calibrated confidence. The authors discuss both the transformative capabilities consistent LMs would unlock and the philosophical objections—such as whether perfect consistency is even desirable for creative or context-sensitive tasks.

Abstract: Despite ever-increasing sophistication in language model (LM) pre- and post-training pipelines, many important failures persist: models overcondition on user framing ("sycophancy"), exhibit incomplete logical generalization, and produce confident but incorrect responses. We argue that these failures arise from a modeling assumption permeating all aspects of the pipeline: that behavior can be specified and evaluated independently on single-output pairs. Many model failures are difficult, if not impossible, to detect without reasoning about relationships between a model's responses across inputs. In this position paper, we propose self-consistency as a framework for understanding these failures. We first observe that a wide variety of techniques designed to improve specific aspects of LM behavior-targeting properties as diverse as adversarial robustness and factual coherence-can be understood as special cases of a common "consistency optimization" procedure and addressed with a standard set of optimization tools. We next outline a set of new model properties that could be achieved by optimizing for consistency, and conclude with a discussion of what it would mean to develop generally consistent LMs, including the capabilities they would enable and the objections they raise.

</details>


### [19] [Analysis of Numerical Localisation in LLM Translations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05232)
*Patrizia Kaye*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper extends Tang et al. (2025) by evaluating five commodity-hardware LLMs on numerical localisation (times, numbers, dates) rather than translation. It establishes baselines and tests three accuracy-improvement strategies, finding that embedding localisation principles directly into prompt context yields statistically significant gains over direct translation or alternative methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To extend prior work on numerical translation by investigating how LLMs handle the localisation of temporal and numerical expressions (rather than translation), and to identify practical improvement strategies that work on models deployable on commodity hardware.

Method: Five LLMs capable of running on commodity hardware were selected. A baseline localisation accuracy was computed for each model. Three distinct strategies to improve accuracy were then tested: (1) embedding localisation principles into the prompt context, (2) direct translation, and (3) alternative strategies. Statistical significance testing was applied to compare outcomes.

Result: Embedding localisation principles into the prompt context provided a statistically significant improvement in accuracy over both direct translation and the alternative strategies. This finding contrasts with Tang et al. (2025), where such an approach was not the most effective for translation tasks.

Conclusion: For numerical localisation tasks on commodity-hardware LLMs, in-context embedding of localisation principles is the most effective strategy, differing from the translation-focused findings of Tang et al. (2025).

Abstract: The work of Tang et. al. (2025) on numerical translation is extended by analysing the capability of five large language models (LLMs) for the localisation of times, numbers, and dates instead of translation. Models were selected that could be loaded onto and run on commodity hardware and a baseline quality for each mode is computed, then three different strategies to improve on that accuracy were tested. In contrast to Tang et. al., it was discovered that on the tested LLMs, embedding the localisation principles into the prompt context provided a statistically significant improvement in accuracy compared to direct translation or the alternative strategies.

</details>


### [20] [Constraint-First Reasoning: A Training-Free Protocol for Exploiting Answer-Space Constraints in Mathematical Problem Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05254)
*Hongbo Ma,Bangji Yang,Yunqian Selina Cheng,Jiajun Fan,Hanwen Zhang,Ge Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CFR is a training-free, two-stage prompting method that extracts problem constraints before solving, improving LLM math accuracy on constrained problems via a routed protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often generate mathematically plausible but constraint-violating outputs (e.g., missing modular reductions, wrong formats). Existing chain-of-thought methods lack explicit constraint enforcement, motivating a lightweight, training-free intervention that surfaces and verifies constraints during reasoning.

Method: Constraint-First Reasoning (CFR) is a two-stage prompting protocol: Stage 1 extracts and summarizes all explicit and implicit constraints from the problem statement; Stage 2 solves the problem while checking intermediate and final results against the constraint summary. Routed-CFR adds a text-only regex router that selectively activates CFR only when restrictive cues are detected; otherwise it defaults to direct chain-of-thought (CoT).

Result: CFR improves direct CoT across AIME, CMIMC, BRUMO, and AIMO_AMC benchmarks on multiple model backbones. Ablations include convention-controlled routing experiments, matched prompting baselines, problem-level paired tests, decoding robustness analyses, constraint-quality audits, total-token accounting, and an OlympiadBench evaluation.

Conclusion: CFR is a targeted test-time intervention, not a general-purpose reasoning replacement. Its effectiveness depends on the presence of recoverable constraints and the reliability of Stage 1 constraint extraction.

Abstract: Large language models can derive a plausible mathematical object yet still violate explicit requirements--for example, by omitting a modular reduction, returning a non-integer, or using the wrong encoded answer form. We introduce Constraint-First Reasoning (CFR), a training-free two-stage prompting protocol: Stage 1 extracts and summarizes constraints entailed by the problem, and Stage 2 solves while checking intermediate and final results against that summary. Routed-CFR activates the two-stage protocol only when a text-only regex router detects restrictive cues; otherwise it uses direct chain-of-thought (CoT). Across AIME, CMIMC, BRUMO, and AIMO_AMC, the method improves direct CoT on multiple backbones. We further report convention-controlled routing experiments, matched prompting baselines, problem-level paired tests, decoding robustness, constraint-quality audits, total-token accounting, and an OlympiadBench evaluation. These analyses position CFR as a targeted test-time intervention whose benefit depends on recoverable constraints and reliable Stage 1 extraction, rather than as a general-purpose replacement for mathematical reasoning.

</details>


### [21] [Evidence Lock Before Commitment: A Frozen Interface Degrades LLM-as-Judge Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05353)
*Divyansh Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether persisting extracted evidence across separate LLM calls improves judgment quality. Testing "evidence locking" (extracting criteria/evidence in one call, then making that record the exclusive input for the verdict in a second call) across 24,000 judgments reveals it harms performance: agreement with human preferences drops 4-6 percentage points and answer-order inconsistency rises 8-10 points compared to standard single-call structured judging. The authors conclude that while persisted evidence aids auditability, it should not replace source answers at decision time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based evaluation pipelines often decompose judgment into evidence extraction followed by verdict, under the assumption that an intermediate record preserves all necessary information. However, for reasoning-capable models, visible field order does not reveal internal decision order. The authors seek to test whether forcing the model to rely exclusively on a persisted evidence record—rather than re-examining source answers—affects judgment quality, motivated by the practical appeal of auditable, locked-evidence workflows.

Method: The authors conduct a large-scale empirical comparison across 24,000 judgments spanning three datasets (HelpSteer3, FeedbackQA, CoVal). They compare four protocols: (1) standard pairwise judging, (2) structured one-call judging (extract criteria/evidence and verdict in a single call), (3) two-call evidence locking (extract evidence in call one, verdict from evidence-only in call two), and (4) three-call pointwise locking (evaluate each candidate independently, then compare). Both Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5 serve as judges. Metrics include agreement with released human preferences and answer-order inconsistency.

Result: Evidence locking reduces agreement with human preferences by 4–6 percentage points and increases answer-order inconsistency by 8–10 points relative to structured one-call judging. Pointwise locking is similarly harmful. Structured evidence elicitation (single-call) remains close to standard judging. The degradation pattern holds consistently for both Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5 across all three datasets.

Conclusion: Persisting extracted evidence as the sole input to a verdict call systematically degrades LLM judgment quality. While evidence locking supports auditability and transparency, it should not replace the original source answers at decision time. The finding suggests that reasoning-capable models benefit from having direct access to raw candidate responses when rendering final judgments.

Abstract: LLM judges are often asked to extract criteria and evidence before choosing between candidate answers. This workflow assumes that the intermediate record preserves the information needed for a later verdict. For reasoning-capable models, visible field order does not reveal internal decision order, so we test an observable alternative: persist the evidence in one call and make it the exclusive input to the next. Across 24,000 judgments over HelpSteer3, FeedbackQA, and CoVal, we compare standard pairwise judging, structured one-call judging, two-call evidence locking, and three-call pointwise locking with Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5. Evidence locking reduces agreement with released human preferences by 4 to 6 percentage points and increases answer-order inconsistency by 8 to 10 points relative to structured one-call judging. Pointwise locking is also harmful, while structured evidence elicitation remains close to standard judging. The result holds for both judges and all three datasets. Persisted evidence can support auditability, but it should not replace the source answers at decision time.

</details>


### [22] [The interface of intonation and lexical tone: Boundary phenomena in Mandarin varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05364)
*Cong Zhang,Yiya Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This chapter examines how intonation and lexical tone interact in Mandarin Chinese, particularly at prosodic boundaries, where f0 serves dual roles in encoding both sentence-level functions (e.g., interrogativity) and speaker attitudes. It reviews theoretical models and emerging techniques for analyzing these multi-layered communicative phenomena.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mandarin Chinese presents a unique challenge for prosodic analysis because f0 simultaneously encodes lexical tone (word-level meaning) and intonation (sentence-level meaning and attitude). Understanding how these two functions coexist and interact—especially at intonation boundaries where conflicts arise—is essential for both phonological theory and speech technology applications.

Method: The chapter adopts a review-based approach, synthesizing empirical findings on intonation boundary phenomena in Mandarin varieties. It focuses on acoustic analysis of f0 contours at boundaries, comparing question vs. statement prosody and attitudinal expression. The discussion integrates theoretical models of tone-intonation interaction and surveys emerging analytical techniques.

Result: Key findings include: (1) Intonation and tone interact most visibly at prosodic boundaries, where boundary tones and tonal realization must be coordinated; (2) Mandarin uses systematic f0 modifications at boundaries to distinguish questions from statements and to convey attitudinal nuances; (3) Multiple theoretical frameworks—including autosegmental-metrical approaches and articulatory-based models—offer complementary accounts of these interactions, with emerging computational techniques providing new analytical precision.

Conclusion: The tone-intonation interface in Mandarin is best understood through boundary phenomena, where competing demands on f0 are resolved. The chapter highlights the need for integrative models that can account for how speakers simultaneously encode lexical, sentence-level, and attitudinal meanings within a single f0 channel, and points toward future directions combining theoretical refinement with advanced acoustic and computational methods.

Abstract: This chapter explores the intricate interplay between intonation and tone in Mandarin Chinese varieties, focusing on f0, the primary acoustic cue for both intonation and tone. The main empirical base is intonation boundary phenomena, where intonation and tone intersect and influence each other in conveying a range of sentence-level linguistic functions -- such as question vs. statement -- and a rich array of speakers' attitudinal information. Theoretical models and emerging techniques are also discussed to account for the observed interactions of tonal aspects and boundary phenomena to convey multiple levels of communicative meanings.

</details>


### [23] [FormBharo: Designing and Evaluating a Voice Agent for Conversational Form Filling in Rural India](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06027)
*Aman Dalmia,Sanskriti Midha,Jigar Doshi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FormBharo is a voice agent that uses LLMs combined with rule-based validation to fill structured forms over phone calls for low-literacy populations. Piloted with ARMMAN to enroll Hindi-speaking mothers in maternal care, it is the first such agent for this demographic. The paper introduces FormVoiceAgentBench, a benchmark of 3,760 multi-turn tests showing that rule-based controls help smaller models match frontier models, and that component-level metrics do not predict end-to-end form completion performance. A Pareto-based method is used to balance accuracy, cost, and latency for deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Millions of low-income, low-literacy individuals in India cannot access social benefits that require form-filling. Frontline health workers spend scarce time enrolling beneficiaries one-on-one through spoken conversation. There is a need for a scalable, automated voice-based system that can conduct structured enrollment conversations in Hindi under tight latency and cost constraints, reaching beneficiaries directly over phone calls.

Method: FormBharo pairs LLMs (for transcription, information extraction, and reply generation) with deterministic, rule-based validation and flow-control mechanisms. It operates over phone calls under strict latency and cost budgets. The authors also built FormVoiceAgentBench: a benchmark with human-recorded Hindi audio across 960 simulated calls and 3,760 multi-turn conversation tests, covering transcription, extraction, reply generation, and end-to-end form completion. They evaluate multiple model configurations and use Pareto-based weighted-sum scalarization to select an optimal deployment configuration balancing accuracy, cost, and latency.

Result: Form completion drops by up to ~41 points when LLMs use error-prone real-speech transcripts instead of reference transcripts. Rule-based controls recover many turn-level extraction errors, allowing smaller, cheaper models to match or surpass frontier models on end-to-end form completion. Component-level performance does not predict end-to-end performance: GPT-5.5 led turn-level extraction accuracy on reference transcripts (99.8%) but ranked lower on form completion. Errors propagate and cancel across the pipeline, so only end-to-end evaluation reveals optimal model choice. No single model is best across accuracy, cost, and latency simultaneously.

Conclusion: Rule-based validation is a practical complement to LLMs for robust form-filling voice agents targeting low-resource populations. End-to-end evaluation is essential because component metrics are misleading predictors of overall performance. Deploying such systems requires multi-objective optimization across accuracy, cost, and latency, for which Pareto-based scalarization provides a principled selection method.

Abstract: In India, almost every social benefit starts with a form, yet the people who need these benefits most are often unable to read or write. Reaching them requires a spoken conversation. Today that work falls to frontline health workers who enroll beneficiaries one at a time, a poor use of stretched capacity. We built FormBharo ("fill the form" in Hindi), a voice agent that fills a structured form over a phone call under tight latency and cost budgets by pairing Large Language Models (LLMs) with deterministic, rule-based validation and flow control. It is being piloted with ARMMAN, an NGO running large-scale maternal and child mobile-health programs in India, to enroll low-income, Hindi-speaking mothers in antenatal and postnatal care. To our knowledge, it is the first voice agent piloted to fill an enrollment form for this population. We openly release FormVoiceAgentBench, a benchmark pairing human-recorded Hindi audio with 3,760 multi-turn conversation tests across 960 simulated calls, to evaluate our agent's components (transcription, extraction, reply generation) and end-to-end form completion under real acoustic variations. Form completion drops by up to ~41 points when LLMs receive error-prone real-speech transcripts instead of reference ones. The rule-based controls recover many turn-level extraction errors, helping smaller, cheaper models match or surpass frontier models on form completion. Component performance does not predict end-to-end performance: GPT-5.5 leads turn-level extraction accuracy on reference transcripts (99.8%) but ranks lower on form completion.
