Since errors both propagate and cancel across the pipeline, the optimal model choice of models emerges only through end-to-end evaluation. Finally, no single model is best across accuracy, cost, and latency at once, so we use a Pareto-based weighted-sum scalarization to select a deployable configuration balancing the three.

</details>


### [24] [Mood Matters: How Syntactic Sensitivity Undermines Safety Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05409)
*Alina Klerings,Jannik Brinkmann,Heiner Stuckenschmidt,Simone Paolo Ponzetto*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Post-training alignment introduces syntactic confounders into refusal mechanisms; models can be jailbroken by manipulating non-imperative grammatical forms, a vulnerability traced to linguistically biased fine-tuning data that can be mitigated through increased syntactic diversity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work showed that trivial syntactic changes like tense shifting can bypass safety alignment. The authors aim to determine whether this reflects a broader, systematic failure tied to non-imperative syntactic forms, and to uncover the mechanistic and data-level causes behind such vulnerabilities.

Method: The authors (1) conduct behavioral evaluations across 16 models (up to 70B parameters) testing non-imperative syntactic jailbreaks; (2) apply causal mediation analysis to isolate whether refusal decisions are conditioned on upstream syntactic features; (3) perform steering experiments on these syntactic features to trigger or suppress refusal; and (4) trace the root cause to syntactic biases in open-source post-training data, testing whether increasing syntactic diversity mitigates the issue.

Result: Non-imperative syntactic forms reliably bypass refusal across all 16 tested models. Causal mediation analysis reveals that refusal is partially conditioned on syntactic features in upstream layers. Steering these features directly modulates refusal behavior. The vulnerability is traced to low syntactic diversity in post-training data, and augmenting that diversity reduces susceptibility.

Conclusion: Current alignment techniques inadvertently introduce syntactic confounders, preventing models from grounding refusal decisions purely in semantics. This represents a fundamental limitation of existing safety training paradigms that can be partially addressed through more linguistically diverse fine-tuning data.

Abstract: Large language models typically undergo post-training to align them with safety policies but there exist many sophisticated jailbreaks that sidestep established safeguards. For instance, prior work by Andriushchenko et al. (2025) has found that changing the grammatical tense from present to past can be enough to elicit harmful responses. In this work, we uncover a more general failure of non-imperative syntactic forms. We demonstrate that this syntactic vulnerability exists in 16 models up to 70B parameters, using behavioral evaluation. To investigate the root cause, we apply causal mediation analysis, finding that refusal is partially conditioned on upstream syntactic features. By steering these purely syntactic features we are able to trigger and suppress refusal. Finally, we trace this ill-conditioning to linguistically biased post-training data of open-source models and show that increasing syntactic diversity can mitigate the issue. Our findings suggest that current alignment approaches introduce confounders that prevent a pure semantic grounding of the refusal decision.

</details>


### [25] [Decolonizing Linguistic Policies in Automated Speech Recognition: A Framework for Cross-Culturally Competent Speech AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06141)
*Jay L. Cunningham,Mark Atta Mensah,Richard Martinez,Joao Vieira da Silva Neto,Efi Dawodu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper critiques ASR systems as sites of colonial linguistic policy, introduces the Three Harms taxonomy (Misrecognition, Misalignment, Mistrust) and a seven-layer situatedness model, and proposes a participatory framework for culturally competent ASR co-designed with affected communities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent ASR failures for low-resource, Indigenous, and non-standard language varieties are not merely technical errors — they constitute implicit linguistic policies that reproduce colonial language hierarchies, shaping access to essential services like public healthcare and education.

Method: The authors draw on theoretical frameworks including linguistic capital (Bourdieu), raciolinguistic ideology, language policy research, and decolonial computing to analyze how data curation, evaluation metrics, and model priors encode linguistic discrimination. They synthesize these analyses into a novel Three Harms (3M) taxonomy and a seven-layer situatedness model for characterizing linguistic diversity in ASR systems. They then develop a participatory framework and minimum audit protocol.

Result: The paper delivers three conceptual contributions: (1) the 3M taxonomy — Misrecognition (speakers erased/misclassified), Misalignment (systems optimized for dominant varieties), and Mistrust (eroded user confidence from repeated failures); (2) a seven-layer situatedness model mapping where linguistic diversity must be addressed across the ASR pipeline; and (3) a participatory framework positioning affected communities as co-designers, evaluators, and governance partners rather than passive data subjects.

Conclusion: ASR systems embed colonial language ideologies through technical design choices. Addressing this requires shifting from purely engineering-centric approaches toward community-governed, culturally competent ASR development, with the proposed audit protocol serving as a concrete mechanism for accountability and harm reduction.

Abstract: This paper focuses on automatic speech recognition (ASR) and ASR-mediated voice interfaces that shape access to public services, healthcare, and education. We argue that persistent failures for low-resource, Indigenous, and non-standard language varieties are not only technical errors, but also implicit linguistic policies that reproduce colonial language hierarchies. Drawing on linguistic capital, raciolinguistic ideology, language policy research, and decolonial computing, we show how data, metrics, and model priors determine whose voices become machine-legible. We introduce the Three Harms (3M) taxonomy---Misrecognition, Misalignment, and Mistrust---and a seven-layer situatedness model for linguistic diversity in ASR and ASR-mediated voice interfaces. We then propose a participatory framework and minimum audit protocol for culturally competent ASR, positioning affected communities as co-designers, evaluators, and governance partners.

</details>


### [26] [Example-Guided Prompting for Document-Level Text Simplification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05447)
*Marina Litvak,Ariel Perstin,Ilan Shtilman,Michael Färber*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Retrieval-augmented prompting with parallel simplification examples consistently improves document-level text simplification across LLMs, matching or surpassing supervised and planning-based systems without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prompt-based LLMs for document-level simplification produce inconsistent outputs because textual instructions alone provide insufficient guidance for complex, discourse-aware transformations. The authors investigate whether retrieved examples can fill this gap.

Method: Example-guided prompting: augment LLM prompts with relevant simplification examples retrieved from a parallel simplification corpus. Evaluated on OneStopEnglish using multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, compared against prompt-only baselines, supervised T5, and the planning-based PlanSimp system.

Result: Retrieval-augmented prompting consistently improves simplification quality over prompt-only generation and achieves competitive or superior performance versus T5 and PlanSimp. Benefits vary across LLMs, suggesting that effective use of retrieved examples depends on a model's contextual integration ability.

Conclusion: Retrieved examples provide an effective, fine-tuning-free method for improving document-level simplification, but model-specific factors influence how well contextual examples are exploited during generation.

Abstract: Document-level text simplification requires large language models (LLMs) to rewrite complex documents while preserving meaning, readability, and discourse coherence. Although prompt-based LLMs have shown promising performance, they often produce inconsistent simplifications because textual instructions alone provide limited guidance for complex document-level transformations. We investigate whether retrieved document-simplification examples can improve document-level generation by augmenting prompts with examples selected from a parallel simplification corpus. This example-guided prompting approach enables LLMs to exploit relevant simplification patterns without task-specific fine-tuning. Experiments on the OneStopEnglish corpus using multiple state-of-the-art LLMs show that incorporating retrieved examples consistently improves simplification quality over prompt-only generation and achieves competitive or superior performance compared with representative supervised (T5) and planning-based (PlanSimp) document simplification systems. Furthermore, we find that the benefits of example-guided prompting vary across LLMs, suggesting that effective use of retrieved examples depends on a model's ability to integrate contextual information during generation.

</details>


### [27] [DBLAST: Dependent Block Drafting for Stochastic Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05448)
*Amirmohammad Karimi,Chao Gao,Negar Hassanpour*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DBLast proposes a dependent block drafter for speculative decoding that models inter-token dependencies via a low-rank latent mixture, coupled with an acceptance-oriented training objective, improving accepted draft length particularly under high-entropy stochastic decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing block and diffusion drafters for speculative decoding assume conditional independence among tokens in a block, which is adequate for greedy decoding but breaks down under non-greedy, stochastic sampling where multiple plausible continuations exist. This mismatch degrades accepted draft length as target distribution entropy increases.

Method: DBLast introduces a dependent block drafter using a low-rank latent mixture over token positions to capture inter-token dependencies, combined with an acceptance-oriented training objective that directly optimizes the expected verified length (rather than standard next-token prediction loss).

Result: Experiments with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, MT-Bench, HumanEval, and creative-writing benchmarks show consistent improvements in accepted length over independent block sampling, with particularly pronounced gains in higher-entropy decoding regimes.

Conclusion: Modeling dependencies across draft block positions and aligning training with the verification objective are both critical for effective non-greedy speculative decoding; DBLast demonstrates that these two design choices jointly yield substantial gains over independent block drafters.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language models' inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple future tokens and a target model to verify them. While recent block and diffusion-style drafters can predict several positions in a single pass, their training and sampling procedures are typically optimized for greedy decoding or assume that positions in the draft block are conditionally independent. This assumption becomes brittle in non-greedy speculative decoding, where the target distribution is deliberately stochastic and multiple continuations become plausible. We study this mismatch for block diffusion drafters and show that the accepted draft length degrades as the entropy of the target sampling distribution increases. We propose a dependent block drafter based on a low-rank latent mixture over token positions, complemented by an acceptance-oriented training objective that directly targets the expected verified length. Experiments with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, MT-Bench, HumanEval, and creative-writing benchmarks show that our approach, namely DBLast, consistently improves accepted length over independent block sampling, especially in higher-entropy decoding regimes.

</details>


### [28] [Different Perturbations, Different Mechanisms: Understanding Continued Pre-training for Zero-Shot Dialect Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05510)
*Aarohi Srivastava,David Chiang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Systematic study of perturbation-based continued pre-training (CPT) for multilingual dialect robustness in LLMs. Six training conditions across nine German, Italian, and Arabic dialect tasks are compared. Character-noised CPT consistently improves zero-shot dialect robustness while preserving standard variety performance. Methods with similar downstream performance induce distinct internal mechanisms (adaptation patterns, representational alignment, prediction repair), offering practical CPT selection guidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work on perturbation-based CPT for dialect robustness evaluates strategies in isolation and provides limited insight into why they work, lacking a systematic understanding of the underlying mechanisms.

Method: Systematic comparison of six perturbation-based CPT conditions across nine dialect tasks in German, Italian, and Arabic. Analysis of language model adaptation patterns, representational alignment, and prediction repair mechanisms to explain why different perturbation strategies succeed.

Result: Character-noised CPT consistently improves zero-shot dialect robustness while largely preserving standard variety performance. Methods with similar downstream performance induce distinct robustness mechanisms, exhibiting different patterns of LM adaptation, representational alignment, and prediction repair.

Conclusion: Perturbation-based CPT is effective for dialect robustness, but different perturbation strategies achieve similar outcomes through distinct internal mechanisms. This mechanistic understanding enables more informed CPT strategy selection for multilingual and dialectal NLP settings.

Abstract: Dialectal variation remains a major challenge for multilingual language models. Perturbation-based continued pre-training (CPT) has emerged as a promising approach to improving robustness, yet existing work largely evaluates individual perturbation strategies in isolation and provides limited insight into why they work. We present a systematic study of perturbation-based CPT for multilingual dialect robustness in LLMs, comparing six training conditions across nine German, Italian, and Arabic dialect tasks. Perturbation-based CPT, especially character-noised CPT, consistently improves zero-shot dialect robustness while largely preserving standard variety performance. More importantly, we show that methods with similar downstream performance induce distinct mechanisms of robustness, exhibiting different patterns of language model adaptation, representational alignment, and prediction repair. Our results provide a more complete understanding of how synthetic surface variation improves robustness and offer practical guidance for selecting CPT strategies in multilingual and dialectal settings.

</details>


### [29] [Where Models Converge and Humans Diverge: A Coverage Framework for Distributional Pluralism in Open-Ended Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05576)
*Zini Yang,Emily Wenger,Richard So*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs produce plausible but narrow content concentrated near the center of the human writing distribution. The paper proposes two metrics—LLM Coverage (LLM-Cov) and In-Boundary Rate (IBR)—to systematically measure the distributional breadth ("cultural reach") of LLM-generated text compared to human writing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior work has noted a distributional "gap" between LLM-generated and human-authored text (LLMs produce "average" writing; humans produce stylistically irregular, diverse content), no systematic framework exists to measure this gap. The authors aim to fill this methodological void.

Method: The authors propose a human-grounded framework that uses the empirical distribution of human writing on a given topic as a reference. Two metrics are introduced: (1) LLM Coverage (LLM-Cov), which quantifies how much of the human response distribution is covered by LLM outputs, and (2) In-Boundary Rate (IBR), which measures the proportion of LLM-generated content that falls within the boundary of the human distribution. These metrics jointly separate plausibility from distributional breadth. The framework is applied across ideation and narrative tasks using the Harry Potter fanfiction domain as a case study.

Result: Current LLMs produce content that is plausible (high IBR) but distributionally narrow (low LLM-Cov), clustering near the center of the human response space rather than spanning its full breadth.

Conclusion: The proposed framework enables rigorous, quantitative assessment of the distributional breadth—termed "cultural reach"—of LLM-authored content, providing researchers with tools to evaluate and improve the diversity of machine-generated text.

Abstract: When a large language model (LLM) writes Harry Potter fanfiction, it reliably produces fundamental elements of the Hogwarts universe, such as recognizable places and characters. Human-written Harry Potter fanfictions, however, typically include these fundamentals and much more, incorporating stylistically irregular content and relationship-diverse plotlines. This gap between LLM and human writing has been noted across a variety of domains. LLMs tend to produce "average" writing, while human writing contains more diverse content that covers a broader distribution. Existing work has shown the existence of this distributional "gap", but no work has proposed a systematic way to measure it. Our paper proposes a human-grounded framework that uses the empirical distribution of human writing on a topic to measure the distributional breadth of LLM-generated content on that same topic. We propose two metrics, LLM Coverage (LLM-Cov) and In-Boundary Rate (IBR), that separate the plausibility of LLM content from its distributional breadth. Across ideation and narrative tasks, we find that current LLMs produce plausible but narrow content that concentrates near the center of the human response space. Our framework can enable researchers to better assess the distributional breadth of LLM-authored content, which we term its "cultural reach".

</details>


### [30] [SkillZip: Contract-Preserving Graph Compression for Scalable Agent Skill Libraries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05604)
*Xingyu Tan,Xiaoyang Wang,Qing Liu,Xiwei Xu,Xin Yuan,Liming Zhu,Wenjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SkillZip is an execution-aware procedural abstraction framework that compresses reusable LLM agent skills by converting recurring contract-valid motifs into reversible ported macros, preserving contract boundaries, dependency closure, and verifier reachability while achieving a 3.46x compression ratio and outperforming baselines by up to 12.2 points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents accumulate reusable skill packages in growing libraries, a fundamental unit mismatch arises: skills are retrieved as whole packages, compressed as flat text, and converted to execution graphs only post-retrieval. This prevents reliable reuse below the whole-skill level, fails to preserve procedural contracts during compression, and cannot maintain executable, expandable compressed routines. The authors identify the need for a contract-bearing procedural unit that enables smallest-sufficient-context retrieval under budget constraints.

Method: SkillZip introduces an execution-aware procedural abstraction framework operating on section-level graphs. It: (1) rewrites recurring contract-valid motifs into reversible ported macros while preserving boundary signatures, dependency closure, verifier reachability, and source-level expansion; (2) at inference time, hydrates a compact dependency-closed context and expands macros only when needed; and (3) provides ReZip, a mechanism that integrates new skills and revises risky macros using execution evidence.

Result: On technical and embodied agent benchmarks, SkillZip outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 12.2 points, achieves a 3.46x compression ratio with 99.2% dependency preservation and 98.7% verifier reachability. Scaling analyses demonstrate robust retrieval across skill libraries ranging from 200 to 100K skills.

Conclusion: SkillZip solves the unit mismatch problem in LLM agent skill retrieval by introducing contract-preserving compression at the procedural graph level. The reversible macro abstraction enables reliable sub-skill reuse, dynamic expansion, and library evolution, establishing a new paradigm for scalable, execution-aware skill management in agent systems.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents whose procedural knowledge is stored in reusable skill packages and loaded at inference time. As skill libraries grow, a central challenge is to expose the smallest sufficient executable context under a limited context budget. Existing systems struggle to reuse routines below the whole-skill level, preserve procedural contracts during compression, keep compressed routines executable and expandable, and update the compressed library as skills evolve. These challenges reveal a unit mismatch: skills are retrieved as packages, compressed as text, and converted into execution graphs only after retrieval, whereas reliable reuse requires a contract-bearing procedural unit. We propose SkillZip, an execution-aware procedural abstraction framework that performs contract-preserving compression over section-level graphs. SkillZip rewrites recurring contract-valid motifs into reversible ported macros while preserving boundary signatures, dependency closure, verifier reachability, and source-level expansion. At inference time, it hydrates a compact, dependency-closed context and expands macros only when required. ReZip further integrates new skills and revises risky macros using execution evidence. Comprehensive experiments1 on technical and embodied agent benchmarks show SkillZip consistently outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 12.2 points, while achieving a 3.46x compression ratio with 99.2% dependency preservation and 98.7% verifier reachability. Scaling analyses further confirm robust retrieval across skill libraries ranging from 200 to 100K skills.

</details>


### [31] [FOCUS: Decoupling Expert Personas in LLMs to Enhance Domain Expert Capabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05611)
*Guanyu Wang,Zidi Zhang,Xu Chu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FOCUS proposes orthogonal decomposition and gated selection to decouple LLM personas across domains, enabling adaptive persona activation without cross-domain interference, improving accuracy on financial, legal, medical, and cross-domain benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing persona control methods for LLMs suffer from cross-domain coupling: activating an expert persona in one domain (e.g., finance) can lead to overly aggressive behavior in high-caution domains (e.g., healthcare) or excessive conservatism in risk-sensitive domains. This coupling limits safe and effective deployment across diverse real-world tasks.

Method: FOCUS (Fine-tuning with Orthogonal Control for Uncoupled personaS) operates in three stages: (1) automatic extraction of expert persona vectors from LLMs, (2) orthogonal decomposition to decouple domain-specific personas, eliminating cross-domain interference, and (3) an expert gating module that adaptively controls persona activation based on task context. A two-stage training strategy with a gated selection regularizer ensures proper persona activation for both single-domain and cross-domain tasks.

Result: Experiments on financial, legal, medical, and cross-domain benchmarks demonstrate that FOCUS improves task accuracy and outperforms existing persona control methods.

Conclusion: FOCUS effectively decouples domain-specific personas in LLMs through orthogonal decomposition and adaptive gating, resolving cross-domain coupling issues and enabling safer, more accurate multi-domain deployment.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can exhibit diverse personas, and activating expert personas has been shown to improve domain expertise and task accuracy. However, existing persona control methods often suffer from cross-domain coupling, which may lead to overly aggressive behavior in high-caution domains such as healthcare, or excessive conservatism in risk-sensitive domains such as financial trading. To address this issue, we propose FOCUS (\textbf{\underline{F}}ine-tuning with \textbf{\underline{O}}rthogonal \textbf{\underline{C}}ontrol for \textbf{\underline{U}}ncoupled persona\textbf{\underline{S}}). FOCUS first automatically extracts expert persona vectors from LLMs, then applies orthogonal decomposition to decouple domain-specific expert personas, and finally introduces an expert gating module to adaptively control persona activation according to task contexts. With a two-stage training strategy and a gated selection regularizer, the model learns to activate appropriate personas for both single-domain and cross-domain tasks. Experiments on financial, legal, medical, and cross-domain benchmarks show that FOCUS improves task accuracy and outperforms existing persona control methods. Our code is available at \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/openpersona-48F4}{this url}.

</details>


### [32] [Human-Like Anaphor Resolution in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05630)
*Keane Zhang,Varshini Chinta,Raj Sanjay Shah,Sashank Varma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study tests whether cognitive factors known to influence human anaphor resolution (discourse structure, situation-model properties, semantic factors) similarly affect five open-weight LLMs, using surprisal as a proxy for reading time and comprehension accuracy. Results reveal selective alignment: LLMs show human-like sensitivity to discourse prominence and distance, but weak sensitivity to semantic interference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether Large Language Models process anaphor resolution in ways that align with human cognitive processing, specifically testing whether established psycholinguistic factors — discourse structure, situation-model properties, and semantic interference — similarly modulate model behavior.

Method: Five open-weight LLMs (GPT-2-XL, Llama-3.1-8B, Pythia-12B, Mistral-7B, Mistral-24B) were evaluated on anaphor resolution. The authors used two behavioral measures: (1) surprisal at the anaphor as a linking hypothesis for human reading times (processing difficulty), and (2) model accuracy versus human accuracy on comprehension questions probing antecedent identification.

Result: LLMs exhibited selective cognitive alignment: human-like sensitivity emerged for discourse prominence and distance-based factors, but sensitivity to semantic interference effects was weaker or absent across models.

Conclusion: The findings delimit the boundary conditions under which LLMs approximate human anaphor resolution, suggesting that while surface-level structural factors are well-captured, deeper semantic integration during resolution remains a challenge for current models.

Abstract: Anaphors are expressions that refer to other expressions, called antecedents. The process of connecting the two is called resolution. Cognitive science has identified multiple factors that affect the speed and success of anaphor resolution, including discourse structure, situation-model properties, and semantic factors. Here, we investigate whether these factors also affect anaphor resolution in five Large Language Models (LLMs) with open weights: GPT-2-XL, Llama-3.1-8B, Pythia-12B, Mistral-7B, and Mistral-24B. To model processing difficulty, we adopt the standard linking hypothesis that relates human reading times to model surprisal at the anaphor. As a second behavioral measure, we compare model accuracy to human accuracy on comprehension questions probing the antecedents of anaphors. The results show selective cognitive alignment: some LLMs exhibit human-like sensitivity to discourse prominence and distance-based factors in anaphor resolution, while showing weaker or absent sensitivity to semantic interference effects. These findings delimit the conditions under which LLMs approximate human anaphor resolution.

</details>


### [33] [Relay, Don't Route: Adaptive Population Handoff for Cost-Efficient LLM-Driven Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05651)
*Sichun Luo,Yi Huang,Guanzhi Deng,Haibo Wang,Haochen Luo,Lei Li,Zefa Hu,Junlan Feng,Qi Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Cheap-strong model handoff at the population level, guided by a bandit scheduler using "Relay Gain," outperforms per-query budget allocation in LLM-driven evolutionary search across nearly all tested settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-driven evolutionary search is stateful, but existing budget-allocation methods treat it as stateless (per-query). Strong models are costly; cheap models can recover much early progress. The goal is to optimally combine cheap and strong models under a fixed inference budget by exploiting the population-level structure of evolution.

Method: Proposes a training-free framework with adaptive population handoff. A cheap model explores multiple short evolutionary trajectories allocated by a bandit scheduler. "Relay Gain" — the marginal improvement of a compact, quality-diverse candidate bank — serves as the scheduler reward and triggers handoff. Curated candidates then seed a strong model population for refinement.

Result: Across four benchmarks and three budget levels, the method achieves the highest mean score in 11 of 12 settings, outperforming competitive baselines.

Conclusion: In stateful evolutionary search, budget allocation should be organized around the population rather than individual queries; population-level handoff between cheap and strong models is both more effective and cost-efficient.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven evolution has shown promise for program search and algorithm discovery, but relying on strong models throughout long evolutionary runs is costly. A natural alternative is to combine cheap and strong models under a fixed inference budget. However, existing approaches typically allocate models at the level of individual queries or mutation steps, overlooking that evolutionary search is \textit{stateful}: each generated candidate changes the population from which subsequent mutations are produced.
  We empirically analyze LLM-driven evolutionary trajectories and find that search progress is strongly front-loaded, early trajectory performance is informative but noisy, and cheap models recover much of the early progress achieved by strong models at lower cost. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textbf{\model}, a training-free framework that shifts budget allocation from individual calls to evolving populations through adaptive \textit{population handoff}. A cheap model explores multiple trajectories in short blocks allocated by a bandit scheduler. Relay Gain, defined as the marginal improvement of a compact, quality-diverse candidate bank constructed for handoff, serves as the scheduler reward and determines when to hand off. The curated candidates initialize a shared strong model population for refinement. Across four benchmarks and three budgets, \model achieves the highest mean score in 11 of 12 settings, outperforming competitive baselines. Our results suggest that in stateful search, budget allocation should be organized around the population, not the individual call.

</details>


### [34] [Answer First, Reason Later: Commitment Order in Diffusion LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05687)
*Jewon Yeom,Jaewon Sok,Seonghyeon Park,Jeongjae Park,Hwiyeong Lee,Taesup Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Masked diffusion LMs fail at reasoning because unconstrained commitment order causes premature answer finalization (collapse to answer-only outputs). A frontier-gated commitment mechanism causally recovers the full performance gap while preserving parallel decoding speed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) are marketed on their ability to commit tokens in any order, but the authors investigate whether this freedom actually harms reasoning performance. They aim to identify why dLLMs fail on reasoning benchmarks and find a minimal intervention to fix the issue.

Method: The authors analyze LLaDA-8B on GSM8K by logging every token commitment during decoding. They use a 2×2 prompt-decoder design (with/without chain-of-thought × ordered/unconstrained decoding) to decompose the failure into a collapse channel and an order channel. They then introduce frontier-gated commitment — a single-knob intervention that restricts which masked positions can be sampled based on a frontier window — and validate on Dream-7B and MATH-500.

Result: Unconstrained decoding commits the final answer at only 15–24% of the trajectory while half the reasoning region remains masked, collapsing to answer-only outputs on up to 90% of problems. Chain-of-thought helps only under ordered commitment (+34.8 pp interaction; 95% CI [26.8, 42.8]). Frontier-gated commitment recovers the full gap (0.528→0.852 accuracy) while preserving up to 4× parallel decoding. The optimal frontier window flips from w=1 at full refinement to unconstrained at 8 tokens/step.

Conclusion: The freedom to commit tokens in any order is the axis of failure for dLLMs on reasoning tasks. Frontier-gated commitment — a simple, efficiency-motivated intervention — causally fixes the reasoning pathology. This reframes existing window-style samplers as addressing a fundamental reasoning problem rather than merely improving efficiency.

Abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) can commit tokens in any order -- a freedom marketed as their core advantage over autoregressive decoding. We show that on reasoning tasks this freedom is instead the axis of failure. Logging every commitment during decoding of LLaDA-8B on GSM8K, we find that unconstrained (pure) decoding commits the final answer at 15-24% of the trajectory while half the reasoning region is still masked, and collapses to answer-only outputs on up to 90% of problems as the canvas grows. The cause is not the model's termination beliefs -- EOS "pressure" is nearly identical across decoders -- but reachability: whether the sampler may act on those beliefs at distant positions. A 2x2 prompt-decoder design shows that chain-of-thought helps only under ordered commitment (interaction +34.8 percentage points, 95% CI [26.8, 42.8]; without reasoning text the decoders are indistinguishable), an interaction we decompose into a collapse channel and an order channel and replicate on Dream-7B and MATH-500. A single-knob intervention -- frontier-gated commitment -- causally recovers the full gap (0.528 to 0.852) while preserving up to 4x parallel decoding, along a measured frontier whose optimal window flips from w=1 at full refinement to unconstrained at 8 tokens/step. Our results reframe existing window-style samplers, previously motivated by efficiency, as the minimal fix for a reasoning pathology they were never designed to address.

</details>


### [35] [Sparse Mutual Information Graph Averaging for Improving Random Indexing Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05724)
*Sriram Loganathan,Gokul Anand,Aung Bo Bo,Yourui Shao,William B. Andreopoulos*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether sparse PPMI graph-based weighted averaging can repair weak Random Indexing (RI) word embeddings without gradient training. On a fairytales corpus, PPMI top-K graph averaging improves RI analogy accuracy from ~19.4% to ~30.7%, but the method underperforms neural baselines (CBOW, Skip-gram, SVD-based approaches) on broader benchmarks like text8 and SimLex-999.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore whether sparse word embedding pipelines — specifically Random Indexing (RI) — can be improved without resorting to dense matrix factorization or gradient-based training, maintaining the computational efficiency of sparse, count-based methods while boosting semantic quality.

Method: Random Indexing (RI) vectors are first generated as a sparse initialization. These are then refined via weighted averaging over a sparse Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (PPMI) graph with top-K pruning. The approach is evaluated on a fairytales corpus using a 272-question Google family-category analogy subset, and compared against PPMI+SVD, Binary+SVD, CBOW, Skip-gram, and Bloom filter sketches.

Result: PPMI top-K graph averaging raises RI accuracy from 19.4±0.7% to 30.7±2.9% (best seed: 34.6%). However, the same neighborhood averaging degrades performance for PPMI+SVD, Binary+SVD, CBOW, and Skip-gram. The method is not competitive with neural baselines on text8 and yields near-zero strict similarity correlation on SimLex-999. Bloom filter sketches underperform RI in the tested configuration.

Conclusion: PPMI graph averaging with top-K pruning is a useful non-gradient repair mechanism specifically for weak RI embeddings, but it does not generalize as an effective post-processing step for stronger neural or SVD-based embeddings, and remains uncompetitive on standard benchmarks.

Abstract: Sparse word embedding pipelines can avoid dense co-occurrence matrix materialization, dense factorization, and gradient training while still relying on sparse global corpus statistics. This paper studies Random Indexing (RI) vectors refined by weighted averaging on a sparse Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (PPMI) graph. On a fairytales corpus, the covered semantic analogy set consists of 272 Google family- category questions. On this family subset, PPMI top-K graph averaging repairs a weak RI initialization, improving accuracy from 19.4+-0.7% to 30.7+-2.9% across five seeds. Under the single tested runs, the same neighborhood averaging reduces family- subset analogy accuracy for PPMI+SVD (singular value decom- position), Binary+SVD, CBOW, and Skip-gram. Thus the method is not competitive with neural baselines on text8 and gives near- zero strict similarity correlation on SimLex-999. While Bloom filter sketches underperform RI in the tested configuration, we find that PPMI graph averaging with top-K pruning is a useful non-gradient repair for weak RI embeddings. On the fairytales dataset, PPMI top-K=50 graph averaging improves RI with accuracy going from 19.4+-0.7% to 30.7+-2.9%, and performing best with a seed42 of 34.6%.

</details>


### [36] [Mitigating Scoring Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge via Random Number Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05726)
*Yuma Asato,Kiyoaki Shirai,Natthawut Kertkeidkachorn*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM evaluators suffer from scoring bias, producing skewed score distributions regardless of context. The authors propose measuring an LLM's latent numerical bias via random number generation prompts, then rectifying token generation probabilities during evaluation to correct for this bias. The method outperforms baselines across four evaluation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge has become a popular paradigm for automatic text evaluation, but LLM evaluators exhibit scoring bias — systematically favoring certain scores independent of input quality. Existing calibration methods are insufficient, motivating a principled approach to measure and correct the latent numerical bias inherent in LLMs.

Method: The method has two stages: (1) Latent numerical bias measurement — the LLM is prompted to generate random number tokens, and the deviation of the observed distribution from uniform reveals its inherent number preference. Task-specific bias is captured by incorporating task definitions into these prompts. (2) Bias rectification — during actual evaluation, the token generation probabilities for score outputs are adjusted/adjusted by the measured latent bias distribution to produce debiased scores.

Result: Experiments on four tasks — LLM alignment evaluation, summarization evaluation, Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), and Semantic Textual Relatedness (STR) — show the proposed method outperforms both an unmodified LLM evaluator and prior calibration methods. The study also finds that scoring bias varies across different LLMs, tasks, and score ranges, underscoring the need for case-specific bias measurement.

Conclusion: Latent numerical bias is a measurable property of LLMs that systematically skews their scoring behavior. Rectifying evaluation probabilities against this measured bias is an effective, task-adaptive debiasing strategy. The variability of bias across LLMs and tasks confirms that one-size-fits-all calibration is insufficient.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are often used as evaluators of text quality, known as LLM-as-a-Judge, which can outperform conventional automatic evaluation metrics that rely on reference texts. However, LLM evaluators tend to generate particular scores regardless of the context of the evaluated text, which is known as scoring bias. This study proposes a novel method to mitigate this scoring bias. An LLM is instructed to randomly generate number tokens, and the latent numerical bias of the LLM is identified by measuring the deviation of the observed distribution of numbers from the uniform distribution. A definition of a downstream task, for which an LLM evaluator is used, is added to the prompts for random number generation to measure task-specific latent number bias. In the evaluation by an LLM, the token generation probabilities for a given input are rectified considering the LLM's latent number bias. Results of the experiment on four different tasks, evaluation of LLM alignment, evaluation of summarization, Semantic Textual Similarity, and Semantic Textual Relatedness, demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms the baselines, including an LLM without debiasing and previous calibration methods. In addition, it is confirmed that scoring bias varies across LLMs, tasks, and score ranges, indicating the importance of measuring latent number bias as the case may be.

</details>


### [37] [Once a Response, Always a Response: Detecting LLM-generated Text via Latent Prompt Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05741)
*Hongrui Bao,Yubing Ren,Yanan Cao,Jinhan You,Fang Fang,Shi Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EchoPrompt is a training-free LLM-generated text detector that identifies machine text by measuring how much a restored generic prompt boosts likelihood in an instruction-tuned model versus a base model, achieving SOTA zero-shot detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing zero-shot detectors rely on probability-based statistical discrepancies but fail to model the distinct generation mechanism of LLMs — namely, that generated text is conditioned on an upstream prompt. This gap limits detection robustness and motivates a detection approach that explicitly leverages the prompt-conditioned nature of machine-generated text.

Method: EchoPrompt is a training-free detector based on latent prompt restoration. It prepends a unified generic prefix (restoring an assistant-response context) to candidate text, measures the resulting likelihood gain using an instruction-tuned model, calibrates this gain against the corresponding base model, and aggregates the differences into a score quantifying latent prompt dependency.

Result: Extensive experiments show EchoPrompt achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot detectors and maintains strong robustness across challenging evaluation settings.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling the latent prompt dependency inherent in LLM generation — via prompt restoration and likelihood calibration — yields a highly effective and robust zero-shot detection method, outperforming existing probability-based approaches.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent and convincing text at scale, creating growing risks for misinformation dissemination, educational misuse, and platform governance. These concerns make robust detection of machine-generated text increasingly necessary. Recent zero-shot detectors mainly exploit probability-based statistical discrepancies, but they do not explicitly account for the training process of LLMs, which leaves a distinct generation mechanism insufficiently modeled and limits detection robustness. To address this issue, we propose EchoPrompt, a training-free detector based on latent prompt restoration. Our key intuition is that machine-generated text is typically produced conditioned on an upstream prompt, and this hidden dependency can be partially reactivated by prepending a unified generic prefix. Specifically, EchoPrompt restores a generic assistant-response context, measures the induced likelihood gain with an instruction-tuned model, calibrates it against the corresponding base model, and aggregates the resulting differences into a score that quantifies latent prompt dependency. Extensive experiments show that EchoPrompt achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot detectors while maintaining strong robustness across challenging evaluation settings.

</details>


### [38] [How to Recognize New Words: A Comparison Between Context Biasing Methods and Speech LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05759)
*Christian Huber,Alexander Waibel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Compares context biasing methods and speech LLMs for rare word recognition in ASR, finding context biasing reduces biased WER by up to 88% with minimal side effects, while speech LLMs perform well on read speech but struggle with non-read speech, distractor words, and prompt ordering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rare and new words (named entities, acronyms, domain-specific terms) remain a persistent challenge in ASR because they are scarce in training data. There is a need to systematically compare emerging strategies — context biasing versus speech LLMs — to understand their trade-offs for reliable rare word recognition.

Method: The authors compare two context biasing methods built on Whisper against three speech large language models (LLMs). Evaluation uses read and non-read speech datasets, measuring biased WER, unbiased WER, and overall WER. They also test sensitivity to distractor count and prompt word order for speech LLMs.

Result: Context biasing methods reduce biased WER by up to 88% relative with negligible impact on unbiased words. Speech LLMs achieve strong results on read speech but generalize poorly to non-read speech. Speech LLMs also show sensitivity to distractor words and the order of words in the prompt.

Conclusion: Context biasing offers robust, targeted improvements for rare word recognition with minimal side effects, making it preferable for general deployment. Speech LLMs are viable for read speech scenarios but require caution due to their sensitivity to distractors, prompt design, and domain mismatch. The paper characterizes trade-offs to inform method selection.

Abstract: Recognizing new and rare words - named entities, acronyms, domain specific special words, and other items scarce in training data - remains a key challenge for automatic speech recognition (ASR). We compare two strategies for this: context biasing methods, where an ASR model is extended such that during inference a word list can be supplied, and speech large language models (LLMs) prompted with context directly. We evaluate two context biasing methods based on Whisper against three speech LLMs across read and non-read speech, reporting biased, unbiased, and overall word error rate (WER). The context biasing methods cut biased WER by up to 88% relative while leaving other words largely unaffected. Speech LLMs excel on read speech but generalize less well to non-read speech, and prove sensitive to distractor count and prompt word order. We characterize the resulting trade-offs to guide method selection.

</details>


### [39] [Task-Conditional Flow Matching for Balanced Multilingual Text Embedding Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05785)
*Tirth Bhatt,Naren Kumar S,Mayank Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TCFM is a multilingual embedding adaptation framework that uses different training objectives for different tasks — Flow Matching for translation and aligned objectives for retrieval/classification — combined with teacher-guided preservation and a three-stage curriculum, achieving SOTA on the Indic Massive Text Embedding Benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multilingual text embedding models typically use a single training objective across all tasks, but different tasks (translation, retrieval, classification, pair-classification) have fundamentally different learning dynamics and optimization needs. This one-size-fits-all approach is suboptimal.

Method: TCFM is a task-conditional adaptation framework. It selectively applies Flow Matching specifically to translation tasks while using objectives better aligned to the learning dynamics of retrieval, classification, and pair-classification tasks. It also incorporates teacher-guided representation preservation to retain knowledge from the original model, and a three-stage curriculum learning strategy to ensure stable adaptation.

Result: TCFM establishes new state-of-the-art results on the Indic Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, consistently improving embedding quality across diverse multilingual tasks and demonstrating generalization across different embedding model families.

Conclusion: Task-conditional objective selection, rather than a uniform training objective, is crucial for optimal multilingual embedding adaptation. The combination of Flow Matching for translation, aligned objectives for other tasks, teacher-guided preservation, and curriculum learning yields robust SOTA performance. Code and datasets will be publicly released.

Abstract: Multilingual text embedding models are commonly adapted using a single training objective across diverse tasks, despite different tasks requiring fundamentally different optimization strategies. We introduce Task-Conditional Flow Matching (TCFM), a multilingual embedding adaptation framework that selectively applies Flow Matching to translation tasks while optimizing retrieval, classification, and pair-classification tasks with objectives better aligned to their learning dynamics. TCFM further combines teacher-guided representation preservation with a three-stage curriculum to enable stable adaptation. Evaluated on the Indic Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, TCFM establishes a new state-of-the-art, consistently improving embedding quality across a diverse set of multilingual tasks and generalizing across embedding model families. We will publicly release the codebase and datasets upon acceptance of the paper.

</details>


### [40] [On-Policy Delta Distillation for Multilingual Math Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05802)
*Byeongho Heo,Jaehui Hwang,Sangdoo Yun,Dongyoon Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates On-Policy Distillation (OPD) and its variant OPD² for multilingual mathematical reasoning in English, Korean, and Japanese. OPD² uses the probability gap between a post-trained teacher and its base model as a learning signal. Experiments show OPD² outperforms OPD, especially in Korean and Japanese, narrowing the English-Korean gap. English-only OPD improves non-English performance but causes language shift toward English, emphasizing the need for multilingual data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-Policy Distillation is gaining traction for LLM post-training, but its effectiveness in multilingual settings has not been adequately studied. The authors aim to fill this gap by evaluating OPD and its advanced variant OPD² across English, Korean, and Japanese for mathematical reasoning tasks.

Method: The paper compares two approaches: (1) standard On-Policy Distillation (OPD), and (2) On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD²), which uses the probability gap between a post-trained teacher model and its base model as the learning signal. Experiments are conducted using the Qwen3 model family on mathematical reasoning tasks across three languages: English, Korean, and Japanese. The study also ablates the effect of using English-only training data versus multilingual data.

Result: OPD² consistently outperforms standard OPD, with particularly strong gains in Korean and Japanese. It generally narrows the English-Korean performance gap. English-only OPD improves Korean and Japanese performance but tends to shift model responses toward English, demonstrating that multilingual training data is crucial for preserving target-language generation.

Conclusion: OPD² is an effective distillation method for multilingual mathematical reasoning, outperforming standard OPD while reducing cross-lingual performance disparities. The language shift observed with English-only training underscores the importance of incorporating multilingual data to maintain target-language fidelity in distilled models.

Abstract: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) is emerging as a promising alternative to reinforcement learning for LLM post-training, yet its effectiveness in multilingual settings remains underexplored. We study OPD and its advanced variant, On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD$^2$), for mathematical reasoning in English, Korean, and Japanese. OPD$^2$ improves OPD by using the probability gap between a post-trained teacher and its base model as the learning signal. Experiments with Qwen3 show that OPD$^2$ consistently outperforms the original OPD, with particularly strong improvements in Korean and Japanese, and generally narrows the English-Korean performance gap. We further find that English-only OPD can also increase performance for Korean and Japanese, but often shifts the responses toward English, highlighting the importance of multilingual data to preserving target-language responses.

</details>


### [41] [Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05806)
*Chang Shi,Tim Pearce,Manan Tomar,Siddhartha Sen,John Langford*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HiLP introduces a hierarchical auxiliary latent prediction objective that mitigates error accumulation in latent-space rollouts, improving long-horizon reasoning, coding performance, and speculative decoding efficiency over standard NTP, MTP, and NextLat.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Next-Token Prediction uses teacher forcing, which is suboptimal for long-horizon reasoning and planning. Existing alternatives like Multi-Token Prediction have limited horizons, while Next-Latent prediction suffers from compounding errors during multi-step latent rollout. There is a need for an objective that enables longer-horizon coherent representations without succumbing to error accumulation.

Method: Hierarchical Latent Prediction (HiLP) introduces an auxiliary prediction task at a higher-level abstract latent space. This hierarchical structure reduces error accumulation during latent-space rollouts by providing a coarser, more stable prediction target alongside the finer-grained latent predictions.

Result: HiLP produces longer-horizon coherent belief state representations. It demonstrates effectiveness on coding and multi-step reasoning benchmarks and offers improved speculative decoding efficiency compared to baselines.

Conclusion: HiLP successfully addresses the limitations of prior auxiliary training objectives by introducing hierarchical abstraction into latent prediction, yielding better long-horizon representations and practical gains in both reasoning benchmarks and decoding efficiency.

Abstract: While standard Next-Token Prediction (NTP) lays the foundation of language model pre- training, its teacher-forced training paradigm may not be optimal for long-horizon reasoning and planning. Recent works such as Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) and Next-Latent prediction (NextLat) try to mitigate the problem through predicting multiple future tokens and self-supervised prediction in the latent space. However, those auxiliary objectives either have a limited horizon or suffer from compounding error from multi-step rollout. We introduce Hierarchical Latent Prediction (HiLP), which introduces an auxiliary higher-level abstract latent to help reduce the error accumulation effect in latent-space rollouts. Experiments show that HiLP can lead to longer-horizon coherent belief state representation and demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across coding and multi-step reasoning benchmarks, and offers more speculative decoding efficiency.

</details>


### [42] [M$^3$R-Bench: A Unified Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Metaphor Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05817)
*Hong Jiang,Junnan Zhu,Jingwang Huang,Xiao Sun,Yuming Yang,Jiang Zhong,Ruirui Chen,Jingman Shi,Hao Wu,Nayu Liu,Xinyi Jiang,Kaiwen Wei*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: M$^3$R-Bench is a multimodal metaphor reasoning benchmark with 1,000 evidence-grounded image-text instances, accompanied by M$^3$R-Reasoner, a model using curriculum-based reasoning supervision and task-aware RL that significantly outperforms larger proprietary MLLMs on metaphor understanding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing metaphor benchmarks evaluate via isolated subtasks without evidence-grounded explanations, making it impossible to assess whether models truly establish Target-Source mappings grounded in both visual and textual cues.

Method: The authors construct M$^3$R-Bench, a unified benchmark with 1,000 image-text instances annotated for metaphor occurrence, Target-Source mapping, sentiment, and stage-wise explanations (evidence identification → mapping establishment → sentiment inference). They then propose M$^3$R-Reasoner, which combines curriculum-based reasoning supervision with task-aware reinforcement learning to align model reasoning with metaphor interpretation.

Result: Evaluations reveal existing models suffer from cross-modal evidence-mapping mismatch: overlooking visual evidence and relying on superficial textual cues. M$^3$R-Reasoner (8B backbone) outperforms larger proprietary MLLMs across four unified-task metrics, improving Visual Evidence and Sentiment Justification scores over GPT-5.5 by 28.45 and 30.11 points, and surpassing Claude-Sonnet-4.6 by 8.00 points in mean rubric score.

Conclusion: M$^3$R-Bench fills a critical gap in multimodal metaphor evaluation, and M$^3$R-Reasoner demonstrates that targeted reasoning alignment can overcome the evidence-mapping mismatch, enabling smaller models to surpass much larger proprietary systems.

Abstract: Metaphor enables the understanding of abstract concepts through cross-domain mappings while conveying affective attitudes. In multimodal scenarios, visual and textual information jointly construct Target--Source mappings, requiring both conceptual understanding and cross-modal reasoning. However, existing benchmarks mainly evaluate metaphor understanding through isolated subtasks and lack evidence-grounded explanations, making it difficult to assess whether models establish mappings grounded in visual and textual cues.To address these limitations, we introduce M$^3$R-Bench, a unified and evidence-grounded benchmark containing 1,000 image--text instances with human-verified annotations. Guided by Conceptual Metaphor Theory and theories of nonliteral language understanding, M$^3$R-Bench provides joint annotations for metaphor occurrence, Target--Source mapping, sentiment, and stage-wise explanations following ``evidence identification--mapping establishment--sentiment inference.''Evaluations on M$^3$R-Bench reveal that existing models often overlook visual evidence, rely on superficial textual cues, and produce inaccurate Target--Source mappings, exposing a cross-modal evidence--mapping mismatch. To address this mismatch, we propose M$^3$R-Reasoner, which combines curriculum-based reasoning supervision with task-aware reinforcement learning to align model reasoning with metaphor interpretation. Experiments show that, with only an 8B-parameter backbone, M$^3$R-Reasoner outperforms larger proprietary MLLMs across four unified-task metrics and improves Visual Evidence and Sentiment Justification scores over GPT-5.5 by 28.45 and 30.11 points, respectively, while surpassing Claude-Sonnet-4.6 by 8.00 points in mean rubric score. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/hongshi4/M3R-Bench.

</details>


### [43] [Decomposed Entailment for Factuality Checking and Hallucination Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05823)
*Achir Oukelmoun,Nasredine Semmar,Gaël De Chalendar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HallDetect is a lightweight, reference-free, black-box hallucination detection framework that decomposes generated text into atomic claims, verifies each against multi-scale source chunks using a contrastive entailment model, and aggregates results with an asymmetric scoring mechanism. It outperforms comparably resourced baselines across three of four source-grounded generation benchmarks while providing interpretable error localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM reliability is undermined by factual inconsistencies (hallucinations) where generated content lacks support from source material. Existing detection approaches are often computationally expensive, require reference texts, or assume white-box access. A need exists for a lightweight, reference-free, black-box method applicable across diverse source-grounded generation tasks beyond just summarization.

Method: HallDetect employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) decomposition of generated output into atomic factual claims, (2) verification of each claim via a compact encoder-based entailment model using a contrastive formulation against a multi-scale library of source chunks (retrieved at different granularities), and (3) asymmetric aggregation where a single confidently contradicted claim suffices to flag the entire response as hallucinated. All components operate under 4-bit quantization with consumer-grade hardware. The framework also produces a claim-to-span audit trail for error localization.

Result: Under a controlled protocol where all methods share 4-bit quantized backbones and consumer-grade hardware, HallDetect outperforms comparably resourced generative and embedding-based baselines on three out of four benchmarks. Performance remains stable across different backbone model families.

Conclusion: HallDetect provides an effective, resource-efficient solution for hallucination detection that is both model-agnostic (black-box) and reference-free, with broader applicability across source-grounded generation tasks. Its asymmetric scoring and audit trail capabilities further enhance practical utility by enabling precise error localization.

Abstract: The reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) is often compromised by factual inconsistencies, including hallucinations---cases where generated content is not supported by the underlying source. We present HallDetect, a lightweight, reference-free, and black-box framework for hallucination detection that we evaluate not only on summarization but across a broader range of source-grounded generation settings. HallDetect builds on decomposition-based factuality evaluation: generated content is decomposed into atomic claims, each verified by a compact encoder-based entailment model through a contrastive formulation over a multi-scale library of source chunks, and aggregated with an asymmetric score in which a single confidently contradicted claim flags the response. Under a controlled protocol in which all methods share the same 4-bit quantized backbones and consumer-grade hardware budget, HallDetect outperforms comparably resourced generative and embedding-based baselines on three of four benchmarks while remaining stable across backbone families, and yields a claim-to-span audit trail that localizes each error.

</details>


### [44] [MoCA: Implicit Social Context Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05825)
*Wenhao Xu,Kaiwen Zhang,Hao Li,Maowei You,Yongzheng Ji,Siyuan Zuo,Jingxuan Yu,Sina A,Xinyao Tan,Bobo Li,Hao Fei,Mong-Li Lee,Wynne Hsu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces MoCA (Implicit Social Context Analysis), a novel multimodal benchmark for modeling implicit social communication across affection, intent, and stance. Proposes CoDAR, a conflict-driven abductive reasoning framework that infers hidden mental states. MLLMs struggle on this task; CoDAR improves performance but a large gap to human-level reasoning remains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human social communication is highly implicit — meaning is conveyed through indirect, culturally grounded signals rather than explicit statements. Despite the pervasiveness of such implicit social contexts in real-world interactions, there is no formal, systematic framework for studying them computationally.

Method: (1) MoCA Benchmark: 3,108 multimodal instances from real-world sources with fine-grained cognitive annotations capturing who expresses what to whom, plus how and why. Three dimensions: affection, intent, stance. (2) CoDAR Framework: Conflict-Driven Abductive Reasoning that models the discrepancy between observed expressions and expected truthful behavior as cognitive conflict, enabling inference of hidden mental states.

Result: State-of-the-art multimodal LLMs struggle significantly on MoCA due to reliance on explicit cues and poor reasoning over latent social contexts. CoDAR substantially improves model performance, yet a large gap from human reasoning remains, underscoring the fundamental difficulty of implicit social understanding.

Conclusion: Implicit social context understanding remains a fundamentally difficult open problem. While CoDAR advances the state of the art, the persistent gap to human-level performance highlights the need for further research into computational reasoning over latent, culturally grounded social signals.

Abstract: Human social communication, such as affection and intent, is often conveyed in highly implicit ways, where underlying meanings are expressed through indirect, socially and culturally grounded signals rather than explicit statements. Such implicit social contexts are pervasive in real-world interactions, yet there remains a lack of a formal and systematic framework for studying them. In this paper, we introduce Implicit Social Context Analysis (MoCA), a novel task that systematically models implicit social scenarios along three key dimensions: affection, intent, and stance. We construct a high-quality benchmark containing 3,108 multimodal instances collected from real-world sources, with fine-grained cognitive annotations revealing who expresses what toward whom, as well as how and why it is conveyed. Using the MoCA dataset, we show that state-of-the-art multimodal large language models struggle significantly with this task because of their reliance on explicit cues and limited ability to reason over latent social contexts. To address this challenge, we propose Conflict-Driven Abductive Reasoning (CoDAR), a novel framework that models the discrepancy between observed expressions and expected truthful behavior as cognitive conflict, thereby enabling the inference of hidden mental states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoDAR substantially improves model performance. Nevertheless, a large gap from human reasoning remains, highlighting the fundamental difficulty of implicit social understanding.

</details>


### [45] [Enhancing Social Intelligence in LLMs with Hierarchical Reasoning and Utterance-Level Goal Rewarding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05832)
*Xiaofeng Wang,Kakam Chong,Shuai Xiao,DeXin Kong,Qingyuan Tian,Chen Ju,Xu Yan,Shuai Zhao,Fei Huang,Rui Wang,Shuguang Han,jufeng chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes TSR (Think-Strategy-Response), a hierarchical framework inspired by the Theory of Planned Behavior, and LHRL-VGR, a novel reinforcement learning algorithm that dynamically routes rewards based on goal achievement variance. Fine-tuning a Qwen2.5-7B agent with this approach surpasses GPT-4o by 7.32% on the SOTOPIA social negotiation benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs perform well on structured tasks but fail at dynamic social interactions requiring long-term goal coordination and rapid adaptation. Existing methods apply uniform goal-based rewards to every utterance, ignoring turn-specific objectives and the rationale behind strategic choices.

Method: The TSR framework decomposes social dialogue hierarchically: high-level strategic planning and low-level linguistic execution. Optimization uses LHRL-VGR, a linearized hierarchical RL algorithm with variance-gated rewards that dynamically balances goal completion and strategy adherence based on the variance of goal achievement scores.

Result: On the SOTOPIA benchmark, a Qwen2.5-7B agent fine-tuned with TSR + LHRL-VGR surpasses the GPT-4o baseline by 7.32% in goal completion success, achieving state-of-the-art performance in multi-agent social negotiation.

Conclusion: Hierarchical decomposition of social dialogue into strategic planning and linguistic execution, combined with variance-gated dynamic reward routing, effectively enables smaller LLMs to outperform much larger proprietary models on social negotiation tasks.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel in structured tasks but struggle with dynamic social interactions, where success requires long-term goal coordination and rapid adaptation. Current methods often apply uniform goal-based rewards to every utterance, overlooking the specificity of objectives at each dialogue turn and failing to account for the rationale of potential strategies. Inspired by the Theory of Planned Behavior, we propose the Think-Strategy-Response (TSR) framework, which decomposes social dialogue into two hierarchical stages: high-level strategic planning and low-level linguistic execution. To optimize TSR, we introduce Linearized Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Variance-Gated Rewards (LHRL-VGR), a novel algorithm that dynamically routes rewards - balancing goal completion and strategy adherence - based on the variance of goal achievement scores. Experiments on the SOTOPIA benchmark show that our approach fine-tunes a Qwen2.5-7B agent to surpass the GPT-4o baseline by 7.32% in goal completion success, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in multi-agent social negotiation tasks.

</details>


### [46] [MameLoshnLM: Yiddish Language Model and Evaluation Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05850)
*Uri Katz,Omer Goldman,Tomasz Limisiewicz,Reut Tsarfaty,Noah A. Smith*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MameLoshnLM is the first open-source 8B-parameter Yiddish language model, built by continuing pretraining of Llama 3.1 8B on a new high-quality corpus (Oytser). It outperforms similarly sized baselines on a new multi-task Yiddish benchmark (Kashes) and better captures lexical/morphological patterns, revealing failure modes of noisy multilingual data for low-resource languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Yiddish has a rich textual tradition but suffers from limited digital presence and scarce evaluation resources. Existing multilingual corpora and benchmarks are noisy, machine-translated, and misclassified, making them poor proxies. There is a clear need for high-quality, curated resources and a dedicated Yiddish LM to advance NLP for this historically rich but digitally underrepresented language.

Method: The authors introduce two key resources: (1) Oytser, a high-quality Yiddish pretraining corpus blending contemporary web-native sources with literary materials, and (2) Kashes, a multi-task benchmark covering translation, linguistic analysis, information extraction, and language understanding. They then perform continued pretraining of Llama 3.1 8B on Oytser to produce MameLoshnLM.

Result: MameLoshnLM outperforms open baselines of similar scale across all Kashes benchmark tasks. Beyond quantitative gains, it better captures language-defining lexical and morphological patterns compared to general-purpose multilingual models, highlighting the inadequacy of noisy web-scale multilingual data for low-resource languages.

Conclusion: The work provides both a foundation for Yiddish NLP and a replicable template for developing language models for historically rich but digitally underrepresented languages, demonstrating that curated, high-quality data yields substantial improvements over noisy multilingual corpora.

Abstract: We present MameLoshnLM, the first open-source 8B-parameter language model built specifically for Yiddish. Despite Yiddish's rich textual tradition, its limited digital presence and the scarcity of reliable evaluation resources have constrained progress in Yiddish language modeling. Existing multilingual corpora and benchmarks are often poor proxies for the language, containing substantial amounts of noisy, machine-translated, and misclassified text. We address these gaps by introducing Oytser, a high-quality Yiddish pretraining corpus that combines contemporary web-native sources with literary materials, and Kashes, a multi-task benchmark spanning translation, linguistic analysis, information extraction, and language understanding. Using these resources, we continue pretraining Llama 3.1 8B to obtain MameLoshnLM. Across the tasks in the benchmark, MameLoshnLM outperforms open baselines of similar scale. Our analyses show that these gains are not only quantitative: relative to general-purpose multilingual models, MameLoshnLM better captures language-defining lexical and morphological patterns, pointing to a broader failure mode of noisy web-scale multilingual data for low-resource languages. Our results provide both a foundation for Yiddish NLP and a practical template for language model development in historically rich but digitally underrepresented languages.

</details>


### [47] [Mapping Similarity Spaces across Embedding Models with Synthetic Query Probing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05857)
*Marcin Rozmus,Peter van der Putten*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Similarity scores from different embedding models are not directly comparable due to differing geometric properties. This paper introduces Synthetic Query Probing to learn mappings between score distributions, enabling cross-model calibration and threshold portability without accessing the embeddings themselves.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems depend on similarity thresholds for retrieval, but these thresholds cannot be reused across embedding models because each model produces scores in its own geometric space. This complicates model migration and forces practitioners to re-tune thresholds from scratch.

Method: Synthetic Query Probing generates queries directly from documents to form controlled query-chunk pairs, enabling large-scale, reference-free comparison of cross-model similarity behavior. Score conversion functions (linear, isotonic, and quantile mappings) are learned to map score distributions between models, evaluated on SciFact and a proprietary corpus.

Result: Models largely agree on relative rankings, but absolute scores exhibit systematic distortions. Isotonic regression performs best for mapping score distributions. Learned mappings partially align embedding spaces and improve threshold portability across models.

Conclusion: Cross-model calibration of similarity scores is both necessary and feasible. Synthetic Query Probing offers a scalable, reference-free framework for analyzing and correcting embedding comparability, with isotonic regression being the most effective mapping method.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems rely on similarity scores to retrieve relevant content, yet scores are not directly comparable across embedding models due to differing geometric properties, complicating model migration and limiting threshold reuse. We study how similarity scores can be related by learning mappings between score distributions rather than embeddings. We introduce Synthetic Query Probing, generating queries from documents to create controlled query-chunk pairs, enabling large-scale, reference-free analysis of cross-model similarity behavior. We evaluate the approach on multiple embedding configurations and learn score conversion functions using linear, isotonic, and quantile mappings. Experiments on SciFact and a proprietary corpus show that while models largely agree on rankings, their absolute scores exhibit systematic distortions. Learned mappings partially align these spaces and improve threshold portability, with isotonic regression performing best. Our results highlight the need for cross-model calibration and position Synthetic Query Probing as a scalable framework for analyzing embedding comparability.

</details>


### [48] [MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05872)
*Paweł Batorski,Abtin Pourhadi,Akylgali Aitaza,Przemysław Spurek,Paul Swoboda*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MACRO proposes a Markov chain-based dynamic layer routing framework for LLMs that learns task-specific execution paths (skipping, repeating, residual additions) without modifying model weights, achieving +5% accuracy over baselines and 7.2% over prior routing methods with 9.4x faster route search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dynamic layer routing methods for LLMs suffer from key limitations: they require weight updates, expensive per-instance search loops, or ground-truth labels at inference time. A method is needed that can learn effective routing policies without these constraints.

Method: MACRO formulates layer routing as a context-dependent Markov policy conditioned on layer indices, computation budget phases, directional displacements, and operator context. It supports skip, repeat, and residual hidden-state addition operations. The Markov route distribution is learned via feedback on training data and decoded using a top-k Viterbi algorithm to extract high-probability candidate programs. No underlying model parameters are modified.

Result: MACRO achieves +5.0% average accuracy over unrouted baselines across reasoning and knowledge benchmarks on multiple open-weight LLMs, with largest gains on smaller models. It outperforms Dr. LLM (the best dynamic routing approach) by +7.2% while reducing route-search time 9.4x from 14.8 to 1.6 hours.

Conclusion: MACRO demonstrates that task-specific layer routing via learned Markov policies can significantly improve LLM performance without weight modification, offering both superior accuracy and computational efficiency compared to prior routing methods.
