Abstract: Standard Large Language Models (LLMs) execute layers sequentially. Dynamic layer routing, i.e. search for a different execution path through layers involving layer repetitions, skips and other moves, can improve performance. Existing routing approaches often require updating model weights, running expensive search loops per test instance, or demand ground-truth labels during inference. In this work, we propose Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers (MACRO), a framework that learns task-specific routes over LLM architectures without modifying underlying parameters. MACRO models layer routing as a context-dependent Markov policy conditioned on layer indices, computation budget phases, directional displacements, and operator context, supporting skip, repeat, and residual hidden-state addition operations. The Markov route distribution is updated via feedback on training data and decoded using a top-k Viterbi algorithm to isolate high-probability candidate programs. We evaluate MACRO across diverse reasoning and knowledge benchmarks on multiple open-weight LLMs. MACRO achieves a +5.0% average accuracy improvement over the unrouted baselines, with largest gains on small models. We outperform the best dynamic routing approach Dr. LLM by +7.2%, while reducing route-search time 9.4x (from 14.8 to 1.6 hours). Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/MACRO.

</details>


### [49] [Causal Episodic Memory for Feedback-Driven Agent Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05906)
*Khang Nhat Hoang Vo,Tam Minh Chu,Anh Trac Duc Dinh,Thuyen Vinh Ha Bui,Tho Quan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MERIT is a training-free, memory-augmented LLM agent for Text-to-SQL repair that stores both successful corrections and observed failures in a dual-polarity memory. By retrieving relevant past experiences during iterative repair (without parameter updates), it improves execution accuracy on Spider (66.34% → 69.79%) and BIRD (47.35% → 48.44%) compared to stateless repair, though gains on BIRD are weaker and it does not reliably outperform untyped dynamic retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agents that iteratively repair SQL failures typically discard corrected outputs after each episode, forcing the model to rediscover similar fixes from scratch. The authors investigate whether persisting finalized repair outcomes—both successful corrections and failed directions—can be retrieved and reused across episodes to improve Text-to-SQL repair without any parameter updates, and under what conditions such cross-query memory is beneficial.

Method: MERIT maintains an online dual-polarity memory: positive entries store oracle-verified successful corrections, negative entries store observed unsuccessful directions. Only memories from earlier finalized episodes are eligible for retrieval. A deterministic classifier assigns each failure a coarse type, conditioning a hybrid lexical-dense retriever. The frozen base model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) then generates each revision using retrieved relevant experiences, with identical initial predictions and repair budgets as baselines.

Result: MERIT improves execution accuracy over stateless iterative repair from 66.34% to 69.79% on Spider and 47.35% to 48.44% on BIRD. Paired analyses confirm the Spider gain but show weaker evidence on BIRD. MERIT is not reliably separable from untyped dynamic retrieval on either benchmark. Reflexion-style memory reaches 51.24% on BIRD but at substantially higher inference cost. Ablations reveal negative memory contributes modestly, type conditioning and lexical-dense ranking benefits are dataset-dependent, and schema-local experience provides the most consistent benefit.

Conclusion: Causal cross-query memory can improve repair in Text-to-SQL, but gains are dataset-sensitive and the simpler untyped dynamic retrieval is not reliably outperformed. Schema-local experience is the most consistently valuable memory signal, while broader memory representations (e.g., Reflexion-style) may be preferable in some settings despite higher cost.

Abstract: LLM agents that repair failures often discard successful corrections, forcing later episodes to rediscover similar solutions. We study whether finalized repair outcomes can improve subsequent Text-to-SQL episodes without parameter updates. We introduce MERIT, a training-free agent that maintains an online dual-polarity memory of oracle-verified corrections and observed unsuccessful directions. Under oracle-assisted benchmark feedback, only memories from earlier finalized episodes are eligible for retrieval. A deterministic classifier assigns a coarse failure type, which conditions a hybrid lexical-dense retriever before the frozen model generates each revision. Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with identical initial predictions and repair budgets, MERIT improves execution accuracy over stateless iterative repair from \(66.34\%\) to \(69.79\%\) on Spider and from \(47.35\%\) to \(48.44\%\) on BIRD. Paired analyses provide clear evidence for the Spider gain but weaker evidence on BIRD. MERIT is not reliably separated from untyped dynamic retrieval on either benchmark, while Reflexion-style memory reaches \(51.24\%\) on BIRD at substantially higher inference cost. Ablations show that negative memory contributes modestly, the value of type conditioning and lexical--dense ranking is dataset dependent, and schema-local experience provides the most consistent benefit. These results clarify when causal cross-query memory improves repair and when broader memory representations remain preferable.

</details>


### [50] [Clinical Communication Processing with Models Trained on LLM-Generated Synthetic Data: A Structured Survey and Novel Application Case Studies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05993)
*Alexander Apartsin,Yehudit Aperstein*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Clinical communication conveys critical information through role-dependent, nuanced language that lacks structured annotation. This survey argues that synthetic clinical communication generated via large language models can bootstrap NLP systems for channels and languages lacking real-world labeled data, and it supports this with 13 case studies spanning EMS reports, nurse handoffs, triage, and discharge communication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Authentic clinical communication (patient-clinician exchanges, handoffs, triage) is rich in meaning but rarely captured as well-annotated corpora due to privacy, fragmentation, and annotation cost. This scarcity impedes healthcare NLP for communication channels where information is conveyed rather than coded in structured records.

Method: Structured narrative survey organizing the literature by (1) source representation, (2) communication form and participants, (3) generation method, and (4) downstream task. The survey is complemented by 13 novel case studies that generate synthetic clinical communication using large language models, covering EMS pre-arrival reports, field-radio casualty documentation, nurse handoffs, patient-portal triage, and low-resource discharge communication. Systems are evaluated on held-out synthetic data with some train-on-synthetic, test-on-authentic pilots.

Result: Synthetic clinical communication can bootstrap NLP systems for diverse clinical channels and languages. Fine-tuned encoder models prove competitive against zero-shot baselines. Deliberately degraded communication improves robustness. However, most evaluations remain on held-out synthetic data; train-on-synthetic, test-on-authentic evidence is still limited.

Conclusion: Synthetic clinical communication is becoming a practical research resource. To mature into reusable clinical infrastructure, it requires authentic-data transfer, safety validation, and external validation demonstrating real-world generalization.

Abstract: Much clinical value is conveyed not through structured records but through communication: exchanges in which patients describe symptoms, clinicians reason and give instructions, ambulances hand over to emergency departments, and nurses pass on a shift. Such language differs from tabular data because meaning depends on speaker role, intent, causality, uncertainty, omission, and channel noise. Healthcare natural language processing must therefore interpret information as conveyed rather than coded. This requires well-annotated corpora, which are scarce because authentic exchanges are private, fragmented, and costly to annotate. Large language models offer a way forward by transforming clinical sources, such as records, diagnostic labels, symptom lists, or care plans, into written and transcribed communication for downstream models. We present a structured narrative survey organized by source representation, communication form and participants, generation method, and downstream task, complemented by thirteen novel case studies. These build clinical NLP systems for communication channels and languages without labeled real-world data, including EMS pre-arrival reports, field-radio casualty documentation, nurse handoffs, patient-portal triage, and low-resource discharge communication. They show that synthetic communication can bootstrap such systems. Findings include the competitiveness of fine-tuned encoder models over evaluated zero-shot baselines and the value of deliberately degraded communication for robustness. The main limitation is that most studies evaluate on held-out synthetic communication, while train-on-synthetic, test-on-authentic evidence remains limited. We conclude that syn-thetic clinical communication is becoming a practical research resource; establishing it as reusable clinical infrastructure will require authentic-data transfer, safety and external validation.

</details>


### [51] [EpiBench: Can LLMs Understand Epitopes for Antibody Drug Discovery?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06022)
*Zirui Wang,Jiaqi Wang,Qinghan Wang,Yuzhi Xu,Gang Du,Tingjun Hou,Odin Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EpiBench is a new benchmark with 1,609 curated samples for evaluating how well LLMs reason about antibody epitopes from sequence data alone. It covers five epitope-related tasks, and testing nine LLMs reveals they capture partial signals but struggle with antibody-specific grounding, long-context localization, and biological reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Epitope understanding is central to antibody drug discovery, yet no benchmark exists for evaluating whether LLMs can infer epitope information directly from antigen/antibody sequences across the full antibody development workflow. Existing resources focus on isolated prediction tasks or require structural data.

Method: The authors introduce EpiBench, a closed-book, sequence-based, automatically scorable benchmark with five tasks: targetable region discovery, antibody-conditioned epitope identification, epitope binning, functional epitope assessment, and antibody escape assessment. Samples are grounded in structural contacts, functional B-cell assays, and deep mutational scanning escape measurements, with controlled sampling to mitigate shortcut artifacts. Nine general-purpose LLMs are evaluated with task-specific baselines, antigen length stratification, explicit-reasoning comparison, and failure-mode inspection.

Result: Current LLMs capture partial epitope-related signals but exhibit clear limitations in antibody-specific sequence grounding, long-context residue localization, and biologically grounded reasoning. Performance varies across the five tasks, with systematic failure modes identified.

Conclusion: EpiBench serves as a diagnostic testbed for measuring and improving sequence-aware biomedical LLMs. It highlights the gap between current LLM capabilities and the demands of reliable epitope reasoning for antibody discovery, providing a foundation for future model development.

Abstract: Epitopes determine where antibodies bind antigens and shape downstream therapeutic properties such as functional blockade and escape resistance, making epitope understanding central to antibody drug discovery. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong biomedical reasoning ability, it remains unclear whether they can infer epitope information directly from antigen and antibody sequences. Existing epitope resources typically focus on isolated prediction tasks or rely on specialized structural settings, while general protein benchmarks do not evaluate epitope-centered decisions across the antibody development workflow. To address this gap, we introduce EpiBench, a closed-book, sequence-based, and automatically scorable benchmark for evaluating epitope reasoning in LLMs. EpiBench contains 1,609 curated samples grounded in structural antibody--antigen contacts, curated functional B-cell assays, and deep mutational scanning escape measurements. It covers five connected tasks: targetable region discovery, antibody-conditioned epitope identification, epitope binning, functional epitope assessment, and antibody escape assessment, with controlled sampling to reduce shortcut-based evaluation artifacts. We evaluate nine general-purpose LLMs and analyze their behavior through task-specific baselines, antigen length stratification, explicit-reasoning comparison, and failure-mode inspection. The results show that current LLMs capture partial epitope-related signals but remain limited in antibody-specific sequence grounding, long-context residue localization, and biologically grounded reasoning. Therefore, EpiBench provides a diagnostic testbed for measuring and improving sequence-aware biomedical LLMs toward reliable LLM-assisted antibody discovery.

</details>


### [52] [Training-Free Token-Level Steering for LLM Personalized Co-Writing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06069)
*Wenhao Mao,Chengbin Hou,Weixiao Wang,Jialiang Zhu,Min Liu,Yibin Hao,Hairong Lv*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SteerWrite is a training-free framework for personalized co-writing that adapts LLMs to specialized domains using token-level steering, outperforming fine-tuning and RAG baselines while reducing editing effort.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs lack specialized domain knowledge for personalization. Fine-tuning is computationally expensive and poorly suited for rapidly changing data. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) cannot provide fine-grained, token-level control. Additionally, co-writing interfaces remain underexploited outside coding, with chat interfaces still dominant.

Method: SteerWrite is a training-free framework that adapts a base LLM to specialized domains through token-level steering without any gradient updates. It incorporates specific design choices tailored for small datasets, enabling effective personalization in a co-writing paradigm.

Result: SteerWrite achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse datasets, evaluation metrics, and model architectures, and significantly reduces the human editing effort required in personalized co-writing scenarios.

Conclusion: SteerWrite demonstrates that training-free, token-level steering is a viable and effective alternative to fine-tuning and RAG for personalized LLM co-writing, especially in data-scarce specialized domains.

Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) show great promise for personalization, they often lack specialized domain knowledge. Conventional solutions like fine-tuning struggle with high computational costs and rapid data updates, while Retrieval-Augmented Generation fails to provide fine-grained, token-level steering. Furthermore, chat-based interfaces remain dominant, whereas productive co-writing paradigms have not yet been well exploited beyond the coding domain. To this end, we introduce SteerWrite, a training-free framework designed for personalized co-writing. Our method effectively adapts the base model to specialized domains without gradient updates, with specific designs tailored to small datasets. Experiments demonstrate that SteerWrite achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse datasets, metrics, and models, significantly reducing human editing effort.

</details>


### [53] [Beyond Sequence Order: Syntax-Informed Positional Embeddings for Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06111)
*Haris Riaz,Hyungji Kim,Mihai Surdeanu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SiPE introduces syntax-informed positional embeddings that inject dependency parse priors into Transformer positional embeddings across all three PE families (absolute, relative, rotary), improving both syntactic generalization (SyntaxGym +10.3%) and real-world language understanding (GLUE +8.2%) while reducing perplexity (-9.0%), unlike prior syntax-injection methods that typically degrade perplexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard positional embeddings encode token distance/order but ignore syntactic structure. Existing syntax-injection methods either marginalize over many parses at inference (high cost) or discard syntax at runtime, and most degrade perplexity. The authors aim to inject syntactic priors efficiently into positional embeddings without modifying self-attention or architecture, establishing a better trade-off between syntactic supervision and inference cost.

Method: SiPE learns a lightweight syntactic prior from dependency parses during pretraining and injects it into absolute, relative, and rotary positional embeddings for both encoders and decoders. The injection strategy is architecture-dependent: for autoregressive decoders with relative PE, the prior is multiplicatively coupled with the relative-position attention term; for encoders, it is added directly to input embeddings. Only a single parse is used at inference time, avoiding multi-parse marginalization.

Result: SiPE improves SyntaxGym benchmark scores by up to 10.3%, reduces perplexity by 9.0% over a base model without syntactic supervision, and raises GLUE benchmark scores by up to 8.2%. Unlike nearly all prior syntax-injection methods, SiPE does not degrade perplexity.

Conclusion: SiPE establishes a new Pareto frontier between syntactic supervision and inference cost by conditioning on a single parse rather than marginalizing over many. It demonstrates that syntax-informed positional embeddings can simultaneously improve syntactic generalization and real-world language understanding without architectural modifications or inference overhead.

Abstract: Positional embeddings (PE) in Transformers encode token distance and order but are largely agnostic to \textit{syntactic structure}. We introduce \textbf{S}yntax-\textbf{i}nformed \textbf{P}ositional \textbf{E}mbeddings (\textbf{SiPE}), which learns a lightweight syntactic prior from dependency parses during pretraining and injects it across all three dominant PE families (absolute, relative, rotary), for both encoders and decoders, leaving self-attention and the rest of the architecture untouched. We isolate \emph{where} and \emph{how} the prior should enter the model, and find it depends on the architecture: for autoregressive decoders that use relative PE, the prior is strongest when coupled multiplicatively with the relative-position term of the attention score, outperforming injection into the input embeddings, into self-attention, or into the positional and attention terms jointly---while for encoders it is best added directly to the input embeddings, composing with each encoder's native positional mechanism. We find that models pre-trained with SiPE improve on the SyntaxGym benchmark by up to $10.3\%$ while simultaneously reducing perplexity by $9.0\%$ over a base model with no syntactic supervision---a metric nearly every existing syntax-injection method instead degrades. Crucially, these gains extend beyond syntactic generalization: SiPE also improves real-world language understanding, raising scores on the GLUE benchmark by up to $8.2\%$ over a model trained without it. Unlike existing syntactic language models that marginalize over many parses at inference or discard syntax at runtime, SiPE conditions on a single parse, establishing a new Pareto frontier between syntactic supervision and inference cost.

</details>


### [54] [Routing Is Least Learnable Where It Is Most Valuable: Bounds on Representation Routing for Web Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06171)
*Jiaming Wei,Zekun Wu,Adriano Koshiyama,Maria Perez-Ortiz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether dynamically choosing a web agent's observation mode (text, pixels, or both) per task yields benefits over a fixed mode. Across 48 site-model combinations, modes are found complementary, but run-to-run noise (12-14% outcome variation) erodes apparent gains. Cost-bound analysis shows 9.5-30.6% savings by routing only unsolved tasks to the cheapest mode. However, five routing policies fail to robustly beat a single well-chosen mode, with the core obstruction being that routing supervision is produced at the agent's success rate — weaker agents yield fewer labels precisely where routing would help most.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Web agents typically use a fixed observation modality (text, pixels, or both) across all tasks. The authors question whether this one-size-fits-all choice leaves performance on the table and investigate what gains per-task mode selection could offer, both in success rate and cost efficiency.

Method: The authors evaluate six observation modes across eight site-model combinations on VisualWebArena and WebArena. They measure: (1) mode complementarity and structural failure differences, (2) run-to-run noise by rerunning identical mode-task pairs, (3) oracle routing gains after accounting for noise, (4) cost bounds by routing only unsolved tasks to the cheapest mode, and (5) five practical routing policies (task-text rule, confidence cascade, pooled cost tiers, etc.) against a fixed-mode baseline.

Result: Modes are complementary with structurally different failures. Apparent oracle gains are inflated by 12-14% run-to-run outcome variation; a second run of the same mode matches the gain of adding a new one. Cost-bound routing yields 9.5-30.6% savings across all cells at unchanged success. None of the five routing policies robustly beats a well-chosen fixed mode. The central finding: routing supervision correlates 0.95 with agent strength, so weaker agents — where routing is most needed — produce the fewest training labels.

Conclusion: The failure of dynamic mode routing is not inherent to routing but to today's agents: label scarcity and routing opportunity rise together. Stronger future agents could overturn this result. The paper provides rerun noise bands and a full measurement protocol to guide future work.

Abstract: Web agents observe a browser through text, pixels, or both, and the choice is usually fixed once for all tasks. We measure six observation modes across eight site-model combinations (cells) on VisualWebArena and WebArena and ask what choosing per task would buy. The modes are complementary: each solves tasks the others miss, they fail in structurally different ways, and the best choice reverses between task sets. The obvious prize, an oracle that picks a winning mode for every task, looks large but is inflated by run-to-run noise: rerunning the same mode on the same tasks changes 12-14% of outcomes, so a second run of a mode already in hand gains about as much as adding a new one. What survives is a cost bound: sending only the tasks no mode solves to the cheapest mode cuts cost by 9.5-30.6% in 8 of 8 cells at unchanged success. We then test five routing policies (picking the mode, deciding when to spend on the strong mode, a zero-cost rule read off the task text, a confidence cascade, and pooled cost tiers), and none robustly beats simply fixing one well-chosen mode; the one exception is a fragile result in our sparsest cell. The central obstruction is that routing supervision is produced at the agent's success rate: the weaker the agent, the fewer labels a router gets, exactly where routing would be most valuable. This limit belongs to today's agents rather than to routing itself. Label supply and routing opportunity rise together (correlation 0.95 across cells), so a stronger agent can overturn the result, and we report the rerun noise bands and the full measurement protocol.

</details>


### [55] [NeSy-RAG: Neuro-Symbolic RAG for Explainable Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06292)
*Jonas Gann,Michael Gertz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: NeSy-RAG combines retrieval-augmented generation with neuro-symbolic reasoning by converting retrieved text into executable Prolog modules, enabling transparent, attributable reasoning with automatic detection of missing user context. It achieves 61.1% accuracy on ShARC, significantly outperforming a standard RAG baseline (42.8%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RAG systems suffer from three key limitations: (1) intermediate reasoning steps are opaque and difficult to verify, (2) reasoning cannot be reliably attributed to specific evidence sources, and (3) missing user-specific context is rarely detected systematically, leading to incomplete or incorrect answers. The authors aim to address all three issues simultaneously.

Method: NeSy-RAG is a modular neuro-symbolic framework that works as follows: (1) For each retrieved text chunk, the system generates Prolog modules containing semantically meaningful predicates encoding Boolean claims, which may be conditioned on user facts. (2) Predicates are retrieved using joint natural language–code embeddings and composed into Prolog queries. (3) A symbolic knowledge-gap detection mechanism identifies missing user facts whose truth values affect the query outcome and triggers follow-up interactions to solicit them. (4) Executing the Prolog queries yields deterministic answers with transparent execution traces linking each reasoning step to its source chunk.

Result: On the ShARC benchmark, without any domain-specific training, NeSy-RAG achieves 61.1% accuracy, compared to 42.8% for a same-model RAG baseline — a substantial improvement of over 18 percentage points.

Conclusion: The neuro-symbolic approach of synthesizing attributable, executable Prolog modules from retrieved text offers a promising direction for making RAG systems more transparent, verifiable, and context-aware, particularly in settings requiring multi-step reasoning with incomplete user information.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves question answering by grounding large language models (LLMs) in external knowledge such as text corpora. However, its reasoning process remains largely opaque: intermediate reasoning steps are difficult to verify and cannot be reliably attributed to specific evidence. Moreover, missing user-specific context is rarely detected systematically, often leading to incomplete or incorrect output.
  We propose NeSy-RAG, a modular neuro-symbolic RAG framework that synthesizes attributable Prolog modules from retrieved text chunks. For each chunk, the system generates semantically meaningful predicates that encode Boolean claims, which may depend on user facts. Using joint natural language-code embeddings, predicates are retrieved and composed into Prolog queries. To address incomplete user context, we introduce a symbolic knowledge-gap detection mechanism that identifies missing user facts whose truth values affect the query outcome and automatically triggers follow-up interactions.
  Executing the resulting Prolog queries yields deterministic answers together with transparent execution traces that link each reasoning step to its originating source. On the ShARC benchmark, without domain-specific training, NeSy-RAG achieves 61.1% accuracy, outperforming a same-model RAG baseline that achieves 42.8% accuracy.

</details>


### [56] [Benchmarking and Enhancing LLMs for Rule-Intensive Review of National Standard Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06312)
*Tao Wang,Qihao Yang,Rongjiao Liang,Lianghong Lin,Haitao Wang,Xinyu Cao,Tianyong Hao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GB/T-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on rule-intensive review of Chinese national standard documents, featuring 7,306 traceable error instances across 25 error types. Experiments with 14 LLMs reveal a large human-AI gap (0.3280 vs 0.6640 CMCS), partially bridged by the proposed GB/T-Reviewer multi-agent framework (0.5094).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for professional tasks, but their ability to perform intrinsic quality review of rule-intensive, highly structured documents (like national standards) remains underevaluated. Existing benchmarks focus on domain QA rather than document review, and human expert review is costly and unscalable.

Method: The authors introduce (1) GB/T-Bench, built on Chinese GB/T standards, with a hierarchical taxonomy of 25 error types across five dimensions; (2) a controllable counterexample generation mechanism using deterministic rules and constrained LLM rewriting to produce 7,306 labeled error instances from 488 documents; (3) a diagnosis-oriented evaluation protocol requiring exact matches on error location, dimension, and type; and (4) GB/T-Reviewer, a multi-agent framework that decomposes review into global inspection, targeted diagnosis, rule scanning, and result verification.

Result: The strongest standalone LLM achieves only 0.3280 CMCS versus 0.6640 for human experts, revealing a substantial gap. GB/T-Reviewer boosts the best CMCS to 0.5094, demonstrating that structured multi-agent coordination significantly improves performance on rule-intensive document review.

Conclusion: Rule-intensive document review remains a major challenge for LLMs, but structured skill coordination via multi-agent architectures offers a promising path forward. The work lays groundwork for trustworthy AI applications in standardization and other high-stakes document domains.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support complex professional tasks, yet their capabilities in rule-intensive document review remain insufficiently evaluated. National standard documents, such as China GB/T standards, offer a representative testbed: they are lengthy, highly structured, and governed by explicit rules for scope, terminology, normative wording, and cross-section consistency. Existing benchmarks focus on domain knowledge and question answering, largely overlooking intrinsic quality review for professional documents. Such reviews rely heavily on human experts, making them costly and difficult to scale. To bridge this gap, we introduce GB/T-Bench, the first benchmark for the structured review of national standard documents. Its GB/T Review Taxonomy is a hierarchical schema covering document structure, scope alignment, normative modality, terminology consistency, and normative references, with 25 diagnosable error types. A controllable counterexample generation mechanism combines deterministic rules and constrained LLM rewriting to process 488 documents into 7,306 traceable review error instances for evaluation. We also develop a diagnosis-oriented evaluation protocol requiring exact matches on error location, review dimension, and error type, plus document-level coverage metrics. We further propose GB/T-Reviewer, a multi-agent framework that converts review knowledge into specialized skills and coordinates global inspection, targeted diagnosis, rule scanning, and result verification. Experiments with 14 mainstream LLMs reveal a substantial human-LLM gap: the strongest model achieves only 0.3280 CMCS versus 0.6640 for experts. GB/T-Reviewer raises the best CMCS to 0.5094, showing the value of structured skill coordination for rule-intensive document review. This work paves the way for trustworthy AI in standardization and other high-stakes document domains.

</details>


### [57] [Benchmarking the Benchmarks: Evaluating Benchmarks for Conversational Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06329)
*Noam Koren,Roy Bar-Haim,Abigail Goldsteen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a reference-free framework using LLM judges to automatically evaluate the quality of conversational-agent benchmarks along three axes—consistency, complexity, and policy coverage—and validates it against human annotations and controlled perturbations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmarks for task-oriented conversational agents are rarely assessed for quality, yet poor benchmarks (inconsistent tasks, simplistic scenarios, limited policy coverage) produce unreliable evaluations. No existing framework systematically diagnoses benchmark weaknesses without requiring gold references.

Method: A reference-free evaluation framework employing LLM judges to score benchmarks on three metrics: consistency (logical coherence across dialogue turns), complexity (richness of scenarios and interaction patterns), and policy coverage (breadth of agent behaviors tested). The framework also provides actionable diagnostics. Validation includes agreement with human annotations, testing across LLMs of varying capabilities, and controlled quality-degrading perturbations.

Result: The proposed metrics consistently distinguish between benchmark quality levels across different domains and judge models. The framework achieves agreement with independent human annotations and effectively identifies quality degradation under controlled perturbations. It also proves applicable to both synthetically generated and manually curated benchmarks.

Conclusion: The framework offers a practical, scalable approach for evaluating the quality of both synthetic and manually curated conversational-agent benchmarks, enabling more reliable downstream agent evaluations.

Abstract: Task-oriented conversational agents are evaluated using curated or automatically generated benchmarks, yet benchmark quality is rarely assessed. Poor benchmarks may contain inconsistent tasks, simplistic scenarios, or limited policy coverage, leading to unreliable evaluations. We introduce a reference-free framework that uses LLM judges to assess benchmark consistency, complexity, and policy coverage, while providing actionable diagnostics of weaknesses. We validate the framework by demonstrating agreement with independent human annotations and by evaluating benchmarks generated by LLMs of varying capabilities, as well as benchmarks subjected to controlled quality-degrading perturbations. Across domains and judge models, the proposed metrics consistently distinguish between benchmark quality levels. We further demonstrate the framework's applicability to manually curated benchmarks. Our framework offers a practical approach for evaluating synthetic and manually curated conversational-agent benchmarks.

</details>


### [58] [RP-OPSD: Reasoning-Pivot-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation for Multilingual Reasoning Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06347)
*Xinye Wang,Junxiao Liu,Shujian Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RP-OPSD improves multilingual reasoning transfer in LLMs by concentrating privileged distillation on "reasoning pivots" — critical decision tokens that advance or redirect reasoning — identified via distributional shift between teacher views with and without an English reference solution. It outperforms baselines across 17 languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) methods for multilingual reasoning transfer provide dense token-level supervision but fail to explicitly prioritize the most critical reasoning signals for cross-lingual transfer. The authors characterize target-language reasoning as comprising both surface text generation and "reasoning pivots" (decisions advancing or redirecting reasoning), motivating distillation that concentrates on these pivots.

Method: RP-OPSD (Reasoning-Pivot-guided On-Policy Self-Distillation) uses the distributional shift between matched teacher views — one with and one without an English reference solution — as an operational proxy to identify reasoning pivots. This proxy guides where to concentrate privileged distillation and reference anchoring during training.

Result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks spanning 17 languages and multiple difficulty levels show RP-OPSD outperforms strong multilingual reasoning baselines and existing OPSD variants. Analysis shows the method concentrates privileged distillation on reasoning-control and problem-conditioned state-update tokens while downweighting surface-realization tokens.

Conclusion: RP-OPSD effectively enhances multilingual reasoning transfer by explicitly targeting reasoning pivots through a principled distributional-shift proxy, yielding superior cross-lingual performance and providing interpretable insight into which token types matter most for reasoning transfer.

Abstract: Multilingual reasoning transfer is crucial for extending reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) beyond high-resource languages. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) and its variants have emerged as a promising paradigm, providing dense token-level supervision on student-generated rollouts, yet their objectives do not explicitly prioritize reasoning signals most critical to cross-lingual transfer. We characterize that target-language reasoning comprises the generation of both surface text and reasoning pivots, which are decisions that advance or redirect the reasoning process and shape subsequent inference. This motivates concentrating privileged distillation around such pivots. We therefore propose RP-OPSD, Reasoning-Pivot-guided On-Policy Self-Distillation, using the distributional shift between matched teacher views with and without an English reference solution as an operational proxy to guide privileged distillation and reference anchoring. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks covering 17 languages and multiple difficulty levels show that our method outperforms strong multilingual reasoning baselines and OPSD variants. Further analysis reveals that RP-OPSD concentrates privileged distillation on reasoning-control and problem-condistioned state-update tokens, while downweighting it for tokens that mainly support surface realization. Our code is available at https://github.com/NJUNLP/RP-OPSD.

</details>


### [59] [The Bitter Lesson of Tool Calling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06370)
*Ishan Patel,Sahil Sen,Elias Lumer,Vamse Kumar Subbiah*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper empirically compares programmatic tool calling (PTC), where tools are invoked via typed Python stubs in code, against native JSON tool calling across 14 language models on the BFCL v4 benchmark. PTC matches or outperforms JSON calling in 11/14 models overall and 13/14 under parallel fan-out, with notable gains (e.g., 10.6% for GPT-5.6) and greater robustness under context rot.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While code-capable LLMs can use programmatic tool calling to chain and parallelize tool invocations more naturally than rigid JSON calls, no systematic evaluation of PTC against JSON tool calling exists on an established benchmark across model generations under realistic task conditions.

Method: The authors evaluate 14 language models on the BFCL v4 benchmark, comparing two paradigms: (1) native JSON tool calling, where tools are called via structured JSON; and (2) programmatic tool calling (PTC), where tools are exposed as typed Python stubs that models invoke through code, with execution and results completed in a single agent turn. They assess performance overall, under parallel fan-out scenarios, and under context rot conditions.

Result: PTC matched or exceeded JSON tool calling in 11 of 14 models overall, with GPT-5.6 achieving a 10.6% improvement. Under parallel fan-out, PTC matched or outperformed in 13 of 14 models. Under context rot, the JSON baseline degraded by 2.3% on average while PTC remained stable.

Conclusion: Programmatic tool calling is a viable, robust alternative to JSON tool calling, with performance that tracks model capability across release generations and provides particular advantages in parallel execution and resilience to context degradation.

Abstract: Tool use transforms LLMs into agents that act beyond their training data, and for code-capable models, programmatic tool calling extends this further by replacing rigid JSON calls with scripts that chain and parallelize naturally. However, a systematic evaluation of tools as code on an established benchmark across current and prior model generations under real-world task conditions has not been conducted. In this work, we empirically compare programmatic tool calling (PTC) to native JSON tool calling across 14 language models on BFCL v4. In the programmatic tool calling paradigm, tools are exposed as typed Python stubs that the model invokes through code, with execution and results handled in a single agent turn. Programmatic tool calling matches or exceeds native JSON tool calling in 11 of 14 models on BFCL v4, with the GPT-5.6 family achieving a 10.6% improvement over the JSON tool calling baseline. Further, it matches or outperforms baseline in 13 of 14 models under parallel fan-out, and holds stable under context rot conditions where baseline degrades 2.3% on average. Our results demonstrate that programmatic tool calling is a viable and robust alternative to JSON tool calling, with performance tracking model capability across release generations.

</details>


### [60] [Learning When to Trust via Selective Context Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06377)
*Xian Sun,Wei Chow,Yingshuo Wang,Junhao Liu,Wei Gao,Qing Wu,Lingdong Kong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MIST is a benchmark for evaluating selective trust in language models across four matched context conditions. The authors propose SCOPE, a DPO-based training method that reduces susceptibility to misleading signals while preserving the ability to use trustworthy context, arguing models should be judged on selective trust rather than blind resistance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models that condition on external signals are vulnerable to misleading context flipping correct answers. Training models to simply resist all context makes them robust but useless when context is trustworthy. The key insight is reframing robustness as "selective trust" — models should distinguish between trustworthy and misleading signals rather than ignoring all context uniformly.

Method: Two main contributions: (1) MIST, a human-annotated benchmark with reasoning items rendered under four matched conditions: clean (no context), misleading (incorrect hint), correct-context, and irrelevant-context. Evaluation uses SC2W, a paired metric measuring how often misleading signals flip clean-correct answers. (2) SCOPE, a training method that mines clean-correct/misleading-wrong failure pairs and applies Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) over preference pairs balanced equally across all four conditions, rather than focusing solely on misleading items.

Result: Susceptibility to misleading signals is universal across tested models. SCOPE substantially reduces SC2W on popular open-source models while preserving accuracy when context is clean, correct, or irrelevant.

Conclusion: Models should be evaluated on selective trust — the ability to appropriately use or disregard context — rather than on resistance to misleading signals alone. SCOPE demonstrates that balanced DPO training across diverse context conditions effectively improves this capability.

Abstract: Language models increasingly condition their answers on external signals, and a single misleading one can turn a correct answer wrong. The obvious remedy, training models to resist such signals, hides a failure mode: a model that ignores all context looks robust yet is useless when the context is worth trusting. We recast the problem as selective trust and introduce MIST, a human-annotated benchmark that renders each reasoning item under four matched conditions (clean, misleading, correct-context, and irrelevant-context), together with SC2W, a paired metric counting how often a misleading signal flips a clean-correct answer to wrong. Across a comprehensive benchmark study, we observe that such a susceptibility is universal. We then propose SCOPE, which mines clean-correct/misleading-wrong failures and optimizes a standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objective over matched preference pairs balanced equally across all four conditions, rather than over misleading items alone. Our approach substantially reduces SC2W on popular open-sourced models while preserving accuracy when the added context is clean, correct, or irrelevant. With this work, we argue that models should be judged on selective trust, not on resistance alone.

</details>

### [61] [Agentic Nesting: A New Methodology for Existing Enterprise Application Integration and Services](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05159)
*Xi Wang,Kun Li,Xianyao Ling,Gang Yin,Liang Zhang,Jiang Wu,Wenbo Lei,Jun Xu,Annie Wang,Fu Zhang,Weizhe Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes "Agentic Nesting," a multi-agent framework that encapsulates legacy enterprise applications as autonomous AI agents organized in hierarchical stewardship topologies, enabling natural-language interaction and cross-application orchestration through a central orchestrator with a unified conversational interface.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprises suffer from severe data silos and process fragmentation due to heterogeneous business systems. Existing integration approaches (ESB, API gateways, RPA) suffer from high architectural coupling, rising O&M costs, and limited intelligence, making it difficult to effectively leverage and orchestrate already-built applications.

Method: The Agentic Nesting framework encapsulates each legacy application as an autonomous AI agent within a hierarchically nested, layered stewardship topology. A digital agent proxy is extracted from each application to enable natural-language interaction and autonomous manipulation. A central orchestrator handles task decomposition and dynamic dispatching across agents, exposing a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process orchestration.

Result: The paper contributes two novel paradigms: "Application-as-Agent" (encapsulating apps as AI agents) and "Conversation-as-Integration" (using natural language as the integration medium). It also demonstrates generalization potential for heterogeneous system coordination and large-scale data application scenarios.

Conclusion: Agentic Nesting offers a more intelligent, loosely-coupled alternative to traditional enterprise application integration by re-conceptualizing applications as conversational AI agents organized in nested hierarchies, with promising applicability across heterogeneous system coordination and large-scale data contexts.

Abstract: Enterprise operations extensively rely on multiple heterogeneous business systems and information applications, which also result in severe data silos and process fragmentation. Enterprises have invested considerable financial and material resources in building these applications, however, effectively leveraging and orchestrating them remains a formidable challenge. Conventional approaches to enterprise application integration, encompassing middleware architectures such as Enterprise Service Bus (ESB), API gateway infrastructures, and Robotic Process Automation (RPA), suffer from inherent limitations like high architectural coupling, escalating operation and maintenance costs, and limited intelligence capabilities. This paper proposes Agentic Nesting, a multi-agent collaboration framework in which existing enterprise applications are encapsulated as autonomous AI agents within a hierarchically nested structure. Rather than flat interconnection, agents are organized into layered stewardship topologies that mirror the compositional complexity of enterprise ecosystems. The framework extracts a digital agent proxy from each legacy application to enable natural-language interaction and autonomous manipulation, coordinates multiple agents through a central orchestrator for task decomposition and dynamic dispatching, and exposes a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process orchestration. The main contributions of this paper are the proposition of the "Application-as-Agent" integration paradigm and the "Conversation-as-Integration" interaction philosophy, together with an exploration of the generalization potential of this methodology in scenarios encompassing heterogeneous system coordination, and large-scale data applications.

</details>


### [62] [The Ignition Index: Measuring Global Workspace Dynamics in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05160)
*Saman Rahbar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces the Ignition Index (I), a scalar metric derived from sigmoid-fitting to per-layer probe accuracy curves, which quantitatively captures Global Workspace Theory's all-or-none ignition dynamics in transformer LMs. The metric shows 9.6-fold selectivity for linguistic structure over spurious correlations, reveals architecture-dependent ignition patterns (feedforward > SSM, recurrent models ignite along recurrence axis), and detects a phase transition in Pythia-410M at training step 256.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global Workspace Theory (GWT) predicts all-or-none "ignition" dynamics during conscious information processing, but no validated quantitative metric exists to operationalize this prediction in artificial neural networks. The authors aim to bridge GWT's theoretical predictions with mechanistic interpretability by providing an empirically validated, architecture-discriminative scalar metric.

Method: The Ignition Index fits a four-parameter sigmoid function to per-layer linear probe accuracy curves as a function of input signal strength. The steepness parameter β̂ is extracted: high β̂ indicates abrupt ignition-like transitions; low β̂ indicates graded build-up. The metric is validated across 11 models from 5 architecture families, with shuffled-label controls to establish 9.6-fold selectivity for genuine linguistic structure (Mann-Whitney U-test, p < 0.001). PELT changepoint detection is used to identify phase transitions during training.

Result: Key findings: (1) Feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89% in aggregate β̂ (p < 1e-13, Cohen's d = 0.52); Mamba shows near-linear profiles consistent with absent global broadcast. (2) Huginn-3.5B exhibits 2.12× higher ignition along its iteration axis vs. depth axis, showing recurrent architectures manifest workspace-like transitions along recurrence. (3) Pythia-410M shows a PELT-detected phase transition at training step 256 (+67%), preceding induction-head formation. (4) Hypotheses linking ignition to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed, suggesting saturation of ignition mechanisms in transformers.

Conclusion: The Ignition Index is the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability, offering 9.6-fold measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability not previously characterized. The findings have implications for understanding how different architectures implement (or fail to implement) global workspace-like information integration.

Abstract: We introduce the Ignition Index (I), a validated scalar metric that operationalizes Global Workspace Theory's (GWT) all-or-none ignition prediction in transformer language models. The metric fits a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength, extracting steepness parameter beta-hat: high values indicate abrupt, ignition-like transitions; low values indicate graded build-up. Across 11 models spanning five architecture families, shuffled-label controls demonstrate 9.6-fold selectivity for genuine linguistic structure over spurious probe capacity (p < 0.001, Mann-Whitney U-test). We find: (1) Feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89% in aggregate beta-hat (p < 1e-13, Cohen's d = 0.52), with Mamba exhibiting near-linear profiles consistent with absent global broadcast. (2) Huginn-3.5B exhibits 2.12-fold higher ignition along its iteration axis than its depth axis, demonstrating that recurrent architectures manifest workspace-like transitions along the recurrence dimension. (3) Pythia-410M shows a PELT-detected phase transition at training step 256 (+67%), preceding induction-head formation. (4) Hypotheses linking ignition to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed, suggesting transformer architectures may saturate available ignition mechanisms. The Ignition Index provides the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability, with 9.6-fold measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability not previously characterized in the scaling literature. Code: https://github.com/saman-rahbar/ignition-index

</details>


### [63] [Woodpecker Distillation: Weak Models Diagnose Reasoning Bugs in Strong Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05168)
*Dayu Wang,Jiaye Yang,Weikang Li,Jiahui Liang,Yang Li,Deguo Xia,Jizhou Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs fail reasoning tasks due to localized intermediate-step bugs rather than global incompetence. Weak-model patches can repair these bugs, but direct imitation fails to internalize the correction. Woodpecker Distillation instead uses contrastive local interventions to construct a corrective teacher distribution from successful vs. unsuccessful patches and distills this into the strong model, outperforming direct imitation baselines on math reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models often fail at reasoning tasks not because of global incompetence, but due to localized reasoning bugs in intermediate steps. While weak probe models can generate patches that redirect reasoning toward correct solutions, this corrective effect cannot be reliably internalized through direct fine-tuning on those patches or repaired trajectories. The core insight is that the useful signal lies in how the intervention reshapes the model's future reasoning distribution, not in the intervention text itself.

Method: The authors propose Woodpecker Distillation, a weak-to-strong training framework that leverages contrastive local interventions. At a given reasoning prefix, a weak probe model generates both successful and unsuccessful patches. The method contrasts these two outcomes, constructing a corrective teacher distribution derived from the induced future token predictions of the successful patch relative to the unsuccessful one. This distributional signal is then distilled into the strong model, teaching it to internally produce reasoning trajectories that align with the corrected distribution without requiring explicit patch insertion at inference time.

Result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance and outperforms direct imitation baselines, confirming that the contrastive distributional signal is more effective than simply imitating the text of successful patches or repaired trajectories.

Conclusion: Localized intermediate-step bugs are a key failure mode in LLM reasoning, and they are repairable via weak-model interventions. However, internalizing this repair requires more than behavioral cloning — it requires learning from the distributional shift induced by corrective patches. Woodpecker Distillation provides an effective weak-to-strong training approach that captures this signal through contrastive distillation, yielding reliable reasoning improvements.

Abstract: Large language models often fail on reasoning tasks despite possessing the capability to solve them. We argue that many such failures arise from localized reasoning bugs in intermediate steps rather than from global incompetence. We show that these bugs are frequently repairable: inserting a short patch generated by a weak probe model after the same strong-model reasoning prefix can redirect the trajectory toward a correct solution.
  However, this corrective effect is not reliably internalized by directly fine-tuning on weak patches or repaired trajectories, suggesting that the useful signal lies not in the intervention text itself, but in how it reshapes the model's future reasoning distribution. We therefore propose Woodpecker Distillation, a weak-to-strong training framework that learns from contrastive local interventions. Our method contrasts successful and unsuccessful weak-model patches at the same prefix, constructs a corrective teacher distribution from their induced future token predictions, and distills this signal into the strong model.
  Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance and outperforms direct imitation baselines.

</details>


### [64] [From Continuous Predictors to Clinical Thresholds: Early Evidence on Performance Trade-offs of Guideline-Based Categorisation for Ischaemic Stroke Outcome Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05203)
*Esra Zihni,Katryna Cisek,Hamzah Ziadeh,Hendrik Knoche,Robert Mikulik,John D. Kelleher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Clinician-aligned categorical encodings of continuous predictors, based on stroke guidelines, yield statistically comparable predictive performance to continuous models in two of three treatment cohorts, with preserved global feature importance rankings, making guideline-based discretisation a viable design choice for stroke outcome prediction models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite strong predictive accuracy of ML models for 90-day stroke outcomes, clinical adoption is hindered because model explanations (e.g., continuous predictor importance) do not align with clinicians' guideline-based, threshold-driven reasoning. A user study with clinicians motivated the exploration of whether continuous predictors can be replaced with clinically meaningful categorical encodings without performance loss.

Method: Using a multi-centre European registry stratified into three treatment cohorts, the authors trained standard gradient-boosted models with continuous predictors and fully categorised gradient-boosted models using stroke guideline-aligned, treatment-specific thresholds. They compared predictive performance and global feature importance rankings between the two approaches.

Result: Fully categorised models were statistically indistinguishable from continuous models in two treatment cohorts, but showed a significant drop in accuracy in one cohort. Global feature importance rankings remained consistent across all cohorts, indicating that the core hierarchy of prognostic factors is preserved under discretisation.

Conclusion: Guideline-based categorisation is a viable design choice for stroke outcome prediction models, offering a path toward better clinical alignment without necessarily compromising predictive performance.

Abstract: Machine learning models achieve strong predictive accuracy for 90-day outcome prediction in acute ischaemic stroke, yet clinical adoption is limited by the misalignment of model explanations with clinicians' reasoning. Motivated by a clinician user study calling for clinical guideline-aligned cut-offs, we ask whether continuous predictors can be replaced by clinically informed categorical encodings without sacrificing performance. On a multi-centre European registry stratified into three treatment cohorts, we compare standard and fully categorised gradient-boosted models, the latter using stroke guideline-aligned, treatment-specific thresholds. The fully categorised models are statistically indistinguishable from their continuous counterparts in two of the treatment cohorts, with a significant drop in predictive accuracy in one cohort. Global feature importance rankings remain consistent, suggesting that discretising continuous predictors into guideline-based categories preserves the core hierarchy of prognostic factors across all treatment groups. Guideline-based categorisation is thus a viable design choice for stroke-outcome models.

</details>


### [65] [DoctorAgents: an agentic framework to iteratively refine AutoML pipeline for small clinical temporal data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05375)
*Ruilin Wang,Bo-Hong Wang,Elizabeth Kourbatski,Jun Bai,Hegang Chen,Ziyang Song,Gilles Boire,Marie Hudson,Yue Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DoctorAgents reformulates AutoML for small clinical data as reasoning-driven refinement using specialized LLM agents that perform targeted pipeline updates via textual gradient descent, outperforming traditional AutoML baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical ML faces challenges of scarce, heterogeneous, temporally complex data. Existing AutoML systems rely on brute-force search over predefined spaces, lacking reasoning and memory — making them inefficient and ineffective for small clinical datasets.

Method: DoctorAgents is an agentic AI framework with three specialized LLM agents (generation, validation, refinement). It reformulates AutoML from exhaustive search to reasoning-driven iterative refinement, using textual gradient descent — backpropagating natural-language feedback to perform targeted pipeline updates without brute-force search.

Result: Experiments across diverse clinical tasks demonstrate that DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines while producing more interpretable, task-specific representations.

Conclusion: Reasoning-driven refinement via LLM agents with textual gradient descent offers a more effective and interpretable alternative to brute-force AutoML for small, complex clinical data, enabling more reliable deployment of ML in high-stakes medical settings.

Abstract: Clinical machine learning (ML) has the potential to support high-stakes medical decision-making, but reliable deployment is often constrained by scarce, heterogeneous, and temporal complexity. Developing effective ML pipelines for such data remains time-consuming and error-prone, while existing automated machine learning (AutoML) systems only partially address this challenge because they largely rely on brute-force search over predefined spaces and lack explicit reasoning and memory. We therefore reformulate AutoML for small clinical data from exhaustive search to reasoning-driven refinement. We propose DoctorAgents, an agentic AI framework that autonomously constructs and optimizes end-to-end ML pipelines through specialized large language model (LLM) agents for generation, validation, and refinement. DoctorAgents backpropagates natural-language feedback through textual gradient descent to perform targeted updates without exhaustive search. Experiments across diverse clinical tasks show that DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines while producing more interpretable task-specific representations.

</details>


### [66] [SkillTrace: Multi-Trace Provenance Auditing for LLM-Agent Skill Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05204)
*Jialuo Chen,Minghe Wang,Lingqi Jiang,Jianan Ma,Xinhao Deng,Xiaohu Du,Ruixiao Lin,Yunhao Feng,Linkang Du,Jingyi Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKILLTRACE is a multi-trace provenance auditing framework for detecting reuse in LLM-agent skill marketplaces. It extracts three traces (Expression, Implementation, Operational) and uses a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) to capture structural similarities. On a benchmark of 820 reuse positives and 751 negatives, it achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898, and scales effectively to a wild audit of 36,446 skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-agent ecosystems are increasingly built on reusable skills — mixed-modality artifacts combining metadata, natural language, code, tools, and workflows. Traditional code clone detectors fail here because skill reuse evidence is distributed across textual, implementation, and operational dimensions; a detector focused on only one modality (e.g., source code) misses reuse that preserves only a different part of the skill. A provenance-aware, multi-trace auditing approach is needed.

Method: SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces at ingestion: (1) Expression Trace (authored text/metadata), (2) Implementation Trace (code/tool fragments), and (3) Operational Trace, represented as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) capturing activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure. An LLM assists only during Operational-trace extraction, performed once at ingestion. At audit time, SKILLTRACE compares cached traces deterministically, calibrates each trace against same-function strict negatives, and reports which trace(s) support a reuse decision.

Result: On SKILLTRACE-BENCH (820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors + 751 negative controls), SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898. A wild audit of 36,446 skills demonstrates that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond what repository-level baselines can provide.

Conclusion: Multi-trace provenance auditing is both necessary and effective for detecting skill reuse in LLM-agent marketplaces. By separating evidence into Expression, Implementation, and Operational traces — and limiting LLM involvement to a one-time ingestion step — SKILLTRACE provides scalable, interpretable, and high-accuracy reuse detection that outperforms single-modality and whole-package approaches.

Abstract: LLM-agent ecosystems are rapidly growing around reusable skills: mixed-modality packages of metadata, natural-language instructions, code, tools, references, and operational workflows. As skills become marketplace artifacts, auditing their reuse is no longer the same problem as ordinary code clone detection. Existing detectors target single-modality source code or whole-package similarity, yet skill reuse evidence is distributed across authored text, implementation fragments, and operational structure. As a result, they can miss reuse that preserves only one part of a skill. We present SKILLTRACE, a multi-trace provenance auditing framework for LLM-agent skill reuse. SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces: Expression, Implementation, and Operational. It represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) that captures activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure. An LLM assists only the Operational-trace extraction, once at ingestion; at audit time SKILLTRACE compares cached traces deterministically, calibrates each trace against same-function strict negatives, and reports which trace supports a reuse decision. On SKILLTRACE-BENCH, with 820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors and 751 negative controls, SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898. A 36,446-skill wild audit further shows that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.

</details>


### [67] [Adaptive Arena-based Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts for Open-Ended Care Plan Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05391)
*Truong Thanh Hung Nguyen,Hoang-Loc Cao,Phuc Ho,Phuc Truong Loc Nguyen,René Richard,Hung Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CANOE is a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework for care plan coordination that uses argumentative computation (A-QBAF) with role-specialized agents, human-in-the-loop contestation, and deterministic recomputation. Medically fine-tuned models achieve the best clinical safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure provides faithful explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Monolithic LLM pipelines cannot perform care plan coordination in a transparent or safe manner, as the task demands synthesizing heterogeneous clinical, functional, and psychosocial information across multiple professional disciplines.

Method: CANOE comprises five modules: (1) complexity assessment, (2) adaptive team recruitment, (3) role-based argumentative computation using an Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), where agents generate supporting/attacking arguments resolved via arena-based clash resolution with acceptability score propagation, (4) human-in-the-loop contestation allowing care planners to accept, reject, edit, or add arguments, and (5) care-plan synthesis with deterministic recomputation.

Result: Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG using ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge showed that medically fine-tuned models achieve the strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure provides faithful explanation and human contestability.

Conclusion: CANOE successfully addresses transparency and safety limitations of monolithic LLM pipelines in care plan coordination through its neuro-symbolic, argumentation-based multi-agent architecture, with empirical evidence supporting both clinical correctness from fine-tuned models and explainability from the argumentative framework.

Abstract: Care plan coordination demands synthesizing heterogeneous clinical, functional, and psychosocial information across multiple professional disciplines, where monolithic LLM pipelines cannot perform in a transparent or safe manner. We present CANOE (Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts), a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework that addresses these limitations through five modules: complexity assessment, adaptive team recruitment, role-based argumentative computation via an Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), human-in-the-loop contestation, and care-plan synthesis. Role-specialized agents generate supporting and attacking arguments for candidate interventions; conflicts are resolved through arena-based clash resolution before acceptability scores propagate across the argumentation graph. Care planners may accept, reject, edit, or add arguments, and the framework will deterministically recompute the final plan. Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG using ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge shows that medically fine-tuned models achieve the strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure provides faithful explanation and human contestability.

</details>


### [68] [Abstract Event Causal Rules: Induction and Application](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05205)
*Ziwei Zheng,Peiqiong Chen,Bang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Abstract Event Causal Rules (AECR), a relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that generalizes concrete cause-effect pairs into reusable abstract causal logic. A multi-agent system with similarity-constrained clustering distills trustworthy AECRs from noisy data, and an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE) injects these rules into event prediction tasks, yielding consistent gains—especially for rare and unseen events.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing instance-level causal pairs for event-centric systems exhibit severe generalization deficits when encountering low-frequency, long-tail, or unseen event combinations. The authors aim to overcome this brittleness by lifting causal knowledge from concrete instance pairs to abstract, reusable causal rules at the relation level.

Method: (1) AECR formulation: a relation-level abstraction that preserves intrinsic causal relationships while generalizing beyond specific event instances. (2) CACI system: a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction framework combined with similarity-constrained clustering to distill high-quality AECRs from noisy raw causal data. Two AECR knowledge bases are constructed. (3) AR-GCAE: an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder that integrates retrieved AECRs into the Causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) benchmark via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion.

Result: Quantitative experiments on the CGEP benchmark show that AECRs substantially strengthen generalization in event causal reasoning, yielding consistent performance improvements in event prediction. The most significant gains are observed on rare and unseen event samples, directly addressing the long-tail generalization problem.

Conclusion: Abstract causal rules at the relation level provide a powerful mechanism for improving generalization in event-centric causal reasoning systems, particularly for low-frequency and unseen scenarios. The AECR paradigm, CACI distillation pipeline, and AR-GCAE integration method collectively demonstrate practical utility and robustness.

Abstract: Event-centric intelligent analytical systems heavily depend on explicit causal event knowledge for risk early warning, decision-making support and narrative comprehension. Nevertheless, existing instance-level causal pairs suffer severe generalization deficits on low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations. To address this limitation, this work proposes Abstract Event Causal Rule (AECR), a novel relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that transforms concrete cause-effect pairs into generalized abstract causal logic while retaining their intrinsic causal relationships. We design a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system coupled with similarity-constrained clustering to distill trustworthy AECRs from noisy raw causal data, based on which two complete AECR knowledge bases are built. To validate the practical utility of abstract causal knowledge, we propose an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE), which injects the retrieved AECRs into the causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) benchmark task via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion. Quantitative experimental results reveal that applying AECRs substantially strengthens the generalization capacity of event causal reasoning and brings consistent performance improvements to event prediction, with the most prominent gains observed on rare and unseen event samples.

</details>


### [69] [Otter: A Time-Aware, History-Conditioned Human Chess AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05206)
*Tarun Kumar S*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Otter is a lightweight (15.3M params) human chess move-prediction AI that models play as a time-aware, sequential process. It uses move history and clock pressure conditioning to predict human moves, achieving 55.23% top-1 accuracy, surpassing Maia 2 with fewer parameters and less data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior human chess models like Maia 2 treat each position in isolation, ignoring the sequential and temporal nature of real human play. The authors argue that human move selection depends on opening repertoire, intra-game behavioral tendencies (positional drift), and time pressure — all of which are lost in position-only modeling. They aim to capture these dynamics with a compact model.

Method: Otter uses two conditioning signals: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves to capture sequential patterns like opening preferences and behavioral drift; (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. The 15.3M-parameter model is trained on 6.1B positions from 117M Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.

Result: Otter achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, outperforming Maia 2 (the prior SOTA) with far fewer parameters and less training data. Accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900–1999 Elo bracket across 11 brackets (<1100 to ≥2000).

Conclusion: Modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches, even with a smaller model. The findings suggest that temporal and sequential context are critical for faithfully modeling human decision-making in chess. All code, models, and training logs are publicly released.

Abstract: Otter is a 15.3M-parameter human chess AI that predicts human move selection by modeling play as a time-aware, sequential process rather than treating each position in isolation. It combines two conditioning signals: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves, capturing opening preferences, positional drift, and intra-game behavioral tendencies; and (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. Otter is trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.
  Otter achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, surpassing the prior state-of-the-art human chess model, Maia 2, with far fewer parameters and less training data. Across 11 Elo brackets (<1100 to >=2000), accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 bracket. These results show that modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches, using a smaller model. Code, trained models, and complete training logs are publicly released.

</details>


### [70] [SearchAuditor: Auditing and Attributing Failures in Long-Horizon Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05212)
*Zhixiang Liang,Yifei Liu,Yidan Huang,Haozhe Zhao,Beichen Huang,Jiaqi Wang,Nan Duan,Qiong Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SearchAuditBench is a benchmark of 1,243 failed search-agent trajectories with expert annotations for error localization, root cause attribution, and repair. The proposed SearchAuditor framework uses multi-perspective auditing with evidence-grounded adjudication, achieving a 32.3% end-to-end pass rate versus 26.6% for the best baseline, and enabling better error recovery when repairs are applied.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep search agents produce fluent but incorrect answers due to small reasoning errors propagating through long, noisy trajectories. Manually diagnosing these failures is extremely difficult given the length of execution traces (averaging 73.1 messages, 65.1K tokens), creating a need for automated auditing to reduce human burden.

Method: The authors introduce two contributions: (1) SearchAuditBench, a benchmark of 1,243 failed trajectories from eight open-weight models across five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics; and (2) SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that localizes failures, attributes root causes, and proposes repairs through evidence-grounded adjudication.

Result: The strongest baseline (GPT-5.5) achieves only 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across frontier models, reaching 32.3% end-to-end pass rate. Additionally, resuming failed trajectories with SearchAuditor's repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.

Conclusion: Automated auditing of deep search agent failures remains a challenging open problem, with even the best methods achieving modest pass rates. However, the SearchAuditor framework demonstrates measurable improvements over baselines and shows practical utility in recovering failed agent runs.
