Abstract: Deep search agents tackle challenging questions through long-horizon web interactions, a process that is both complex and fragile: small reasoning errors may propagate through long, noisy trajectories into fluent but incorrect answers. Diagnosing such failures is difficult, requiring the manual inspection of extremely long execution traces, which could be beyond human capacity. We therefore introduce SearchAuditBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM auditors can localize, attribute, and repair these failures, thereby reducing the human burden. SearchAuditBench comprises 1,243 failed trajectories, averaging 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, collected from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics. We further propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that effectively localizes, attributes, and repairs search-agent failures through evidence-grounded adjudication. Experimental results show that even the strongest baseline, when powered by a frontier model like GPT-5.5, attains only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. In contrast, our SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving an end-to-end pass rate of 32.3%, and resuming failed runs with its repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.

</details>


### [71] [PD-GS: Phoneme-Driven 3DGS for Audio-Driven Talking Heads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05218)
*Ao Fu,Yi Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PD-GS augments 3D Gaussian Splatting with phoneme tokens from forced alignment to improve lip articulation, reducing "leaky mouth" artifacts while maintaining smooth audio-driven dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3DGS-based talking-head methods rely on continuous acoustic embeddings under a regression objective, which biases predictions toward averaged mouth shapes and fails to capture discrete articulatory events like bilabial closures, resulting in over-smoothed, leaky mouth artifacts. Self-supervised speech features lack explicit frame-aligned linguistic targets to disambiguate closure-level events.

Method: PD-GS introduces two key components: (1) time-aligned phoneme tokens extracted via an ASR and forced-alignment pipeline, providing explicit phonetic targets; (2) a Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM) that uses a learned gating mechanism to adaptively blend continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings, preserving smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. Training uses monocular video with image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision.

Result: On the HDTF dataset, PD-GS achieves state-of-the-art lip geometry (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, producing more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

Conclusion: Explicit phoneme-level supervision via forced alignment effectively addresses the "leaky mouth" problem in 3DGS-based talking heads, demonstrating that discrete linguistic targets complement continuous acoustic embeddings for faithful lip articulation.

Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables fast, photorealistic talking-head rendering, yet accurate lip articulation remains elusive: mouth motion is often over-smoothed and may violate hard articulatory constraints such as bilabial closures, producing the notorious ``leaky mouth'' artifact. A key difficulty is that brief, discrete articulatory events are inferred from a continuous acoustic embedding under a regression objective, which biases predictions toward averaged mouth configurations. While modern self-supervised speech encoders provide rich prosodic and phonetic cues, they do not provide an explicit, frame-aligned linguistic target that reliably disambiguates closure-level events. We propose \textbf{Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS)}, which augments a 3DGS talker with time-aligned phoneme tokens obtained from an automatic ASR and forced-alignment pipeline. Our core component, the \textbf{Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM)}, adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings through a learned gate, allowing the model to preserve smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. PD-GS is trained purely from monocular video using image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision. On HDTF, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry among the compared baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, yielding more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

</details>


### [72] [From Siloed Algorithms to Compliance-First Agentic Platforms: A Multi-Layered Architecture for Hospital AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06112)
*Manideep Dhar,Ritwik Singh,Sharat Chandra Kumar Manikonda*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with interoperable layers — agent orchestration, policy-as-code compliance, and privacy-preserving data fabric — demonstrating end-to-end triage, workflow optimization, and compliance logging on synthetic hospital data to move from siloed AI pilots to governed, ROI-focused platforms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 70–80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints, despite explosive market growth. Most deployments remain isolated point solutions in departmental silos, causing duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value.

Method: Proposes a layered Agentic AI architecture with three novel extensions: (i) Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent clinical/operational/financial workflows; (ii) Compliance and Policy Layer centralizing policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, EU AI Act, DISHA, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC standards; (iii) Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric integrating federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into HIMS flows. Validated via a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open prototype implementation.

Result: Demonstrated end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access.

Conclusion: The architecture provides hospital leaders with a pragmatic blueprint to transition from ad hoc AI tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused platform adaptable to on-premise, hybrid, and cloud-native deployments.

Abstract: Hospitals are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence for triage, imaging, scheduling etc., yet most deployments remain isolated point solutions locked inside departmental silos, resulting in duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. Despite explosive growth of AI in healthcare market and accelerating investment, an estimated 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale, largely due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. This research proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with multiple interoperable layers, extending existing hospital AI platform models with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational, and financial domains, (ii) a Compliance and Policy Layer that centralizes policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, DISHA Act, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC security and safety standards, and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric that plugs federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into real-world Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) flows. Using a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open, ready-to-deploy prototype implementation, this study demonstrates the end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access. The resulting architecture offers hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint to move from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform that can be tailored to on-premise, hybrid and cloud-native deployments.

</details>


### [73] [When Privileged Guidance Misaligns: State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05219)
*Junzhuo Liu,Weiwei Li,Jun Ling,Peng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SMRC-SD addresses state-reference mismatch in privileged on-policy distillation for multi-turn agents by matching student states to reference trajectories and applying state-conditioned distillation only at matched turns, significantly improving task success on ALFWorld and WebShop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In privileged on-policy distillation for multi-turn agents, the student's divergent actions cause its rollout to reach states not covered by the privileged reference trajectory. Applying distillation indiscriminately creates state-reference mismatch, where the reference provides unreliable guidance for the student's actual execution state.

Method: SMRC-SD operates in two stages: (1) State-Matched Routing — at each turn, it verifies whether the student's current execution state matches a supported state along a reference trajectory, applying distillation only at matched states; (2) Contextualized Self-Distillation — for matched states, it constructs state-conditioned teacher context from the successful trajectory to ground supervision in the state actually reached.

Result: With Qwen3-1.7B, SMRC-SD improves task success from 0.746 to 0.865 on ALFWorld and from 0.574 to 0.693 on WebShop. Controlled ablation studies confirm that both state-matched routing and state-compatible teacher context construction independently contribute to performance gains.

Conclusion: Explicitly managing state-reference alignment via state-matched routing and contextualized distillation is an effective strategy for privileged on-policy distillation in interactive environments, yielding substantial and consistent improvements over unconditional full-path distillation.

Abstract: Privileged on-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multi-turn agents by allowing a synchronized teacher to re-score the student's response at every turn with access to training-only references, such as successful trajectories. In interactive environments, however, the student's preceding actions continually change the execution state. As the student takes different actions or completes subgoals in a different order, its rollout may reach states not covered by the reference, making the reference an unreliable source of guidance for the state actually reached. Applying privileged distillation indiscriminately therefore creates state--reference mismatch. This mismatch motivates a central objective: providing privileged reference guidance that remains compatible with the student's current execution state. We introduce State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation (SMRC-SD), which explicitly determines when and how a privileged trajectory should guide an on-policy student. At each turn, SMRC-SD verifies whether the student's current execution state matches a supported state along the reference trajectory. Distillation is applied only at matched states, filtering out turns for which the reference lacks locally compatible guidance. For each matched state, SMRC-SD further constructs state-conditioned teacher context from the successful trajectory, grounding supervision in the state actually reached. Across ALFWorld and WebShop, SMRC-SD consistently outperforms unconditional successful full-path distillation. With Qwen3-1.7B, it improves task success from $0.746$ to $0.865$ on ALFWorld and from $0.574$ to $0.693$ on WebShop. Controlled routing and context ablations support both selecting locally supported turns and constructing state-compatible teacher context as contributors to these gains. Code is available at https://github.com/liujunzhuo/SMRC-SD.

</details>


### [74] [Small Foundation Models of Human Cognition and Behaviour](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05224)
*Nick Oh,Fernand Gobet*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Training small LMs (0.6–1B) on 10.7M human choices from 160 experiments achieves near-ceiling in-distribution performance matching 70B models, but out-of-distribution generalization reveals a steep scaling gradient favoring larger models. Diagnostic ablations show models rely on stimuli/feedback (75.7% of learned information), not mere choice-history shortcuts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether the scale of LM-based cognitive proxies is necessary for capturing human-like decision-making, and to investigate whether these models genuinely learn task structure or merely exploit statistical shortcuts like choice history.

Method: Fourteen models (135M–14B parameters, four architecture families) were fine-tuned on Psych-101 (10.7M trial-level choices, 160 experiments). Evaluation included in-distribution (held-out participants) and out-of-distribution (novel task structure) tests. Two diagnostics: (1) progressive stripping of four prompt channels (instructions, stimuli, feedback, choice history) across 27 experiments; (2) trial-order permutation to assess sensitivity to sequential structure.

Result: In-distribution performance hits a ceiling across scales; 0.6–1B matches a 70B baseline. Out-of-distribution shows a steep scaling curve, with larger models generalizing better. Masking stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information, ruling out choice-history-only exploitation. Permutation reveals invariance on independent-trial tasks but sensitivity on response-dependent sequential tasks.

Conclusion: Small cognitively fine-tuned models can serve as noise-ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, but their generalization scope is bounded by training paradigm coverage. True task-structure learning—not shortcut exploitation—underpins their behavior.

Abstract: Large language models fine-tuned on human behavioural data have emerged as general-purpose cognitive proxies, but the scale this requires, and whether these models process task structure or exploit statistical shortcuts, remain open questions. We train fourteen models from 135M to 14B parameters across four architecture families on Psych-101, a dataset of 10.7 million trial-level choices from 160 experiments. In-distribution, scale barely matters. The models fall within a narrow band, as though against a ceiling, and 0.6B to 1B parameters suffice to match a 70B baseline on held-out participants. Out-of-distribution, that band opens into a markedly steeper scaling gradient, with larger models clearly advantaged in generalisation to novel task structure. To determine what information these models use, we run two diagnostics. We progressively strip four prompt channels -- task instructions, experimental stimuli, outcome feedback, and choice history -- across 27 experiments, and permute trial order. Masking the content of stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information and pushes models below chance, demonstrating that choice history alone does not account for performance. Permutation reveals invariance on tasks with independent trials but sensitivity where trial order is determined by prior responses. Small cognitively fine-tuned models therefore show promise as noise ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, though their scope remains bounded by the paradigms seen in training.

</details>


### [75] [Project2Task: Graph-Guided Project-Level Planning for Autonomous Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05225)
*Huirui Xu,Runtao Xu,Shuo Ren,Jiajun Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Project2Task is a graph-guided planning layer that decomposes a research project brief into a structured portfolio of bounded, dependency-aware tasks. It uses innovation atoms and a directed lineage graph with a Bernoulli block-model objective to select optimal decomposition strategies (horizontal, vertical, or hybrid), then generates explicit task contracts with clear boundaries, dependencies, and execution order. On a benchmark of 10 project briefs (~30 tasks), Project2Task achieves a manuscript-based quality score of 7.15 vs. 4.58 (baseline) and boosts downstream execution accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759 when integrated with AutoResearchClaw.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing autonomous research systems treat a research project as a single oversized task or produce flat, vague, overlapping task sets without proper dependency management. Research projects are long-horizon agendas requiring multiple bounded tasks with distinct objectives, parallel alternatives, and dependency-aware sequencing — a gap that existing single-task systems fail to address.

Method: Project2Task introduces: (1) innovation atoms — candidate contributions represented as nodes in a directed lineage graph; (2) a lightweight Bernoulli block-model objective that selects among horizontal, vertical, and hybrid portfolio decompositions; (3) bounded task generation with explicit contribution ownership, overlap repair, and missing execution field filling; and (4) dependency-aware task contracts specifying objectives, inputs, expected artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order, all independent of any specific downstream executor.

Result: On a benchmark of 10 project briefs yielding ~30 tasks, Project2Task achieves an average manuscript-based portfolio quality score of 7.15, compared with 4.58 for the Brief Baseline and 5.31 for the Topic-only Setting. When its contracts are integrated with the AutoResearchClaw executor, downstream task accuracy increases from 0.536 to 0.759.

Conclusion: Explicit project-to-task planning via graph-guided decomposition and structured task contracts significantly improves the coherence, non-redundancy, and executability of research-task portfolios, demonstrating clear value over flat or underspecified task generation approaches.

Abstract: Research agents can increasingly search literature, propose hypotheses, generate code, run experiments, and draft manuscripts from a single topic. However, a research project is not merely a larger task: it is a long-horizon agenda that must be advanced through multiple bounded tasks with distinct but related objectives, parallel alternatives, and dependency-aware sequences. Existing single-task systems often treat the project as one oversized task, produce a flat set of vague or overlapping tasks, or leave task boundaries and execution order to manual coordination. We introduce Project2Task, a graph-guided project-level planning layer for autonomous research. Given a project brief, it represents candidate contributions as innovation atoms and organizes them in a directed lineage graph. A lightweight Bernoulli block-model objective selects among horizontal, vertical, and hybrid portfolio decompositions. Project2Task then generates bounded tasks with explicit contribution ownership, repairs overlaps and missing execution fields, and emits dependency-aware task contracts that specify objectives, inputs, expected artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order. The contracts are independent of any particular downstream research executor and support integration of task outputs into a coherent project-level result. On a benchmark of ten project briefs yielding roughly 30 tasks, manuscript-based portfolio evaluation gives Project2Task an average quality score of 7.15, compared with 4.58 for the Brief Baseline and 5.31 for the Topic-only Setting. Integrating its contracts with AutoResearchClaw increases average downstream task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759. These results demonstrate the value of explicit project-to-task planning for producing coherent, non-redundant, and executable research-task portfolios.

</details>


### [76] [TriQua: Reconciling Granularity and Context in Factuality Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05228)
*Jin Liu,Steffen Thoma,Achim Rettinger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TriQua introduces an adaptive factuality evaluation framework that models simple facts as triples and complex facts as hyperrelational facts with contextual qualifiers, achieving better alignment with human judgment and outperforming existing decomposition-based verification methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing "decompose-then-verify" approaches face a trade-off: atomic facts (single-information sentences) lose crucial context, while broader statements lack the granularity needed for precise factuality assessment. A more flexible fact representation is needed.

Method: TriQua models facts adaptively by complexity — simple claims are extracted as standard (subject, relation, object) triples, while complex claims become hyperrelational facts with auxiliary contextual qualifiers attached. Verification then annotates concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers, and TriQuaScore quantifies factuality of these structured units.

Result: TriQuaScore strongly correlates with human-annotated factuality scores. TriQua demonstrates robust decomposition quality and outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks on evidence-based fact verification tasks.

Conclusion: Adaptive fact representation — atomic triples for simple claims and hyperrelational facts for complex ones — effectively resolves the context-vs-granularity trade-off in LLM factuality evaluation, yielding both accurate verification and fine-grained explainability.

Abstract: The "decompose-then-verify" paradigm for LLM factuality evaluation faces a fundamental trade-off: atomic facts, i.e., one sentence conveying one unit of information, often omit essential context, while broader statements lack the granularity needed for precise assessment. To address this, we introduce TriQua, a framework that flexibly models facts based on their complexity. Simple claims are extracted as standard triples, while complex claims are represented as hyperrelational facts by attaching auxiliary contextual qualifiers. This adaptive structure preserves the necessary context for accurate retrieval and verification without sacrificing atomicity. Furthermore, TriQua's verification process directly annotates concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers, providing fine-grained explainability for error detection. Alongside the framework, we propose TriQuaScore to quantify the factuality of these structured fact units. Empirical evaluations show that TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human annotated factuality scores, TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality, and outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.

</details>


### [77] [Beyond Top-K: Replacing Black-Box Retrieval with Interpretable Agentic Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06305)
*Sagar Tamang,Ayush Vyas,Tabarakul Hazarika*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper critiques chunk-and-embed retrieval for financial documents where table rows dominate, causing figures to be separated from their units and headers. It proposes READ, an embedding-free agentic system using lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded reads, achieving 58.8% accuracy vs. 15.7% for dense retrieval on 51 verified questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RAG pipelines chunk text and use dense embeddings, but this is structurally unsound for financial documents (statements, audit reports, regulatory returns) where 86.8% of content is table rows. Chunk boundaries separate numbers from their units (e.g., lakh vs. crore — a 100x error) and from their fiscal-year headers. The authors argue this failure is measurable and systematic.

Method: The authors propose READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search), where an agent reads raw documents via three deterministic operations exposed over the Model Context Protocol: (1) normalized lexical search, (2) structural navigation (table-aware), and (3) bounded span reads. This produces a replayable audit trail rather than opaque similarity scores. A table-aware chunker ("steelman") is built as a baseline. Evaluation uses 51 verified questions on a 780-page government financial report, comparing against dense retrieval, BM25, and a top-k agent variant.

Result: READ achieves 58.8% accuracy vs. dense retrieval's 15.7% (p_Holm = 2×10⁻⁵). Against a tuned dense retriever (35.3%), READ still leads by 23.5 points (p_Holm = 0.017). A top-k-based agent reaches only 27.5%, showing the gain comes from the interface design, not iteration. The table-aware chunker fixes the unit problem but still leaves 27–30% of numeric chunks without fiscal-year headers at all chunk sizes. BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, so the result separates embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval rather than agentic from lexical search.

Conclusion: For table-heavy, numerically-dense documents, embedding-based retrieval is structurally inappropriate. Embedding-free, deterministic agentic interfaces using lexical search and structural navigation outperform dense retrieval significantly. The key performance driver is the interface design (deterministic operations vs. opaque similarity), not agentic iteration. BM25's parity with READ suggests the critical distinction is embedding-based vs. embedding-free, not agentic vs. non-agentic.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over long documents is dominated by one design: chunk the text, embed the chunks, and surface the top-k nearest neighbours of the query. We argue that for an important class of documents -- financial statements, audit reports, regulatory returns -- this design is structurally unsound, and we make the argument measurable. On a 780-page government financial report, 86.8% of content lines are table rows, thousands of near-identical figures compete in one embedding space, and a figure inherits its unit from a header a median of 13 lines above it -- so a chunk boundary routinely separates a number from whether it is in lakh or crore, an error of two orders of magnitude. A table-aware chunker built as a steelman fixes the unit problem but leaves 27-30% of numeric chunks with no fiscal-year header at every chunk size we tried. We propose READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search), in which an agent reads the raw document through three deterministic operations -- normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads -- exposed over the Model Context Protocol, so a trajectory is a replayable audit trail, not an opaque similarity score. On 51 verified questions READ answers 58.8% against dense retrieval's 15.7% (p_Holm = 2 x 10^-5) -- or 35.3% tuned, which READ still leads by 23.5 points (p_Holm = 0.017). An agent given the same loop but a top-k tool reaches only 27.5%, locating the gain in the interface rather than in iteration. We also report what the evidence does not support: BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, so our result separates embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval, not agentic from lexical search.

</details>


### [78] [Coherence-Oriented Dream Scene Visualisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05233)
*Azra Açıl,Simon Colton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DSV (Dream Scene Visualiser) converts written dream descriptions into coherent four-panel image sequences using an LLM for chronological segmentation and a text-to-image model with regeneration for quality control. Evaluated on 50 DreamBank visualisations using CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dreams are emotionally intense experiences that are inherently difficult to communicate. Bridging the gap between subjective dream narratives and visual representation can help with dream interpretation, sharing, and analysis.

Method: A pipeline: (1) an LLM splits the dream description into four chronological parts; (2) a text-to-image model generates images for each part with mechanisms to maintain visual coherence across the sequence; (3) an iterative regeneration step replaces any image that insufficiently matches the corresponding text prompt. Evaluation uses 50 dream visualisations from the DreamBank dataset.

Result: Objective evaluation via vision-language models (CLIP, DINOv2, Qwen2-VL) reports metrics on image quality, text-image fidelity, and cross-panel visual coherence.

Conclusion: The DSV system demonstrates a functional pipeline for transforming subjective dream narratives into coherent visual sequences, validated through multi-model objective assessment. The regeneration mechanism ensures fidelity, while chronological segmentation preserves narrative flow.

Abstract: Dreams can be emotionally intense but difficult to communicate. We describe the Dream Scene Visualiser (DSV) system which turns written dream descriptions into a temporal sequence of four panel images visualising the dream. This starts with a large language model prompted to split a dream description into four chronological parts. Then a text-to-image model produces images for each part with visual coherence maintained across the sequence, and DSV regenerates any image not suitably matching the text. We evaluate DSV over 50 visualisations from dream descriptions in DreamBank, and report quality, fidelity and coherence results via objective measures employing the CLIP, DINOv2 and Qwen2-VL vision-language models.

</details>


### [79] [Search2Skill: Skill Distillation Beyond Knowledge Boundaries Via Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05245)
*Muyang Ye,Tian Lan,Feihu Jiang,Yongshi Ye,Wuyunsiqin,Bin Zhu,Qianghuai Jia,Zhao Xu,Weihua Luo,Ye Wang,Jinyang Zhang,Longyue Wang,Lingfeng Bao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Search2Skill is a framework that enables LLM agents to autonomously identify capability gaps, search external sources for missing domain knowledge, and distill retrieved evidence into reusable skills, outperforming existing baselines across eight expert domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-evolving skill methods for LLM agents rely on the model's internal parametric knowledge or trajectories, limiting them to what the agent already knows. Professional domain conventions and standard procedures often fall outside this boundary and cannot be elicited from the agent alone, creating a capability gap.

Method: Search2Skill automatically detects capability gaps, searches external knowledge sources to fill those gaps, and distills retrieved evidence into structured reusable skills. The framework is optimized via a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves three components: when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills.

Result: Across eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks, Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under streaming and held-out evaluation protocols. Ablations show gains stem from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and acquired skills transfer across model scales.

Conclusion: Search2Skill demonstrates that bridging the gap between internal model knowledge and external domain expertise via structured skill distillation enables robust self-evolution of LLM agents in expert domains, with skills that are both effective and transferable.

Abstract: Reusable skills, which encapsulate the procedural knowledge required to solve real-world professional tasks, offer LLM-based agents a path toward self-evolution in expert domains. Existing self-evolving skill methods construct skills internally from the model's parametric knowledge or trajectories, and are therefore bounded by what the model already knows. However, the domain conventions and standard procedures underlying professional skills often lie beyond this boundary and are hard to elicit from the agent alone. To address this issue, we therefore propose a novel framework, Search2Skill, that automatically identifies the agent's capability gaps, searches external sources to address them, and distills the retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. Specifically, Search2Skill is optimized by a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills. Experiments on eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks show that Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under both streaming and held-out evaluation protocols. Further analyses show that the gains arise from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and that the acquired skills transfer across model scales.

</details>


### [80] [LUNAR: Benchmarking Personalized Large Language Models on UNiversal User BehAvioR Logs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05246)
*Jiahao Zhang,Yongzhi Tong,Zelin Fu,Pengde Zhao,Yanmei Jiang,Jiang Feng,Min Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LUNAR is a novel benchmark for evaluating cross-domain behavioral personalization in LLMs using synthesized longitudinal app interaction histories. It reveals that access to behavioral logs is necessary but insufficient — effective personalization hinges on evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks rely on textual personas or isolated behavioral signals, failing to evaluate cross-domain personalization grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities. There is a need for a benchmark that captures realistic, multi-domain, longitudinal behavioral patterns while addressing data sparsity and privacy concerns.

Method: The authors introduce LUNAR, a benchmark using a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns across four daily-life domains (clothing, food, housing, mobility). Fidelity analyses validate alignment with real behavioral distributions. Experiments across 19 mainstream LLMs evaluate personalization under varying context strategies (fine-grained retrieval vs. compressed memory) and analyze the privacy-personalization trade-off.

Result: Neither more context nor larger models guarantee better personalization. Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records consistently outperforms compressed memory representations. Stronger personalization correlates with reduced privacy protection. Evidence selection and cross-domain integration emerge as critical bottlenecks rather than model scale or context quantity.

Conclusion: The paper identifies evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control as three key challenges for personalized LLMs. LUNAR provides a foundational benchmark for advancing research on personalization that is both behaviorally grounded and privacy-aware.

Abstract: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks primarily rely on textual personas or isolated behavioral signals, providing limited evaluation of cross-domain behavioral personalization, where responses must be grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities. To address this gap, we introduce LUNAR, the first benchmark for evaluating how LLMs personalize responses from longitudinal app interaction histories across universal daily-life domains, including clothing, food, housing, and mobility. To support scalable benchmark construction while mitigating data sparsity and privacy concerns, LUNAR uses a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns. Fidelity analyses show closer alignment with real behavioral distributions than other synthetic benchmarks. Experiments on 19 mainstream LLMs show that access to behavioral logs is necessary but not sufficient for deep personalization: neither more context nor larger models guarantees better performance; effective personalization depends on selecting and integrating relevant evidence across domains. Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records consistently outperforms compressed memory, while stronger personalization can come at the cost of privacy protection. These findings identify evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control as key challenges for personalized LLMs.

</details>


### [81] [WorldClaw: Agentic 3D Open-World Generation at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05248)
*Chunchao Guo,Jinpeng Li,Yang Li,Zilong Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WorldClaw is an agentic, coarse-to-fine framework that generates large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from text prompts by jointly maintaining global spatial coherence, rich local content, and explicit editable assets through planning agents, terrain generation, and render-based refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches struggle to generate large-scale, open-world 3D scenes from text because they fail to simultaneously preserve global spatial coherence, produce rich local detail, and output explicit, editable assets suitable for downstream reuse. A unified framework addressing all three requirements is lacking.

Method: WorldClaw employs a fully agentic, coarse-to-fine pipeline: (1) planning agents translate a text prompt into structured specifications covering regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations; (2) a globally coherent terrain foundation is built from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative/procedural materials, and a region-aware height field; (3) for detail-demanding regions, terrain-conditioned compositions are generated, editable textured meshes are reconstructed and placed on the terrain; (4) render-based agents iteratively refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contact points.

Result: Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes demonstrating coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, consistent global terrain structure, and editable instance-level assets.

Conclusion: WorldClaw demonstrates that an agentic, coarse-to-fine framework can successfully bridge global consistency and local richness in open-world 3D scene generation, producing explicit, editable assets suitable for downstream applications.

Abstract: Generating large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from open-ended text remains challenging because a system must jointly maintain global spatial coherence, rich local content, and explicit assets suitable for downstream editing and reuse. We present WorldClaw, a fully agentic, coarse-to-fine framework for open-world 3D scene generation. Planning agents translate a text prompt into a structured specification of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations. WorldClaw then builds a globally coherent terrain foundation from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative or procedural materials, and a region-aware height field. For detail-demanding regions, it generates terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructs editable textured meshes, and recovers their placement on the terrain; render-based agents further refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts. Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets while preserving a consistent global terrain structure.

</details>


### [82] [Posture and Sustainment Optimization Under Adversarial Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05256)
*Amelie Norris,Alyssa Lee,Natan Vidra,Spurthi Setty*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the unsolved Pre-commitment posture problem in military planning by proposing CEV and RobustCEV optimizers that outperform greedy baselines, recovering up to 19.8% and 158% efficiency respectively against static and adaptive adversarial threats.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current military posture planning relies on greedy heuristics that maximize value while ignoring geographic coverage, making them vulnerable to adversaries targeting high-strategic-value locations. A formally rigorous, adversarially robust optimization approach is critically needed but remains unsolved.

Method: The Pre-commitment posture problem is modeled as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. Two optimizers are introduced: (1) the Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer, which maximizes scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency over a distribution of threat scenarios; and (2) the RobustCEV extension, which iterates against a Bayesian adversary that adaptively updates its targeting distribution based on observed placement.

Result: Experiments in an Indo-Pacific basing environment (20 assets, 5 locations) show: (1) the greedy baseline suffers a 25.1% permanent posture efficiency penalty and 57.3% scenario-weighted readiness collapse under value-correlated threat; (2) CEV recovers up to 19.8% efficiency with only 5–20 curated scenarios; (3) RobustCEV achieves up to 158% efficiency gain over a naive optimizer against an adaptive adversary with a deceptive prior. Statistical significance was validated via paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition.

Conclusion: The performance gaps are structural properties of placement strategies, not sampling artifacts. CEV and RobustCEV provide substantial robustness and efficiency improvements over greedy heuristics, demonstrating the value of scenario-weighted and adversarially adaptive optimization for joint operational posture planning.

Abstract: Pre-commitment posture, the assignment of military assets to theater locations before conflict scenarios resolve, is a critical and formally unsolved problem in joint operational planning. Current practice relies on greedy heuristics that maximize value and ignore geographic coverage and are structurally vulnerable to adversaries that target high-strategic value locations. This paper presents a scenario-weighted adversarially robust posture optimization engine for the Posture and sustainability allocation (PSA) problem, modeled as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. We introduce the Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer, which places assets by maximizing scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency over a distribution of threat scenarios, and the RobustCEV extension, which iterates against a Bayesian adversary that updates its targeting distribution in response to observed placement. Across three experiments in an Indo-Pacific basing environment with 20 assets and 5 theater locations, we demonstrate that: (1) the greedy baseline incurs a permanent 25.1% posture efficiency penalty due to geographic under-coverage and a 57.3% scenario-weighted readiness collapse under value-correlated adversarial threat; (2) the CEV optimizer recovers up to 19.8% efficiency over greedy when the threat distribution carries a geographic signal, with a curated set of 5 to 20 scenarios sufficient to capture the majority of this gain; and (3) the RobustCEV extension recovers up to 158% efficiency relative to a naive optimizer when an adaptive adversary employs a deceptive threat prior. All findings are validated using paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition, confirming that the performance gaps reported are structural properties of placement strategies rather than sampling artifacts.

</details>


### [83] [OrchestraBench: Evaluating Multi-Agent Orchestration Failure Modes, Recovery, and Decomposition Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05263)
*Yidian Chen,Yingzi Gu,Natan Vidra,Spurthi Setty,Sharon Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OrchestraBench is a failure-injection benchmark for multi-agent orchestration frameworks that measures cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery, revealing that intent-based routers dramatically outperform keyword routers on adversarial inputs, that failure-handling tiers exist across MAST modes (only tool faults recover fully), and that cascade radius grows with pipeline depth while containment gains stem from trusted-state signals rather than autonomous detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-agent orchestration benchmarks report only task accuracy without diagnosing why pipelines fail, where cascades originate, or which routing decisions cause breakdowns. This diagnostic gap prevents systematic improvement of failure-handling mechanisms in production orchestrators.

Method: A controlled, seed-reproducible failure-injection harness applied over templated enterprise workflows. Key techniques: (1) comparison of routing policies (keyword/flag vs. intent-reasoning model) with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests on 26 gold-labelled cases; (2) controlled mechanism probes using a Claude agent over a verifiable arithmetic dependency chain, testing five MAST failure modes across three model sizes (Sonnet, Opus, Haiku); (3) cascade radius measurement across pipeline depths 3–7; (4) trusted-state repair ablation to isolate the source of containment gains; (5) blind retry experiments to assess detection and attribution necessity.

Result: The keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases (misleading/missing surface flags) while the intent-reasoning model router scored 100%, matching the oracle. Failure-handling tiers across five MAST modes: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent/semantic modes never recovered (0.0). This ordering persisted across the loan-approval workflow reframing and all three model sizes. Cascade radius increased with depth (mean 0.9 at depth 3 to 4.7 at depth 7). Trusted-state repair ablation showed containment gains came primarily from the trusted-state signal, not autonomous detection. Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased time to detection.

Conclusion: Detection and attribution are necessary for effective failure containment; retry alone is insufficient. Intent-based routing is essential for adversarial robustness. The persistent failure-handling tier ordering across contexts suggests fundamental limits in current orchestrator recovery capabilities for latent and semantic faults. Results are characterized as controlled-chain mechanism probes, not general domain-workload claims.

Abstract: Multi-agent orchestration frameworks are moving from demos to production, yet benchmarks typically report task accuracy without diagnosing why a pipeline failed, where a cascade began, or which routing decision caused the breakdown. OrchestraBench evaluates failure, recovery, and decomposition through a controlled, seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows. It introduces cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery as primary metrics and compares routing policies with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. On a 26-case gold-labelled diagnostic, a keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases with misleading or missing surface flags, whereas an intent-reasoning model router scored 100%, matching the oracle. Controlled mechanism probes with a real Claude agent over a verifiable arithmetic dependency chain revealed three failure-handling tiers across five MAST modes: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent or semantic modes never recovered (0.0). This ordering persisted when the computation was reframed as a loan-approval workflow and across Sonnet, Opus, and Haiku, although absolute rates shifted with context. Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased time to detection, indicating that detection and attribution are necessary for containment. Cascade radius increased with pipeline depth (mean 0.9 to 4.7 across depths 3-7). A trusted-state repair ablation showed that apparent containment gains primarily came from the trusted-state signal rather than autonomous detection. These results are controlled-chain mechanism probes, not domain-workload claims.

</details>


### [84] [Epistemic Trustworthiness in Generative AI: A Normative Framework for Warranted Reliance in High-Stakes Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05602)
*Nimisha Karnatak,Max Van Kleek,Nigel Shadbolt*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper argues that responsible deployment of generative AI in high-stakes contexts requires a new evaluative standard: epistemically warranted reliance. The authors propose a constitutive normative framework with three necessary conditions — epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice — and demonstrate through case analyses how failures in these dimensions produce harms not captured by standard metrics like accuracy or fairness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI evaluation frameworks focus on accuracy, fairness, explainability, safety, and user trust, but none directly addresses the normative question: when are users epistemically justified in relying on AI outputs? The authors identify a gap between behavioral reliance (users acting on outputs) and epistemically warranted reliance (users being justified in treating outputs as premises in their reasoning), particularly urgent as generative AI enters high-stakes professional domains like law, medicine, and hiring.

Method: The authors draw on philosophical theories of epistemic trustworthiness — specifically competence and audience-orientation accounts — to derive a constitutive normative framework with three jointly necessary, non-fungible conditions: (1) epistemic humility (communicating limits of competence), (2) epistemic access (enabling inspection, questioning, and contestation), and (3) resistance to epistemic injustice (recognizing users as legitimate epistemic agents). They validate the framework through case analyses in legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring contexts.

Result: Case analyses reveal that failures of epistemic humility, access, and resistance to epistemic injustice produce consequential harms — such as unjustified legal decisions, eroded clinical judgment, and marginalized applicant knowledge — that standard measures of accuracy, fairness, and usability fail to capture or remediate on their own.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that GenAI design and evaluation should be reoriented around epistemically warranted reliance rather than output correctness alone, and they outline practical implications for system design, auditing, and governance that operationalize the three normative conditions.

Abstract: Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes professional contexts, where their outputs shape what users believe, how they reason, and what they treat as settled. This raises a central question for responsible AI: under what conditions is reliance on generative AI outputs epistemically warranted rather than behaviourally induced? Existing frameworks largely ask whether AI outputs are accurate, fair, explainable, safe, or trusted by users. These questions remain necessary, and each can contribute to warranted reliance. However, they do not directly specify warranted reliance as a distinct evaluative target: the conditions under which users are justified in treating AI outputs as inputs into their own reasoning. We argue that this requires an account of epistemic trustworthiness: what makes a system epistemically worthy of reliance. Drawing on philosophical accounts of trustworthiness as competence and audience-orientation, we develop a constitutive normative framework comprising three jointly necessary and non-fungible conditions. First, epistemic humility requires systems to represent and communicate the limits of their competence. Second, epistemic access requires systems to enable users to inspect, question, and contest outputs in context. Third, resistance to epistemic injustice requires systems to recognise users as legitimate epistemic agents and avoid marginalising their knowledge and experience. Through real-world case analyses in legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring, we show how failures of epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice can produce consequential harms that standard measures of accuracy, fairness, and usability do not address on their own. We conclude by outlining design and evaluation implications for GenAI systems organised around epistemically warranted reliance rather than output correctness alone.

</details>


### [85] [Agentic self-driving microscopy benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalize to unseen tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05266)
*Nathan S Johnson,Ian Abshire*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study develops a benchmark and trace-logging framework to systematically evaluate how different LLM agent architectures (1-, 2-, and 3-agent topologies, five LLMs, RAG parameters) perform on microscopy control tasks. While the framework enables effective qualification, regression testing, and direct comparison across 105 configurations (1,949 test runs), surrogate models could not reliably predict agent performance on unseen tasks, indicating the heterogeneous benchmark suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Research into LLM agentic control of scientific instruments (microscopes, synchrotron beamlines) is nascent and lacks established engineering paradigms. Researchers face many design choices (LLM selection, agent count, delegation rules, RAG parameters) but lack systematic methods to evaluate whether these choices generalize to unseen tasks. The study aims to fill this gap by providing both a comparative evaluation framework and testing whether benchmark performance predicts generalization.

Method: The authors built a benchmark and trace-logging framework encompassing 53 microscopy tests. They systematically evaluated 105 agent configurations varying: agent graph topologies (one-, two-, and three-agent systems), five different LLMs, RAG and context parameters, and operational constraints. In total, 1,949 individual test runs and 49,109 RAG retrievals were logged. Surrogate models were then trained on agent architecture and test results to attempt prediction of performance on unseen tasks.

Result: Direct comparisons revealed clear, measurable differences across configurations in latency, token consumption, cost, and failure modes. However, surrogate models trained on architecture and test outcomes failed to reliably predict agent performance on new, unseen microscopy tasks. This indicates that while the benchmark is useful for qualification, regression testing, and diagnosis, it does not support building a task-independent global configuration model.

Conclusion: The proposed benchmark and logging framework is valuable for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison of microscope agent configurations. However, the heterogeneity of the current test suite precludes generalizing performance predictions to unseen tasks, highlighting a fundamental limitation of current benchmarking approaches for agentic scientific instrument control.

Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly being developed to control a wide range of scientific characterization tools including microscopes and synchrotron beamlines. Research into agentic control of physical infrastructure is nascent and there are few well-established paradigms for how to engineer an agentic system. There are many choices to make when designing a microscopy agent, including the choice of LLM, the number of agents to use, agent responsibilities and delegation rules, retrieval-augmented generation parameters, and more. When designing and optimizing an agentic microscope controller, researchers not only want to ensure that the agent can correctly perform known tasks but also that the agent can generalize to new tasks that it has not encountered before. In this study, we develop a benchmark and trace-logging framework that reveals a) how different choices of agent architecture impact performance at microscopy tasks and b) the limitations of benchmarks for predicting if a particular agent will perform well on unseen microscopy tasks. The framework was used to evaluate one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies, five LLMs, RAG and context parameters, and operational constraints across 53 microscopy benchmark tests. In total, 105 agent configurations, 1,949 individual test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals were recorded. Direct comparisons showed clear differences in latency, token use, cost, and failure mode between configurations. However, surrogate models trained on agent architecture and test results did not reliably predict an agent's performance on new, unseen tasks. These results show that these benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the current heterogeneous test suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model.

</details>


### [86] [Unified Agent: Managing Interactions across Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05729)
*Xinshuang Liu,Runfa Blark Li,Shaoxiu Wei,Xin Lin,Truong Nguyen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a cross-device, cross-time agent benchmark and proposes "Unified Agent," a stateful design that maintains a compact, action-ready state of engagement evidence, facts, and standing requests. It significantly outperforms four published agent designs across multiple MLLM settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI agent systems fail at cross-device, cross-time scenarios because single-agent systems treating devices as tools lack effective state management across time, while multi-agent systems don't maintain the compact carried state needed for cross-device requests. Observations are scattered across devices and moments, but mainstream designs are not built around this reality.

Method: The authors (1) construct a benchmark of user-agent interaction across devices and time to compare state designs, and (2) instantiate the "Unified Agent" — a stateful agent that carries interaction evidence across devices and moments, combining this carried state with current observations to decide actions. They compare it against adaptations of four published designs, and evaluate robustness across different MLLM families, capabilities, and reasoning effort levels.

Result: Unified Agent significantly outperforms all four adapted published designs in the default setting. The performance advantage remains consistent across changes in MLLM family, capability, and reasoning effort, demonstrating that the state-design advantage is robust across MLLM settings.

Conclusion: Effectively designed state that organizes engagement evidence, stated facts, and standing requests in a compact, action-ready form is critical for cross-device, cross-time agent performance. The Unified Agent design principle proves robust and superior, and the benchmark plus code/data will be open-sourced on GitHub.

Abstract: As capabilities rapidly increase, AI agents can move from running inside one app to acting across a user's devices over time. Yet existing agent systems still fall short in this scenario. This is because observations are scattered across devices and moments, but mainstream systems are not designed around this fact: a single agent that treats devices as tools lacks effective state management for all devices across time, and multi-agent systems coordinate across agents but do not maintain the compact carried state a cross-device, cross-time request needs. We argue that the agent should maintain an effectively designed state that organizes engagement evidence, stated facts, and the standing request in a compact, action-ready form for deciding its action given the current observation. To compare state designs, we construct a benchmark of user-agent interaction across devices and time. We instantiate this principle in Unified Agent, a stateful agent that carries interaction evidence across devices and moments and uses it with the current observation to act. In the default setting, it significantly outperforms our adaptations of four published designs. Across changes in multimodal large language model (MLLM) family, capability, and reasoning effort, it remains ahead of all compared systems, demonstrating that the state-design advantage is robust across MLLM settings. Our code and data will be publicly available on GitHub.

</details>


### [87] [CASCADE: An Agentic Regulatory Network Framework for Patient-Data-Validated Downstream Perturbation Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05359)
*Jose A. Bird*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CASCADE is an agentic framework using ARACNe regulatory networks via MCP to predict transcriptional effects of gene perturbations. The paper validates direction-of-change predictions using TCGA copy-number amplification as a dosage proxy for knockdown, showing strong concordance for MYC across multiple cancer types, and benchmarks LLM grounding of natural-language requests into tool calls, revealing schema and ambiguity-resolution failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior validation of gene perturbation prediction tools relies on gene-set membership (whether predicted genes are known cancer genes). The authors argue this is insufficient and propose instead testing whether predicted transcriptional direction of change matches actual patient tumor data, using focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown.

Method: They use ARACNe-inferred regulatory networks exposed through MCP within an agentic framework (CASCADE). Validation leverages TCGA patient tumor data: focal copy-number amplification of a gene serves as a dosage proxy (inverse of knockdown). Predicted direction of change for knockdown targets is compared against real amplified-vs-non-amplified tumor expression. Concordance is tested via permutation baselines and PAM50 subtype controls, with replication in METABRIC. MSigDB gene-set baselines are compared via Fisher's exact test. The approach is extended to 15 additional genes. Separately, LLM grounding of natural-language requests into MCP tool calls is benchmarked across 35 queries using exact-match scoring.

Result: For MYC, CASCADE's predicted knockdown targets show concordance of 90.0% (BRCA), 72.0% (COAD), 85.7% (STAD) — all significant (p<0.0013), surviving PAM50 control and replicating in METABRIC (87.2%). Against MSigDB baselines, CASCADE's accuracy does not exceed existing public knowledge of MYC/E2F-driven biology, though its direction-calling outperforms a uniform guess. Extension to 15 genes shows gene-specific validity: proliferation-machinery regulators mostly replicate; lineage-identity transcription factors and CCND2 consistently fail. LLM benchmarking: a local model achieves 71.4% exact match, a larger model 85.7%. Schema and gene-alias failures resolve with scale or server-side correction. Both models default to wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries; a targeted fix fails because its trigger condition never fires.

Conclusion: Direction-of-change validation against real tumor data offers a more rigorous standard than gene-set membership. CASCADE performs well for MYC and proliferation regulators but not universally — lineage-identity TFs and CCND2 fail, suggesting a hedged, post-hoc hypothesis about biological scope. LLM agent grounding shows promise but exposes failures in schema handling and ambiguity resolution that scaling alone does not fully address.

Abstract: CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts downstream transcriptional effects of gene perturbation from precomputed
  ARACNe regulatory networks, exposed via MCP. Prior work validates such tools by checking whether predicted genes are
  known cancer genes (membership); we instead test whether the predicted direction of change matches reality, using
  focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown against real TCGA patient
  tumor data.
  For MYC, CASCADE's predicted knockdown targets show strong concordance with real amplified-vs-non-amplified tumor
  expression across three cancer types (BRCA: 90.0%, COAD: 72.0%, STAD: 85.7%; all p<0.0013), well above permutation
  baselines, surviving a PAM50 subtype control and replicating in an independent cohort (METABRIC, 87.2%). Compared
  against curated MSigDB gene-set baselines via Fisher's exact test, CASCADE's accuracy is not shown to exceed existing
  public knowledge of MYC- or E2F-driven biology, though its gene-specific direction-calling clearly outperforms a naive
  uniform guess.
  Extending to fifteen additional genes, validation proves gene-specific rather than universal: proliferation-machinery
  regulators mostly replicate, while lineage-identity transcription factors and one cyclin-D paralog (CCND2)
  consistently fail, a pattern we discuss as a hedged, post-hoc hypothesis.
  We separately benchmark whether an LLM-based agent correctly grounds natural-language requests into CASCADE's real MCP
  tool calls. Across 35 queries, a documented local model reaches 71.4% exact match (85.7% for a larger model); schema
  and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the
  wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries, a failure a targeted fix could not resolve because its trigger condition
  never occurs.

</details>


### [88] [Counterfactual Analysis via Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05367)
*Zonghao Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper explores using GPT-3.5 for counterfactual ROI prediction in online lending, finding that prompt engineering improves GPT's predictive performance (R² from 1.97% to 2.84%), approaching gradient-boosted regression (3.48%), and demonstrates GPT's capacity for logically coherent causal reasoning under alternative interest rate scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Counterfactual analysis is essential for evaluating hypothetical policy scenarios, particularly in online lending where predicting ROI under alternative interest rate schemes informs decision-making. The authors seek to assess whether LLMs like GPT-3.5 can serve as viable tools for this task, potentially offering a more accessible alternative to traditional machine learning approaches.

Method: The study employs GPT-3.5 for counterfactual ROI prediction in online lending. First, the authors benchmark GPT's predictive accuracy against advanced ML models (e.g., gradient-boosted regression). They then apply prompt engineering techniques to enhance GPT's performance. Finally, they use GPT to generate counterfactual ROI estimates under various hypothetical interest rate schemes, evaluating the logical coherence and causal reasoning quality of the model's outputs.

Result: Prompt engineering raised GPT's R-squared from 1.97% to 2.84%, narrowing the gap with gradient-boosted regression's 3.48%. GPT also demonstrated logical coherence and plausible causal reasoning when generating counterfactual ROI predictions across alternative interest rate scenarios.

Conclusion: LLMs, particularly GPT-3.5, show promise as effective tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending. With appropriate prompt engineering, their predictive performance approaches that of specialized ML models, and they exhibit meaningful causal reasoning capabilities. The authors suggest broader applicability of LLMs in predictive and decision-making contexts.

Abstract: Counterfactual analysis aims to predict potential outcomes under hypothetical scenarios, offering valuable insights for decision-making. This paper investigates the application of large language models (LLMs), specifically the GPT-3.5 model, for counterfactual analysis. We focus on the online lending context, where the counterfactual return on investment (ROI) is crucial for evaluating different interest rate schemes. We begin by assessing the predictive performance of GPT and comparing it with advanced machine learning algorithms. The results show that prompt engineering can significantly enhance GPT's predictions, with the R-squared increasing from 1.97% to 2.84%, closely approaching the 3.48% achieved by gradient-boosted regression. Subsequently, we utilize GPT to generate counterfactual ROIs under a set of alternative interest rates. GPT exhibits logical coherence and causal reasoning in its responses. The findings underscore the potential of LLMs as effective tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending, suggesting broader applications for LLMs in various predictive and decision-making contexts.

</details>


### [89] [C$^3$PO: Evaluating Cross-Modal Composition and Counterfactual Performance in Omnimodal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05381)
*Swapnanil Mukherjee,Agyeya Negi,Tanuja Ganu,Ponnurangam Kumaraguru*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: C$^3$PO is a benchmark of 3,404 multimodal samples (video, audio, image, text) diagnosing cross-modal reasoning failures in MLLMs. It reveals that 86-95% of failures come from modality dominance (over-reliance on text), and mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness. The best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) achieves 73.17% vs. human 88.64%, with open-source models collapsing under counterfactual conflict.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLMs exhibit reasoning heavily biased toward a dominant modality (typically text), leading to brittle cross-modal reasoning. Existing benchmarks lack targeted diagnosis of when and why cross-modal reasoning fails, particularly distinguishing between fusing dispersed evidence versus resolving deliberate cross-modal contradictions.

Method: The authors introduce C$^3$PO, a benchmark with 3,404 samples covering video, audio, image, and text. It evaluates two core abilities: Information Composition (IC — fusing dispersed evidence) and Counterfactual Conflict (CC — resolving deliberate cross-modal contradictions). The benchmark uses a paired IC/CC structure with a four-tier difficulty design. Samples are generated via a fully automatic pipeline using 25 logically grounded templates. Attention probe analysis is conducted to measure modality dominance, and mid-layer attention entropy is tracked as a predictor of correctness.

Result: Humans achieve 88.64% accuracy; the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches only 73.17%, with open-source models collapsing under conflict conditions. 86-95% of failures are attributed to modality dominance: models fixate on one modality (87-95% of attention on text) while ignoring contradictory evidence. Mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness — sustained cross-modal exploration succeeds, while premature attention collapse leads to failure. A 56-point accuracy gap between equally complex templates demonstrates that performance depends on modalities' structural roles in conflict resolution, not merely modality combinations.

Conclusion: Multimodal perception does not guarantee robust cross-modal reasoning. Architectures must enable sustained cross-modal attention to avoid premature commitment to a single modality. The findings call for designing MLLMs that maintain balanced, dynamic attention across modalities during reasoning.

Abstract: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can process diverse sensory inputs, yet their reasoning remains heavily biased toward a dominant modality, resulting in brittle cross-modal reasoning. We introduce C$^3$PO, a benchmark of 3,404 samples spanning video, audio, image, and text, evaluating two abilities: information composition (fusing dispersed evidence) and counterfactual conflict (resolving deliberate contradictions). C$^3$PO's paired IC/CC structure and four-tier design enable targeted diagnosis of when and why cross-modal reasoning fails. Built through a fully automatic pipeline using 25 logically grounded templates, C$^3$PO reveals that while humans achieve 88.64% accuracy, the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches only 73.17%, with open-source models collapsing under conflict. Through attention probes, we find 86-95% of failures stem from modality dominance: models commit to one modality while ignoring contradictory evidence, concentrating 87-95% of attention on text. Mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness-sustained exploration succeeds, premature collapse fails. The 56-point accuracy gap between equally complex templates reveals that performance depends on modalities' structural roles in conflict resolution, not combinations. These findings show multimodal perception does not guarantee robust reasoning; architectures must enable sustained cross-modal attention to avoid premature

</details>


### [90] [Evaluating and Improving Pedagogical Fit in LLM-Based AI Tutors with the Pedagogical Suitability Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05411)
*Benjamin Barlog,Hudson Craig,Zedong Peng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a composite metric evaluating LLM tutoring responses not just for correctness but for alignment with learner readiness and curricular progression. Testing four LLMs across 240 scenarios shows PSI-guided feedback improved 82.3% of weak cases, suggesting pedagogical alignment is measurable and improvable regardless of model category.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as AI tutors, but existing evaluations focus primarily on answer correctness and quality, neglecting whether responses are pedagogically appropriate — i.e., matched to the learner's current knowledge foundation, the course sequence, and the timing of concept introduction. This instructional fit is critical in classroom settings but remains under-measured.

Method: The authors introduce the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a composite metric comprising six theory-informed sub-scores that assess alignment with learner readiness and curricular progression. They evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, Qwen3) across 240 scenario-based evaluations using paired standard and defective prompts. A PSI-guided regeneration protocol is then applied to 62 weak-performing cases, with focused manual evaluation to validate whether PSI-identified weaknesses and regenerations correspond to human-judged instructional improvements.

Result: Baseline PSI scores across the four models ranged from 0.557 to 0.638, with modest differences and no clear separation between open-weight and closed models. Under prompt perturbations, overall PSI remained stable (Δ = -0.002) but sub-score trade-offs emerged. PSI-guided feedback substantially improved weak cases: 51 of 62 (82.3%) showed improvement. Manual evaluation confirmed that PSI-identified weaknesses were instructionally meaningful and that PSI-guided regenerations aligned with human-judged improvement.

Conclusion: Learner- and curriculum-aware alignment may matter more for effective AI tutoring than model category alone. Such alignment is both measurable (via PSI) and improvable (via PSI-guided regeneration), suggesting that pedagogical suitability should be a core dimension of LLM tutor evaluation and refinement.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as AI tutors, but a correct answer is not always a pedagogically appropriate one. In classroom learning, effective help depends not only on correctness, but also on whether a response matches the learner's current foundation, the course sequence, and the timing of concept introduction. Existing evaluations focus mainly on answer quality, leaving this instructional fit under-measured. We present the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a composite metric of six theory-informed sub-scores that evaluates how well LLM-generated tutoring responses align with learner readiness and curricular progression, and we further use PSI as a structured feedback signal for response improvement. We evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, and Qwen3) across 240 scenario-based evaluations using paired standard and defective prompts, then apply a PSI-guided regeneration protocol to 62 weak-performing cases. Baseline differences across the four tested models were modest overall (PSI range: 0.557 to 0.638), and open-weight and closed models did not exhibit a clear separation in pedagogical fit. Under the tested prompt perturbations, overall PSI remained largely stable (Delta = -0.002), though sub-score trade-offs emerged. More importantly, PSI-guided feedback substantially improved weak-performing cases: 51 of 62 cases improved (82.3%). Focused manual evaluation of the 62 PSI-selected weak cases provides initial evidence that the identified weaknesses are instructionally meaningful and that many PSI-guided regenerations correspond to human-judged improvement. These results suggest that learner- and curriculum-aware alignment may matter more for effective tutoring than model category alone, and that such alignment is both measurable and improvable.

</details>


### [91] [Negotiating Risk Boundaries in AI for Policing Through Mixed-Stakeholder Deliberation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05418)
*Mackenzie Jorgensen,Jo Reilly,Alex Sutherland,Miri Zilka*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A mixed-stakeholder workshop with 30 participants (community members, police, academics) evaluated 13 AI policing use cases through a racial bias lens. Participants were broadly open to AI, rejecting only three — most notably recidivism risk assessment on principled grounds. Centering racial equity did not narrow debate; instead, discussions converged on universal questions of efficacy, genuine benefit, and equitable distribution, mirroring the curb-cut effect in inclusive design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI adoption in UK policing is accelerating, and racial bias is a documented risk. Yet affected community representatives are rarely included in decision-making about AI deployment. The study seeks to fill this gap by directly engaging those communities in deliberation, testing whether foregrounding racial equity enriches or constrains the risk-benefit analysis.

Method: A mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop involving 30 participants — community representatives, police officers, and academics. Participants assessed 13 AI use cases in policing through structured deliberation, with an explicit framing around racial bias. Qualitative analysis of the discussions was conducted to identify patterns in reasoning and acceptance/rejection thresholds.

Result: Participants were broadly receptive to AI, rejecting only 3 of 13 use cases outright. Recidivism risk assessment was the most prominently rejected, with objections targeting the fundamental premise rather than technical implementation. Crucially, centering racial bias did not narrow deliberation; instead, discussions converged on three universal questions: Does the tool work? Does it deliver genuine benefit? Will that benefit reach everyone? This mirrors the curb-cut effect.
