Conclusion: Incorporating a racial bias lens from the outset does not constrain deliberation but rather elevates it toward universal design principles. The findings support integrating affected community voices and equity considerations early in AI procurement and deployment decisions, as this approach surfaces foundational questions that benefit all users — akin to the curb-cut effect in inclusive design.

Abstract: AI tools are being increasingly adopted in policing in the UK and worldwide. Racial bias is a known and well-documented risk, yet representatives of affected communities are rarely included in decisions about AI adoption. We present results from a mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop bringing together 30 community representatives, police officers, and academics to assess the risks of 13 AI use cases in policing, with an explicit focus on racial bias. We found that participants were broadly open to AI adoption, rejecting only three use cases outright, most notably recidivism risk assessment, where objections targeted the premise rather than the implementation. Our analysis reveals that foregrounding racial equity did not narrow the deliberation. Instead, discussions gravitated toward a fundamental set of questions: does this tool actually work, will it deliver genuine benefit, and will that benefit extend to everyone? This integrated reasoning, reminiscent of the curb-cut effect in inclusive design, highlights the benefit of incorporating the racial bias lens into the risk-benefit analysis of AI use cases from the outset.

</details>


### [92] [SCP-NL2TL: Selective Conformal Prediction with Semantic Verification for Natural Language to Temporal Logic Specifications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05439)
*Yixuan Wang,Licheng Luo,Yu Fu,Kaidi Xu,Yue Dong,Mingyu Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a selective translation framework for NL-to-formal-specification tasks that uses conformal risk control to decide when to trust or abstain from generated specifications, with distribution-free reliability guarantees and OOD detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NL-to-formal-specification translators blindly output a specification for every input, even unreliable ones, posing safety risks. There is a need for systems that know when they are uncertain and can abstain rather than execute incorrect specifications in safety-critical applications.

Method: The framework uses two complementary black-box reliability signals: (1) back-translation fidelity — translating the generated formal specification back to NL and measuring semantic similarity; (2) dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence — measuring consistency across multiple generations. These signals are combined and calibrated via conformal risk control into an accept/abstain decision with a distribution-free bound on the incorrect-acceptance rate. A conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens OOD inputs before translation.

Result: Experiments across STL, LTL, and SpaTiaL demonstrate improved translation reliability, robustness under cross-tier distribution shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention. The two signals fail on different errors and jointly separate incorrect translations more sharply than either alone.

Conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for trustworthy NL interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may not be reliable, with a general framework applicable across formal specification languages.

Abstract: Translating natural language instructions into machine-interpretable formal specifications enables robots and autonomous systems to plan, reason, and formally verify their behavior. However, existing translation models typically generate a specification for every input, even when the result is unreliable or fails to capture the user's intent, creating risks in safety-critical applications. Inspired by selective conformal prediction, we propose a selective translation framework that not only generates formal specifications but also determines when they can be trusted. Reliability is scored by two complementary black-box signals, the fidelity of the specification back-translated into natural language and the dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence, which fail on different errors and jointly separate incorrect translations more sharply than either alone. Conformal risk control calibrates this score into a decision that accepts a specification or abstains, with a distribution-free bound on the rate at which incorrect specifications are accepted for execution, and a conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens out-of-distribution inputs before any translation is attempted. The proposed framework is general across formal specification languages, with experiments on Signal Temporal Logic (STL), Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), and geometric Spatio-Temporal Logic (SpaTiaL) demonstrating improved translation reliability, robustness under the evaluated cross-tier shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may not be reliable.

</details>


### [93] [Stochasticity Is Not the Hard Part: Reduction and Complexity in Instructional Sequencing over Prerequisite DAGs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05455)
*Zonglin Han,Yichen Chen,Jiawen Jiang,Tongan Shi,Kristian A. Stevens*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Instructional sequencing under prerequisite constraints is studied as a stochastic shortest-path problem. The stochasticity can be eliminated exactly by collapsing to a deterministic problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals. The problem remains NP-hard even under restrictive conditions (via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments), but becomes polynomial-time solvable when transfer preferences and prerequisites are jointly acyclic or when prerequisite width is fixed. A diagnostic metric bounds optimization value, and empirical validation on 70K+ CS course interactions confirms both easy and hard regimes exist.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When students learn interconnected concepts with prerequisite dependencies, instructors face the question of optimal sequencing: when does order matter, and how costly is finding the best order? Prior work lacks a rigorous treatment combining both stochastic learning outcomes and prerequisite constraints in a unified optimization framework.

Method: The authors model instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem where attempting a concept succeeds with state-dependent probability. They prove this stochastic problem collapses exactly to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals. Complexity is analyzed via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments. Tractable cases are identified (jointly acyclic transfer/preferences, fixed prerequisite width solvable via dynamic programming). A diagnostic metric mΔ is introduced, and experiments use 70,893 interactions from an introductory CS course plus constructed hard instances evaluated with A* search.

Result: Key theoretical results: (1) exact collapse from stochastic to deterministic; (2) NP-hardness even with no prerequisites, unit costs, uniform binary transfer, and success probability ≥1/2; (3) polynomial-time DP when prerequisite width is fixed; (4) any topological order of the residual joint graph is optimal when transfer preferences and prerequisites are jointly acyclic. Empirically, the diagnostic certifies the CS course data as doubly easy (low optimization value, small search space), while constructed hard instances show myopic sequencing suffers large regret, yet A* with consistent heuristics expands only linearly many states.

Conclusion: Instructional sequencing exhibits a sharp dichotomy: it is NP-hard in general but admits efficient algorithms under realistic structural assumptions. The mΔ diagnostic can determine upfront whether optimization is worth pursuing. Real educational data often falls in the easy regime, but hard instances are constructible, where informed search (A*) remains tractable despite the hardness.

Abstract: When a student must learn concepts connected by prerequisite dependencies, when does the order of instruction matter, and what does it cost to find the best one? We study instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem in which attempting a concept succeeds with a state-dependent probability and failure leaves the learner state unchanged. We first prove that this stochasticity can be eliminated exactly: the problem collapses to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals, preserving optimal values and actions. The collapse removes stochastic complexity but not combinatorial complexity: optimal sequencing remains NP-hard -- via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments -- even with no prerequisite edges, unit costs, uniform binary nonnegative transfer, and success probabilities at least $1/2$. Hardness is not uniform: when realizable transfer preferences remain jointly acyclic with the prerequisites, any topological order of the residual joint graph is optimal, and fixed prerequisite width yields polynomial-time exact dynamic programming. A computable diagnostic, $mΔ$, bounds the value of sequencing before optimization. On 70,893 interactions from an introductory CS course, the diagnostic certifies a doubly easy regime -- little value to optimize and little space to search -- while constructed transfer instances realize the challenging regime, where myopic sequencing suffers large regret yet exact A* with a consistent heuristic expands only linearly many states on that family.

</details>


### [94] [Recursive Synthesis for Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05466)
*Zhongzhi Li,Yucheng Shi,Zongxia Li,Ruhan Wang,Anhao Li,Zixun Huang,Junyao Yang,Lei Ke,Ninghao Liu,Haitao Mi,Leowei Liang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RST is a recursive verified synthesis framework that generates long-horizon terminal-agent tasks at scale (~$0.05/task), producing 37,484 tasks across 15 rounds with steadily increasing difficulty. Fine-tuning on trajectories from these tasks yields up to 10-point gains on terminal benchmarks, with recursion showing no ceiling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-quality long-horizon training data for terminal agents is prohibitively expensive (hundreds to thousands of dollars per task) because instructions, environments, reference solutions, and verifiers must remain mutually consistent. Human authoring doesn't scale, and direct LLM generation often breaks these dependencies.

Method: RST is a recursive verified synthesis framework: starting from verified seed tasks, it extends the reference solution, realigns the verifier and instruction to the new workflow, validates results in a fresh sandbox, and reuses accepted tasks as seeds for subsequent rounds. This process iterates over 15 rounds, producing 37,484 tasks.

Result: Task difficulty increases substantially across rounds (median solution lines: 67→374; median commands: 40→244; DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 drops from 90% at R1 to 2.5% at R15). Fine-tuning Qwen3.5 models on rejection-sampled trajectories yields up to 10-point improvements on Terminal-Bench 2, Terminal-Bench Hard, and Long-Horizon Terminal Bench. Agentic PPO lifts Qwen3.5-27B to 49.44%, 32.00%, and 22.07% (relative gains of 20.0%, 41.2%, 21.9%). Recursion shows no ceiling after 15 rounds.

Conclusion: RST enables scalable, low-cost synthesis of increasingly difficult terminal-agent tasks. Training on these synthetic tasks yields substantial performance gains, and the recursive process shows no signs of plateauing, suggesting further scaling potential.

Abstract: High-quality long-horizon training data for terminal agents is expensive to produce, often costing hundreds to thousands of dollars per task, because each task must keep the instruction, environment, reference solution, and verifier mutually consistent. Human authoring does not scale, and direct generation with large language models (LLMs) often breaks these dependencies. We present Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks (RST), a recursive verified synthesis framework for constructing long-horizon terminal-agent tasks at scale. Starting from verified seed tasks, RST extends the reference solution, realigns the verifier and instruction to the new workflow, validates the result in a fresh sandbox, and reuses accepted tasks as seeds for subsequent rounds. Across fifteen recursive rounds, RST produces 37,484 synthesized terminal-agent tasks at roughly \$0.05 per task. Task difficulty increases substantially over rounds: the median reference solution grows from 67 to 374 lines, the median number of executed commands grows from 40 to 244, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 drops from 90\% at $R_1$ to 2.5\% at $R_{15}$. To demonstrate training utility, we collect rejection-sampled Qwen3.5 trajectories on the synthesized tasks and use them for supervised fine-tuning. Fine-tuning on these trajectories improves Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B by up to 10 points on Terminal-Bench~2, Terminal-Bench Hard, and Long-Horizon Terminal Bench, while agentic PPO lifts Qwen3.5-27B to 49.44\%, 32.00\%, and 22.07\% on the three benchmarks, corresponding to relative gains of 20.0\%, 41.2\%, and 21.9\% over the base model. Moreover, after 15 rounds, the recursion shows no ceiling: synthesis yield and validation rates remain stable as difficulty keeps climbing, indicating that the process can continue well beyond the scale reported here.

</details>


### [95] [Innovation-Residual Auditing of Autonomous Analysis Agents: Localization, Detection Limits, Error Control, and Identifiability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05490)
*Ahmed Hassoon,Mark Dredze*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the reliability of automated audits for autonomous data analysis agents. It shows that how an audit scores operations determines whether errors can be localized, quantifies error spread across operations, provides statistical procedures to control false flag rates under exchangeability assumptions, examines how guarantees degrade with model imperfection or data-dependent selection, and establishes a fundamental limit: errors below a magnitude threshold are indistinguishable from natural variation, with this threshold bounded primarily by representation dimension rather than training data volume.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous agents increasingly perform end-to-end data analyses without step-by-step human supervision. When errors occur, identifying which specific operation caused the failure is critical. A recent approach flags suspicious operations by comparing them against a model trained on sound analyses, without requiring labeled mistakes. However, the reliability of such audits has not been formally studied, motivating this paper's rigorous theoretical and empirical analysis.

Method: The authors formalize the audit problem, contrasting two scoring paradigms: (1) scoring operations based on surprise given the immediately preceding operation (Markov-style), and (2) scoring against a longer reconstruction of the intended analysis. They derive how errors propagate under each scheme, develop procedures to control the false flagging rate within a single analysis relying on exchangeability of sound analyses rather than model correctness, quantify degradation under model misspecification and data-dependent selection, and prove a fundamental lower bound on detectable error magnitude rooted in the representation's dimensionality.

Result: Key findings include: (a) predecessor-based scoring cannot distinguish inherited errors from correct operations, localizing one mistake to a single flag; (b) reconstruction-based scoring spreads a single error across multiple operations, with a quantified spreading rate; (c) false flag rate can be controlled under exchangeability, with explicit bounds on how guarantees weaken under model imperfection or selection effects; (d) a fundamental identifiability limit exists—errors below a threshold set by representation dimension are indistinguishable from natural variation, and this threshold falls slowly (under 2% reduction for a 100× increase in training data at current representation sizes).

Conclusion: The reliability of automated audits for autonomous analysis agents depends crucially on the scoring mechanism, with a sharp trade-off between error localization precision and false flag proliferation. Statistical guarantees are achievable under mild exchangeability conditions, but a hard identifiability barrier tied to representation dimension—not dataset size—limits what any audit can detect. Scaling training data yields diminishing returns, so improving representation quality is the more effective path to more sensitive audits.

Abstract: Autonomous agents now carry out entire data analyses, selecting cohorts, joining tables, and fitting models with little step-by-step supervision. When such an analysis turns out to be wrong, someone must determine which operation caused it. A recent approach does this without any labelled mistakes, learning instead from analyses known to be sound and flagging operations that depart from what that model predicts; how reliable such audits are has not been studied. This paper supplies that analysis. The choice of score determines whether an error can be localized at all. If each operation is scored by how surprising it is given the operation immediately preceding it, then operations that merely inherit an earlier error are indistinguishable from correct ones, so one mistake produces one flag; scores computed against a longer reconstruction of the intended analysis instead spread a single mistake across many operations. We quantify how far they spread, and how to choose the comparison length when an error accumulates gradually rather than at once. We then give procedures that control the proportion of falsely flagged operations within a single audited analysis, requiring only that sound analyses be exchangeable rather than that the fitted model be correct, and we quantify how much the guarantees weaken when the model is imperfect or when the analysis was selected for review in a way that depends on its content. Finally we establish a limit on what any such audit can report: errors below a certain magnitude cannot be attributed at all, being indistinguishable from ordinary variation among sound analyses. This limit falls so slowly as more sound analyses are collected that at the representation sizes now in use a hundredfold increase reduces it by under two percent, so the dimension of the representation rather than the volume of training data is the binding constraint.

</details>


### [96] [EcoAgent-Bench: Evaluating Economic Decision-Making in Budget-Constrained LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05519)
*Jie Wu,Ming Gong,Feixiang Cheng,Qinqin Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EcoAgent-Bench evaluates LLM agents not just on task completion but on economical action selection under explicit budgets. Across 304 tasks, agents struggle with both micro success (3.9-24.0%) and economic consistency (≤7.3%), revealing that budget-constrained completion and cost-efficient action selection are distinct, challenging properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard agent benchmarks treat resource consumption as a secondary metric, ignoring that in real deployment, deciding whether to escalate (to a stronger model, broader search, or human) is a core part of the task. There is no existing benchmark that jointly evaluates task accuracy and cost-efficiency under an explicit budget constraint with priced actions.

Method: The authors introduce EcoAgent-Bench with 304 real-derived tasks across five families (adapted from GAIA, HotpotQA, MuSiQue). Each task specifies priced actions and an explicit budget. Tasks test four agent decisions: avoiding unnecessary escalation, escalating when local evidence is insufficient, selecting an appropriate model tier, and stopping on unsupported premises. Seven LLM agents are evaluated in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings, alongside four oracle scripted controls. Beyond micro-averaged accuracy, the paper introduces an economic-consistency score (the minimum accuracy across upgrade-oriented and save-oriented family groups) to penalize one-sided policies like always-escalate.

Result: Tool-API agents achieve only 3.9–24.0% micro strict success, with at most 7.3% economic consistency. Agents either prematurely stop before warranted escalation or overspend on cheap tasks. A budget threshold sweep on GPT-5.4 shifts its escalation rate from 0% to merely 3%, indicating current models are largely insensitive to budget signals.

Conclusion: Task completion under a budget and economical action selection are distinct properties that current LLM agents fail to exhibit jointly. The benchmark, transformation pipeline, frozen evaluation environments, and result artifacts are released to enable further study of cost-aware agent decision-making.

Abstract: Agent benchmarks usually measure task completion and treat resource use as an auxiliary statistic. In deployment, however, the choice among a local lookup, broad search, composite research tool, stronger model, or human escalation is part of the task itself. We introduce EcoAgent-Bench, in which every task specifies priced actions and an explicit budget. Its 304 real-derived tasks span five families adapted from GAIA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, and test four decisions: avoiding unnecessary escalation, escalating when local evidence is insufficient, selecting a model tier, and stopping on unsupported premises. We evaluate seven LLM agents in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings, together with four oracle scripted controls. Micro-averaged accuracy rewards one-sided policies: always-escalate controls achieve high micro success while failing save-oriented tasks. We therefore also report an economic-consistency score (the worse of accuracy on upgrade-oriented and save-oriented family groups) which exposes this failure. Tool-API agents attain only 3.9-24.0% micro strict success (at most 7.3% economic consistency), often either stopping before warranted escalation or overspending on cheap tasks. A threshold-crossing budget sweep changes GPT-5.4's escalation rate from 0% to only 3%. These results show that completion under a budget and economical action selection are distinct properties. We release the task bundle, transformation pipeline, frozen evaluation environments, and integrity-bound result artifacts needed to study both.

</details>


### [97] [Hyper-ES: Effective Evolution Strategies for LLM Reasoning via Descent Direction Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05541)
*Yu Gu,Zhi Zheng,Yunpeng Ba,Xialiang Tong,Mingxuan Yuan,Zhenkun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hyper-ES is a subspace-based Evolution Strategy framework that combines a few gradient-based fine-tuning runs to construct a compact adaptation subspace, then applies CMA-ES to optimize model merging coefficients within that subspace, achieving better mathematical reasoning performance than GRPO-LoRA with 10% fewer gradient updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Directly applying Evolution Strategy (ES) to billion-parameter LLMs fails because random perturbations in high-dimensional parameter spaces are nearly orthogonal to useful update directions, causing unstable optimization. The authors aim to circumvent this weakness by restricting ES search to a low-dimensional, semantically meaningful subspace.

Method: Hyper-ES operates in two stages: (1) A small number of inexpensive gradient-based fine-tuning runs produce distinct descent directions, whose span forms a compact adaptation subspace capturing useful reasoning updates. (2) CMA-ES then optimizes layer-wise DARE-TIES merging coefficients within this subspace, searching over combinations of meaningful descent directions rather than arbitrary full-model perturbations.

Result: Evaluated on three backbone models (Qwen2.5-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill) across six mathematical reasoning datasets, Hyper-ES consistently outperforms GRPO-LoRA by 1% while requiring 10% fewer space-consuming gradient updates.

Conclusion: Hyper-ES demonstrates that combining gradient-based descent directions with ES-based coefficient optimization in a low-dimensional subspace is an effective and resource-efficient strategy for LLM reasoning fine-tuning, outperforming existing RL-based methods like GRPO-LoRA.

Abstract: Evolution Strategy (ES) is a promising alternative to gradient-based fine-tuning for resource-constrained Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. However, directly applying ES to billion-parameter LLMs is highly ineffective. In such high-dimensional parameter spaces, most random perturbations are nearly orthogonal to useful update directions, leading to unstable optimization. We propose Hyper-ES, a subspace-based ES framework that avoids the weakness of ES in full-parameter search while exploiting its strength in low-dimensional optimization. Instead of asking ES to discover useful directions from random perturbations in the LLM parameter space, Hyper-ES first performs a small number of inexpensive gradient-based fine-tuning runs to obtain descent directions. Although each direction may provide only a limited improvement on its own, their span forms a compact adaptation subspace that captures useful reasoning updates. Hyper-ES then applies CMA-ES to optimize layer-wise DARE-TIES merging coefficients within this subspace, allowing ES to search over combinations of meaningful descent directions rather than over arbitrary full-model perturbations. We evaluate Hyper-ES on three Qwen2.5-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill backbones across six mathematical reasoning datasets. Results show that Hyper-ES consistently outperforms GRPO-LoRA by 1% while requiring 10% fewer space-consuming gradient updates. Code at https://github.com/kuangrepi/Hyper-ES.

</details>


### [98] [SkillTV-Bench: Benchmarking How Well Judges Perform on Skill-Augmented Agentic Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05573)
*Zhi Han,Chenxi Zeng,Liuhaichen Yang,Zihan Guo,Ming Zhou,Yang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillTV-Bench introduces a benchmark and method for skill-aware trajectory verification of LLM agents, where procedural knowledge from task-time skills guides inspection and verdicts. An automated evolution loop refines a reusable JudgeSkill, improving agent judge accuracy by 14.8 pp and boosting rollout selection success from 22.9% to 45.5%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents performing long-horizon tasks require verification of complete execution trajectories, not just final responses. For skill-augmented agents, effective verification depends on procedural knowledge encoded in task-time skills — this knowledge specifies what evidence to inspect and which failures are task-critical. Existing judge benchmarks are inadequate because they expose final responses or static trajectories and rarely integrate task-time skills with inspectable artifacts and environments.

Method: The authors introduce SkillTV-Bench, a 681-case benchmark comprising real agent trajectories from 50 tasks across 11 domains, designed to evaluate skill-aware trajectory verification. They propose SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge into a reusable JudgeSkill that guides an agent judge to plan targeted inspections and issue evidence-grounded verdicts. An automated evolution loop on a disjoint development pool refines the JudgeSkill using misjudged cases.

Result: On SkillTV-Bench, the refined JudgeSkill improves the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points. In offline rollout-pool selection experiments, it increases selected-trajectory success rate from 22.9% with a single rollout to 45.5% with ten rollouts.

Conclusion: Skill-aware trajectory verification, guided by externalized JudgeSkills refined through automated evolution, substantially improves both verification accuracy and trajectory selection for skill-augmented LLM agents. The benchmark and method are open-sourced.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly execute long-horizon tasks through tool use and environment interaction, shifting evaluation from final-response scoring to verification of complete executions. For skill-augmented agents, verification additionally requires the procedural knowledge encoded in task-time skills, because this knowledge indicates what evidence to inspect and which failures are task-critical. However, existing judge benchmarks often expose final responses or static trajectories, and rarely combine task-time skills with directly inspectable artifacts and environments. We therefore introduce SkillTV-Bench, a 681-case benchmark of real agent trajectories from 50 tasks across eleven domains, designed to evaluate skill-aware trajectory verification for both LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge methods. Additionally, we propose SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge as a reusable JudgeSkill that guides an agent judge to plan targeted inspections and issue evidence-grounded verdicts. On a disjoint development pool, an automated evolution loop further refines the JudgeSkill using misjudged cases. On SkillTV-Bench, the refined skill increases the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points. In offline rollout-pool selection, it increases selected-trajectory success from 22.9% with one rollout to 45.5% with ten rollouts. The code and data are available at https://github.com/HanZhi306/SkillTV-Bench

</details>


### [99] [DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05695)
*Wenhao Lin,Chenyu Yu,Xingwei Lin,Sicong Cao,Xiang Chen,Lei Xue,Le Yu,Letian Sha,Chunming Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DreamGuard is a proactive guardrail for LLM agents that uses a risk-aware world model with recurrent latent states to predict both immediate and long-horizon risks, outperforming reactive baselines in safety-utility trade-offs with only 25ms latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing runtime guardrails for LLM agents are predominantly reactive, evaluating only the apparent safety of the current action without modeling how risk accumulates across a trajectory. This creates a blind spot for long-horizon risks, where individually benign actions can gradually lead to hazardous states—potentially causing irreversible harm to external systems, user data, and downstream services.

Method: DreamGuard introduces a risk-aware world model that maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the agent's trajectory. It predicts future latent states and derives two complementary signals: immediate-hazard evidence (for the current action) and prefix-risk evidence (for long-horizon trajectory risk). These multi-horizon signals are fused into intervention decisions made before action execution.

Result: DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines across four benchmarks and an online guardrail evaluation. It achieves the best safety-utility trade-off among all evaluated guardrails while maintaining an average end-to-end latency of 25 ms per call.

Conclusion: A proactive, world-model-based approach to LLM agent safety can effectively capture both immediate and long-horizon risks, overcoming a key limitation of reactive guardrails. DreamGuard demonstrates that this can be done with minimal latency overhead, making it practical for real-world deployment.

Abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents increasingly invoke external tools and interact with real-world systems, unsafe actions may cause irreversible consequences on external states, user data, and downstream services. Recent runtime guardrails mitigate such risks by checking proposed actions before execution, but many remain reactive: they primarily assess the apparent safety of the current action, lacking an explicit model of how risk evolves across the trajectory. This limitation creates a critical blind spot for long-horizon risks, where individually benign-looking actions can gradually drift the agent toward hazardous states. In response, we propose DreamGuard, a proactive guardrail for LLM agents built around a risk-aware world model. The world model maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the trajectory and predicts future latent states from which DreamGuard derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence. It then fuses these multi-horizon signals into intervention decisions before execution. Experiments across four benchmarks and an online guardrail evaluation show that DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines, achieves the best safety-utility trade-off among evaluated guardrails, and maintains an average end-to-end latency of 25 ms per call.

</details>


### [100] [StepReflect: Structured UI Transition Reflection for Mobile GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05587)
*Linqiang Guo,Wei Liu,Li Gu,Yang Wang,Tse-Hsun,Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StepReflect reframes GUI action reflection as structured prediction, achieving 82.16% transition accuracy (11.83 points above GPT-5.2) with an 8B model, while improving task success and reducing API costs for mobile GUI agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mobile GUI agents rely on costly, open-ended multimodal reasoning after each action for reflection. This approach poorly aligns with the inherently structured nature of GUI state transitions, motivating a more efficient, structured prediction formulation.

Method: StepReflect formulates per-step GUI reflection as supervised structured prediction using explicit transition specifications and paired visual evidence. Training proceeds via a staged pipeline: supervised fine-tuning, teacher-student distillation, and preference- and reward-based refinement. The resulting model is 8B parameters.

Result: Offline: 82.16% transition-level accuracy on AndroidWorld, outperforming zero-shot GPT-5.2 by 11.83 points. Online: Higher task success in 3 of 4 agent configurations (M3A, Agent-SAMA, MAI-UI-8B, Seed-2.0-Pro), within one successful task of GPT-5.2 Reflection Agent in the fourth. Reduced paid API charges across all four configurations.

Conclusion: StepReflect establishes a practical, locally deployable alternative to repeated frontier-model reflection for long-horizon mobile GUI agents, combining stronger accuracy with lower operational cost.

Abstract: Autonomous mobile GUI agents require accurate action reflection for reliable long-horizon execution. Existing approaches rely on open-ended multimodal reasoning after each action, which is costly and poorly matched to the structured nature of GUI state transitions. We propose StepReflect, which formulates per-step GUI reflection as supervised structured prediction conditioned on explicit transition specifications and paired visual evidence. StepReflect is trained through a staged pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning, teacher-student distillation, and preference- and reward-based refinement. Offline, the resulting 8B model achieves 82.16% transition-level accuracy on AndroidWorld, exceeding zero-shot GPT-5.2 by 11.83 percentage points under the same structured input. Online, across M3A, Agent-SAMA, MAI-UI-8B, and Seed-2.0-Pro, StepReflect achieves higher task success in three of four agent configurations and remains within one successful task of the GPT-5.2 Reflection Agent in the fourth. It also reduces paid API charges relative to GPT-based reflection in all four configurations. These results establish StepReflect as a practical, locally deployable alternative to repeated frontier-model reflection for long-horizon mobile GUI agents.

</details>


### [101] [ChainClaw: A Layered Agent Framework for Reliable On-Chain Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05790)
*Jiacheng Wei,Zhaoxin Fan,Xin Wen,Yuqin Lan,Dongrun Li,Wenjun Wu,Faguo Wu,Xiao Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ChainClaw is a blockchain-native LLM agent framework that addresses three fundamental gaps (Reactivity, Irreversibility, Observability) in deploying LLM agents on-chain through a layered architecture with event-driven orchestration, simulation-based safety, and on-chain monitoring, outperforming baselines on safety and task completion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose LLM agents fail in blockchain environments because on-chain execution is stateful, adversarial, and economically irreversible. Existing agent frameworks make assumptions that break down under these conditions, revealing three critical gaps: Reactivity (inability to respond to on-chain events in real time), Irreversibility (no safety mechanism against costly, permanent mistakes), and Observability (limited ability to read and monitor on-chain state).

Method: ChainClaw is built on OpenClaw and features a layered architecture: (1) an event-driven orchestration layer for real-time reactivity via event ingestion and simulation feedback; (2) a simulation-based safety intelligence layer providing a pre-execution safety pipeline with transaction simulation and action guards to prevent irreversible errors; (3) an on-chain monitoring runtime layer with an on-chain read adapter and transaction monitor for observability. These layers are unified by a cross-layer memory subsystem.

Result: ChainClaw was evaluated on a purpose-built benchmark covering seven tasks across four categories and five dimensions. It consistently outperformed representative baselines on both safety metrics and task completion rates.

Conclusion: The three identified gaps (Reactivity, Irreversibility, Observability) are critical barriers for LLM agents in blockchain settings, and ChainClaw's layered architecture effectively bridges these gaps, enabling safer and more reliable autonomous on-chain execution.

Abstract: General-purpose large language model agents have achieved strong performance on tool-augmented tasks, yet they rely on assumptions break down in blockchain environments. On-chain execution is stateful, adversarial, and economically irreversible, exposing three fundamental gaps: Reactivity, Irreversibility, and Observability. We propose ChainClaw, a blockchain-native agent framework built on OpenClaw, that addresses all three gaps through a layered architecture comprising an event-driven orchestration layer, a simulation-based safety intelligence layer, and an on-chain monitoring runtime layer, unified by a cross-layer memory subsystem. ChainClaw closes the Reactivity gap via event ingestion and simulation feedback, the Irreversibility gap via a pre-execution safety pipeline with transaction simulation and action guard, and the Observability gap via an on-chain read adapter and transaction monitor. We evaluate ChainClaw on a purpose-built benchmark covering seven tasks across four categories and five dimensions. ChainClaw consistently outperforms representative baselines on both safety and task completion.

</details>


### [102] [Measuring and Detecting Harmful AI Sycophancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05624)
*Bohan Jiang,Dawei Li,Yasin Silva,Huan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces PSRS (preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy), where LLMs flip their initial stance to match user preferences. Using the CAP framework, the authors collect 290,460 labeled responses across 17 LLMs and 12 domains, revealing PSRS rates of 5–56%. They show that PSRS can be detected from single responses, but detector generalization to unseen models remains challenging, and they propose an initial mitigation approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work has identified sycophancy in LLMs as potentially harmful but has focused primarily on measuring degrees of sycophancy. The authors argue that a specific harmful subtype — preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS) — demands attention, particularly the question of whether it can be detected automatically from a single response, which is critical for scalable moderation and safety.

Method: The authors propose CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a data collection framework that elicits an initial model stance, then exposes the model to a user's stated preference to observe whether stance reversal occurs. They apply CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, generating 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday-advice domains. They then train detectors on response text alone and evaluate both in-distribution detection performance and cross-model generalization.

Result: PSRS rates vary substantially across models (5%–56%), with more capable models exhibiting lower sycophancy. Detection from a single response is feasible but requires learning subtle textual patterns. Cross-model generalization proves difficult: detector performance degrades on unseen models. The authors propose an initial approach to mitigate this generalization gap.

Conclusion: PSRS is a measurable and detectable form of harmful sycophancy in LLMs. While detection is achievable in-distribution, cross-model generalization remains an open challenge. The authors commit to releasing their dataset and code to facilitate further research on this safety problem.

Abstract: Sycophantic responses are becoming pervasive in large language models (LLMs), and prior work has pointed out that some of them could be harmful. This paper focuses on one harmful sycophancy: preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS), where a model reverses an initial stance merely to align with a user's stated preference. While existing research mainly measures how sycophantic a model is, we go further and ask whether PSRS can also be detected automatically from a single response. To investigate this at scale, we introduce CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a framework for collecting labeled PSRS data. Applying CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, we collect 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday-advice domains. We organize our study around three research questions. (1) How often does PSRS occur? (2) How well can it be detected? (3) How does detection generalize to unseen models? We first reveal that PSRS rates range from 5% to 56% across LLMs, with more capable models being less sycophantic. Next, we show that detecting PSRS is feasible from the response text alone, and detectors need to learn subtle PSRS patterns from the training data. Because new LLMs appear rapidly, detectors inevitably encounter unseen models, making cross-model generalization an important framework goal. We demonstrate that detection performance drops on unseen models and propose an initial approach to address this challenge. We will release our dataset and code to support future research.

</details>


### [103] [SkillHEX: Improving Agent Skills via Hypothesis-Driven Autonomous Exploration and Exploitation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05628)
*Yuru Feng,Yaoqi Chen,Beidi Zhao,Qianxi Zhang,Xinjiang Wang,Jianan Lu,Zhirui Wang,Shusen Xu,Zengzhong Li,Qi Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillHEX introduces a closed-loop framework that combines hypothesis-driven self-verification with evidence-guided tree search to enable autonomous, on-demand skill evolution for LLMs at test time, overcoming sparse reward and exploitation trap issues that plague existing greedy refinement methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual maintenance of LLM agent skills is costly, unscalable, and prone to misalignment. Real-world deployments demand autonomous skill evolution at test time under tight interaction budgets and without training/validation sets. This setting creates a sparse reward problem where multiple latent failure causes are conflated, making greedy single-skill refinement vulnerable to exploitation traps—early misdiagnoses waste limited trials on unproductive trajectories.

Method: SkillHEX is a closed-loop framework with two core components: (1) hypothesis-driven self-verification that translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable diagnostic tests, yielding dense reward signals without extra environment interactions; and (2) evidence-guided tree search over persistent skill-revision branches, dynamically balancing exploitation of supported edits with exploration of plausible alternatives.

Result: Evaluated across 87 tasks from SkillsBench, SkillHEX achieves average pass rates of 55.9% (GPT-5.3-Codex) and 57.9% (Claude Opus 4.7) under a five-iteration budget, outperforming existing self-evolving methods.

Conclusion: SkillHEX demonstrates that pairing diagnostic self-verification with tree-structured exploration effectively addresses sparse reward and exploitation trap challenges in test-time skill evolution, enabling LLM agents to autonomously improve procedural skills under realistic deployment constraints.

Abstract: Although agent skills equip LLMs with reusable procedural knowledge, manual maintenance suffers from high costs, unscalability, and misalignment. Real-world deployments thus require autonomous, on-demand skill evolution at test time, constrained by limited interaction budgets and a lack of training or validation sets. This setting introduces a severe sparse reward challenge, where outcomes conflate multiple latent failure causes. Under such ambiguity, existing methods that greedily refine a single incumbent skill are particularly vulnerable to an exploitation trap, allowing early misdiagnoses to exhaust limited trials along unproductive trajectories. To address this, we introduce SkillHEX, a closed-loop framework coupling hypothesis-driven self-verification with evidence-guided tree search. SkillHEX translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable tests, producing diagnostic evidence as dense reward without additional environment attempts. This evidence guides a search over persistent skill-revision branches, dynamically balancing the exploitation of supported edits with the exploration of plausible alternatives. Evaluated on 87 tasks from SkillsBench, SkillHEX outperforms existing self-evolving methods and achieves an average pass rate of 55.9% and 57.9% using GPT-5.3-Codex and Claude Opus 4.7 under a five-iteration budget, respectively.

</details>


### [104] [Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) Model: A Computational Account of What Makes Design Options Worth Trying](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05642)
*Shimon Honda,Takuma Miyaguchi,Koji Koizumi,Takanori Sano,Tristan Briard,Hideyoshi Yanagisawa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The B-EUR model quantifies the value of a design action as its expected reduction in epistemic uncertainty. Simulations and human experiments reveal that epistemic value follows an inverted-U with generalizability and increases with outcome discriminability, explaining how uncertainty perception drives action selection in design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address an open question in the Uncertainty Driven Action (UDA) model: how changes in uncertainty perception determine which actions a designer selects. The authors seek a computational account of how candidate design actions are evaluated under uncertainty.

Method: The B-EUR model formalizes candidate-action value as Bayesian expected reduction of epistemic uncertainty about action–outcome relations. Simulations and human experiments employed a graph-shape guessing task under limited trial budgets, manipulating two environmental properties: generalizability (knowledge transfer across neighboring candidates) and outcome discriminability (distinguishability of outcome differences).

Result: Simulations showed epistemic value had an inverted-U relationship with generalizability and increased with outcome discriminability. Human experiments replicated the inverted-U pattern for subjective value and enjoyment ratings; choice behavior reflected sensitivity to both environmental properties.

Conclusion: The B-EUR model offers a computational framework for evaluating candidate actions in uncertainty-driven design. It provides practical implications for constructing prototype sets, framing design problems, and organizing feedback to promote informative exploration.

Abstract: This paper proposes the Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) model, which formalizes the value of trying a candidate design action as its expected reduction of epistemic uncertainty about action--outcome relations. The model addresses one part of the Uncertainty Driven Action (UDA) model's open question concerning how changes in uncertainty perception determine action selection. We examine two environmental properties: generalizability, or how far knowledge from one trial extends to neighboring candidates, and outcome discriminability, or how clearly differences among outcomes can be distinguished.
  We tested the model through simulations and human experiments using a graph-shape guessing task that isolates learning about action--outcome relations under a limited trial budget. Epistemic value followed an inverted-U-shaped relationship with generalizability and increased with outcome discriminability in the simulations. In the human experiments, the subjective value of trying and enjoyment followed inverted-U-shaped relationships with generalizability, while choice behavior reflected both properties.
  The B-EUR model provides a computational account of candidate-action evaluation within uncertainty-driven design activity and offers implications for constructing prototype sets, framing design problems, and organizing feedback to support informative exploration.

</details>


### [105] [Refining Over Resampling: Test-Time Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05643)
*Ahsan Bilal,Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin,Muhammad Umer,Lena Trigg,Ali Subhan,Muhammad Ali,Dean F. Hougen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a verifier-free breadth–depth refinement framework for test-time scaling that first samples diverse reasoning rollouts (breadth), then iteratively self-corrects each (depth), and finally aggregates via majority voting. This outperforms sampling-only, verifier-based selection, beam search, and lookahead decoding across multiple math benchmarks and model sizes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test-time compute scaling via wider sampling suffers from diminishing returns because new rollouts tend to repeat existing answer patterns rather than contributing genuine reasoning diversity. Verifier-based selection depends on well-calibrated external reward models, which may not always be available or reliable. The authors aim to use test-time compute more effectively by refining existing trajectories rather than merely sampling more or relying on external verifiers.

Method: The proposed breadth–depth refinement framework operates in three stages: (1) Breadth — sample multiple independent reasoning rollouts from the policy model to preserve diverse initial solution attempts. (2) Depth — refine each individual rollout through iterative self-critique and self-correction, where the model identifies and repairs local reasoning errors. (3) Aggregation — combine the refined answers via majority voting to produce the final output. The method is verifier-free, requiring no external reward model.

Result: Evaluated across AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500 using multiple open-weight models, the method consistently improved over greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-N, beam search, and lookahead decoding. Notable results: Qwen2.5-1.5B reached 58.0% on MATH500 (up from the strongest verifier-based baseline) and 32.5% on AMC (up from 25.0%).

Conclusion: Test-time compute is more effective when used to refine sampled trajectories (via self-critique and self-correction) rather than only to sample more candidates or rely on verifier-guided selection. The breadth–depth framework demonstrates that combining diverse exploration with targeted local repair yields stronger reasoning performance across diverse math benchmarks.

Abstract: Test-time scaling improves LLM reasoning by using additional inference compute, but wider sampling alone can suffer from diminishing returns: new rollouts often repeat existing answer patterns instead of adding useful reasoning diversity. Verifier-based selection offers an alternative, but its performance depends on the calibration of an external reward model. We propose a verifier-free breadth--depth refinement framework that uses test-time compute to both explore and improve candidate solutions. The method samples multiple independent reasoning rollouts, refines each rollout through iterative self-critique and self-correction, and aggregates the refined answers by majority voting. Breadth preserves diverse initial attempts, while depth repairs local reasoning errors before aggregation. Across AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500, our method consistently improves over greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-$N$, beam search, and lookahead decoding across multiple open-weight models. For instance, with Qwen2.5-1.5B, accuracy increases from the strongest verifier-based baseline to $58.0\%$ on MATH500, and from $25.0\%$ to $32.5\%$ on AMC. These results show that test-time compute can be more effective when used to refine sampled trajectories rather than only to sample more candidates or rely on verifier-guided selection.

</details>


### [106] [A Unified Framework for Trajectory Prediction with Explicit Planning and Reaction Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05673)
*Jiaheng Chen,Jiaxing Li,Tinghe Zhang,Chaopeng Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: INTraJ proposes a two-stage trajectory prediction framework that decomposes social influence into a planning stage (anticipating others' futures to construct reference trajectories) and a reaction stage (recovering local adjustments from residuals), achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing trajectory prediction methods inadequately distinguish functional roles of social influence. The authors observe that agents plan by anticipating others' future behaviors first, then make local reactive adjustments — i.e., planning precedes reaction. Current methods fail to capture this staged nature of social interaction.

Method: INTraJ is a unified framework that decomposes social influence into two stages: (1) a planning stage that constructs reference trajectories using future social information, and (2) a reaction stage that recovers local adjustments from the residual between full-context prediction and the reference. The framework supports both multi-target and single-target paradigms.

Result: Extensive experiments on Argoverse 2, Argoverse 2-ped, ETH/UCY, and SDD demonstrate consistent improvements, particularly in Final Displacement Error (FDE) and long-horizon consistency. State-of-the-art performance was achieved in several settings.

Conclusion: INTraJ reframes trajectory prediction as a planning-driven two-stage process, validating that staged social modeling is critical for stable predictions. Code is publicly available.

Abstract: Trajectory prediction has shifted toward structured formulations with explicit social modeling. However, existing methods inadequately distinguish the functional roles of social influence in trajectory planning. Observing that agents typically form motion plans by anticipating others' future behaviors before making local reactive adjustments, we identify social interactions as playing staged roles, namely planning precedes reaction. We propose INTraJ, a unified framework that decomposes social influence into two stages: a planning stage constructs reference trajectories using future social information, and a reaction stage recovers local adjustments from the residual between full-context prediction and the reference. INTraJ supports both multi-target and single-target paradigms. Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks, including Argoverse 2, Argoverse 2-ped, ETH/UCY, and SDD, demonstrate consistent improvements, particularly in FDE and long-horizon consistency, with state-of-the-art performance achieved in several settings. INTraJ reframes trajectory prediction as a planning-driven two-stage process, validating that staged social modeling is critical for stable predictions. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/11isnotavailable/INTraJ.

</details>


### [107] [Grounded Well-Condition Anomaly Detection on the Volve Field: Constructed Labels, a Baseline, and a Dual-Head Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05685)
*Gospel Bassey,Vincent Fakiyesi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses the gap between controlled test-rig benchmarks and real-world industrial monitoring by creating verified anomaly labels for the open Volve field dataset. The authors validate labels against engineering documentation, test their learnability with unsupervised and supervised models, and release all artifacts publicly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most public machine-condition monitoring benchmarks use controlled test rigs with artificially induced faults and known event labels. Real production environments provide only raw sensor histories without fault annotations, forcing anomaly-detection methods to self-generate labels — a process where hidden assumptions can easily go unnoticed. The authors aim to bridge this gap using real field data where labels must be constructed and validated rigorously.

Method: The authors use the open Volve field dataset from Equinor. First, they construct anomaly labels grounded in the field's engineering documentation, ensuring each label corresponds to physically plausible failure modes, and release the reasoning (provenance) behind every label. Second, they test label learnability via two approaches: (1) an unsupervised baseline to check whether detected anomalies align with the constructed labels without label exposure, and (2) a compact dual-head supervised model — adapted from prior work on metal-part defect detection — that simultaneously predicts event presence and event type. Evaluation includes cross-well generalization.

Result: The unsupervised detector identified the same anomalous regions as the rule-based labels, confirming the labels are not arbitrary. The dual-head supervised model successfully recovered both event presence and event type on unseen wells, though it localized events in time only approximately. The paper transparently reports both successes and failures along with all underlying assumptions.

Conclusion: Grounded, physically verifiable anomaly labels can be constructed for real-world field data and are learnable. Unsupervised methods independently corroborate the label quality, and a compact supervised model generalizes across wells for event detection and classification — though temporal precision remains a challenge. Full transparency via open release of data, labels, provenance, models, and code sets a new standard for reproducible industrial condition monitoring research.

Abstract: Most public benchmarks for machine-condition monitoring come from test rigs, where faults are induced on purpose and every event is known. Real production fields rarely offer that. They give you sensor histories with no fault log attached, which is exactly the situation where an anomaly-detection method has to invent its own labels, and where quiet assumptions can slip in unnoticed. We work with the open Volve field data released by Equinor and take two things seriously that such datasets usually skip. First, we build anomaly labels that are not just patterns in the numbers but are checked against what the field's own engineering documents say can physically go wrong, and we release the reasoning behind every label. Second, we test whether those constructed labels are learnable at all, using both an unsupervised baseline and a small dual-head model that marks when an event happens and what kind it is, an idea we carry over from earlier work on defect detection in metal parts. The results are honest. An unsupervised detector that never sees the labels still lands on the same regions our rules flagged, which tells us the labels are not arbitrary. A compact supervised model recovers event presence and event type well across wells it has never seen, and locates events in time only roughly. We report what worked, what did not, and every assumption in between. The dataset, grounded labels, per-label provenance, baseline scores, trained model, and code are released publicly under CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0.

</details>


### [108] [Shaping Human-AI Interactions to Provide Improvement Pathways and Balance Competing Objectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05710)
*Keziah Naggita*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This thesis investigates the design of human-AI interaction loops where individuals strategically adapt their behavior based on beliefs about AI systems. It proposes principles and methods to help users form accurate beliefs, encourage genuine improvement, discourage gaming, and maintain AI system objectives, advancing human-centered machine learning through theory, experiments, and empirical evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployed AI systems create feedback loops: evaluated individuals form beliefs about the system and strategically adapt their behavior to influence outcomes. This raises three core challenges: helping users develop accurate mental models to improve efficiently, discouraging manipulative gaming while encouraging genuine improvement, and ensuring the AI system itself continues to meet its objectives (e.g., accuracy). Existing work lacks a unified framework addressing these intertwined goals from both the human and system perspectives.

Method: The thesis is structured into three complementary parts examining human-AI interactions from dual perspectives (evaluated individuals and AI systems). Methodologically, it integrates four approaches: theoretical analysis (formalizing interaction dynamics), data-driven modeling (capturing real-world behavioral patterns), human-subject experiments (testing behavioral responses), and empirical evaluations on real-world and semi-synthetic datasets.

Result: The thesis delivers principles and methods for designing AI systems that: (1) enable individuals to develop accurate beliefs about system operation, facilitating improvement at minimal cost; (2) incentivize genuine improvement while discouraging gaming behaviors; and (3) preserve the AI system's intended objectives. The work advances human-centered machine learning by aligning system design with human needs, values, and capabilities.

Conclusion: Human-AI interaction loops require careful co-design from both the evaluator and evaluee perspectives. By integrating theoretical, empirical, and experimental methods, the thesis provides a principled foundation for building AI systems that remain effective in strategic, adaptive environments while supporting the humans who interact with them.

Abstract: When an AI system is deployed, the individuals who use and or are evaluated by it form beliefs about how the system operates and use those beliefs to strategically present their preferences, behaviors, or attributes. The system then responds with feedback or a decision outcome, thereby creating a human-AI interaction loop. This thesis studies how to design and shape such interactions to achieve three goals: (1) help individuals develop accurate beliefs about the AI systems so they can improve and or secure favorable outcomes at minimal cost, (2) encourage improvement and or discourage gaming behaviors, and (3) ensure that the AI system continues to achieve its intended objectives, such as maximizing accuracy. To address these goals, the thesis is organized into three complementary parts that examine and study human-AI interactions from the perspectives of both evaluated individuals and AI systems. Together, the work presented in this thesis advances human-centered machine learning by providing principles and methods for designing AI systems that align with human needs, values, and capabilities. Methodologically, this thesis integrates theoretical analysis, data-driven modeling, human-subject experiments, and empirical evaluations on real-world and semi-synthetic datasets.

</details>


### [109] [RA-CAD: Learning Post-Execution Critique for State-Aware Text-to-CAD Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05714)
*Shuhao Yan,Changhao He,Xi Peng,Peng Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RA-CAD introduces a state-aware agent that generates parametric CAD code through an iterative Generate-Execute-Critique-Rewrite loop, where critique becomes a learnable policy optimized via Group Relative Policy Optimization, achieving SOTA on CADFusion and Text2CAD benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing text-to-CAD methods use fixed, externally supplied, or separately optimized critique mechanisms but fail to optimize how feedback is interpreted and translated into effective corrective actions during generation. This leaves a feedback-utilization gap that limits iterative refinement quality.

Method: RA-CAD employs a two-stage training pipeline: (1) CAD Code Bootstrapping (CCB) using supervised fine-tuning on parametric CAD code to establish fundamental coding capabilities; (2) Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization (FAO) using trajectory-level Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) over the full Generate-Execute-Critique-Rewrite loop. The agent produces explicit post-execution critiques as intermediate policy actions, and both code and critique sequences receive terminal rewards based on F1 score and Chamfer Distance, making critique an outcome-aligned, learnable policy decision.

Result: RA-CAD achieves state-of-the-art execution validity and geometric quality on CADFusion and Text2CAD benchmarks, outperforming both existing methods and strong proprietary language models.

Conclusion: The state-aware agent formulation, where critique is treated as a learnable policy action optimized via trajectory-level GRPO with geometric rewards, effectively bridges the feedback-utilization gap in text-to-CAD generation, enabling superior iterative code refinement.

Abstract: Text-to-CAD generation translates natural-language design intent into editable and executable parametric computer-aided design (CAD) codes, reducing the expertise and effort required for manual modeling. Existing methods incorporate fixed, externally supplied, prompt-induced, or separately optimized critique mechanisms to optimize the generation process, but they do not necessarily optimize how feedback is interpreted and translated into effective corrective actions throughout the generation process. To bridge this feedback-utilization gap, we present RA-CAD (ReAct Agent for CAD), a state-aware agent that interacts with the CAD environment through a Generate--Execute--Critique--Rewrite loop. At each iteration, RA-CAD executes the current code and observes its outcome. Conditioned on the design instruction, current code, and execution feedback, the agent then generates an explicit post-execution critique as an intermediate policy action. This critique either validates the current result for termination or provides revision-oriented guidance that conditions the next rewrite. CAD Code Bootstrapping (CCB) first establishes fundamental parametric CAD coding capabilities through supervised fine-tuning. Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization (FAO) subsequently applies trajectory-level Group Relative Policy Optimization to both policy-generated code and critique sequences, assigning terminal F1 and Chamfer Distance rewards to the complete interaction trajectory. This formulation makes critique an outcome-aligned, learnable policy decision rather than an unoptimized auxiliary output. Experiments on CADFusion and Text2CAD show that RA-CAD achieves state-of-the-art execution validity and geometric quality compared with existing methods and strong proprietary language models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed state-aware text-to-CAD agent.

</details>


### [110] [BlockPython: A Process-Aware Agent-Supported Platform for the Transition from Block-Based to Python Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05716)
*Jesse Yusuf Chan,Haoming Wang,Mingwei Xu,Xianlong Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BlockPython is a learning platform that supports the transition from block-based to text-based programming through bidirectional block–Python translation, a four-stage learning workflow, and process-aware support mechanisms that diagnose learner difficulties using continuously collected evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learners transitioning from block-based to text-based programming face a cognitive gap: they must translate visible, concrete program structures into abstract textual syntax (Python). This gap separates understanding computational concepts from expressing them in code, and existing approaches lack integrated, evidence-driven support for bridging it.

Method: BlockPython implements: (1) bidirectional translation between blocks and Python; (2) a four-stage workflow — Task Decomposition, Block-Based Practice, Code Challenge, and Extended Interaction — that progressively connects program structure, runtime behavior, and textual code; (3) continuous collection of process evidence (block artifacts, code versions, run outcomes, support usage, dialogue); and (4) a dual support system combining a rule-based engine for execution/evaluation/stage control with an AI learning assistant that uses verified evidence to provide explanations, prompts, and guiding questions.

Result: The paper is a design report; it does not present empirical results. It describes the design rationale, learning workflow, and process-aware support mechanisms, and positions BlockPython as a reference architecture for supporting block-to-text transition and learning process analysis.

Conclusion: BlockPython offers a structured, evidence-driven approach to easing the block-to-text programming transition. By tightly integrating bidirectional translation, staged progression, and process-aware diagnosis, the platform addresses both computational understanding and syntactic expression difficulties, serving as a system-design reference for future learning environments.

Abstract: The transition from block-based to text-based programming requires learners to convert visible program structures into abstract textual expressions, which may create a cognitive gap between understanding computational concepts and expressing them in Python syntax. To support this transition, we designed and implemented BlockPython. The platform centers on bidirectional translation between blocks and Python and guides learners through four stages: Task Decomposition, Block-Based Practice, Code Challenge, and Extended Interaction. Across these stages, learners progressively establish connections among program structure, runtime behavior, and textual code. During learning, the platform continuously collects process evidence, including block artifacts, code versions, run outcomes, use of support, and dialogue. Deterministic diagnosis, program visualization, and the learning assistant use this evidence to identify different difficulties in computational understanding and Python expression. The rule-based system is responsible for program execution, objective evaluation, and stage control, while the learning assistant uses verified evidence to provide explanations, prompts, and guiding questions. This report describes the design rationale, learning workflow, and process-aware support mechanisms of BlockPython and provides a system-design reference for supporting the transition from block-based to text-based programming and for analyzing learning processes.

</details>


### [111] [Subliminal Learning is Non-Semantic Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05734)
*Ethan Hadley,Eren Gultepe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Subliminal Learning (SL) transfers biases from teacher to student models via synthetic data. This paper investigates SL mechanisms, finding that Gaussian weight noise amplifies transfer, steering vectors can generate subliminal data, students inherit the teacher's intervention type, and subliminal data gradients linearly correlate with steering vectors — suggesting pathways for data auditing in synthetic-data-driven training pipelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Subliminal Learning poses safety and predictability risks because hidden biases can be transferred through seemingly innocuous synthetic data, evading standard input auditing. Understanding the mechanisms and enablers of SL is critical as synthetic data becomes central to frontier model training.

Method: The authors (1) add Gaussian noise to teacher and student model weights to probe the role of non-semantic weight structures in SL; (2) apply steering vectors (in addition to prompting and finetuning) to teachers to generate subliminal data; (3) analyze student activations to assess whether the intervention type is inherited; and (4) examine whether gradients of steered subliminal data exhibit linear correlation with teacher steering vectors for auditing potential.

Result: Gaussian weight noise increased subliminal transfer magnitude by 1.9× in Gemma and 1.3× in Llama, implicating non-semantic weight structures. Steering vectors successfully produce subliminal data. Student models inherit not only the teacher's semantic bias but also the intervention type: steered students imitate steering vectors, prompted students do not. Gradients of steered subliminal data linearly correlate with teacher steering vectors, showing promise for data auditing.

Conclusion: SL is mediated substantially by non-semantic, weight-level structures rather than purely semantic signals. The inheritance of intervention type and the linear correlation between subliminal data gradients and steering vectors open avenues for detecting hidden signals, a capability increasingly vital as synthetic data dominates training pipelines.

Abstract: Subliminal Learning (SL) is a surprising type of generalization displayed by modern language models. It allows the transfer of a bias or behavior from a teacher model to a student by distilling from seemingly unrelated or random synthetic data from the teacher. This presents challenges in ensuring AI systems remain predictable and are trained safely, as standard auditing of the input data would not catch the hidden subliminal signal. Here, we investigate several open questions as to the enabling mechanisms and drivers of SL. First is the nature of the process by which biases are encoded in the data. We find that by adding Gaussian noise to the weights of the teacher and student models, the magnitude of subliminal transfer is increased by a factor of 1.9 in Gemma and 1.3 in Llama, suggesting that non-semantic weight structures play a crucial role. We show that steering vectors can be applied to the teacher to produce subliminal data, in addition to prompting and finetuning as used in previous studies. Analysis of the activations of the student models that have been trained on steered and prompted data demonstrates that students inherit not just the semantic meaning of the teacher's bias, but also the type of intervention that was used to apply it: steered students imitate steering vectors, prompted students do not. Additionally, the gradients of steered subliminal data show a linear correlation with the teacher's steering vectors, showing promise for data auditing. More broadly, as synthetic data becomes central to frontier training pipelines, being able to see the latent signals hidden in training data becomes paramount.

</details>


### [112] [When Do Prompt-Side Agent Playbooks Transfer? Accuracy, Cost, and Runtime Shift in Agent Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05778)
*Weihong Lin,Lin Sun,Xiangzheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Frozen playbook transfer across tool-using language agents is evaluated under a shared distill–validate–transfer protocol across three benchmarks. Transfer shows conditional benefits under controlled settings but suffers from compatibility-sensitive heterogeneity, cost inflation under context-runtime shifts, and inconsistent statistical significance. The authors conclude that frozen transfer is a conditional cold-start option, not a default reuse strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prompt-side playbooks improve tool-using language agents without retraining, but their portability beyond the original (source) setting remains unclear. The work investigates whether frozen playbooks can be effectively transferred across domains, tasks, or runtime configurations, addressing a gap in understanding the robustness and generalizability of playbook-based agent augmentation.

Method: A shared distill–validate–transfer protocol is applied across three benchmarks: ALFWorld, TAU2-Bench, and XBench-DeepSearch. Playbooks are first distilled in a source setting, then transferred frozen to target settings. Evaluations include controlled greedy decoding comparisons, budget-matched demonstration baselines, aggregate and route-level statistical contrasts with Holm correction, and analysis of artifact–runtime pairing effects.

Result: On ALFWorld, frozen transfer is beneficial under controlled greedy decoding, with distilled guidance outperforming five fixed demonstrations in one near-budget-matched comparison. On TAU2-Bench, a modest average matched-domain advantage is found, but global Holm correction retains only 1 of 135 route-level effects, revealing compatibility-sensitive heterogeneity. On XBench-DeepSearch, runtime pairing preserves first-try heuristics but induces repeated queries, delayed stopping, and substantial cost inflation after a context-runtime shift. Across all benchmarks, both transferred and target-derived playbooks require target-side validation of success, termination, protocol compatibility, and cost.

Conclusion: Frozen playbook transfer is a conditional cold-start option rather than a reuse-by-default strategy or a universally preferable alternative to target-side redistillation. Its effectiveness depends heavily on compatibility between source and target settings, and target-side validation remains essential regardless of the playbook's origin.

Abstract: Prompt-side playbooks can improve tool-using language agents without retraining, but their portability beyond the source setting is unclear. We study frozen playbook transfer under a shared distill--validate--transfer protocol. On ALFWorld, transfer is beneficial under controlled greedy decoding and, in one near-budget-matched comparison, distilled guidance outperforms five fixed demonstrations. On TAU2-Bench, a prespecified aggregate contrast supports a modest average matched-domain advantage, but global Holm correction retains only one of 135 route-level effects; the remaining grid provides descriptive evidence of compatibility-sensitive heterogeneity.
