On XBench-DeepSearch, one artifact--runtime pairing preserves useful first-try heuristics while producing repeated queries, delayed stopping, and substantial cost inflation after a context-runtime shift. Across benchmarks, transferred and target-derived playbooks both require target-side validation of success, termination, protocol compatibility, and cost. Frozen transfer is therefore a conditional cold-start option, not a reuse-by-default strategy or a universally preferable alternative to target-side redistillation.

</details>


### [113] [Activity Frames: Deterministic Screen-Activity Compilation for Agent Memory and Replay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05784)
*Nossa Iyamu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A deterministic, zero-model pipeline compiles passive screen capture into structured, auditable agent memory, achieving 86x compression and 98.4% QA accuracy—outperforming LLM summaries—while also providing the first empirical measurements of routine overhead ratio (60–343x) and delegable recurrence (~8%) for agent cost modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current computer-use agents rely on conversational memory (what the user said), forcing them to expensively re-derive routines the user has already performed. The authors aim to shift agent memory to record what the user actually did, eliminating redundant frontier-model inference and enabling precise, auditable recall of past activity.

Method: A deterministic, zero-model pipeline segments passively captured screen activity into typed activity frames and bounded episodes. Each frame carries application, site, timing, input volume, and evidence pointers to raw capture rows. The approach uses no ML model in the loop, making output byte-identical, cacheable, and mechanically auditable. The same compiler also serves as a demand-side cost instrument that reads passive, pre-delegation human activity to measure two parameters: Routine Overhead Ratio R and routine recurrence h.

Result: On a single-user corpus of 128,756 frames over 51 days: (1) a day's raw capture is reduced 86x to a prompt-ready context block in 68 ms; (2) an agent reading that block achieves 98.4% QA accuracy (Wilson 95% CI 91.7–99.7%) vs. an independent oracle, compared to 66–80% for LLM summaries; (3) a mid-tier model reading the block matches frontier-model performance; (4) first empirical R values reported at 60–343x; (5) delegable recurrence of 9.0% in-sample and 7.7% out-of-sample, with a realistic all-fleet token ceiling near 8%; (6) compiled routines replay deterministically with zero model tokens on guard-matched hits.

Conclusion: Passive screen compilation offers a practical, auditable, and highly accurate alternative to LLM-based summarization for agent memory, while simultaneously providing the first measured parameters for agent-cost models. The deterministic design yields strong compression, verifiability, and zero-inference replay, with all artifacts released open-source.

Abstract: Computer-use agents pay full frontier inference to re-derive routines their user has already performed, because an agent's memory today records what the user said, not what the user did. We compile passively captured screen activity into agent memory with a deterministic, zero-model pipeline: it segments a local capture stream into typed activity frames, bounded episodes carrying application, site, timing, input volume, and evidence pointers back to the raw rows, with no model in the loop, so the output is byte-identical, cacheable, and mechanically auditable. On one professional's single-user corpus of 128,756 frames over 51 active days, the compiler reduces a day of raw capture to a prompt-ready context block 86x smaller in 68 ms, and an agent reading that block answers questions about the day at 98.4% accuracy (Wilson 95% CI 91.7-99.7%) against an independent oracle, versus 66-80% for an LLM summary of the same capture, a mid-tier model reading the block matching a frontier one.
  The same compiler doubles as a demand-side cost instrument. Read off passive, pre-delegation human activity rather than agent rollouts, it supplies two parameters that agent-cost models assume but, to our knowledge, have not measured: the Routine Overhead Ratio R and the routine recurrence h. We report first values of R, a modeled upper bound, at 60-343x, and a delegable recurrence of 9.0% in-sample and 7.7% out-of-sample, for a realistic all-fleet token ceiling near 8%; a compiled routine replays deterministically with the model out of the loop, demonstrated live at zero model tokens on a guard-matched hit. Schema, compiler, and evaluation harness are open.

</details>


### [114] [When Agentic AI Meets Integrated Sensing and Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05792)
*Kai Li,Conggai Li,Sarah Ali Siddiqui,Syed Sohail Ahmed,Xin Yuan,Shenghong Li,Wei Ni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This survey introduces AISAC (Agentic Integrated Sensing and Communication), a paradigm framing ISAC as a goal-driven closed-loop system. It proposes a six-stage framework and five maturity levels to unify fragmented research, audits existing work against agentic criteria revealing major gaps, and identifies key open challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research on learning-based sensing, resource allocation, RIS, edge intelligence, multi-agent coordination, and resilient networking for ISAC has developed in isolation. There is no unified framework that captures the transition from function-oriented physical-layer ISAC to goal-driven, closed-loop agentic systems.

Method: The paper proposes a six-stage closed-loop framework (observation, contextualization, reasoning and prediction, planning and orchestration, execution and collaboration, feedback and resilience) and defines five levels of agentic maturity. It then reviews and audits representative studies against nine agentic-specific evaluation criteria using this framework.

Result: An audit reveals no existing system reports more than one or two of the nine agentic evaluation criteria, exposing a significant gap between claimed and demonstrated agentic maturity across the literature.

Conclusion: Open challenges remain in physical-to-semantic grounding, predictive world models, real-time agent-PHY interaction, safe tool use, heterogeneous multi-agent collaboration, benchmarking, and resource-efficient autonomy, which must be addressed for AISAC to mature into fully closed-loop intelligent systems.

Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) from a function-oriented physical-layer technology into a goal-driven, closed-loop intelligent system, a paradigm we term AISAC. Existing work on learning-based sensing, resource allocation, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), edge intelligence, multi-agent coordination, and resilient networking has developed largely in isolation. This survey unifies the literature within a six-stage closed-loop framework comprising observation, contextualization, reasoning and prediction, planning and orchestration, execution and collaboration, and feedback and resilience. It also introduces five levels of agentic maturity, ranging from physical-layer primitives to fully closed-loop agentic ISAC. We use this framework to review advances in multimodal intelligence, large language models, reinforcement learning, federated learning, RIS-assisted control, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) and vehicular networks, and AI-native network management, and analyze privacy, security, resilience, and sustainability as cross-cutting requirements of the full perception-reasoning-action loop. An audit of representative studies against nine agentic-specific evaluation criteria shows that no system reports more than one or two of them, exposing a gap between claimed and demonstrated agentic maturity. We identify open challenges in physical-to-semantic grounding, predictive world models, real-time agent-PHY interaction, safe tool use, heterogeneous multi-agent collaboration, benchmarking, and resource-efficient autonomy.

</details>


### [115] [When Self-Evolution Backfires: Pre-Commit Gating against Skill Contamination in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05810)
*Linfang Shang,Ming Xu,Yiding Sun,Tianle Xia,Lingxiang Hu,Lan Xu,Ning Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Self-evolving agents suffer a capability-contamination phase transition where accumulating skills beyond a critical pool size degrades performance due to irreversible cross-round contamination chains. The proposed Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG) uses three complementary critics and marginal-gain subset selection to filter skills pre-admission, achieving superior performance with far fewer skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors identify a fundamental failure mode in self-evolving agents: skill accumulation is non-monotonic. Beyond a critical skill pool size, performance degrades because defective skills, once admitted, become reference material for distilling subsequent skills, creating irreversible cross-round contamination chains. Post-hoc removal of bad skills cannot fix the damage their descendants have inherited.

Method: Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG) is a progressive trust hierarchy for skill admission. It employs three heterogeneous critics: (1) structural validity, (2) behavioral harmlessness, and (3) semantic consistency, which filter each candidate skill individually. A marginal-gain subset selection step then removes combinatorial contamination at the top tier before skills enter the runtime context, functioning as a pre-commit gate rather than a post-hoc fix.

Result: On Terminal-Bench 2, unconditional accumulation peaks then degrades as the pool grows; post-hoc removal recovers only a small fraction of performance — confirming irreversibility. VaG improves monotonically every round, reaching 72% pass@1 with a pool ~5x smaller. The frozen VaG skill pool transfers positively to four other backbones and a second benchmark without re-evolution. Ablations show the three critics are complementary and non-substitutable, each intercepting largely disjoint harmful skill classes.

Conclusion: Skill admission in self-evolving agents must be a pre-commit decision, not a post-hoc fix, because contamination is structurally irreversible. VaG's progressive trust hierarchy with heterogeneous critics effectively gates harmful skills before they propagate, enabling monotonic improvement, sample efficiency, and cross-model transferability.

Abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate capability by distilling reusable skills from their execution trajectories, but we find this process is not monotonic: past a critical pool size, newly added skills degrade performance instead of improving it. We formalize this capability-contamination phase transition and trace it to a structural cause: once a defective skill enters the decision context, it becomes reference material for distilling later skills, forming cross-round contamination chains. We further show the contamination is structurally irreversible: removing a source skill after the fact cannot erase the flawed reasoning its descendants have already inherited, so post-hoc rollback recovers only a small fraction of the lost performance. This makes skill admission a pre-commit necessity rather than a post-hoc fix, and motivates Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG): a progressive trust hierarchy whose three heterogeneous critics - structural validity, behavioral harmlessness, and semantic consistency - filter each skill individually, coupled with a marginal-gain subset selection that removes combinatorial contamination at the top tier before skills reach the runtime context. On Terminal-Bench 2, unconditional accumulation rises to a peak and then degrades, giving back most of its gains as the pool keeps growing, and post-hoc removal of the culprit skills recovers only a small part of the drop - the empirical signature of irreversibility. In contrast, VaG improves every round, reaching 72% pass@1 with a pool roughly 5x smaller, and its frozen skill pool transfers positively to four other backbones and a second benchmark without re-evolution. Ablations confirm the three critics are complementary and mutually non-substitutable, each intercepting a largely disjoint class of harmful skills.

</details>


### [116] [Cautious Context Steering for Language Model Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05813)
*Gihoon Kim,Jeyoung Lee,Suhan Woo,Sekwon Oh,Minsu Jeon,Hyounsoo Han,Euntai Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CCS adds a lightweight adapter to a frozen LM that learns per-token gating of user context influence, improving personalized generation across domains without per-user training and at lower inference cost than Context Steering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing personalization methods (per-user adapters, user-dependent reward models) suffer from data sparsity and poor generalization. ICL and Context Steering (CoS) avoid per-user training but are suboptimal: ICL provides uncontrolled context influence, while CoS uses a fixed steering coefficient and requires two forward passes per token. A method is needed that adaptively modulates context influence per decoding step without the inference overhead of CoS.

Method: Cautious Context Steering (CCS) trains a lightweight adapter on a frozen backbone LM. The adapter learns, at each token position, a gating mechanism that decides whether and how strongly to incorporate user context into the next-token prediction. Training uses an oracle context-conditioned LM as supervision — the adapter learns to mimic the oracle when context is beneficial and default to the base LM otherwise. Only a single CCS adapter is trained on one dataset, requiring no per-user fine-tuning.

Result: A single CCS adapter trained on one dataset improves generation quality both in-domain and across four out-of-distribution personalization benchmarks, demonstrating robust generalization to unseen users and domains. CCS also avoids the additional context-conditioned forward pass required by CoS, substantially reducing inference cost.

Conclusion: CCS offers an effective and efficient personalization approach: it adaptively modulates user context influence per token via a single portable adapter, generalizes robustly across users and domains, and reduces inference cost compared to CoS.

Abstract: Personalizing language models (LMs) to individual user preferences is essential for aligning responses with diverse goals and backgrounds. Existing methods typically train a separate adapter for each user or learn a reward model whose scores depend on the user. Despite explicitly optimizing for each user, these methods must learn from limited observations and therefore suffer from data sparsity and poor generalization to unseen users and domains. In-context learning (ICL) and Context Steering (CoS) can instead provide more effective personalization by conditioning the base LM directly on user context and leveraging its pretrained capabilities without per-user training. Yet neither adapts the influence of that context across decoding steps: ICL leaves it uncontrolled, whereas CoS applies a fixed steering coefficient and requires two LM forward passes per step. We propose Cautious Context Steering (CCS), which adds a lightweight adapter to a frozen backbone LM to decide at each token whether and how strongly user context should affect generation. The adapter learns this behavior from an oracle context-conditioned LM and preserves the base LM when the context is not helpful. A single CCS adapter trained on only one dataset improves generation quality both in-domain and across four out-of-distribution personalization benchmarks, demonstrating robust generalization to new users and domains. CCS also avoids per-user fine-tuning and the additional context-conditioned forward pass required by CoS, substantially reducing inference cost.

</details>


### [117] [ViSR-KGC: Visual Subgraph Reasoning with Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Knowledge Graph Completion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05833)
*Jiafan Li,Mengxue Yang,Jiaqi Zhu,Liang Chang,Ying Li,Hongan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ViSR-KGC proposes a visual subgraph reasoning framework for multimodal knowledge graph completion that converts query-aware subgraphs into visual images, enabling vision-language models to perform link prediction by jointly leveraging structural topology, multimodal evidence, and commonsense knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embedding-based methods struggle with limited relation-specific evidence; LLM-based linearization loses structural topology and visual information; and VLMs cannot natively interpret structured graph topology. A method is needed that bridges representation learning, multimodal reasoning, and graph structure interpretation.

Method: ViSR-KGC first extracts a compact, query-aware subgraph from the MMKG using learned multimodal embeddings. The subgraph is then rendered into a visually interpretable image via an empirically selected layout strategy. This image, along with entity images, textual descriptions, and candidate answers, forms a unified prompt for a VLM to infer the missing entity.

Result: The paper reports empirical comparison of layout strategies for subgraph visualization and demonstrates that the VLM can effectively reason over the combined visual and textual prompt to perform KGC.

Conclusion: By integrating representation learning for global topology, VLMs for local multimodal analysis, and pretrained commonsense knowledge, ViSR-KGC bridges the gap between structured graph reasoning and multimodal understanding, enabling effective MMKGC.

Abstract: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) aims to infer missing entities or relations from incomplete graph structures, and has evolved into multimodal knowledge graph completion (MMKGC), where entities are associated with multiple modalities such as text and images. Traditional representation learning approaches follow the embedding-based paradigm and may struggle when relation-specific evidence is limited. Meanwhile, LLM-based reasoning methods typically linearize graph structures into textual prompts, which obscures structural topology and neglects vital visual information. While vision-language models (VLMs) excel at multimodal reasoning, they cannot natively interpret structured graph topology, particularly when it comes to knowledge graphs where nodes and edges carry complex semantics. To bridge this gap, we propose ViSR-KGC, a visual subgraph reasoning approach for KGC. It integrates three complementary capabilities to capture semantic correlations: identifying global topology dependencies via representation learning, analyzing local multimodal evidence using VLMs, and providing necessary commonsense knowledge inherent in pre-trained models. Based on learned multimodal embeddings, our framework first extracts a compact and query-aware subgraph from the MMKG. Then, this subgraph is transformed into a visually interpretable image using a layout strategy selected through empirical comparison.Finally, the visualized subgraph, entity images, textual descriptions, and candidate answers are combined into a unified prompt, enabling the VLM to infer the missing entity.

</details>


### [118] [Runtime Observability for Heterogeneous Attention Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05863)
*Fanzhe Wei,Li Liu,Ziyang Wang,Chenyu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a runtime observability contract for modern attention memory systems (KV caches, latent caches, learned sparse selectors, recurrent states), with formal composition rules and machine-adjudicated risk tracking, validated on DeepSeek-V4 with compressed-KV, where it localizes silent corruptions to precise structural boundaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern LLM serving systems employ diverse memory architectures (plain KV, latent, sparse, recurrent), each failing under compression in distinct ways. There is no unified framework for observing, composing, and certifying memory behavior across these heterogeneous classes under runtime constraints, nor a principled method to track risk budgets and attribute failures.

Method: The authors define a runtime observability contract covering four memory classes with three operators. They instantiate it on six model configurations across five architecture families, composing per-stage bounds into a request-level risk ledger. Contracts carry error metrics as types, with composition only allowed when metrics match (enforced by machine-checked type discipline). When formal certification fails, the system automatically degrades to empirical measurement, with a three-tier hierarchy: certified, partially certified, empirical — composition inherits the weakest tier. Two bridge proofs reconcile mismatched metrics. A fused CUDA-graph probe observes a declared one-layer subset within the serving noise floor. The system runs under eight-way concurrency with per-request budgets and fail-closed identity attribution, validated on 12.4M entry reads.

Result: The risk ledger holds its budget with zero violations across 12.4M reads under eight-way concurrency. Applied to a served DeepSeek-V4 stack with packed compressed-KV, the machinery localizes silent corruption to a precise structural boundary — exact in the eviction-free identity-isolated regime. A discrimination campaign correctly rejected two of the authors' own confounded inferences. All claims receive one of three machine-determined tiers, with composition inheriting the weakest.

Conclusion: A unified typed contract framework can provide rigorous, composable runtime observability across heterogeneous attention memory systems, enabling certified risk budgeting with zero violations. The approach bridges formal verification and empirical measurement where purely formal methods are infeasible, demonstrated convincingly on production-scale DeepSeek-V4 with silent corruption localization. All results are reproducible from shipped artifacts.

Abstract: Modern models no longer keep a plain KV cache: latent caches, learned sparse selectors and recurrent states each carry the model's memory in a different form, and each fails differently under compression. We give a runtime observability contract that covers all four memory classes with three operators, instantiate it on six model configurations across five architecture families, and compose the per-stage bounds into an executable request-level risk ledger. Contracts carry their error metric as a type -- composition is only defined when metrics match, and this check rejected our own first composed chain; the repaired chain crosses metrics through two proved bridges, and whatever no formal system can certify is measured instead, dropping the composed tier to empirical automatically: every claim is certified, partially certified, or empirical, composition inherits the weakest tier, and the tier is decided by the machine. Replayed over $12.4$M entry reads and run under eight-way concurrency with per-request budgets and fail-closed identity attribution, the ledger quantifies the honest trade-off on today's witness and holds its risk budget with zero violations. A fused always-on probe observes a declared one-layer subset under CUDA graphs inside the serving noise floor. Applied to a served DeepSeek-V4 stack with a packed compressed-KV prototype, the same machinery localizes a silent corruption to a precise structural boundary -- exact in the eviction-free, identity-isolated regime, with every observed failure in an eviction or slot-reuse regime -- through a machine-adjudicated discrimination campaign whose calculus rejected two of our own confounded inferences along the way. All artifacts, guards, and the Lean development are released at https://github.com/metask-ai/witprobe-attention-memory; every number in this paper regenerates from the shipped artifacts by one command.

</details>


### [119] [Seeing Is Not Deciding: Can Multimodal LLMs Act as Effective CEOs?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05864)
*Yuyang Dai,Xueqing Peng,Yuxia Wang,Preslav Nakov,Zhuohan Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: C-SUITEBENCH evaluates multimodal LLMs as CEO agents across 50 scenarios. While visual inputs improve evidence-centric reasoning (especially risk forecasting), they paradoxically degrade resource allocation decisions due to signal crowding during decoding — revealing that visual perception and constrained action are separable bottlenecks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based decision-making agents are text-only, leaving it unclear whether models can effectively perceive and integrate visual business evidence to improve executive decision quality in high-stakes settings.

Method: The authors introduce C-SUITEBENCH, a controlled multimodal benchmark with five decision tasks under paired text-only and multimodal conditions across 50 scenarios. Nine frontier models are evaluated in the role of CEO, with ablation experiments isolating the effects of individual vs. combined visual channels.

Result: Multimodal inputs consistently improve evidence-centric reasoning, with largest gains in risk forecasting and board-facing justification. However, a "multimodal integration paradox" emerges: adding visual information degrades constrained resource allocation across all nine models. Ablations reveal this stems from signal crowding — individual visual channels help, but their combination disrupts constraint satisfaction during decoding.

Conclusion: Visual perception and constrained action are separable bottlenecks in multimodal agents. Indiscriminate visual augmentation can harm high-stakes decision-making, motivating selective grounding strategies rather than uniform multimodal enrichment for future executive AI systems.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly applied as autonomous decision-making agents. However, in executive business decisions, existing benchmarks are limited to textonly settings. This makes it unclear whether models can perceive visual business evidence and effectively integrate it to improve decision quality. We introduce C-SUITEBENCH, a controlled multimodal benchmark that includes five decision tasks under paired text-only and multimodal conditions across 50 scenarios. We place nine frontier models in the role of a chief executive officer and evaluate their decision-making ability. Multimodal inputs consistently improve evidence-centric reasoning, with the largest and most reliable gains appearing in risk forecasting and board-facing justification. However, we uncover a multimodal integration paradox: adding visual business information degrades constrained resource allocation for all nine models, even as visual grounding itself improves. Ablation experiments reveal that this failure emerges from signal crowding, although each visual channel helps individually, their combination disrupts constraint satisfaction during decoding. These findings demonstrate that visual perception and constrained action are separable bottlenecks in multimodal agents, and that indiscriminate visual augmentation can harm high-stakes decision making, motivating selective grounding strategies for future executive AI systems.

</details>


### [120] [Improving Interoperability among Defence and National Security Ontologies: Analysis and Evaluation Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05867)
*Jonathon Dilworth,Pedro Giesteira Cotovio,David Herron,Paul Cripps,Nigel Dewdney,Catia Pesquita,Ernesto Jiménez-Ruiz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper surveys over 60 publicly available defence and national security ontologies and introduces a new OAEI track featuring eight matching tasks with consensus alignments and manually-curated silver-standard mappings to benchmark ontology alignment systems in this domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the proliferation of ontologies and knowledge graphs in defence and national security—developed by academia, industry, and government—achieving interoperability across them remains a major challenge due to the domain's breadth and specialisation. There is a lack of standardised benchmarks to evaluate ontology alignment systems in this domain.

Method: The authors analysed and documented over 60 publicly available defence/national security ontologies. They then constructed a new OAEI track comprising eight ontology matching tasks. Consensus alignments were derived by aggregating outputs from several state-of-the-art ontology alignment systems. A subset of unique mappings (those suggested by only one system) together with the consensus alignment were manually validated to produce a silver-standard reference alignment.

Result: A comprehensive survey of 60+ defence and national security ontologies was produced. A new OAEI benchmark track was established with eight matching tasks, complete with consensus alignments and silver-standard mappings derived from both automated aggregation and manual curation.

Conclusion: The new OAEI track provides a foundational benchmarking resource for ontology alignment in the defence and national security domain, facilitating systematic evaluation and progress toward semantic interoperability across heterogeneous defence ontologies.

Abstract: The use of ontologies and knowledge graphs is becoming increasingly widespread in the defence and national security domain. Numerous ontologies have been developed through initiatives led by academia, industry, and government. Achieving interoperability across diverse defence and national security ontologies remains a major challenge due to the domain's breadth and specialisation. In this work, we analyse and document over 60 publicly available ontologies and introduce a new track for the Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative (OAEI). This track comprises eight matching tasks, consensus alignments and manually-curated (silver-standard) mappings. The consensus alignments are derived by aggregating the outputs of several state-of-the-art ontology alignment systems. The silver-standard is obtained from the manual validation of the consensus alignment together with a subset of the unique mappings (i.e., mappings suggested by only one system).

</details>


### [121] [Personalized Deep Research Query Refinement with Graph-Scaffolded Evidence Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05876)
*Soojin Yoon,Dongha Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: G-STEER refines user requests into personalized research specifications for deep research agents by learning a clarification policy from an Intent Elicitation Graph, balancing coverage of framing factors against evidence acquisition costs. It achieves superior personalization while asking significantly fewer user questions than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalized deep research requires user requests to reflect individual goals, constraints, preferences, and evaluation criteria. Existing approaches either embed user context within the research pipeline or into the input specification. The authors focus on refining the user request into a personalized research specification before feeding it to an unchanged deep research agent. The core challenge is resolving three interdependent decisions: identifying relevant framing factors, assessing whether available user context supports them, and determining whether to retrieve user memory, ask the user, or stop and refine.

Method: G-STEER structures framing factors as elicitation targets in an Intent Elicitation Graph that captures their dependencies. It learns a clarification policy from graph-scaffolded trajectories that span diverse factor dependencies and evidence conditions. During inference, the policy selects actions (retrieve memory, ask user, or stop/refine) to produce a refined query, optimizing for target coverage while minimizing evidence acquisition costs.

Result: G-STEER achieves the strongest overall weighted target coverage and the highest downstream report personalization across two evaluated deep research agents (DRAs), while asking approximately one third as many user questions as a strong clarification baseline.

Conclusion: G-STEER offers an effective approach to personalized deep research by decoupling user context incorporation from the research pipeline itself. By learning a clarification policy grounded in an Intent Elicitation Graph, it efficiently resolves what to elicit and how, yielding high-quality personalized specifications with substantially lower user burden.

Abstract: User requests serve as research specifications for deep research agents, shaping what evidence to seek and how to synthesize it. In personalized deep research, these specifications must additionally reflect user goals, constraints, preferences, and evaluation criteria. User context can be incorporated either within the deep research pipeline or into the research specification provided as its input. We focus on the latter, refining the user request into a personalized research specification before passing it to an unchanged deep research agent. This requires resolving three coupled decisions: which framing factors are relevant, whether the available user context sufficiently supports them, and whether to retrieve user memory, ask the user, or stop and refine the query. For training, G-STEER organizes framing factors as elicitation targets in an Intent Elicitation Graph that captures their dependencies. It learns a clarification policy from graph-scaffolded trajectories spanning diverse factor dependencies and evidence conditions. The policy produces a refined query while balancing target coverage against the costs of evidence acquisition. Experiments show that G-STEER achieves the strongest overall weighted target coverage and the highest downstream report personalization across both evaluated DRAs, while asking roughly one third as many user questions as a strong clarification baseline.

</details>


### [122] [AppDeltaWorld: Transition-Grounded Delta Code World Model for Mobile GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05891)
*Weikai Xu,Yunren Feng,Haoxiang Lei,Kun Huang,Yuxuan Liu,Kang Zhao,Xiaolin Hu,Shuo Shang,Bo An*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AppDeltaWorld is a world model for mobile GUI agents that predicts the next GUI state as a reachable code update (delta HTML) rather than raw images/text. It retrieves app-specific HTML references, generates executable HTML conditioned on current screen/action/predicted next-screen text, and inserts visual assets before rendering. It achieves state-of-the-art fidelity on CMGUIBench-500 and enables filtered closed-loop SFT data construction and test-time RL that boost mobile agent performance across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real mobile GUI trajectories are hard to collect for sensitive/privacy-critical apps, and existing simulated environments are expensive to scale. Current GUI world models suffer from unstable generation, limited modality coverage (text-only or image-only), and inconsistent action-transition logic. A better world model is needed that can faithfully simulate app interactions for training mobile agents without relying on real app data.

Method: AppDeltaWorld is a transition-grounded delta code world model operating at two levels: Level-1 retrieves app-specific HTML references under action-transition constraints; Level-2 generates executable HTML conditioned on the current screen, action, predicted next-screen text, and retrieved structure. Visual assets are inserted into image slots before browser rendering. The delta-code formulation predicts reachable code updates rather than unconstrained images/text. This world model supports filtered closed-loop SFT data construction and test-time reinforcement learning for policy adaptation.

Result: AppDeltaWorld achieves highest fidelity on CMGUIBench-500 under Code2World evaluation, with clear gains in structural layout and UI element reconstruction over image-only and code-only baselines. As a training environment, AppDeltaAgent (trained with AppDeltaWorld-filtered SFT data) achieves SOTA on AndroidLens and consistent gains on MobileGym and MobileWorld. Test-time RL using the world model yields further improvements without additional real app interactions.

Conclusion: AppDeltaWorld demonstrates that a transition-grounded delta code approach to GUI world modeling overcomes key limitations of prior image/text-based world models, enabling both high-fidelity simulation and effective training data construction. Combined with test-time RL, it provides a practical path for improving mobile GUI agents without requiring additional costly or privacy-sensitive real-world data collection.

Abstract: Mobile GUI agents can operate apps through pixel perception and touch actions, making them a promising interface for collecting and improving long-horizon mobile interaction policies. However, real trajectories are difficult to obtain for sensitive apps and privacy-critical operations. At the same time, existing simulated environments are costly to scale up, and GUI world models still suffer from unstable generation, limited modality coverage, and inconsistent action-transition logic. To address these limitations, we propose AppDeltaWorld, a transition-grounded delta code world model that predicts the next GUI as a reachable code update rather than as an unconstrained image or text description. AppDeltaWorld retrieves app-specific Level-1 HTML references under an action-transition constraint, generates Level-2 executable HTML conditioned on the current screen, action, predicted next-screen text, and retrieved structure, and inserts generated visual assets into image slots before browser rendering. As a world model, AppDeltaWorld achieves the highest fidelity on CMGUIBench-500 under Code2World evaluation, with clear gains in structural layout and UI element reconstruction over image-only and code-only baselines. As a training environment, AppDeltaWorld supports filtered closed-loop SFT data construction that, when combined with public supervision, enables AppDeltaAgent to achieve state-of-the-art performance on AndroidLens and consistent gains on MobileGym and MobileWorld. Moreover, world-model-based test-time reinforcement learning enables policy adaptation and shows further improvements without additional interaction with real apps.

</details>


### [123] [ECG-LENS: Lead-Aware Clinical Context Enriched ECG Report Generation and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05893)
*Akanta Das,Tasinul Islam Ahon,Ahmed Mahir Sultan Rumi,Md Mahbubur Rahman,Tausif Amim Shadly,Tanzima Hashem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ECG-LENS is an end-to-end framework for generating clinical ECG reports that integrates multi-lead signal modeling, diagnosis-aware representations, and clinically grounded text generation, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on PTB-XL and MIMIC-IV-ECG with a new ECG-specific evaluation metric, F1-ECGBERT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automating multi-lead ECG report generation is challenging due to the need for subtle temporal morphology analysis and coherent diagnostic reasoning in dense clinical terminology. Existing systems focus on classification, and current report-generation methods produce outputs inadequate for clinical use.

Method: ECG-LENS uses lead-wise encoders for localized waveform morphology, a global encoder for inter-lead dependencies, diagnosis-aware representations fused with clinically enriched textual prompts, and a GPT-2 decoder guided by these fused signals. An ECG-specific preprocessing strategy filters for clinically meaningful findings. A new BERT-based metric, F1-ECGBERT, measures diagnostic label agreement between generated and reference reports.

Result: ECG-LENS achieves absolute gains of 4.0% in METEOR, 6.3% in ROUGE-L, and 11.5% in F1-ECGBERT over the strongest baselines on PTB-XL (in-domain) and MIMIC-IV-ECG (cross-domain).

Conclusion: Jointly modeling multi-lead signals with diagnosis-aware conditioning and a clinically focused preprocessing strategy significantly improves automated ECG report generation. F1-ECGBERT provides a more clinically meaningful alternative to lexical metrics.

Abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG) is one of the most widely used non-invasive tools for diagnosing cardiovascular disease, but transforming multi-lead ECG recordings into reliable clinical reports remains challenging. Automating ECG report generation could reduce clinicians' interpretive workload, improve diagnostic efficiency, and expand access to cardiac assessment in underserved communities. Unlike image-based report-generation tasks, ECG interpretation requires the analysis of subtle temporal morphologies, followed by coherent diagnostic reasoning expressed in dense clinical terminology. Existing systems predominantly focus on classification, while current report-generation methods often produce outputs that remain inadequate for practical clinical use. To address these challenges, we propose ECG-LENS, an end-to-end ECG report-generation framework that jointly integrates multi-lead signal modeling, diagnosis-aware representations, and clinically grounded text generation. ECG-LENS combines lead-wise encoders that preserve localized waveform morphology with a global encoder that captures inter-lead dependencies. To guide report generation, we fuse signal representations with clinically enriched textual prompts that condition a GPT-2 decoder. We further introduce an ECG-specific report-preprocessing strategy that helps the model focus on clinically meaningful findings. Finally, because lexical metrics may under- or overestimate report quality, we propose F1-ECGBERT, a BERT-based, ECG-specific metric that measures agreement between diagnostic labels extracted from generated and reference reports. In-domain experiments on PTB-XL and cross-domain evaluation on MIMIC-IV-ECG show that ECG-LENS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with absolute gains of 4.0%, 6.3%, and 11.5% in METEOR, ROUGE-L, and F1-ECGBERT, respectively, over the strongest baselines.

</details>


### [124] [GSBF: Gaussian Splatting for Environment-Aware Beamforming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05896)
*Yijie Bian,Wei Guo,Zixin Wang,Shenghui Song,Jun Zhang,Khaled B. Letaief*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GSBF uses 3D Gaussian splatting with bidirectional spherical Gaussian kernels to render angular propagator maps from environment geometry, enabling direct beam synthesis from AP pose and user position without instantaneous CSI or iterative optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional MIMO beamforming requires accurate instantaneous CSI and iterative optimization, causing high pilot overhead and computational complexity. Since radio propagation is governed by physical geometry, a persistent environment representation can eliminate these requirements.

Method: GSBF models environmental scattering via reciprocity-preserving bidirectional spherical Gaussian (Bi-SG) kernels within a 3D Gaussian splatting framework. It performs two-sided electromagnetic rasterization to render an angular propagator map, then aggregates through an over-complete array-manifold dictionary and projects to constant-modulus beamformers.

Result: Simulations show GSBF consistently outperforms baselines including exhaustive beam alignment (EBA) while achieving lower latency.

Conclusion: Environment-aware beamforming via 3D Gaussian splatting enables efficient, low-latency beam synthesis without online CSI, offering a promising alternative to conventional beamforming approaches.

Abstract: Beamforming plays a key role in multiple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) communication systems. However, conventional beamforming design normally requires accurate instantaneous channel state information (CSI) and iterative optimization, which incur substantial pilot overhead and computational complexity. Recognizing that radio propagation is intrinsically governed by the physical geometry, we develop a 3D Gaussian splatting for environment-aware beamforming (GSBF) pipeline based on multi-modal data, which characterizes the environment through a persistent 3D Gaussian representation. Specifically, GSBF models the environmental scattering response with reciprocity-preserving bidirectional spherical Gaussian (Bi-SG) kernels and performs two-sided electromagnetic rasterization to render an angular propagator map. The rendered map is then aggregated through an over-complete array-manifold dictionary and projected to the constant-modulus beamformers, thereby synthesizing beams directly from the access point (AP) pose and user position without online instantaneous CSI. Simulations demonstrate that GSBF consistently outperforms baselines such as exhaustive beam alignment (EBA) with lower latency.

</details>


### [125] [CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910)
*Arthur Nijdam,Paul Stankovski Wagner,Sara Ramezanian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CourseGraph is an automated methodology using BERT-based semantic representation and a Random Forest classifier to detect course overlap between a student's home curriculum and external courses taken abroad, addressing a key challenge in student mobility programs like Erasmus+.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Student mobility programs (e.g., Erasmus+) allow students to take courses at other universities, but this creates a practical challenge: ensuring that external courses do not substantially overlap with courses already in the student's home curriculum. Currently, this assessment is done manually by curriculum administrators, which is time-consuming and lacks automation.

Method: CourseGraph extracts course titles, descriptions, and learning outcomes from course webpages. This textual information is then semantically encoded using a BERT-based language model to compute pairwise similarity between courses. Finally, a Random Forest classifier uses these similarity features to determine whether a candidate external course overlaps with a course in the student's home curriculum.

Result: The methodology was evaluated on two datasets: (1) the Computer Science program at Eindhoven University of Technology, containing courses with known substantial overlap, and (2) six approved international programs from Lund University's Computer Science program with corresponding administrative decisions. Experimental results demonstrate that CourseGraph effectively identifies overlapping courses.

Conclusion: CourseGraph provides an effective, automated approach for identifying overlapping courses and supporting curriculum alignment across universities, reducing the manual burden on curriculum administrators in student mobility contexts.

Abstract: Student mobility programs such as Erasmus+ enable students to take courses at other universities, broadening their academic and cultural horizons. However, this flexibility also leads to a practical challenge: ensuring that students do not take courses elsewhere that substantially overlap with courses in their home curriculum. In this work, we propose CourseGraph, a methodology that automates the evaluation of external courses based on insights obtained from the process followed by curriculum administrators when assessing courses for inclusion in a degree program. Course- Graph extracts information such as course titles, descriptions, and learning outcomes from the course webpage. Then, this information is represented semantically using a BERT-based language model, after which the pair-wise similarity between courses can be computed. This information is then used by a Random Forest classifier to determine whether a candidate course abroad overlaps with a course already contained in the student's curriculum. We evaluate CourseGraph using (1) the Computer Science program at Eindhoven University of Technology, which contains information about courses with substantial overlap, and (2) six approved international programs from students enrolled in the Computer Science program at Lund University, including the corresponding decisions made by a curriculum administrator. The experimental results indicate that CourseGraph provides an effective approach for identifying overlapping courses and supporting curriculum alignment across universities.

</details>


### [126] [GAUGE: A Measurement-Grounded Benchmark for Physical Fidelity in Simulation Engines and Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05948)
*Shuai Wang,Yaxin Feng,Xuekun Jiang,Shihan Tian,Ningyu Yan,Xing Shen,Chaoyang Lyu,Hui Wang,Yunsong Zhou,Hanqing Wang,Jiangmiao Pang,Yang Xiang,Xing Gao,Chunhua Shen,Weinan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GAUGE is a real-world-grounded diagnostic benchmark with 22 task families for jointly evaluating physics engines and generative video world models on physical fidelity. It reveals no simulator is uniformly faithful, with largest errors in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation, while video models can produce correct equation forms but wrong physical parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of physical fidelity for simulators and video world models are conducted in isolation, rely on perceptual similarity or human judgment, and provide limited insight into which specific physical principles or parameters are violated. There is no unified benchmark grounded in real-world data for jointly diagnosing physics engines and generative world models.

Method: GAUGE comprises 22 controlled task families across rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects. Tasks are grounded in real-world trajectories with calibrated physical metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables covering collision, friction, momentum transfer, oscillation, self-contact, and deformation. Three physics engines (Isaac Sim, Genesis, Newton) are benchmarked on 14 task families using generalized trajectory errors, and six image-to-video models are evaluated on 5 rigid-body tasks via physical-law consistency and temporal stability of inferred parameters.

Result: No physics engine is uniformly faithful; the largest discrepancies occur in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation. Video world models can generate trajectories matching the expected equation form while recovering incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing.

Conclusion: GAUGE provides a foundation for developing more physically faithful simulators and world models for embodied intelligence by enabling systematic, real-world-grounded diagnosis of physical fidelity across multiple simulators and generative models.

Abstract: Physics engines facilitate large-scale training and evaluation for embodied intelligence, while generative video world models are emerging as implicit simulators of future states and interactions. However, existing evaluations of physical fidelity are often conducted in isolation and rely heavily on perceptual similarity or human judgments, providing limited insight into which physical principles or parameters are violated. We introduce GAUGE, a real-world-grounded diagnostic benchmark for jointly evaluating how numerical simulators and generative video world models reproduce or deviate from real-world physics. It comprises 22 controlled task families covering rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects. Grounded in real-world trajectories and paired with calibrated physical metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables, these tasks cover fundamental physical processes including collision, friction, momentum transfer, oscillation, self-contact, and deformation across diverse materials and conditions. We benchmark Isaac Sim, Genesis, and Newton on 14 task families using generalized trajectory errors, and evaluate 6 image-to-video models on 5 rigid-body tasks by testing physical-law consistency and the temporal stability of inferred parameters. Our results reveal no uniformly faithful physics engine, with the largest discrepancies arising in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation. We further find that video world models can produce trajectories with the expected equation form while recovering incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing. GAUGE lays the groundwork for developing more physically faithful simulators and world models for embodied intelligence.

</details>


### [127] [VLMs for Videogame Data Annotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05949)
*Katrin Schmid,Iuri Frosio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VLMs struggle to annotate video game frames with reliable reward signals due to synthetic variability and physics non-compliance. The paper examines VLM limitations, proposes countermeasures (output mixing, prompt optimization), and analyzes how sequence length, resolution, and batching affect annotation quality and token cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLM and AI agent adoption in video games is hindered by extreme variability of synthetic scenarios and poor real-world physics compliance. There is a need to assess whether VLMs can reliably annotate game frame sequences with reward signals for applications like conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning, and to understand their failure modes.

Method: Empirical evaluation of VLMs on video game frame annotation tasks, primarily racing games but also other genres. The authors test VLM performance on basic game-state questions, then explore countermeasures including VLM output mixing and prompt optimization. They systematically vary input sequence length, resolution, and question batching to measure effects on annotation quality and token consumption.

Result: VLMs often fail to answer basic questions about racing video game frames. Output mixing and prompt optimization help mitigate these failures. Input sequence length, resolution, and question batching significantly influence both annotation quality and token consumption.

Conclusion: VLMs are currently unreliable for out-of-the-box video game frame annotation with reward signals. Practical deployment requires careful tuning of input parameters and mitigation strategies like output mixing and prompt engineering to improve reliability and manage computational cost.

Abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents have revolutionized how engineers approach complex problems in real-world applications. Their adoption in video games is on the other hand limited by the extreme variability of the synthetic scenarios and their poor compliance with real-world physics. Here we investigate the use of VLMs for annotating video game frame sequences with reward signals, a task with several potential applications including, among others, conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning. We show that VLMs often struggle to answer basic questions on racing video games (although we observed a similar behavior on other game genres) and discuss countermeasures such as VLM output mixing and prompt optimization. We also show how input sequence length, resolution, and question batching affect the annotation quality and its token consumption.

</details>


### [128] [Training a Conditioned Video Game Agent on a VLM Annotated Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05954)
*Katrin Schmid,Iuri Frosio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes using Vision Language Models to annotate video game datasets with human-defined rewards, enabling offline RL training of a return-conditioned agent, while discussing early experimental challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional RL for video games faces three key pain points: (1) requiring access to the game engine for reward collection, (2) laborious trial-and-error reward design and weighting, and (3) difficulty interpreting how sparse rewards shape learned policies. The authors seek to bypass these issues by leveraging VLMs for automated reward annotation.

Method: The approach uses Vision Language Models (VLMs) to annotate pre-collected video game datasets by extracting human-defined reward signals directly from gameplay frames. These reward-annotated datasets then serve as input for offline RL, which trains a return-conditioned agent — an agent that modulates its behavior based on desired return targets rather than relying on environment-interactive reward collection.

Result: The paper presents early experimental findings demonstrating that offline RL with VLM-annotated rewards can train a conditioned agent responsive to desired returns. However, the authors also report emerging difficulties and limitations encountered during these initial experiments, though specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: VLM-based reward annotation combined with offline RL offers a promising direction to reduce the engineering burden of reward design in game-playing agents, but significant challenges remain that require further investigation.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a powerful but far from easy-to-use technique for policy learning. In the specific case of video games, access to the game engine is required to get rewards for training (e.g. to collect rewards from the environment). Furthermore, the proper identification and weighting of the rewards generally requires a difficult trial-and-error approach. Lastly, rewards are often sparse and understanding how they eventually affect the learned policy is a non-trivial exercise. To ease these issues we propose annotating a video game dataset with Vision Language Models (VLMs) instructed to extract human defined rewards. We show that offline RL can then be used to train a conditioned agent that responds accordingly to the desired returns and we discuss the difficulties and limitations that emerged in our early experiments.

</details>


### [129] [Stability of Ranking-dependent Pair-wise Comparison Patterns in the Analytic Hierarchy Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05958)
*Vitaliy Tsyganok,Sergii Kadenko,Oleh Andriichuk*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper compares three pairwise comparison methods in AHP — Best-Worst, Top 2, and Maximum Difference — to determine which incomplete ranking-dependent pattern is most stable against expert errors, aiming to reduce comparisons without sacrificing credibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the quality of expert data and reduce the cognitive burden on experts by leveraging ordinal information to minimize the number of pairwise comparisons needed, while maintaining result credibility in uncertain decision-making environments.

Method: The authors analytically determine conditions for comparability among the three methods (Best-Worst, Top 2, Maximum Difference) regarding stability to expert errors, then conduct a simulation experiment to empirically compare their performance.

Result: The research identifies the most stable incomplete ranking-dependent pairwise comparison pattern and demonstrates that the number of comparisons can be significantly reduced without loss of credibility in expert session results.

Conclusion: The findings contribute to algorithmic, cognitive, and applied aspects of decision support in uncertain environments by providing a more efficient and error-resilient approach to pairwise comparisons in AHP.

Abstract: The paper addresses several ranking-dependent decision support methods. Ordinal information on compared objects can be used to improve the quality of expert data during estimation and help reduce the number of comparisons that the experts need to perform. In the paper we compare three incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison patterns which can be used in the Analytic Hierarchy Process - Best-worst method, Best-Second Best (Top 2) method, and the original maximum difference method. The first two comparison patterns (and respective methods) are incomplete, while the third can be a complete one. We determine conditions under which these three methods can be compared in terms of stability to expert errors. We also present the results of a simulation-type experiment, in which the three methods are compared. The research allows us to define the most stable incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison pattern and reduce the number of comparisons without loss of credibility of expert session results. The research contributes to algorithmic, cognitive, and applied aspects of decision support in uncertain environments.

</details>


### [130] [Temporal Bridges for Spatial Resolution: Enhancing Climate Data Super-Resolution with Bidirectional Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05981)
*Yichen Zhang,Yixiong Xiao,Congxi Xiao,Jingbo Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a temporal-enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment for climate data super-resolution, addressing the limitation of existing methods that only use single-frame spatial information by explicitly modeling temporal correlations between consecutive frames to improve SR performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-resolution climate data is expensive to obtain, motivating data-driven super-resolution from low-resolution inputs. Existing deep learning methods focus only on single-frame spatial information and neglect temporal correlations across frames. Additionally, climate data's stochastic and noisy nature makes standard temporal alignment methods like optical flow ineffective, creating a gap for a framework that can capture implicit temporal dependencies in climate data SR.

Method: The proposed framework consists of three components: (1) Paired Latent Mapping, which unifies latent spaces to achieve spatial alignment and noise reduction; (2) Bidirectional Temporal Alignment, which captures temporal correlations by training forward and backward networks on consecutive latent frames; and (3) Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution, which jointly optimizes the entire framework for climate data SR.

Result: Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrated the superior performance of the proposed framework compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: The Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment effectively bridges temporal information to enhance spatial resolution in climate data super-resolution, overcoming limitations of prior single-frame approaches and establishing a viable solution for capturing implicit temporal correlations in stochastic climate data.

Abstract: High-resolution climate data is crucial for meteorological predictions and for informing decision support across diverse domains. However, the acquisition of such high-resolution climate information is often prohibitively costly, necessitating the development of data-driven meteorological prediction models. These models aim to generate fine-grained climate data from low-resolution inputs, a process termed climate data super-resolution (SR). Nevertheless, recent advancements in deep learning for climate data SR have primarily focused on leveraging single-frame spatial information, largely neglecting the temporal correlations between different time frames that could enhance SR outcomes. Furthermore, climate data are inherently stochastic and noisy, rendering widely used temporal alignment methods, such as optical flow models, ineffective in this context. Consequently, the development of a framework tailored for climate data SR that effectively captures implicit temporal correlations remains an unresolved challenge. To this end, we propose a novel Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment. In essence, our framework establishes a temporal bridge to enhance spatial resolution in climate data SR through bidirectional alignment, leading to improved SR performance. Within this framework, Paired Latent Mapping achieves spatial alignment and noise reduction by unifying latent spaces. Then a Bidirectional Temporal Alignment captures temporal correlations by training forward and backward networks on consecutive latent frames. Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution then optimizes the entire framework for climate data SR. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrated the superior performance of our framework.

</details>


### [131] [AgentOPSD: Recursive Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05987)
*Zi-Han Wang,Zhengxi Lu,Zhiyuan Yao,Jinyang Wu,Jie Wu,Zhengzhou Cai,Yueqing Sun,Ziang Ye,Linji Hao,Qi Gu,Xunliang Cai,Yongliang Shen,Yujiu Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentOPSD is a critic-free, recursive credit assignment method for agentic RL that converts sparse outcome rewards into turn-level signals using Bayesian belief updates in log-odds space, outperforming GRPO and self-distillation baselines on long-horizon benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RL with verifiable rewards computes trajectory-level advantages but fails to identify the few critical decisions that drive outcomes in long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks. While privileged self-distillation offers denser supervision, it is unclear how such local signals should represent sequential credit assignment.

Method: AgentOPSD operates in three stages: (1) token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps are aggregated into turn-level evidence; (2) a Bayesian belief state is recursively updated in log-odds space using this evidence; (3) turn-level credit signals are derived from the marginal belief revision between consecutive states, producing a principled reweighting scheme. The method requires no critic network and no extra rollouts, integrating directly with standard policy optimization.

Result: AgentOPSD achieves 89.1% success on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B, outperforming GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines. Gains are validated across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA using Qwen2.5 at 3B and 7B scales. Ablations confirm that turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive belief updates are key drivers of performance.

Conclusion: AgentOPSD provides an effective, principled framework for turn-level credit assignment in agentic RL, demonstrating that recursive Bayesian belief updates over aggregated token-level signals can reliably identify pivotal decisions and improve policy optimization without additional computational overhead.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards constructs trajectory-level advantage estimates, yet it often fails to credit the few pivotal decisions that determine outcomes in long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks. Recent work introduces privileged self-distillation for credit assignment, providing denser supervision, but it remains unclear how such local signals should represent sequential credit. We propose AgentOPSD, a critic-free, recursive method for turn-level credit assignment in agentic reinforcement learning. AgentOPSD aggregates token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and recursively updates a Bayesian belief state in log-odds space. This yields a principled reweighting scheme that converts sparse outcome supervision into turn-level credit signals and identifies pivotal turns through the marginal belief revision between consecutive states. The method is fully compatible with standard policy optimization and requires neither an additional critic nor extra rollouts. We evaluate AgentOPSD on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA using Qwen2.5 models at two scales (3B and 7B). AgentOPSD outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines, achieving 89.1% success on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablation studies attribute the gains to turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive belief updates.

</details>


### [132] [OPERA: Operator-residual feedback for reliable autonomous optical experiments with language-model agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05990)
*Ning Xu,Xiang Zheng,Fuqiang Zhong,Huadong Wang,Xiaolong Wu,Zhiyuan Liu,Hui Ning*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPERA is an operator-residual framework for autonomous optical experiments that replaces score-only feedback with physically interpretable operators and residuals, dramatically reducing decisions that increase scores without genuine physical improvement (from 23.6–39.0% to 0.9–1.9%) and improving target attainment and budget efficiency across multiple optical tasks and instruments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous agents in experimental settings typically rely on abstract scores for decision-making, but these scores can be gamed or misaligned with actual physical success. The authors identify a critical failure mode: score increases that do not correspond to real experimental improvement, motivating a framework grounded in physically measurable evidence rather than black-box scoring.

Method: OPERA frames experimental actions as optical operators (executable changes to measurement, control, or reconstruction) and evaluates outcomes via physically interpretable residuals (departures from specified physical conditions). The agent selects, combines, or generates operators guided by these residuals, while independent evaluation uses a withheld reference. Protocols are developed in digital twins and then transferred to real optical instruments.

Result: Across three optical tasks, score-only feedback yielded score increases without physical improvement in 23.6–39.0% of decisions, versus only 0.9–1.9% for operator-residual feedback. Operator-residual feedback also increased the probability of reaching and maintaining task targets and reduced experimental budgets. In structured-light reconstruction, transferred protocols achieved a lower projection budget in repeated physical experiments across three instruments.

Conclusion: Operators and residuals together provide a principled alternative to score-based feedback for autonomous experimentation, grounding agent decisions in measurable physical evidence, improving reliability, and enabling successful transfer from simulation to real-world optical instruments.

Abstract: Autonomous agents choose actions using scores that may not reflect experimental success. We developed OPERA, an operator-residual framework for optical experiments. It represents experimental actions as optical operators and evaluates their outcomes using physically interpretable residuals. Operators specify executable changes to measurement, control or reconstruction, while residuals report departures from specified physical conditions. The agent uses both to select, combine or generate operators, and physical performance is evaluated independently against a withheld reference. Across three optical tasks, score-only feedback produced score increases without physical improvement in 23.6--39.0\% of decisions, compared with 0.9--1.9\% for operator-residual feedback. Operator-residual feedback increased the probability of reaching and maintaining task targets and reduced experimental budgets. Protocols selected in digital twins were transferred to three optical instruments, and repeated experiments showed a lower projection budget in structured-light reconstruction. Together, operators and residuals guide autonomous decisions using measurable physical evidence.

</details>


### [133] [Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Herd-Level Cattle Growth Pattern and Weight Gain Forecasting in Grazing-Based Production Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06001)
*Muhammad Riaz Hasib Hossain,Rafiqul Islam,Shawn R. McGrath,Md Zahidul Islam,David W. Lamb*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A hybrid ML framework forecasts herd-level cattle weight using sparse automated sensing data. The cascade GB→RF→NN architecture performed best (R²=0.889, RMSE=21.32 kg), outperforming ARIMA/LSTM/GRU baselines, with age, rainfall, and temperature as dominant predictors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commercial grazing systems produce irregular, sparse livestock observations that undermine traditional cattle growth forecasting methods. Reliable weight prediction is needed for feed allocation, grazing management, and marketing decisions, but existing sequential models (ARIMA, LSTM, GRU) lack robustness under heterogeneous, sparse sensing conditions.

Method: The authors developed a hybrid machine learning framework using automated sensing data (2022–2024, southeastern Australia). Weekly live weight, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors were structured into forecasting datasets. Herd-level trajectories were obtained by temporally aggregating animal-level predictions. Four hybrid architecture families were evaluated: residual, stacked, cascade, and ensemble-assisted frameworks, benchmarked against ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU. Feature importance analysis was performed to identify dominant predictors.

Result: The cascade GB→RF→NN architecture achieved the best independent test performance: R²=0.889, RMSE=21.319 kg, MAE=15.462 kg. Hybrid architectures demonstrated greater robustness than recurrent sequential models under sparse observation conditions. Forecasting error increased progressively across extended prediction horizons. Feature importance identified animal age, rainfall, and temperature as the dominant predictors of herd-level growth.

Conclusion: Hybrid ML architectures—particularly the cascade design combining gradient boosting, random forest, and neural networks—offer superior robustness and accuracy for cattle weight forecasting in commercial grazing systems with irregular sensing. The framework can support operational decisions in feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing.

Abstract: Commercial grazing systems yield irregular livestock observations, which challenge cattle growth forecasting. This study developed a hybrid machine learning framework for herd level cattle weight forecasting using automated sensing observations collected between 2022 and 2024 in southeastern Australia. Weekly live weight observations, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors were integrated into structured forecasting datasets. Herd level forecasting trajectories were generated through temporal aggregation of animal level predictions. Four hybrid architecture families were evaluated, including residual, stacked, cascade, and ensemble assisted frameworks. ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU models were used as comparative baselines. Independent testing demonstrated strong predictive agreement across multiple forecasting horizons. The cascade GB to RF to NN architecture achieved the best performance, with a test R^2 of 0.889, RMSE of 21.319 kg, and MAE of 15.462 kg. Hybrid architectures maintained greater robustness than recurrent sequential models under sparse observation conditions. Forecasting error increased progressively across extended prediction horizons. Feature importance analysis identified animal age, rainfall, and temperature as dominant predictors influencing herd level growth forecasting. The proposed framework may support feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing decisions under heterogeneous sensing environments.

</details>


### [134] [HERALD: Counterfactual Audits and Minimal Repairs for Proof-of-Retrieval Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06012)
*Zhuowen Liu,Bohan Cui,YinShang Guo,Yuting Wang,Hao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HERALD is an offline audit framework that identifies and repairs vulnerabilities in search-agent reward functions, specifically a citation-laundering attack. The minimal repair—adding a penalty for citing non-retrieved corpus passages (R[L])—reduces attack success rate to near zero while maintaining downstream task performance on most benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Search-agent reward functions are composite (answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, anti-hacking), creating optimization loopholes: a high reward score does not guarantee that cited evidence was actually retrieved. Attackers can exploit this gap via citation laundering—citing corpus passages absent from retrieved evidence—and standard penalties may inadvertently cancel each other out, leaving policies vulnerable.

Method: The authors propose HERALD, an offline audit methodology with three components: (1) exact same-question interventions that isolate candidate-visible information from oracle information; (2) enumeration of detector contracts (reward penalty terms) prior to policy optimization; and (3) a full 2³ ablation over search deletion resistance, fake ID detection, and the novel citation-laundering detector L. The audit is applied to four Qwen3-8B agent pools across HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue. The repair R[L] is validated via 5M-token matched training with 256 paired questions per benchmark, evaluated on exact match (EM) non-inferiority, citation precision/recall, unsupported citation rates, and laundering attackability.

Result: The baseline reward R₀ rejects search deletion and fake ID attacks but fails against label-free citation laundering. The 2³ ablation identifies R[L] (penalizing citation of non-retrieved passages) as the inclusion-minimal repair, achieving zero empirical attack success rate with a 0.50% one-sided cluster upper bound. The gap persists across pool rules, a visible BM25 attacker, and four models. Broader hardening remains vulnerable when oracle support-ID penalties are removed. Under matched training, R[L] meets EM non-inferiority on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but not MuSiQue. Citation precision improves by 2.02 points, support recall by 1.46, unsupported citations drop by 1.69, and laundering attackability falls on 2Wiki and MuSiQue. Natural L is not reduced, and the detector fires in only 18 of 58,368 training trajectories—demonstrating sparse but effective learning signal.

Conclusion: HERALD successfully decouples robust reward scoring, sparse learning signal, and policy transfer. The minimal repair R[L] provides a principled defense against citation laundering without degrading natural behavior, though transfer gaps remain on MuSiQue, and broader hardening is fragile when support-ID penalties are absent.

Abstract: Search-agent rewards mix answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, and anti-hacking terms; a high score therefore need not imply that cited evidence was retrieved, and added penalties can cancel. We introduce HERALD, an offline audit that applies exact same-question interventions, separates candidate-visible from oracle information, and enumerates detector contracts before policy optimization. On four Qwen3-8B pools from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, $R_0$ rejects search deletion and fake IDs, but a label-free citation-laundering attack succeeds. A complete $2^3$ ablation identifies targeted strengthening of $L$---citing a corpus passage absent from the retrieved evidence---as the observed inclusion-minimal repair: $R[L]$ has zero empirical ASR with a 0.50% one-sided cluster upper bound. The gap persists across pool rules, a visible BM25 attacker, and four models; broader hardening remains vulnerable when the attack removes an oracle support-ID penalty.
