Under strict 5M-token matched training evaluated on 256 paired questions per benchmark, $R[L]$ meets the EM non-inferiority gate on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but not MuSiQue. Equal-suite citation precision and support recall improve by 2.02 and 1.46 points, unsupported citations fall by 1.69, and laundering attackability falls on 2Wiki and MuSiQue. Natural $L$ is not reduced, and the detector appears in only 18 of 58,368 training trajectories. HERALD thus separates robust scoring, sparse learning signal, and policy transfer.

</details>


### [135] [From Economic Agents to Agentic Economies: A Systems Blueprint for Economic World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06020)
*Jiale Han,Xiang Li,Jing Qian,Wenyuan Gu,Pin Gao,Ye Luo,Hongyuan Zha,Dacheng Tao,Benyou Wang,Lin William Cong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a roadmap for building Economic World Models (EWMs)—generative simulations where heterogeneous agents, institutions, and markets co-evolve from within. It defines a six-level capability ladder spanning fixed-rule agents to sim-to-real economic twins and surveys the literature, finding that current work clusters at lower levels while higher-level capabilities (self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, empirical alignment) remain scarce.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing economic simulation environments lack integrated, generative architectures where agents, market mechanisms, and institutions adapt and co-evolve endogenously. Most work stops at fixed or adaptive agent behaviors without persistent empirical alignment or evolving institutional frameworks, limiting their utility as high-fidelity sandboxes for human decision-makers and as substrates for training, evaluating, and safeguarding AI agents.

Method: The authors (1) conceptualize EWMs as generative engines producing macro dynamics from micro-level agent interactions; (2) organize EWM systems into a six-level capability ladder: Level 1 (fixed rule-based agent worlds), Level 2 (LLM-based agent worlds), Level 3 (adaptive agent worlds), Level 4 (self-evolving agents), Level 5 (evolving institutional worlds), and Level 6 (sim-to-real economic twins); (3) conduct a systematic literature survey across these levels to map the current research landscape; and (4) synthesize findings into an implementation blueprint with concrete design choices, architectures, and an open resource repository.

Result: The literature survey reveals that most existing work concentrates at Levels 1–3 (rule-based, LLM-based, and adaptive agents), while systems featuring self-evolving agents (Level 4), endogenous institutional evolution (Level 5), and persistent sim-to-real empirical alignment (Level 6) remain rare. This gap highlights significant underexplored research frontiers across the higher capability tiers.

Conclusion: Building next-generation EWMs requires advancing beyond lower-level agent simulations toward integrated systems with self-evolving agents, co-evolving institutions, and validated alignment with real-world data. The paper's implementation blueprint and curated resources aim to accelerate progress toward high-fidelity economic sandboxes useful for both human policy-making and AI agent development.

Abstract: Economic World Models (EWMs) are generative economic models that simulate how economies evolve from within by modeling heterogeneous agents, their beliefs and actions, and the market and institutional mechanisms through which their interactions produce aggregate outcomes. This paper develops an implementation roadmap for building economic world models as generative engines in which heterogeneous agents act, interact, adapt, and co-evolve with markets and institutions, thereby producing economic dynamics from the inside. We organize EWM systems into a six-level capability ladder, from fixed rule-based agent worlds to adaptive and LLM-based agent worlds, self-evolving agents, evolving institutional worlds, and sim-to-real economic twins aligned with real observations. A systematic literature survey across these levels reveals that existing work remains concentrated in lower-level agent and simulation environments, while systems with self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare. By translating the EWM agenda into an implementation blueprint, this paper aims to accelerate the development of the next generation of economic simulation environments that can serve as high-fidelity sandboxes for human decision-makers and as training, planning, evaluation, and safety substrates for AI agents. We release a curated paper list and related resources to support future research.

</details>


### [136] [Integrating Implicit and Explicit Relational Biases through Graph-Based Multiple Instance Learning: A Case Study in Skin Lesion Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06037)
*Rafał Buler,Jakub Buler,Maciej Bobowicz,Michał Grochowski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a dual-level relational framework for image classification that combines implicit patch-level relationship learning (via a convolutional masked autoencoder) with explicit graph-based message passing. Tested on skin lesion diagnosis benchmarks (ISIC-2018, ISIC-2019), the combined approach outperforms both the baseline EfficientNetB3 and implicit-only modeling, with the grid-structured Graph Attention Network achieving the best results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard convolutional neural networks have limited capacity to capture structural dependencies among image patches. The authors aim to bridge the gap between implicit representation learning and explicit structural modeling by introducing relational inductive biases at two levels: self-supervised patch relationship learning and graph-based message passing.

Method: The framework operates in stages: (1) an EfficientNetB3 baseline for standard classification; (2) a patch-based strategy using a convolutional masked autoencoder (ConvMAE) pretrained via self-supervised reconstruction to learn implicit inter-patch relationships; (3) explicit relational modeling where learned patch embeddings are organized into graph topologies (grid-based, random, k-nearest neighbour) and processed via a Graph Attention Network (GAT) for message passing and final classification.

Result: On ISIC-2018: baseline balanced accuracy 76.17%, implicit-only 77.12%, full grid-GAT 79.27%. On ISIC-2019: implicit-only 59.84%, combined implicit+explicit 60.67%. The grid-structured GAT with both implicit and explicit relational modeling consistently yielded the highest performance across both benchmarks.

Conclusion: Combining implicit inter-patch relational learning with explicit graph-based message passing provides complementary structural information that improves classification accuracy. The dual-level relational framework effectively enhances skin lesion diagnosis performance, suggesting that hybrid implicit-explicit structural modeling is a promising direction for image classification tasks requiring fine-grained dependency capture.

Abstract: Relational inductive biases are essential for capturing structural dependencies among data. This study investigates a dual-level relational framework for image classification, bridging the gap between implicit representation learning and explicit structural modelling. We begin by establishing a baseline using an EfficientNetB3 architecture. To move beyond standard convolutional biases, we adopt a patch-based strategy, employing a convolutional masked autoencoder to learn implicit inter-patch relationships through self-supervised reconstruction. We then extend this approach by incorporating explicit relational modelling, organizing the learned embeddings into various graph topologies, including grid-based, random, and k-nearest neighbour structures. Experimental results on the ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019 skin lesion diagnosis benchmarks show that combining implicit inter-patch modelling with explicit graph-based message passing yields the best performance. On the ISIC-2018 test set, the baseline model achieves a balanced accuracy of 76.17%, which improves to 77.12% with implicit patch-based relational modelling. The fully integrated grid-structured Graph Attention Network further increases performance to 79.27%. Similarly, on ISIC-2019, the implicit approach reaches 59.84% balanced accuracy, while the combination of implicit and explicit modelling yields 60.67%.

</details>


### [137] [When History Lies: Evaluating and Improving Tool Use under Misleading Multi-Turn Histories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06057)
*Xiaoqing Wu,Xingyu Fan,Feifei Li,Wenhui Que*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Historical tool-calling traces can mislead agents even when structurally valid — a phenomenon the authors term "history pollution." They introduce a paired benchmark (Original/Polluted/Oracle) and a teacher-student distillation method that transfers oracle-conditioned policies to students observing only polluted history, achieving significant accuracy gains (87% on 1.7B, 93% on 8B models) while generalizing to clean histories and unseen tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In persistent tool-calling interactions, accumulated dialogue and tool traces become stale over time. While structurally valid, these historical traces may no longer be authoritative for current requests, yet agents continue to rely on them — leading to incorrect decisions, reuse of deprecated entities, and outdated interface conventions. The authors identify this as a distinct and underexplored bottleneck in tool-use reliability.

Method: The authors contribute: (1) **bench**: a paired benchmark with three synchronized views (Original, Polluted, Oracle State) that preserve system policy, tools, request, and gold action while introducing targeted pollution; (2) **Eleven gold-preserving interventions** isolating failures across decision state, entity binding, and interface execution; (3) **ours**: a teacher-student framework where an Oracle-conditioned teacher (accessing clean state) supervises a student that only sees polluted history, using soft supervision on student-generated prefixes rather than full-sequence distillation.

Result: On Qwen3-1.7B, pollution flips 32.1% of previously correct decisions. The proposed method achieves 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy, outperforming Gold-SFT (66.3%), Oracle sequence distillation (82.3%), and off-policy token distillation (85.0%). An 8B teacher raises the 1.7B student to 91.9%; an 8B student reaches 93.0%. Policies transfer to clean histories, unseen functions, regenerated contexts, external tool-use benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop QA.

Conclusion: History reliability is established as a distinct tool-use bottleneck, separate from general reasoning or instruction-following failures. Reliable-state policy transfer via teacher-student distillation with soft prefix supervision offers an effective, scalable solution that produces policies robust across diverse conditions without sacrificing performance on clean inputs.

Abstract: Tool-calling agents infer task state from accumulated dialogue and tool traces. In persistent interactions, however, historical traces may remain structurally valid and semantically plausible after they cease to be authoritative for the current request. We show that such history can hijack a policy the model already possesses: on Qwen3-1.7B, pollution flips 32.1% of decisions that are correct under the original trajectory and frequently induces reuse of corrupted entities or interface conventions. We introduce bench, a paired benchmark with synchronized Original, Polluted, and Oracle State views that preserve the system policy, current tools, latest request, and gold next action. Eleven gold-preserving interventions isolate failures in decision state, entity binding, and interface execution across complete calls and non-call decisions. We further propose ours, which transfers an Oracle-conditioned teacher policy to a student observing only polluted history through soft supervision on student-generated prefixes. On Qwen3-1.7B, ours achieves 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy, outperforming Gold-SFT (66.3%), Oracle sequence distillation (82.3%), and off-policy token distillation (85.0%). The method scales consistently: an 8B teacher raises the same compact 1.7B student to 91.9%, while an 8B student reaches 93.0%. The resulting policies further transfer to clean histories, unseen functions, independently regenerated evaluation contexts, external tool-use benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop question answering. These results establish history reliability as a distinct tool-use bottleneck and demonstrate reliable-state policy transfer as an effective and scalable solution.

</details>


### [138] [Signal or Spurious Cue? A Randomized Audit of Survey-Country Metadata in LLM Social Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06085)
*Yifan Lyu,Xinran Li,Jiaqi Qiao,Xiujuan Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an audit experiment testing whether disclosing that a country label is randomly assigned (i.e., non-informative) reduces LLMs' reliance on that label when forecasting survey responses. While verified survey-country metadata usefully lowers Brier loss, disclosing the random origin of a label fails to attenuate the models' country-directed forecast shifts. The study spans five API models, six countries, and seven targets, with an accompanying dataset (PROV-FORECAST) of 14,400 paired probability distributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs increasingly serve as simulators of human survey responses, but they may be sensitive to metadata cues like country labels. When such labels are informative (verified survey country), they improve forecasts; when assigned randomly, they may still redirect forecasts—introducing bias. The study investigates whether transparency about a label's random, record-independent origin can mitigate this spurious uptake, a question with implications for fairness, audit methodology, and the responsible deployment of LLMs in social science and policy contexts.

Method: A within-record audit design compares opaque random labels against disclosed-random labels. For each of 72 records (primary panel), five fixed API models generate probability distributions over seven development-selected targets across six countries. Independent population anchors and recorded human answers serve as ground truth. The key metrics are: (1) country-direction shift (deviation attributable to label), (2) paired attenuation (reduction in shift when random origin is disclosed), (3) reduction in held-out Brier loss from verified country metadata, and (4) random-label regret. A non-overlapping mixed-coverage consistency panel replicates the analysis.

Result: Both opaque and disclosed-random labels produced country-direction shifts of 0.214, with paired attenuation of 0.0003 (95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166])—effectively zero. Verified country metadata reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]); random-label regret included zero. The consistency panel replicated the positive disclosed-random movement and verified utility, but attenuation remained uncertain. Disclosure thus did not reliably attenuate random-label uptake across either panel.

Conclusion: Verified survey-country metadata is useful for improving LLM forecast accuracy, but LLMs are vulnerable to random (non-informative) country labels, and merely disclosing the label's random origin does not reliably correct this spurious reliance. This suggests that transparency alone is insufficient as a debiasing mechanism; more robust interventions are needed. The PROV-FORECAST dataset provides a benchmark for future work on metadata sensitivity in LLM-based survey simulation.

Abstract: Survey-country metadata can improve an LLM's forecast of an individual response when informative, yet the same cue may redirect the forecast when assigned at random. A within-record audit tests whether disclosing a random label's uniform, record-independent origin reduces its country-directed uptake, and whether verified survey country lowers held-out Brier loss. Independent population anchors and recorded human answers measure direction and consequence across five fixed API models, six countries, and seven development-selected targets. In the primary post-review 72-record panel, opaque and disclosed-random labels each produced country-direction shifts of 0.214. Paired attenuation was 0.0003 (95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166]). Verified country reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while random-label regret included zero. A non-overlapping mixed-coverage consistency panel retained positive disclosed-random movement and verified utility, while attenuation remained uncertain. On the selected targets, verified metadata was useful in both panels, but disclosure did not reliably attenuate random-label uptake. PROV-FORECAST contains 14,400 paired item-level probability distributions from the corrected panel.

</details>


### [139] [Evaluating Investment Logic in Large Language Models: A Real-World Benchmark Towards Personalzied Financial Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06108)
*Yuanhong Jiang,Jingjie Zou,Zhenghong Lin,Xusheng Yu,Qiqi Huang,Shuai Jia,Shijie Dai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InvestLogicBench is a process-native benchmark for financial LLMs that evaluates the full decision chain (Profile→Event→Reasoning→Decision→Outcome) using 201K real investor decisions. It reveals that current LLMs produce polished but weakly grounded reasoning that outcome-only evaluation misses, and argues that the P→E→R→D→O framework should become a standard data-system interface for personalized, consequential agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation paradigms for financial LLMs are fundamentally misaligned with the personalized nature of investment competence. Static QA omits investor agency (different profiles warrant different actions from the same evidence), while terminal P&L cannot distinguish grounded, profile-consistent decisions from lucky ones. The authors argue the community is using the wrong ruler for consequential agents and need a process-oriented benchmark that captures the full reasoning chain under profile constraints.

Method: The authors construct InvestLogicBench, comprising 201,247 documented decisions from 151 real-world investors. Each episode instantiates a structured P→E→R→D→O trace: Profile (investor goals, horizons, portfolios, risk boundaries), Events (point-in-time observable market evidence), Reasoning (structured investment logic), Decision (executable action), and Outcome (delayed result). The benchmark supports three evaluation modes: comprehension, profile-conditioned generation, and end-to-end replay. Four leading LLMs are evaluated on both logical plausibility and event grounding.

Result: Across four leading LLMs, logical plausibility scores near 4/5, while event grounding scores are starkly lower at 0.8–2.8/5. Return-based metrics and process-quality metrics also exhibit significant disagreement. This exposes a pattern of polished but weakly grounded reasoning — LLMs generate plausible-sounding investment logic that is insufficiently anchored to the actual market events in the profile, a flaw that outcome-only (P&L) evaluation completely obscures.

Conclusion: The P→E→R→D→O framework should serve as a data-system interface standard for personalized, consequential agents, requiring versioned profiles, temporal provenance, inspectable retrieval, decision ledgers, and replayable outcomes. Finance serves as a stress test for a broader class of agentic systems where decisions are profile-dependent, consequential, and require auditable reasoning chains beyond terminal metrics.

Abstract: Investment competence is inherently personalized: the same market evidence can justify different actions for investors with different goals, horizons, portfolios, and risk boundaries. Yet financial LLMs are evaluated either by static question answering or by terminal profit and loss. The former omits agency; the latter cannot reveal whether a profitable action was grounded, profile-consistent, or merely lucky. We ask whether the community is using the wrong ruler for consequential agents.
  We introduce \textsc{InvestLogicBench}, a process-native benchmark containing 201,247 documented decisions from 151 real-world investors. Each episode instantiates a \textbf{P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O} trace: investor \textit{Profile}, observable market \textit{Events}, investment \textit{Reasoning}, executable \textit{Decision}, and delayed \textit{Outcome}. The release includes profile construction, point-in-time event binding, structured logic, horizons, outcomes, and post-mortems, and supports comprehension, profile-conditioned generation, and end-to-end replay. Across four leading LLMs, logical plausibility remains near 4/5 while event grounding is only 0.8--2.8/5; return and process quality also disagree. These results expose polished but weakly grounded reasoning that outcome-only evaluation hides. We further argue that P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O should be a data-system interface, requiring versioned profiles, temporal provenance, inspectable retrieval, decision ledgers, and replayable outcomes. Finance is our stress test for a broader class of personalized, consequential agents.

</details>


### [140] [ECHO: A Locally-Deployable Agentic Health Assistant with Temporal Memory, Safety Guardrails, and Speech Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06110)
*Abdulkadir Külçe,Alihan Esen,Cağla Fikir,Berke Kurt,Kuzey Arar,Gökhan Ercan,Faik Boray Tek*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ECHO is a locally-deployable conversational health assistant combining an agentic chatbot (94.9% tool pass rate), a two-stage safety layer (88.8% accuracy, 90.6% unsafe recall), and a multimodal speech assessment module (macro F1 0.652), all running on consumer hardware with full data privacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term chronic care management requires persistent, privacy-preserving conversational AI that can safely handle clinical queries, but existing solutions either depend on cloud services (risking data privacy) or lack multimodal assessment capabilities and robust safety mechanisms for health contexts.

Method: ECHO integrates three modules: (1) a ReAct-loop agentic chatbot orchestrated via LangGraph with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for cross-session memory; (2) a two-stage hybrid safety layer combining a rule-based filter (<1ms for crisis/jailbreak) with a signed GNN using APPNP-style propagation for boundary-case intent classification; (3) a multimodal speech module fusing Whisper acoustic embeddings and BERT text embeddings via cross-attention for estimating emotion, depression, and pain.

Result: The agentic chatbot achieved a 94.9% tool-execution pass rate on 59 scenarios (GPT-5 Mini). The safety GNN reached 88.8% accuracy and 90.6% unsafe recall on a 2,537-query Turkish health dataset, outperforming zero-shot Llama 3.3 70B. The speech module attained a mean macro F1 of 0.652. The full system runs locally on consumer hardware with no external data transmission.

Conclusion: ECHO demonstrates that a fully local, privacy-compliant (GDPR/KVKK) conversational health assistant with competitive clinical tool use, robust safety filtering, and multimodal affect assessment is feasible on consumer-grade hardware, offering a viable paradigm for long-term chronic care management without compromising patient data sovereignty.

Abstract: This paper presents ECHO (Enhanced Care \& Health Observer), a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for long-term chronic care management. ECHO integrates three complementary software modules developed under shared supervision as a unified system. The core module is an agentic chatbot built on a ReAct loop orchestrated via LangGraph, equipped with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for persistent cross-session memory; it achieves a 94.9\% tool-execution pass rate across a 59-scenario benchmark with GPT-5 Mini. A two-stage hybrid safety layer intercepts all incoming queries: a rule-based layer handles explicit crisis signals and jailbreak attempts in under 1ms, while a signed graph neural network (GNN) with APPNP-style propagation classifies boundary cases by clinical intent, achieving 88.8\% accuracy and 90.6\% unsafe recall on a 2,537-query annotated Turkish health dataset while outperforming zero-shot LLM baselines including Llama 3.3 70B. A multimodal speech assessment module combining Whisper acoustic encoding and BERT text encoding with cross-attention fusion estimates emotion, depression, and pain, reaching a mean macro F1 of 0.652. The full system is implemented as a web application that can run entirely on consumer hardware, with no patient data transmitted to external services, supporting compliance with GDPR and KVKK.

</details>


### [141] [Mind the Gaps: Mixture-of-Minds for Human Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06115)
*Pranav Dahiya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Anacreon is an audience simulation model that achieves state-of-the-art individual-level prediction accuracy (0.775 ordinal alignment) on survey responses by clustering individuals, training cluster-specific adapters on a Gemma 12B base, and augmenting data with chain-of-emotion and distribution-balancing techniques.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing statistical methods and LLM-based simulators capture population-level central tendencies well but fail at the individual level — they flatten heterogeneity, carry social biases, and suffer from prompt brittleness. The goal is to faithfully simulate individuals to draw valid aggregate insights.

Method: Anacreon uses: (1) an authorship embedding to separate individuals; (2) clustering of a real qualitative corpus around seed people; (3) a "mixture of minds" — training a dedicated LoRA adapter for each cluster on a Gemma 4 12B base; (4) harvesting demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text; (5) chain-of-emotion augmentation; (6) response-option shuffling to reduce prompt brittleness; and (7) training-distribution balancing to mitigate positive bias.

Result: Anacreon achieves state-of-the-art ordinal alignment of 0.775 on a large externally sourced survey, with only small residual bias.

Conclusion: The work represents progress toward drawing aggregate insight from faithfully simulated individuals, bridging the gap between population-level and individual-level prediction in audience simulation.

Abstract: Predicting how a population will answer a new question is a long-standing goal. Statistical methods succeed at the level of the mass but falter at the level of the individual. Large language model simulators inherit this gap. They recover a population's central tendencies while flattening its heterogeneity, and they carry social biases and prompt brittleness that distort individual predictions. This paper introduces Anacreon, an audience simulation model that targets the individual level within a narrow, well-specified domain. Anacreon learns an authorship embedding that separates individuals, clusters a real qualitative corpus around seed people, and trains a dedicated adapter for each cluster, a mixture of minds, on a Gemma~4 12B base. It harvests demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text, and augments each record with a chain-of-emotion. It reduces prompt brittleness by shuffling response options and reduces positive bias by balancing the training distribution. On a large, externally sourced survey, Anacreon reaches a state-of-the-art ordinal alignment of 0.775, the individual-level accuracy measure on which the field has converged, with a small residual bias. The work is a step toward drawing aggregate insight from faithfully simulated individuals.

</details>


### [142] [Poli-Bias: Understanding and Measuring Large Language Model Biases in International Political Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06123)
*Massi-Nissa Abboud,Aladin Djuhera,Elena Cabrio,Holger Boche*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Poli-Bias is a counterfactual framework that measures political bias in LLMs by swapping country identities in legally equivalent conflict scenarios and decomposing response disparities into five interpretable dimensions, revealing systematic unequal treatment across 13 models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches to measuring political bias in LLMs rely on single metrics that fail to capture subtle, multi-faceted disparities in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning when models encounter legally equivalent scenarios involving different countries.

Method: The authors introduce Poli-Bias, a counterfactual framework that constructs paired prompts where country identities are systematically swapped across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks. Rather than producing a single bias score, the framework decomposes response disparities into five interpretable dimensions to reveal how unequal treatment manifests.

Result: Evaluating 13 contemporary LLMs across diverse model families and sizes, the authors find that country identities and user affiliations systematically affect how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law.

Conclusion: Poli-Bias establishes a fine-grained, multi-dimensional framework for auditing political even-handedness and sycophancy in LLMs, moving beyond simplistic bias metrics to capture the nuanced ways unequal treatment emerges in model outputs.

Abstract: Measuring political bias in large language models (LLMs) remains challenging as it can manifest through subtle differences in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning that are difficult to capture with a single metric. In this work, we introduce Poli-Bias, a counterfactual framework for measuring whether LLMs treat legally equivalent conflict scenarios differently depending on the countries involved. Poli-Bias compares responses to paired prompts in which country identities are systematically swapped across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks. Rather than reducing bias to a single judgment, our framework decomposes response disparities into five interpretable dimensions, revealing how and where unequal treatment manifests. Across 13 contemporary LLMs spanning diverse model families and sizes, we find that country identities and user affiliations can systematically affect how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law. Our results thus establish Poli-Bias as a fine-grained framework for auditing political even-handedness and sycophancy in LLMs.

</details>


### [143] [Contextual Information Policy Optimization for Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06128)
*Xingyu Guo,Wei Chen,Linlin Yang,Baochang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CIPO is an evidence-oriented RL framework that provides turn-level credit for retrieval-grounded reasoning steps, reducing confirmation bias and improving how search agents use external evidence during multi-step reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current search agents optimize for final-answer correctness, encouraging prior-driven reasoning where agents use retrieval merely to confirm internal biases rather than genuinely incorporating external evidence. This leads to confirmation bias and inefficient evidence use.

Method: CIPO assigns dense, turn-level credit to actions influenced by retrieved information, combined with a global outcome reward. It requires no human process annotations or additional reward models.

Result: CIPO reduces prior-driven reasoning and achieves strong performance across seven in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks.

Conclusion: Explicitly aligning policy optimization with evidence use via turn-level credit assignment effectively mitigates confirmation bias and improves the reliability of search-augmented LLM agents.

Abstract: Search agents extend large language models beyond static parametric memory by enabling them to acquire and use ex ternal evidence during multi-step reasoning. For knowledge intensive tasks involving complex or evolving information, their reliability depends not only on retrieving relevant ev idence but also on using it to guide subsequent reasoning. However, existing methods primarily reward final-answer cor rectness or intermediate progress, without directly assessing whether post-retrieval actions are grounded in the retrieved evidence. This misalignment encourages prior-driven reason ing: agents form conclusions based on internal knowledge and use retrieval mainly to confirm them, resulting in confirma tion bias and inefficient evidenceuse.Toaddressthisissue, we propose Contextual Information Policy Optimization (CIPO), an evidence-oriented reinforcement learning framework that explicitly aligns policy optimization with external evidence use. CIPO assigns dense, turn-level credit to reasoning ac tions influenced by retrieved information, while combining this evidence-use signal with a global outcome reward to pre serveanswercorrectness.Withthismanner,CIPOdiscourages evidence-detached guesses and promotes reasoning trajecto ries in which retrieved facts can guide or revise subsequent reasoning. Importantly, CIPO requires neither human process annotations nor an additional reward model. Extensive exper iments on seven in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks show that CIPO reduces the prevalence of prior-driven rea soning and achieves excellent performance on most tasks.

</details>


### [144] [FinEvo-Bench: A Longitudinal Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents in Professional Financial Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06144)
*Bo Deng,Kang Zhou,Lifan Guo,Chongyang Tao,Xuanren Chen,Chenggang Xie,Renzhao Liang,Feng Chen,Chi Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FinEvo-Bench is a longitudinal benchmark for evaluating both task performance and self-evolution in financial AI agents, using 120 real-case tasks across 6 domains. Evolving agents outperformed non-evolving controls by 9.33–19.37 points, with Letta achieving the highest score (91.65) and Codex showing the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent benchmarks evaluate tasks independently and cannot measure whether experience from one task improves performance on later tasks. Current self-evolution benchmarks also fail to jointly cover professional workflows, open-ended deliverables, and multi-aspect evaluation. There is a need for a benchmark that assesses both professional competence and the ability to leverage prior experience for continuous improvement.

Method: The authors introduce FinEvo-Bench, comprising 120 real-case-grounded tasks across 20 business scenes in six financial domains. Each scene contains 6 related but distinct cases sharing a professionally defined procedure and a manually reviewed rubric for quality and compliance. Four self-evolving agent scaffolds (all using Qwen3.7-Max backbone) and paired non-evolving controls are tested on three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams. An independent Claude Code scoring agent (backed by Claude Opus 4.6) evaluates all outputs. Evolution strategies include skill-only, memory-only, and combined memory-skill approaches, with comparisons between rubric feedback and reference-answer feedback.

Result: Letta achieves the highest evolved score (91.65) and the fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task). Codex achieves the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Across all scaffolds, evolving conditions raise scores by 9.33–19.37 points and reduce compliance issues by 0.12–0.44 per task. Within-scene rank analysis shows paired score gains at ranks 4–6 exceed those at ranks 1–3 by 6.10–8.70 points, indicating cumulative improvement. Skill-only evolution outperforms both memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution in Claude Code. Rubric feedback yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback across all four scaffolds.

Conclusion: FinEvo-Bench effectively measures both professional task performance and self-evolution ability in AI agents, revealing that evolving agents significantly benefit from retained experience, particularly in later related tasks. The benchmark provides a rigorous framework for evaluating how effectively agents turn prior experience into later improvement in professional financial settings.

Abstract: Most agent benchmarks evaluate tasks independently and cannot measure whether experience from one task helps with later tasks. Existing self-evolution benchmarks do not jointly cover professional workflows, open-ended deliverables, and multi-aspect evaluation. We introduce FinEvo-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark with 120 real-case-grounded tasks, 20 business scenes across six financial domains. Institution-provided professional procedures define the required operations and constraints. Eligible institution-provided and publicly documented cases supply the task facts. Each scene contains six related but substantively distinct cases that share a professional procedure and a manually reviewed rubric for task quality and financial compliance. We compare four self-evolving agent scaffolds using the same Qwen3.7-Max backbone and three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams. Paired non-evolving controls estimate each scaffold's self-evolution gain from retained experience, while an independent Claude Code scoring agent backed by Claude Opus 4.6 evaluates all outputs. Letta achieves the highest evolved score (91.65) and fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task); Codex achieves the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Across scaffolds, the evolving condition raises scores by 9.33-19.37 points and reduces compliance issues by 0.12-0.44 per task. Paired score gains at within-scene ranks 4-6 exceed those at ranks 1-3 by 6.10-8.70 points. In Claude Code, skill-only evolution produces higher task quality and fewer compliance issues than memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution. Across all four scaffolds, rubric feedback also yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback. FinEvo-Bench measures both professional performance and self-evolution ability: how effectively an agent turns prior experience into later improvement.

</details>


### [145] [Schema-Guided Hierarchical Information Extraction and Semantic Evaluation Using Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06167)
*Modhurita Mitra,Jan-Willem Versteeg,Maarten D. Schermer,Shiva Nadi Najafabadi,Marie L. De Bruin,Lourens T. Bloem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A schema-based framework using generative AI (Claude Opus 3) extracts complex nested information from unstructured text in a single zero-shot call, followed by a path-based semantic matching algorithm for automated evaluation against a gold standard. Achieved >90% F1 on 12/14 attributes from NICE documents, ~30× faster than human experts, with demonstrated generalisability across models, organisations, and languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extracting complex, hierarchical, and nested structured information from unstructured text documents is time-consuming and labour-intensive when performed by human domain experts. There is a need for a unified, systematic framework that can perform such extraction efficiently using generative AI and automatically evaluate the quality of results against a gold standard, while handling variable-cardinality attributes and domain-specific considerations.

Method: The authors propose a schema-based framework comprising two stages: (1) Information extraction via a single zero-shot generative AI call, where the schema serves as an information model encoding domain knowledge to extract hierarchical, nested information with variable-cardinality attributes. (2) Automated semantic evaluation using a path-based semantic matching algorithm to align nested, variable-cardinality attributes between extracted results and a gold standard, followed by generative AI-based semantic comparison with a rubric classifying matches as exact, semantic, useful, or non-match according to domain-specific criteria.

Result: Using Claude Opus 3 on NICE (health technology assessment) documents, 12 out of 14 attributes achieved F1 scores >90%. Extraction time was approximately 30× faster than human domain experts. The framework demonstrated generalisability across different generative AI models and transferability across different HTA organisations and languages.

Conclusion: The schema-based generative AI framework provides a highly accurate, efficient, and generalisable solution for extracting and evaluating complex structured information from unstructured text, offering significant time savings over manual human extraction while maintaining high semantic fidelity.

Abstract: We present a schema-based framework for extracting complex, structured information from unstructured text documents using generative AI, followed by automated semantic evaluation of the extracted information against a gold standard. The schema, serving as an information model encoding domain knowledge, provides a unified, systematic, and consistent framework for extraction of hierarchical, nested information, with attributes of variable cardinality, and subsequent evaluation of the results. Information extraction from a document is performed in a single call to the model, in zero-shot mode.
  In the evaluation step, we introduce a path-based semantic matching algorithm to align the nested, variable-cardinality attributes in the extracted results with those in the gold standard. We use generative AI for semantic comparison of the extracted and gold standard values of an attribute, and introduce a rubric to classify the result of the comparison, according to domain-specific considerations, as an exact, semantic, useful, or non-match.
  We were able to extract 12 out of 14 attributes with an F1 score of $>$90\% from documents published by the health technology assessment organisation NICE, using the generative AI model Claude Opus 3. The time needed to extract the attributes from a document was $\sim$30 times lower than the time taken by a human domain expert. We further demonstrate generalisability of this framework across different generative AI models and transferability across different HTA organisations and languages.

</details>


### [146] [PaDoc: Layout-Grounded Parallel Decoding for Document Parsing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06146)
*Hao Yu,Jiabo Zhan,Kang Liu,Linnan Zhao,Dongxu Yue,Rui Chen,Jinglin Wang,Chong Sun,Chen Li,Jing Lyu,Chun Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PaDoc is a layout-grounded document parser that factorizes page parsing into concurrent layout and content branches over a shared representation, reducing decoding depth while maintaining full-page context. It achieves state-of-the-art results on OmniDocBench and significantly improves throughput and latency over sequential baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing end-to-end document parsers serialize entire pages into a single autoregressive sequence, creating long decoding paths that grow with content length. Crop-based two-stage parsers expose parallelism but incur repeated visual prefills and lose full-page context. The goal is to retain full-page context while eliminating sequential dependencies among regions.

Method: PaDoc treats the predicted layout as a branching structure over a shared page representation. Under a region-sufficiency assumption, it derives a prefix-conditioned factorization where the layout stream and regional content branches advance concurrently, reducing decoding depth to the longest layout-content path. This is realized in a single MLLM with (1) packed variable-length ancestor attention for standard next-token training and (2) masked parallel decoding for inference, where a vLLM backend serves branches as concurrent requests with cache-resident shared-prefix reuse.

Result: On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc achieves 91.1 Overall Layout F1, 94.24 Overall score (top-tier among end-to-end parsers), best Text Edit (0.038), and Formula CDM (95.59). On a 384-page subset with one A800 GPU, it is the fastest end-to-end parser at five concurrency levels, with 67.4-118% valid-page throughput improvement and 39.2-54.9% P95 latency reduction over a same-backbone Sequential SFT baseline.

Conclusion: PaDoc demonstrates that layout-grounded branching factorization within a single MLLM can simultaneously achieve state-of-the-art parsing accuracy and substantial inference speedups by exposing region-level parallelism while preserving full-page context.

Abstract: End-to-end document parsers provide a unified interface, but serialize page layouts and regional contents into one autoregressive sequence. This formulation forces independent regions onto a decoding path whose length grows with the total content, whereas crop-based two-stage parsers expose region-level parallelism at the cost of repeated visual prefills and fragmented page context. To retain full-page context while removing dependencies, we propose PaDoc, a layout-grounded parser that treats the predicted layout as a branching structure over a shared page representation. Under a region-sufficiency assumption, we derive a prefix-conditioned factorization in which the layout stream and regional content branches advance concurrently, reducing the decoding depth to the longest layout-content path. We realize this factorization within a single MLLM: packed variable-length ancestor attention preserves the visibility under standard next-token training, while masked parallel decoding creates branches that the evaluated vLLM backend serves as concurrent requests with cache-resident shared-prefix reuse. On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc attains an Overall layout F1 of 91.1 and, among end-to-end parsers, a top-tier Overall score of 94.24 together with the best Text Edit (0.038) and Formula CDM (95.59). On a 384-page subset and one A800 GPU, it is the fastest end-to-end parser at five concurrency levels, improving valid-page throughput by 67.4-118% and reducing P95 latency by 39.2-54.9% relative to a same-backbone Sequential SFT baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/Longin-Yu/Padoc

</details>


### [147] [HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06301)
*Varun Ursekar,Apaar Shanker,Yash Maurya,Shehab Yasser,Vijay S. Kalmath,Veronica Chatrath,Yuan Xue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HarnessOpt-Bench is a benchmark for measuring LLMs' ability to optimize agentic system harnesses (prompts, tools, control flow, memory, orchestration) under expensive, stochastic evaluation. Evaluating 5 frontier LLMs across 4 tasks over 111 scored runs reveals that optimizer models differ more than their coding harnesses, native harnesses are not consistently better, and gains vary substantially by task—establishing harness optimization as a measurable, discriminative capability with significant room for improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are deployed in agentic systems, performance depends on both model weights and the surrounding "harness"—the prompts, tools, control flow, memory, and orchestration code. Automated harness optimization is a critical capability, yet the community lacks a standardized protocol for measuring how well frontier LLMs perform this task. The benchmark fills this gap.

Method: HarnessOpt-Bench provides an end-to-end optimization setting: an optimizer (LLM + coding harness) receives a target agent's seed harness, graded evaluation feedback, and a fixed evaluation budget. It iteratively edits the harness and nominates a final candidate. Scoring uses normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition inaccessible during search. A trusted execution environment enforces the evaluation boundary, meters resource usage, and preserves candidate versions for audit.

Result: Evaluating 5 frontier LLMs as optimizers across 4 downstream tasks (111 scored runs) shows: (1) optimizer model choice matters more than the coding harness used; (2) native harnesses are not consistently superior; (3) performance gains vary substantially across tasks and seed regimes.

Conclusion: Harness optimization is a measurable and discriminative capability for frontier LLMs. Current models show meaningful but inconsistent gains, indicating substantial room for improvement in automated harness optimization.

Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed within agentic systems, their capabilities depend not only on the model weights but also on the harness: the prompts, tools, control flow, memory, and orchestration code surrounding them. This makes automated harness optimization -- the iterative and evaluation-guided improvement of a harness by an AI system -- both an important route to improving AI systems and a demanding capability for AI systems themselves. Yet the community lacks a common protocol for measuring how well frontier LLMs perform at this task. We introduce HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization under expensive and stochastic evaluation. An optimizer, an LLM paired with a coding harness, receives a target agent's seed harness, graded evaluation feedback, and a fixed target-evaluation budget. It edits the harness and nominates a final candidate, which is scored by its normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition that remains inaccessible throughout search. A trusted execution environment enforces the evaluation boundary, meters target-agent resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit. We evaluate 5 frontier LLMs as optimizers both under a shared coding harness and under their native harnesses across 4 downstream tasks, over 111 scored runs. Experiment results show that optimizer models separate more than the coding harnesses they act through, native harnesses are not consistently superior, and gains vary substantially across tasks and seed regimes. These results establish harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with large space for improvement.

</details>


### [148] [CogVis: Must Open-Vocabulary Change Detection Perceive the Scene Anew for Every Query?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06150)
*Zijie Wang,Chen Zhong,Wei He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CogVis is a cognitive memory-guided framework for Open-Vocabulary Change Detection that decouples temporal perception from semantic discrimination using a perception-memory-verification paradigm, achieving SOTA performance across seven benchmarks while improving inference throughput by 28.50%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing OVCD methods entangle temporal perception, semantic discrimination, and region verification, leading to unstable results and redundant computation. The authors seek to address this by taking inspiration from human visual change perception, where change evidence and semantic decisions are processed separately.

Method: CogVis reformulates OVCD as a perception-memory-verification paradigm with three modules: (1) Scene Change Perceptron (SCP) extracts a reusable, category-agnostic change prior from frozen bi-temporal features, decoupling temporal evidence from semantic decisions; (2) Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC) dynamically estimates an image-query-specific decision threshold to compensate for category-dependent score shifts; (3) Adaptive Region Filter (ARF) filters connected candidates using learned semantic, temporal, and structural reliability.

Result: CogVis achieves state-of-the-art performance across seven benchmarks covering semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment. By sharing scene-level change perception across queries, it avoids redundant category-agnostic temporal perception and improves inference throughput by 28.50%.

Conclusion: The perception-memory-verification paradigm effectively decouples change perception from semantic reasoning, resulting in both superior accuracy and improved computational efficiency for open-vocabulary change detection.

Abstract: Earth-surface monitoring requires change detection models capable of recognizing arbitrary semantic categories. Open-Vocabulary Change Detection (OVCD) addresses this need. However, existing methods often entangle temporal perception, semantic discrimination, and region verification, causing unstable results and redundant computation. Inspired by human visual change perception, we propose CogVis, a cognitive memory-guided framework that reformulates OVCD as a perception-memory-verification paradigm. CogVis first employs a Scene Change Perceptron (SCP) to extract a reusable, category-agnostic change prior from frozen bi-temporal features, thereby decoupling temporal evidence from semantic category decisions. A Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC) then compensates for category-dependent score shifts by dynamically estimating an image-query-specific decision threshold. Finally, an Adaptive Region Filter (ARF) filters connected candidates using learned semantic, temporal, and structural reliability. Experiments on seven benchmarks spanning semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment show that CogVis achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated datasets. By sharing scene-level change perception, CogVis further avoids repeating category-agnostic temporal perception across queries and improves inference throughput by 28.50%.

</details>


### [149] [iARCS: Iterative Agentic RL for Controllable 3D Scene Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06161)
*Saugat Adhikari,Ashok Prasad Neupane,Pramish Paudel,Ajad Chhatkuli,Danda Pani Paudel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: iARCS is an iterative agentic RL framework that adapts pretrained scene generators to meet natural-language task constraints. It uses universal-reward pretraining for physical plausibility, then task-specific fine-tuning with LLM-generated reward programs refined from feedback. It improves constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance tasks while maintaining scene diversity, and the generated data can improve downstream training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing synthetic 3D scene generators prioritize perceptual realism but fail to reliably satisfy functional constraints like accessibility, traversability, and spatial rule compliance, limiting the utility of synthetic data for embodied AI and computer vision training tasks where these properties are essential.

Method: iARCS proposes a two-stage iterative agentic reinforcement learning framework: (1) universal-reward pretraining to enhance physical plausibility and layout quality of a pretrained scene generator, followed by (2) task-specific fine-tuning using LLM-generated reward programs that are iteratively refined based on training feedback, all driven by natural-language task specifications.

Result: iARCS demonstrates improved constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance-focused tasks, effective task-specific constraint optimization, and competitive scene diversity compared to baselines. It also shows that iARCS-generated data can improve a base generator for downstream training.

Conclusion: iARCS serves not only as a controllable scene editing method but more importantly as a practical synthetic data generation tool, bridging the gap between perceptual realism and functional constraint satisfaction in generated 3D scenes for embodied AI applications.

Abstract: Synthetic 3D scene generation is increasingly used as a data source for computer vision and embodied AI, but existing generators often optimize perceptual realism without reliably satisfying task-critical functional constraints. This mismatch limits the usefulness of synthetic data for downstream training, where accessibility, traversability, and spatial rule compliance are often essential. We present iARCS, an iterative agentic reinforcement learning framework that adapts a pretrained scene generator to natural-language task requirements. iARCS uses a two-stage strategy: universal-reward pretraining to improve physical plausibility and layout quality, followed by task-specific fine-tuning with LLM-generated reward programs that are iteratively refined from training feedback. Experiments show improved constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance-focused tasks, effective task-specific constraint optimization, and competitive scene diversity. We further show that data generated by iARCS improves a base generator, supporting its value as a practical synthetic data generation tool rather than only a controllable scene editing method.

</details>


### [150] [MicroEvo: Knowledge-Guided LLM Sampling for Efficient Microarchitecture Design Space Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06183)
*Jia Xiong,Runkai Li,Chenxu Niu,Guangyuan Gao,Changwen Xing,Yifan Zhang,Xinlai Wan,Jieran Cui,Chen Bai,Yusheng Hua,Ying Wang,Ming Ling,Xi Wang,Tao Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MicroEvo integrates LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search for multi-objective microarchitecture design space exploration, using evolutionary operators, Pareto-aware tree policies, and active knowledge accumulation to improve Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% and search efficiency by 10.6x over NSGA-II.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Microarchitecture design space exploration is hindered by vast search spaces and costly PPA (Power, Performance, Area) evaluations, limiting simulation budgets. Existing methods are blind to microarchitectural dependencies and fail to learn iteratively, resulting in wasted evaluations and weak Pareto convergence.

Method: MicroEvo couples off-the-shelf LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). It features: (1) LLM-driven evolutionary operators, (2) a Pareto-aware tree policy balancing Pareto contribution and diversity, (3) an active knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts and reuses optimization insights, and (4) state-aware directives for online search behavior adaptation.

Result: MicroEvo improves Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% over NSGA-II, achieves 10.6x higher search efficiency, and demonstrates strong scalability to a complex industrial-scale core.

Conclusion: MicroEvo effectively addresses the multi-objective microarchitecture optimization challenge by leveraging LLM-guided evolutionary search with MCTS and knowledge reuse, significantly outperforming traditional methods in both solution quality and search efficiency, and scaling well to industrial designs.

Abstract: Microarchitecture design space exploration suffers from expansive search spaces and expensive PPA evaluation, leaving only a small simulation budget for design decision-making. Existing methods perform blind search without considering microarchitectural dependencies and fail to learn from the iterative search effectively, leading to wasted evaluations and weak Pareto convergence. In this paper, we propose MicroEvo, a knowledge-guided framework that couples off-the-shelf LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for multi-objective microarchitecture optimization. MicroEvo combines LLM-driven evolutionary operators, a Pareto-aware tree policy that balances Pareto contribution and diversity, an active knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts and reuses optimization insights, and state-aware directives that adapt the search behavior online. Experiments show that MicroEvo improves Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% over NSGA-II and achieves 10.6x higher search efficiency, and also demonstrates strong scalability to a complex industrial-scale core. The code repository is available at: https://github.com/GEAR-SEU/MicroEvo-ICCAD-26.

</details>


### [151] [Comparative Approaches to Agent Retrieval over Large Skill Libraries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06196)
*Indivara Kolluru,Nathan Sportsman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: For skill retrieval in agent systems, a hybrid dense-lexical ranker achieves 73.5% top-5 accuracy, while augmenting it with a typed knowledge graph not only fails to improve retrieval but significantly degrades performance (-11.2 points). The graph's edges largely recapitulate what the ranker already surfaces (98.6% overlap), revealing that structural augmentation cannot extend retrieval reach when the graph topology is bound to the same embedding neighbourhood. Evaluation on author-written queries inflates hit@5 by up to 44 points, masking these null effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agents with large skill libraries face a retrieval problem: loading all skills into context is expensive, and autonomous sequencing lacks structure. The paper investigates whether adding a typed knowledge graph encoding workflow relations (prerequisites, data flow, ordering) can improve retrieval over a strong hybrid ranker, and under what conditions structural interdependence aids retrieval.

Method: The authors compare two systems over a corpus of 690 skills: (1) a hybrid ranker combining lexical (BM25) and dense-embedding retrieval, loading skills sparsely on demand, and (2) the same ranker augmented with a typed knowledge graph whose edges encode workflow relations. Graph edges are drawn from both an LLM-generated layer and a local embedding pass. Evaluation uses 117 realistic, non-echoing queries, measuring hit@5, with ablation on edge source, graph topology, and evaluation query construction (author-written vs. realistic).

Result: The hybrid ranker alone achieves 73.5% ± 8.0 hit@5. Substituting graph neighbours for ranked results at matched token budget significantly reduces performance by 11.2 points (p = 0.0007). The LLM-generated edge layer adds no benefit over embedding-derived neighbours. Critically, 73% of ranker-missed queries are unreachable through the graph, and 98.6% of typed edges connect skills already co-surfaced by the ranker, confirming a pre-filter topology bound. Author-written queries inflate hit@5 by up to 44 points.

Conclusion: Adding structural knowledge graphs does not improve retrieval over a strong ranker when the graph's topology is bounded by the same embedding neighbourhood the ranker already searches. The graph can enrich relation semantics but cannot extend retrieval reach. Structural augmentation is only optimal when the graph introduces genuinely novel connections beyond the ranker's coverage.

Abstract: Agents backed by large skill libraries must decide which skills to load and in what order. Loading the entire library into context is expensive and provides no structure for autonomous sequencing. We study two systems for this problem over a corpus of 690 skills: a hybrid ranker combining lexical and dense-embedding retrieval for sparse, on-demand loading, and a typed knowledge graph encoding workflow relations such as prerequisites, data flow, and ordering. On a set of 117 realistic, non-echoing queries, the hybrid ranker retrieves the correct skill within the top five in 73.5% +/- 8.0 of cases, leaving roughly a quarter of queries unserved. When used as the design intended (substituting graph neighbours for additional ranked results at matched token budget), the graph is significantly worse (-11.2 points, p = 0.0007). Its LLM-generated edge layer adds nothing over neighbours obtained free from a local embedding pass, and 73% of the queries the ranker misses are not reachable through the graph at all. We attribute this to a pre-filter topology bound. Because the graph's candidate edges are drawn from the same embedding neighbourhood the ranker already searches, 98.6% of typed edges connect skills the ranker had already surfaced together. The graph can enrich relation semantics but cannot extend retrieval reach. We further show that evaluating on author-written queries overstates hit@5 by up to 44 points, which would have hidden these results entirely. Our contribution is a mechanistic account of why added structure does not improve retrieval over a strong ranker, and identify the conditions under which adding structural interdependence into the retrieval is optimal.

</details>


### [152] [EnvACE: Internalizing Environment Dynamics via World Rehearsal for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06197)
*Zishan Xu,Zhiyuan Yao,Yuxin Chen,Yifu Guo,Zhengxi Lu,Yuquan Lu,Jinyang Huang,Yan Xu,Yasheng Wang,Weinan Zhang,Xingshan Zeng,Weiwen Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EnvACE introduces world rehearsal, where an LLM agent internally simulates environment responses to its own actions during training, replacing costly external environment interaction. The policy jointly learns acting and environment modeling end-to-end via task rewards, internalizing a world model that supports decision making. The method outperforms environment-scaling baselines across multiple benchmarks and enables private pre-execution rehearsal at test time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training LLM agents for long-horizon tool use requires interaction with executable environments, which are expensive to construct, verify, and ground. The authors aim to bypass the need for external simulators or real environments by having the agent learn an internal world model through self-simulated rehearsal.

Method: EnvACE is an agentic reinforcement learning method based on world rehearsal. The policy alternates between two roles: (1) acting — generating a tool call, and (2) rehearsal — playing the environment to produce the response induced by that action. Subsequent decisions are conditioned on the rehearsed response. Both roles are jointly optimized end-to-end using task-success rewards, allowing the policy to internalize action–environment response relationships in its parameters as an agent world model.

Result: EnvACE achieves strong, transferable performance across BFCL-v4, tau²-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench, outperforming environment-scaling baselines overall. Controlled studies show world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning across model scales. At test time, the internalized world model enables private rehearsal before committed execution, yielding further gains under a moderate rehearsal budget without additional external interaction.

Conclusion: World rehearsal offers a viable alternative to external environment scaling for LLM agent training, internalizing environment dynamics within the policy itself and enabling both more efficient training and improved test-time performance through private rehearsal.

Abstract: Training large language model agents for long-horizon tool use typically relies on interactions with real or synthesized executable environments, whose construction and verification are costly, or on external simulators that are difficult to ground. We introduce EnvACE, an agentic reinforcement learning method that replaces external environment interaction during training with world rehearsal. The policy alternates between acting and rehearsal: it first generates a tool call, then plays the role of the environment to produce the response induced by that action, and conditions subsequent decisions on the rehearsed response. Both roles are jointly optimized end-to-end using task-success rewards. Through world rehearsal, the policy internalizes the relationship between actions and their environment responses in its parameters, yielding an agent world model that directly supports decision making. Across BFCL-v4, tau^2-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench, EnvACE achieves strong and transferable performance, outperforming environment-scaling baselines in the overall evaluation. Controlled studies further show that world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning across model scales. At test time, the internalized world model enables private rehearsal before committed execution, yielding further gains under a moderate rehearsal budget without additional external interaction. Our findings establish world rehearsal as a new path toward scaling LLM agent training beyond the constraints of external environments. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Within-yao/EnvACE.

</details>


### [153] [TS-RAG: Retrieval Augmented Generation for Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06223)
*Yixiong Xiao,Congxi Xiao,Jingbo Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TS-RAG proposes a retrieval-augmented generation framework for time series forecasting that uses specially designed reference tokens to fuse retrieved similar sequences with input sequences, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG has proven effective in NLP but remains underexplored in time series forecasting. Time series models lack the large scale and generative capabilities of LLMs, so simply concatenating retrieved sequences (as in NLP) is ineffective. A specialized approach is needed to leverage retrieval for improving forecasting accuracy.

Method: TS-RAG introduces a framework with specially designed reference tokens that effectively fuse information from the input sequence with retrieved similar historical sequences. This enables more robust capture of complex temporal dynamics, rather than naive concatenation of reference sequences into the prompt.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate that TS-RAG achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance across several real-world forecasting benchmarks.

Conclusion: RAG can be effectively adapted to time series forecasting through carefully designed fusion mechanisms (reference tokens), overcoming the limitations of smaller-scale time series models and enabling them to benefit from retrieved relevant temporal patterns.

Abstract: While deep learning models, particularly transformer-based architectures, have shown impressive performance in time series forecasting, the application of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in this domain remains limited. Since RAG has proven effective in enhancing the capabilities of large language models by incorporating relevant external information, retrieving similar time series sequences as references might also improve accuracy in time series forecasting tasks. However, most time series models are constrained by limited training data, smaller parameter scales, and a lack of the extensive generative capabilities found in large language models. Simply concatenating reference sequences into the prompt, as done in language models, may not yield the expected results. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach, TS-RAG, which leverages RAG to enhance forecasting performance. The framework introduces specially designed reference tokens to effectively fuse information from the input sequence with that from retrieved similar sequences, enabling a more robust capture of complex temporal dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that TS-RAG achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance across several real-world forecasting benchmarks.

</details>


### [154] [DASH: Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons for On-Policy Self-Distillation of Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06243)
*ZhiYan Hou,Xinyu Tang,Hongyan An,Jianjin Zhang,Weizhen Wang,Yunyun Han,Gengsheng Li,Xiangzhao Hao,Haiyun Guo,Wenbin Hu,Jinqiao Wang,Yafeng Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DASH improves on-policy self-distillation for RLVR by using adaptive temporal gating to weight token-level supervision based on divergence histories, yielding consistent gains over standard OPSD across math reasoning benchmarks without extra forward passes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard OPSD assigns uniform importance to every local divergence between teacher and student, ignoring the temporal context — i.e., the sequence of divergences that preceded a given token. Since identical divergence magnitudes can arise after different mismatch histories, treating them identically leaves useful temporal information unexploited.

Method: DASH (Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons) computes the gap between each local token-level distillation signal and the sequence-level mean, maps this gap through an adaptive propagation gate, and uses the resulting gates to control backward multi-step aggregation of supervision weights. This allows token-level weights to adapt based on the evolution of local divergences during autoregressive generation.

Result: Across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three model scales, DASH consistently outperforms matched vanilla OPSD reruns at every scale on every benchmark.

Conclusion: DASH provides a lightweight, temporally-aware enhancement to OPSD that requires no additional teacher or student forward passes, yet reliably improves reasoning performance by adapting supervision to the trajectory of divergence during generation.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models using automatically verifiable outcome signals, but these signals are typically sparse and at the sequence-level. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) mitigates this sparsity by querying a privileged teacher at student-visited prefixes and providing dense token-level distributional supervision. Although this dense supervision alleviates signal sparsity, we find that standard OPSD still underexploits the temporal structure of the rollout. It assigns every local divergence the same coefficient, regardless of its position or the divergence sequence in which it occurs. In on-policy autoregressive generation, the same divergence magnitude can follow different discrepancy histories, reflecting different evolutions of the mismatch between the teacher and student. Since the local scalar alone cannot distinguish these temporal contexts, standard OPSD cannot adapt its token-level weights to the realized discrepancy sequence. To address this limitation, we propose Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons (DASH). DASH maps the gap between each local distillation signal and the sequence-level mean to an adaptive propagation gate and then uses these gates to control backward multi-step aggregation. By doing so, DASH adjusts token-level supervision weights according to how local divergences evolve during generation. Experiments on three mathematical reasoning benchmarks across three model scales show that DASH improves over our matched vanilla OPSD reruns on every benchmark at all three scales. DASH reuses the teacher and student distributions that OPSD already computes, so the gains require no additional teacher or student forward pass.
  Code: https://github.com/DBtxy/DASH-OPSD

</details>


### [155] [Improving the Realism of Synthetic Clinical Benchmarks Under Utility Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06265)
*Omid Bazgir,Md Nasir,Jacob Hoffman,Yang Yang,Manu Agrawal,Anusua Trivedi,Vinay Rao Dandin,Chris Gibbons,Christine Swisher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Synthetic clinical benchmarks can pass utility checks while remaining structurally unrealistic. The authors propose utility-constrained realism improvement — revising benchmarks to increase realism metrics (missingness structure, simplicity, plausibility, population alignment) while maintaining an operational utility floor. Applied to a Synthea-derived care-gap benchmark, deterministic revisions improved realism substantially, whereas naive densification preserved unrealistic templating. Utility alone should not be treated as sufficient evidence of realism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic clinical benchmarks for enterprise AI agents often pass downstream utility checks yet retain structural unrealism, particularly in privacy-sensitive healthcare settings where real operational data is inaccessible. There is a need to explicitly optimize benchmark realism without breaking existing utility validation pipelines.

Method: The authors frame benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement: modify datasets to maximize realism while remaining above a predefined operational utility threshold. They instantiate this on a care-gap benchmark built from Synthea-generated patients run through demonstration EHR workflows and processed by the same downstream pipeline as operational data. Realism is quantified via four dimensions: missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment. Two deterministic revision strategies are compared against a naive densification baseline.

Result: The baseline benchmark exhibits severe thinness: 79.44% sampled-pair missingness, only 12.75% actionable rows, 38.94% of patients with zero actionable measures, and 100% top-three token concentration. Both deterministic revisions improve all realism panels while staying above the utility floor. Naive densification fails, preserving unrealistic templating patterns. The authors also demonstrate that internal benchmark realism and fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are related but distinct objectives.

Conclusion: Synthetic benchmark quality must be optimized explicitly, treating utility as a constraint rather than sufficient evidence of realism. Benchmark realism and source fidelity to operational data are separate concerns that both warrant targeted optimization.

Abstract: Synthetic clinical benchmarks for enterprise AI agents can pass existing utility checks and still remain structurally unrealistic, especially in privacy-sensitive healthcare settings where operational data are hard to access. We study how to improve such benchmarks without breaking the downstream utility checks already used in practice.
  We formulate benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement: dataset changes should increase realism while staying above an operational utility floor. We instantiate this idea on a care-gap benchmark derived from Synthea-generated patients exercised through demonstration electronic health record workflows and then processed by the same downstream pipeline as operational data. Realism is measured through missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment.
  The baseline benchmark is extremely thin: sampled-pair missingness is 79.44%, only 12.75% of rows are actionable, 38.94% of patients have zero actionable measures, and top-three token concentration reaches 100.0%. Two deterministic revisions improve these panels while remaining above the current utility floor, whereas a naive densification control preserves unrealistic templating. We further show that internal benchmark realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are related but distinct objectives. These results suggest that synthetic benchmark quality should be optimized explicitly, with utility treated as one constraint rather than as sufficient evidence of realism.

</details>


### [156] [The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use: A Causal Audit of Thinking with Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06270)
*Zhiheng Wang,Bo Peng,Lai Wei,Chaochao Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper audits whether visual tool-use (e.g., crop-and-zoom) in multimodal LLMs causally contributes to answers.
