### [163] [Mixed Uncertainty in One View: Co-Visualizing Statistical Variability and Qualitative Confidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05487)
*Racquel Fygenson,Lace Padilla,Laura E. Matzen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Three preregistered studies (n=923) examine how different visual encoding techniques (text, icons, color, transparency, blurred stroke) for representing qualitative confidence alongside quantitative confidence intervals in line charts influence non-experts' decision making, finding that non-textual encodings can effectively convey qualitative confidence and offering actionable design guidelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior research shows that communicating both quantitative uncertainty and qualitative confidence affects decision making, little is known about how the visual presentation of these dual uncertainty forms influences judgments, particularly in time-series line chart forecasts.

Method: Three preregistered human-subjects experiments (total n=923) tested non-experts' decision making responses to line chart forecasts. Experiment 1 replicated prior findings by showing qualitative confidence (via text) alongside confidence intervals. Experiments 2 and 3 compared multiple non-textual encoding techniques — including icons, color, transparency, and a blurred stroke design — for representing qualitative confidence either separately from or integrated into quantitative confidence intervals.

Result: Experiment 1 confirmed that presenting qualitative confidence alongside statistical variability alters decision-making patterns, replicating prior work in the time-series line chart context. Experiments 2 and 3 demonstrated that several non-textual encoding techniques produce similar effects to text-based representations in how participants incorporate qualitative confidence into their judgments.

Conclusion: Non-textual visual encodings can effectively convey qualitative confidence alongside quantitative uncertainty in line chart forecasts. The findings provide actionable design guidelines for visualization practitioners seeking to represent multiple uncertainty forms simultaneously.

Abstract: Forecasting involves multiple forms of uncertainty, including both uncertainties that can be quantified directly (quantitative uncertainty) and those that must be expressed through experts' subjective judgments about the forecast and its context (qualitative confidence). Past work has established that conveying both quantitative uncertainty and qualitative confidence in forecasts can alter readers' decision making, but little research investigates the impact of how these forms of uncertainty are presented. In this work, we present three preregistered human-subjects studies (total n = 923) on how different methods of visualizing qualitative uncertainty alongside line charts' confidence intervals affects non-experts' decision making. In particular, we investigate representing qualitative uncertainty separately via text and icons, and integrated into quantitative confidence intervals via color, transparency, and a blurred stroke design. In Experiment 1, we confirm that showing qualitative confidence alongside statistical variability can change patterns of decision making, replicating findings from previous work in the new context of time-series line charts. In Experiments 2 and 3, we find several non-textual encoding techniques that produce similar effects in participants' incorporation of qualitative confidence into their judgments. Our findings suggest actionable guidelines for visualization designers who seek to represent multiple forms of uncertainty for a single line chart forecast. A free copy of this paper and all supplemental materials are available at https://osf.io/7ya2c/overview.

</details>


### [164] [Turing's Frist Imitation Game: Design Concepts and a Human-Approximates-Machine Reading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05558)
*Sharon Temtsin,Christoph Bartneck*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper analyzes Turing's 1948 "Intelligent Machinery" report, integrating its key design concepts—machine fallibility, exclusion of physical features, the human judge's role, and search as central to intellect—and argues that restricting the human contestant to a poor chess player in the imitation game makes human behavior more machine-like, reframing the game as a human-approximates-machine test.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish Turing's 1948 report as a crucial conceptual source for his later imitation games and to offer a novel interpretation of the chess-based imitation game that broadens the framework beyond the standard "can machines imitate humans?" question.

Method: Conceptual analysis and historical integration of Turing's 1948 report, focusing on distilling four design concepts (machine fallibility, exclusion of physical features, the human judge, search as intellectual activity) and applying them to reinterpret the chess-based imitation game.

Result: The paper identifies four integrated design concepts in the 1948 report; it further argues that using a poor chess player as the human contestant amplifies the role of intellectual search, rendering human performance more comparable to machine behavior, and thus reframes the imitation game as a human-approximates-machine test.

Conclusion: The 1948 chess-based imitation game should be understood as a human-approximates-machine game, demonstrating that Turing's framework can investigate not only machine imitation of humans but also the conditions under which human intelligence becomes machine-like, thereby extending the scope of the imitation game paradigm.

Abstract: This paper examines Turing's 1948 report, "Intelligent Machinery", as an important conceptual source for the later imitation games. Its first contribution is to identify and integrate the design concepts underlying the 1948 chess-based imitation game: the possibility that intelligent machines may make mistakes, the exclusion of irrelevant physical features, the role of the human judge, and Turing's claim that intellectual activity consists mainly of search. The paper's second contribution is to argue that restricting the human contestant to a rather poor chess player increases the role of intellectual search and makes human behaviour more comparable to machine behaviour. This interpretation presents the 1948 game as a human-approximates-machine game and suggests that the imitation game framework can be used not only to ask whether machines imitate humans, but also to examine when human intelligence becomes machine-like under specific task constraints.

</details>


### [165] [A Multi-Layer System for Ultra-High-Resolution Static 360-Degree Telepresence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05570)
*Jiapeng Chi,Gerd Bruder,Carsten Neumann,Carolina Cruz-Neira,Dirk Reiners*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A multi-layer system for static 360-degree telepresence that combines an 8K panoramic camera with a rotatable 4K PTZ camera to achieve ultra-high-resolution backgrounds through tile-based offline stitching and real-time dynamic updates, outperforming video super-resolution baselines while balancing fidelity and interactivity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 360-degree telepresence is limited by capture and display resolution. Existing installations often use fixed viewpoints and static scenes, yet optimization strategies specifically designed for such constrained setups have been underexplored.

Method: A three-layer representation: (1) a tile-based ultra-high-resolution panoramic background layer created by offline stitching 4K PTZ camera scans onto an 8K base panorama, yielding spatial tiles with resolution beyond native capture; (2) a dynamic update layer that composites foreground motions from the 8K stream using real-time high-resolution background matting; (3) a region-of-interest 4K layer that streams a real-time PTZ view of a user-selected region and progressively updates corresponding background tiles.

Result: Evaluated via comparisons against representative video super-resolution approaches and a user study on perceived detail and immersion. Results show that tile-based background refinement with user-guided updates effectively balances panoramic fidelity and interactivity.

Conclusion: Tile-based background refinement combined with user-guided updates offers a practical approach to balancing panoramic fidelity and interactivity in static 360-degree telepresence systems.

Abstract: 360-degree video telepresence offers strong immersive potential but remains constrained by the limited resolution of current capture and display hardware. Many telepresence installations feature fixed viewpoints and largely static scenes, yet optimization strategies tailored to such setups have received limited attention. We present a multi-layer, ultra-high-resolution system for static 360-degree telepresence that combines an 8K panoramic camera with a rotatable 4K pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) camera. Our approach builds a three-layer representation: (1) a tile-based ultra-high-resolution panoramic background, generated by offline stitching high-detail 4K PTZ scans onto the base 8K panorama to achieve effective resolution beyond native capture, and represented as a set of spatial tiles; (2) a dynamic update layer that composites foreground motions from the 8K stream via real-time high-resolution background matting; and (3) a region-of-interest 4K layer that streams a real-time PTZ view of the selected region and additionally updates the corresponding background tiles over time. We evaluate the proposed system through comparisons with representative video super-resolution approaches and a user study assessing perceived detail and immersive experience. Our results indicate that tile-based background refinement, together with user-guided updates, provides a practical way to balance panoramic fidelity and interactivity in static 360-degree telepresence.

</details>


### [166] [Toward Resilient Human-AI Collaboration: A Lifecycle Taxonomy of Sociotechnical Risks and Cascading Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05614)
*Md Foysal Ahmed,Isaac Kobby Anni,Md Main Uddin Rony*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper synthesizes fragmented literature on human-AI collaboration risks into a unified, lifecycle-oriented framework spanning task allocation, interaction, feedback, and adoption. It identifies six recurring cross-domain risk clusters and proposes a conceptual interaction model showing how sociotechnical drivers create cascading failure pathways that undermine team performance and human well-being.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems are deployed in high-stakes domains (healthcare, journalism, education, defense, etc.), human-AI collaboration becomes critical. However, existing research examines sociotechnical risks in isolation, obscuring recurring failure mechanisms that cut across domains. There is a need for a unified framework that reveals interconnected patterns rather than treating risks as independent problems.

Method: The authors conduct a lifecycle-oriented synthesis of human-AI collaboration risks, organizing evidence from diverse application domains across four stages: task allocation, interaction, feedback, and adoption. From this synthesis, they derive six cross-domain risk clusters and develop a conceptual interaction model illustrating how risks emerge from sociotechnical drivers, interact through cascading pathways, and impact team performance and well-being.

Result: The analysis yields six recurring cross-domain risk clusters: (1) Trust Miscalibration, (2) Cognitive Burden, (3) Accountability Gap, (4) Capability Erosion, (5) Goal Misalignment, and (6) AI Anxiety and Technostress. The conceptual model reveals that most collaboration failures originate from interconnected sociotechnical dynamics rather than isolated technical deficiencies, explaining why piecemeal interventions frequently produce unintended consequences.

Conclusion: The paper provides a unified, lifecycle-oriented framework that integrates previously fragmented literature on human-AI collaboration risks. This foundation supports future empirical research, lifecycle-oriented governance, and the design of more resilient, trustworthy, and human-centered human-AI collaboration systems.

Abstract: As AI systems become increasingly integrated into consequential domains such as healthcare, journalism, education, scientific research, organizational decision-making, and defense, effective human-AI collaboration has emerged as a critical challenge. However, the sociotechnical risks that undermine collaboration are often studied in isolation, obscuring the recurring failure mechanisms that cut across domains. This paper presents a lifecycle-oriented synthesis of human-AI collaboration risks spanning four stages: task allocation, interaction, feedback, and adoption. Drawing on evidence from diverse application domains, we identify six recurring cross-domain risk clusters: Trust Miscalibration, Cognitive Burden, Accountability Gap, Capability Erosion, Goal Misalignment, and AI Anxiety and Technostress. We further propose a conceptual interaction model that illustrates how these risks emerge from sociotechnical drivers, interact through cascading pathways, and ultimately affect team performance and human well-being. Our analysis shows that many collaboration failures stem not from isolated technical deficiencies but from interconnected sociotechnical dynamics, helping explain why piecemeal interventions frequently create unintended consequences. By synthesizing fragmented literature into a unified framework, this work provides a foundation for future empirical research, lifecycle-oriented governance, and the design of more resilient, trustworthy, and human-centered human-AI collaboration systems.

</details>


### [167] [CaRing: Preventing Carpal Tunnel Syndrome based on Daily Activities from Always-Available Input Device](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05619)
*Shuowei Li,Houdong Liang,Xingjian Dong*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: CaRing is an index-finger-worn ring that uses an optical flow sensor to detect when mouse use starts and ends, aiming to prevent Carpal Tunnel Syndrome. It establishes a per-session zero point while the hand rests on the desk, enabling threshold-based detection without per-user calibration, achieving ~90% detection accuracy within two seconds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome involves permanent median nerve damage, and preventing it requires detecting mouse use patterns. Existing approaches (software timers, wrist-worn devices) fail to capture actual finger movement — the key indicator of mouse interaction. A wearable that directly senses finger motion at the index finger's base knuckle can fill this gap.

Method: CaRing is worn on the base knuckle of the index finger and employs an optical flow sensor to track finger displacement. Displacement readings are accumulated into a running value. At the start of each session, a zero point is measured while the hand rests on the desk. Start and end thresholds are defined relative to this session-specific zero point, eliminating the need for per-user parameter tuning. Detection is evaluated on 35 recordings from a 10-user lab study.

Result: Approximately 90% of mouse-use start and end events were detected within two seconds of the researcher-labeled ground truth, across 35 recordings from ten users.

Conclusion: CaRing demonstrates that an optical-flow-based ring sensor with a session-relative zero-point formulation can reliably detect mouse use onset and cessation without per-user calibration, offering a promising approach for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome prevention through accurate activity monitoring.

Abstract: We present CaRing, a ring worn on the base knuckle of the index finger, a wearable system for detecting the start and end of mouse use to help prevent Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, in which the damage to the median nerve is permanent. CaRing senses finger movement, which neither a software timer nor a wrist-worn device detects. The displacement reported by an optical flow sensor is accumulated into a running value, then a zero point is measured while the hand rests on the desk at the start of each session. With this formulation, the start and end thresholds are expressed relative to the session's zero point. CaRing does not introduce any per-user parameter. We empirically demonstrate that approximately $90\%$ of start and end events are detected within two seconds of the researcher's label, using 35 recordings and a lab study with ten users.

</details>


### [168] [ASIDE: From Conflict Participants to Co-Observers Through Dyadic Spectator Reflection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05690)
*Xinyi Zhang,Jingting He,Zicheng Zhu,Yuxin Su*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: ASIDE is a system that helps couples reflect on past text-based conflicts by generating a pixel-art theatrical replay with AI-inferred inner states, allowing each partner to independently annotate their own and their partner's perspectives before jointly reviewing where their interpretations diverged.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI reflection tools are single-user and cannot surface interpretive gaps between two people, while dyadic tools support co-expression but do not make divergent understandings inspectable. There is no tool that lets partners externalize their interpretations independently and then encounter those differences together.

Method: The authors introduce Dyadic Spectator Reflection (DSR), a two-phase structure: (1) externalize independently, (2) encounter together. ASIDE implements DSR by generating a pixel-art theatrical replay of a past chat conflict with AI-generated inner-state hypotheses for each conversational turn. Partners separately confirm their own inner states and edit interpretations of the other's. After both finish, they view the co-annotated scene and Divergence Cards that juxtapose their confirmed account against their partner's reading at specific conversational beats. An exploratory study was conducted with 10 real couples revisiting actual text-based conflicts.

Result: Participants reported that the theatrical replay helped them "step out of their roles" and observe the conflict together from a shared spectator position, enabling more reflective joint sense-making about their disagreement.

Conclusion: DSR is contributed as a reusable interaction structure for dyadic reflection, and the study provides an exploratory account of how partners used this structure to revisit past text-based conflicts from a shared observer perspective.

Abstract: When people argue over text, they share a record of what was said but may hold different accounts of what it meant. Existing AI reflection tools typically work from one person's account, while dyadic tools support co-expression without making interpretation gaps inspectable. We present ASIDE, a system for Dyadic Spectator Reflection (DSR). DSR follows the sequence externalize independently, then encounter together. From a past chat conflict, ASIDE creates a pixel-art theatrical replay with revisable AI-generated inner-state hypotheses. Partners first confirm hypotheses about themselves and separately edit their interpretations of the other. After both finish, they view the co-annotated scene together and review Divergence Cards that pair a confirmed account with the partner's reading at a specific conversational beat. In an exploratory study with 10 couples who revisited real text-based conflicts, participants described the theatrical replay as helping them step out of their roles and observe the conflict together. We contribute DSR as a reusable interaction structure for dyadic reflection and an exploratory account of how partners used it to revisit past text-based conflicts from a shared observer position.

</details>


### [169] [SpaceVLA: Spatially Grounded VLA for Robotic Manipulation with User-Authored Grasp and Place Anchors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05730)
*Daniia Zinniatullina,Iaroslav Kolomiets,Mikhail Konenkov,Miguel Altamirano Cabrera,Dzmitry Tsetserukou*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Introduces Visual Intent Anchors, an XR pipeline that overlays user-specified grasp/placement regions onto images for VLA models, achieving 91.25% grasp success with sub-centimeter precision in Unity pick-and-place tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLA models follow language commands but lack explicit spatial intent for manipulation, making it difficult to specify precise grasp and placement locations through language alone.

Method: An XR pipeline lets users delineate grasp and placement regions, which are rendered as image-space overlays. OpenVLA-7B is fine-tuned with LoRA on 200 Unity demonstrations with temporally subsampled annotated observations. The policy predicts tokenized 7-DoF incremental actions from marked RGB frames and language input.

Result: In closed-loop Unity evaluation, the policy attains 91.25% grasp success rate, with mean grasp error of 0.5 cm and mean placement error of 0.7 cm.

Conclusion: Visual intent anchors effectively bridge the spatial intent gap in VLA models, enabling precise, user-guided robotic manipulation with minimal spatial error in a simulated environment.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models follow language commands but often lack explicit spatial intent for manipulation. We present Visual Intent Anchors, an XR pipeline that lets users specify grasp and placement regions and renders them as image-space overlays for VLA control. We collect 200 Unity pick-and-place demonstrations and fine-tune OpenVLA-7B with LoRA on temporally subsampled annotated observations. The policy predicts tokenized 7-DoF incremental actions from marked RGB observations and language. We evaluate the policy in closed-loop Unity trials, achieving a grasp success rate of 91.25% and mean grasp and placement errors of 0.5 cm and 0.7 cm, respectively.

</details>


### [170] [Temporal Tracking of Reeb-Space Sheets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05837)
*Mohit Sharma,Petar Hristov,Talha Bin Masood,Ingrid Hotz*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A framework for tracking Reeb space sheets across timesteps in time-varying bivariate fields, using complementary similarity measures in both spatial and range domains, demonstrated on synthetic and molecular electronic structure data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While topological methods like merge trees are well-established for tracking features in univariate time-varying data, analogous approaches for bivariate fields remain underexplored. Reeb spaces naturally extend topological analysis to multivariate data via interconnected sheets, but establishing temporal correspondences between sheets across timesteps is difficult due to structural complexity, noise sensitivity, and the lack of meaningful similarity measures.

Method: The authors propose a framework that establishes correspondences between Reeb space sheets in consecutive timesteps using two complementary similarity measures: one defined in the spatial domain (capturing geometric overlap of fiber pre-images) and one defined in the range space (capturing proximity in the bivariate scalar field domain). These measures are combined to reliably track sheets over time.

Result: Evaluation on a synthetic torus dataset and two time-varying molecular electronic structure datasets shows that the sheet tracking reveals persistent structures and highlights intervals of significant temporal change. The approach demonstrates that Reeb space sheets can serve as trackable topological features.

Conclusion: Reeb space sheets are viable as trackable topological structures for time-varying bivariate data. The proposed framework provides a foundation for visual analysis of such data, successfully identifying both stable, persistent features and dynamic temporal events.

Abstract: Time-varying bivariate fields arise in many scientific applications, where the relationship between two scalar quantities evolves over time. While topological methods such as merge trees provide an effective framework for identifying and tracking features in univariate data, analogous approaches for bivariate fields remain comparatively underexplored. Reeb spaces extend topological analysis to multivariate data by representing fiber connectivity through a collection of interconnected sheets, making these sheets natural candidates for describing bivariate structures. However, establishing temporal correspondences between sheets is challenging due to the structural complexity of Reeb spaces, sensitivity to noise, and the difficulty of defining meaningful similarity measures across timesteps. We present a framework for tracking Reeb space sheets in time-varying bivariate fields. The method establishes correspondences between sheets in consecutive timesteps using complementary similarity measures defined in the spatial domain and the range space. We evaluate the method on a synthetic torus dataset and two time-varying molecular electronic structure datasets. The results show that Reeb space sheet tracking reveals persistent structures and highlights interesting intervals of temporal change. Overall, the results demonstrate that Reeb space sheets can serve as trackable topological structures and provide a foundation for the visual analysis of time-varying bivariate data.

</details>


### [171] [Topic Matters: How Linguistic Properties can Shape Reading Behaviour in Selective Exposure Studies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05942)
*Thomas Krämer,Dagmar Kern,Thomas Kosch,Daniel Hienert*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Texts across controversial topics differ systematically in linguistic properties, which in turn shape reading behavior in eye-tracking studies — introducing a critical methodological confound in selective exposure research that must be accounted for.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Selective exposure research routinely uses eye tracking and assumes that texts on different controversial topics are comparable after basic controls. The authors challenge this assumption, arguing that topic-dependent linguistic features may systematically influence how readers allocate attention, potentially confounding experimental results.

Method: A laboratory study with 68 participants who searched for and read news articles on two controversial topics: climate change and migration policy. The authors analyzed linguistic features of the texts and corresponding eye-tracking measures to assess systematic differences in both textual characteristics and reading behavior across topics.

Result: Systematic differences were found in both textual characteristics (linguistic features) and reading behavior (eye-tracking measures) between the two topics, confirming that topic-dependent linguistic properties relate to differences in how users read and allocate attention.

Conclusion: Topic-specific linguistic properties constitute a significant methodological confound in selective exposure research. Researchers must account for these properties when interpreting eye-tracking measures and when designing systems aimed at mitigating biased information consumption.

Abstract: Research on selective exposure frequently relies on eye tracking to study reading behaviour, often assuming that texts across different controversial topics are comparable once basic controls are applied. This assumption is problematic if topic-dependent linguistic properties systematically shape how users read and allocate attention. We therefore examine whether such properties relate to differences in reading behaviour in selective exposure contexts. We analyse linguistic features and eye-tracking data from a laboratory study in which 68 participants searched for and read news articles on climate change and migration policy. Our results reveal systematic differences in both textual characteristics and reading behaviour across topics. These findings identify an important methodological confound in selective exposure research and highlight the need to account for topic-specific linguistic properties when interpreting eye-tracking measures and designing systems intended to mitigate biased information consumption.

</details>


### [172] [A Modular Workflow for Multimodal Reading Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05966)
*Thomas Krämer,Thomas Kosch,Dagmar Kern,Daniel Hienert*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A modular, web-based workflow integrating eye tracking, EEG, and interaction data for real-time multimodal experiments in naturalistic online reading, enabling online gaze-derived metrics and post-task neural/behavioral analysis within a single lab session.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional reading research relies heavily on self-report measures and lacks ecological validity. There is a need for an integrated, reusable experimental framework that combines multiple physiological and behavioral sensors to study naturalistic online reading in real time, enabling empirical validation of cognitive constructs in ecologically valid contexts.

Method: The authors developed a web-based modular workflow that (1) integrates eye tracking, EEG, and mouse/keyboard interaction data; (2) synchronizes all streams via Lab Streaming Layer (LSL); (3) maps gaze data to browser-based text at word, sentence, and AOI levels; (4) computes gaze-derived measures online during the experiment; and (5) performs fixation-triggered segmentation of EEG and other streams immediately post-task. A use case on selective exposure in online news search and reading validates the approach.

Result: The workflow successfully produces behavioral, neural, and linguistic metrics that support selecting text passages for targeted post-task rating or labeling within the same lab session. It enables real-time gaze-derived measures and immediate post-task processing of synchronized EEG data, demonstrating feasibility for multimodal reading research in ecological settings.

Conclusion: The workflow provides a general, reusable basis for multimodal research on reading and related cognitive processes, bridging the gap between controlled lab paradigms and naturalistic online reading. It supports the empirical validation of constructs typically operationalized via self-report, offering a foundation for future studies requiring synchronized physiological and behavioral data in web-based environments.

Abstract: We introduce a web-based modular workflow for real-time multimodal experiments in naturalistic online reading. The workflow integrates eye tracking, EEG, and interaction data from mouse and keyboard, synchronizes them via Lab Streaming Layer, and links gaze to browser-based text at the word, sentence, and AOI levels. It is designed as a reusable experimental procedure that can be adapted to different sensors, tasks, and analysis goals. As a use case, we apply the workflow to a study of selective exposure in online news search and reading. During the experiment, gaze-derived measures are computed online, while EEG and other synchronized streams are processed immediately after task sessions based on fixation-triggered segmentation. The resulting behavioral, neural, and linguistic metrics support selecting text passages for targeted post-task rating or labelling within the same lab session. The workflow thus provides a general basis for multimodal research on reading and related cognitive processes, and supports the empirical validation, in ecological contexts, of constructs that are typically operationalised through self-report measures.

</details>


### [173] [PoseForge: Editable Pose Analytics for AI-Assisted Sports Coaching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05971)
*Shuvam Swapnil Dash,Arpit Narechania*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: PoseForge is an open-source visual analytics system that extracts 3D skeletal poses from single-camera sports videos, computes kinematic metrics, compares them against norms, and enables interactive pose correction via mouse or natural-language input, validated with eleven cricket experts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Raw sports footage lacks quantitative tools for motion analysis and simulation of valid corrective adjustments. Coaches need interpretable kinematic feedback to diagnose technique flaws and explore corrections, especially in low-resource settings without expensive multi-camera motion capture.

Method: Formative interviews with 11 cricket experts informed design. PoseForge extracts 3D skeletal poses from monocular video using pose estimation, computes kinematic metrics (e.g., feet gap, elbow angle), compares them against scientifically derived norms, and integrates an AI coach for targeted natural-language suggestions. Users can modify poses via mouse interaction or natural-language commands, with inverse kinematics ensuring anatomical plausibility and real-time metric updates.

Result: Evaluation with the same 11 cricket experts demonstrated PoseForge's effectiveness for diagnosing movement issues and exploring corrective alternatives, with applicability shown for academy, grassroots, and low-resource coaching contexts.

Conclusion: PoseForge successfully bridges the gap between raw video footage and actionable biomechanical feedback, enabling interactive movement analysis and correction. Future work includes expanding sport-specific metrics and longitudinal tracking capabilities.

Abstract: Athletic coaching increasingly relies on video analysis, yet raw footage lacks tools to quantify motion or simulate valid technique corrections. Drawing on formative interviews with eleven cricket experts (coaches, performance analysts, captains, and players), we introduce PoseForge, a visual analytics system that extracts 3D skeletal poses from single-camera sports videos for interactive movement analysis. In a cricket batting case study, PoseForge computes interpretable kinematic metrics such as feet gap and elbow angle, compares them against scientifically derived norms, and uses an AI coach to suggest targeted adjustments, presented visually and through natural-language feedback (e.g., "increase feet gap by 10 cm"). Users can directly modify poses via mouse interaction or natural-language instructions, with inverse kinematics maintaining anatomical plausibility and real-time updates of metrics and comparisons. An evaluation with the same eleven cricket experts found PoseForge effective for diagnosing movement issues and exploring corrective alternatives, highlighting its applicability in low-resource, academy, and grassroots coaching settings, while identifying opportunities for enhanced sport-specific metrics and longitudinal tracking. PoseForge is available as open-source software at https://github.com/DataVisards/PoseForge.

</details>


### [174] [OneEmo: A Unified Multimodal Reasoning Model for Emotion Perception, Understanding, and Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06013)
*Jiahao Huang,Zheng Lian,Jingyi Zhang,Zhide Chen,Xiaojiang Peng,Shaonan Wang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: OneEmo is a unified multimodal affective model that jointly masters emotion perception, comprehension, and interaction. It uses a curated dataset (EmoWorld-130K) with human-in-the-loop reasoning trajectories and a novel multi-task RL strategy (Emo-Chord) to achieve SOTA performance, outperforming similarly sized models and rivaling larger commercial ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM research on emotional intelligence is fragmented across isolated tasks (perception, comprehension, interaction), ignoring inter-task synergy and leaving latent reasoning capabilities underexploited. A unified approach is needed to harness mutual benefits from multi-task learning.

Method: First, construct EmoWorld-130K, a comprehensive dataset using a human-in-the-loop workflow to distill specialized affective knowledge into explicit reasoning trajectories. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on this corpus enables multi-task mutual learning. Second, propose Emo-Chord, a novel reinforcement learning strategy that stabilizes optimization through unified multi-task reward allocation to unlock latent reasoning potential.

Result: OneEmo achieves state-of-the-art performance against similarly sized baselines across most benchmarks. Despite significantly fewer parameters than commercial models, it delivers highly competitive results.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that unified multi-task training with structured reasoning trajectories and stable multi-task RL can produce a highly capable, interpretable affective generalist, paving the way for more reliable affective computing.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in emotional intelligence. However, prevailing research predominantly focuses on task-specific specialization, often neglecting inter-task synergy and leaving latent reasoning potential underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce OneEmo, a unified affective generalist capable of mastering emotion perception, comprehension, and interaction. For this purpose, we first construct EmoWorld-130K, a comprehensive dataset that distills specialized affective knowledge into explicit reasoning trajectories via a human-in-the-loop workflow. Supervised fine-tuning on this corpus reveals significant mutual benefits derived from multi-task learning. Second, to fully unlock the latent reasoning potential, we propose Emo-Chord, a novel reinforcement learning strategy that stabilizes optimization through unified multi-task reward allocation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OneEmo achieves state-of-the-art performance against similarly sized baselines across most benchmarks. Notably, despite having significantly fewer parameters than commercial models, OneEmo delivers highly competitive results. This paper paves the way for more reliable and interpretable affective computing. The code is available at https://github.com/waHAHJIAHAO/OneEmo.

</details>


### [175] [Cleo: A Transparent and Controllable Chatbot for Conversational Commerce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06068)
*Kevin Schott,Jan Lattenkamp,Daniel Hienert,Dagmar Kern*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Cleo is a conversational product advisor combining a deterministic ranking engine with a constrained LLM to deliver transparent, controllable, and hallucination-mitigated product recommendations, featuring per-attribute loss explanations and natural-language comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing conversational commerce systems suffer from LLM opacity, unpredictability, and the cognitive burden of comparing complex product specifications. Traditional faceted search lacks conversational fluidity, while purely LLM-based recommenders risk hallucination and persuasive bias.

Method: A hybrid architecture separates deterministic ranking (categorical filters + numeric loss functions over 3,638 product specs) from constrained LLM-based language generation. The LLM reflects on interpreted user needs for transparency, while an auditable ranking mechanism exposes per-attribute loss values. Generation is grounded strictly to catalog evidence to prevent hallucination.

Result: The system delivers four contributions: (1) transparent need reflection and auditable rankings, (2) controllable hybrid architecture, (3) decision support via natural-language comparisons and highlights, and (4) an extensible experimental platform for IR/HCI research. A live demonstration showcases real-time re-ranking, loss inspection, and AI-generated multi-item comparisons.

Conclusion: Cleo advances conversational system design by demonstrating that fluid conversation and algorithmic transparency are compatible goals, offering a practical blueprint for transparent, controllable product advisors in online commerce.

Abstract: We demonstrate Cleo, a transparent and controllable conversational product advisor that addresses the challenges of opacity, unpredictability of LLMs, and the complexity of comparisons in conversational commerce. With our chatbot system, we make four contributions: First, we introduce transparency by prompting the LLM to reflect on interpreted user needs, while an auditable ranking mechanism reveals loss values per attribute, explaining ranking decisions. Second, we propose controllability through a hybrid architecture separating deterministic ranking from language generation. A ranker applies categorical filters and numeric loss functions over 3,638 product specifications. Meanwhile, a constrained LLM generates grounded descriptions constrained to catalog evidence, thus mitigating the risk of hallucinated or persuasive content. Third, we provide decision support in the form of natural-language comparisons and a highlights feature. These aim to reduce mental workload by contextualizing specifications relative to user needs. Fourth, we contribute an extensible experimental system for IR and HCI researchers, as well as practitioners of conversational search and recommendation. Unlike traditional faceted search or opaque LLM-only recommenders, our approach allows for fluid conversation while maintaining algorithmic transparency. In a live demonstration, attendees will experience information needs elicitation and reflection, conversational refinement with real-time re-ranking, inspection of per-attribute loss explanations, and AI-generated multi-item comparisons. The system aims to advance the design of transparent and controllable conversational systems that provide support for decision-making during online product search.

</details>


### [176] ["I don't know anything about laptops!" - User Perception of Digital Product Advisors Adapting to Their Knowledge Levels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06091)
*Kevin Schott,Andrea Papenmeier,Daniel Hienert,Dagmar Kern*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A study on chatbot-assisted laptop search examined how augmenting technical product information with performance categories and/or attribute explanations affects novice and expert users. Findings show novices benefit significantly from explanations, while experts are not negatively affected, leading to four design guidelines for inclusive conversational commerce interfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conversational commerce agents must adapt their communication style to users with varying domain knowledge, but how to effectively present complex product information to both novices and experts remains an open challenge. The study aims to identify strategies for knowledge-level adaptation that support shared understanding without disadvantaging either user group.

Method: A between-subjects experiment (n=251) using a chatbot-assisted laptop search scenario with four conditions: technical information only (T), technical + performance categories (TC), technical + attribute explanations (TE), and technical + categories + explanations (TCE). Both novice and expert participants rated perceptions of helpfulness, information quantity appropriateness, and perceived learning across conditions.

Result: Novices perceived TE and TCE conditions as significantly more helpful and reported higher perceived learning than T or TC alone. They also rated TCE as more appropriate in information quantity than T and TC. Experts showed no significant differences across any conditions, indicating supplementary information for novices does not harm expert experience.

Conclusion: The authors distill four design guidelines: (1) use TCE (technical + categories + explanations) by default; (2) maintain a single inclusive interface for all users; (3) avoid standalone performance categories without explanations; and (4) support user agency and personalize to the stated use case.

Abstract: Conversational commerce uses digital assistants to support the search process and decision-making in e-commerce. Effective communication in these interactions can be facilitated by assistants adapting their communication style to users and supporting shared understanding. An open challenge in this context is adapting the presentation of complex product information to users with varying levels of domain knowledge. To investigate strategies for such knowledge-level adaptation, we set up a chatbot-assisted laptop search scenario. In a between-subjects experiment (n = 251), we examined novice and expert perceptions of product attribute recommendations presented as technical information only (T), or augmented with performance categories (TC), attribute explanations (TE), or both (TCE). For novices, approaches with explanations (TE, TCE) were perceived as more helpful and led to higher perceived learning than those without. Novices also rated the combined approach (TCE) more appropriate than the baseline (T) and TC in terms of information quantity, indicating that explanations are crucial to understand and benefit from performance categories. Critically, experts showed no significant differences across conditions, suggesting that providing supplementary information beneficial to novices did not detract from their experience. We distill these findings into four concrete design guidelines for inclusive text-based product advisors in technical domains: use TCE by default; keep a single inclusive interface; avoid standalone categories; and support user agency and personalize to the stated use case.

</details>


### [177] [Divergent Perceptuomotor Recalibration in Virtual Reality and Video-Passthrough Mixed Reality on the Same Head-Mounted Display](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06132)
*Xiaoye Michael Wang,Grant Monahan,Timothy N. Welsh*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: VR and MR-VPT delivered on the same headset produce opposite initial pointing biases (undershooting vs. overshooting), different adaptation rates, and distinct aftereffects, demonstrating that perceptuomotor recalibration is shaped by the visual information available in each modality, not just display hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VR and MR-VPT can run on identical headsets, yet it remains unclear whether these modalities yield comparable perceptuomotor behavior. Differences in visual-feedback pipelines and the availability of action-relevant visual information (e.g., synthetically rendered vs. passthrough-preserved body and environment) may lead to distinct patterns of movement planning and adaptation.

Method: Forty adults were assigned to either a VR or MR-VPT group using the same headset. Participants performed a visually guided manual pointing task in unmediated reality (UR) before and after exposure to their assigned XR modality. Baseline UR performance, pointing biases during XR exposure, adaptation trajectories, and post-exposure aftereffects were compared between groups.

Result: (1) Baseline UR performance was equivalent across groups. (2) Initial biases during XR exposure were opposite: VR group undershot targets, MR-VPT group overshot. (3) Adaptation patterns diverged: VR adapted more slowly with stronger distance-dependent undershooting. (4) Post-XR, both groups exhibited undershooting aftereffects, with the VR group showing persistent residual undershoot indicative of incomplete de-adaptation.

Conclusion: Perceptuomotor recalibration is influenced not only by display-level constraints but critically by the action-relevant visual information available in the interaction environment. Consequently, perceptuomotor interaction techniques must be validated separately in VR and MR-VPT, even when implemented on identical hardware.

Abstract: Virtual reality (VR) and video-passthrough mixed reality (MR-VPT) can be delivered on the same headset, but it is unclear whether these two interaction modalities produce comparable perceptuomotor behavior. Although delivery through the same headset controls many display-level characteristics, VR and MR-VPT differ in both their visual-feedback pipelines and the action-relevant visual information available to guide movement, such as whether the surrounding environment and the user's body are synthetically rendered or preserved through passthrough. This study compared visually guided manual pointing in VR and MR-VPT using the same headset. Forty adults were assigned to either a VR or MR-VPT group and completed a pointing task in the physical, unmediated reality (UR) before and after performing the same task in their assigned XR modality. The analyses revealed numerous important insights. First, groups had comparable baseline performance in UR prior to XR exposure. Second, the two modalities produced opposite initial biases during XR exposure: the VR group undershot the target, whereas the MR-VPT group overshot. Third, although both groups reduced error with continued exposure to XR, there were differences in the patterns of adaptation: the VR group adapted more slowly and exhibited stronger distance-dependent undershooting than the MR-VPT group. Finally, after XR exposure, both groups showed significant undershooting aftereffects with the VR group retaining a persistent residual undershoot, suggesting incomplete de-adaptation. The results suggest that perceptuomotor recalibration is shaped not only by display-level constraints but also by the action-relevant visual information available within the interaction environment. These findings highlight the need to validate perceptuomotor interaction techniques separately in VR and MR-VPT, even when they are implemented on the same hardware.

</details>


### [178] [Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06151)
*Thomas H. Costello,Nathaniel Rabb,Michael Nicholas Stagnaro,Gordon Pennycook,David Rand*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Conversational dialogues with a large language model significantly reduced belief in emerging conspiracy theories following two high-profile assassination events, with effects persisting one to two months later.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conspiracy theories that emerge in the immediate aftermath of major societal events pose a significant challenge. The authors aimed to test whether scalable, cognitively-focused interventions using LLMs could counter these beliefs during the critical window when they are still forming.

Method: Two randomized controlled experiments were conducted shortly after real-world crises: the July 2024 Trump assassination attempt (N=472) and the September 2025 Charlie Kirk assassination (N=1,035). U.S. adults holding conspiratorial views engaged in multi-turn conversations with an LLM prompted to reduce conspiracy belief. Control conditions included chatting with an LLM about an irrelevant topic or viewing a static fact sheet. Follow-up surveys assessed downstream effects on different conspiracies one to two months later.

Result: The LLM treatment significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments compared to controls. Downstream effects were observed: reduced belief in unrelated conspiracies one to two months later following subsequent crisis events.

Conclusion: LLM-based conversational interventions show promise as scalable, cognitively-focused tools to reduce conspiracy beliefs as they emerge, with effects that generalize and persist beyond the original target conspiracy.

Abstract: The emergence of conspiracy theories in the wake of major events is a significant societal challenge. Here we test whether conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) can reduce belief in immediately unfolding conspiracies. In experiments conducted in the days following the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump and the September 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, U.S. adults (Experiment 1: N = 472; Experiment 2: N = 1035) holding conspiratorial views about the crisis event engaged in a multi-turn conversation with an LLM prompted to reduce their conspiracy belief. Compared to control participants who either discussed an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewed a static fact sheet, participants in the LLM treatment showed significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments. We also found evidence of downstream effects of the LLM treatment, observing reduced belief in different conspiracies one to two months later in the wake of subsequent crisis events. These results shed light on the psychology of emerging conspiracies and highlight the potential for scalable, cognitively-focused interventions to counteract misinformation in the immediate aftermath of high-profile societal events.

</details>


### [179] [What Current AI Benchmarks Leave Unmeasured: Modality, Search, Citations, and Implications (for Safety Evaluations)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06202)
*Ro Encarnación,Tina Behzad,Emma Lurie,Danaé Metaxa*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper audits the reliability of LLM benchmark evaluations by comparing ChatGPT's chat UI and API across two benchmarks (BBQ and SafetyBench) under different search conditions. Findings reveal that modality, web search, and repeated runs significantly affect accuracy, consistency, citation grounding, and abstention behavior — with accuracy dropping up to 8 points with search enabled and inconsistent responses in up to 21% of repeated prompts. The authors argue that AI safety evaluations must account for these factors to reflect real-world deployment behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM benchmark evaluations typically use a single modality (API), single-run prompts, and report only accuracy — ignoring deployment-relevant factors like web search, response consistency across runs, and differences between user-facing interfaces and APIs. This creates a gap between evaluation conditions and real-world deployment behavior, potentially undermining AI safety assessments.

Method: The authors conducted a stratified audit of one widely-used LLM (OpenAI's ChatGPT) across two modalities (chat UI vs. API), with and without web search enabled. They sampled 401 prompts from BBQ and SafetyBench benchmarks, collected 4,812 total responses over three repeated runs per prompt, and evaluated multiple output dimensions: accuracy, response consistency (run-to-run), response text similarity, citation grounding, and abstention behavior.

Result: Key findings: (1) Chat UI responses were less accurate than API responses on both benchmarks with search disabled. (2) Enabling web search reduced accuracy by up to 8 percentage points and reversed modality performance trends for one benchmark. (3) Repeated runs produced inconsistent responses in up to 21% of prompts. (4) The two modalities grounded answers in different citations. (5) Abstention behavior was inconsistent across both modalities.

Conclusion: Reporting only simple accuracy metrics obscures important behavioral variation relevant to AI safety. The authors argue that evaluations should systematically account for modality, multi-run consistency, search conditions, and response-level behaviors to better reflect how deployed AI systems behave in practice.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) benchmark evaluations are routinely used to support claims about model safety, reliability, and deployment readiness. Yet most evaluations rely on a single access modality (model APIs), perform a single run per prompt, and report accuracy as the primary outcome metric, without accounting for conditions such as web search that may have effects on model behavior in deployment. We audit these assumptions for one of the most widely-used LLMs, comparing two modalities, ChatGPT's chat UI and OpenAI's API, with and without web search enabled. We use a stratified total sample of 401 prompts from two popular benchmarks, BBQ and SafetyBench, collecting 4,812 total responses across three repeated runs per prompt. Beyond standard performance measures, we evaluate model output dimensions including response consistency, response text similarity, citation grounding, and abstention behavior. For instance, chat UI responses were less accurate than API responses on both benchmarks with search disabled. Enabling web search reduced accuracy by up to 8 percentage points, and even reversed the direction of modality performance trends for one benchmark. Repeated runs of the same prompt produced inconsistent responses in up to 21\% of prompts. The two modalities also grounded answers in different citations, and abstention behavior was also inconsistent across both modalities. These results illustrate that, even within a model family, reporting only simple accuracy metrics can obscure important forms of model behavioral variation relevant to AI safety assessments. We argue that AI safety evaluations should systematically account for modality, multi-run consistency, search conditions, and response-level behaviors to better reflect how deployed AI systems behave in practice.

</details>

# cs.CR [[Back]](#toc)

### [180] [Post-Hoc Trajectory-Risk Certification for Modular LLM-Based Security Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05199)
*Zhenpeng Li*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Autonomous security agent pipelines require trajectory-level conformal prediction guarantees, but naive composition fails. The paper shows Bonferroni is conservative, pairwise-correlation extensions beyond two stages are invalid, and proposes a valid spanning-tree approach with sample-complexity bounds. Experiments on two-stage intrusion detection reveal that coarse-to-fine label artifacts inflate correlation, and modular certificates cost only 0.6% coverage on average.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous security agents use staged pipelines (e.g., classify traffic, then attribute attacks). Each stage can be independently calibrated with split conformal prediction for finite-sample coverage, but these per-stage guarantees do not compose into a trajectory-level guarantee across the full chain. Existing approaches like Bonferroni allocation are distribution-free but overly conservative under correlated errors, and no valid method existed for three or more stages with pairwise correlations.

Method: The authors formally analyze the composition of conformal prediction sets across multi-stage pipelines. They prove that extending pairwise-correlation bounds to three or more stages yields a lower bound (invalid for coverage) rather than an upper bound, and derive a valid spanning-tree alternative. They distinguish between dependence of stages and certifiability of that dependence from finite audit samples, providing matching upper and information-theoretic lower sample-complexity bounds. They identify a spurious correlation artifact from coarse-to-fine label selection. Empirically, they evaluate on a two-stage intrusion-detection pipeline using 6 open LLMs and 2 datasets, comparing direct trajectory audit, Bonferroni, and a modular certificate using per-stage certificates with pairwise overlap bounds.

Result: (1) Coarse-to-fine label selection creates near-perfect measured correlation without learned dependence; removing this artifact drops measured correlation from ~1 to 0–0.78. (2) Direct trajectory audit is 13.7% tighter than Bonferroni once sufficient audit sample size is reached, but worse when undersized. (3) Modular certificates yield a positive average gain of 0.6% over baselines. (4) Same-model, cross-model, and permuted-pairing tests show residual dependence stems from shared sample difficulty, not shared model representations. (5) Average trajectory coverage across 12 configurations is 92.7% ± 2.4% at α = 0.10. (6) Under cross-dataset deployment, single-step miscoverage hits 100% even at 78% accuracy, demonstrating distribution shift destroys calibrated confidence before raw accuracy degrades.

Conclusion: Valid trajectory-level conformal guarantees for multi-stage pipelines require careful handling of inter-stage dependence. The spanning-tree approach provides a theoretically sound alternative to invalid pairwise-correlation extensions and conservative Bonferroni. Practical deployment must account for spurious correlation artifacts and ensure sufficient audit sample sizes. The catastrophic failure of calibration under distribution shift underscores that conformal guarantees are brittle to deployment mismatch, even when accuracy remains reasonable.

Abstract: Autonomous security agents operate as staged pipelines, such as classifying network traffic and then attributing attacks to a specific technique. Split conformal prediction gives each stage finite-sample coverage, but deployment requires a trajectory-level guarantee across the full chain. These guarantees do not compose automatically when stages are independently trained and calibrated. Bonferroni allocation is distribution-free but conservative under correlated errors. We show that a natural pairwise-correlation extension to three or more stages is invalid because it gives a lower rather than an upper bound, and derive a valid spanning-tree alternative. We distinguish whether stages are dependent from whether an audit sample is large enough to certify that dependence, and give matching upper and information-theoretic lower sample-complexity bounds. We also show that coarse-to-fine label selection can create near-perfect measured correlation without learned dependence.
  On a two-stage intrusion-detection pipeline across 6 open LLMs and 2 datasets, removing this artifact reduces measured correlation from near 1 to 0-0.78. A direct audit of trajectory failure becomes 13.7% tighter than Bonferroni once the audit reaches the required sample size, but is worse when undersized. A modular certificate using per-stage certificates and a pairwise overlap bound yields a positive average gain of 0.6%, quantifying the cost of lacking joint access. Same-model, cross-model, and permuted-pairing tests show that residual dependence reflects shared sample difficulty, not shared model representations. Average trajectory coverage across 12 configurations is 92.7% +/- 2.4% at alpha = 0.10. Under cross-dataset deployment, single-step miscoverage reaches 100% even when accuracy remains 78%, showing that distribution shift destroys calibrated confidence before raw accuracy.

</details>


### [181] [ASTELD: A Six-Axis Classification Framework for Autonomous AI Agents - Design, Evaluation, and an OpenClaw Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05201)
*Siyuan Li,Peng Shu,Churan Yu,Peilong Wang,Ruidong Zhang,Bowen Guo,Xinliang Li,Ruiyu Yan,Arif Hassan Zidan,Yi Pan,Wei Ruan,Lifeng Chen,Junhao Chen,Zhaojun Ding,Yiwei Li,Zhengliang Liu,Haixing Dai,Lin Zhao,Yu Bao,Xiang Li,Wei Zhang,Tianming Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ASTELD is a six-axis classification framework for autonomous AI agents (Architecture, Security, Tool integration, Execution, Level of autonomy, Deployment) that enables systematic comparison of agent platforms, reveals cross-platform patterns, identifies ecosystem fragmentation, and exposes a critical design gap: no platform combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous AI agent platforms vary widely in architecture, security, tool integration, execution models, autonomy levels, and deployment strategies, yet no common classification scheme exists to systematically compare these design choices. This taxonomic gap hinders platform evaluation, framework selection, and identification of unoccupied design regions.

Method: The authors synthesize prior agent taxonomies with observable platform properties and explicit category-assignment rules to construct ASTELD. They evaluate its utility by mapping eight representative agent frameworks onto the six axes, conducting an in-depth case study of OpenClaw (including 50+ derivatives), and performing vulnerability taxonomy, institutional assessment, and governance analyses.

Result: ASTELD successfully discriminates all eight platforms; reveals a security-accessibility diagonal, strong execution-architecture coupling, and capability convergence with persistent architectural differentiation; shows innovation concentrates on Security, Execution, and Deployment axes in OpenClaw derivatives; and identifies a consequential empty region: no system combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security.

Conclusion: ASTELD provides a reproducible method for comparing agent platforms, identifying unoccupied design regions, guiding framework selection, and organizing future empirical research. The framework exposes actionable gaps in the design space, particularly the absence of locally-deployed, enterprise-secure agents.

Abstract: Autonomous AI agent platforms differ substantially in architecture, security, tool integration, execution, autonomy, and deployment, yet the field lacks a common classification scheme for comparing these design choices. We propose ASTELD, an operational six-axis classification framework for autonomous AI agents: Architecture pattern, Security posture, Tool integration model, Execution paradigm, Level of autonomy and human control, and Deployment topology. ASTELD is constructed by synthesizing prior agent taxonomies with observable platform properties and explicit category-assignment rules. We evaluate its discriminative and explanatory utility by mapping eight representative frameworks and by using OpenClaw as an in-depth case study. The resulting profiles separate all eight platforms under their dominant configurations and reveal three cross-platform patterns: a security-accessibility diagonal, strong execution-architecture coupling, and capability convergence with persistent architectural differentiation. We further classify 50+ OpenClaw derivatives and find that innovation concentrates on the Security, Execution, and Deployment axes, indicating that ASTELD can explain where ecosystem fragmentation occurs. The OpenClaw case study also supplies a six-category vulnerability taxonomy, evidence from five institutional assessments, and adoption and governance analyses that connect platform coordinates to observed risks. These results position ASTELD as a reproducible method for comparing agent platforms, identifying unoccupied design regions, guiding framework selection, and organizing future empirical research. The analysis also exposes a consequential empty region: none of the evaluated systems combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security.

</details>


### [182] [A Survey of Adversarial Efficiency Degradation for Vision Transformer by Exploiting Input-adaptive Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05217)
*Anadi Goyal,Nandish Chattopadhyay,Anupam Chattopadhyay,Chandan Karfa*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This survey analyzes adversarial efficiency degradation attacks on Vision Transformers that exploit input-adaptive inference mechanisms (token pruning, early halting). It compares SlowFormer and DeSparsify attacks across A-ViT, ATS, and AdaViT frameworks, standardizes evaluation metrics (GFLOPs, accuracy loss, Attack Success), and examines defenses for low-power deployment settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ViTs increasingly use input-adaptive inference (token pruning, early halting) to meet energy/latency constraints in mobile/embedded settings. However, these optimizations create new attack surfaces. Understanding how adversaries can reverse computational savings is critical for designing lightweight countermeasures suitable for low-power deployment.

Method: The paper is a survey that unifies and compares two representative attacks — SlowFormer (universal adversarial patch) and DeSparsify (per-image perturbations) — across three token-pruning frameworks: A-ViT, ATS, and AdaViT. It standardizes evaluation using GFLOPs, accuracy loss, and an Attack Success (AS) metric that quantifies how much compute savings an attack reverses. Analysis is organized around three questions regarding attack surfaces, practical attack operation, and existing defenses.

Result: Input-adaptive optimizations inherently create vulnerability surfaces for efficiency degradation. Both SlowFormer and DeSparsify can reverse computational savings without necessarily degrading accuracy. The AS metric provides a standardized way to quantify attack impact. Certain token-pruning frameworks are more vulnerable than others, and existing defenses show varying degrees of effectiveness at restoring efficiency under attack.

Conclusion: Adversarial efficiency degradation is an underexplored threat to input-adaptive ViTs. Designing countermeasures requires balancing risk mitigation with lightweight overhead, as deployments occur in resource-constrained settings. Standardized evaluation (GFLOPs, AS metric) is essential for comparing attacks and defenses meaningfully.

Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) increasingly rely on input-adaptive inference, such as token pruning and early halting, to meet energy and latency budgets. This survey examines a recent class of adversarial efficiency degradation attacks that target these mechanisms to increase computation without necessarily degrading accuracy. We unify and compare two representative attacks, SlowFormer (a universal adversarial patch) and DeSparsify (per-image perturbations), across three popular token-pruning frameworks: A-ViT, ATS, and AdaViT. We standardize reporting using GFLOPs, accuracy loss, and an Attack Success (AS) metric that measures how much of the model's compute savings the attack takes away. Understanding these attacks is crucial for designing countermeasures that not only mitigate risk but also remain lightweight, since deployment often occurs in low-power settings such as mobile or embedded devices. To organize our analysis, we focus on three questions: how input-adaptive optimizations (e.g., token pruning and early halting) create attack surfaces for efficiency degradation; how such attacks operate in practice and which optimizations are most vulnerable; and which defenses exist today and whether they meaningfully restore efficiency under attack.

</details>


### [183] [CyberBridge: Bridging the Gap Between Cybersecurity Education and Industry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05231)
*Arthur Nijdam,Paul Stankovski Wagner,Sara Ramezanian*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: CyberBridge is an interpretable framework that uses sentence-BERT embeddings to automatically map cybersecurity job descriptions to professional role profiles by decomposing them into Knowledge, Skill, and Task (KST) statements, supporting job recommendation, market analysis, and curriculum planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid evolution of the cybersecurity landscape creates a persistent gap between academic curricula and industry competency expectations. Existing approaches lack interpretability, making it difficult for educators and students to understand why specific job-role mappings are recommended.

Method: CyberBridge decomposes job vacancy descriptions into constituent Knowledge, Skill, and Task (KST) statements, embeds them using a sentence-BERT model for semantic representation, and matches them to the most similar workforce profiles via semantic similarity. A key design feature is interpretability: users can trace each recommendation back to the specific competencies driving the match.

Result: The framework enables three use cases: (1) job recommendation for students based on completed curricula, (2) market analysis for educators to identify in-demand roles, and (3) curriculum planning to assess which programs best prepare students for target cybersecurity roles.

Conclusion: CyberBridge serves as a practical, evidence-based tool for educational institutions to support career guidance and curriculum development in cybersecurity education, bridging the gap between academic training and workforce needs through interpretable competency mapping.

Abstract: This full research paper presents CyberBridge, a framework that automatically maps cybersecurity job descrip- tions to professional role profiles. As the cybersecurity landscape evolves rapidly, it is difficult for academic programs to align curricula with the competencies expected in practice.
  CyberBridge addresses this gap by decomposing a given vacancy description into its constituent Knowledge, Skill, and Task (KST) statements, embedding them using a sentence- BERT model, and matching them to the most semantically similar workforce profiles. A key contribution of our approach is its interpretability. Rather than functioning as a black box, CyberBridge enables users to trace recommendations back to the specific competencies driving each match, providing a human- readable justification for the resulting mappings.
  CyberBridge supports three primary use cases; (1) job recom- mendation, providing students with vacancies and closely match- ing professional roles based on their completed curriculum, (2) market analysis, enabling educators and curriculum developers to analyze which roles are currently in demand, and (3) curriculum planning, assessing which course program best prepares students for in-demand cybersecurity roles.
  As such, CyberBridge can be used by educational institutions as a practical tool for career guidance and evidence-based curriculum development in cybersecurity education.

</details>


### [184] [The Hidden Life of Public Safety Communications Signals: A Comparative Security Analysis of TETRA, TETRAPOL, and P25](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05247)
*Larry Hernandez,Sergey Bratus*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Trunked LMR systems (P25, TETRA, TETRAPOL) expose extensive metadata through their unencrypted signaling plane, allowing passive SDR observers to infer sensitive operational information—including network topology, unit mobility, organizational structure, and even voice content—from local observation alone, revealing a critical gap between content and communication confidentiality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LMR standards focus on encrypting the content (traffic) plane while leaving the signaling plane almost entirely in cleartext. Prior security research has concentrated on content-plane attacks (key recovery, cleartext capture), but the authors argue that comparably sensitive information can be inferred from signaling metadata alone—even if content encryption were perfect. This gap between confidentiality of content and confidentiality of communication represents a significant, underexplored vulnerability for public-safety and critical infrastructure operators.

Method: The authors employ passive, receive-only software-defined radio (SDR) observation across P25, TETRA, and TETRAPOL trunked LMR standards. They analyze the exposed signaling plane to infer: network topology and geography, unit presence and mobility across cells/groups, organizational structure, key domains and key-epoch rotation, and identity obfuscation timing/association patterns. For TETRAPOL specifically, they combine signaling metadata inference with a standards-level confidentiality failure in emergency call handling to demonstrate unencrypted voice extraction. The local sniffing is shown to enable nationwide network mapping capabilities.

Result: The study demonstrates that passive signaling-plane observation enables inference of: (1) operationally sensitive network topology and geography details, (2) unit presence and mobility across cells and groups, (3) organizational structure, (4) security parameters including special key domains and key-epoch rotation, and (5) identity obfuscation defeat through timing and association analysis. The local observation scales to nationwide network mapping. For TETRAPOL, a standards-level failure in emergency call handling combined with signaling metadata tracking enables unencrypted voice extraction.

Conclusion: The signaling plane in trunked LMR standards constitutes a significant confidentiality vulnerability that undermines communication metadata protection, even where content encryption is robust. The authors discuss potential countermeasures and provide specific recommendations for protecting inter-cell, base station, and subscriber identities.

Abstract: Public-safety agencies and critical infrastructure operators rely on trunked land-mobile radio (LMR) systems, based on P25, TETRA, and TETRAPOL. These systems are expected to protect not just the content of a communication but the fact of it. Yet LMR standards leave a stark gap between confidentiality of \emph{content} and of \emph{communication}: underneath an encrypted traffic plane, their signaling plane is almost entirely in the clear. We probe the depth and impact of adversarial inference from this exposed signaling.
  Prior security analyses of these systems have concentrated on the content plane---recovering encryption keys or capturing accidental cleartext. We show that comparably sensitive information can be \emph{inferred from passively observed signaling even if the content encryption were perfect}.
  In particular, we show that across the trunked LMR standards, a passive, receive-only software-defined radio (SDR) observer can recover operationally sensitive network topology and geography details, unit presence, mobility across cells and groups, organizational structure, as well as operational security details such as special key domains and key-epoch rotation. This signaling-plane inference reaches far beyond the observer's direct area of reception, turning \emph{local} sniffing into \emph{nationwide} network mapping capabilities that degrade or defeat LMR standards' identity obfuscation through timing and association. In the case of TETRAPOL, we demonstrate how inference and tracking of such signaling metadata and a standards-level confidentiality failure in emergency call handling enable unencrypted voice extraction.
  Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures and mitigations, including specific recommendations for protecting inter-cell, base station and subscriber identities.

</details>


### [185] [eMicro: Real-Time Multi-Hop Access Control for Microservices with eBPF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05300)
*Rizky Ramadhana Putra,Osama Bajaber,Saimon Amanuel Tsegai,Teryl Taylor,Frederico Araujo,Yuede Ji,Peng Gao*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: eMicro is a path-aware defense system for microservices that prevents multi-hop attacks by enforcing real-time access control over entire service invocation sequences using DFA-encoded policies and eBPF-based in-kernel tracing, achieving microsecond-level policy checks and minimal runtime overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional inter-service access control only checks individual service-to-service requests, leaving systems vulnerable to multi-hop attacks where each hop appears legitimate but the overall request path violates security intent, enabling unauthorized access and data exfiltration.

Method: eMicro employs three core techniques: (1) history-based access control that captures full service invocation sequences rather than single hops; (2) security policies encoded as deterministic finite automata (DFA) for constant-time lookups and compact label propagation; (3) eBPF-based in-kernel request tracing for transparent, low-overhead enforcement requiring no application code modifications.
