Result: Evaluated on DeathStarBench and production cloud traces from Uber, Alibaba, and ByteDance (12 million workflows, thousands of services), eMicro achieves policy checks in 1 microsecond, stores 50 million policies in 100 MB, and reduces propagation overhead by 90% with negligible runtime impact.

Conclusion: eMicro delivers scalable and efficient protection against multi-hop attacks, demonstrating practicality for deployment in large-scale microservice environments.

Abstract: Modern cloud applications often comprise thousands of microservices whose interactions form complex request paths. Traditional inter-service access control restricts individual service-to-service requests, but fails to prevent multi-hop attacks, where each hop appears legitimate yet the overall path violates security intent. This gap leaves systems exposed to unauthorized access and data exfiltration. In this paper, we present eMicro, a path-aware defense system for microservices that prevents such attacks while remaining efficient and deployable. eMicro enforces real-time multi-hop access control through three key techniques: (1) history-based access control extended to capture service invocation sequences; (2) security policies encoded as efficient deterministic finite automaton (DFA), supporting constant-time lookups and compact label propagation; (3) eBPF-based in-kernel request tracing for transparent, low-overhead enforcement without code changes. Evaluations on DeathStarBench and production cloud traces from Uber, Alibaba, and ByteDance, covering 12 million request workflows and thousands of services, demonstrate the scalability of eMicro. eMicro performs policy checks in 1 microsecond, stores 50 million policies in only 100 MB, and reduces propagation overhead by 90% with negligible runtime impact. These results show that eMicro delivers scalable and efficient protection against multi-hop attacks, making it practical for deployment in large-scale microservice environments.

</details>


### [186] [The Trust-Free Aggregation Layer of the Unicity Infrastructure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05316)
*Risto Laanoja,Mike Gault,Dirk Draheim,Ahto Buldas*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Unicity introduces a Layer-2 aggregation layer that uses Radix Sparse Merkle Trees and STARK-based proofs to enable off-chain P2P token transactions with compact, trustless double-spending prevention, achieving 10,000 insertions/sec and millisecond verification on consumer hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable off-chain peer-to-peer token transactions while preventing double-spending with minimal on-chain complexity and storage, without compromising trust.

Method: An Aggregation Layer maintains an append-only key-value repository certified periodically on a Consensus Layer blockchain. It uses Radix Sparse Merkle Trees (RSMTs) to produce a cryptographic digest per round and generates append-only consistency proofs showing that successive digests result solely from adding new key-value pairs. Proof verification is implemented as an Algebraic Intermediate Representation (AIR) circuit using the Plonky3 STARK toolkit, requiring no trusted setup.

Result: The system achieves a throughput of 10,000 insertions per second and millisecond-range verification time on a single consumer-class CPU.

Conclusion: Unicity provides a practical, trustless Layer-2 aggregation architecture for scalable off-chain token transfers, combining append-only Merkle tree consistency proofs with STARK-based verification to deliver high throughput and low-latency proof checking without trusted setup.

Abstract: Unicity is a novel blockchain infrastructure for enabling users to execute off-chain peer-to-peer token transactions while preventing parallel states of tokens (double-spending) with minimal blockchain complexity and storage. A key component of the infrastructure is the Aggregation Layer responsible for storing information about the spent states of tokens and providing compact cryptographic proofs of no double-spending for the users without making any compromises in trust. Aggregation Layer is a layer 2 style service that holds an append-only key-value repository that periodically certifies its state using a traditional blockchain that we call the Consensus Layer. Every time while certifying a changed state the Aggregation Layer provides a cryptographic proof to the Consensus Layer about the append-only consistency of the key-value store. We use the Radix Sparse Merkle Trees (RSMTs) to create the cryptographic digest r_i of the store in every round i and authentication paths of special type in order to prove that the next digest r_{i+1} was obtained while only adding some key-value pairs (k,v) to the repository. The proof verification code is implemented as an Algebraic Intermediate Representation (AIR) circuit on top of the Plonky3 STARK toolkit. Our implementation uses no trusted setup, achieves throughput of 10,000 insertions per second and and millisecond range verification time on a single consumer-class CPU.

</details>


### [187] [S12X Patch Diffing with QBinDiff](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05350)
*Ben Gardiner*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A reverse engineering analysis reveals that a commercial vehicle Brake ECU firmware update, issued as a safety recall, also served as a security patch. The authors extracted firmware from the updater, performed differential binary analysis on S12X architecture images, and identified that the patch addressed undocumented vulnerabilities in legacy protocol processing — while also containing critical flaws of its own.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors sought to determine whether a safety recall firmware update for a commercial vehicle Brake ECU contained undisclosed security fixes. The work addresses the broader concern that automotive recalls may silently patch security vulnerabilities without transparent disclosure to owners or regulators.

Method: Reverse engineering of the firmware updater executable to extract firmware images; differential binary analysis comparing pre- and post-recall firmware images targeting the S12X microcontroller architecture; identification of modified functions and legacy protocol processing routines.

Result: The analysis identified specific code changes that address previously undocumented vulnerabilities in legacy protocol processing. The recall remediation functioned as a covert security patch. Additionally, the patched functionality itself was found to contain critical flaws, suggesting incomplete or flawed remediation.

Conclusion: The safety recall was confirmed to double as a security patch for undocumented vulnerabilities. The presence of critical flaws in the patched code raises concerns about the adequacy of the remediation and highlights the need for greater transparency and rigor in automotive security update practices.

Abstract: This paper presents a reverse engineering analysis of a firmware update for a commercial vehicle Brake ECU. We analyze the updater executable to extract firmware and perform differential binary analysis of the S12X architecture firmware images. Our research identifies specific changes in the recall that address undocumented vulnerabilities in legacy protocol processing. We demonstrate that the patched functionality contained critical flaws. The findings confirm the safety recall remediation was also a security patch.

</details>


### [188] [Robust Context-Aware Detection of Malicious Instructions in Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05430)
*Buzhao Liu,Xinhang Ma,Yevgeniy Vorobeychik*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces a context- and query-aware malicious sentence classifier for defending against indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks on LLM agents, and hardens it against adaptive evasion using two adversarial training methods: embedding-space projected-gradient AT and LLM-based paraphrasing AT, demonstrating superior performance over SOTA baselines under both static and adaptive attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, where malicious instructions are embedded in external text. Existing defenses lack query-relative detection at the segment level and are not hardened against adaptive evasion attacks that adversaries can execute in agentic settings.

Method: 1. Develop a malicious sentence classifier that is both context-aware and query-aware, operating at the segment level. 2. Propose two adversarial training (AT) variants for hardening: (a) feature-space AT using projected-gradient-based optimization in embedding space, and (b) LLM-based paraphrasing that simulates realizable evasion attacks within the AT loop. 3. Parameterize both AT variants to enable a tunable tradeoff between utility and attack robustness.

Result: The proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art IPI defense baselines under static attacks. Under adaptive attacks, both AT variants yield significantly higher utility and lower attack success rates. The optimal AT parameters are domain-dependent, suggesting practical deployment requires domain-specific tuning.

Conclusion: A query- and context-aware segment-level detector with adversarial training provides effective defense against both static and adaptive indirect prompt injection attacks. Domain-dependent tuning of AT parameters is necessary for practical deployment. Code is publicly released.

Abstract: The remarkable instruction-following ability of modern LLMs has enabled their practical use as the minds of agents that can autonomously complete increasingly complex tasks. Therein, however, also lies their vulnerability to attacks which embed malicious instructions in text, common variants of which are known as indirect prompt injection (IPI). A fundamental task in addressing this vulnerability is successful segmentation of a given text into benign and malicious sentences (if any). While a number of approaches for this task have been proposed, no detector combines query-relative detection at the segment level, and none are hardened against adaptive evasion attacks realizable in agentic executions. We address the former limitation by developing an approach for malicious sentence classification that is both context- and query-aware. Next, to harden the resulting classifier against evasion, we present two adversarial training methods. The first is directly adapted feature-space adversarial training (AT) in which evasions are approximated using projected-gradient-based optimization in the embedding space. The second simulates realizable evasion attacks in the AT loop through LLM-based paraphrasing. Crucially, we parametrize both AT variants to facilitate a smooth tradeoff between utility and attack robustness. In extensive experiments using indirect prompt injection benchmarks we show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art IPI defense baselines under static attacks, while in the case of adaptive attacks, our AT variants provide significantly higher utility, lower attack success rate, and often both. Finally, we show that the best AT parameters can depend intimately on the particular application domain. Consequently, domain-dependent tuning of malicious text detectors is likely necessary in practice. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/tavia-liu/CAD.

</details>


### [189] [Quantifying Bitcoin Network Resilience Through Critical Scenario Discovery: A Dual-Layer Framework for Discovering Contentious Fork Conditions in Decentralized Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05461)
*Peter Foytik,Sachin Shetty,Ross Gore,Eranga Bandara*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Using ensemble simulations of real Bitcoin nodes, this paper identifies economic weight distribution—not hashrate majority—as the primary determinant of contentious soft fork outcomes, establishing precise parameter thresholds (economic-support floor at 0.45–0.50, override ceiling at 0.78–0.82, and a pool-commitment flip-point at 0.214) that bound clean resolution versus persistent chain splits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bitcoin consensus emerges from heterogeneous nodes with divergent economic stakes, making it difficult to analytically predict whether a contentious soft fork will resolve cleanly or fracture into a persistent chain split. Controlled experimentation is needed to identify the configuration regions and parameter thresholds that produce each outcome.

Method: The authors apply Scenario Discovery using the Patient Rule Induction Method (PRIM), an ensemble-simulation methodology. They deploy Warnet to run real bitcoind nodes across 1,330 valid scenarios, systematically varying economic weight distribution, mining-pool commitment, pool ideology, hashrate, and difficulty-retarget regime.

Result: Three key findings: (1) an economic-support floor (0.45–0.50) and override ceiling (0.78–0.82) bound the contested space, with an Economic Self-Sustaining Point at 0.74; (2) a pool-commitment flip-point at 0.214 of committed hashrate, where committing the largest pool to the upgrading chain paradoxically reverses the outcome; (3) outcomes resolve on two independent layers—hashrate and economic adoption—governed by different parameters. Individual user nodes exert no detectable influence under modeled economic weightings.

Conclusion: Economic weight distribution, not hashrate majority, is the primary determinant of fork resolution under Bitcoin's operational retarget interval with moderate price divergence. The authors translate their threshold findings into three operational monitoring questions answerable from public data.

Abstract: Bitcoin's consensus depends not only on protocol rules but on the emergent behavior of a heterogeneous network of nodes with divergent economic stakes. Whether a contentious soft fork resolves cleanly or fractures into a persistent chain split is difficult to predict analytically but can be explored through controlled experimentation. This paper applies Scenario Discovery, an ensemble-simulation methodology using the Patient Rule Induction Method (PRIM), to identify the configuration regions that produce contentious fork outcomes. Using Warnet to run real bitcoind nodes across 1,330 valid scenarios spanning economic weight, mining-pool commitment, pool ideology, hashrate, and difficulty-retarget regime, we identify the parameter thresholds separating clean resolution from contested split. We show that economic weight distribution across a partition, not hashrate majority, is the primary determinant of resolution under Bitcoin's operational retarget interval and moderate price divergence. Three findings follow: an economic-support floor (0.45-0.50) and override ceiling (0.78-0.82) bound the contested space, with an Economic Self-Sustaining Point (0.74) between them; a pool-commitment "flip-point" (0.214 of committed hashrate) at which committing the largest pool to the upgrading chain paradoxically reverses the outcome; and outcomes resolve on two independent layers, hashrate and economic adoption, governed by different parameters. Individual user nodes show no detectable influence on fork outcomes under the modeled economic weightings. We close with three monitoring questions, answerable from public data, that translate these thresholds into operational guidance.

</details>


### [190] [Exploring Privacy Leakage and Data Disclosure Violations in the MacOS Application Ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05474)
*Jyotirmay Chauhan,Kostas Solomos,Mir Masood Ali,Jason Polakis*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: First comprehensive study of macOS data collection mechanisms, introducing NutriScan to analyze 1K apps, finding 85% access user-data APIs without disclosure and 49.7% exfiltrate data to trackers, revealing systemic gaps in desktop privacy regulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While privacy risks in web, mobile, and IoT ecosystems have been extensively studied, desktop environments—particularly macOS—remain critically under-examined despite widespread use. The authors aim to fill this gap by investigating how macOS mechanisms regulate and disclose data collection practices.

Method: The authors adopt an app-development-centric perspective, analyzing macOS mechanisms that mediate data access. They develop NutriScan, an analysis framework combining static and dynamic analysis techniques to produce a consolidated view of data practices and disclosures. The framework is applied to dynamically analyze 1,000 macOS apps.

Result: Key findings: (1) 85% of apps access user-data APIs without proper disclosure; (2) 49.7% exfiltrate data to advertising entities and hosting providers, with 12.5% doing so without disclosure; (3) desktop apps are exploited by online trackers for user profiling and device fingerprinting; (4) macOS employs disjoint mechanisms with divergent data abstractions, increasing developer complexity and enabling undisclosed privacy-invasive practices.

Conclusion: The macOS ecosystem suffers from fragmented privacy mechanisms that inadvertently facilitate undisclosed data collection. The authors propose mitigations to streamline data disclosure for developers and strengthen Apple's app vetting process, highlighting the need for desktop environments to receive privacy scrutiny comparable to mobile and web platforms.

Abstract: The systematic and excessive data collection practices of tech companies have rendered online privacy both a necessity and a sought-after commodity. However, while the privacy risks of the web, mobile, and IoT ecosystems have been extensively examined, desktop environments have been largely overlooked. As desktop apps continue to be widely used, they remain a critical yet understudied dimension of user privacy. In this paper, we address this gap by presenting the first, to our knowledge, comprehensive study of the mechanisms designed to regulate and disclose data collection and sharing practices in the macOS ecosystem. We adopt an app-development-centric view, and shed light on the interactions between the various macOS mechanisms that mediate apps' data access. Driven by our findings, we develop NutriScan, an analysis framework that incorporates both static and dynamic analysis techniques to create a consolidated view of macOS apps' data practices and disclosures. We use our system to dynamically analyze 1K macOS apps, and find that 85% of them access user-data APIs without disclosing it. 49.7% also exfiltrate data to advertising entities and hosting providers, 12.5% of which do so without a corresponding disclosure. We find that desktop apps are being leveraged by online trackers to enrich user profiles and device fingerprints, thus shedding new light on the true scope of the online tracking ecosystem. Our analysis reveals how the macOS app ecosystem is comprised of disjoint mechanisms with divergent data abstractions, thus increasing complexity for developers while also facilitating undisclosed privacy-invasive practices. Accordingly, we propose a series of mitigations that aim to both streamline the data disclosure process for developers and improve Apple's app vetting process.

</details>


### [191] [PromptShield Home: Ambient Multimodal Prompt Injection Defense for Smart-Home Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05495)
*He Zhang,Feilong Li,Dingning Long,Yilin Cui,Peijun Zhang,Yuewen Zhang,Qianyao Xu,Xinyi Fu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PromptShield-Home is a benchmark evaluating whether multimodal LLM-based smart-home assistants can distinguish genuine user commands from ambient or injected content (TV speech, on-screen text, overheard conversations). The study compares three abstraction layers—traditional detectors (L0), single MLLM agents (L1), and multi-agent mediation (L2)—finding that detectors over-trigger while MLLMs over-refuse, with their correct sets being largely disjoint. An oracle combining layers reaches 94.1% accuracy versus 76.5% for the best single layer, suggesting learned routing and sensor fusion are preferable to pure MLLM replacement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As smart-home assistants adopt multimodal LLMs that directly perceive video and audio, a home-specific safety concern emerges: the inability to discriminate authentic user commands from ambient speech (TV, radio), on-screen text, or overheard conversations that superficially resemble commands. Existing evaluation paradigms do not capture these home-specific ambiguities, motivating a dedicated benchmark.

Method: The authors introduce PromptShield-Home, a pilot benchmark with realistic smart-home scenarios covering five challenge categories: addressee ambiguity, screen/audio injection, health-monitor false triggers, mixed occupancy, and a legitimate-command floor. Three abstraction layers are compared: (L0) traditional detectors (keyword spotting, voice biometrics), (L1) a single MLLM agent in vision-only, vision+ASR, and audio-visual configurations, and (L2) multi-agent mediation via voting, role specialists, and cross-model arbitration. Given label skew toward inaction, the authors report unsafe-execution and safe-completion rates separately. They also compute an oracle upper bound by selecting the correct layer per instance.

Result: A constant always-block predictor achieves 82% accuracy due to label imbalance, rendering aggregate accuracy misleading. Detectors (L0) act on nearly everything, while all MLLM configurations (L1) over-refuse, completing almost no genuine commands and missing every true fall scenario. The correct prediction sets of L0 and L1 are largely disjoint. An oracle that always picks the right layer reaches 94.1%, compared to 76.5% for the best single layer—a 17.6-point gap demonstrating complementary strengths. No operational router is implemented; this is reported as an upper bound.

Conclusion: Home-agent safety is best served by learned routing and sensor fusion that combine traditional detectors with MLLMs, rather than wholesale replacement of detectors with an MLLM. The complementary failure modes and disjoint correct sets indicate that a hybrid architecture can substantially outperform either paradigm alone.

Abstract: Smart-home assistants increasingly use multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that perceive video and audio directly. This raises a safety question specific to the home: can the agent tell a genuine user command from ambient or externally-sourced content, television speech, on-screen text, or an overheard conversation, that merely looks like a command? We introduce PromptShield-Home, a pilot benchmark of realistic smart-home scenarios spanning addressee ambiguity, screen/audio injection, health-monitor false triggers, mixed occupancy, and a legitimate-command floor, and use it to compare three abstraction layers: traditional detectors (L0), a single MLLM agent (L1; vision, vision+ASR, and audio-visual), and multi-agent mediation (L2; voting, role specialists, cross-model arbitration). Because the label distribution is skewed toward inaction, aggregate accuracy is misleading, a constant always-block predictor scores 82%, so we report unsafe-execution and safe-completion rates separately. The two paradigms fail in opposite ways: detectors act on everything, while every MLLM configuration over-refuses, completing almost no genuine command and missing a true fall in every case. Crucially, their correct sets are disjoint: an oracle that always picks the right layer reaches 94.1%, against 76.5% for the best single layer. We report this as an upper bound, not a system - no router is implemented - and argue that home-agent safety is best served by learned routing and sensor fusion, not by replacing detectors with an MLLM.

</details>


### [192] [Behavioral Residualization for Unsupervised Intrusion Detection in Automotive CAN Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05548)
*Chandan Hegde,Mukundh R Reddy*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes "per-ID behavioral residualization," a CAN bus feature representation that subtracts each arbitration ID's normal baseline from windowed temporal/protocol/payload features. This representation, rather than any specific detector, drives significant performance gains across multiple unsupervised detectors—achieving strong results on realistic attacks that reuse legitimate IDs, while transparently quantifying failure modes (novel-ID flooding and cross-ID fuzzing).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CAN intrusion detection systems rely on presence-based features (novel IDs, frozen bytes, anomalous DLC) that work well on simplistic public datasets but fail against attackers who reuse legitimate arbitration IDs. There is a need for a representation that enables detection of sophisticated, ID-reusing attacks on more realistic datasets.

Method: The authors introduce per-ID behavioral residualization: for each arbitration ID, fourteen temporal, protocol, and payload features are extracted from sliding windows. These features are then residualized by subtracting each ID's normal behavioral baseline, producing deviations that feed into any of six unsupervised anomaly detectors. The method is evaluated on two datasets (HCRL and the more realistic ROAD) across five random seeds.

Result: Residualization improved mean F1 in the majority of evaluations: 21/24 on HCRL and 30/36 on ROAD across five seeds. On ROAD's targeted signal-manipulation attacks (where legitimate IDs are reused), the representation achieved recall ≥ 0.99 with high ROC-AUC. Two failure modes were quantified: novel-ID flooding (HCRL DoS, F1=0.02) and cross-ID fuzzing (ROAD, F1=0.27), establishing the representation's coverage boundary.

Conclusion: The per-ID behavioral residualization representation is the primary driver of detection performance, not the choice of detector. It enables strong detection of ID-reusing attacks but has clear, quantifiable limitations against novel-ID flooding and cross-ID fuzzing. The authors advocate reporting these boundaries to define operational coverage for CAN intrusion detection systems.

Abstract: Modern vehicles rely on the Controller Area Network (CAN) bus, whose design prioritizes low cost and real-time performance but provides no message authentication or encryption. An attacker with physical or remote access can therefore inject arbitrary frames, making intrusion detection an important defense-in-depth mechanism.
  Most published CAN intrusion detection systems rely on presence-based features, such as novel arbitration IDs, frozen payload bytes, or anomalous DLC values. These features perform well on public datasets containing easily separable attacks but fail when attackers reuse legitimate arbitration IDs. We present per-ID behavioral residualization, a CAN-specific representation that extracts fourteen temporal, protocol, and payload features from sliding windows and residualizes them against each arbitration ID's normal baseline. Our central claim is that this representation, rather than any individual detector, drives the performance gains.
  Across six unsupervised detectors and two datasets, residualization improves mean F1 in the majority of evaluations (21/24 on HCRL and 30/36 on ROAD across five seeds). On the more realistic ROAD dataset, where attacks reuse legitimate IDs, the representation achieves recall >= 0.99 with high ROC-AUC on targeted signal-manipulation attacks. Two limitations are explicitly quantified: novel-ID flooding (HCRL DoS, F1 = 0.02) and cross-ID fuzzing (ROAD, F1 = 0.27), defining the measured coverage boundary of the proposed representation.

</details>


### [193] [A Self-Explainable Deep Architecture for Security Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05552)
*Ananth Shreekumar,Jyun-Jhu Syu,Muslum Ozgur Ozmen,Dongyan Xu,Z. Berkay Celik*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: XSec is a self-explainable deep architecture for security applications that uses mask-based feature extraction and prototype learning during training to generate interpretable, deterministic explanations at inference time — achieving 97.33% average accuracy across five security scenarios while dramatically reducing explanation latency compared to post-hoc methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning models are increasingly deployed in security-critical applications, but their black-box nature undermines transparency. Existing explanation methods (visual explanations, post-hoc approaches) suffer from three key limitations: (1) reduced faithfulness from local approximation errors, (2) instability from reliance on randomness, and (3) computational inefficiency that precludes real-time use. These shortcomings are especially problematic in security domains where trustworthy, timely explanations are essential.

Method: The authors propose XSec, a self-explainable deep architecture. During training, XSec employs a novel mask-based mechanism to select informative sub-features from the input data and learns class-representative prototypes. At test time, a dedicated similarity layer computes similarity scores between input sub-features and learned prototypes, producing inherently interpretable explanations without requiring any post-hoc analysis. Because the architecture is self-explainable by design, explanations are deterministic for a fixed model and input.

Result: XSec achieves an average classification accuracy of 97.33% across five diverse security scenarios with minimal performance degradation. It generates deterministic explanations and substantially reduces explanation latency compared to both approximation-based and perturbation-based post-hoc explanation methods.

Conclusion: XSec successfully extends self-explainable AI to the security domain, reconciling high deep learning performance with the critical need for interpretability. The approach demonstrates that built-in explainability can match the accuracy of black-box models while providing faithful, stable, and computationally efficient explanations suitable for real-time security applications.

Abstract: Deep learning models have become integral to security applications due to their ability to model complex relationships in data and detect sophisticated threats. However, their complexity makes it difficult to understand how predictions are generated, posing significant challenges for interpretability, particularly in security applications where transparency is critical. Existing explanation methods, such as visual explanation techniques and post-hoc approaches, suffer from several limitations: reduced faithfulness due to local approximation errors, instability caused by reliance on randomness, and computational inefficiency that hinders real-time usage. To address these issues, we introduce XSec, a self-explainable deep architecture developed for security applications. During training, XSec uses a novel mask-based approach to extract informative sub-features from the data and learns prototypes, representative patterns that characterize each class. XSec then leverages the prototypes in a dedicated similarity layer at test time to compute similarity scores and generates interpretable explanations without the need for post-hoc analysis. We evaluate XSec across five diverse security scenarios, demonstrating its ability to achieve an average classification accuracy of 97.33% with minimal performance compromise. XSec produces deterministic explanations for a fixed trained model and input and substantially reduces explanation latency compared with approximation-based and perturbation-based post-hoc methods. Through this effort, we extend the applicability of self-explainable AI to security applications, bridging the gap between deep learning performance and the need for explainability in critical scenarios.

</details>


### [194] [When Experience Becomes Instruction: Trajectory Poisoning in Self-Evolving Agent Skill Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05563)
*Jialuo Chen,Lingqi Jiang,Xinhao Deng,Xiaohu Du,Jianan Ma,Yunhao Feng,Yuqi Qing,Zhihao Yuan,Linkang Du,Jingyi Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PoisonedEvolution is a trajectory-poisoning attack against self-evolving skill (SES) systems that manipulates the evidence promotion process, achieving 91% success on SkillClaw and 61.5% on Trace2Skill with only 10% attacker support, exposing a critical security boundary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-evolving skill systems automatically distill agent interaction trajectories into persistent, trusted skills. This "promotion" process treats collected experience as trustworthy evidence for skill creation. The authors identify that this evidence pipeline lacks security scrutiny and investigate whether an attacker with limited access can subvert it to embed malicious behaviors, thereby exposing a novel attack surface in agent evolution architectures.

Method: The authors formalize three necessary conditions for artifact poisoning — Inclusion (attacker evidence enters the pool), Evolution Attribution (evidence appears causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable), and Realization (the skill is ultimately promoted). They design PoisonedEvolution as a skill-visible black-box attack where the attacker can inspect a target skill and inject bounded trajectory records but cannot observe private pools, evolution logic, or edit the skill bank. They evaluate four security-effect families using inert canary specifications across two distinct evolution architectures (SkillClaw and Trace2Skill) with six mainstream LLM evolvers, and conduct ablations on recurring support, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding.

Result: At 10% attacker support, PoisonedEvolution successfully embeds target behaviors in 546/600 trials (91.0% Success Embedding Rate) on SkillClaw and 369/600 trials (61.5% SER) on Trace2Skill. A controlled study shows three consistent attacker records suffice in a 30-record batch, while a single record is substantially weaker. Ablation results identify recurring support, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding as the primary determinants of attack success.

Conclusion: The evidence promotion mechanism in self-evolving skill systems constitutes a previously unrecognized security boundary. Even a skill-visible black-box attacker with only bounded trajectory-injection capability can reliably poison the skill bank. The Attribution bottleneck — requiring behaviors to appear causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable — can be gamed through careful trajectory crafting, indicating that current SES architectures lack sufficient safeguards against adversarial evidence.

Abstract: Self-evolving skill (SES) systems distill agent trajectories into persistent skills, allowing untrusted experience to become trusted instruction. We introduce PoisonedEvolution, a trajectory-poisoning attack on this promotion process. Our skill-visible black-box attacker can inspect a target skill and contribute bounded evidence, but cannot observe private pools or evolution logic or edit the skill bank. Artifact poisoning requires Inclusion, Evolution Attribution, and Realization. Attribution is the distinctive bottleneck: the target behavior must appear causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable before promotion. We evaluate four representative security-effect families using inert canary specifications. At 10% attacker support, across six mainstream LLM evolvers in SkillClaw, PoisonedEvolution embeds target behaviors in 546/600 trials (91.0% SER). On the structurally different Trace2Skill pipeline at the same ratio, it embeds target behaviors in 369/600 trials (61.5% SER), demonstrating transfer across evolution architectures. In a representative controlled study, three consistent attacker records suffice in a 30-record batch, whereas a single record is much weaker. Ablations identify recurring support, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding as the main determinants of success. These findings expose evidence promotion as a security boundary for self-evolving agents.

</details>


### [195] [Detecting Safety Training Modification in Language Models via Activation Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05578)
*Glen Messenger*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AMS detects safety-training modifications in LLMs by measuring activation-space geometry of safety-relevant concepts. Tested across 14 model configurations, it identifies four modification signatures with varying detectability, achieving 71% accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As open-weight LLMs proliferate, malicious actors can modify safety training through weight manipulation or fine-tuning. There is a need for tools that can audit models and detect such safety-training modifications without requiring behavioral testing alone, which can be noisy and incomplete.

Method: AMS measures the geometric structure of safety-relevant concepts in activation space, specifically computing sigma (separation between harmful and benign content class representations) and direction similarity. It implements a two-tier detection scheme: Tier 1 uses sigma thresholds to detect collapsed separation, and Tier 2 uses direction-similarity verification to detect rotated refusal directions. The tool was validated across 14 model configurations spanning 4 architecture families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral) and 4 safety-modification categories (instruction-tuned, base, abliterated, uncensored fine-tunes). Behavioral compliance was measured using 20 stratified JailbreakBench prompts per model.

Result: Leave-one-out cross-validation achieved 71% accuracy (10/14). Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on sigma had median width 3.4 sigma. Harmful-content sigma predicted jailbreak compliance with Pearson r = -0.546 (p = 0.043). The mechanistic analysis revealed a four-class taxonomy: (1) training removal collapses cluster separation; (2) weight-orthogonalization abliteration collapses separation and rotates refusal direction; (3) rotation-without-collapse abliteration preserves separation while rotating direction; (4) behavioral fine-tuning preserves both magnitude and direction. Tier 1 detects classes 1-2; Tier 2 detects class 3; class 4 is undetectable by activation-only probing.

Conclusion: AMS provides a practical activation-space auditing approach for detecting certain safety-training modifications, but acknowledges limitations: single-run measurement noise, threshold calibration challenges, and the fundamental undetectability of purely behavioral safety modifications that leave activation structure intact—representing an open problem.

Abstract: We introduce AMS (Activation-based Model Scanner), a tool that detects modifications to safety training in language models by measuring the geometric structure of safety-relevant concepts in activation space. Safety training creates measurable separation between harmful and benign content classes; certain safety modifications collapse or rotate this structure, while others leave it intact. We validate AMS across 14 model configurations spanning 4 architecture families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral) and four safety-modification categories (instruction-tuned, base, abliterated, uncensored fine-tunes). Leave-one-out cross-validation of thresholds achieves 71% accuracy (10/14); bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on sigma point estimates have median width 3.4 sigma. We measure behavioral compliance on 20 stratified JailbreakBench prompts per model and find that sigma on the harmful-content concept predicts compliance with Pearson r = -0.546 (p = 0.043), directionally but with meaningful noise. Mechanistic analysis identifies a four-class taxonomy of safety-training modifications distinguished by activation-space signature: training removal collapses cluster separation; weight-orthogonalization abliteration both collapses separation and rotates the refusal direction; rotation-without-collapse abliteration preserves separation while rotating direction; and behavioral fine-tuning preserves both magnitude and direction. AMS's Tier 1 sigma-threshold detects the first two classes; Tier 2 direction-similarity verification detects the third. The fourth is undetectable by activation-only probing and represents a documented failure mode. We discuss threshold calibration, limitations of single-run measurement, and the open problem of detecting behavioral-only safety modifications.

</details>


### [196] [Enhancing Anomaly Resilience in Research Networks: A Large-Scale Forecasting Benchmark for Dynamic Security Baselining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05605)
*Mohammad Arafath Uddin Shariff,Byrav Ramamurthy*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: RENs face a security challenge where legitimate scientific elephant flows are statistically indistinguishable from DDoS attacks. The paper benchmarks six forecasting model families on a 57-day Internet2 dataset (13.7B packets, 10 routers) across 960 configurations, finding that advanced architectures like TiDE reduce prediction error by 30-42% over traditional methods, enabling better distinction between scientific bursts and real anomalies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Research and Education Networks (RENs) exhibit massive, bursty elephant flows as part of normal scientific data transfers. These legitimate traffic patterns are statistically identical to volumetric DDoS attacks, causing conventional anomaly detection systems to suffer from high false-positive rates. This paradox blinds operators to genuine threats, necessitating a traffic forecasting approach that can establish accurate dynamic baselines to differentiate normal scientific bursts from attacks.

Method: The authors leverage a 57-day dataset from Internet2 spanning 10 backbone routers (13.7 billion packets). They benchmark six model families — ranging from classical SARIMA to modern long-sequence architectures (TiDE, PatchTST) — across 960 experimental configurations. A novel anomaly-integration strategy is introduced during training to improve model robustness against noise. Performance is evaluated via prediction error reduction and statistical significance testing ($p < 0.001$).

Result: Advanced architectures, particularly TiDE, reduce baseline prediction error by 30-42% compared to traditional methods ($p < 0.001$). The anomaly-integration strategy improves model robustness by 3.3% under noisy conditions. The framework significantly enhances the distinction between legitimate scientific bursts and potential anomalies.

Conclusion: This work provides the first statistically validated forecasting framework for distinguishing scientific workflows from network attacks in RENs. It enables more autonomous and resilient network security operations by establishing high-fidelity dynamic security baselines that reduce false positives and improve anomaly detection fidelity.

Abstract: Research and Education Networks (RENs) serve as critical infrastructure for scientific discovery, yet they face a unique security paradox: their normal traffic patterns which are characterized by massive, bursty "elephant flows" are statistically indistinguishable from volumetric attacks such as DDoS to conventional monitoring systems. This similarity leads to high false-positive rates in anomaly detection, blinding security operators to genuine threats. In this paper, we propose and evaluate a high-fidelity traffic forecasting framework designed to establish dynamic security baselines for RENs. Leveraging an exclusive 57-day Internet2 dataset spanning ten backbone routers (13.7 billion packets), we perform the first large-scale benchmark of anomaly-aware forecasting models in this domain. We systematically evaluate six model families, from SARIMA to state-of-the-art long-sequence architectures (TiDE, PatchTST), across 960 experimental configurations. Our results demonstrate that these advanced architectures, particularly TiDE, reduce baseline prediction error by 30-42% compared to traditional methods ($p < 0.001$), significantly improving the distinction between legitimate scientific bursts and potential anomalies. Furthermore, we introduce a novel anomaly-integration strategy that improves model robustness by 3.3% in the presence of noise. This work provides the first statistically validated framework for distinguishing scientific workflows from network attacks, enabling more autonomous and resilient network security operations.

</details>


### [197] [Breaking Customized LLMs for Coding: Automated Red Teaming for Instruction Backdoor Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05659)
*Yuchen Chen,Wei Cheng,Yuan Xiao,Wising Sun,Chunrong Fang,Yang Liu,Zhenyu Chen,Baowen Xu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ARIA is an automated red-teaming framework that uses an attacker LLM to iteratively generate covert and effective backdoored instructions for LLM customization platforms, achieving high attack success rates (0.945) while evading detection and maintaining clean-task utility across code intelligence tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM customization platforms enable users to build task-specific models by embedding instructions into system prompts, but this introduces instruction backdoor attacks. Existing attacks have two critical limitations: they rely on explicit trigger patterns that are easily detected, and they require substantial manual effort to craft task-specific backdoored instructions, limiting scalability.

Method: ARIA employs an attacker LLM that iteratively generates and refines backdoored instructions. The refinement process is guided by structured feedback from the target LLM across three dimensions: stealthiness (evading detection), clean-task utility (preserving normal performance), and backdoor effectiveness (triggering malicious behavior). The framework is evaluated on three code intelligence tasks using four representative LLMs against three baseline attacks.

Result: ARIA achieves the highest attack success rate of 0.945 while maintaining the best clean-task utility across all tasks. It generalizes well across programming languages, remains robust to generation temperature variations, achieves a false negative rate of up to 1.000 in evading platform-side and user-side detection, and stays effective against existing defense methods.

Conclusion: ARIA demonstrates strong generalizability and robustness as an automated red-teaming tool for instruction backdoor attacks, significantly outperforming existing attacks in effectiveness, stealth, and scalability. The work highlights a serious security vulnerability in LLM customization platforms.

Abstract: LLM customization platforms allow users to build task-specific models for code intelligence tasks by embedding instructions into system prompts, without modifying the underlying model parameters. While these platforms lower the barrier to developing customized LLMs, they also introduce a new attack surface: instruction backdoor attacks, in which adversaries implant hidden malicious behaviors into customized instructions. However, existing attacks suffer from two key limitations. First, they often rely on explicit trigger patterns readily detected by platform-side or user-side inspection. Second, they require substantial manual effort to craft task-specific backdoored instructions, limiting their scalability.
  In this paper, we propose ARIA, an automated red-teaming framework for crafting covert and effective backdoored instructions against customized LLMs. ARIA leverages an attacker LLM to iteratively generate and refine backdoored instructions, guided by structured feedback from the target LLM along three dimensions: stealthiness, clean-task utility, and backdoor effectiveness. We evaluate ARIA on three code intelligence tasks, using four representative LLMs, and compare it with three baseline attacks. Experimental results show that ARIA achieves the highest attack success rate of 0.945, while maintaining the best clean-task utility across all tasks. ARIA also generalizes well across programming languages and remains robust to generation temperature. Furthermore, ARIA significantly outperforms existing attacks in evading platform-side and user-side detection, achieving a false negative rate of up to 1.000, and stays effective against existing defense methods, demonstrating its strong generalizability and robustness.

</details>


### [198] [Algebraic Cryptanalytic Extraction on Hard-Label Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05736)
*Zirui Chen,Shi Tang,Zhengchao Gao,Yongjia Su,Lingyue Qin,Xiaoyang Dong*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes an Approximate Signature Vector (ASV) method that transforms Carlini et al.'s SVD-based hard-label model extraction attack into an algebraic framework using inner-product operations, drastically reducing clustering complexity. It also extends the attack to max-pooling CNNs via a kernel-centric clustering scheme, filling a cryptanalysis gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Carlini et al. (EUROCRYPT 2025) presented a polynomial-time hard-label model extraction attack, but its reliance on SVD for dual-point clustering incurs O(n²·(d^(k))³) complexity, making it computationally prohibitive in practice. The authors aim to eliminate this bottleneck and extend hard-label extraction to CNNs with max-pooling.

Method: The authors reframe the geometric hard-label attack algebraically and introduce the Approximate Signature Vector (ASV) method. ASV replaces SVD-based rank checking with inner-product operations, exploiting that (1) high-dimensional random vectors are nearly orthogonal and (2) practical DNN neurons learn disentangled features. This reduces average clustering complexity to O(n·(d^(k))³). For CNNs, they propose an advanced ASV with kernel-centric (rather than neuron-centric) clustering, leveraging convolutional weight sharing.

Result: Experiments on a 64-64×4-10 FCNN and LeNet-5 (CNN with max-pooling) show that ASV drastically reduces clustering time and improves overall model extraction efficiency. The CNN variant achieves the first successful hard-label extraction against max-pooling CNNs.

Conclusion: The ASV method effectively overcomes the computational bottleneck in Carlini et al.'s attack by replacing costly SVD with lightweight inner-product operations, and the kernel-centric extension successfully breaks hard-label security in max-pooling CNNs for the first time, advancing model extraction cryptanalysis significantly.

Abstract: Although the state-of-the-art neural network model extraction attack in the hard-label setting by Carlini et al. at EUROCRYPT 2025 has polynomial-time complexity in theory, its dual-point clustering relies on singular value decomposition (SVD) with a time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n^2 \cdot (d^{(k)})^3)$, resulting in huge runtime in practice. To address this computational bottleneck, this work transforms Carlini et al.'s geometric-view hard-label attack into an algebraic framework, and proposes a novel Approximate Signature Vector (ASV) method to achieve efficient parameter extraction on Fully Connected Neural Networks (FCNNs) by leveraging two key observations: high-dimensional random vectors are nearly orthogonal, and neurons in practical DNNs tend to learn disentangled features. The proposed ASV method replaces SVD-based rank checking with simple inner-product operations, reducing the clustering complexity to $\mathcal{O}(n \cdot (d^{(k)})^3)$ on average. Furthermore, this paper presents the first model extraction attack against hard-label max-pooling Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by proposing an advanced ASV method with a kernel-centric clustering scheme instead of the neuron-centric clustering, which fully exploits the property of weight sharing in convolutions and fills the cryptanalysis gap. Experiments on a 64-64$\times$4-10 FCNN and LeNet-5 (CNN) with max pooling demonstrate that our ASV method drastically cuts clustering time, and improves the overall efficiency in the model extraction.

</details>


### [199] [ABC: Numerical Data Collection under Local Differential Privacy without Prior Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05737)
*Incheol Baek,Hyungbin Kim,Yon Dohn Chung*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Existing LDP mechanisms for numerical data require a predefined domain, but choosing the wrong domain causes clipping or excessive noise. This paper proposes ABC (Adaptive Bounding of Clipping regions), an adaptive LDP framework where users send perturbed data plus a clipping signal, allowing the data collector to iteratively adjust the domain to fit the true data distribution without prior knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Local Differential Privacy mechanisms for numerical data collection suffer from a fundamental domain dilemma: a too-narrow domain clips out-of-range values (information loss), while a too-wide domain injects excessive noise (quality degradation). Since the true data range is often unknown in practice, there is a critical need for methods that can dynamically estimate the data domain without prior knowledge.

Method: The authors propose the Adaptive Bounding of Clipping regions (ABC) method within an adaptive LDP framework. Each user transmits two pieces of information: (1) their numerical data perturbed under the current domain, and (2) a privatized binary signal indicating whether their original value was clipped. The data collector aggregates these clipping signals and iteratively adjusts the domain bounds to converge toward an appropriate range that fits the underlying data distribution.

Result: Empirical evaluations show the framework significantly improves numerical data collection quality across multiple datasets and underlying LDP mechanisms. The estimated range successfully converges in practice, and comprehensive ablation studies demonstrate robustness to hyperparameters.

Conclusion: The ABC method effectively resolves the domain prior knowledge problem in LDP for numerical data by enabling dynamic, iterative domain estimation. It converges to an appropriate range, improves data quality, and is robust to hyperparameter choices.

Abstract: Local Differential Privacy (LDP) provides strong privacy guarantees for collecting numerical data. A fundamental challenge, however, is that existing LDP mechanisms require a predefined data domain, which is often unknown in practice. This lack of prior knowledge creates a critical dilemma for the data collector: if the chosen domain is too narrow, values outside the range are clipped, leading to information loss. Conversely, if the domain is too wide, excessive noise is added during the privatization process, which degrades the quality of collected data. This highlights the need for methods that can dynamically estimate the data domain.
  In this work, we propose an adaptive LDP framework that addresses this problem. In our method, each user sends two pieces of information: their perturbed numerical data, and a privatized signal indicating if their original value was clipped by the current domain. By aggregating these signals, our proposed method, Adaptive Bounding of Clipping regions (ABC) method, iteratively adjusts the domain to fit the underlying data distribution without prior knowledge. Our theoretical analysis shows that the estimated data domain converges to an appropriate range.
  In the empirical evaluation, the results demonstrate that our framework significantly improves the quality of numerical data collection across various datasets and underlying LDP mechanisms. We also show that the estimated range successfully converges in practice and our approach is robust to its hyperparameters through comprehensive ablation studies.

</details>


### [200] [On the Figures of Merit for Quantum Software Security: Toward a Benchmarking Rubric](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05831)
*Badhon Rahman,Majid Haghparast,Tommi Mikkonen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper identifies a gap in measuring quantum software security, proposes a structured set of Security Figures of Merit (S-FoMs) aligned with ISO/IEC 25010, maps them to the QaaS pipeline, and defines a benchmarking rubric that aggregates these into a unified Quantum Software Security Posture (QSSP) score.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantum computing performance has well-established metrics (qubit count, Quantum Volume, CLOPS), and software-quality metrics are emerging, but security measurement for quantum software remains largely absent. Existing ad hoc indicators like TVD and DFC are technique-specific and incompatible, creating a critical measurement gap that hinders security-aware evaluation of Quantum-as-a-Service stacks.

Method: The authors (i) characterize a three-layer measurement gap in quantum software security, (ii) propose a structured S-FoM set organized by ISO/IEC 25010 security sub-characteristics (confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation, accountability, authenticity), mapped to the QaaS pipeline and classified by measurement maturity, and (iii) define a benchmarking rubric that normalizes and aggregates individual S-FoMs into a composite Quantum Software Security Posture (QSSP) score. An illustrative reanalysis of published obfuscation techniques validates the framework.

Result: The paper delivers a structured taxonomy of quantum software security metrics (S-FoMs), a maturity-based classification, a pipeline-to-characteristic mapping, and a normalized aggregation rubric (QSSP). The reanalysis demonstrates how existing obfuscation techniques can be consistently evaluated under the proposed framework, revealing their previously incomparable security properties.

Conclusion: Security of quantum software deserves parity with performance benchmarking. The proposed S-FoM framework and QSSP score represent a first step toward standardized, security-aware benchmarking of the Quantum Software Stack, enabling practitioners to make informed risk assessments across the QaaS pipeline.

Abstract: Quantum software is increasingly provided through multi-tenant and cloud-based Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) stacks. A growing concern about the diverse attack vectors across the pipeline has been demonstrated in recent research. Yet the community has converged on three mature pillars: Scale (Qubit Count), Quality (Quantum Volume), and Speed (Circuit Layer Operations per Second (CLOPS)) for the merit performance figures. Moreover, it has also begun to define software-quality metrics. However, the security of quantum software remains largely unmeasured. A few quantitative security indicators, such as Total Variation Distance (TVD) and Degree of Functional Corruption (DFC), exist. Although they were introduced ad hoc for individual circuit obfuscation techniques, they are incompatible. We assert that the security of quantum software deserves the same attention as the performance: an explicit set of Security Figures of Merit (S-FoMs). The research of this paper is threefold: (i) characterizes a three-layer measurement gap, (ii) proposes a structured S-FoM set organized by ISO/IEC 25010 security sub-characteristics, QaaS pipeline mapping, and measurement maturity, and (iii) defines a benchmarking rubric that normalizes and aggregates S-FoMs into a combined Quantum Software Security Posture (QSSP) score. Additionally, an illustrative reanalysis of published obfuscation techniques has been presented. Our aim is a first step toward security-aware benchmarking of the Quantum Software Stack (QSS).

</details>


### [201] [An End-to-End Threat Model for the Quantum-as-a-Service Pipeline](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05836)
*Badhon Rahman,Majid Haghparast,Tommi Mikkonen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a six-stage decomposition of the QaaS workflow with STRIDE threat modeling, identifying attack vectors across quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible tiers, while highlighting underexplored repudiation/elevation-of-privilege threats and three cross-stage attack chains with amplified impact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing attacks on QaaS platforms (calibration tampering, SWAP attacks, QubitHammer, etc.) are studied in isolation using disparate terminology, and current STRIDE-based threat modeling for quantum systems lacks a holistic, stack-aware view. There is a need for a structured, end-to-end threat framework that unifies these attacks and exposes gaps.

Method: The authors decompose the QaaS workflow into a six-stage pipeline model and apply STRIDE threat modeling across each stage. They construct a matrix mapping attack vectors into three tiers: quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible. They further analyze underexplored STRIDE categories (repudiation and elevation-of-privilege) and trace three cross-stage attack chains.

Result: The resulting threat matrix systematically categorizes known and plausible attack vectors at each pipeline stage. The analysis reveals that repudiation and elevation-of-privilege are critically underexplored in quantum contexts and demonstrates three cross-stage attack chains that compound impact beyond single-stage attacks.

Conclusion: A structured, stage-decomposed STRIDE approach is essential for comprehensive threat modeling of QaaS platforms. The work identifies significant security blind spots and urges quantum security research to address cross-stage attack chains and neglected threat categories.

Abstract: Cloud-based accessing of Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) platforms such as IBM Quantum, IonQ Cloud, and Amazon Braket is becoming popular day by day. Hybrid quantum-classical algorithms (VQE, QAOA, QML) transfer data via a long layered pipeline of orchestration, compilation, and execution. Recent works have demonstrated various critical attacks at individual stages: Calibration tampering, SWAP attacks, QubitHammer, and so on. However, these attacks remain separated because of their own terminology, and existing STRIDE-based threat modeling in the context of quantum lacks a structured view towards the QaaS stack itself. We address this concern by decomposing the workflow into six-stage model with STRIDE threat modeling. Our matrix demonstrated attack vectors in quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible tiers for each of the stages. We further investigate the underexplored sections (repudiation and elevation-of-privilege) and distinguish three different cross-stage attack chains with higher impacts.

</details>


### [202] [RustGo: Fairly Directed Greybox Fuzzing for Enforcing Rust Memory Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05870)
*Dongyeon Yu,Jiun Min,Yewan Na,Mijung Kim,Taegyu Kim,Yuseok Jeon*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: RustGo is a directed greybox fuzzer for Rust that focuses on unsafe code regions by statically identifying potential memory bug targets and pruning irrelevant paths, achieving faster bug discovery and finding 13 previously unknown bugs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fuzzers waste resources on safe Rust code (≈90% of codebases) whose memory safety is already guaranteed by the compiler. Unsafe Rust code, where memory bugs can still occur, represents a small fraction but is not specifically targeted, leading to inefficient fuzzing.

Method: RustGo uses Rust-specific static analysis to automatically identify potential memory bug targets and prune irrelevant execution paths. For each target, it maintains an independent fuzzing state and applies dynamic pruning to ensure balanced, focused fuzzing across all identified targets.

Result: RustGo prunes 78.49% of irrelevant paths on average, reaches targets 2.09× to 5.08× faster than existing fuzzers, and discovers 13 previously unknown bugs (six RUSTSEC IDs, one CVE ID).

Conclusion: Targeted fuzzing of unsafe Rust code regions, guided by static analysis and dynamic pruning, significantly improves fuzzing efficiency and bug discovery effectiveness compared to whole-program fuzzing approaches.

Abstract: Rust is a popular systems programming language that provides strong memory safety and introduces low-performance overhead. While Rust guarantees memory safety through strict security policies, such as ownership, memory bugs can still occur in unsafe-related Rust codes where these policies are not fully enforced. Although such unsafe Rust code accounts for only a small portion of the entire code (e.g., 10%), existing approaches fuzz the entire code-including safe Rust, whose memory safety is already enforced by the Rust compiler-resulting in inefficient use of fuzzing resources. In this paper, we propose RustGo, the new Rust-directed greybox fuzzer that effectively and fairly focuses on code regions potentially containing memory bugs. For this, RustGo automatically identifies potential memory bug targets and accurately prunes the paths irrelevant to each target by leveraging Rust-specific static analysis. For each identified target, RustGo includes a new fuzzing approach that maintains an independent state and applies dynamic pruning to maximize balanced and focused fuzzing. We evaluate RustGo on various real-world Rust applications. On average, RustGo prunes 78.49% of irrelevant paths, reaches targets x 2.09 to x 5.08 faster than existing fuzzers, and identifies 13 unknown bugs (six assigned RUSTSEC IDs and one assigned CVE ID).

</details>


### [203] [The Vulnerability With No CVE: Managing Persistent Gaps Between Mandate and Authority in AI Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05884)
*Shayell Aharon Salomon Amir Shaked Matan Noga*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes Agentic Posture Vulnerability (APV), a task-conditioned vulnerability-management abstraction that provides a durable record for composed agent-control exposures in persistent, multi-component agent deployments, along with patterns, a lifecycle, and operational guidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing frameworks identify agentic risks (excessive agency, weak authorization, inadequate controls) but lack a mechanism to manage persistent deployed agent instances that span components and outlive single events. Security programs need a way to track enduring posture-level exposures rather than just runtime manifestations.

Method: The authors define APV conceptually, distinguish it from CVE vulnerabilities, OWASP Excessive Agency, Agent Baseline controls, and runtime authorization gaps. They provide a thresholded definition, identify six recurring APV patterns, specify a vulnerability lifecycle, propose a minimum record schema, a control-and-closure matrix, and outline tooling implications and a research agenda.

Result: Six recurring APV patterns are identified. A complete operational framework is provided: a thresholded definition, a vulnerability lifecycle with closure criteria (authority narrowed, control added, risk accepted, or closure verified), a minimum record structure, and a control-and-closure matrix linking controls to closure actions.

Conclusion: APV operationalizes existing risk classes (excessive agency, authorization weaknesses, control-composition gaps) into a durable, manageable vulnerability abstraction suitable for persistent agent deployments, bridging the gap between control frameworks and day-to-day security operations.

Abstract: Existing guidance identifies excessive agency, excessive permission, weak task-bound authorization, and inadequate agent controls as important risks. Control frameworks also describe capabilities for constraining, authorizing, observing, validating, and responding to agent activity. Yet security programs still need a way to manage persistent deployed instances that span components and outlive any one event.
  We propose the agentic posture vulnerability (APV) as a task-conditioned vulnerability-management abstraction: a durable record for a composed agent-control exposure. One posture may produce different runtime manifestations across tasks; APV links those manifestations to the invariant posture and remains open until authority is narrowed, a missing control is added, risk is accepted, or closure is verified. APV is not proposed as a new root-cause class of risk; it operationalizes existing excessive-agency, authorization, and control-composition weaknesses.
  We distinguish APVs from CVE-addressable product defects, OWASP Excessive Agency, Agent Baseline control outcomes, and the runtime authorization-execution gap. We then provide a field vignette, a thresholded definition, six recurring APV patterns, a vulnerability lifecycle, a minimum record, a control-and-closure matrix, tooling implications, and a testable research agenda.

</details>


### [204] [Tool Demo: Topology analysis with GPML for detection of cyberattacks in Water Distribution Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05902)
*Majed Jaber,Abdul Qadir Khan,Ankush Meshram,Julien Michel,Côme Frappé - - Vialatoux,Pierre Parrend*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A topology-driven cyberattack detection method for water distribution networks that transforms raw traffic into dynamic graphs, extracts community and spectral metrics, and evaluates on three industrial datasets (HITL, SWaT, CrossTest), demonstrating improved detection of both cyber and physical attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Water distribution networks integrate physical processes with communication networks via industrial control systems, making them susceptible to cyberattacks that alter traffic patterns and network behavior. Existing detection methods relying on raw traffic or protocol information fail to capture structural changes induced by such attacks, motivating a topology-driven approach.

Method: The authors propose a Graph Processing for Machine Learning (GPML) framework that: (1) transforms raw network traffic into dynamic graphs, (2) extracts community metrics and spectral metrics from these graphs, and (3) analyzes structural and communication modifications over time to detect anomalies indicative of cyberattacks.

Result: Spectral and community graph metrics consistently improved model performance for detecting both cyber and physical attacks across all three evaluated datasets: HITL, SWaT, and CrossTest.

Conclusion: A topology-driven, graph-based detection approach that leverages community and spectral features effectively identifies cyberattacks in water distribution networks by capturing structural changes that traditional raw-traffic or protocol-based methods overlook.

Abstract: Water distribution networks depends on industrial control systems to integrate the physical process with communication network, making them vulnerable to cyberattacks that alter the traffic pattern and network behavior. Traditional detection approaches that rely on raw traffic or protocol information often oversee structural changes that are induced by such attacks. In this work, we presents a topology-driven approach for detection of cyberattacks in water distribution networks based on Graph Processing for Machine Learning (GPML) framework. The raw traffic is transformed into dynamic graphs, from which community and spectral metrics are extracted and analyzed for any structural and communication modifications with time. The proposed methodology is evaluated on three industrial water distribution datasets such as HITL, SWaT, and CrossTest. Spectral and community graph metrics improve the model performance in detection of cyber and pyhiscal attacks across the three datasets.

</details>


### [205] [MMAligner: Safeguarding Multimodal Large Language Models through Representation Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05909)
*Shenyi Zhang,Keyan Guo,Zihao Wang,Xuebin Li,Lingchen Zhao,Hongxin Hu,Chao Shen,Qian Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MLLMs refuse unsafe text but not equivalent multimodal inputs due to representation shift. The paper proposes MMAligner, which realigns unsafe multimodal representations into the model's pre-existing refusal boundary, achieving ~99% refusal rate with minimal utility loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs exhibit a safety disparity: they refuse unsafe text prompts but generate harmful responses to semantically equivalent multimodal inputs. Existing defenses (external guardrails, safety fine-tuning) are suboptimal—adding overhead, sacrificing utility, or requiring large datasets. The authors aim to identify the root cause of this gap geometrically.

Method: The authors perform geometric analysis of MLLM representations, revealing a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary across modalities. They find that unsafe multimodal inputs undergo a representation shift that places them outside this boundary. Based on this insight, they propose MMAligner, which applies three constraints: (1) a hard lower bound to ensure refusal, (2) a soft upper bound to prevent excessive modification, and (3) a preservation objective for benign inputs, thereby calibrating unsafe multimodal representations into the refusal region.

Result: MMAligner achieves an average refusal rate of 99% on unsafe multimodal inputs with less than 2% utility degradation and minimal training data across multiple open-source MLLMs, substantially outperforming existing baselines on the safety-utility trade-off.

Conclusion: Multimodal safety degradation is caused by representation misalignment, not absence of safety capability. MMAligner effectively corrects this by realigning representations into the existing refusal subspace, offering a lightweight and effective safeguarding method.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often refuse unsafe text prompts yet generate harmful responses to semantically equivalent multimodal inputs. Existing defenses either rely on external guardrails, which add inference overhead without repairing intrinsic flaws, or safety fine-tuning, which treats alignment as black-box optimization and may sacrifice utility or require large multimodal datasets. To identify the cause of this safety disparity, we analyze MLLM representations geometrically. We find that safety mechanisms learned from text persist across modalities: a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary remain effective, and representations inside this boundary consistently trigger refusals. However, unsafe multimodal inputs undergo a representation shift that places most of them outside the boundary, allowing them to bypass the model's intrinsic safety mechanism. This indicates that multimodal safety degradation stems from representation misalignment rather than the absence of safety capability. Based on this finding, we propose MMAligner, a safeguarding method that calibrates unsafe multimodal representations into the pre-existing refusal region. MMAligner applies a hard lower bound to ensure refusal, a soft upper bound to avoid excessive modification, and a preservation objective for benign inputs. Experiments across multiple open-source MLLMs show that MMAligner raises the average refusal rate on unsafe multimodal inputs to 99% with less than 2% utility degradation and minimal training data, substantially improving the safety-utility trade-off over existing baselines. (*Due to the notification from arXiv, "The Abstract field cannot be longer than 1,920 characters", the Abstract that appeared is shortened.)

</details>


### [206] [A Note on the Influence of a Zero Length Nonce on GCM and GMAC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06061)
*Yaobin Shen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A simple attack recovers the GCM/GMAC hash key when a zero-length nonce is permitted, enabling arbitrary ciphertext/message forgery. The attack applies to the ISO/IEC version but not the NIST version, which mandates a minimum one-bit nonce.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper is motivated by a gap between two major standards for GCM/GMAC: the ISO/IEC version permits zero-length nonces, while the NIST version explicitly forbids them. The authors aim to demonstrate that this seemingly minor specification difference has serious security implications, showing that the ISO/IEC allowance creates a practical attack vector for hash key recovery.

Method: The attack exploits the use of a zero-length nonce in GCM/GMAC. The authors show that when an empty (zero-length) nonce is used, the authentication mechanism leaks the hash key H used in the GHASH polynomial evaluation. Specifically, with a zero-length nonce, the initial counter block and the authentication tag computation simplify in a way that allows direct algebraic recovery of H from observed ciphertext/tag pairs, breaking the confidentiality and integrity guarantees of the scheme.

Result: The attack successfully recovers the hash key H of GCM/GMAC when a zero-length nonce is allowed. Once H is known, the adversary can forge arbitrary authenticated ciphertexts or messages at will. The ISO/IEC version is vulnerable; the NIST version is immune due to its minimum nonce length requirement of one bit.

Conclusion: The ISO/IEC standard's permissiveness regarding zero-length nonces constitutes a critical security vulnerability in GCM/GMAC. The NIST requirement of at least a one-bit nonce is vindicated as a necessary security measure. This highlights how subtle differences between cryptographic standards can lead to significant security gaps.

Abstract: In this note, we show a simple attack that can recover the hash key of GCM and GMAC by using a zero length nonce. After recovering the hash key, the adversary can forge an arbitrary ciphertext or message as she wants. We note that the ISO/IEC version of GCM and GMAC allows the nonce to be a zero length string, while the NIST version of GCM and GMAC explicitly requires the nonce to be at least one bit. Hence, our attack works for the ISO/IEC version and cannot work for the NIST version.

</details>


### [207] [dfence: Fine-Grained Speculation Barriers for Efficient and Effective Hardware-Software Protection in the Spectre Era (Extended Version)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06124)
*Davide Davoli,Marton Bognar,Lesly-Ann Daniel,Benjamin Grégoire,Frank Piessens,Tamara Rezk*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: dfence is a new CPU instruction that generalizes Speculative Load Hardening to mitigate both Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL attacks. It allows developers to annotate sensitive registers so hardware prevents transient leakage, achieves &lt;1% average overhead, and is paired with a type system for static verification of correct placement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing software mitigations for speculative execution attacks are limited: Speculative Load Hardening (SLH) only addresses Spectre-PHT and requires error-prone manual speculative masks; SSBD for Spectre-STL incurs high overhead and lacks fine-grained control. A unified, low-overhead hardware-software solution is needed.

Method: The authors introduce dfence, a new CPU instruction that generalizes SLH. Developers annotate sensitive registers, and the hardware transparently prevents transient leakage of those register values. The instruction is implemented in the Proteus CPU. Additionally, a type system is designed to statically verify correct dfence placement in code.

Result: dfence achieves less than 1% average performance overhead on the evaluated benchmarks while providing unified protection against both Spectre-PHT (Bounds Check Bypass) and Spectre-STL (Speculative Store Bypass).

Conclusion: dfence demonstrates that a single, minimal hardware instruction can provide broad, low-overhead defense against key Spectre variants. Coupled with static type-checking for correct usage, it offers a practical and secure path for adoption in future processors.
