Abstract: Speculative execution attacks such as Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL remain a critical security concern in modern processors. While software-based mitigations like Speculative Load Hardening (SLH) offer effective protection against Spectre-PHT, they are limited in scope and require software-managed speculative masks, which can be error-prone and costly. Defenses against Spectre-STL, such as the Speculative Store Bypass Disable bit (SSBD), incur additional performance overhead and lack fine-grained control. In this work, we introduce dfence, a new CPU instruction that generalizes SLH to mitigate both Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL with minimal hardware support. dfence enables developers to annotate sensitive registers, with the hardware ensuring that these values do not leak transiently. We implement dfence in the Proteus CPU and evaluate its security and performance, demonstrating less than 1% average performance overhead for our benchmarks. In addition, to support easy and secure adoption, we design a type system that statically verifies the correct placement of dfence instructions in code.

</details>


### [208] [Hardware Keystores for AI Agent Signing Workflows: A Zero-Trust MCP Enforcement Architecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06130)
*Leo Sambrook,Sampo Sovio*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: To prevent AI agents from exposing private cryptographic keys, the authors replace software-stored keys with hardware-confined keys via PKCS#11 and wrap them in a five-layer Zero-Trust enforcement stack. Evaluation against 12 AgentDojo injection scenarios shows baseline ASR of 19.3% reduced to 0% with protection, and zero false positives on benign tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents routinely perform cryptographic operations (signing, authentication, certificate issuance) but store private keys in software-accessible locations (plaintext files, env vars, container memory). This creates a critical vulnerability: any process with read privileges can exfiltrate raw key material. A recent production incident demonstrated this severity—private keys were stolen from a widely deployed framework via email injection in under five minutes. The authors seek to enforce both key confidentiality and content-aware authorization for key use.

Method: 1. Replace software-resident keys with hardware-confined keys accessible through a vendor-neutral PKCS#11 interface. A hardware keystore (HSM, TPM, smart card) executes cryptographic operations on-device; the host receives only results via opaque handles. 2. Surround hardware confinement with a five-layer Zero-Trust enforcement stack: session identity (SAGA), scope bounds (Smax), semantic validation (RAV), taint tracking, and the hardware execution boundary. 3. Evaluate against 12 injection scenarios derived from AgentDojo's ImportantInstructionsAttack template, running four LLM models (gpt-oss-120b, Qwen2.5-72B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash) with n=192 combined.

Result: Baseline Attack Success Rate (ASR): 19.3% [95% CI: 14.3%, 25.4%]. Protected ASR: 0% (Wilson 95% CI upper bound 2.0%). Zero false positives across four benign task scenarios.

Conclusion: Hardware-confined keys combined with the five-layer Zero-Trust enforcement stack effectively eliminate prompt-injection-driven key exfiltration in AI agents, reducing ASR from 19.3% to 0% with no false positives, demonstrating a practical and robust defense against a real-world class of supply-chain and agent-security threats.

Abstract: AI agents performing cryptographic operations (signing Git commits, authenticating API calls, issuing certificates) currently store private keys in software-accessible locations: plaintext files, environment variables, or container memory. Any process with sufficient read privileges can extract the raw key material. A recent production incident demonstrated the practical severity: private keys were exfiltrated from a widely deployed framework via email injection in under five minutes. We aim to enforce both key confidentiality and content-aware authorisation for key use. To that end, we replace software-resident keys with hardware-confined keys accessible through a vendor-neutral PKCS#11 interface. A hardware keystore (HSM, TPM, smart card) executes cryptographic operations on-device; the host receives only the result via opaque handles. Hardware confinement is the primary contribution; it is enabled by a surrounding five-layer Zero-Trust enforcement stack comprising session identity (SAGA), scope bounds (Smax), semantic validation (RAV), taint tracking, and the hardware execution boundary. We evaluate against 12 injection scenarios derived from AgentDojo's ImportantInstructionsAttack template (Debenedetti et al., arXiv:2406.13352). We run four LLM models; three follow injections in baseline mode (gpt-oss-120b, Qwen2.5-72B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, n=192 combined). Baseline Attack Success Rate (ASR): 19.3% [14.3%, 25.4%]; protected ASR: 0% (Wilson 95% CI upper bound 2.0%). Zero false positives across four benign task scenarios.

</details>


### [209] [Reversible Unlearnable Examples: Towards the Copyright Protection in Deep Learning Era](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06211)
*Binze Wang,Jinyu Tian,Xingrun Wang,Xiaochen Yuan,Jianqing Li*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a unified copyright protection mechanism that simultaneously prevents unauthorized model training via unlearnable perturbations (based on minimizing mutual information) and enables watermark-based ownership verification through a dual extraction strategy, addressing the negative interaction between availability attacks and watermarking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing copyright protection methods address only one threat at a time: either unauthorized model training (via unlearnable examples) or data leakage (via watermarking). Simply combining these two techniques fails due to negative interactions — unlearnable perturbations interfere with watermark extraction. A comprehensive solution addressing both threats simultaneously is lacking.

Method: The method has two components: (1) Generating unlearnable perturbations by minimizing mutual information between model inputs and outputs, forcing models to learn uncorrelated features that do not generalize, thereby preventing unauthorized training. (2) A dual extraction strategy using two distinct watermark extractors to decouple watermark extraction from the unlearnable perturbations, eliminating their side impact on watermark recovery.

Result: Extensive experiments on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and Pets datasets demonstrate that the proposed method provides comprehensive copyright protection, effectively preventing unauthorized model training while preserving reliable watermark extraction.

Conclusion: The proposed mechanism successfully unifies protection against both illegal model training and malicious data leakage, overcoming the negative interaction between availability attacks and watermarking. The code is publicly available.

Abstract: Significant advancements in deep learning have been made possible by the utilization of large datasets, underscoring the critical importance of copyright protection. Adding meticulously designed perturbations to examples, making them unlearnable has become a crucial approach for safeguarding data copyright. Existing methods for creating unlearnable examples overlook the risk of data leakage, which can threaten data ownership. Thus, copyright protection in deep learning faces two main threats: illegal model training and malicious data leakage. We investigate that these two threats cannot be solved by straightforwardly combining existing availability attacks and watermarking techniques as their negative interaction effects. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a novel copyright protection mechanism for the aforementioned security concerns. Considering that the prevention of unauthorized model training requires powerful generalizability of unlearnable perturbations, we generate perturbations to induce the model to learn uncorrelated features of input images. It works by minimizing the mutual information of the input and output of the model. On the other hand, to eliminate the side impact of unlearnable perturbations on the watermark extraction, we design a dual extraction strategy by using two distinct watermark extractors. Extensive experiments on the image datasets {ImageNet, CIFAR10, and Pets} show that our proposed method could provide comprehensive copyright protection to images. The code is available at {https://github.com/Yeah21/ReversibleUnlearnableExamples}.

</details>


### [210] [Game Hopping in Lean](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06261)
*Stefan Dziembowski,Grzegorz Fabiański,Daniele Micciancio,Rafał Stefański*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: HOPSCOTCH is a Lean 4 framework for mechanizing game-based cryptographic proofs using a shallow embedding, with a formal game-hopping object, a computational soundness theorem, and a state-abstraction methodology for observational equivalence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mechanized frameworks for game-based cryptographic proofs are either deep embeddings with limited integration into general-purpose proof assistants, or lack a formal, inspectable representation of the game-hopping argument itself. The authors aim to provide a shallow-embedded framework in Lean 4 that tightly integrates with Mathlib, supports the standard game-hopping paradigm, and yields explicit, verifiable proof objects with concrete advantage bounds.

Method: HOPSCOTCH uses a shallow embedding in Lean 4: oracles and reductions are ordinary Lean definitions. Security is defined as indistinguishability between stateful probabilistic oracles. Game-hopping proofs are represented as explicit formal objects whose constructors mirror standard game-hopping steps. A general computational soundness theorem interprets these proof objects by constructing reductions against the assumptions used and deriving concrete advantage bounds. Observational equivalence between oracles is established via a state-abstraction methodology that handles adding/forgetting state and eager-to-lazy sampling transformations.

Result: The framework is validated through formalized proofs of: (1) IND-CCA security of encrypt-then-MAC, (2) ElGamal security from DDH, (3) the implication from one-time secrecy to public-key IND-CPA security, and (4) the GGM pseudorandom-function construction. The GGM proof is claimed to be the first mechanized proof for non-constant depth.

Conclusion: HOPSCOTCH demonstrates that shallow embeddings can effectively mechanize game-based cryptographic proofs with tight integration into a general-purpose proof assistant, while retaining the structure and inspectability of game-hopping arguments through explicit proof objects and a soundness theorem that yields concrete bounds.

Abstract: We present HOPSCOTCH, a Lean 4 framework for mechanizing computationally sound, game-based cryptographic proofs. Security definitions are expressed as indistinguishability between stateful probabilistic oracles, and proofs follow the standard game-hopping paradigm. HOPSCOTCH uses a shallow embedding: oracles and reductions are ordinary Lean definitions, enabling direct integration with the full Lean ecosystem, including general mathematical theories from Mathlib, such as finite-group theory. A game-hopping proof in HOPSCOTCH is represented as an explicit formal object whose constructors correspond to the standard steps of a game-hopping argument, making proofs easier to construct, automate, and inspect. We prove a general computational soundness theorem that interprets these proof objects by constructing reductions against the assumptions they use and deriving a concrete bound on the advantage of any distinguisher. Observational equivalence between oracles is established using a state-abstraction methodology: a simple yet powerful approach that supports transformations such as adding or forgetting state and replacing eager sampling with lazy sampling. We illustrate the framework with formalized proofs of the IND-CCA security of encrypt-then-MAC, the security of ElGamal encryption from DDH, the implication from one-time secrecy to public-key IND-CPA security, and the GGM pseudorandom-function construction. To the best of our knowledge, the last is the first mechanized proof of GGM for non-constant depth.

</details>


### [211] [A Sound Translation from Tamarin to ProVerif: Enabling Comparative Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06315)
*Kevin Morio,Yavor Ivanov,Robert Künnemann*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A sound translation from Tamarin to ProVerif is presented, enabling rigorous comparison of the two protocol verification tools. The translation covers a large subset of Tamarin's features with formal soundness and completeness guarantees, and evaluation on 121 models shows 246/247 non-XOR tasks agree, with ProVerif being faster in 92.3% of cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tamarin and ProVerif are leading security protocol verifiers with fundamentally different formalisms—Tamarin uses multiset rewrite rules with sound-and-complete verification, while ProVerif uses applied-pi calculus with fast but potentially incomplete results. A systematic, rigorous comparison has been challenging due to these foundational differences. The authors aim to bridge this gap with a faithful translation.

Method: The authors develop a sound translation from Tamarin to ProVerif, introducing novel techniques for (1) formula rewriting, (2) encoding multiset rewrite semantics into ProVerif's process calculus, and (3) handling simultaneous events. They formally prove soundness (any ProVerif-verified property holds in the original Tamarin model) and completeness (exists-trace properties not involving attacker knowledge are preserved) within the faithful fragment. XOR and other best-effort encodings are treated separately.

Result: Evaluation on 121 Tamarin models covering 566 lemma tasks shows: the translation handles 562/566 tasks. Among non-XOR tasks with definitive results from both tools, 246/247 agree (the sole discrepancy is flagged as using an incomplete model). For 362 tasks where Tamarin returns a Boolean result and ProVerif completes, ProVerif is faster in 334 cases (92.3%), with median speedup of 6.74x and peak-memory ratio of 6.24x.

Conclusion: The translation establishes a rigorous bridge between Tamarin and ProVerif, enabling systematic comparison and allowing users to leverage ProVerif's speed while retaining Tamarin's modeling expressiveness. The high agreement rate (246/247) validates the translation's fidelity, and ProVerif's substantial performance advantages (6.74x faster, 6.24x less memory) demonstrate practical benefits.

Abstract: Tamarin and ProVerif are two prominent tools for the formal verification of security protocols. They share the same high-level goal but differ significantly in their underlying formalisms and verification techniques, making a systematic comparison challenging: Tamarin uses multiset rewrite rules with sound and complete verification, whereas ProVerif employs an extension of the applied-pi calculus that provides fast but potentially incomplete results.
  We present a sound translation from Tamarin to ProVerif that enables a rigorous comparison of the two tools. It introduces novel techniques for formula rewriting, encoding multiset rewrite semantics, and handling simultaneous events, supporting an extensive subset of Tamarin's features, including multiset rewrite rules, lemmas, and restrictions, while precisely characterizing the cases where faithful translation is not possible. We provide formal proofs: within the faithful fragment, soundness ensures that any property verified in ProVerif also holds in the original Tamarin model, and completeness ensures that exists-trace properties not involving attacker knowledge are preserved. Best-effort encodings, in particular XOR, are reported separately and are outside these guarantees.
  Finally, we evaluate our translation on 121 Tamarin models. The translation covers 562 of 566 lemma tasks. Among non-XOR tasks with definitive results from both tools, 246 of 247 agree, with the remaining verdict explicitly flagged as using an incomplete model. Among the 362 tasks for which Tamarin returns a Boolean result and ProVerif completes with a logical result, ProVerif is faster in 334 cases (92.3%), with median per-task runtime and peak-memory ratios of 6.74x and 6.24x, respectively.

</details>

### [212] [BioMedJImpact: A Comprehensive Dataset and LLM Pipeline for AI Engagement and Scientific Impact Analysis of Biomedical Journals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05227)
*Ruiyu Wang,Yuzhang Xie,Xiao Hu,Carl Yang,Jiaying Lu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: BioMedJImpact is a large-scale dataset of 1.74M PubMed Central articles across 2,744 biomedical journals, integrating bibliometric indicators, collaboration features, and an LLM-derived AI engagement rate. Analysis reveals larger author teams correlate with higher citation impact, while AI engagement rate positively associates with Impact Factor only in 2019. The LLM pipeline is validated via human evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing resources for assessing journal impact rarely capture how collaboration patterns and AI research jointly shape venue prestige in biomedicine. There is a need for a comprehensive, content-aware dataset that integrates both collaboration metrics and AI engagement to enable more nuanced scientometric analysis.

Method: The authors constructed BioMedJImpact from 1.74M PubMed Central articles across 2,744 journals. They designed a reproducible three-stage LLM pipeline to extract an AI engagement rate (proportion of AI-related articles per journal-year). The dataset integrates bibliometric indicators, collaboration features, and this AI engagement rate. They then analyzed how collaboration intensity and AI engagement rate jointly influence scientific impact across two temporal subsets: 2016–2019 and 2020–2023. Human evaluation was conducted to validate the LLM pipeline for AI relevance detection and subfield classification consistency.

Result: Two main patterns emerged: (1) journals with larger author teams tend to have higher citation impact; (2) AI engagement rate is positively associated with Impact Factor, but only in the 2019 subset. Human evaluation confirmed substantial agreement in AI relevance detection and consistent subfield classification, validating the LLM pipeline.

Conclusion: BioMedJImpact offers a validated, scalable framework for content-aware scientometric analysis at the intersection of biomedicine and AI, providing both a comprehensive dataset and a reproducible methodology for assessing how collaboration and AI research jointly shape journal prestige.

Abstract: Assessing journal impact is central to scholarly communication, yet existing resources rarely capture how collaboration and artificial intelligence (AI) research jointly shape venue prestige in biomedicine. We present BioMedJImpact, a large-scale, biomedical-oriented dataset built from 1.74 million PubMed Central articles across 2,744 journals. BioMedJImpact integrates bibliometric indicators, collaboration features, and an LLM-derived AI engagement rate, defined as the proportion of AI-related articles within each journal-year. Specifically, AI engagement rate is extracted through a reproducible three-stage LLM pipeline. We analyze how collaboration intensity and AI engagement rate jointly influence scientific impact across two temporal subsets (2016-2019, 2020-2023). Two main patterns emerge: journals with larger author teams tend to have higher citation impact, while AI engagement rate is positively associated with Impact Factor only in the 2019 subset. To validate the LLM pipeline for deriving the AI engagement rate, we conduct human evaluation, confirming substantial agreement in AI relevance detection and consistent subfield classification. Together, BioMedJImpact provides both a comprehensive dataset at the interface of biomedicine and AI and a validated framework for scalable, content-aware scientometric analysis. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/JonathanWry/BioMedJImpact.

</details>


### [213] [From Trajectories to Evidence: Auditable Experimental Records for Industrial Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05235)
*Zijie Zhuang,Changxin Lao,Pengbo Xu,Hanwen Xu,Ruochen Yang,Yingzhi He,Peng Zhang,Jiangxia Cao,Yusheng Huang,Guohong Mu,Jian Liang,Ruiming Tang,Shuang Yang,Zhaojie Liu,Wenwu Ou,Kun Gai*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of converting completed research trajectories (multi-round ML experiments) into reliable evidence. The authors propose a framework with pre-execution artifact verification, post-execution claim qualification, and an LLM-assisted controller that applies, defers, or rejects findings. They reveal non-monotonic trajectory evolution and demonstrate positive online lifts from candidates produced through the workflow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In industrial recommendation systems, research agents conduct multi-round ML experiments, but completed trajectories are not automatically trustworthy evidence. Generated artifacts may be unsupported or incomplete, experimental rounds may be invalid or confounded, and later modifications can obscure earlier findings. There is a need to systematically determine what a completed research process has actually established.

Method: The authors introduce an evidence-grounded framework with two phases: (1) a context-isolated generate–verify–repair process that checks artifacts for evidence violations and missing downstream requirements before release (bounded verification of consequential artifacts), and (2) post-execution validity and attribution checks that consolidate evidence across rounds, qualify intervention-level claims as actionable repairs, diagnostic guards, or withheld findings, and preserve admitted claims as auditable records with explicit provenance and applicability boundaries. A hybrid LLM-assisted controller then applies, defers, or rejects records based on available target evidence.

Result: Record audits characterize which claims survive qualification. Downstream diagnostics identify affirmative applicability judgment as a bottleneck for the tested controller. Across paper-to-target adaptations, later rounds often improve on the first, while final rounds frequently underperform an earlier best, exposing non-monotonic trajectory evolution. Candidates produced through the complete workflow yielded positive online lifts relative to deployed baselines.

Conclusion: Trajectory-to-evidence conversion is a critical but underexamined problem. The proposed evidence-grounded framework, combining bounded verification, post-execution claim qualification, and an LLM-assisted controller, effectively surfaces which claims are genuinely supported, reveals non-monotonic progress across experimental rounds, and produces candidates with positive real-world impact.

Abstract: Research agents increasingly conduct multi-round machine-learning experiments in industrial recommendation settings and retain the resulting trajectories to guide later decisions. Yet a completed trajectory is not automatically evidence: generated artifacts may be unsupported or incomplete, executed rounds may be invalid or confounded, and later modifications may obscure earlier findings. We study \textbf{trajectory-to-evidence conversion}, asking what a completed research process has actually established. We introduce an evidence-grounded framework that couples bounded verification of consequential artifacts with post-execution claim qualification. A context-isolated generate--verify--repair process checks artifacts for evidence violations and missing downstream requirements before release. After execution, validity and attribution checks consolidate evidence across rounds, qualify intervention-level claims as actionable repairs, diagnostic guards, or withheld findings, and preserve admitted claims as auditable records with explicit provenance and applicability boundaries. A hybrid LLM-assisted controller subsequently applies, defers, or rejects records based on available target evidence. Record audits characterize which claims survive qualification, while downstream diagnostics identify affirmative applicability judgment as a bottleneck for the tested controller. Across paper-to-target adaptations, later rounds often improve on the first, while final rounds frequently underperform an earlier best, exposing non-monotonic trajectory evolution. Candidates produced through the complete workflow also yielded positive online lifts relative to deployed baselines.

</details>


### [214] [Cross-platform epistemic verification for improving factual reliability in AI-generated news summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05302)
*Zhuo Xie,Haoze Ni*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: MECV is a post-hoc hallucination correction framework that uses multi-source evidence aggregation and a multi-LLM jury with contradiction-aware consensus scoring to improve factual consistency in AI-generated news summaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-generated news summaries suffer from factual hallucinations, and single-source verification is insufficient. The authors aim to leverage heterogeneous evidence and consensus mechanisms to better detect and correct unsupported claims.

Method: MECV aggregates evidence from three sources: source document, Wikipedia, and open-web retrieval. A multi-LLM jury (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-Chat) performs contradiction-aware consensus scoring to estimate factual reliability. Unsupported claims are revised via iterative minimal-edit refinement, with Qwen-Plus as orchestrator. Evaluated on SummEdits benchmark.

Result: MECV improves factual consistency while preserving semantic structure. Agreement across heterogeneous evidence sources serves as a useful signal for identifying factual uncertainty, including in financial news aggregation.

Conclusion: Multi-source consensus-based verification offers a promising direction for improving factual reliability in AI-generated news summarization, contributing to trustworthy AI and automated journalism.

Abstract: This study proposes Multi-source Evidence Consen- sus Verification (MECV), a post-hoc hallucination cor- rection framework for AI-generated news summariza- tion. Instead of depending on a single retrieval channel, MECV aggregates evidence from multiple heterogeneous sources, including the source document, Wikipedia, and open-web retrieval. The framework further incorporates a multi-LLM jury mechanism that estimates factual reliabil- ity through contradiction-aware consensus scoring across verifier models. Claims identified as potentially unsup- ported are revised through iterative minimal-edit refine- ment. The proposed framework is evaluated on the SummEd- its benchmark using GPT-4o-mini and DeepSeek-Chat as the verifier jury, with Qwen-Plus as the orchestra- tor. Experimental results show that MECV improves fac- tual consistency while preserving the semantic structure of the original summaries. The findings further suggest that agreement across heterogeneous evidence sources can serve as a useful signal for identifying factual uncertainty in AI-generated summaries, including in information- sensitive domains such as financial news aggregation. This study contributes to research on trustworthy AI and automated journalism by introducing a multi-source verification framework for hallucination correction and demonstrating the value of consensus-based verification for improving factual reliability in AI-generated news summarization.

</details>


### [215] [Robustness and User-Perceived Value of Popularity Calibration in Music Recommendation: A User Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05402)
*Oleg Lesota,Gustavo Escobedo,Bruce Ferwerda,Simone Kopeinik,Dominik Kowald,Elisabeth Lex,Markus Schedl*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether popularity-calibrated music recommendations are actually preferred by users. Through a user study, the authors find that while users can perceive differences in popularity composition, they do not clearly prefer calibrated lists. The study also reveals that the standard JSD-based calibration metric's relationship with perceived popularity is unstable, depending on item familiarity, list composition, and history availability. Computational and user-judged popularity labels show only weak alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work on popularity calibration relies heavily on offline metrics and assumes users prefer lists matching their historical consumption profile, yet user studies are scarce and prior findings show mixed effects on user experience. The robustness of calibration metrics under varying familiarity and incomplete history remains unclear. This paper aims to critically examine the perceived value and measurement reliability of popularity calibration in music recommendation.

Method: The authors conduct a user study with personalized music track lists constructed from participants' recent listening histories. Using a controlled naive recommender, they generate three types of lists: highpop-heavy, lowpop-heavy, and calibrated. They measure whether users perceive differences between these lists, whether calibrated lists are preferred, how JSD-based popularity calibration behaves under different familiarity and history-availability conditions, and how well computational popularity labels align with users' own judgments.

Result: Users can perceive differences in popularity composition across lists but do not clearly prefer calibrated ones. The relationship between JSD and perceived popularity is conditional on item familiarity, list composition, and available user history. Computational popularity labels align only weakly with users' own popularity judgments.

Conclusion: Popularity calibration as both an offline metric and a user-facing construct warrants more critical scrutiny. The findings challenge common assumptions that calibrated recommendations inherently improve user experience, and highlight measurement validity concerns with JSD-based calibration in real-world settings.

Abstract: Popularity calibration in recommender systems has been studied both as a form of user-centered personalization and as an indicator of popularity bias. Most existing work evaluates calibration through offline metrics, often assuming that users prefer recommendation lists whose popularity distribution matches their historical consumption profile. However, user studies on calibration remain limited, and existing findings suggest that calibrated recommendations do not necessarily have a strong effect on user experience. Moreover, although prior work has shown that calibration metrics can correlate with users' perceptions of recommendation lists, the robustness of this relation remains unclear under different levels of item familiarity and incomplete user-history information. In this work, we study the perceived value and measurement reliability of popularity calibration in music recommendation. We construct personalized track lists from users' recent listening histories and use a controlled naive recommender to create lists with different popularity compositions: highpop-heavy, lowpop-heavy, and calibrated. We investigate whether users perceive differences between these lists, whether calibrated lists are preferred, how robust JSD-based popularity calibration is under different familiarity and history-availability conditions, and how computational popularity labels align with users' own popularity judgments. Our results show that users perceive differences in popularity composition, but do not clearly prefer calibrated lists. We further find that the relation between JSD and perceived popularity depends on item familiarity, list composition, and available user history, while computational and user-judged popularity labels only weakly align. These findings contribute to a more critical understanding of popularity calibration as both an offline metric and a user-facing construct.

</details>


### [216] [A Mechanistic Analysis of Gender Sensitivity in Dense Retrieval Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05467)
*Catherine Chen,Maarten de Rijke,Carsten Eickhoff*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper mechanistically analyzes bi-encoder dense retrieval models to localize gender bias, finding it originates in input embeddings and concentrates in a small set of late-layer attention heads that mix gender and term-matching signals. Steering at these two levels yields distinct effects: embedding-level intervention non-specifically neutralizes score differences, while attention-level steering produces directional shifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work documents that dense retrieval models exhibit gender bias (scoring male-gendered documents higher), but the internal mechanisms producing these disparities remain poorly understood. The authors aim to open the black box and identify where and how gender sensitivity arises within bi-encoder architectures.

Method: The authors perform a mechanistic analysis of bi-encoder retrieval models using causal mediation analysis and activation patching. They trace gender signals from input embeddings through transformer layers, localizing them to specific attention heads. They then test two types of steering interventions — embedding-level and attention-level — and compare their effects on retrieval score disparities.

Result: Gender sensitivity originates in input embeddings and propagates through a small subset of late-layer attention heads that jointly encode both gender information and term-matching (relevance) signals. Embedding-level steering non-specifically neutralizes score differences across the board, while attention-level steering enables directional control over gender-biased scoring.

Conclusion: The findings provide a mechanistic foundation for targeted debiasing of dense retrieval models. A key challenge is that gender and relevance signals are entangled within shared model components (the identified attention heads), making disentanglement difficult without degrading retrieval quality.

Abstract: While gender bias in dense retrieval models is well documented, with prior work showing that models often score male-gendered documents higher than female or neutral variants, the internal mechanisms producing these disparities are poorly understood. In this paper, we mechanistically analyze bi-encoder models to localize gender sensitivity, finding that the signal originates in input embeddings and propagates through a small set of late-layer attention heads that carry both gender and term-matching signals. Guided by these findings, we test steering interventions at both identified points and find distinct effects: embedding-level steering non-specifically neutralizes score differences, while attention-level steering produces directional shifts. Our findings provide a mechanistic basis for targeted debiasing and highlight the challenge of disentangling gender from relevance signals in shared model components.

</details>


### [217] [An Ontology-Based Framework for Student Profiling and Content Personalization in Higher Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05489)
*José Luiz M. Morais,Arlindo F. da Conceição,Cacilda Encarnação Augusto Alvarenga,Daniela Musa*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper explores how to improve self-paced e-learning in higher education by using ontologies and a computational architecture to store and manage student profiles and learning process data, enabling better pedagogical models for distance education.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The expansion of digital technologies and virtual learning environments in distance education has shifted the teaching-learning paradigm, demanding greater student protagonism. Existing pedagogical models need rethinking to better achieve learning objectives in self-paced and e-learning contexts.

Method: Qualitative, bibliographic research that discusses techniques for electronic and automatic monitoring and recording of learning process outcomes. The study proposes the use of ontologies to store educational process information and presents a computational architecture designed for this purpose.

Result: The paper identifies key aspects for implementing and improving self-paced e-learning, highlights the importance of systems that store and manage student profiles (both content and access patterns), and delivers a proposal for an ontology-based computational architecture to manage educational data.

Conclusion: Effective self-paced e-learning requires robust mechanisms for tracking, storing, and managing student profile data. Ontology-based computational architectures offer a promising approach to organizing educational process information, thereby supporting more adaptive and effective pedagogical models in distance higher education.

Abstract: The expansion of access to Digital Information and Communication Technologies and the offer of distance or semi-distance education courses that make use of virtual learning environments brought changes in the teaching and learning processes, requiring that the student be even more protagonist in this process. The present study aimed to identify important aspects to be considered in the implementation and improvement of self-paced learning and e-learning in higher education courses, with the purpose of rethinking pedagogical models of courses offered at a distance so that they reach even more of your learning objectives. The research is characterized as qualitative, of bibliographic nature, and discusses techniques to monitor and record, electronically and automatically, the results of the process and learning. The importance of processes that store and manage the student's profile is highlighted, both in terms of content and forms of access. The article proposes the use of ontologies to store information about the educational process and presents a computational architecture for this purpose.

</details>


### [218] [EXCISE: Query-Side Exclusion for Late-Interaction Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05497)
*Mohammed Ali,Abdelrahman Abdallah,Adam Jatowt*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Late-interaction retrievers (e.g., ColBERT) suffer from "exclusion inversion," where additive MaxSim scoring inadvertently boosts documents matching excluded terms. EXCISE tackles this at query time using lightweight query-side modules (1.5M parameters) to identify excluded topics and re-rank shortlists, dramatically improving exclusion handling while matching frozen baselines on standard retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Late-interaction multi-vector retrievers like ColBERT use additive MaxSim scoring, which causes exclusion inversion: when a query specifies "X but not Z," documents containing Z receive inappropriately high scores because every token contributes positively. The authors show this is a fundamental limitation—no static readout of frozen vectors can recover the exclusion constraint—because identifying the excluded topic depends on the query alone, not the document representations.

Method: EXCISE (EXClusion Inversion Suppression Engine) applies two query-side modules at inference time without modifying the index: (1) a lightweight topic identification module and a re-embedding module (1.5M parameters total) that re-encode a 100-document shortlist from the frozen retriever, and (2) a parameter-free demotion rule that suppresses candidates matching the identified excluded topic. The authors also introduce X-BENCH, a tiered evaluation benchmark covering explicit, implicit, and compound exclusion queries with no-harm and Boolean accuracy controls.

Result: On ExcluIR, EXCISE raises exclusion success@10 from 0.058 to 0.691 and Boolean NOT accuracy from 0.25–0.29 to 0.90–0.92. Across six collections and three backbones (18 backbone–collection cells), EXCISE is the strongest system against both frozen and fine-tuned baselines. Pooled over 1,860 queries, it outperforms every fine-tuned cross-encoder—each of which suffers degraded no-harm nDCG@10—while EXCISE matches its frozen baseline's performance on standard retrieval.

Conclusion: Exclusion inversion is an inherent limitation of late-interaction scoring that cannot be resolved by re-weighting frozen vectors. EXCISE provides an effective, index-agnostic query-time solution that dramatically improves exclusion handling without sacrificing standard retrieval quality, making it practical for real-world deployment.

Abstract: Late-interaction retrievers handle exclusion queries poorly. When a user asks for X but not Z, the additive MaxSim score promotes documents covering Z, a problem we call exclusion inversion. We show that no readout of the frozen vectors recovers the constraint, because the difficulty lies in identifying the excluded topic, which depends on the query alone. EXCISE operates at query time and corrects the inversion while leaving the index frozen. Two query-side modules totalling 1.5M parameters identify the topic and re-embed a 100-document shortlist, and a parameter-free rule demotes candidates matching that topic. Across six collections and three backbones, EXCISE is the strongest system in all eighteen backbone-collection cells against that backbone's own frozen and fine-tuned baselines. It raises exclusion success@10 on ExcluIR from 0.058 to 0.691 and raises Boolean NOT accuracy from 0.25-0.29 to 0.90-0.92. Pooled over 1,860 queries, it outperforms every fine-tuned cross-encoder, each of which loses no-harm nDCG@10, whereas EXCISE matches its frozen baseline on its strongest backbone. We release X-BENCH, a tiered benchmark of explicit, implicit, and compound exclusions with no-harm and Boolean controls.

</details>


### [219] [omni-macos: On-Device Omni-Modal Search on Apple Silicon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05543)
*Han Xiao*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Omni-macos is a fully local, privacy-preserving multimodal search engine that runs embedding, indexing, and storage entirely on a Mac, keeping all user data on-device and operating within a user-defined memory budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal search engines assume server-side infrastructure, requiring files and queries to leave the user's machine. This raises privacy concerns and introduces network latency. The goal is to build a search engine that runs entirely on-device — on the same Mac where the files reside — so no data ever leaves the machine.

Method: The system employs a background indexer and an interactive search box constrained by a user-set memory budget. It re-encodes only chunks affected by file edits, offloads smaller GPU work units during interactive typing, serves queries from a quantized index replica with exact rescoring, and propagates the memory budget to allocators leveraging Apple's unified memory architecture.

Result: The system was evaluated on five Macs spanning an 8× range of accelerator width and a 32× range of memory, each indexing its own local files. Quantitative measurements of each mechanism are reported.

Conclusion: A fully on-device, memory-budgeted multimodal search engine is feasible on consumer Mac hardware, enabling private, low-latency search across diverse file types without any data leaving the machine.

Abstract: A search engine that embeds text, code, documents, images, audio and video into the same representation space has to run its encoder and keep its index somewhere, and almost every component built for the purpose assumes a server. We present omni-macos, which runs that whole engine, encoder, index and store, on the Mac the files are already on, so no file, query or vector ever leaves the machine. It keeps a background indexer and an interactive search box inside one memory budget the user sets: it re-encodes only the chunks an edit changes, hands the GPU smaller units while the user is typing, answers queries from a quantized replica with exact rescoring, and propagates that budget to the allocators that draw on unified memory. We measure every mechanism on five Macs spanning an eightfold range of accelerator width and a thirty-twofold range of memory, each one indexing its own local files.

</details>


### [220] [Is Personalized Modality Weighting Actually Personalized? A Controlled Audit of Per-User Weighting Claims in Multimodal Recommenders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05655)
*Jingyuan Zheng,Xin Zhang,Yang Gu,Dongjing Wang,Yuxiang Wang,Xudong Shen,Haiping Zhang,Youhuizi Li,Dongjin Yu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper audits per-user modality weighting in multimodal recommenders and finds that a single global modality weight captures nearly all gains, with per-user personalization adding no consistent benefit. The authors propose a two-contrast audit framework (real-GM and real-shuf) as a minimum standard for evaluating personalization claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on per-user modality weighting in billion-scale multimodal recommenders claims ranking gains from user-specific modality preferences, but these evaluations have not isolated genuine user-specific signals from mere global modality weighting combined with increased model capacity. A rigorous audit is needed to determine whether personalized modality weighting truly provides value beyond a single global weight.

Method: The authors propose a two-contrast audit principle: (1) real-GM (utility gap): comparing per-user implementations against a single global modality weight; (2) real-shuf (identifiability gap): comparing real per-user weights against eval-time permutation of user-weight bindings. Six per-user implementations (user modality-strength vectors, attention gates, meta-weight hypernetworks, low-rank guided weights) are reduced onto one shared collaborative backbone and tested across three short-video corpora and one cross-domain e-commerce corpus. A monotone signal-implant dose-response experiment verifies the harness can detect user-specific structure when present.

Result: A single global weight delivers nearly all content gain (+1.9/+3.6/+3.5 pp over no-modality baseline, p < .001). Per-user weighting adds no consistent utility: no implementation wins across all corpora and metrics; positive gaps are small (≤0.9 pp) and flip. The real-shuf control reaches +128% of content gain for heads that simultaneously lose to the global weight. Decoupling gate input from the shared collaborative embedding collapses inflated real-shuf to near zero. The signal-implant experiment shows capture AUROC rising from 0.57→0.89 and 0.64→1.00, confirming the harness would detect user-specific structure if present. All findings replicate on the e-commerce corpus.

Conclusion: Per-user modality weighting provides negligible benefit beyond a single global weight. The dissociation between real-shuf and real-GM is traced to gates reading shared collaborative embeddings rather than genuine user-specific signal. The authors recommend reporting both real-GM and real-shuf as a minimum evidentiary standard for personalization claims in multimodal recommenders.

Abstract: Per-user modality weighting is deployed at billion-user scale in multimodal recommenders, through user modality-strength vectors, attention gates, meta-weight hypernetworks, and low-rank guided weights, each claiming a ranking gain from user-specific modality preference. Yet, to our knowledge, prior evaluations do not isolate a genuinely user-specific signal from a global modality weight plus model capacity. We audit this family with a two-contrast audit principle, reducing six implementations onto one shared collaborative backbone and measuring a utility gap (real-GM) against a single global modality weight and an identifiability gap (real-shuf) against an eval-time permutation of the user-weight binding. Across three independent short-video corpora, a single global weight already delivers nearly all of the content gain (+1.9/+3.6/+3.5pp over a no-modality baseline, p < .001). Making the weight per-user adds no consistent utility: no implementation wins on all corpora and metrics, and the few positive gaps are small (<=0.9pp) and flip. The shuffle control is necessary but not sufficient, since real-shuf reaches +128% of the content gain for heads that simultaneously lose to the global weight. We trace this dissociation to gates reading the shared collaborative embedding: decoupling the gate input collapses the inflated real-shuf to near zero while the utility conclusion stands. A monotone signal-implant dose-response (capture AUROC rising from 0.57 to 0.89 and from 0.64 to 1.00) verifies the harness would detect user-specific structure if present, and every finding replicates on a fourth, cross-domain e-commerce corpus. We propose reporting real-GM alongside real-shuf as a minimum evidentiary standard for personalization claims.

</details>


### [221] [Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade - Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06213)
*Anna Lipkina,Daria Tikhonovich,Viktor Yanush,Mariia Ulianova,Oleg Sorokin,Vladislav Dodonov,Ilya Murzin,Denis Burshtein,Nikolay Savushkin*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Gryphon-v2 is a unified generate-and-rank architecture that replaces multi-stage recommendation cascades with a single end-to-end model. It uses an autoregressive decoder to generate Semantic-ID candidates and a distilled Ranking Module to score them, achieving a 1.41% increase in active users at Yandex Music while matching production latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial recommender systems rely on multi-stage cascades (candidate generators, pre-rankers, final rankers) that incur repeated user-history processing, complex feature pipelines, and multiple serving stages. While Semantic-ID-based generative retrieval simplifies this, next-item prediction alone fails to capture the fine-grained preferences that production ranking objectives encode. The authors aim to unify generation and ranking into one model without adding expensive second models to the serving path.

Method: Gryphon-v2 encodes user history once, generates Semantic-ID candidates via an autoregressive decoder, resolves them to catalog items, and ranks them with an item-level Ranking Module reusing shared encoder states. A training-only high-capacity Teacher Ranker is distilled into the Ranking Module using Rollout Distillation: teacher scores serve as the sole ranking supervision, collected over two complementary distributions — decoder rollouts (matching serving-time generation) and logged impressions (real user exposures).

Result: In an online A/B experiment at Yandex Music, a single Gryphon-v2 model replaced a production cascade of 15+ candidate generators, pre-ranking, and final ranking. The deployment yielded a 1.41% increase in active users at serving latency comparable to the production cascade.

Conclusion: A generative retriever paired with a Ranking Module distilled from a Teacher Ranker is a practically viable end-to-end alternative to production multi-stage recommendation cascades, delivering both simplification and improved user engagement.

Abstract: Industrial recommender systems are commonly deployed as multi-stage cascades with separate candidate generators, pre-rankers, and final rankers. Although effective, these cascades require repeated user-history processing, complex feature pipelines, and multiple serving stages. Semantic-ID-based generative retrieval offers a path toward simpler end-to-end systems, but next-item prediction alone does not capture the fine-grained preferences encoded by production ranking objectives. We present Gryphon-v2, a unified generate-and-rank architecture for end-to-end recommendation. The model encodes a user history once, generates Semantic-ID candidates with an autoregressive decoder, resolves them to catalogue items, and ranks them with an item-level Ranking Module that reuses the shared encoder states. To transfer fine-grained production ranking preferences without adding an expensive second model to the serving path, we distill a high-capacity, training-only Teacher Ranker into the Ranking Module. Gryphon-v2 is trained with Rollout Distillation: teacher scores are the only ranking supervision, and they are collected over two complementary candidate distributions. Rollouts from the current decoder expose the Ranking Module to candidates produced by the same generation mechanism used at serving time, while logged impressions cover items users were actually shown. In an online A/B experiment on a large-scale recommendation surface at Yandex Music, a single Gryphon-v2 model replaces a production cascade comprising more than 15 candidate generators, pre-ranking, and final ranking. The deployment increases the number of active users by 1.41% at serving latency comparable to the production cascade. These results support the practical viability of a generative retriever with a Ranking Module distilled from the Teacher Ranker as an end-to-end alternative to a production cascade.

</details>
