### [222] [Towards a Risk Assessment of Malicious Skill Files in Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05223)
*Rui Yang,Michael Fu,Kla Tantithamthavorn,Chetan Arora,Joey Chua*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper investigates the security vulnerability of autonomous coding agents' "skill interface"—folders of instructions/scripts that agents dynamically load. The authors demonstrate that malicious shell commands can be disguised within natural-language skill files, achieving exploitation rates of 95.5-96.1% against Gemini CLI and 71.6-74.0% against Qwen Code, with explicit safety recognition occurring in only 1.99% of runs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous coding agents are increasingly deployed in enterprise settings with delegated authority over connected systems. The agent skills interface—which allows dynamic loading of instruction/script folders to specialize agent behavior—represents an understudied attack surface. The authors aim to expose how adversarial actors can weaponize this interface by embedding malicious shell commands within benign-appearing natural-language skill files, thereby bypassing safety mechanisms.

Method: The authors make three contributions: (1) An adversarial skill-synthesis method employing six LLMs across four model families to transform 471 real-world shell commands into seemingly innocuous skills, producing a benchmark of 2,826 skills mapped to 11 MITRE ATT&CK tactics. (2) A reproducible evaluation pipeline incorporating run stratification, evidence anchoring, a refusal veto, and a deterministic declared-intent override mechanism, adjudicated by a three-judge LLM-as-a-judge panel validated against a blind human gold standard (Cohen's κ = 0.85). (3) Large-scale empirical characterization of two enterprise-grade agents (Gemini CLI and Qwen Code) across 5,629 completed runs.

Result: Gemini CLI was exploited in 95.5–96.1% of runs, and Qwen Code in 71.6–74.0% (ranging from raw majority vote to declared-intent-corrected estimates, both within the human gold standard). Exploitation rates were nearly invariant to the generating model used. Explicit safety recognition—where the agent identified and refused a malicious skill—occurred in only 1.99% of all runs.

Conclusion: Enterprises must assess and mitigate skill-interface risk before adopting autonomous coding agents. The near-total vulnerability of current enterprise-grade agents to adversarial skill injection, combined with negligible safety recognition rates, constitutes a critical security concern. The authors release their code and dataset to facilitate further research and mitigation development.

Abstract: Autonomous coding agents are increasingly embedded in enterprise software workflows with delegated authority over connected systems. Central to this architecture is the agent skills interface: folders of instructions and scripts that agents load dynamically to specialize their behavior. This interface also widens the attack surface, letting malicious shell commands hide within natural-language skill files. We make three contributions. First, an adversarial skill-synthesis method using six LLMs across four families to transform 471 real-world shell commands into benign-appearing skills, released as a benchmark of 2,826 skills mapped to 11 MITRE ATT&CK tactics. Second, a reproducible evaluation pipeline coupling run stratification, evidence anchoring, a refusal veto, and a deterministic declared-intent override with a three-judge LLM-as-a-judge panel, validated against a blind human gold standard (Cohen's kappa = 0.85). Third, a large-scale characterization of two enterprise-grade agents across 5,629 completed runs. Gemini CLI is exploited in 95.5-96.1% of runs and Qwen Code in 71.6-74.0% (raw majority vote to declared-intent-corrected estimate, both within the human gold standard), nearly invariant to the generating model. Explicit safety recognition occurs in only 1.99% of runs. Enterprises must assess and mitigate skill-interface risk before adopting coding agents. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/awsm-research/AgentJailbreak

</details>


### [223] [Improving Debugging in Verification-Aware Languages Through Automated Fault Localization: A Case Study in Dafny](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05399)
*Álvaro Silva,Isabel Amaral,João Pascoal Faria,Alexandra Mendes*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates automated fault localization for verification-aware languages (specifically Dafny), comparing state-based and counterexample-based approaches. Using a mutant dataset from DafnyBench with EXAM score evaluation, results show counterexample-based methods significantly outperform state-based localization. Structured single-trace ranking provides the largest improvement, while multi-trace aggregation further enhances robustness by increasing coverage and reducing solver-introduced path bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When verification fails in languages like Dafny, feedback is limited to the immediate error condition (e.g., a violated postcondition) rather than the root cause. While Dafny's counterexamples offer concrete execution traces, they expose only a single failing path per assertion failure, forcing developers to manually inspect the entire trace to locate faults. This motivates the need for automated fault localization techniques tailored to verification-aware languages.

Method: The authors compare two paradigms: (1) state-based localization, replicating AutoFix's "snapshot" methodology using inferred invariants and predicates to identify suspicious program states; and (2) counterexample-based localization, a family of techniques progressing from raw counterexample extraction, to structured single-trace ranking, to multi-trace aggregation. Evaluation uses MutDafny to generate mutants from DafnyBench, with effectiveness measured by the EXAM score.

Result: Counterexample-based approaches substantially outperform state-based localization. Structured ranking over a single trace yields the largest improvement over raw counterexample output. Multi-trace aggregation provides additional gains in robustness and debugging utility by increasing coverage and reducing path bias introduced by the solver.

Conclusion: Effective fault localization in verification-aware languages depends on both using counterexample information and on how that information is structured and diversified. The findings advocate for moving beyond single-trace counterexamples toward structured and aggregated approaches for practical debugging support.

Abstract: Verification-aware languages, like Dafny, integrate formal specifications directly into source code to enable static correctness checks. However, when verification fails, the feedback provided is often limited to the specific condition of the error, such as a violated postcondition, rather than the root cause of the fault. While Dafny's counterexample features provide concrete execution traces, these typically expose a single failing path per assertion failure, leaving the developer to manually look through the entire trace to locate the error.
  This paper investigates automated fault localization for verification-aware languages by comparing two paradigms: state-based and counterexample-based localization. Our state-based localization strategy replicates the ``snapshot'' methodology of AutoFix by inferring invariants and predicates to identify suspicious program states. The counterexample-based strategy consists of a family of techniques that progressively enrich the use of verifier output: from raw counterexample extraction, to structured single-trace ranking, and to multi-trace aggregation.
  To validate these methods, we present an evaluation framework using MutDafny to generate a diverse mutant dataset from DafnyBench and measure localization effectiveness using the EXAM score. Our results show that counterexample-based approaches substantially outperform state-based localization in this setting. Structured ranking over a single trace yields the largest improvement over raw counterexample output, while multi-trace aggregation provides additional gains in robustness and debugging utility by increasing coverage and reducing path bias introduced by the solver. These findings demonstrate that effective fault localization in verification-aware languages depends both on using counterexample information, and how that information is structured and diversified.

</details>


### [224] [Reasoning from Traces: Divergence-Guided Agentic Repair of WebAssembly Discrepancies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05521)
*Liyan Huang,Kaicheng Wang,Weihang Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: WasmMend is a system that automatically repairs functional discrepancies between WebAssembly and native binaries compiled from the same C/C++ source. It uses differential trace analysis to localize divergent functions, then employs LLM agents for root-cause reasoning and patch generation, achieving a 70% fix rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-compiling C/C++ code to Wasm and native binaries often produces runtime discrepancies due to library implementation differences or compiler bugs. These root causes are hidden beneath source code, making even advanced LLM-based repair agents ineffective. A dedicated, divergence-guided repair system is needed.

Method: WasmMend operates in two stages: (1) a novel differential trace analysis that identifies the specific function where Wasm and native executions first diverge, and (2) LLM agents guided by this localization to reason about root causes and generate patches that resolve the divergent behavior.

Result: On real-world C/C++ projects, WasmMend achieves a 70.0% fix rate, outperforming the agentic baseline (50.2%) and an LLM-based instrumentation-augmented approach (54.5%).

Conclusion: Divergence-guided reasoning significantly improves cross-platform repair. By converting undirected exploration into focused reasoning via differential trace analysis, WasmMend substantially outperforms existing LLM-based repair methods for Native-Wasm functional discrepancies.

Abstract: WebAssembly (Wasm) promises seamless reuse of C/C++ codebases as portable, fast, sandboxed binaries. In practice, however, this promise often falls short: recent studies show that cross-compiling the same C/C++ source to Wasm and native binaries frequently leads to runtime discrepancies, owing to library implementation differences or compiler bugs. Since the root causes lie in the platform-level runtime and are hidden beneath the source code, even state-of-the-art LLM-based repair agents often fail to fix these discrepancies. In this paper, we present WasmMend, the first system to automatically repair Native-Wasm functional discrepancies. WasmMend converts the undirected exploration to a focused reasoning task in two stages: First, a novel differential trace analysis approach localizes the function where Wasm and native executions initially diverge; guided by this localization, LLM agents then reason about the root causes and generate patches that eliminate the divergent behavior. Experiments on real-world C/C++ projects show that WasmMend achieves a fix rate of 70.0%, compared to 50.2% for the agentic baseline and 54.5\% for the approach augmented with repair-time LLM-based instrumentation, demonstrating the value of divergence-guided reasoning for cross-platform repair.

</details>


### [225] [Exploring Dependence, Overreliance, and Addiction Related Behaviors Associated with Large Language Model Use Among Software Engineers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05561)
*Ronnie de Souza Santos,Italo Santos,Matheus de Moraes Leça,Cleyton Magalhaes,Mairieli Wessel*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A survey of 119 software practitioners reveals that LLM use in professional development has become habitual, characterized primarily by functional dependence and overreliance patterns (e.g., prioritizing LLMs over documentation/peers), while addiction-related behaviors remain rare and mainly manifest as difficulty moderating use or emotional attachment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The widespread integration of LLMs into software engineering workflows has raised concerns about developers' dependence, overreliance, and potential addiction-related behaviors, yet empirical evidence on how these behavioral patterns manifest in professional practice remains limited.

Method: An exploratory survey of 119 software practitioners, analyzed using descriptive statistics and qualitative thematic analysis of open-ended responses.

Result: Participants reported functional dependence on LLMs for routine tasks due to productivity gains. Overreliance patterns emerged, including prioritizing LLMs over documentation and peer consultation, though verification behaviors persisted. Addiction-related behaviors were uncommon, limited to difficulty moderating use and emotional attachment rather than impaired control.

Conclusion: LLMs are becoming a habitual part of software engineering practice. While most use is functional, the findings underscore the need to promote appropriate reliance through trust calibration, professional judgment, and verification practices.

Abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) has changed how software engineers perform everyday development activities. While these systems provide substantial support for tasks such as code generation, debugging, and documentation, their increasing integration into professional workflows has also raised questions regarding developers' reliance on these tools and the emergence of dependence, overreliance, and addiction-related behaviors. This study investigates how software engineers experience the use of LLMs during professional software development, with attention to behavioral patterns associated with dependence, overreliance, and addiction-related behaviors. An exploratory survey was conducted with 119 software practitioners. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and qualitative thematic analysis of participants' open-ended responses. Participants primarily described functional dependence, with LLMs becoming integrated into routine software engineering activities because of the productivity and efficiency they provide. Responses also suggested patterns consistent with overreliance, particularly through prioritizing LLMs over documentation or peer consultation while continuing to verify generated outputs. Reports associated with addiction-related behaviors were less common and primarily reflected difficulty moderating use or emotional attachment to the technology rather than impaired control. The findings suggest that LLMs are becoming a habitual component of professional software engineering practice. While most reported use appears functional, the results indicate the importance of promoting appropriate reliance by supporting trust calibration, professional judgment, and verification throughout software development.

</details>


### [226] [JTA: Joint Testability Architecture for Scenario-Based Validation of Safety-Critical Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05594)
*Wenyao Xue,Jiandi Wang,Yichen Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: JTA treats the scenario, test system, and system under test as a unified analysis object, characterizing validation capability along controllability, observability, and isolability dimensions through a structured architecture of three domains, three bridges, and an iterative refinement loop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing testability research is artifact-centric and lacks architectural support for reasoning about the combined capability of the scenario, test system, and system under test. Safety-critical software validation requires critical scenario construction, evidence alignment, and actionable attribution of abnormal outcomes, which current approaches do not holistically address.

Method: JTA introduces three dimensions (controllability, observability, isolability), three domains, three bridges, and an analysis-design-evaluation-refinement loop. It employs scenario contracts, joint capability assessment, validation blind-spot identification, and bridge-oriented design actions to map capability gaps to concrete improvements. An illustrative case study applies JTA to ArduPilot failsafe validation.

Result: The ArduPilot case study reveals that link-loss scenarios are comparatively mature in validation capability, while state-estimation anomaly scenarios remain harder to validate due to weaker evidence alignment and attribution semantics.

Conclusion: JTA is not a replacement for existing testing or safety-analysis techniques; rather, it provides an architectural basis for modeling, designing, and assessing scenario-based validation in safety-critical software systems.

Abstract: Validation adequacy in safety-critical software depends on more than the system under test. Critical scenarios must be constructed under controlled conditions, execution evidence must be aligned into verdict-ready form, and abnormal outcomes must be attributable to actionable causes. Existing testability research remains largely artifact-centric and offers little architectural support for reasoning about the combined capability of the scenario, the test system, and the system under test. Joint Testability Architecture (JTA) addresses this gap by treating those three elements as a single object of analysis and design. It characterizes validation capability along three dimensions--controllability, observability, and isolability--and organizes them through three domains, three bridges, and an analysis-design-evaluation-refinement loop. JTA also introduces scenario contracts, joint capability assessment, validation blind-spot identification, and bridge-oriented design actions that map capability gaps to concrete improvements in control points, evidence organization, and attribution boundaries. An illustrative analysis of ArduPilot failsafe validation shows that link-loss scenarios are comparatively mature, whereas state-estimation anomaly scenarios remain harder to validate because evidence alignment and attribution semantics are weaker. JTA is not a replacement for existing testing or safety-analysis techniques; it provides an architectural basis for modeling, designing, and assessing scenario-based validation in safety-critical software.

</details>


### [227] [Towards Competence-Based Management for Open Source Software Projects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05599)
*Sabahat Younas,Márcia Moraes,Fabio Santos*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a competence assessment model for open-source software contributors using code metrics from their contributions to predict the competence level needed for tasks, aiming to identify and train replacements for disengaging core contributors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Core contributors disengaging from OSS projects poses a survival risk. Finding replacements is difficult and time-consuming due to insufficient knowledge about candidates' actual competences, which prior studies fail to adequately capture in terms of competence depth and levels.

Method: The authors collect code metrics related to source code from contributor contributions and propose a competence model that predicts the competence level required to solve specific tasks, enabling proper assessment of contributor capabilities.

Result: The paper provides a replication package containing code, data, and documentation, but the abstract does not specify quantitative experimental results or evaluation metrics.

Conclusion: Properly assessing contributors' competences through code-metric-based modeling can help identify and train candidates to replace core contributors, thereby mitigating the risk of project abandonment due to contributor disengagement.

Abstract: Contributors to Open Source Software (OSS) projects are vital to maintaining the health of both communities and projects. However, the number of projects experiencing core contributors' disengagement has increased to the point that it risks the projects' survival. Finding new contributors to replace the workforce is challenging and time-intensive due to several factors, including a lack of precise knowledge about potential candidates' competences, which may need to be confirmed through interviews and exams. Previous studies provided indications of the contributor's competences, although they lack depth in understanding competence levels, which can result in poor knowledge about the contributor's capabilities. To address this gap, we assess contributors' competence by collecting code metrics related to source code from contributions. We also propose a competence model able to predict the competence level required to solve tasks. By properly assessing contributors' competences, we can identify and train candidates to replace core contributors. Our replication package, including code, data, and documentation, is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21605122

</details>


### [228] [Keeping Models and Code in Sync: Roundtrip Engineering for Tactical Domain-Driven Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05612)
*Weixing Zhang,Mario Herb,Wai Chung Dorothy Cheng,Michael Wagner,Bowen Jiang,Tianhai Liu,Anne Koziolek*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: JDomInO is a bidirectional synchronization toolchain that keeps Java code and domain-driven design (DDD) models aligned through a shared metamodel, generating code from models (forward) and reconstructing models from code (reverse), with potential applications as a context layer for AI code assistants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In DDD practice, the shared vocabulary between domain model and code degrades over time as code changes outpace model updates, or model revisions fail to propagate to the codebase. This drift undermines the utility of DDD's ubiquitous language.

Method: JDomInO implements a bidirectional synchronization toolchain built on a shared metamodel covering 12 tactical DDD building block types. The forward path deterministically generates Java code structure from a domain model specification. The reverse path reconstructs a domain model from existing Java code through mapping logic. Validation used a Hotel Management scenario.

Result: The forward path was fully validated on a Hotel Management scenario covering all 12 building block types. The reverse path's mapping logic passed unit testing, with end-to-end validation still in progress. The authors also propose using JDomInO's structured domain model output as a precision context layer for AI code assistants to enforce aggregate boundaries and DDD semantics.

Conclusion: JDomInO demonstrates feasibility of bidirectional DDD model-code synchronization, with forward generation fully validated and reverse reconstruction partially validated. The structured domain model shows promise as a semantic enrichment layer for AI-assisted development in DDD contexts.

Abstract: Domain-Driven Design gives teams a shared vocabulary for complex business logic, but that vocabulary only stays useful as long as the model and the code agree with each other. In practice, they drift apart: code changes outpace the model, or model revisions never make it into the codebase. This paper presents JDomInO, a bidirectional synchronization toolchain for tactical DDD that keeps a Java codebase and its domain model connected through a shared metamodel, with the goal of keeping the two in sync as the system evolves. JDomInO generates Java code structure deterministically from a domain model (forward path) and reconstructs a domain model from existing Java code (reverse path). The forward path has been fully validated on a Hotel Management scenario covering all 12 building block types in the metamodel; the reverse path's mapping logic has passed unit testing, with end-to-end validation underway. We also outline how the structured domain model produced by JDomInO could serve as a precision context layer for AI code assistants, helping them respect aggregate boundaries and DDD semantics that raw source code alone does not convey.

</details>


### [229] [Agent-Based Test Assertion Generation via Diverse Perspective Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05822)
*Dong Wang,Qiaoyu Han,Lin Yang,Jianyi Zhou,Guangtai Liang,Junjie Chen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AssertMate is an agent-based framework for automated unit test assertion generation that combines static analysis, multi-perspective expected value prediction (code generation, RAG, and CoT reasoning), and an LLM-as-a-Judge selection mechanism, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art techniques like ChatAssert on the Defects4J benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based assertion generation approaches (e.g., ChatAssert) suffer from modest accuracy, heavy reliance on oversampling, and vulnerability to model randomness due to one-shot prompting. A more robust, multi-perspective approach is needed to improve reliability and quality.

Method: AssertMate consists of three components: (1) actual value construction using static analysis and type-aware heuristics to identify assertion targets; (2) multi-perspective expected value prediction employing three agents — code generation, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning; and (3) an LLM-as-a-Judge collaboration mechanism that selects the most appropriate assertion from the candidates.

Result: On Defects4J, AssertMate significantly outperforms SOTA techniques in compilation success, pass rates, and bug detection. Integration with EvoSuite yields superior mutation coverage and kill counts. Ablation studies confirm each component contributes significantly and complementarily.

Conclusion: Aggregating diverse perspectives through a multi-agent framework substantially enhances LLM-based assertion generation effectiveness. AssertMate demonstrates both strong standalone performance and practical utility when integrated with existing test generation tools like EvoSuite.

Abstract: Test assertions are critical elements of unit tests, serving as checkpoints to validate expected behavior and ensure software correctness. Numerous techniques have been proposed to automate assertion generation, with recent progress notably driven by large language models (LLMs). Despite the promise, existing approaches such as ChatAssert suffer from modest accuracy, heavy reliance on oversampling, and vulnerability to model randomness due to one-shot prompting. To address these limitations, we propose AssertMate, a novel agent-based assertion generation framework that enhances the quality and reliability of LLM-generated assertions through three key components: (1) actual value construction that identifies assertion targets via static analysis and type-aware heuristics; (2) multi-perspective expected value prediction using code generation, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning agents; and (3) an LLM-as-a-Judge collaboration mechanism to select the most appropriate assertion. Evaluation on the Defects4J benchmark demonstrates that AssertMate significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in compilation success and pass rates, along with substantially higher bug detection capabilities. Integration with EvoSuite further validates AssertMate's practicality, yielding superior mutation coverage and kill counts. Ablation studies reveal that each of the three components makes a significant and complementary contribution to the overall performance. This work affirms the great potential of aggregating diverse perspectives to enhance the effectiveness of LLM-based assertion generation.

</details>


### [230] [CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05886)
*Wuya Chen,Yihao yang,Yang Cao,Yue Lin*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CodeGrep is a 14B retrieval agent trained with GRPO to offload repository exploration from LLM coding agents. By issuing multi-turn parallel grep, glob, and read calls, it improves precision to 0.677 (vs. 0.375 for BM25) and reduces token costs by 19% and rounds by 15% on SWE-Bench Verified, while maintaining resolve rate. The paper also introduces CATM for mining supervision from agent trajectories and a Git-worktree RL environment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern LLM coding agents (Claude Code, OpenHands) waste substantial token budgets on repository exploration (grep, glob, view_file) rather than actual patching. A 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, with many calls spent on file discovery. Existing retrieval methods like BM25 lack sufficient precision (0.375) and can actually degrade downstream agent performance. The goal is to build a retrieval agent precise enough to reduce rollout cost without harming resolve rates.

Method: CodeGrep is a 14B retrieval model trained end-to-end with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It performs multi-turn parallel grep, glob, and read tool calls and returns candidate files to a frozen downstream coding agent. Supervision is mined from 67K open-source agent trajectories using CATM (Context-Aware Trajectory Mining). Training uses a custom Git-worktree environment for multi-turn agent RL. A key design choice: the efficiency signal is applied at the advantage layer rather than the reward layer, which reduces KL drift and translates cleanly into downstream efficiency gains.

Result: On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep achieves a 27.0% resolve rate vs. 25.8% for the no-retrieval baseline, with 15% fewer rounds and 19% fewer tokens on resolved instances. The paper identifies a precision threshold effect: BM25 (precision 0.375) degrades the agent, Jina (0.445) is neutral, and CodeGrep (0.677) crosses the threshold where retrieval begins reducing rollout cost. Applying efficiency signal at the advantage layer rather than reward layer reduces KL drift.

Conclusion: A dedicated retrieval agent (CodeGrep) can offload repository exploration from coding agents, improving efficiency without sacrificing resolve rate — but only if retrieval precision exceeds a critical threshold (~0.677). Training such an agent with GRPO, CATM-mined supervision, and advantage-layer efficiency signals is effective. The model, pipeline, RL environment, and evaluation harnesses will be open-sourced.

Abstract: Modern LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenHands share a common inefficiency: they spend much of their token budget finding the file to patch, rather than patching it. On SWE-Bench Verified, a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, with many calls spent on grep, glob, and view_file during repository exploration. We introduce CodeGrep, a 14B retrieval agent trained end-to-end with GRPO to issue multi-turn parallel grep, glob, and read tool calls and return candidate files to a frozen downstream coding agent.
  On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep preserves resolve rate while substantially improving efficiency: 27.0% versus 25.8% for the no-retrieval baseline, with 15% fewer rounds and 19% fewer tokens on resolved instances. Across retrievers, downstream utility follows a precision threshold: BM25 with precision 0.375 degrades the agent, Jina with precision 0.445 is neutral, and CodeGrep with precision 0.677 crosses the threshold at which retrieval begins to reduce rollout cost. To enable this study, we mine supervision from 67K open-source agent trajectories using CATM and build a Git-worktree environment for multi-turn agent RL. In our setting, applying the efficiency signal at the advantage layer rather than the reward layer reduces KL drift and translates cleanly into downstream efficiency. We will release the model, training pipeline, RL environment, and evaluation harnesses.

</details>


### [231] [Mapping the Emerging Curriculum for AI-Assisted Software Engineering via Syllabus Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05898)
*Francis Geng,Anshul Shah,Mia Chen,Paul Denny,Juho Leinonen,Bill Griswold,Gerald Soosai Raj,Leo Porter*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Analysis of 23 university syllabi on Generative AI in software engineering reveals how courses are being designed for AI-assisted development workflows, characterizing learning objectives, assessments, topics, and tools to guide future curriculum design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As Generative AI coding tools reshape professional software development, universities are creating courses to prepare students. There is a need to empirically understand how this emerging curricular area is being defined and to derive evidence-based guidance for future curriculum design.

Method: The authors analyzed 23 publicly available syllabi and course materials from upper-division, credit-bearing courses that explicitly address Generative AI in software engineering. They employed iterative qualitative coding to characterize courses across four dimensions: learning objectives, assessments, topics, and documented AI tools.

Result: The analysis revealed both commonalities and differences among the courses, providing a structured characterization of how AI-assisted development is currently being taught. Specific patterns in learning objectives, assessment methods, topical coverage, and tool selection were identified across institutions.

Conclusion: The findings offer a foundational empirical picture of this nascent curricular area, enabling researchers and educators to study existing approaches and design more informed future courses on Generative AI in software engineering.

Abstract: As Generative AI coding tools reshape professional software development, universities have begun designing courses to prepare students for AI-assisted development workflows. By analyzing the syllabi of these courses, we can gather empirical evidence about these courses, reveal how this emerging curricular area is being defined, and gain guidance for future curriculum design. We analyzed 23 publicly available syllabi and course materials of upper-division, credit-bearing courses that meet specific criteria, including explicitly addressing Generative AI in software engineering. Through iterative qualitative coding, we characterized courses' learning objectives, assessments, topics, and documented AI tools. Our analysis reveals commonalities and differences among these courses that allow researchers and educators to study and develop future courses.

</details>


### [232] [Escaping the Self-Repair Trap: Improving Test Oracle Generation via Dual-Context Awareness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05917)
*Kefan Li,Hongyue Yu,Yuan Yuan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LLM-based regression oracle generation suffers from the "Self-Repair Trap," where iterative repair optimizes execution success at the expense of fault-revealing capability. The authors propose DCAware, a non-iterative framework that uses structured static context and selectively retrieved dynamic states to produce high-quality oracles without feedback loops.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Iterative self-repair methods for regression-oracle completion optimize for execution success, but this proxy objective is misaligned with the true goal of generating fault-revealing oracles. This misalignment creates a feedback-driven degeneration ("Self-Repair Trap") where models converge on trivial assertions that pass easily but detect few faults.

Method: DCAware is a non-iterative framework that integrates structured static context (program structure, types, control flow) with selectively retrieved dynamic states (runtime values, execution traces). It avoids multi-round repair entirely, instead focusing on high signal-to-noise contextual grounding to enable precise oracle generation in a single pass.

Result: Extensive experiments using execution and mutation testing show DCAware consistently improves fault-revealing effectiveness while maintaining high execution success rates, outperforming prior iterative repair methods at substantially lower computational cost.

Conclusion: Improving contextual quality is more effective than adding iterative repair complexity for regression-oracle generation. The Self-Repair Trap reveals a fundamental limitation of feedback-driven repair pipelines in this setting.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for regression-oracle completion, where a test prefix is given and the current program version is treated as expected behavior. Recent approaches increasingly rely on iterative self-repair and execution feedback, but optimizing execution success does not necessarily yield strong fault-revealing oracles. This objective, widely adopted in repair-based methods, serves only as a proxy and may be misaligned with the true goal of oracle generation. Such misalignment biases the repair process, giving rise to a feedback-driven degeneration that we term the Self-Repair Trap, where iterative repair progressively drives models toward assertions that are easier to satisfy but less effective at detecting faults. To address this issue, we propose DCAware, a computationally efficient, non-iterative framework that prioritizes high signal-to-noise contextual grounding over multi-round repair. DCAware integrates structured static context with selectively retrieved dynamic states, enabling precise and robust oracle generation without iterative feedback loops. Extensive experiments based on execution and mutation testing show that DCAware consistently improves fault-revealing effectiveness while maintaining high execution success, outperforming prior methods with substantially lower computational cost. Our results suggest that improving contextual quality is more effective than adding iterative repair complexity in the studied regression-oracle setting.

</details>


### [233] [Expertise-Based Developer Assignment for Long-Term Software Components in Open-Source Projects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05919)
*Faheem Ullah,Babar Shah,William Shanks,Ayesha Mohsin,Abrar Ullah*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A web application that models developer expertise from Git commit history to automatically assign developers to tasks in new projects; caching improved speed by 9.86×, and 72.4% of tasks had the target developer in the top 10 recommendations (out of 47).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assigning tasks misaligned with a developer's expertise leads to slower completion and less maintainable code. Existing automated assignment research focuses on specific short-term jobs, but there is little work on matching developers to expertise-specific long-term components of a new project.

Method: The authors built a web application that models developer expertise from their prior Git commit history and uses this profile to automatically assign developers to optimal tasks within a new project. Server-side data caching was employed to improve performance.

Result: Server-side data caching improved worst-case speeds by a factor of 9.86. In evaluation, 72.4% of tasks had their correct target developer ranked within the top 10 recommendations out of a pool of 47 possible developers.

Conclusion: The proposed expertise-based assignment system shows strong recall (top-10 accuracy of 72.4%) and benefits significantly from caching optimizations, demonstrating feasibility for automating developer-to-task matching in new software projects.

Abstract: Open-source software development through GitHub has enabled countless software projects to be developed by developers from across the world. Assigning the right task to the right developer enables teams to work efficiently. Assigning a task which is not representative of a developer's expertise results in slower completion time and less maintainable code. Whilst much work has been done to automate this assignment for specific jobs, there is little work addressing the assignment of developers to expertise-specific long-term components of a new project. This paper produces a web application that models developers' expertise based on their previous Git commits and automatically assigns them to an optimal task within a new project. Testing showed that the system's speed varies depending on the back-end model used but server-side data caching improved worst-case speeds by a factor of 9.86. 72.4% of tasks had their target developer listed in the top 10, out of a possible 47.

</details>


### [234] [Sensor-Level Fault Diagnosis for Automotive Software Validation Using Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05921)
*Mohammad Abboush,Hamza Ouarrad,Andreas Rausch*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A two-phase framework uses small, fine-tuned open-source LLMs to detect and diagnose faults in automotive HIL sensor data. Anomalous recordings are first isolated via automated requirement checking, then described textually and fed to a 4-bit LoRA-adapted LLM that outputs fault locations with written justifications. The smallest model matched the largest at 81.6% accuracy on a gasoline-engine case study, with performance depending on convergence rather than parameter count.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automotive HIL validation generates massive multivariate sensor data that manual review cannot scale to handle. Existing threshold-based tools only flag deviations without diagnosis, while data-driven classifiers need large labeled datasets and produce opaque decisions that conflict with ISO 26262 traceability requirements. The paper asks whether instruction-tuned LLMs can provide data-efficient, interpretable fault detection and diagnosis suitable for safety-critical validation workflows.

Method: A two-phase pipeline: (1) Automated requirement checking on a dSPACE real-time platform isolates recordings violating safety requirements. (2) Only those anomalous recordings are analyzed — sliding windows extract statistical, relational, and contextual descriptors from signals, which are embedded in a fixed textual prompt. A 4-bit quantized, low-rank-adapted (LoRA) instruction-tuned LLM maps the description to a predicted fault location with a written justification. Four open-source model families (2B–8B parameters) are adapted and evaluated on a gasoline-engine case study with six injected fault classes.

Result: The smallest model matched the largest at 81.6% accuracy. A comparably sized model failed to converge entirely, showing that diagnostic competence under task-specific adaptation depends on convergence behavior, not parameter count. The entire adapt-and-evaluate cycle fits on a single commodity GPU accelerator.

Conclusion: Instruction-tuned LLMs with LoRA adaptation can serve as data-efficient, interpretable fault diagnosis engines for automotive HIL validation, offering traceable written justifications aligned with ISO 26262 requirements. Model size matters less than successful convergence, and the approach is computationally accessible on commodity hardware.

Abstract: The pre-series validation of automotive software on hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) platforms produces large volumes of multivariate sensor recordings whose assessment against functional safety requirements exceeds what manual review can sustain at campaign scale. Threshold-based tooling reports that a deviation has occurred but neither identifies its nature nor locates its source, while data-driven classifiers, although accurate, rely on large labelled datasets and return opaque decisions that sit uneasily with the traceability demanded by ISO 26262. This study examines whether open-source instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs), given a textual description of sensor behaviour, can serve as data-efficient and interpretable engines for fault detection and diagnosis inside the validation loop. A two-phase framework is proposed: automated requirement checking on a dSPACE real-time platform first isolates the recordings that violate a safety requirement, and only these are inspected, with sliding windows of the signals reduced to statistical, relational, and contextual descriptors, embedded in a fixed prompt, and mapped by a 4-bit low-rank-adapted LLM to a fault location accompanied by a written justification. Four model families ranging from two to eight billion parameters were adapted and tested on a gasoline-engine case study spanning six injected fault classes. The smallest model matched the largest at 81.6\% accuracy, whereas a comparably sized model failed to converge, indicating that diagnostic competence under task-specific adaptation follows convergence rather than parameter count, with the entire adapt-and-evaluate cycle fitting on a single commodity accelerator.

</details>


### [235] [AgentExecutor: Partial Code Execution via Agentic Context Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05959)
*Junkai Chen,Chengran Yang,Xing Hu,Zhenhao Li,Xin Xia,David Lo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgentExecutor is a multi-agent LLM framework for partial code execution that uses a three-phase design — environment preparation, iterative refinement via dynamic exploration, and prefix evolution via program synthesis — achieving up to 94% code coverage, outperforming Treefix by 19.9% while reducing execution time by up to 80.3% and cost by 56.6%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing partial code execution tools like LExecutor and Treefix are limited by restricted action spaces, insufficient feedback mechanisms, and rigid optimization strategies, hindering both effectiveness and efficiency when executing arbitrary code snippets with missing context and incomplete dependencies.

Method: AgentExecutor employs a multi-agent LLM framework with three phases: (1) execution environment preparation, (2) dynamic exploration with iterative refinement enabling diverse operations like creating resource files and resolving environment configurations, and (3) prefix evolution via program synthesis. It incorporates adaptive optimization strategies including coverage-guided context pruning and leverages agents capable of thinking, acting, and receiving iterative feedback to autonomously explore a richer action space.

Result: On Stack Overflow snippets and open-source project code datasets, AgentExecutor achieved up to 94% and 90% code coverage respectively, outperforming state-of-the-art Treefix by 19.9% and 13.8%. It also reduced execution time by up to 80.3% and execution cost by up to 56.6%.

Conclusion: AgentExecutor provides an effective and efficient solution for partial code execution, demonstrating that multi-agent LLM frameworks with adaptive optimization and richer action spaces can significantly advance the state of the art in dynamic program analysis.

Abstract: Executing code snippets is essential for dynamic program analysis, but it remains challenging to execute an arbitrary code snippet due to issues like missing context and incomplete dependencies. Existing approaches to partial code execution, such as LExecutor and Treefix, leverage the power of language models to infer missing information and enable execution. However, they suffer from (i) limited action spaces and feedback, and (ii) rigid optimization strategies, which restrict their effectiveness and efficiency. In this paper, we propose AgentExecutor, a novel multi-agent framework for partial code execution. Our approach introduces a three-phase design: execution environment preparation, dynamic exploration with iterative refinement, and prefix evolution via program synthesis. Supported by the power of LLM agents who can think, act, and get feedback iteratively, AgentExecutor is able to autonomously explore a richer action space, enabling diverse operations such as creating resource files and resolving environment configuration. Furthermore, it adopts adaptive optimization strategies, including coverage-guided context pruning and prefix evolution via program synthesis, to systematically improve the execution quality of partial code. We evaluate AgentExecutor on two widely used datasets comprising Stack Overflow snippets and open-source project code. The results show that AgentExecutor achieves up to 94% and 90% code coverage, outperforming the state-of-the-art approach Treefix by 19.9% and 13.8%, respectively. In addition, AgentExecutor significantly reduces execution time (by up to 80.3%) and cost (by up to 56.6%). These findings demonstrate that AgentExecutor provides an effective and efficient solution for partial code execution.

</details>


### [236] [LangChoiceBench: Measuring and Explaining Programming-Language Choice in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06041)
*Lukas Twist,Twm Stone,Helen Yannakoudakis,Jie M. Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Introduces LangChoiceBench, a benchmark for measuring LLMs' Python preference in project-level code generation. Evaluates 25 LLMs across 28 projects, finding heavy Python over-selection, low recommendation-implementation consistency, and identifies failure modes including "phantom evidence."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs exhibit strong Python preferences in project-level code generation, but no systematic benchmark exists to measure this across models. This gap hinders understanding of language selection bias and its downstream effects.

Method: LangChoiceBench comprises 28 projects spanning 7 software domains where Python is suboptimal. Researchers evaluated 25 diverse LLMs (both open-weight and proprietary), measuring Python preference, recommendation-implementation consistency, and language diversity. Additionally, 9,826 reasoning traces were analyzed to characterize decision-making patterns.

Result: Python is heavily over-selected even when it's a poor fit. Recommendation-implementation consistency is low. Smaller open-weight models exhibit stronger Python preference and lower language diversity. Most Python choices are automatic or ease-driven rather than requirements-driven. Two failure modes identified: "phantom evidence" (fabricating contextual support for Python) and code contradicting the model's own stated language choice.

Conclusion: LLMs systematically over-prefer Python, relying on superficial heuristics rather than project-appropriate reasoning. The identified failure modes (phantom evidence, self-contradiction) highlight brittleness in LLM decision-making for language selection at the project level.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to exhibit strong Python preferences when generating project-level code, but there is currently no systematic way to measure this behaviour across new models. To bridge this gap, we introduce LangChoiceBench, a project-level code-generation benchmark for measuring Python preference, recommendation-implementation consistency, and language diversity. LangChoiceBench covers 28 projects across seven software areas where Python is often a poor default. We evaluate 25 diverse LLMs and find that Python remains heavily over-selected, recommendation-implementation consistency is low, and smaller open-weight models generally show stronger Python preference and lower language diversity. We further analyse 9,826 reasoning traces and find that most Python choices are automatic or driven primarily by ease, rather than explicit consideration of project requirements. In a smaller but important set of cases, models fabricate contextual support for choosing Python - a failure mode we call phantom evidence - or produce code that contradicts the language selected in their own reasoning.

</details>


### [237] [In Terms of Explainability: Refining Requirements for Self-Explainable Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06049)
*Arno Leue,Akhila Bairy,Maike Schwammberger*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes unified definitions and a structured taxonomy for explainability in autonomous software-intensive systems, addressing the lack of universal standards by combining existing definitions and introducing explanation goodness/correctness as a key requirement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous and software-intensive systems are increasingly complex and responsible, yet no universally applicable definition or development guide for (self-)explainable systems exists. The EU AI Act and IEEE 7001-2021 recognize the need for explainability standards, motivating the authors to fill this gap.

Method: The authors analyze and synthesize existing definitions of explainability from the literature, derive a structured set of explainability requirements, and construct a taxonomy. They further propose incorporating "explanation goodness" (correctness of explanations) into the unified definitions.

Result: A unified definitional framework and a structured taxonomy of explainability requirements are produced. The taxonomy supports the development of formal standards and facilitates certification or auditing of explainable systems.

Conclusion: Establishing a uniform taxonomy for explainability is a crucial step toward formal standardization, certification, and auditing of (self-)explainable autonomous systems, directly supporting regulatory efforts like the EU AI Act and IEEE 7001-2021.

Abstract: Autonomous and software-intensive systems have been growing in occurrence, complexity, and assumed responsibility. Due to the high complexity of these systems, properties like transparency and explainability must be a focus of investigation. To date, no universally applicable definition and guide for the development of (self-)explainable systems exists. A need for explainability standards has already been recognized in the EU AI Act and the IEEE Transparency Standard 7001-2021. To address this need, we propose unified definitions in explainability based on an analysis and combination of existing definitions. Additionally, we present structured explainability requirements that are necessary to build (self-)explainable systems. By analysing the resulting taxonomy, we propose the incorporation of explanation goodness and thus correctness of explanations into the unified definitions. With our approach, we support the development of formal standards for (self-)explainable systems. Establishing such a uniform taxonomy also is a beneficial step towards certifying or auditing explainable systems.

</details>


### [238] [DCAS: Decoupling CLI Agent Scaffolding to Internalize Planning across Scaffolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06113)
*Kishanthan Thangarajah,Boyuan Chen,Ahmed E. Hassan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Fine-tuned CLI agents suffer cross-scaffold performance degradation because scaffold-specific planning conventions become baked into the model during training. The authors propose DCAS, a routing layer that enables cross-scaffold evaluation and planning-aware data collection, and show that decoupling planning from the scaffold yields consistent gains across non-training scaffolds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-source CLI-based software-engineering agents are almost exclusively trained on trajectory data from a single scaffold (OpenHands). Models fine-tuned on this data perform well under that scaffold but degrade significantly under others — a gap not present in base models. The authors hypothesize that planning structure (both explicit pre-execution plans and implicit structural conventions) is the scaffold-specific behavior responsible for this brittleness.

Method: The authors introduce DCAS (Decoupling CLI Agent Scaffolding), a backend-substitution interception layer that transparently routes API traffic between any CLI scaffold and any backend model without scaffold modification. DCAS enables cross-scaffold evaluation and planning-aware trajectory collection. They then conduct a controlled plan-source intervention to isolate the impact of planning quality and fine-tune a model on DCAS-collected planning-aware trajectories under a single scaffold to test cross-scaffold generalization.

Result: Planning quality is confirmed as a high-leverage component, with gains from improved planning exceeding the cross-scaffold performance drops. A model fine-tuned on DCAS-collected planning-aware trajectories from a single scaffold shows consistent improvement across non-training scaffolds. The two senses of planning (explicit and implicit) are empirically separable in training data.

Conclusion: Closing the cross-scaffold generalization gap requires moving planning from a fixed scaffold artifact to a learned model capability. DCAS provides both a diagnostic tool and a remedy by enabling planning-aware data collection that transfers across scaffolds.

Abstract: CLI-based software-engineering agents have matured rapidly, yet the open ecosystem has converged on a single training environment: trajectory datasets used to fine-tune open models are collected almost exclusively under OpenHands. Models fine-tuned on this data score well under OpenHands but degrade substantially when deployed under any non-training scaffold. Untrained base models do not show this divergence, indicating the gap is fine-tuning-induced and tied to the conventions of the training scaffold. We argue that a load-bearing scaffold-specific behavior is planning structure, in two senses this paper distinguishes: explicit planning, a pre-execution plan produced as a first-class artifact, and implicit planning, the structural conventions that shape execution throughout the agent loop. Under this hypothesis, closing the gap requires moving planning from a fixed scaffold artifact to a learned model capability. We introduce Decoupling CLI Agent Scaffolding (DCAS), a backend-substitution interception layer that routes API traffic between any CLI scaffold and any backend model without modifying the scaffold, enabling cross-scaffold evaluation and planning-aware trajectory collection. Using DCAS, a controlled plan-source intervention confirms planning quality is a high-leverage component, with gains exceeding the cross-scaffold drops we observe. A model fine-tuned on a small set of DCAS-collected planning-aware trajectories under a single scaffold gains consistently across non-training scaffolds, and the two senses of planning are empirically separable in training data.

</details>


### [239] [Learning Globally Reusable Skills for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06153)
*Chen Yang,Jiashuo Tian,Ziqi Wang,Xinyin Liu,Meiru Ye,Junjie Chen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: GSE is a globalized skill evolution framework for LLM agents that uses a Skill Relation Graph and cluster-based consolidation to jointly optimize skill compatibility and generalization, significantly outperforming existing methods on software engineering tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent skill evolution methods treat updates as isolated local changes, ignoring inter-skill relationships and producing overfitted updates that fail to generalize across tasks.

Method: GSE introduces three core components: (1) a Skill Relation Graph (SRG) that explicitly models and co-evolves inter-skill relationships; (2) cluster-based skill consolidation that abstracts reusable capabilities from local updates; and (3) replay-driven verification to prevent overfitting and behavioral regression.

Result: On bug-revealing test generation and false-positive bug report filtering, GSE outperforms existing evolution techniques with precision improvements of 6.1%–34.1% (test generation) and 15.4%–96.4% (filtering), recall gains of 31.8%–180.0% and 13.1%–19.8%, respectively. An industrial deployment yielded a 61.4% F1-score improvement.

Conclusion: GSE demonstrates that jointly optimizing skill compatibility and generalization via structured inter-skill modeling yields substantial and consistent gains across both academic benchmarks and real-world industrial deployment.

Abstract: Automated skill evolution enables Large Language Model (LLM) agents to continuously improve without expensive retraining. However, existing approaches typically treat skill evolution as a sequence of local updates, overlooking relationships among skills and often producing overfitted skill updates that fail to generalize across tasks. We propose GSE, a globalized skill evolution framework that jointly optimizes skill compatibility and skill generalization. To preserve consistency across the skill bank, GSE maintains a Skill Relation Graph (SRG) that explicitly models and co-evolves inter-skill relationships. To improve generalization, GSE performs cluster-based skill consolidation to abstract reusable capabilities from local updates and employs replay-driven verification to prevent overfitting and behavioral regressions. We evaluate GSE on two representative software engineering tasks: bug-revealing test generation and false-positive bug report filtering. Across two state-of-the-art coding agents, OpenHands and mini-SWE-agent, GSE consistently achieves the best precision, recall, and F1-score. Compared with existing evolution techniques, GSE improves precision and recall by 6.1%~34.1% and 31.8%~180.0% for test generation, and by 15.4%~96.4% and 13.1%~19.8% for false-positive filtering. Deployment on an internal industrial agent further yields a 61.4% improvement in F1-score, demonstrating the effectiveness and generalizability of GSE for evolving effective skills.

</details>


### [240] [Predicting Agile Success: The Critical Few Factors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06228)
*Ridewaan Hanslo,Maureen Tanner*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study identifies critical success factors (CSF) for Agile software development projects using a positivist approach and PLS-SEM analysis, resulting in a novel model to evaluate and measure Agile project success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite Agile projects outperforming traditional approaches, their overall success rate remains low, with many projects challenged or failed. This is attributed to insufficient rigorous evaluation against CSFs and contemporary success criteria, motivating the need to empirically identify factors that Agile practitioners perceive as critical to project success.

Method: A positivist (quantitative) research approach was employed. Data were collected from Agile practitioners and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS software to test hypotheses and identify statistically significant relationships between constructs representing CSFs and project success criteria.

Result: The analysis revealed that a subset of critical factors have statistically significant relationships with Agile project success. A novel evaluation model was developed based on these empirically validated CSFs.

Conclusion: The study contributes a validated model that practitioners and organizations can use to rigorously evaluate and measure Agile software development project success, addressing the gap between Agile adoption and consistently successful outcomes.

Abstract: While Agile projects are more successful than traditional software development project management approaches, their overall success rate remains relatively low, with a high percentage of projects still deemed challenged or failed. This low project success rate is attributed to projects not being rigorously evaluated against critical success factors (CSF) of Agile projects and contemporary project success criteria. To identify the CSF that contribute to Agile software development project success as perceived by Agile practitioners, this study used a positivist approach to investigate the CSF of Agile software development projects. PLS-SEM with SmartPLS was used to analyse the data and test the hypotheses to identify significant relationships between the constructs and project success criteria. This research found that a few critical factors significantly contribute to Agile project success. The study developed a novel model that can be used to evaluate and measure project success.

</details>


### [241] [Automatic Translation of Unstructured Requirements into Linear Temporal Logic through Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06287)
*Alexandra Newcomb,Omar Ochoa*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper evaluates six modern LLMs on translating unstructured natural language requirements into Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas using few-shot prompting. Across 15 requirements and 450 candidate formulas, results show LLMs can achieve practically significant performance without fine-tuning, suggesting viability as front-end assistants in semi-automated formalization workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Translating unstructured natural language requirements into formal specifications (specifically LTL) is a persistent bottleneck in requirements engineering for safety- and mission-critical systems. Manual formalization is labor-intensive and error-prone, yet mathematically precise specifications are essential for verification. The authors investigate whether contemporary off-the-shelf LLMs can help bridge this gap without requiring task-specific fine-tuning.

Method: Six modern LLMs were evaluated using a few-shot prompting strategy on a heterogeneous benchmark of 15 structurally varied requirements. For each requirement-model pair, five independent stochastic generations were collected, producing 450 candidate LTL formulas total. Performance was assessed via: (1) manual semantic evaluation of correctness, (2) pass@k metrics for k ∈ {1, 3, 5}, and (3) a self-consistency measure capturing syntactic reproducibility across trials. Additionally, natural language explanations and timeline-based visualizations were explored for interpretability.

Result: Current general-purpose LLMs can achieve practically significant performance on unstructured NL-to-LTL translation without task-specific fine-tuning. The pass@k analysis and self-consistency results indicate that aggregating multiple generations improves reliability, and model-produced explanations paired with timeline visualizations enhance understandability for non-experts.

Conclusion: Modern LLMs are becoming viable front-end assistants for semi-automated formalization workflows, reducing the manual effort required to produce LTL specifications from natural language requirements. The findings support integrating LLMs into requirements engineering toolchains, with complementary use of explanations and visualizations to bridge the expertise gap.

Abstract: Automatically translating unstructured natural language requirements into formal specifications remains a challenge in requirements engineering and formal methods, particularly for safety- and mission-critical systems whose verification depends on mathematically precise specifications. This paper evaluates whether contemporary off-the-shelf Large Language Models (LLMs) can help bridge this gap by generating Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas directly from unstructured requirements. The study examines six modern LLMs using a few-shot prompting strategy on a heterogeneous benchmark of 15 structurally varied requirements. Five independent generations were collected for each requirement-model pair, yielding 450 candidate LTL formulas in total. Performance was assessed through manual semantic evaluation, pass@k for k in {1, 3, 5}, and a self-consistency measure capturing syntactic reproducibility across stochastic trials. The results indicate that current general-purpose LLMs can achieve practically significant performance on the unstructured NL-to-LTL task without task-specific fine-tuning. The study also considers understandability for non-experts by pairing generated formulas with model-produced natural language explanations and discussing the complementary use of timeline-based LTL visualization. The findings suggest that modern LLMs are becoming viable front-end assistants for semi-automated formalization workflows.

</details>


### [242] [A Study of LLMs' Preferences for Libraries and Programming Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17181)
*Lukas Twist,Mark Harman,Don Syme,Joost Noppen,Helen Yannakoudakis,Detlef Nauck,Jie M. Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: First empirical study on LLMs' library and programming language preferences in code generation, revealing systematic overuse of popular libraries (e.g., NumPy in 45% of unnecessary cases) and a strong default bias toward Python (58% of cases where it is suboptimal), with Rust entirely unused. Highlights need for fine-tuning, data diversification, and benchmarks targeting selection fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing code generation evaluations focus narrowly on functional correctness and syntactic validity, completely overlooking how LLMs make critical design decisions—specifically which libraries and programming languages to use. This gap is significant because inappropriate library/language choices can lead to inefficiency, bloat, and suboptimal solutions in real-world software engineering.

Method: The authors conducted an empirical study across eight diverse LLMs, systematically analyzing their code generation outputs to quantify (1) library usage patterns, specifically measuring unnecessary overuse of popular libraries like NumPy relative to ground-truth solutions, and (2) programming language preferences, particularly in high-performance project initialization tasks where Python is not the optimal choice.

Result: LLMs exhibit a strong overuse bias toward widely adopted libraries: in up to 45% of cases, NumPy usage was unnecessary and deviated from ground-truth solutions. A significant default preference for Python was observed: even for high-performance tasks where Python is suboptimal, it remained the dominant choice in 58% of cases, while Rust was never selected.

Conclusion: LLMs prioritize familiarity and popularity over task-specific optimality when making library and language choices. This underscores the urgent need for targeted fine-tuning strategies, training data diversification, and new evaluation benchmarks that explicitly measure fidelity in language and library selection.

Abstract: Despite the rapid progress of large language models (LLMs) in code generation, existing evaluations focus on functional correctness or syntactic validity, overlooking how LLMs make critical design choices such as which library or programming language to use. To fill this gap, we perform the first empirical study of LLMs' preferences for libraries and programming languages when generating code, covering eight diverse LLMs. We observe a strong tendency to overuse widely adopted libraries such as NumPy; in up to 45% of cases, this usage is not required and deviates from the ground-truth solutions. The LLMs we study also show a significant preference toward Python as their default language. For high-performance project initialisation tasks where Python is not the optimal language, it remains the dominant choice in 58% of cases, and Rust is not used once. These results highlight how LLMs prioritise familiarity and popularity over suitability and task-specific optimality; underscoring the need for targeted fine-tuning, data diversification, and evaluation benchmarks that explicitly measure language and library selection fidelity.

</details>

### [243] [MS-MLB: An Open Machine Learning Benchmark for Blood-Based MS Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05196)
*Adam Simson,Ankush Dutta,Quang Bui*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MS-MLB is a reproducible open benchmark for classifying Multiple Sclerosis versus healthy controls from whole blood RNA expression data (GSE17048). It provides a standardized, leakage-controlled pipeline with nested cross-validation and holdout evaluation. Gradient Boosting achieved the top MS Research Score of 93.83 (AUC-ROC 0.989). The benchmark includes an external model submission pathway and is intended for research comparison only, not clinical diagnosis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Blood RNA expression data may harbor disease-associated immune signals for MS, but no standardized, reproducible benchmark exists for comparing ML methods on this task. The authors address the gap between prior heterogeneous studies and the need for a fair, leakage-controlled evaluation framework that researchers can rerun without reconfiguration, while explicitly clarifying that such classifiers cannot replace clinical diagnosis.

Method: MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression cohort converted into a binary MS vs. healthy control classification task. The pipeline includes nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC and precision-recall analysis, calibration measurement (Brier score), and an exploratory composite metric called the MS Research Score. Multiple algorithms are evaluated under a shared, leakage-controlled framework with a documented external model submission pathway.

Result: Gradient Boosting ranked first on the holdout set with an MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, F1 score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050.

Conclusion: MS-MLB provides the first open, reproducible benchmark for MS vs. healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA data with a built-in external submission pathway. The framework enables fair algorithmic comparison for research purposes but has not been clinically validated and should not be used for diagnosis.

Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed through clinical assessment, magnetic resonance imaging, laboratory evidence when appropriate, and exclusion of better explanations. Blood RNA expression data may contain disease associated immune signal, but a blood RNA classifier cannot be treated as a replacement for clinical diagnosis. This paper presents MS-MLB (Multiple Sclerosis Machine Learning Benchmark), a reproducible open benchmark for machine learning based MS research classification from whole blood RNA expression data. MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 cohort, converts it into an MS versus healthy control task, and evaluates multiple algorithms under a shared, leakage controlled pipeline that a researcher can rerun without reconfiguring the evaluation. The evaluation includes nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC and precision recall analysis, calibration measurement, and an exploratory MS Research Score. In the final benchmark summary, Gradient Boosting ranked first by MS Research Score on the holdout set, with an MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, $F_{1}$ score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050. Prior studies have applied machine learning to MS blood transcriptomic data, including PBMC stage classification and whole blood diagnostic signature modeling. The contribution here is different and narrower. To our knowledge, MS-MLB is the first open benchmark focused on MS versus healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression data with a documented external model submission pathway built into the framework. The score is intended for research comparison only and has not been clinically validated. The benchmark is accessible here: https://github.com/duckyquang/MS-MLB.

</details>


### [244] [IFlowNets: Extending Generative Samplers to Learn Strategies in Incomplete Information Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05422)
*Conor M. Artman,Nicholas Di,Scott Perkins*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IFlowNets extends generative flow networks to incomplete information games, fixing invalid density constraints from prior work (AFlowNets), and shows comparable or better performance than OSMCCFR and RL baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work (AFlowNets) applied generative flow networks to complete information games, but the constraints used are inadmissible for incomplete information settings—yielding invalid player strategy densities and training objectives. A proper generalization is needed.

Method: The authors propose IFlowNets, a generalization of AFlowNets that establishes valid density constraints and training objectives for incomplete information games. They prove the inadmissibility of prior constraints and demonstrate that IFlowNets strictly generalizes AFlowNets.

Result: In preliminary experiments on three standard game environments, IFlowNets perform comparably to or better than Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret (OSMCCFR) and standard RL-based methods in both performance and computational speed.

Conclusion: IFlowNets successfully extends generative flow networks to incomplete information games, resolving theoretical issues in prior work, and demonstrates competitive empirical performance against established baselines.

Abstract: While many algorithms blend reinforcement learning (RL) with counterfactual regret (CFR) methods to leverage tradeoffs in computational speed and performance, there are fewer investigations into generative sampling frameworks in game theoretic applications in incomplete information games. We extend a generative flow network framework, Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets), to incomplete information games, called Information Flow Networks (IFNs). We prove that previously established constraints for generative flow networks in complete information games are inadmissible for obtaining valid densities (corresponding to player strategies) and a valid training objective. We show that our proposed generalization, IFlowNets, alleviates this issue and strictly generalizes AFlowNets. In preliminary results for three standard game environments, IFlowNets perform comparably to or better than Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret (OSMCCFR) and standard RL-based methods in performance and speed.

</details>


### [245] [When Do Corrective Features Help? An Agent for Corrective Feature Discovery on Black-Box Forecasters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05207)
*Fangxin Wang,Ziyi Zhang,Diyi Zhuang,Langzhou He,Shiyu Wang,Baichuan Mo,Philip S. Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRAFTER proposes a post-hoc correction framework that mines interpretable features from a frozen forecaster's residuals using both compositional search and LLM-generated features, then applies a validation-gated corrector. It consistently outperforms dedicated feature-engineering systems across diverse datasets and backbones, doubling correction gains and reducing weak backbone error by up to 27%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frozen pretrained forecasters exhibit structured, recurring failures that are expensive to fix via fine-tuning. The core insight is that prior feature engineering models the data-generating process, whereas correcting a frozen model requires modeling the model-failure process — a fundamentally different objective that existing systems are not designed for.

Method: CRAFTER uses two complementary feature generators: (1) compositional search over raw input channels, and (2) an LLM that proposes named feature combinations, binary flags, and short executable code. A validation-grounded gate accepts or rejects every candidate irrespective of its source. A validation-selected corrector then applies the accepted features or leaves the forecast unchanged. This source-agnostic design also serves as an instrumentation framework for attributing forecast improvements to specific feature sources.
