Result: Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER surpasses every dedicated feature-engineering system at every feature budget. It roughly doubles the improvement achieved by a corrector alone and reduces the error of the weakest backbones by up to 27%. Gains are robust across different LLM backends and persist even when applied on top of fine-tuned backbones.

Conclusion: Corrective feature discovery — modeling the failure process rather than the data-generating process — is a highly effective strategy for post-hoc forecast correction. The source-agnostic, validation-gated architecture of CRAFTER provides both a practical tool for improving frozen forecasters and a principled instrument for ablating the contribution of different feature sources.

Abstract: Frozen pretrained forecasters often fail in structured, recurring ways that are costly to repair through fine-tuning. We study corrective feature discovery: mining interpretable features of a frozen forecaster's residual to drive a lightweight post-hoc corrector. Prior automated feature engineering models the data-generating process; corrective features instead model the model-failure process. We present CRAFTER (Corrective Residual Agent with Feature-based Temporal Exploration and Reasoning), which keeps the backbone frozen and mines its residual with two complementary generators: a compositional search over the raw input channels, and a large language model (LLM) that proposes named feature combinations, binary flags, and short executable code. A single validation-grounded gate accepts or rejects every candidate regardless of its origin, and a validation-selected corrector applies the accepted features or leaves the forecast unchanged. This source-agnostic pipeline also allows prior feature-engineering systems to be evaluated under identical conditions, making CRAFTER an instrument for attributing forecast improvements to the feature source alone. Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER surpasses every dedicated feature-engineering system at every feature budget, roughly doubling the improvement achieved by the corrector alone and reducing the error of the weakest backbones by up to 27%. These gains are robust across different LLM backends and persist even when applied on top of fine-tuned backbones.

</details>


### [246] [Hybrid-Adaptive Thread Tuning to Mitigate Simulation Execution Bottlenecks in High-Performance Reinforcement Learning Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06025)
*Jiming Su,Hantao Hua,Lujia Yin,Yiping Yao,Feng Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoThread is a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method that uses a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) predictor combined with an M/M/1 queueing model to dynamically optimize thread counts for RL inference under simulation bottlenecks, achieving up to 1.8× throughput gains and 83.8% execution time reduction over state-of-the-art methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In simulation-in-the-loop RL systems, simulator-side execution imposes significant overhead. Workloads are highly dynamic, and existing multithreaded strategies fail to adapt thread configurations before or during execution, leading to resource contention, scheduling inefficiency, and degraded throughput. The empirical insight that the ratio of task execution time to scheduling time governs optimal thread count drives the need for an adaptive solution.

Method: AutoThread employs a three-component approach: (1) a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) serving as a thread-count predictor, (2) a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model that constrains and guides the PINO predictions for fast, accurate estimation under dynamic workloads, and (3) load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for residual prediction errors and iteratively refine resource allocation during runtime.

Result: AutoThread achieves an average speedup improvement of 18.4% over static thread-tuning strategies. It delivers 1.7× and 1.8× the average throughput of XGBoost and Reinforcer, respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8% compared with state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: By combining physics-informed neural operators with queueing-theoretic constraints and online fine-tuning, AutoThread effectively mitigates simulation bottlenecks in RL inference. The method demonstrates substantial throughput and latency improvements over both static and learning-based baselines, establishing a practical framework for adaptive thread management in dynamic simulation-in-the-loop environments.

Abstract: In simulation-in-the-loop decision-making systems, reinforcement learning (RL) inference is often constrained by simulator-side execution overhead, where workloads are highly dynamic and sensitive to runtime thread configurations. Existing multithreaded strategies struggle to match thread resources before or during execution, causing resource contention, scheduling overhead, and reduced throughput. Through empirical analysis, we identify the ratio of task execution time to scheduling time as the key factor determining the optimal thread count. Building on this insight, we propose AutoThread, a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method for mitigating simulation bottlenecks in RL inference. AutoThread employs a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) as a thread-count predictor and incorporates a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model to constrain and guide prediction, enabling fast and accurate estimation under dynamic workloads. It further performs load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for prediction errors and refine resource allocation. Experiments show that AutoThread improves average speedup by 18.4\% over static strategies, achieves average throughput of 1.7x and 1.8x that of XGBoost and Reinforcer, respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8\% compared with state-of-the-art methods. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/suchenjm/AutoThread.

</details>


### [247] [PPDL: LLM-Based Flows as Probabilistic Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05234)
*Louis Mandel,Guillaume Baudart,Mandana Vaziri,Martin Hirzel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a probabilistic programming language for building LLM-based application flows, allowing developers to quantify and propagate uncertainty across multi-step LLM calls and experiment with inference scaling techniques without extra code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs produce outputs with unclear confidence, and this uncertainty compounds in multi-call flows, undermining trust in LLM-based applications. Existing approaches require significant additional code to handle uncertainty and inference scaling.

Method: Introduce a probabilistic language that natively integrates uncertainty quantification and propagation into the programming model for LLM flows. The language supports inference scaling experimentation declaratively within the flow logic, requiring no extra boilerplate code.

Result: An experimental study demonstrates the uncertainty quantification and propagation capabilities. A case study applies the approach to build a theorem-proving agent for the Rocq theorem prover.

Conclusion: The probabilistic programming approach effectively addresses uncertainty management in LLM-based flows, improving reliability and trustworthiness without burdening developers with additional implementation overhead.

Abstract: Building reliable applications that leverage large language models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge. While LLMs offer impressive capabilities across diverse tasks, their outputs often lack accuracy and provide no clear measure of confidence. This uncertainty compounds in flows of multiple calls to LLMs and other tools, making it difficult for developers and end-users to trust the results. This paper introduces a probabilistic language for programming LLM-based flows. It enables developers to quantify and propagate uncertainty throughout the application's flow, and experiment with different inference scaling techniques without adding a single line of code beyond the flow's logic. We present an experimental study to demonstrate this capability, and a case study building a theorem proving agent for the Rocq theorem prover.

</details>


### [248] [Does Latent Context Help? A Controlled Evaluation of Inverse Reinforcement Learning in Arctic Shipping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06105)
*Vaishnav Vaidheeswaran,Dilith Jayakody,Biruk Ambaw,Jaswanth Kumar,Md Mahbub Alam,Gabriel Spadon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In a controlled study of Arctic shipping navigation, a nonlinear inverse reinforcement learning model improved performance by 50.9% over a linear baseline, but adding latent vessel-specific context reduced performance by 16.5%. Apparent behavioral variation was explained by observable route and environmental features rather than hidden vessel preferences, challenging the value of latent-context meta-IRL and arguing for simpler, more interpretable reward models in safety-critical domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-assisted Arctic navigation requires interpretable and robust reward models. While meta-IRL methods using latent context variables promise to capture heterogeneous preferences, it is unclear whether these latent variables recover genuinely hidden preferences or merely re-encode observable state information. This uncertainty threatens the trustworthiness and reliability of AI deployment in safety-critical maritime operations.

Method: The authors conducted a controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels spanning nine Arctic shipping seasons. They compared three model architectures: a linear shared reward model, a nonlinear shared reward model, and a latent-context model built on the same nonlinear architecture. Evaluation included behavioral analysis, context probes, and a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation to determine whether vessel-specific variation reflects hidden preferences or observable conditions. Models were assessed across multiple metrics: held-out likelihood, predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer.

Result: The nonlinear reward model improved held-out likelihood by 50.9% over the linear baseline. However, adding vessel-specific latent context reduced performance by 16.5% relative to the nonlinear shared model. Feature-hiding ablation and context probes revealed that apparent vessel-level variation is predominantly explained by observable route and environmental conditions rather than hidden vessel-specific factors. Different evaluation metrics produced divergent model rankings, demonstrating that no single metric suffices to evaluate learned reward quality.

Conclusion: Before introducing per-vessel latent context in meta-IRL, researchers should test whether observable features already explain behavioral variation. Favoring simpler, more interpretable models without unnecessary latent variables supports trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains like Arctic navigation.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted navigation can help Arctic shipping adapt to rapidly changing sea-ice conditions, but reliable deployment requires reward models that are interpretable and robust to changing environments. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a framework for recovering such rewards from vessel trajectories, while recent meta-IRL methods introduce latent context variables to capture behavioral heterogeneity. However, it remains unclear whether these latent representations recover genuinely hidden preferences or simply re-encode information already available in the observed state. We conduct a controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels across nine Arctic shipping seasons, comparing a linear shared reward, a nonlinear shared reward, and a latent-context model built on the same nonlinear architecture. The nonlinear reward improves held-out likelihood by 50.9% over the linear baseline, whereas adding vessel-specific latent context reduces performance by 16.5%. Behavioral analysis, context probes, and a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation show that apparent vessel-level variation is largely explained by observable route and environmental conditions rather than hidden vessel-specific factors. Moreover, predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer yield different model rankings, demonstrating that no single metric is sufficient to evaluate learned rewards. These findings motivate testing whether the observed route, environmental, and vessel features already explain behavioral variation before adding per-vessel latent context. This supports more trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains.

</details>


### [249] [Decoupling Perception from Description: Computation-Grounded Representation Alignment between Multivariate Time Series and Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05238)
*Xinran Feng,Yi Xie,Chao Zhang,Ruikun Li,Wanyun Ling,Ziyue Li,Chenxi Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies a self-supervision trap in training time-series-language models: LLMs are used as labelers but can only describe what they already perceive, creating a ceiling on data quality. This is exacerbated in multivariate settings where cross-variable patterns matter most but labeling LLMs are least capable. The authors resolve this trilemma (reliable, realistic, scalable) by decoupling perception from description—deterministic code computes statistics from real multivariate series, and the LLM verbalizes them. Their 4B-parameter model, CGTime, outperforms much larger models on multivariate understanding tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches to training multimodal time-series-language models suffer from a self-supervision trap: LLMs are tasked with both perceiving and describing time series, so label quality is bounded by the model's own perceptual limits. This problem is compounded in the multivariate setting, where meaningful patterns (cross-channel correlation, lead-lag relationships, co-occurring anomalies) are most salient but also where labeling LLMs are least reliable. The result is a trilemma—existing methods can be reliable, realistic, or scalable, but never all three simultaneously.

Method: The authors propose decoupling perception from description. Deterministic computational routines extract a comprehensive set of statistics from real, open-source multivariate time series. These precomputed facts serve as ground-truth perceptual features. An LLM is then trained to generate natural language descriptions that verbalize these precomputed statistics, grounding language generation in verified numerical computation rather than unreliable model perception. This yields CGTime, a 4B-parameter computation-grounded time-series-language model.

Result: CGTime achieves the best multivariate fact score on the held-out benchmark: 0.283 versus 0.173 (GPT-4o-mini) and 0.203 (GPT-5.4-nano). This superiority is statistically significant, surviving Holm-corrected paired significance tests against every baseline. CGTime also generates captions with more verifiable numerical facts stated accurately and covers a broader range of statistical properties than competing models.

Conclusion: Decoupling perception (via deterministic computation) from description (via LLM verbalization) resolves the self-supervision trap in time-series-language modeling. The resulting CGTime model demonstrates that a relatively small (4B-parameter), computation-grounded model can significantly outperform much larger general-purpose models on multivariate time series understanding, offering a scalable and reliable path forward.

Abstract: Training multimodal models to align time series with language runs into a self-supervision trap. The usual recipe asks an LLM to read a series and write a description, so label quality is capped by the perceptual skill the model is supposed to learn. The data can never teach more than the labeler already knows. A second gap makes this worse: most datasets use a single variable, but the patterns that matter (cross-channel correlation, lead-lag structure, co-occurring anomalies) appear only with several variables, right where the labeling LLM's limits are most exposed. These two problems create a trilemma: existing methods are reliable, realistic, or scalable, but none achieves all three. We resolve this by decoupling perception from description. Deterministic code computes a set of statistics from real, open-source multivariate series; the LLM verbalizes those precomputed facts. Perception, which LLMs do poorly, is handled by computation, while the LLM handles expression. This produces CGTime, our 4B-parameter computation-grounded time-series-language model. CGTime outperforms far larger general-purpose models on multivariate understanding tasks: it attains the best multivariate fact score on our held-out benchmark (0.283 vs. 0.173 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.203 for GPT-5.4-nano), a gap that survives Holm-corrected paired significance tests against every baseline. It also states verifiable numerical facts in generated captions more accurately and covers a broader range of statistical properties.

</details>


### [250] [Disentangling 3D Modeling from Spatial Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05242)
*Haoze Sun,Jiequan Cui,Qingshan Xu,Richang Hong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DiSR framework disentangles 3D perception from reasoning by using off-the-shelf perception models to generate structured 3D evidence, then fine-tuning an LLM with LoRA to reason over that explicit geometry — achieving competitive spatial reasoning without large-scale end-to-end training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing spatial reasoning approaches jointly learn implicit 3D perception and reasoning via large-scale training, which is computationally expensive and opaque. The authors observe that modern perception models already excel at estimating continuous 3D geometry, while LLMs are naturally strong at compositional, symbolic reasoning. This motivates a clean separation of these two capabilities.

Method: The Disentangled Spatial Reasoner (DiSR) uses off-the-shelf expert perception models to reconstruct the physical world into structured 3D evidence (explicit geometric representations). A large language model is then fine-tuned with LoRA to perform reasoning directly over this explicit geometric evidence, without requiring large-scale 3D VQA training or complex tool-use policies.

Result: DiSR achieves competitive performance on popular spatial reasoning benchmarks, matching or approaching end-to-end models, while offering superior interpretability, modularity, and computational efficiency.

Conclusion: Explicitly separating perception from reasoning is a scalable and effective alternative to end-to-end modeling for spatial intelligence, enabling modular systems that leverage the complementary strengths of specialized perception models and LLMs.

Abstract: In this work, we explore an alternative paradigm for spatial reasoning by explicitly disentangling 3D perception from reasoning, rather than jointly acquiring implicit 3D perception and reasoning through large-scale training. Our key observation is that modern perception models excel at estimating continuous 3D geometry, whereas large language models (LLMs) are particularly effective at compositional and symbolic reasoning. Motivated by these complementary strengths, we propose the Disentangled Spatial Reasoner (DiSR), a simple yet effective framework that reconstructs the physical world into structured 3D evidence using off-the-shelf expert perception models and fine-tunes an LLM with LoRA to perform reasoning solely over this explicit geometric evidence. Without large-scale 3D VQA training or complex tool-use policies, DiSR achieves competitive performance on popular spatial reasoning benchmarks. Beyond its strong performance, DiSR offers improved interpretability, modularity, and computational efficiency, demonstrating that explicit separation of perception and reasoning is a scalable and effective alternative paradigm to end-to-end modeling for spatial intelligence.

</details>


### [251] [Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05571)
*Mohammad Asadi,Soheil Hor,Bardiya Akhbari,Jack W. O'Sullivan,Tahoura Nedaee,Layne C. Price,Raviteja Anantha,Euan Ashley,Ehsan Adeli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Align-RAG is a training-free method that aligns retrieved past-future windows to a frozen Time Series Foundation Model via amplitude rescaling and phase shifting, outperforming trained retrieval adapters and establishing closed-form alignment as a new default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior retrieval-augmented forecasting methods assume frozen TSFMs cannot dynamically incorporate retrieved context and therefore require learned fusion modules (trained adapters). The authors challenge this assumption, hypothesizing that frozen backbones can already support in-context use of retrievals if the retrieved examples are properly aligned before being fed into the model.

Method: Align-RAG applies two closed-form operations to each retrieved past-future window before it enters the frozen backbone's context: (1) per-pair amplitude rescaling to match the query's scale, and (2) integer-lag phase shifting to temporally align the retrieved pattern with the query. No learned parameters are involved. The method is evaluated by comparing the frozen backbone's prediction shift under aligned demonstrations to the closed-form ridge prediction shift on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control to rule out simple futures-averaging.

Result: Align-RAG outperforms the state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter on Chronos-Bolt across all seven benchmark datasets (average -3.75% MSE). On four additional frozen TSFMs with diverse architectures, it improves zero-shot MSE by 2.5% to 13.7% per backbone without any per-backbone tuning. Analysis shows aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts that track a closed-form ridge predictor, confirming frozen TSFMs can dynamically use retrievals in-context.

Conclusion: Frozen TSFMs already possess the capacity for dynamic in-context use of retrievals; learned fusion modules are unnecessary for this purpose. Closed-form alignment (Align-RAG) should serve as the default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before any fusion module is trained.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented forecasting promises to adapt frozen Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) to new domains without fine-tuning, but recent methods typically rely on learned fusion modules, i.e., trained adapters that merge retrieved examples into the backbone's forecast, based on the assumption that frozen backbones cannot dynamically incorporate retrieved context on their own. We show this assumption is unnecessary. We introduce Align-RAG, a training-free method that applies a closed-form per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift to retrieved past-future windows before they enter a frozen backbone's context. With no learned parameters, Align-RAG outperforms the state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter on a frozen Chronos-Bolt on all seven datasets of the standard benchmark (avg -3.75% MSE), showing that the gains previously attributed to learned fusion are recoverable without any training. Align-RAG further improves zero-shot MSE on four additional frozen TSFMs with various architectures by 2.5% to 13.7% per backbone with no per-backbone tuning. To probe why alignment helps, we compare the frozen backbone's prediction shift under aligned demonstrations to the closed-form ridge prediction shift on the same pairs. We find that aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts that track a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control ruling out a futures-averaging account. Together, these results indicate that frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals, and that closed-form alignment should be the default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before any fusion module is trained. Code available at: https://github.com/masadi-99/align-rag

</details>


### [252] [Marginal Matching Does Not License Factorized Sampling: Auditing Conditional Style Leakage in Factorized Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05243)
*Duong Bach,Hai Nguyen Hong,Cuong Do*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Factorized generative models that only match the marginal distribution of a style variable to a Gaussian prior fail to ensure class independence. The paper proves that marginal matching leaves class-conditional distributions unconstrained, enabling style latents to remain highly predictive of labels. Experiments show near-zero global MMD coexisting with 74–100% linear probe accuracy, demonstrating that marginal divergence metrics cannot certify style-class independence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many factorized generative models claim that matching the marginal distribution of a style latent z_s to a Gaussian prior ensures independence from class information. The authors challenge this widespread interpretation, arguing that marginal alignment is insufficient to guarantee the intended factorization between style and class, and that commonly reported metrics do not actually verify the property they are claimed to certify.

Method: The authors derive an exact decomposition showing that marginal matching is only one of four conditions needed for factorized sampling. They empirically evaluate a case-study model and four baselines, measuring global MMD, linear probe accuracy, clustering accuracy, and externally evaluated class-conditional generation. Six independent perturbations (model capacity, curriculum, prior geometry, supervision, across two datasets) are tested, along with four mitigation strategies and two post-hoc correction approaches (conditional prior and empirical style bank).

Result: Models achieve near-zero global MMD while linear probes recover labels with 74–100% accuracy. The case-study model reaches 99.15% clustering accuracy but only 16% success on class-conditional generation. Leakage persists under all six perturbations. Mitigation strategies reduce probe accuracy to 21–46% without improving within-class dependence. A post-hoc conditional prior reaches 0.97 class generation on MNIST but only 0.41 on CIFAR-10; an empirical style bank achieves 0.88 on CIFAR-10.

Conclusion: No divergence computed solely on the marginal distribution of the style latent can certify independence from class labels. Reporting marginal statistics alone does not verify the factorization property commonly claimed in factorized generative models, and the community should adopt class-conditional evaluation metrics to properly validate style-class disentanglement.

Abstract: Factorized generative models commonly regularize a latent style variable z_s by matching its marginal distribution to a fixed Gaussian prior and interpret this as evidence that the style representation is independent of class information. We show that this interpretation is incorrect. Matching only the marginal distribution places no constraint on the class-conditional distributions, allowing the latent style to remain highly predictive of the label despite appearing perfectly Gaussian in aggregate. We derive an exact decomposition showing that this mismatch is one of four conditions required for factorized sampling, and demonstrate that eliminating it is necessary but not sufficient to obtain the intended factorization.
  Empirically, our case-study model and four representative latent baselines achieve near-zero global MMD while still allowing a linear probe to recover class labels with 74%--100% accuracy (10% chance level). Our model reaches 99.15% clustering accuracy, whereas externally evaluated class-conditional generation succeeds only 16% of the time. This leakage remains under six independent perturbations involving model capacity, curriculum, prior geometry, and supervision across two datasets. Four mitigation strategies reduce probe accuracy to 21%--46%, although they leave within-class dependence largely unchanged. A post-hoc conditional prior improves externally evaluated class generation to 0.97 on MNIST without retraining but reaches only 0.41 on CIFAR-10, while an empirical style bank achieves 0.88 on CIFAR-10. These results demonstrate that no divergence computed solely on the marginal distribution of the style latent can certify independence from class labels, and that reporting marginal statistics alone does not verify the property commonly claimed in factorized generative models.

</details>


### [253] [PRISM: Priority-aware Rubric Internalization via Structured Multimodal Data Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05249)
*Xiaomin He,Dongling Xiao,Jiahao Xie,Ruiqi Lu,Qianle Wang,Zhongbin Guo,Wanxuan Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PRISM introduces rubric comprehension — a paradigm where MLLMs act as executors that verify typed, prioritized rules before forming a judgment. The framework synthesizes 10K training samples and an evaluation benchmark (PRISM-Eval) with deterministic metrics, improving Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5% to 30.1% Strict accuracy while preserving general performance, with gains transferring across multiple MLLM architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world multimodal instructions often contain multiple requirements with unequal importance, yet existing training data reduce instruction following to single-question answering. This creates a gap: models are evaluated against rubrics but not trained to explicitly follow them. The authors aim to bridge this gap by reframing the model as an executor that verifies each rubric rule before producing an overall judgment.

Method: The PRISM framework consists of four stages: (1) persona–task pair generation, (2) prefix-guided rule set construction, (3) quality-filtered rubric creation, and (4) structured verification trace synthesis. The PRISM-Eval benchmark uses Loose and Strict metrics based on deterministic matching against fixed labels, eliminating the need for inference-time judge models. Only 10K synthesized samples are used for training.

Result: PRISM raises Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5% to 30.1% Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval while maintaining average performance on general benchmarks. The improvements transfer to four additional open-source MLLMs across both dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures.

Conclusion: Structured rubric supervision offers a scalable path toward multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following, with compact synthetic data proving sufficient to induce significant gains.

Abstract: Real-world multimodal instructions often bundle multiple requirements with unequal importance, yet most multimodal training data still reduce instruction following to answering one self-contained question. We study this gap through \textbf{rubric comprehension}, which casts the model not as a generator measured against rubrics but as an \textbf{executor} that follows them: given an image and a typed, prioritized rubric, the model must verify each rule before producing an overall judgment. To support this setting, we propose \textbf{PRISM}, a four-stage data synthesis framework that produces persona--task pairs, prefix-guided rule sets, quality-filtered rubrics, and structured verification traces. We further introduce \textbf{PRISM-Eval}, whose Loose and Strict metrics use deterministic matching against fixed labels and therefore require no inference-time judge model. With only 10K synthesized samples, PRISM lifts Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5\% to 30.1\% Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval while preserving average performance on general benchmarks, and the gains transfer to four additional open-source MLLMs across dense and MoE architectures, suggesting that structured rubric supervision is a scalable path toward multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following.

</details>


### [254] [Beyond Full-Model Rollback: AuroSFT for Adapter-State Multi-Task Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05250)
*Yue Han,Ziniu Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AuroSFT introduces a parameter-efficient multi-task SFT framework that replaces full-model checkpoints with compact, mergeable adapter states, enabling task-wise rollback at peak generalization without the storage and deployment costs of msft.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-task SFT trains heterogeneous data as a single optimization problem, but different tasks peak in generalization at different training stages. The existing msft approach addresses this via task-wise roll-out, exclusion, and rollback, but materializes scheduler state as full-model checkpoints, incurring prohibitive storage, restoration, and deployment costs.

Method: AuroSFT freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only injected adapters. It rolls back adapter checkpoints at task-wise validation peaks and continues training on the remaining active mixture. Each adapter uses an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer applied to a low-rank weight factor (not sample representations), keeping updates linear in the input, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into the frozen projection.

Result: Under a retained-backbone comparison protocol, AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy versus 59.85% for the corresponding msft reference row, and obtains higher accuracy on all five evaluated backbones.

Conclusion: AuroSFT successfully addresses the storage and deployment inefficiencies of msft by reformulating checkpointed state as lightweight, mergeable adapter states, while preserving or exceeding the accuracy gains of overfitting-aware multi-task scheduling.

Abstract: Multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) often casts a heterogeneous data mixture as a single optimization problem, even though different tasks may reach their best generalization at different times. msft exposes this mismatch through task-wise roll-out, exclusion, and rollback, but its original formulation materializes the scheduler state as full-model checkpoints, making stage transitions costly to store, restore, and deploy. This paper introduces AuroSFT, a parameter-efficient framework that recasts the carried state of overfitting-aware multi-task SFT as a compact, mergeable adapter state. AuroSFT freezes the pretrained backbone, trains only injected adapters, rolls back adapter checkpoints at task-wise peaks, and continues on the remaining active mixture. At the layer level, each adapter applies an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer to a low-rank weight factor rather than to the sample representation. The resulting update remains linear in the input, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into the frozen projection. Under the retained-backbone comparison protocol, AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy, compared with 59.85% for the corresponding msft reference row, and obtains higher accuracy on all five backbones. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroSFT-80D1.

</details>


### [255] [Beyond Rotations: AuroOFT for Expressive Quantized Orthogonal Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05253)
*Yue Han,Dianlin Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AuroOFT augments quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (QOFT) with a zero-initialized gated low-rank nonlinear residual branch, enabling input-dependent corrections while preserving quantization compatibility and initialization equivalence. It achieves significant accuracy gains over QOFT and QLoRA with fewer trainable parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: QOFT enables parameter-efficient adaptation of low-bit quantized language models via structured activation rotations, but its updates are limited to linear orthogonal transformations, lacking the capacity for input-dependent nonlinear corrections that could improve task performance.

Method: AuroOFT retains QOFT as a stable, quantization-compatible branch and adds a parallel zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer. Activations are mapped into an RMS-normalized compact latent space, processed with adaptive nonlinear bases using bounded or token-dependent gating. Zero-initialized up-projection ensures functional equivalence to QOFT at initialization, while orthogonality is preserved as a branch-level stability property rather than enforced on the combined nonlinear layer.

Result: Under matched protocols, AuroOFT improves Macro-6 over QOFT by 1.30–2.70% on 1.5B/3B Qwen2.5 models, exceeds QLoRA by 6.52–10.62%, and reduces trainable parameters by 32.3–44.7% relative to QLoRA.

Conclusion: AuroOFT effectively combines the stability and quantization compatibility of orthogonal fine-tuning with the expressive capacity of nonlinear low-rank adapters, yielding substantial accuracy and efficiency gains. The small math diagnostic set is used only for protocol-sensitivity checks, not as a primary benchmark.

Abstract: Quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (qoft) enables parameter-efficient adaptation of low-bit language models by learning structured activation rotations before frozen quantized weights. However, its task-specific updates remain constrained to linear orthogonal transformations, limiting input-dependent nonlinear corrections. We introduce AuroOFT, which keeps qoft as a stable quantization-compatible branch while attaching a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer. AuroOFT maps activations into an RMS-normalized compact latent space and uses adaptive nonlinear bases with bounded or token-dependent gating. The zero-initialized up projection makes AuroOFT functionally identical to qoft at initialization, while orthogonality remains a branch-level stability property rather than a property of the combined nonlinear layer. Under matched data, optimization, decoding, and parser protocols, AuroOFT improves Macro-6 over matched qoft by 1.30-2.70% on the 1.5B/3B Qwen2.5 settings, exceeds QLoRA by 6.52-10.62%, and saves 32.3-44.7% trainable parameters relative to QLoRA in representative scales. The small exam-style multiple-choice math set is treated only as a protocol-sensitivity diagnostic. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroOFT-F3FD.

</details>


### [256] [An Emerging Retail Portfolio Management Application: Personalized, Tax-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Natural Language Goals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05255)
*Ramin Pishehvar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A fully functional, integration-tested application that provides personalized, tax-aware portfolio management for retail investors using a three-phase reinforcement learning system, bridging the gap between static robo-advisors and institutional-grade tools — currently pre-deployment with preliminary backtest validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retail investors are underserved: existing robo-advisors rely on static, rule-based allocation, while institutional-grade tax-aware portfolio management systems demand high account minimums and inaccessible technology stacks. There is a clear gap for personalized, adaptive portfolio management accessible to individual investors.

Method: The system comprises a FastAPI backend with a web dashboard that accepts plain-language investment goals, routes them to one of six investment mandates, and generates broker-integrated portfolio recommendations via a three-phase RL pipeline: (1) a self-supervised cross-asset encoder, (2) a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) allocation policy with a learned intent router, and (3) a lightweight LoRA adapter for personalizing recommendations from revealed brokerage behavior without full model retraining. The system is integration-tested against Alpaca's live brokerage API (paper-trading mode) with features including multi-user authentication, preview-before-apply confirmation, daily email digests, and an auditable action-integrity chain. Validation uses 14-day walk-forward backtests with bootstrapped confidence intervals.

Result: The system is functionally complete and end-to-end integration-tested, but has not yet been exposed to real end-users. Preliminary 14-day walk-forward backtests with bootstrapped confidence intervals are reported as pre-deployment validation, not production performance. The authors also report practical engineering lessons including silently-inactive integration paths, hanging third-party API calls, and the value of end-to-end empirical verification over trusting checkpoint metadata.

Conclusion: The application demonstrates a concrete, emerging solution for bringing personalized RL-based portfolio management to retail investors, with a clear deployment path. The engineering lessons learned — particularly around live API integration pitfalls and the necessity of end-to-end verification — generalize to other applied RL systems relying on external, live data sources.

Abstract: Retail investors lack access to the kind of personalized, tax-aware portfolio management that institutional clients take for granted -- existing robo-advisors use static, rule-based allocation, and institutional-grade systems require account minimums and technology stacks unavailable to individual investors. We present a fully built, integration-tested application that closes this gap: a FastAPI backend and web dashboard that let a user describe an investment goal in plain language (e.g. "I want steady growth but need to sell some shares next month for a down payment"), routes that goal to one of six investment mandates, and produces a live, broker-integrated portfolio recommendation from athree-phase reinforcement learning system -- a self-supervised cross-asset encoder, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) allocation policy with a learned intent router, and a lightweight LoRA adapter that personalizes recommendations from an individual's revealed brokerage behavior without retraining the shared model. The system is functionally complete and integration-tested end-to-end against a live brokerage API (Alpaca, paper-trading mode), including multi-user authentication, a trust first preview-before-apply confirmation flow, daily email digests, and an auditable action-integrity chain, but has not yet been opened to real end-users; we report this honestly as an emerging, pre-deployment application with a concrete path to full deployment, alongside 14-day walk-forward backtests (bootstrapped confidence intervals included) as preliminary, pre-deployment validation rather than production performance. We also report several practical engineering lessons -- silently-inactive integration paths, hanging third-party API calls, and the value of end-to-end empirical verification over trusting checkpoint metadata -- that we believe generalize to other applied RL systems built on external, live data sources.

</details>


### [257] [Evaluating Machine Learning Models for Post-Wildfire Debris-Flow Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05265)
*Quinn Ledingham,Zhengsen Xu,Yimin Zhu,Zack Dewis,Mabel Heffring,Saeid Taleghanidoozdoozan,Motasem Alkayid,Megan Greenwood,Lincoln Linlin Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates 15 machine learning models for post-wildfire debris-flow prediction, finding TabPFN achieves the best performance. SHAP analysis reveals short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation as top predictors. Synthetic data augmentation using TabPFN-generated samples further improves model performance, particularly for deep learning models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-wildfire debris-flow prediction is critical for hazard mitigation, but is complicated by overlapping event classes in feature space, limited training data, and the need for model interpretability. A systematic evaluation of ML models addressing these challenges is lacking.

Method: The authors compare 15 machine learning models (including TabPFN) using basin-scale observations from the western United States. They employ repeated stratified cross-validation with threat score as the metric. SHAP is used for feature importance analysis. Synthetic data augmentation is performed using TabPFN-generated samples to address data scarcity.

Result: TabPFN achieves the highest unaugmented performance (threat score = 0.637), closely followed by tree-based models. SHAP analysis shows short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation are the most important features; burn severity and terrain features contribute less. Synthetic augmentation improves all models except CNN, with deep learning models gaining the largest mean increase (+0.041 in threat score).

Conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive framework combining rigorous model benchmarking, interpretable feature analysis (SHAP), and synthetic data augmentation to improve post-wildfire debris-flow prediction, addressing key challenges of data scarcity and model interpretability.

Abstract: Prediction of post-wildfire debris flows is critical for mitigating hazards to communities, infrastructure, and resources during intense rainfall in recently burned areas. However, identifying reliable machine learning models is complicated by overlapping debris-flow and non-debris-flow events in feature space, the need for model interpretability, and limited training data. This paper addresses these challenges through a systematic evaluation of machine learning models in terms of predictive performance, feature importance, and synthetic data augmentation. Using basin-scale observations of post-wildfire debris-flow events across the western United States, we compare 15 models, including the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN). Repeated stratified cross-validation shows that TabPFN achieves the highest unaugmented performance with a threat score of 0.637, closely followed by the best tree-based models. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are used to identify the features driving predictions, revealing that short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation consistently rank highest, while burn severity and terrain features contribute less. We further evaluate synthetic data augmentation using TabPFN-generated samples to address the scarcity of debris-flow observations. Synthetic augmentation improves the performance of all models except CNN, with the largest mean threat score increase of +0.041 among the deep learning models. By combining rigorous model benchmarking, interpretable feature analysis, and synthetic data augmentation, this work provides a comprehensive framework for improving post-wildfire debris-flow prediction.

</details>


### [258] [Rectifying Geometric Misalignment: Online Source-Free Adaptation for Class-Imbalanced EEG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05315)
*Shiwen Chu,Shanglin Li,Motoaki Kawanabe,Reinmar Kobler*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OSPDIM is a source-free online unsupervised domain adaptation method for EEG-based BCIs that corrects geometric bias from label shifts on the Riemannian manifold via tangent-space bias optimization with information maximization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Riemannian alignment methods like RCT assume balanced class priors, but real-world online BCI scenarios suffer from dynamic label distribution shifts (label shift), causing geometric misalignment of target data on the SPD manifold.

Method: OSPDIM introduces a manifold-constrained bias parameter into the tangent space mapping of SPD matrices, optimized online via information maximization to correct geometric skew from imbalanced data streams—without requiring source data or global batch statistics.

Result: Simulations on 2D SPD matrices visually confirm geometry rectification where standard centering fails. Extensive motor imagery experiments show OSPDIM significantly outperforms Riemannian baselines, especially under severe class imbalance.

Conclusion: OSPDIM provides a robust, plug-and-play solution for online BCI systems by addressing label shift on the Riemannian manifold, outperforming existing methods in challenging imbalanced streaming settings.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) based Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) often require unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) to generalize across subjects and sessions. While Riemannian alignment methods like the Riemannian Centering Transformation (RCT) are effective for handling covariate shifts, they implicitly assume balanced class priors. However, in realistic online BCI scenarios, the label distributions vary dynamically (label shift), causing standard alignment techniques to geometrically misalign the target data distributions. In this work, we propose OSPDIM (Online SPD manifold information maximization), a source-free online UDA framework designed to address label shifts on the Riemannian manifold. OSPDIM introduces a manifold-constrained bias parameter into the tangent space mapping, which is optimized via information maximization to correct the geometric skew caused by imbalanced data streams. Unlike offline methods relying on global batch statistics, OSPDIM estimates and corrects geometric bias on-the-fly. Simulations on 2D SPD matrices visually demonstrate that OSPDIM successfully rectifies the misalignment where standard centering fails. Extensive experiments on multiple motor imagery datasets show that OSPDIM significantly outperforms standard Riemannian baselines, particularly in challenging online adaptation scenarios with severe class imbalance, offering a robust solution for practical, plug-and-play BCI systems.

</details>


### [259] [QEvict: Recoverable Quantized KV Eviction for Attention-Drift-Robust Long-Context Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05326)
*Ayushman Garg,Akshita Gupta,Shaswata Bhattacharya,Abhishek Gupta,Sandeep Kumar,Manoj Kumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QEvict introduces a three-tier KV-cache management scheme that replaces irreversible token eviction with recoverable eviction, using full-precision, quantized recoverable, and deleted tiers to preserve broader historical context under fixed memory budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard KV-cache eviction policies based on attention scores make irreversible decisions — once a token is evicted, it cannot be recovered. The authors demonstrate this is problematic because token and window importance drifts during decoding, causing evicted states to later become important again. Current policies permanently discard states that would receive substantial attention under full-cache models.

Method: The authors first introduce two diagnostics: Future Missed Mass (measuring future attention assigned to discarded states) and Global LIR (measuring reactivation of historically inactive regions). They then propose QEvict, which maintains three tiers: (1) high-confidence windows in full precision, (2) intermediate windows in a quantized recoverable tier, and (3) deletion of only the lowest-confidence windows. Cumulative attention scores dynamically update window importance; when a quantized window becomes important again, it is dequantized and promoted to full precision.

Result: Across long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks, QEvict consistently improves over representative eviction and quantization baselines, reducing missed attention and improving information retention under a fixed memory budget.

Conclusion: Recoverable eviction is superior to binary retain-or-delete policies. By maintaining a quantized recoverable tier, QEvict preserves broader context while retaining exact precision for critical regions, addressing the attention-drift problem inherent in standard eviction methods.

Abstract: Autoregressive large language model inference is increasingly constrained by the memory footprint of the Key-Value (KV) cache. A dominant line of work reduces this footprint by evicting tokens that appear unimportant under attention-derived scores. However, such policies make an implicit irreversible decision: once a token is evicted, it cannot become useful again. We show that this assumption is brittle during decoding. Token and window importance drift as generated queries evolve, causing standard eviction policies to permanently discard states that later receive substantial attention under the full-cache model. To characterize this behaviour, we introduce Future Missed Mass and Global LIR, two diagnostics that measure future attention assigned to discarded states and the reactivation of historically inactive regions. We propose QEvict, a three-tier KV-cache management scheme that replaces binary retain-or-delete eviction with recoverable eviction. QEvict maintains high-confidence windows in full precision, stores intermediate windows in a quantized recoverable tier, and deletes only the lowest-confidence windows. During decoding, cumulative attention scores update window importance and when a quantized window becomes important again, it is dequantized and promoted to the full-precision. Under a fixed memory budget, this design preserves broader historical context while retaining exact full precision for the most important regions. Across long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks, QEvict consistently improves over representative eviction and quantization baselines, reducing missed attention and improving information retention

</details>


### [260] [DG-FedReuse: Proxy-Gradient-Gated Cached-Update Reuse with Matched Sparse Uplink Accounting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05358)
*Rahil Aftab,Vineet Kumar Rakesh,Soumya Mazumdar,Tapas Samanta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DG-FedReuse proposes a federated learning mechanism where selected clients can reuse age-decayed cached model updates when a head-gradient discrepancy proxy is below a threshold, combined with adaptive Top-K compression. It achieves 83-85% uplink savings but with modest accuracy trade-offs (-5.29 to -0.14 pp), and the savings are sensitive to whether downlink is included in the accounting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated learning incurs substantial communication costs from repeated local optimization and model-update transmission. The authors aim to reduce uplink communication by allowing clients to skip transmitting fresh updates when their local gradient direction has not changed substantially, instead reusing aged cached updates — without requiring additional client-side computation or protocol changes beyond simulator-level logic.

Method: DG-FedReuse operates at the simulator level. Selected clients may contribute age-decayed cached updates when a stochastic head-gradient discrepancy proxy falls below a round-dependent threshold. Constraints include a hard cache-age limit and a minimum quota of fresh-client updates. Fresh updates are compressed using an adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation. The study uses 50 virtual clients with Dirichlet label heterogeneity (α=0.5) across six image-classification datasets, evaluated over three seeds at a 90-round budget. Both uplink-only and symmetric uplink+downlink accounting are considered.

Result: At 90 rounds, DG-FedReuse yields 83.36–85.42% modeled update-data-field uplink saving versus 76.88% for matched Top-K FedAvg. Seed-aligned accuracy differences range from -5.29 to -0.14 percentage points. Best-observed test accuracies (exploratory, test-controlled checkpointing) range from -2.38 to +0.45 pp relative to matched FedAvg. When symmetric dense-model downlink is included, headline saving drops to 41.68–42.71%, with only 3.24–4.27 pp incremental gain over Top-K FedAvg.

Conclusion: The caching-via-discrepancy reuse rule can substantially reduce modeled uplink data volume with manageable accuracy loss, but the communication savings are highly sensitive to whether downlink transmission is accounted for. The study explicitly disclaims generalization beyond the implemented simulator, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime/energy savings, faster convergence, or superiority over existing stale-update and lazy-aggregation methods.

Abstract: Federated learning repeatedly incurs local optimization and model-update transmission. We study DG-FedReuse, a simulator-level mechanism that allows selected clients to contribute age-decayed cached updates when a stochastic head-gradient discrepancy proxy remains below a round-dependent threshold. A hard cache-age limit and minimum fresh-client quota constrain reuse, while fresh updates use an adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation. Experiments cover six image-classification datasets, 50 virtual clients, Dirichlet label heterogeneity (α=0.5), and three seeds. At a common 90-round budget, DG-FedReuse yields 83.36-85.42% modeled update-data-field uplink saving, compared with 76.88% for matched Top-K FedAvg; the seed-aligned accuracy differences range from -5.29 to -0.14 percentage points. Best-observed test accuracies obtained under test-controlled checkpointing are retained only as exploratory archival evidence and range from -2.38 to +0.45 percentage points relative to matched FedAvg. A symmetric dense-model-downlink sensitivity reduces the headline saving to 41.68-F42.71% and the incremental gain over Top-K FedAvg to 3.24-4.27 percentage points, demonstrating the dependence of communication conclusions on the accounting boundary. The study characterizes the proposed reuse rule in the implemented simulator; it does not establish unbiased generalization, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime or energy savings, faster convergence, or superiority over existing stale-update and lazy-aggregation methods.

</details>


### [261] [Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs) for Predictive Latent Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05371)
*Hailong Jiang,Emran Hossain,Feng Yu,Jianfeng Zhu,Guilin Zhang,Wulan Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs), a framework that applies quantum-inspired mathematical structures—complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents—to predictive world modeling, and evaluates them on elementary cellular automata, finding promising local predictions but limitations in long-horizon rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current world models rely on classical vector, probabilistic, or transformer-based latent state representations. The authors investigate whether quantum-theoretic mathematical structures (complex amplitudes, density matrices) provide useful inductive biases for learning structured, compact latent states and transition operators in world modeling.

Method: The authors propose QSWMs built on three foundational properties (classical inclusion, predictive sufficiency, structured compactness). They instantiate two variants: complex-valued latents and density-matrix-like latents, both paired with latent transition operators and measurement-inspired decoding. Evaluation is conducted on elementary cellular automata against classical baselines.

Result: Complex-valued QSWMs show promising local predictive potential compared to classical baselines. However, both variants exhibit limitations in long-horizon rollout performance, and density-matrix variants underperform relative to expectations.

Conclusion: Quantum-inspired inductive biases offer some benefits for local prediction in structured world modeling, but scaling to long-horizon tasks remains a challenge. The framework establishes a theoretical foundation for further exploration of quantum-structured latent representations.

Abstract: World models learn latent states that summarize interaction histories, evolve over time, and support prediction, simulation, or planning. Most existing world models represent these states using classical vectors, probability distributions, recurrent hidden states, or transformer activations. In this paper, we introduce Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs), a quantum-inspired framework for predictive world modeling with structured latent states, latent transition operators, and measurement-inspired decoding maps. We study whether mathematical structures inspired by quantum theory, such as complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents, provide useful inductive biases for world modeling. We establish three foundational properties: classical inclusion, predictive sufficiency, and structured compactness. We then instantiate complex-valued and density-matrix-like QSWM variants and evaluate them on elementary cellular automata against strong classical baselines. Results show promising local predictive potential for complex-valued QSWMs, while also revealing limitations in long-horizon rollout, density-matrix variants

</details>


### [262] [Spectral Distillation: From Nonlinear Dynamics to Linear State-Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05416)
*Liane Galanti,Devan Shah,Shlomo Fortgang,Elad Hazan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a provable pipeline for learning nonlinear dynamical systems through compact linear state-space representations. It combines convex Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF) to learn an implicit predictor, followed by spectral-to-LDS distillation to produce an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system, with dimension-free generalization guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning nonlinear dynamical systems typically requires solving non-convex system-identification problems or learning high-dimensional latent representations. The authors aim to bypass these difficulties by using a convex learning approach followed by a principled distillation step, yielding compact linear state-space models with provable guarantees.

Method: The pipeline has two stages: (1) Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method that learns an implicit spectral predictor competitive with the best linear observer for the system; (2) spectral-to-LDS distillation, which converts the implicit predictor into an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system (LDS). The analysis decomposes prediction error into an exponentially small distillation term plus the OSF learning error governed by Luenberger observer complexity.

Result: The main theorem provides a dimension-free guarantee: the average prediction error depends on observer complexity rather than the latent dimension of the nonlinear system. Experiments on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning demonstrate that the train-then-distill pipeline yields compact LDS predictors matching or outperforming directly trained baselines.

Conclusion: This work establishes the first end-to-end provable method for extracting a best-in-hindsight LDS representation of nonlinear dynamics via convex learning followed by distillation, with strong empirical performance and dimension-free theoretical guarantees.

Abstract: Can nonlinear dynamical systems be learned through a compact linear state-space representation, without directly solving a non-convex system-identification problem? We give a provable pipeline for doing so. Starting from observations of an unknown nonlinear dynamical system, we first learn an implicit spectral predictor using Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method that competes with the best linear observer for the system. We then apply spectral-to-LDS distillation to convert this predictor into an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system. Our main theorem shows that the average prediction error of the distilled LDS decomposes into an exponentially-small distillation term and the OSF learning term governed by the Luenberger complexity of the best observer. The guarantee is dimension-free: it depends on observer complexity rather than on the latent dimension needed to represent the nonlinear system. To our knowledge, this yields the first end-to-end provable method for extracting a best-in-hindsight LDS representation of nonlinear dynamics through convex learning followed by provable distillation. Experiments on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning show that the train-then-distill pipeline produces compact LDS predictors that match or outperform directly trained baselines.

</details>


### [263] [Perturbation Sensitivity at Convergence: A Simple Signal for Identifying Spuriously Correlated Samples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05419)
*Nilesh Kumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: After model convergence, spurious-correlation samples are classified by a shared, robust rule, while non-spurious samples exhibit fragile, input-specific configurations. A fixed perturbation flips predictions of fragile samples more often, enabling group annotation-free detection. Rebalancing training with detected samples raises worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 57.3% to 80.8%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for identifying spurious-correlation-affected samples without group labels require early-training signals and a carefully chosen intervention epoch, typically tuned with group-labeled validation data. The authors aim to eliminate dependence on group labels and early-stopping hyperparameters entirely.

Method: The method operates on converged models. A fixed perturbation is applied to inputs, and prediction flips are measured. Samples consistent with the spurious correlation share a stable classification rule and are robust to perturbation; the remaining samples are fit via brittle, instance-specific configurations and flip more readily. Detection requires only two forward passes per sample, with no group labels or early-stopping epoch.

Result: Using detected samples to rebalance training improves worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 57.3% to 80.8%, compared to 85.8% with ground-truth group labels.

Conclusion: A usable signal for separating spurious-correlation-consistent samples from others exists post-convergence, based on differential fragility to input perturbation. This enables group-label-free, hyperparameter-free detection and effective worst-group accuracy improvement through rebalancing.

Abstract: Models trained by empirical risk minimization on data containing spurious correlations achieve high average accuracy while failing on subpopulations where the correlation does not hold. Existing methods for identifying the affected samples without group annotations rely on signals from early training, which requires locating the epoch at which to intervene, a hyperparameter typically selected using group-labeled validation data. We show that a usable signal is available after convergence, when loss no longer distinguishes the two populations. Samples consistent with the spurious correlation are classified by a shared rule, while the remaining samples are fit through configurations specific to individual inputs and are correspondingly more fragile. Applying a fixed perturbation to a converged model's inputs flips the predictions of the latter far more often than the former. The resulting procedure requires two forward passes per training sample, no group annotations at any stage, and no early-stopping epoch. Using the detected samples to rebalance training raises worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 57.3% to 80.8%, against 85.8% with ground-truth group labels.

</details>


### [264] [Why the Third Axis Is Freedom](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05423)
*Michael Timothy Bennett*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that Explorative Modeling (XM), which generates K outputs and updates on the closest match, actually optimizes for "freedom" (weakness of behavioral constraint) rather than "exploration" as a third pretraining axis. Freedom—a property of function, not form—was previously shown to predict generalization better than MDL. The author proves XM's loss depends on the probability of missing acceptable outputs (raised to power K), and empirically demonstrates XM increases freedom, with freedom-based selection outperforming validation selection in 29/30 cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To clarify that Explorative Modeling's claimed "third pretraining axis" of exploration is actually freedom—the weakness of behavioral constraints—and to demonstrate that freedom, not generative expressivity, is what drives XM's benefits, particularly for generalization under distribution shift.

Method: The author provides a theoretical proof showing average XM loss relates to the probability a candidate misses an acceptable region, with exploration (K>1) raising this to a power K, thereby increasing match probability with freedom. Empirically, the author conducts: (1) a Forward XM experiment varying K to measure freedom changes, (2) training XM candidate pools and comparing validation-based selection against a freedom selector using unlabeled parent contexts.

Result: Larger K increased or saturated measured freedom, with freedom increasing at every tested value under context-dependent targets. The freedom selector won against validation selection in 29 of 30 cases. Generative expressivity is identified as merely a mode-count proxy for freedom that discards the extension structure crucial to freedom's generalization significance.

Conclusion: XM is a means to an end, with freedom being the actual end. Selecting for freedom improved XM performance under distribution shift, and the "third pretraining axis" is properly understood as freedom (behavioral constraint weakness) rather than exploration or generative expressivity.

Abstract: In generative training, a model produces an output and is penalised for its difference from an example. With one output per comparison, a model that produces one common answer can outperform a model retaining a broader repertoire. Explorative Modeling (XM) produces $K$ outputs per comparison and updates on the closest, claiming exploration as a "third pretraining axis" associated with generative expressivity. Here I show the third axis is actually freedom, meaning the weakness of the constraint implied by a model's behaviour. Previous work showed freedom is a property of function rather than form. Parameters, architecture, minimum-description-length (MDL), and data can vary while the behavioural constraint remains unchanged. It was formally proved that weakest models are likeliest to generalise, and freedom selection beat MDL by 110-500\% in induction experiments. I prove average XM loss depends on the chance a candidate misses an acceptable region, with exploration raising miss probability to power $K$. For $K>1$, match probability rises with freedom. I then demonstrate empirically that XM optimises for freedom. In a Forward XM experiment, larger $K$ increased or saturated measured freedom, and increased freedom at every tested value under context-dependent targets. I trained XM candidate pools and compared validation selection with a freedom selector that read unlabelled parent contexts. Freedom won in 29 of 30 cases. Generative expressivity is a mode-count proxy for freedom, that discards the extension structure that gives freedom its generalisation significance. XM is a means, freedom an end, and selecting for freedom improved XM under distribution shift.

</details>


### [265] [EvoHarness-RL: Learning Self-Evolving Runtime Harness for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05446)
*Xuying Ning,Dongqi Fu,Tianxin Wei,Hanqing Zeng,Yuanchen Bei,Bingxuan Li,Zihao Li,Qifan Wang,Xiang Shen,Yifan Wu,Jiayi Liu,Hong Li,Yinglong Xia,Xiangjun Fan,Hanghang Tong,Jingrui He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces EvoHarness-RL, a framework where LLM agents learn policies for constructing and selectively accessing external harness state (Belief, Progress, Experience) during long-horizon tasks. Combining supervised fine-tuning with cost-aware GRPO, the approach achieves 96.9% on ALFWorld and reveals emergent phenomena: harness annealing (internalizing frequent harness patterns) and harness evolution (adaptive state refinement).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents tackling long-horizon tasks require external execution support (state tracking, tool invocation, outcome verification, experience reuse), but current approaches manually engineer both the external workspace and its usage policy through prompts, heuristics, or domain conventions. This is brittle and suboptimal. The paper addresses the coupled challenges of state formation from noisy interaction traces and runtime control over external-state access by framing them as a unified policy learning problem.

Method: EvoHarness-RL proposes a two-stage training pipeline: (1) Supervised harness fine-tuning (SFT) teaches the base agent the harness action space and how to construct useful external state structured as Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE); (2) Cost-aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) explores coordination policies for selectively reading, updating, and consolidating harness state during long-horizon interactions. The system is evaluated on ALFWorld using a Qwen3-8B LLM.

Result: EvoHarness-RL achieves 96.9% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-8B. Two key emergent dynamics are identified: (1) harness annealing — training internalizes recurring harness-use patterns into model policy, shifting from frequent harness calls toward selective external-state access; (2) harness evolution — progress updates and experience consolidation refine the harness into a compact, task-adaptive state substrate.

Conclusion: Long-horizon agents benefit significantly from trainable policies that learn how to construct and coordinate with external harness workspaces, rather than merely equipping agents with stronger tools or larger memories. The learned coordination between internal policy and external harness state yields both higher task success and more efficient state access patterns.

Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents increasingly rely on external execution support to maintain state, track progress, invoke tools, verify outcomes, and reuse experience across interactions. However, effective harness use raises two coupled challenges: state formation from noisy interaction traces and runtime control over external-state access. Existing agents usually handle both through prompts, heuristics, or domain-specific conventions, leaving the external workspace and its usage policy manually engineered. To address this, we study the problem of harness policy learning, where agents learn harness policies offline and deploy them to construct and update external harness state online during runtime task execution. We introduce EvoHarness-RL, which exposes Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE) as policy-facing harness state. Supervised harness fine-tuning teaches the base agent the harness action space and how to construct useful external state, while cost-aware GRPO explores coordination policies to selectively read, update, and consolidate that state during long-horizon interaction. Instantiated on ALFWorld with a Qwen3-8B LLM, EvoHarness-RL reaches 96.9% success and reveals two key dynamics: harness annealing, where training internalizes recurring harness-use patterns into the model policy and shifts the agent from frequent harness calls toward selective external-state access, and harness evolution, where progress updates and experience consolidation refine the harness into a compact, task-adaptive state substrate. These results suggest that long-horizon agents benefit from trainable policies for constructing and coordinating with external harness workspaces, beyond simply adding stronger tools or larger memories.

</details>


### [266] [Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotopes for Identifiable and Refinable Predictive Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05454)
*Zhen Zhang,Amr Alanwar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ), a novel prediction head for neural networks that decomposes predictive uncertainty into three distinct sources—discrete mode choice, bounded systematic drift, and irreducible noise—using binary, bounded, and stochastic generators within a zonotope framework that supports closed-form likelihood, algebraic future-step coupling, identifiability guarantees, and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing probabilistic prediction heads (Gaussian mixtures or single conformal regions) fail to separate three distinct sources of uncertainty commonly present in real-world prediction tasks: discrete choice among modes, bounded systematic drift within a chosen mode, and irreducible stochastic noise. The authors aim to address this gap with a unified representation that disentangles these uncertainty sources.

Method: The HProbZ output head represents the three uncertainty sources as binary, bounded, and stochastic generators of a zonotope. The bounded generator is shared across prediction steps, coupling future predictions algebraically so that observing one step refines the predictive distribution at all remaining steps in a single forward pass. The model admits a closed-form likelihood via convolution and is shown to be identifiable up to permutation. It also provides analytic per-mode risk and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets at inference time.

Result: The three generators are proven identifiable from the likelihood up to permutation, and the HProbZ density is representationally distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture. Empirical analysis on representative prediction benchmarks demonstrates effectiveness relative to same-encoder mixture baselines, while offering structural properties that mixture or convex-conformal predictors do not jointly provide.

Conclusion: The HProbZ offers a principled, interpretable decomposition of predictive uncertainty with formal identifiability guarantees and practical benefits (closed-form likelihood, coupled multi-step refinement, per-mode risk, multi-modal conformal sets) that existing approaches—mixtures or conformal predictors—cannot jointly deliver, making it a compelling alternative for uncertainty-aware prediction.

Abstract: Probabilistic prediction heads in neural networks typically output either a Gaussian mixture or a single conformal region. Neither separates the distinct sources of uncertainty often present in real prediction tasks: a discrete choice among modes, bounded systematic drift within the chosen mode, and irreducible stochastic noise. We introduce the Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ), an output head that represents these three sources as binary, bounded, and stochastic generators of a zonotope, and admits a closed-form likelihood by convolution. Sharing the bounded generator across prediction steps couples future predictions algebraically, so observing one step refines the predictive distribution at every remaining step in a single forward pass. We establish that the three generators are identifiable from the likelihood up to permutation, and that an HProbZ density is representationally distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture. The same shared structure provides analytic per-mode risk and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets at inference time. Empirical analysis on representative prediction benchmarks supports the effectiveness of the design relative to same-encoder mixture baselines, while offering structural properties that mixture or convex-conformal predictors do not jointly provide.

</details>
