### [267] [Matrix Zonotopic Attention: A Context-Adaptive Value Projection for Set Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05472)
*Zhen Zhang,Amr Alanwar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multi-head attention suffers from asymmetry: its routing is input-dependent (softmax) but its value projection is input-independent (fixed linear map). The authors introduce Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) to quantify how many input-dependent directions a target operator needs, prove that standard attention requires depth proportional to TDOF while context-adaptive values can do it in one layer, and propose Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn) — a drop-in replacement using gated generator matrices — showing selective gains on high-rank combinatorial set tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard multi-head attention has an architectural asymmetry: the softmax routing adapts per-input, but the value projection matrix is fixed across all inputs. This "context-rigid" design limits expressivity for permutation-invariant set functions, particularly those requiring input-dependent output transformations. The authors aim to characterize this limitation theoretically and remedy it with a minimally disruptive architectural change.

Method: The paper (1) defines Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) — the minimal number of input-dependent linear directions needed to exactly represent a target operator; (2) proves a depth-separation result: context-rigid attention needs depth ≥ TDOF, while a single context-adaptive value layer suffices; (3) proposes Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn), where the fixed value matrix is replaced by a matrix-zonotope family: a learned centre plus a sum of generator matrices gated by input-dependent scalars. This reduces to standard attention at initialization, preserves permutation equivariance, and admits a reachability interpretation via zonotope geometry.

Result: Experiments on set-prediction benchmarks confirm the TDOF prediction: MZAttn substantially outperforms parameter-matched standard attention on targets with high-rank, sparsely combinatorial dependence on the input set. On aggregate-statistic targets (low TDOF), the gap is negligible, consistent with the theory that the architectural advantage is selective rather than universal.

Conclusion: The context-rigidity of standard attention is a genuine bottleneck for set functions with high transformation complexity. MZAttn offers a principled, lightweight fix that preserves key properties (equivariance, initialization compatibility) while providing expressivity gains precisely where TDOF predicts. The work opens avenues for applying zonotope-based parameterizations in broader transformer architectures.

Abstract: Multi-head attention combines an input-dependent softmax routing with an input-independent linear value projection, so the per-sample operator mapping aggregated values to outputs is the same for every input set. We study the consequences of this asymmetry for permutation-invariant set targets. We introduce the Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) of a target operator, a complexity measure counting the input-dependent directions an exact representation requires, and present a depth-separation analysis showing that context-rigid attention needs depth proportional to the target's TDOF, whereas a single layer with a context-adaptive value family can represent the same target. Building on this analysis, we propose Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn), which replaces the fixed value projection with a context-adaptive matrix-zonotope family: a centre matrix plus a sum of generator matrices weighted by input-dependent gates. The construction reduces to standard multi-head attention at initialisation, preserves permutation equivariance, and admits a data-driven reachability interpretation. Experiments on a range of set-prediction tasks are consistent with the TDOF prediction that the architectural advantage is selective: it appears on targets that depend on the input set in a high-rank, sparsely combinatorial way, and is small on aggregate-statistic targets where parameter-matched standard attention is already competitive.

</details>


### [268] [KV-Skill: Forging Expertise in the Model's Native Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05475)
*Zhaowei Han,Xiang Zhang,Bing Han,Kai Liu,Danqi Hu,Jie Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KV-Skill introduces external factorized operators for frozen LLMs that store task knowledge separately from the backbone. It supports two paths: registration (converting text skills into operators) and reward learning (learning operators from outcomes). The method consistently outperforms text-in-prompt, SkillOpt, SoftSkill, prefix tuning, and LoRA across multiple benchmarks and backbones, while supporting independent loading of multiple skills without forgetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Task knowledge stored as text in prompts is modular but requires reinterpretation on every use, while weight-based adaptation (e.g., fine-tuning) makes capabilities hard to load, remove, or share independently. The authors seek a middle ground: an external, modular representation that a frozen LLM can read efficiently without adding positions to the prompt, combining the modularity of text with the efficiency of weight-based adaptation.

Method: KV-Skill proposes factorized operators injected into the key-value (KV) representations of a frozen language model through a lightweight shared per-backbone interface. Two complementary paths are offered: (1) Registration — converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains the shared interface; (2) Reward learning — directly optimizes a compact latent operator from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. Critically, neither path consumes prompt positions. A post-hoc rank analysis examines the dimensionality of useful directions in the operators.

Result: On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration achieves 77.2 accuracy vs. 23.4 (source text), 52.0 (SkillOpt), and 64.5 (SoftSkill). Across eight matched settings (varying reward training and parameter budgets), KV-Skill outperforms soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA in seven of eight. Rank analysis shows text-derived operators retain nearly all benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while matched random directions fail. A single shared interface retains three independently loadable KV-Skills with no measurable forgetting.

Conclusion: Task knowledge can be effectively acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external operator, and deployed separately from the backbone. KV-Skill bridges the gap between prompt-based and weight-based knowledge storage, offering modularity, composability, and strong performance without occupying prompt context.

Abstract: Task knowledge is commonly stored either as text in the prompt or as an update to model weights. Text is modular but must be interpreted on every use, while weight adaptation makes the resulting capability difficult to load, remove, or share independently. We introduce KV-Skill, a design space of external factorized operators that a frozen language model reads through a lightweight interface. KV-Skill supports two complementary paths. Registration converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains a shared per-backbone interface. Reward learning develops a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. Neither path adds positions to the prompt. Across ten benchmarks and four backbones from three model families, converting text to a KV-Skill consistently makes the same procedural knowledge more effective. On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration reaches 77.2 accuracy, compared with 23.4 for the source text skill, 52.0 for SkillOpt, and 64.5 for SoftSkill. Under matched reward training and parameter budgets, KV-Skill gives the best result in seven of eight matched settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. A post-hoc rank analysis further shows that text-derived operators retain nearly all of their benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while matched random directions fail. Finally, one shared interface retains three independently loadable KV-Skills without measurable forgetting. These results show that task knowledge can be acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external operator, and deployed separately from the backbone. Code is available at: https://github.com/shawnzhg/KV-Skill

</details>


### [269] [LC-GRPO: Bridging Train-Inference Gap for Flow-Based GRPO with Langevin Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05600)
*Yingqing Guo,Hui Yuan,Zijian He,Mengdi Wang,Zheng Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LC-GRPO introduces a Langevin-corrected sampling scheme for flow-based generative models in GRPO training, replacing the standard SDE rollouts with ODE Euler steps followed by a Langevin correction. This aligns training samples more closely with test-time ODE inference, reducing blur and improving reward optimization without requiring an extra score model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard GRPO for flow models replaces the deterministic ODE sampler with an SDE during training. However, finite-step SDE discretizations diverge from ODE samples, producing blurry rollouts as exploration noise increases. This creates a mismatch between reinforcement learning training samples and test-time ODE generation, degrading both reward optimization and output quality.

Method: LC-GRPO decomposes each rollout transition into two steps: (1) a deterministic ODE Euler step aligned with test-time inference, and (2) a stochastic Langevin correction targeting the marginal distribution at the resulting timestep. The score function for the Langevin step is analytically recovered from the flow velocity via the relationship ∇log p_t = (v_t - ∂_t x_t)/σ_t², eliminating the need for a separate score model. The combined transition remains an isotropic Gaussian with a tractable likelihood, enabling direct policy optimization. Theoretical analysis shows that one Langevin correction step reduces the Wasserstein error of an imperfect ODE Euler step, and that the proposed transition can be more accurate than Euler–Maruyama SDE discretization at matched randomness.

Result: Experiments on SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo demonstrate consistent improvements in reward optimization across text-to-image and text-to-video tasks. LC-GRPO preserves generation quality while substantially narrowing the gap between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic test-time ODE inference.

Conclusion: LC-GRPO provides a principled solution to the train-test mismatch in flow-based GRPO by aligning stochastic rollouts with the deterministic ODE sampler through Langevin correction, achieving better reward optimization and generation quality without additional model components.

Abstract: Flow-based generative models are typically sampled by solving a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), whereas online reinforcement learning requires stochastic rollouts for policy exploration and optimization. Existing GRPO methods for flow models therefore replace the inference-time ODE with a stochastic differential equation (SDE) during training. Although the ODE and SDE share the same marginal distributions in continuous time, their finite-step discretizations can differ substantially. In particular, SDE rollouts often become blurry as the exploration noise increases, creating a mismatch between the samples used for reinforcement learning and those generated by the test-time ODE sampler. We introduce LC-GRPO, a flow-based GRPO framework with Langevin correction. Each rollout transition first takes an inference-aligned ODE Euler step and then applies a stochastic Langevin correction targeting the marginal distribution at the resulting timestep. The required score is recovered directly from the flow velocity, requiring no additional score model, while the resulting transition remains an isotropic Gaussian with a tractable likelihood for policy optimization. We theoretically show that, under suitable conditions, one Langevin correction step reduces the Wasserstein error of an imperfect ODE Euler step. At a matched randomness level, we further show that the proposed transition can be more accurate than the standard Euler--Maruyama discretization of the reverse SDE. Experiments on SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo demonstrate that LC-GRPO consistently improves reward optimization across text-to-image and text-to-video tasks, preserves generation quality, and substantially narrows the gap between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic test-time ODE inference.

</details>


### [270] [GAUGE: Granularity-Adaptive Counterfactual Gating of Evidence for Incomplete Multimodal Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05608)
*Yunping Shi,En Yu,Kairui Guo,Jie Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GAUGE introduces a lightweight counterfactual gating framework that performs fine-grained evidence unit modulation for incomplete multimodal classification, using Taylor-based scoring in a single forward-backward pass, outperforming strong baselines across six benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for incomplete multimodal classification operate at coarse modality level during imputation and fusion, meaning they cannot selectively retain reliable components while suppressing misleading ones within the same recovered modality, which compromises prediction reliability.

Method: GAUGE first imputes missing modalities with a frozen imputer and encodes both observed and recovered inputs as fine-grained evidence units. It then scores the counterfactual effect of replacing each unit with a reference representation using prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores (first-order approximation), computed in a single forward-backward pass. These scores are mapped to continuous gates and converted into additive attention-logit biases for unit-wise modulation without altering the backbone architecture.

Result: Experiments across six benchmarks show GAUGE outperforms strong baselines under diverse incomplete-input settings. A Taylor remainder theoretical analysis further characterizes the approximation error relative to the exact counterfactual effect.

Conclusion: GAUGE establishes a principled and scalable framework for fine-grained evidence control under modality incompleteness, providing both empirical performance gains and theoretical grounding via the Taylor remainder analysis.

Abstract: Multimodal classification typically assumes all modalities are available, yet real-world inputs are often incomplete. Imputation and dynamic fusion can mitigate such incompleteness, but existing methods operate at a coarse modality level and thus cannot retain reliable components while suppressing misleading ones within the same recovered modality, compromising prediction reliability. To address this issue, we propose GAUGE, a lightweight counterfactual gating framework for incomplete multimodal classification. GAUGE first imputes missing modalities with a frozen imputer and encodes observed and recovered inputs uniformly as fine-grained evidence units. Rather than intervening on each unit explicitly, GAUGE scores the counterfactual effect of replacing every unit with a reference representation through prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores, all obtained in a single forward-backward pass. These scores are mapped to continuous gates, which are converted into additive attention-logit biases for unit-wise evidence modulation without altering the backbone architecture. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate that GAUGE outperforms strong baselines across diverse incomplete-input settings. Furthermore, a Taylor remainder theoretical analysis characterizes the error of the first-order approximation relative to the exact counterfactual effect, establishing GAUGE as a principled and scalable framework for fine-grained evidence control under modality incompleteness.

</details>


### [271] [Reasoning Errors Have a Region and a Direction in the Residual-Stream Trajectory of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05660)
*Hamed Damirchi,Ignacio Meza De la Jara,Damith Ranasinghe,Yuhang Liu,Javen Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a three-stream detector that combines residual-stream displacement ("motion") with two views of state ("region" via vector quantization and "direction" via normalized multi-layer states) to better distinguish sound reasoning from flawed reasoning. The method improves selection accuracy by up to 12% over displacement-only methods and 21% over single-layer probing, demonstrating that reasoning validity is best read from state-conditioned motion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distinguishing correct from incorrect reasoning is critical as language models are deployed for verifiable reasoning tasks. Existing trajectory-based methods use layerwise residual-stream displacements, which capture representational change but omit the originating state. However, restoring the full state risks reintroducing shortcut-prone, token-specific information. The paper identifies this trade-off between motion and location and seeks a middle ground — enough state context to interpret motion without the vulnerability of full-state probing.

Method: A three-stream detector architecture is proposed: (1) a motion stream using residual-stream displacements, (2) a coarse region reader employing vector quantization to capture broad state location, and (3) a fine direction reader operating over normalized multi-layer states. These three streams are combined to condition motion interpretation on restricted state context, avoiding full-state probing while restoring sufficient location information.

Result: On unseen reasoning benchmarks, the three-stream detector improves selection accuracy by up to 12% over displacement-only state-of-the-art methods and 21% over single-layer probing baselines. Despite training only on reasoning benchmarks, it also outperforms all compared detectors on factual completion and fact verification tasks, indicating the signal captures general correctness rather than reasoning-type-specific patterns. Ablations confirm that motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals.

Conclusion: Reasoning validity is better read from state-conditioned motion than from either static states or decontextualized trajectories alone. The three-stream design successfully navigates the trade-off between omitting and fully restoring state, offering a robust, generalizable correctness detector applicable even beyond reasoning-specific tasks.

Abstract: As language models are increasingly used for tasks that require verifiable reasoning, reliably distinguishing sound reasoning from flawed reasoning has become an important practical problem. Recent trajectory-based methods seek this signal in layerwise residual-stream displacements, which capture how representations change while attenuating some stable, token-specific information. However, displacement omits the state from which an update originates, whereas restoring the full state risks reintroducing shortcut-prone information. We identify this trade-off and propose a three-stream detector that combines motion with two restricted views of location. A coarse region reader based on vector quantization and a fine direction reader over normalized multi-layer states. This design restores enough state context to interpret the motion without returning to full-state probing. On reasoning benchmarks unseen during training, our method improves selection accuracy by up to 12% over the displacement-only state of the art and 21% over single-layer probing baselines. Although trained only on reasoning benchmarks, it also reads factual completion and fact verification, ahead of every detector we compare against, which places the signal on correctness rather than on a kind of reasoning. Ablations further show that motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals. These results suggest that reasoning validity is better read from state-conditioned motion than from either static states or decontextualized trajectories alone.

</details>


### [272] [Potential Matching Optimal Transport: Continuous Normalizing Flows for Exact $p$-Wasserstein Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05666)
*Lishuo Zhang,Ruizhi Huang,Yang Yu,Lei Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PMOT introduces a potential-flow framework for general p-cost optimal transport, using a scalar potential to parameterize CNF velocity fields. It employs self-induced matching along straight bridges and achieves zero-loss exactness: under regularity assumptions, any zero-loss solution recovers the p-optimal transport map.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extend neural optimal transport beyond the standard quadratic (p=2) case to general p-costs c_p(x,y)=||x-y||^p, enabling learning of p-specific transport maps and dynamics with theoretical exactness guarantees.

Method: PMOT parameterizes the Continuous Normalizing Flow (CNF) velocity field as a scalar potential gradient in the generalized Benamou-Brenier form for exponent p. Training uses a self-induced matching loss along straight bridges defined by the model's own endpoints, combined with flexible terminal distribution matching (e.g., likelihood-based or MMD-based).

Result: The main theoretical result is zero-loss exactness: any zero-loss solution satisfying regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness assumptions recovers the generalized Benamou-Brenier optimality system and the p-optimal transport map. Empirically, PMOT matches p-specific OT references on synthetic benchmarks, remains competitive as a density model on tabular data, and demonstrates flexible sample-based terminal matching via MMD color transfer.

Conclusion: PMOT provides a theoretically grounded, flexible framework for learning p-cost optimal transport maps and dynamics, with strong exactness guarantees and competitive empirical performance across diverse tasks.

Abstract: We introduce Potential Matching Optimal Transport (PMOT), a potential-flow framework for general $p$-cost optimal transport with $c_p(x,y)=\|x-y\|^p$. PMOT parameterizes the CNF velocity field with a scalar potential in the generalized Benamou--Brenier form for the chosen exponent $p$. It trains the potential gradient with a self-induced matching loss along straight bridges determined by the model's own endpoints, while allowing flexible terminal distribution matching. Our main result establishes zero-loss exactness: under the stated regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness assumptions, any zero-loss solution satisfies the generalized Benamou--Brenier optimality system and recovers the corresponding $p$-optimal transport map and dynamics. On synthetic benchmarks, PMOT learns $p$-specific maps that agree with the corresponding $p$-matched OT references. It also remains competitive as a likelihood-based density model on high-dimensional tabular data, and an MMD-based color transformation experiment demonstrates flexible sample-based terminal matching.

</details>


### [273] [When Does Consensus Mean Correctness? Measuring the Agreement-Accuracy Coupling with Semantics-Preserving Re-Rendering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05670)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RENDEQ generates render-equivalent scientific figures from data programs, enabling exact measurement of the agreement–correctness coupling in VLMs. Re-rendering outperforms resampling; agreement outperforms token log-probability on most models. However, fine-tuning on cross-render consensus degrades accuracy, reversing prior natural-image findings — agreement only signals correctness above an error-diffuseness threshold that the objective itself destroys.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work uses input-perturbation agreement both as a reliability signal and a self-training target, assuming agreement tracks correctness. This coupling is rarely measured directly because natural-image perturbations lack guaranteed semantic equivalence and have no exact ground truth. Scientific figures eliminate both confounds: they are generated by data-to-image programs, so re-rendering produces semantically identical images with an exact answer key. The authors exploit this to rigorously measure the agreement–correctness relationship.

Method: The authors build RENDEQ, a generator that produces render-equivalence sets — multiple images from the same underlying data program, varying rendering factors (plotting library, style, etc.) while preserving semantic content. They evaluate three open-weight VLMs, measuring: (1) whether re-rendering beats resampling on accuracy and reliability; (2) whether cross-render agreement outperforms mean token log-probability as a correctness signal; and (3) the effect of fine-tuning on the model's own cross-render consensus. Every finding is replicated across three independent instantiations.

Result: Re-rendering outperforms resampling on both accuracy and reliability metrics. Agreement beats the evidence-carrying baseline (mean token log-probability) on two of three VLMs and ties on the third — though an intermediate buggy replication (traced to a rendering-pipeline failure) initially reversed this. Dispersion is concentrated in one style factor (plotting library), with effect size more than double the next factor and an order of magnitude above the noise floor. Critically, fine-tuning on cross-render consensus inverts: accuracy drops in all five replication runs, opposite to published natural-image results. The interpretation: agreement certifies correctness only when errors are diffuse; optimizing for agreement collapses that diffuseness, destroying the signal.

Conclusion: The agreement–correctness coupling is real but conditional: it holds only above a threshold of error diffuseness. Self-training on agreement is self-defeating because it destroys the very error distribution that makes agreement informative. Scientific-figure render-equivalence sets provide a clean, exact-ground-truth testbed for evaluating reliability signals in VLMs, revealing failure modes that natural-image benchmarks obscure.

Abstract: A model's agreement across perturbed inputs is used both as a label-free reliability signal and as a self-training target, on the premise that agreement tracks correctness. That coupling is rarely measured directly: natural-image perturbations preserve meaning only by assumption, and no exact answer key localizes errors. Scientific figures remove both obstacles, a figure is drawn from data by a program, so redrawing it yields images that are semantically equivalent by construction and share a programmatically exact answer. We build RENDEQ, a generator of such render-equivalence sets, and measure the coupling on three open-weight VLMs, checking every finding across three independent instantiations. Re-rendering beats resampling on both accuracy and reliability. Agreement beats an evidence-carrying baseline, mean token log-probability, on two of three models and ties on the third, reversing an intermediate, buggy replication traced to a rendering-pipeline failure. The dispersion behind this is concentrated in one style factor, the plotting library, more than double the next-largest factor and an order of magnitude above the noise floor. Fine-tuning on the model's own cross-render consensus inverts: accuracy falls in every one of five replication runs, the opposite sign to published results on natural images. Agreement certifies correctness only above a threshold set by how diffuse a model's errors are, and an objective that rewards agreement destroys exactly that diffuseness.

</details>


### [274] [Consistency Has a Computable Blind Spot: A Commutation Theory of Label-Free Reliability for Vision-Language Figure Reading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05675)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formalizes why invariance-based reliability testing for vision-language models has a fundamental blind spot: errors that commute with perturbation edits are undetectable. The authors characterize this via commutativity and centralizers, then propose equivariance as a complementary principle—where correct answers must change predictably under data edits. They operationalize this as the Equivariance-Consistency Score and release the REND-EQUIV benchmark, demonstrating that their theoretical ordering of detectability holds empirically across multiple models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Invariance-based testing (perturb input, expect unchanged output) is widely used to assess vision-language model reliability without labels, but it has a known but under-formalized blind spot: systematic misreading errors can survive perturbations and get falsely certified as correct. The authors aim to rigorously characterize which errors are invisible to which edit suites, and to develop a complementary testing paradigm (equivariance) that catches errors invariance misses.

Method: The paper leverages algebraic characterizations: (1) An error is invisible to an edit iff the two commute, so undetectable errors form the joint centralizer of the edit suite. (2) Equivariance is introduced as the dual relation: when data are edited, the correct answer must change by a computable, known amount. Two matched edits provably yield completeness for affine reading errors. For label permutations, no suite of swap edits is complete, but cyclic relabeling closes most of the gap. (3) The Equivariance-Consistency Score instantiates this theory as a training-free, label-free detector. (4) The REND-EQUIV benchmark pairs matched invariance and equivariance tests over identical data. (5) Empirical validation uses three models and a hand-labeled population selected to avoid circularity, with a second invariance-family method as a sanity check.

Result: The predicted ordering of detectability holds across three models on the hand-labeled population. A second invariance-family method confirms the blind spot is a property of the relation itself, not of any specific implementation. Cyclic relabeling delivers its predicted empirical gain on a matched real sample. The framework also explains a reported inversion in the classifier metamorphic-testing literature: detectability is a joint property of the relation and the fault class, never of the relation alone.

Conclusion: Invariance-based reliability testing has a computable, structural blind spot rooted in commutativity. Equivariance provides a rigorous complementary testing principle. The joint characterization—detectability depends on both the testing relation and the fault class—unifies the proposed framework with prior observations in metamorphic testing, and the REND-EQUIV benchmark offers a concrete tool for label-free, training-free reliability assessment of vision-language models.

Abstract: Label-free reliability for vision-language models rests on invariance: perturb the input and a faithful reader's answer should not change. This has a known blind spot, a systematic misreading survives the perturbation and gets certified wrong, which we show is computable, not just real: an error is invisible to an edit exactly when the two commute, so the errors a suite cannot reach form its joint centralizer, a set that shrinks as edits are added and can be written down rather than guessed at. We act on the complementary relation, equivariance: edit a figure's data and the correct answer must change by a computable amount. Two matched edits are provably complete for affine reading errors; no suite of swap edits is complete for label permutations, and cyclic relabeling closes most of that gap. We instantiate the theory as the Equivariance-Consistency Score, a label-free, training-free detector, and release REND-EQUIV, pairing matched invariance and equivariance sets over identical data. The predicted ordering holds across three models and a hand-labeled population immune to the one circularity in how it is selected; a second invariance-family method confirms the blind spot belongs to the relation, not to any implementation; and cyclic relabeling delivers its predicted gain on a matched real sample. The same characterization explains a reported inversion of this ordering in the classifier metamorphic-testing literature: detectability is a joint property of the relation and the fault class, never of the relation alone.

</details>


### [275] [SEAM: Global consistency beyond local accuracy in scientific machine learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05702)
*Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan,Bum Jun Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SEAM introduces a framework for checking whether local scientific explanations (across regions, sensors, regimes) can be assembled into a globally consistent account, using an explanation-sheaf formalism that detects, locates, and attributes inconsistencies via channel-resolved obstructions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current scientific ML validation practices (subdomain checks, benchmark splits, single-prediction explanations) fail to test whether local explanations cohere into a globally admissible scientific account. There is no computable framework for assessing this local-to-global consistency.

Method: SEAM-Ω instantiates an explanation-sheaf where each region carries state, closure, and observation channels plus contract metadata. Neighboring explanations are compared on overlaps; disagreements become channel-resolved obstructions. The framework supports exact feasibility testing (refuting/retaining accounts), residual-aware regularized records for attribution, separation of inconsistency from non-identifiability, and distribution-shift monitoring of generators. Theorems cover minimum-cost intervention and conservation-contract detectability.

Result: Across 19 experiments with synthetic PDE systems and out-of-distribution FNO monitoring, SEAM detects incompatible explanations even under accurate local predictions, attributing failures to specific channels and overlaps.

Conclusion: SEAM provides a global explanation-consistency audit for existing solvers and learned models, testing whether local explanations form a coherent scientific account — complementing rather than replacing local validation practices.

Abstract: Scientific machine learning commonly validates models at the level of a subdomain, a benchmark split, or an explanation for one prediction. Yet such local checks cannot establish whether the resulting explanations can be assembled into one globally admissible explanation. We introduce Scientific Explanation-Admissibility Machines (SEAM), a generator-agnostic framework that makes this local-to-global consistency question computable across regions, sensors, regimes, and model components. The finite explanation-sheaf instantiation SEAM-$Ω$ represents each region by a structured explanation with state, closure, and observation channels together with optional contract metadata; compares neighboring explanations on their overlaps; and converts disagreement into a channel-resolved obstruction. This obstruction locates inconsistency and tests competing declared accounts by restricting each repair to the revisions that one account permits. Exact feasibility refutes or retains an account; when exact repair is unavailable, residual-aware regularized records provide a separately labeled empirical attribution. The framework also separates inconsistency from non-identifiability and monitors learned generators under distribution shift. We establish theorems for minimum-cost intervention and conservation-contract detectability, together with companion results for identifiability and closure recoverability. Across nineteen experiments involving synthetic partial differential equation systems and out-of-distribution Fourier neural operator (FNO) monitoring, SEAM detects incompatible explanations even when local predictions are accurate, and attributes failures to specific channels and overlaps. SEAM adds a global explanation-consistency audit to existing solvers and learning models, testing whether their local explanations form a coherent scientific account.

</details>


### [276] [Spectral Aliasing Pretext: A novel task for Self-Supervised fault diagnosis in rotating machinery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05705)
*Victor Gialis,Maxime Metz,David Esteve,Abdenour Soualhi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAP is a self-supervised pretraining method for fault diagnosis that reconstructs original spectra from deliberately aliased (undersampled) vibration signals, enabling strong performance with minimal labeled data via linear probing, outperforming fully supervised approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning for machinery fault diagnosis requires extensive labeled data, which is scarce and expensive to obtain in industrial settings. Existing self-supervised methods often rely on data augmentations that may destroy diagnostically relevant signal characteristics. There is a need for a pretraining strategy that learns meaningful fault-related representations from unlabeled vibration data without destructive augmentations.

Method: The authors propose Spectral Aliasing Pretext (SAP), a self-supervised pretraining framework. Unlabeled vibration signals are deliberately undersampled, causing spectral aliasing (frequency folding). A Transformer model is then trained to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum from the aliased version. This pretext task compels the model to learn frequency-domain invariants characteristic of mechanical faults. After pretraining, the model is evaluated using linear probing — freezing the encoder and training only a linear classifier on a small fraction of labeled data. Comparisons are made against full fine-tuning and fully supervised training.

Result: On the CWRU dataset, SAP-pretrained models with linear probing achieved high classification accuracy using only a small fraction of labeled data, with low variance across runs. Full fine-tuning and fully supervised training did not yield more stable or superior results, suggesting that SAP's frozen representations are already highly discriminative and robust.

Conclusion: SAP combined with linear probing is more effective and reliable than fully supervised training for fault diagnosis under limited-label regimes. The approach demonstrates that frequency-domain reconstruction from spectral aliasing is a powerful self-supervised pretext task for learning fault-discriminative representations without destructive augmentations.

Abstract: Deep learning is a new way for machinery fault diagnosis but requires extensive labeled data, a scarce resource in industrial settings. We propose Spectral Aliasing Pretext (SAP), a self-supervised learning method that pretrains models on unlabeled vibration data by exploiting spectral aliasing. We deliberately undersample signals to create folded spectrum, then train a Transformer to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum. This pretext task forces the model to learn frequency-domain invariants characteristic of mechanical faults, without potentially destructive augmentations. Experiments on the CWRU dataset show that SAP learns stable and highly discriminative representations. In a linear probing setting, SAP quickly achieves very high classification performance with only a small fraction of labeled data and low variance. In contrast, full fine-tuning, including fully supervised training, does not lead to more stable or better results. Overall, these findings suggest that SAP combined with linear probing can be more effective and reliable than fully supervised training for fault diagnosis with limited labeled data.

</details>


### [277] [CircuitSteer: Geometrically Aligned Multi-Layer Steering via Sparse Autoencoder Circuits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05732)
*Mehrshad Saadatinia,Parsa Razmara,Ardalan Aryashad,Ali Abbasi,Seyedarmin Azizi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CircuitSteer uses Sparse Autoencoders to identify multi-layer semantic circuits and applies multi-point steering interventions, outperforming single-layer methods like CAA across toxicity, sycophancy, refusal, and emotion-intensity tasks while preserving text fluency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM steering methods (e.g., CAA) rely on fixed single-layer interventions from aggregate activation differences. These fail to sustain consistent behavioral changes across layers and struggle with semantically diverse inputs, limiting steering effectiveness. The authors aim to overcome these limitations through multi-layer, circuit-aware interventions.

Method: CircuitSteer leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract interpretable features across layers, then constructs a feature flow circuit by tracking feature co-activation and measuring geometric alignment (cosine similarity) of decoder weight directions. This isolates the multi-layer subcircuit responsible for the target behavior. Dense steering vectors are synthesized from these sparse features, and multi-point interventions are applied along the circuit to guide the model's internal semantic trajectory.

Result: Evaluated on toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, and refusal tasks across two model families, CircuitSteer was the only method to consistently preserve output fluency while achieving effective behavioral steering. Competing methods either degraded text quality or failed entirely on complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal.

Conclusion: Multi-layer circuit steering with geometrically aligned feature selection provides strictly more robust and effective behavioral control than static single-point interventions, establishing a new state-of-the-art for activation-based LLM steering.

Abstract: Controlling the behavior of large language models (LLMs) remains a critical challenge for AI alignment. Existing steering methods, such as Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), typically rely on fixed single-layer interventions derived from aggregate activation differences. These methods impose a single intervention across semantically diverse inputs and often fail to sustain consistent behavioral changes across layers, limiting the effectiveness of the steering. In this work, we introduce CircuitSteer, a novel framework that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify and manipulate coherent semantic circuits distributed across multiple layers. By constructing a feature flow circuit based on feature co-activation and the geometric alignment of decoder directions, we isolate the specific multi-layer subcircuits responsible for a target behavior. We then synthesize dense steering vectors from these sparse features and apply multi-point interventions to guide the model's internal semantic trajectory. We evaluate CircuitSteer using contrastive examples across a diverse set of tasks, including toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, and refusal, spanning two model families. Across all models and datasets, CircuitSteer is the only method to consistently produce fluency-preserving interventions; competing methods either sacrifice text quality or lack coverage, failing entirely on complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal. These results demonstrate that multi-layer circuit steering, enabled by enforcing geometric alignment among selected features, yields strictly more robust and effective behavioral control than static single-point interventions. Code is available at https://github.com/mehrshad-sdtn/CircuitSteer.

</details>


### [278] [Multivariate Time Series Forecasting needs Cross Variable Loss](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05742)
*Kuiye Ding,Yifan Hu,Hanchen Wang,Hao Xue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies an "objective gap" in Direct Forecasting (DF) for multivariate time series—DF's point-wise loss does not constrain cross-variable structure among future values. The authors propose Cross-Variable Loss (CvLoss), a plug-in regularizer that enforces consistency of residual differences on a cross-variable graph across forecast patches, improving multiple forecasting backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multivariate time series forecasting models primarily exploit cross-variable dependencies in historical observations but neglect dependencies among future values. The dominant Direct Forecasting paradigm uses point-wise objectives that fail to explicitly constrain the co-evolution structure of forecasted variables, creating a mismatch (objective gap) when cross-variable and lagged dependencies exist.

Method: The authors propose CvLoss, a plug-in structural regularizer that operates on a cross-variable graph. It penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences over forecast patches, encouraging consistency across both synchronous (same time step) and asynchronous (lagged) cross-variable interactions. CvLoss is designed as a model-agnostic addition to standard point-wise forecasting objectives.

Result: Experiments show that CvLoss consistently improves competitive forecasting models, outperforms representative learning objectives, and is compatible with a variety of forecasting backbones.

Conclusion: The DF objective is mismatched for multivariate forecasting due to its neglect of cross-variable future dependencies. CvLoss effectively bridges this objective gap by enforcing structural consistency on a cross-variable graph, serving as a general-purpose regularizer that broadly enhances forecasting performance across diverse architectures.

Abstract: Multivariate time series forecasting presents unique challenges because future variables often co-evolve under shared system dynamics. While existing studies mainly focus on cross-variable dependencies in historical observations, dependencies among future values are much less explored. Specifically, modern forecasting models largely follow the Direct Forecasting (DF) paradigm, generating multi-step forecasts with point-wise objectives that do not explicitly constrain cross-variable structure. In this work, we show that the DF objective is mismatched in the presence of cross-variable and lagged dependencies, revealing an objective gap. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{C}ross-\textbf{V}ariable \textbf{Loss} (CvLoss), a plug-in structural regularizer that constrains forecast residuals on a cross-variable graph. CvLoss penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences over forecast patches, encouraging consistency across both synchronous and asynchronous interactions. Our experiments show that CvLoss consistently improves competitive forecasting models, outperforms representative learning objectives, and is compatible with a variety of forecasting backbones.

</details>


### [279] [Equipment-centric workpiece localization in near real-time using deep learning-based vision and event-driven finite state machines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05744)
*Dohyeon Kong,Jaebong Cho,Hyunbo Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A vision-based, equipment-centric framework using multi-camera 3D pose estimation and keypoint-guided 3D CNNs for activity recognition achieves 100% event detection accuracy and 317.8 mm mean localization error in a hot forging factory, enabling continuous workpiece tracking without direct observation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Direct workpiece tracking in hot forging is infeasible due to extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing. Continuous localization remains essential for traceability and process coordination, motivating an indirect, equipment-centric inference approach.

Method: The framework employs multiple static 2D cameras to estimate 3D equipment coordinates in floorplan space. A keypoint-guided attention mechanism within a 3D convolutional neural network recognizes grasp and release activities. Event-driven finite state machines validate these activities as discrete handling events and continuously update workpiece states and locations.

Result: In an operational hot forging factory, the system achieved 100% event detection accuracy within a 33-second tolerance window, 317.8 mm mean localization error, and 21 seconds mean system latency.

Conclusion: The framework successfully bridges vision-based perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning, enabling both visualization of workpiece transfers and quantitative analysis of equipment operations in a challenging industrial environment.

Abstract: Continuous workpiece localization is essential for traceability and process coordination in hot forging, but direct tracking is unreliable because of extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing. This study presents an equipment-centric framework that infers workpiece locations from handling equipment observed by multiple static 2D cameras. The framework estimates floorplan-space 3D equipment coordinates and recognizes grasp and release activities. Event-driven finite state machines validate these activities as discrete handling events and continuously update workpiece states and locations. A keypoint-guided attention mechanism integrated into a 3D convolutional neural network improves activity recognition by focusing on functionally relevant equipment regions. Evaluation in an operational hot forging factory achieved 100\% event detection accuracy within a 33-second tolerance window, a mean localization error of 317.8 mm, and a mean system latency of 21 seconds. The framework connects vision-based perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning and supports visualization of workpiece transfers and quantitative analysis of equipment operations.

</details>


### [280] [Accelerating nanodrug development in continuous flow systems using informed prediction models based on low-cost surrogate nanoparticles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05761)
*Kai Dahms,Eilien Heinrich,Jochen Schmid,Michael Bortz,Iryna Savych,Regina Bleul*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A shape-constrained predictive modeling approach is introduced to accurately estimate nanoparticle size and PDI under varying process conditions, reducing the need for extensive empirical optimization in nanomedicine manufacturing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Nanoparticle properties (size, PDI) are highly sensitive to minor process parameter changes, yet no predictive mathematical frameworks exist, forcing reliance on costly, time-consuming iterative experimental screening.

Method: Shape-constrained modeling informed by experimental data and expert knowledge; systematic preparation of liposomes and lipid nanoparticles using controlled microfluidics under varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and aqueous-to-organic mixing ratios; validated with minimal empirical data for a pharmaceutical application.

Result: The shape-constrained model achieved accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity, substantially reducing the experimental workload required for process development.

Conclusion: Shape-constrained modeling offers a rational, efficient framework for nanomedicine process development, enabling reliable predictions with minimal empirical input and supporting streamlined manufacturing workflows.

Abstract: The development of nanotherapeutics often involves extensive empirical optimization due to the sensitivity of nanoparticle properties, such as size and polydispersity index (PDI), to minor changes in process parameters. Factors like formulation concentration, flow rates, and mixing ratios can significantly influence clinical efficacy and therapeutic outcomes. The absence of predictive mathematical frameworks has made iterative experimental screening necessary, increasing both costs and development time.
  This study introduces and validates a predictive modeling approach based on shape constraints, aiming to enhance the estimation of nanoparticle characteristics across various process conditions. Using controlled microfluidic methods, liposomes and lipid nanoparticles were systematically prepared under varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and aqueous-to-organic mixing ratios.
  The shape-constrained model, informed by both experimental data and expert knowledge, was subsequently validated for a pharmaceutical application using minimal empirical data. Results reveal that shape-constrained modeling facilitates accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity, reducing the need for extensive experimental workflows. This framework supports rational and efficient process development for manufacturing nanomedicine systems.

</details>


### [281] [Neuro-Symbolic Closed-Loop Control of Laser Powder Bed Fusion with an In-Loop Ontology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05773)
*Gisuk Hong,Jaebong Cho,Hyunbo Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture for LPBF that uses an ontology and description-logic reasoner to dynamically set controller constraints, demonstrated by eliminating overhang dross through a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio supplied by a Gaussian process.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) controllers lack geometric awareness, leading to quality defects like overhang dross that depend on melt pool depth — a variable that cannot be directly measured during the build. There is a need for an architecture that can reason about geometric context and enforce appropriate process constraints in real time.

Method: A closed-loop architecture integrating (1) a standards-aligned ontology operating inside the control loop, (2) a description-logic reasoner that classifies geometric features and selects active constraints (e.g., lack-of-fusion floor, monotone guard, energy-density cap), (3) a Gaussian process mapping unmeasurable melt pool depth to observable width via a geometry- and power-dependent ratio, and (4) a constraint-aware predictive controller solving small quadratic programs per scan. Validated on an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to NIST AM-Bench IN625 data.

Result: The architecture eliminated dross produced by a geometry-blind controller, maintained dross at zero with only small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring, degraded gracefully under deliberate plant mismatch, and supported retargeting to new alloys/constraints via ontology edits rather than code changes.

Conclusion: Architectural feasibility is established. The principal next step is experimental calibration of the depth-to-width ratio. The neuro-symbolic approach demonstrates a practical pathway for integrating domain knowledge with learning in manufacturing process control.

Abstract: A geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture is proposed for laser powder bed fusion, in which a standards-aligned ontology operates inside the control loop and couples symbolic reasoning with statistical learning to set the targets of a constraint-aware predictive controller. The ontology links the process objectives and constraints to the signals a controller can observe, and a description-logic reasoner converts them into the references and bounds enforced on each scan. The demonstrated case is overhang dross, a quality limit on the melt pool depth, which governs quality yet cannot be measured during the build, is mapped through a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio onto a bound on the observable width, with the ratio and its calibrated uncertainty supplied by a Gaussian process. The reasoner classifies each upcoming feature and selects the active constraints-adding a lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs, a monotone guard beyond the calibrated range, and an energy-density cap where a process window is declared while running only on changes of geometric context and otherwise leaving a single small quadratic program on the per-scan path. In an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to the NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625, the architecture eliminates the dross produced by a geometry-blind controller, holds dross at zero with only a small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring, degrades gracefully under deliberate plant mismatch, and retargets to new alloys and constraints by editing ontology data rather than code. The results establish architectural feasibility, experimental calibration of the ratio is the principal next step.

</details>


### [282] [GROM: Gradient-Free Rapid One-Shot Machine Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05783)
*Paweł Batorski,Przemysław Spurek,Paul Swoboda*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GROM is a one-shot, closed-form machine unlearning method for LLMs that uses ridge-regularized least-squares to directly edit weight matrices via forward passes only, achieving state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs in seconds while resisting quantization attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current iterative gradient-based unlearning methods (e.g., LoRA fine-tuning) are computationally expensive, lack analytical formulations, and often merely hide targeted knowledge rather than truly removing it — as evidenced by quantization attacks that recover supposedly erased content. A fast, exact, and robust alternative is needed.

Method: GROM frames unlearning as a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem, deriving a closed-form additive update for targeted weight matrices. The update is computed from gradient-free forward passes only (no backpropagation, no iterative convergence), applied in seconds. It suppresses unwanted content while preserving behavior on retained data.

Result: GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News, and WMDP benchmarks, with orders-of-magnitude speed gains over fine-tuning. It also withstands low-bit quantization attacks that recover content from gradient-based baselines.

Conclusion: A direct analytical solution for unlearning is not only feasible but superior to iterative fine-tuning — it is faster, more theoretically principled, and yields more robust removal that survives quantization.

Abstract: Machine unlearning has become a critical capability for safely removing specific, sensitive knowledge from large language models (LLMs). Current state-of-the-art approaches primarily rely on iterative, training-time unlearning via fine-tuning. However, even when utilizing parameter-efficient dimensionality reduction techniques like LoRA, gradient-based optimization remains computationally expensive and lacks explicit analytical formulations. It can also leave the targeted knowledge merely hidden rather than removed, to the point that simply quantizing the unlearned model restores much of what it was supposed to have erased. To resolve this, we propose a novel one-shot unlearning approach, abandoning iterative optimization in favor of a direct, exact analytical solution. We frame the unlearning process as a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem, deriving a closed-form additive update for targeted weight matrices. This update forces the selected layer to suppress unwanted content while strictly preserving its behavior on retained data. Computed from gradient-free forward passes alone, with no backpropagation and no iteration to convergence, GROM applies the weight edit in mere seconds, which makes it orders of magnitude faster than traditional fine-tuning. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News and WMDP, significantly reducing computational overhead without sacrificing overall model performance. Because the update removes the targeted content from the weights instead of masking it, GROM also withstands the low-bit quantization attack that recovers much of the content a gradient-based baseline had appeared to forget. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/GROM.

</details>


### [283] [Predicting Task Difficulty Without Rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05797)
*Stefan Krsteski,Charlotte Meyer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies ex ante difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks, showing that AUC can mask poor estimates, token-level entropy is a useful predictive signal, and residuals between expected and observed difficulty can expose hidden flaws like contamination and infeasibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Estimating task difficulty without costly rollouts is critical for calibrating benchmarks and building training curricula, especially as agents move into long-horizon domains where empirical trial-and-error is computationally prohibitive. Prior work is limited to static tasks or isolated coding environments with narrow features and inaccurate metrics.

Method: The authors conduct a large-scale empirical study of ex ante difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, ML, web navigation, and function calling. They evaluate AUC as a metric, propose token-level entropy as a predictive signal, and analyze residuals between predicted and observed difficulty to detect environment flaws.

Result: AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, token-level entropy serves as a useful predictive signal for task difficulty, and residual analysis between expected and observed difficulty reveals hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.

Conclusion: Reliable ex ante difficulty prediction is feasible and valuable; token-level entropy and residual analysis offer practical tools for benchmark calibration and curriculum design, while AUC alone is insufficient for evaluating prediction quality.

Abstract: Task difficulty dictates an agent's likelihood of success, and estimating it without rollouts means forecasting this directly from a task description before executing costly simulations in stateful environments. Reliable estimates would therefore allow environment designers to calibrate evaluation benchmarks and construct progressive training curricula. This becomes increasingly important as agents move into long-horizon domains, where empirical trial-and-error is a severe computational bottleneck. Prior work on early prediction is limited to static tasks or isolated coding environments, often relying on narrow features and inaccurate evaluation metrics. We study \textit{ex ante} difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, machine learning, web navigation, function calling, and other domains. We show that AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, identify token-level entropy as a useful predictive signal, and show how residuals between expected and observed difficulty can expose hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.

</details>


### [284] [Learning to Rank Tensor Network Contraction Plans for GPU-Accelerated Quantum Circuit Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05819)
*Alfred M. Pastor,Maribel Castillo,Jose M. Badia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a learning-to-rank framework that uses gradient-boosted models to select efficient tensor-network contraction plans for quantum circuit simulation on GPUs, trained on structural features and GPU measurements. Listwise ranking achieves the best decision quality, and the rankings show substantial (though not perfect) stability across GPU architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits via tensor-network contraction is crucial for algorithm development but computationally expensive. Contraction plans with similar theoretical cost can exhibit drastically different GPU performance due to parallelism, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. Exhaustive plan search is infeasible, so a predictive method is needed to select efficient plans before execution.

Method: Each contraction plan is encoded with structural features extracted from its sequence of pairwise contractions. Gradient-boosted decision trees (LambdaMART for listwise, RankNet for pairwise) are trained on GPU execution time measurements. Models are evaluated under in-distribution and circuit-family-shift conditions, plus a backend-shift experiment where models trained on one GPU are tested on another without retraining. Baselines include random selection and the MinFill heuristic.

Result: Learned rankers outperform both random and MinFill baselines. The listwise (LambdaMART) model delivers the strongest overall decision quality. Rankings remain substantially stable across two GPU architectures, and source-trained models retain useful decision quality when evaluated on a different device, though performance is not perfectly backend-independent.

Conclusion: Learning to Rank is a practical approach for reducing contraction-plan search cost in tensor-network simulation. While plan quality rankings generalize reasonably across GPU backends, some backend dependence persists, suggesting that optimal deployment may benefit from device-aware training or calibration.

Abstract: Classical simulation remains essential for developing and validating quantum algorithms, but its cost grows rapidly with circuit size. Tensor-network contraction can reduce this cost by exploiting circuit structure, although its efficiency depends strongly on the chosen contraction plan. On GPUs, plans with similar theoretical complexity may perform very differently because execution also depends on parallelism, reduction structure, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. We present a learning-to-rank framework for selecting efficient contraction plans before executing them. Each plan is represented by structural features derived directly from its sequence of pairwise contractions, and gradient-boosted rankers are trained from GPU measurements using listwise and pairwise objectives. We evaluate the resulting models on diverse circuit families, using separate in-distribution and circuit-family-shift test sets, and compare them with random and MinFill-based baselines. The learned rankers generally identify better plans, with the listwise model providing the strongest overall decision quality. We also study backend shift by comparing empirical plan orderings on two GPU architectures and evaluating the source-trained models on the second device without retraining. The rankings remain substantially, though not perfectly, stable across GPUs, and the models retain useful decision quality. These results support Learning to Rank as a practical way to reduce contraction-plan search, while showing that performance remains partly backend dependent.

</details>


### [285] [Evidential Rule Learning for Interpretable Classification with Abstention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05859)
*Javier Fumanal-Idocin,Javier Andreu-Perez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FERL is a fuzzy rule learning method that produces inherently evidential outputs (belief, plausibility, abstention) in a single forward pass, offering interpretable classification with native uncertainty quantification, strong predictive accuracy, and reliable out-of-distribution detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world deployment of classifiers requires not just accuracy but also transparent evidence for decisions and the ability to abstain when uncertain. Existing rule learners lack native evidential reasoning, while post-hoc calibration methods add complexity (auxiliary heads, held-out sets, repeated inference). There is a need for a unified, interpretable model that provides both accurate predictions and principled uncertainty estimates without extra overhead.

Method: FERL learns interpretable fuzzy rule models whose rule activations are derived from fuzzy memberships. The evidential outputs—belief, plausibility, and abstention—emerge directly from these fuzzy memberships in a single deterministic forward pass, requiring no auxiliary components. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis proving FERL is Lipschitz stable, ensuring smooth variation of evidential outputs with input perturbations.

Result: On a 30-dataset tabular benchmark, FERL achieves statistically significantly higher accuracy (+2.6% over the second-best rule learner). For set predictions, it yields the best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers (u65/u80 = 0.80/0.83) with higher set coverage (0.92 vs. ≤0.82). On tabular near-OOD detection, FERL matches dedicated detectors (77.7 vs. 77.4 AUROC). Under concept-bottleneck evaluation on CUB and AwA2, it is within 2.3 AUROC points of the strongest dedicated detector while achieving best AwA2 AUPR-Out (68.3) and novel-class rejection (57.2), and can name anomalous attributes.

Conclusion: FERL successfully unifies interpretable fuzzy rule learning with native evidential reasoning, delivering competitive or superior accuracy, reliable uncertainty quantification, and strong OOD detection—all without the overhead of post-hoc calibration. Its Lipschitz stability guarantees smooth, trustworthy evidential outputs, making it suitable for safety-critical, transparent deployments.

Abstract: Interpretable classification often requires more than accurate predictions for real-life deployment: models should be transparent about the evidence behind their decisions and abstain when they cannot decide reliably. We introduce Fast Evidential Rule Learning (FERL), a method that learns interpretable, accurate fuzzy rule models whose outputs are evidential. Unlike post-hoc calibration, FERL's belief, plausibility, and abstention capabilities arise directly from the fuzzy memberships in a single deterministic pass, with no auxiliary head, held-out set, or repeated inference. Our theoretical analysis further shows that FERL is Lipschitz stable, which means that its evidential outputs vary smoothly with the input. Against state-of-the-art rule learners, FERL is statistically significantly more accurate across a 30 tabular-dataset benchmark ($+2.6\%$ average accuracy over the second best). Its native set predictions attain the best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers ($u_{65}/u_{80}=0.80/0.83$ vs.\ $0.79/0.80$ for the naive credal classifier), at higher set coverage ($0.92$ vs.\ $\le0.82$). FERL also matches dedicated out-of-distribution detectors on tabular near-OOD detection ($77.7$ vs.\ $77.4$ AUROC for the strongest baseline). Under detector-class-disjoint concept-bottleneck evaluation, its it is within $2.3$ AUROC points of the strongest dedicated detector on both CUB and AwA2, while attaining the best AwA2 AUPR-Out ($68.3$) and novel-class rejection ($57.2$), while being able to name which attributes are anomalous.

</details>


### [286] [Beyond Feature Importance: A Comparative Analysis of Pattern Detection Methods in Cluster Interpretation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05880)
*Benjamin Connor,Anna Jurek-Loughrey,Lu Bai,Muhammad Fahim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Existing explainability methods (Random Forest surrogates, LIME, PCA) fail to consistently detect structured patterns within clustering results, revealing a critical gap that motivates dedicated pattern detection methodologies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current explainability techniques focus on feature importance or local instance-level explanations rather than identifying structured patterns within clusters. This is particularly problematic in domains like healthcare, where interpreting clustering outcomes requires detecting meaningful, structured patterns in high-dimensional data.

Method: The authors conducted a comparative evaluation of three widely used post-hoc analysis methods — Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and principal component analysis (PCA) — for pattern detection in clustering results. A suite of synthetic datasets with systematically injected predefined patterns was introduced to enable controlled evaluation.

Result: Each method can successfully recover relevant features, but none consistently detects all injected pattern types. This demonstrates a systematic limitation across all three techniques when applied to pattern-level cluster interpretation.

Conclusion: A critical gap exists between current explainability tools and the requirements of pattern-level cluster interpretation, underscoring the need for developing dedicated pattern detection methodologies tailored to clustering outcomes.

Abstract: Interpreting clustering outcomes remains a fundamental challenge in data analysis, particularly in domains such as healthcare where meaningful patterns must be extracted from high-dimensional data. While numerous explainability techniques exist, they are primarily designed to assess feature importance or provide local instance-level explanations rather than to identify structured patterns present within clusters. This work presents a comparative evaluation of commonly used post-hoc analysis methods for pattern detection in clustering results. To enable controlled evaluation, we introduce a suite of synthetic datasets in which predefined patterns are systematically injected. Three widely used techniques are evaluated: a Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and principal component analysis. Results demonstrate that although each method can successfully recover relevant features, none consistently detects all injected pattern types. These findings high- light a critical gap between existing explainability tools and the requirements of pattern-level cluster interpretation, motivating the development of dedicated pattern detection methodologies.

</details>


### [287] [Alternating Levenberg-Marquardt Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Fourier-Enhanced Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05892)
*Yulun Wu,Matthieu Barreau,Miguel Aguiar,Karl H. Johansson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FALM-PINN is an optimization framework that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting in PINNs. It uses Fourier-enhanced basis functions in an upper-level problem and solves a nonlinear least-squares problem via Levenberg–Marquardt in a lower-level problem, achieving up to two orders of magnitude improvement in relative L² error over state-of-the-art baselines on high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard PINNs suffer from two key failure modes: (1) spectral bias, where neural networks preferentially learn low-frequency features and underfit high-frequency components; and (2) representation-coefficient coupling, where representation learning and coefficient fitting are entangled within a single nonconvex optimization objective. These issues cause PINNs to fail on PDEs with high-frequency, multi-scale, or strongly nonlinear solutions.

Method: The authors propose FALM-PINN, a bilevel optimization framework. The upper-level subproblem learns a Fourier-enhanced basis that enriches the latent space with high-frequency components, decoupling representation learning. The lower-level subproblem fits projection coefficients on this basis by solving a nonlinear least-squares problem using the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm. For linear PDEs, the framework reduces to a single-step convex optimization. The alternating training scheme is proved to converge globally for both nonlinear and linear cases.

Result: Numerical experiments on challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs demonstrate that FALM-PINN achieves relative L² errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: Decoupling representation learning from coefficient fitting via a Fourier-enhanced alternating Levenberg–Marquardt approach effectively addresses both spectral bias and representation-coefficient coupling in PINNs, yielding significant accuracy gains on previously difficult PDE problems.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often fail to accurately resolve partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency or multi-scale solutions, as well as strongly nonlinear problems. Two factors underlie this difficulty: spectral bias, the tendency of neural networks to underfit high-frequency features; and representation-coefficient coupling, the entanglement of representation learning and coefficient fitting within a single nonconvex optimization objective. In this work, we propose the Fourier-enhanced alternating Levenberg--Marquardt PINN (FALM-PINN), an optimization framework that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting. The upper-level problem learns a Fourier-enhanced basis that enriches the latent space with high-frequency components, while the lower-level problem resolves the coupling by fitting the projection coefficients on this basis, solving a nonlinear least-squares problem with the Levenberg--Marquardt algorithm. The framework applies to general nonlinear and coupled PDE systems, and reduces to a single-step convex optimization problem for linear PDEs. We prove global convergence of the alternating training scheme in both cases. Numerical examples on multiple challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs show that FALM-PINN achieves relative $L^2$ errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [288] [CohortHijack: Robustness of Single Cell Annotation to Companion Cell Removal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05900)
*Arash Vashagh,Yasmin Vashagh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that neighborhood-based refinement in single-cell annotation tools can be manipulated by selectively removing non-target cells from the query cohort, without altering the target cell's expression profile, base prediction, or the trained model — a vulnerability the authors term "CohortHijack."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-cell annotation tools commonly refine initial predictions using neighborhood or cluster-level voting. The authors investigate whether this refinement step introduces a previously unrecognized attack surface: can an adversary change a target cell's final label simply by manipulating which companion cells are included in the query cohort, leaving the target cell itself completely untouched?

Method: The authors introduce CohortHijack, a robustness audit framework that removes selected non-target cells from the query cohort while preserving the target cell's expression profile, base prediction, and the trained model. They evaluate random and structured removal strategies, combined with greedy, multi-start, and beam search algorithms. Experiments were conducted on PBMC3K and Paul15 datasets using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers, with additional evaluation on CellTypist's majority voting mechanism. Ablation studies disabled neighborhood refinement to isolate its causal role.

Result: Structured removal consistently outperformed random removal on the Paul15 dataset. Multi-start search altered 24.33% of linear-SVM target predictions and 19.67% of logistic-regression target predictions while removing only a small fraction of the cohort, with mean collateral changes below 0.4%. Ablations confirmed that the effect disappeared when neighborhood refinement was disabled.
