For CellTypist, independent predictions remained unchanged, but refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals.

Conclusion: Query cohort composition constitutes a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation pipelines that rely on neighborhood-based refinement. This vulnerability allows an adversary to change a target cell's final label without modifying the target cell itself, the base classifier, or the underlying model — highlighting a critical robustness gap in widely used annotation workflows.

Abstract: Many single-cell annotation tools refine an initial cell label using nearby cells or cluster-level voting. We study whether this refinement can be manipulated without changing the target cell. We introduce CohortHijack, a robustness audit that removes selected non-target cells from the query cohort while preserving the target expression profile, base prediction, and trained model. We evaluate random and structured removal methods, together with greedy, multi-start, and beam search, on PBMC3K and Paul15 using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers. Structured removal was consistently stronger than random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search changed 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets while removing a small fraction of the cohort and keeping mean collateral changes below 0.4%. Ablations confirmed that the effect disappeared when neighborhood refinement was disabled. We also evaluated CellTypist majority voting, where independent predictions remained unchanged across all evaluations, but refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals. These findings identify query cohort composition as a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation.

</details>


### [289] [BioM-JEPA: joint-embedding prediction of graph-connected gene blocks in single cells](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05928)
*Yuhao Wang,Zelin Zang,Yuxuan Liu,Zhen Lei,Stan Z. Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BioM-JEPA introduces a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) for single-cell transcriptomics that predicts aggregate representations of graph-connected gene blocks rather than individual genes, producing embeddings with higher effective rank, lower gene-depth bias, and superior performance on perturbation-response benchmarks, while offering substantially higher throughput than scFoundation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current self-supervised models for single-cell transcriptomics reconstruct individual genes, ignoring that transcriptomes are sparse observations of coordinated biological programmes. The authors aim to learn better representations by predicting higher-level biological units—gene blocks—instead of individual tokens.

Method: BioM-JEPA uses a JEPA framework with a student-teacher architecture. Gene blocks are constructed using graph connectivity from protein-association networks and corpus-derived coexpression evidence. The student predicts each target block's aggregate representation from the remaining (context) genes, while an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher provides target representations from the full observed gene set. Linear attention avoids quadratic gene-by-gene matrix computation.

Result: Block-level prediction produced embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth compared to token-prediction, random-block, and reconstruction baselines. On CellBench tasks, frozen BioM-JEPA embeddings retained expression, pathway, and neighbourhood information and achieved the lowest aggregate perturbation-response error. Representations aligned with canonical pancreatic programmes and compositional perturbation relationships. Throughput benchmarks showed 5.75× higher fine-tuning and 3.76× higher held-out embedding throughput versus scFoundation.

Conclusion: Graph-connected gene blocks serve as effective prediction targets for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology, yielding high-quality embeddings that are both biologically meaningful and computationally efficient.

Abstract: Single-cell transcriptomes are sparse observations of coordinated biological programmes, yet most self-supervised models learn by reconstructing individual genes. Here we present BioM-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that instead predicts aggregate representations of graph-connected gene blocks defined by protein-association and corpus-derived coexpression evidence. A student network infers each target-block representation from the remaining genes in a cell, while a slowly updated teacher supplies the corresponding target from the full observed gene set. Under the reported extraction procedure, block-level prediction produced embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth in the tested diagnostics than token-prediction, random-block and reconstruction controls. Across CellBench tasks, frozen BioM-JEPA embeddings retained expression, pathway and neighbourhood information and achieved the lowest aggregate perturbation-response error among the evaluated models. Representation diagnostics were also consistent with canonical pancreatic programmes and compositional relationships between genetic perturbations. Linear attention avoids constructing a quadratic gene-by-gene attention matrix; in a matched one-epoch hPancreas experiment at batch size 8, BioM-JEPA provided 5.75-fold higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76-fold higher held-out embedding throughput than scFoundation. Together, these results support graph-connected gene blocks as useful prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology.

</details>


### [290] [How Far Do Simple Transformations Translate Across Text Embedding Models?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05980)
*Sid Ali Hamideche,Louis Adrien Dufrene,Quentin Lampin,Guillaume Larue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper tests whether simple linear transformations can translate between heterogeneous text embedding models. Across nine diverse models, simple mappings recover shared structure for some pairs but fail for others, contradicting claims of universal latent space compatibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether independently trained text embedding models organize semantic information in a way that allows translation via simple mappings, enabling AI-to-AI latent communication without text decoding.

Method: Evaluate nine embedding models (varying in architecture, pooling, training objective) using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), downstream transfer performance, embedding fidelity, and retrieval metrics to assess the effectiveness of lightweight linear translators.

Result: Simple translators succeed for some compatible model pairs but fail sharply for others. Compatibility is jointly determined by architecture, training objective, pooling strategy, and data distribution. No universal simple mapping exists across all pairs.

Conclusion: Heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings, challenging the latent universality hypothesis often claimed in prior literature.

Abstract: We investigate whether simple transformations can translate representations across heterogeneous text embedding models. Understanding how independently trained models organize semantic information is an enabler for AI-to-AI latent communication without decoding into human-readable text. Focusing on lightweight translators such as linear mappings, we test the literature hypothesis of latent universality in a realistic text setting beyond simplified benchmarks. Across nine embedding models differing in architecture, pooling strategy, and training objective, we evaluate compatibility using CKA, downstream transfer, fidelity, and retrieval. Simple translators recover meaningful shared structure and support transfer for some compatible pairs, but fail sharply for others. Compatibility depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling, and data distribution. Overall, the results show that heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings as often suggested in some literature.

</details>


### [291] [THBKG: A Temporal Biomedical Knowledge Graph for Decision-Aligned Clinical Advancement Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05982)
*Pui Chung Siu,Claudia Cabrera,Mani Mudaliar,Arkaitz Zubiaga*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG) that captures time-stamped evidence for therapeutic target–disease links, enabling retrospective prediction of Phase II clinical trial success. Graph propagation methods outperform direct-evidence baselines, especially for pairs lacking direct evidence at decision time (72.8% of cases), achieving 4.3–4.5× relative success in top-10 ranking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inadequate target–disease linkage accounts for 40–50% of Phase II efficacy failures. Existing biomedical knowledge graphs lack temporal information, making it impossible to reconstruct the evidence profile that existed when a clinical programme was initiated. A temporally-aware KG is needed to fairly evaluate and predict which target–disease hypotheses will succeed.

Method: The authors construct the THBKG with 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across 19 relation types, where each edge carries the year its supporting evidence changed. They define a decision-aligned benchmark: given a target–disease pair entering Phase II, predict advancement to Phase III using only evidence dated before that decision. Graph neural network propagation over the THBKG is compared against direct-evidence baselines. A path-based explainer adapted to the decision-time subgraph decomposes predictions into interpretable evidence landscapes.

Result: Graph propagation over THBKG achieves 4.3–4.5× relative success over direct-evidence models at ranking top-10 pairs per therapeutic area. For the 72.8% of pairs with no direct target–disease evidence at decision time, encoders still rank 5–6× above chance by propagating over indirect biological pathways.

Conclusion: Temporal awareness in biomedical knowledge graphs enables fair retrospective validation of target–disease hypotheses. The THBKG is released as a continually updated resource for studying therapeutic target hypotheses, with explainable predictions decomposable into the evidence landscape behind each decision.

Abstract: Inadequate target--disease linkage accounts for 40--50\% of Phase~II efficacy failures, so anticipating which programmes will advance would let sponsors back the hypotheses most likely to reach patients. What a programme can be judged on is the evidence that supported its linkage \emph{when it entered the clinic}. No existing biomedical knowledge graph allows that evidence profile to be assembled as of a past date. We present the Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG), which describes and predicts therapeutic target--disease links through time: 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across nineteen relation types, each edge carrying the year its evidence changed, so a pair's profile can be recovered as it stood when its own decision fell due. On this graph we define a decision-aligned benchmark that predicts, for a target--disease pair entering Phase~II, whether it advances to Phase~III on evidence datable before that decision. Graph propagation over the THBKG outranks every direct-evidence reference scored under the same decision-aligned protocol, reaching a relative success of 4.3--4.5 at the top ten pairs per therapeutic area. The gain concentrates on the 72.8\% of pairs with no direct target--disease evidence at their decision point, where a direct-edge model has nothing to read: the encoders still rank five- to sixfold above chance, recovering the signal by propagating over the intervening biology. Adapting a path-based explainer to the decision-time subgraph decomposes each prediction into the evidence landscape behind the hypothesis for explainable prediction. We release the THBKG as a continually updated substrate for studying therapeutic target hypotheses by retrospective validation.

</details>


### [292] [Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Reinforcement Learning for Visual Continuous Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05989)
*Xinwei Liu,Junyuan Liang,Jianting Zhang,Wuhui Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OG-SPR is a model-free visual RL algorithm that combines latent self-prediction with next-observation prediction via lightweight adapters, achieving state-of-the-art performance on 28 DMControl tasks, especially on challenging dog and humanoid domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dynamics-based visual RL methods rely on either latent self-prediction or observation prediction alone. The authors argue this is insufficient: observation prediction grounds representations in observation-level dynamics but lacks long-horizon temporal regularization, while standalone self-prediction may over-constrain shared representations. A method combining both objectives effectively is needed.

Method: OG-SPR introduces two auxiliary objectives: (1) multi-step latent self-prediction and (2) next-observation prediction. Crucially, rather than imposing self-prediction directly on the shared encoder representation (which they show can harm performance), OG-SPR uses two lightweight adapter networks that branch off the shared representation. This allows the shared representation to benefit from temporally predictive signals without being forced to directly satisfy the self-prediction objective, avoiding over-constraint.

Result: OG-SPR outperforms state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL methods in aggregate across 28 visual control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite, with especially large gains on challenging domains like dog and humanoid.

Conclusion: Combining latent self-prediction with observation prediction, when properly decoupled via adapters, yields superior visual representations for sample-efficient continuous control compared to using either objective in isolation.

Abstract: Sample-efficient policy learning from pixels is a long-standing challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Recent dynamics-based representation learning methods have significantly improved the sample efficiency of model-free visual RL by learning dynamics-aware representations through auxiliary prediction performed either in latent space (self-prediction) or observation space (observation prediction). However, state-of-the-art methods from both categories still struggle on challenging visual control tasks when training data is limited. We posit that relying on either predictive objective alone may be insufficient. In contrast, observation prediction grounds learned representations in observation-level dynamics, but does not directly regularize the temporal predictability of latent representations over extended horizons. In this paper, we propose Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Representations (OG-SPR), a model-free visual RL algorithm for continuous control that learns representations that are both temporally predictive in latent space and grounded in observation-level dynamics. OG-SPR incorporates two core auxiliary objectives: multi-step latent self-prediction and next-observation prediction. We empirically show that directly imposing latent self-prediction on the shared representation may over-constrain it and does not necessarily improve performance. To address this issue, OG-SPR introduces two lightweight adapters for latent self-prediction, allowing the shared representation to benefit from temporally predictive signals without being forced to directly satisfy the self-prediction objective. Experiments on 28 visual control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite show that OG-SPR improves aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL methods, with particularly pronounced gains in challenging domains such as dog and humanoid.

</details>


### [293] [A Unified Risk View of Uncertainty: Posterior Risk for Disentanglement and Evaluation Beyond Proxies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05995)
*Frieder Wizgall,Georg Tirpitz,Moritz Seiler,Kerstin Ritter,Bálint Mucsányi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a unified definition of predictive uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk, then builds a benchmark using semi-synthetic data with known generative processes to directly compute oracle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties, enabling fine-grained evaluation of disentanglement methods without relying on proxy tasks like OOD detection. Key finding: accurate prediction does not guarantee reliable uncertainty disentanglement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uncertainty disentanglement (separating epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty) is critical for safety-sensitive applications, but current evaluation is hindered by: (1) inconsistent definitions of uncertainty types across the literature, and (2) lack of ground-truth epistemic uncertainty, forcing reliance on proxy tasks (e.g., OOD detection) that provide incomplete targets and limited insight into estimate quality.

Method: The authors (1) propose a unified definition of uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk—the expected loss of a predictor under the distribution of plausible ground-truth functions given the data, combining Bayesian uncertainty over functions with estimator-dependent deviations (capturing misspecification and optimization error); (2) construct a theory-backed benchmark using semi-synthetic datasets with real covariates and known generative processes, enabling direct oracle computation of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, avoiding proxy evaluations.

Result: Accurate prediction does not guarantee reliable uncertainty disentanglement. The benchmark reveals practically useful differences between methods, identifying approaches with meaningful alignment to oracle uncertainty targets while exposing sensitivity to datasets and modeling choices.

Conclusion: The unified posterior-risk-based definition and accompanying benchmark provide a rigorous foundation for evaluating uncertainty disentanglement methods. The findings highlight that predictive accuracy alone is insufficient for assessing uncertainty quality, and that method performance varies substantially across datasets and modeling configurations, underscoring the need for careful method selection in practice.

Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimates are critical in safety-sensitive applications, where understanding the sources of predictive uncertainty is essential. This often requires disentangling epistemic uncertainty from aleatoric uncertainty, yet these uncertainty types are not defined consistently across the literature, making it difficult to assess whether a method produces accurate uncertainty estimates. Evaluation is further complicated by the fact that ground-truth epistemic uncertainty is typically unavailable. Existing benchmarks therefore mostly rely on proxy tasks such as out-of-distribution detection, which do not provide complete ground-truth uncertainty targets and offer limited insight into the structure and quality of uncertainty estimates. We propose a unified definition of uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk, the expected loss of a predictor under the distribution of plausible ground-truth functions given the data. This view combines Bayesian uncertainty over functions with estimator-dependent deviations from the posterior mean, capturing effects such as misspecification and optimization error. This formulation constitutes the foundation of a theory-backed benchmark that enables direct computation of oracle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty using semi-synthetic datasets with real covariates and known generative processes. By avoiding proxy evaluations, the benchmark enables fine-grained analysis of uncertainty estimates. Empirically, we find that accurate prediction does not guarantee reliable uncertainty disentanglement. The benchmark reveals practically useful differences between methods, identifying approaches with meaningful alignment to oracle uncertainty targets while exposing sensitivity to datasets and modeling choices.

</details>


### [294] [Do Tabular Foundation Models Agree with Themselves?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06004)
*Christian Klötergens,Vijaya Krishna Yalavarthi,Lars Schmidt-Thieme,Tom Hanika*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) produce univariate conditional predictions but lack theoretical guarantees about the joint distribution when used autoregressively. The authors propose two consistency criteria—marginalization consistency and factorization consistency—and show that all evaluated TFMs violate both across classification and regression tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TFMs are state-of-the-art for tabular prediction but are fundamentally univariate models. When extended autoregressively to multivariate prediction, the faithfulness of the resulting joint distribution has never been investigated. Since ground-truth posteriors are unknown on real data, direct evaluation against the true posterior is impossible, motivating an alternative diagnostic framework.

Method: The authors propose two necessary conditions for any model to be consistent with some valid joint distribution: (1) marginalization consistency — marginalized conditional distributions must equal directly predicted marginal distributions; (2) factorization consistency — different autoregressive factorization orders must yield the same joint distribution. They then empirically evaluate existing TFMs against both criteria across multiple datasets, covering both classification and regression.

Result: Every TFM evaluated violates both marginalization consistency and factorization consistency across all tested datasets, for both classification and regression tasks. This indicates that TFMs do not correspond to any valid joint distribution.

Conclusion: Current TFMs fail to represent coherent joint distributions when used autoregressively. The proposed consistency criteria offer a practical diagnostic tool for evaluating and guiding future development of tabular models toward faithful multivariate prediction.

Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are currently the best approach to tabular prediction problems. They are constructed as transformers that approximate the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution based on a pre-training prior. These univariate predictors can be converted into multivariate ones autoregressively by sampling one target and adding it to the features.
  However, the faithfulness of the resulting joint has not been investigated. Furthermore, TFMs cannot be evaluated against the posterior itself, at least not on real-world datasets, because the ground-truth distribution is unknown. We therefore propose asking a different question: could a model's predictions result from any joint distribution? To answer this question, we pose two requirements that any such model must satisfy. The first is marginalization consistency, which demands that marginalized conditionals are equal to directly predicted marginals. The second is factorization consistency, which demands that different factorization orders result in equal joint distributions. Every TFM that we evaluate violates both of these requirements for both classification and regression across all datasets.

</details>


### [295] [ProDVI: Programmatic Dynamics Priors for Value Network Initialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06015)
*Xinwei Liu,Junyuan Liang,Jianting Zhang,Wuhui Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProDVI uses LLM-generated Python functions encoding coarse environment dynamics to pretrain value network representations, improving sample efficiency of model-free RL without requiring pre-collected datasets, simulators, or meta-learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL agents suffer from poor sample efficiency partly because they start from scratch. Existing solutions (pretraining on datasets, simulators, or meta-learning) require resources that may be unavailable. The authors aim to leverage LLMs' commonsense and domain knowledge as an accessible alternative for initialization.

Method: ProDVI prompts a code-generating LLM to produce executable Python functions that approximate environment dynamics. These programs generate synthetic transitions used to pretrain the state-action encoder of an actor-critic value network via an auxiliary dynamics prediction objective. The pretrained encoder provides dynamics-aware inductive biases, and only the representation is transferred — the generated programs need not accurately simulate the target environment. Online RL then corrects any inaccuracies using real transitions and rewards.

Result: Experiments on OpenAI Gym and DeepMind Control Suite demonstrate that ProDVI effectively improves the sample efficiency of model-free RL algorithms.

Conclusion: LLM-generated programmatic dynamics priors offer a viable, resource-efficient method for initializing RL agents, with online learning able to overcome inaccuracies in the generated programs.

Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) is notoriously sample inefficient. One contributing factor is that RL agents are typically initialized from scratch, forcing them to acquire task-relevant knowledge through online interaction. Existing approaches obtain informative initializations through pre-collected datasets, high-fidelity simulators, or meta-learning over related tasks, but these prerequisites may be difficult to access or even unavailable. In this paper, we propose Programmatic Dynamics Priors for Value Network Initialization (ProDVI), a framework that leverages the commonsense and domain knowledge encoded in large language models to initialize RL agents without relying on these resources. Specifically, ProDVI prompts a code-generating language model to produce executable Python functions that encode coarse hypotheses about environment dynamics. These functions are then used to generate synthetic transitions. Based on these transitions, we construct an auxiliary dynamics prediction objective to pretrain the state-action encoder of the value network in an actor-critic framework. The learned representation provides dynamics-aware inductive biases before online RL begins. Importantly, the generated programs are used only for representation pretraining and are not required to faithfully simulate the target environment. While the generated programs may be inaccurate, their induced initialization can be corrected through online learning from real transitions and rewards. Experiments on OpenAI Gym and DeepMind Control Suite tasks show that ProDVI can effectively improve the sample efficiency of model-free RL algorithms.

</details>


### [296] [BioKD: Selective Physiology-to-Video Knowledge Distillation via Reliability Gate for Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06023)
*Bojing Hou,Ruohao Li,Yitong Zhu,Hongjun Liu,Luwen Yu,Yuyang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BioKD is a reliability-aware knowledge distillation framework that uses physiological signals as privileged training information to teach a video-based emotion recognition model, incorporating a gating mechanism and progressive distillation to handle noisy supervision, achieving strong results on DEAP and AMIGOS with no physiological input needed at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video-based emotion recognition suffers from ambiguous/socially masked behavioral cues, while physiological signals—though more informative—are intrusive and hard to deploy. Existing cross-modal distillation approaches lack mechanisms to handle the inherent noise and unreliability of physiological supervision.

Method: BioKD employs a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework where physiological signals (teacher) guide a video-based model (student). Key innovations include: (1) a sample-wise reliability-aware gating mechanism that adaptively weights the distillation loss based on estimated teacher reliability per sample, and (2) a progressive distillation strategy that gradually increases distillation strength. The student uses only video at inference.

Result: BioKD achieves 68.01% on DEAP (trial-wise arousal) and 65.29% under subject-wise evaluation, outperforming baselines on both DEAP and AMIGOS for valence and arousal recognition. It mitigates overconfident teacher errors and surpasses entropy-only weighting. No inference-time overhead is introduced relative to the video-only student architecture.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling supervision reliability via reliability-aware gating and progressive distillation is critical for effective physiology-to-video knowledge transfer. BioKD enables practical, deployment-friendly emotion recognition using only video while leveraging physiological signals solely during training.

Abstract: To address the limitations of video-based emotion recognition under ambiguous or socially masked behavioral cues, as well as the poor deployability of physiological signals, this paper proposes a reliability-aware physiology-to-video knowledge distillation framework, termed BioKD. The proposed framework leverages physiological signals as privileged information during training to guide a video-based student model in learning deep affective representations, while relying solely on non-intrusive video inputs at inference time. To cope with the high noise and instability of physiological teacher supervision caused by inter-subject variability, signal artifacts, and temporal inconsistency, BioKD incorporates a sample-wise reliability-aware gating mechanism together with a progressive distillation strategy. By adaptively regulating the strength of knowledge transfer, the framework suppresses negative transfer induced by unreliable physiological supervision and enables more stable cross-modal distillation. Experiments on DEAP and AMIGOS show that BioKD consistently outperforms representative baselines under both trial-wise and subject-wise evaluation protocols for valence and arousal recognition. For example, BioKD achieves 68.01\% on DEAP (trial-wise arousal) and 65.29\% under the more challenging subject-wise setting, demonstrating improved performance under a subject-independent evaluation setting. Further analyses show that BioKD effectively mitigates overconfident teacher errors and outperforms an entropy-only weighting strategy, confirming the importance of explicitly modeling supervision reliability. In addition, BioKD introduces no additional inference-time overhead relative to the same video student architecture and removes the need for physiological sensing and multimodal synchronization.

</details>


### [297] [Dynamic Graph Prompting via Topology-Routed Mixed-Curvature Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06031)
*Quanxin Wang,Xuanting Xie,Bingheng Li,Xingtong Yu,Shuo Wang,Ruiyi Fang,Zhao Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CurvPrompt introduces a topology-routed geometry prompting framework for dynamic graphs that adapts representation geometry over time using a bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts, significantly improving few-shot link prediction and node classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dynamic graph prompting methods operate in a single fixed embedding space, but the authors reveal that temporal shifts in local clustering and degree heterogeneity cause the optimal representation geometry to evolve with local topology. This creates a "geometry under-adaptation" mismatch that prior work fails to address.

Method: CurvPrompt maintains a bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts, each paired with a learnable prompt. A topology-aware gate dynamically routes each node-time instance to a sparse subset of experts, constructing a personalized mixed-curvature representation. Pre-training uses soft routing for a continuous topology-geometry mapping; downstream adaptation switches to hard Top-K routing with uniform weights for parameter efficiency and training stability under extreme label scarcity.

Result: Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that CurvPrompt significantly advances few-shot link prediction and delivers strong, consistent performance on node classification tasks.

Conclusion: The results validate the necessity of geometry-adaptive prompting, showing that dynamically adapting representation geometry to evolving local topology is critical for effective dynamic graph learning under label-scarce settings.

Abstract: Dynamic graph prompting freezes a pre-trained temporal backbone and adapts it to label-scarce downstream tasks using lightweight prompts. However, existing methods operate within a single, fixed embedding space. In this work, we reveal that temporal shifts in local clustering and degree heterogeneity actively reorganize the edge curvature spectrum---indicating that the optimal representation geometry dynamically evolves with local topology over time. We formalize this unaddressed mismatch as geometry under-adaptation. To overcome this limitation, we propose CurvPrompt, a topology-routed geometry prompting framework for dynamic graphs. Instead of relying on a single space, CurvPrompt maintains a bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts, each paired with a learnable prompt. A topology-aware gate dynamically routes each node--time instance to a sparse subset of experts, constructing a personalized mixed-curvature representation. To ensure parameter efficiency and training stability under extreme label scarcity, CurvPrompt employs soft routing during pre-training to build a continuous topology--geometry mapping, and transitions to hard Top-K routing with uniform weights during downstream adaptation. Extensive experiments across four benchmark datasets show that CurvPrompt significantly advances few-shot link prediction while delivering strong, consistent performance on node classification tasks, validating the necessity of geometry-adaptive prompting.

</details>


### [298] [Kastor: An efficient fine-tuning strategy for generative emulation of PDE simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06107)
*Guillaume Couairon,Alexis Jacq,Yu-Han Wu,Renu Singh,Yana Hasson,Quentin Berthet,Romuald Elie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Kastor proposes a methodology to adapt deterministic physics foundation models into generative surrogates using three key innovations: (1) a two-stage inference scheme with causal auto-regression and non-causal temporal super-resolution to reduce error accumulation, (2) Mean Prediction Regularization (MPR) to constrain generative outputs, and (3) spatial gradient matching for improved physical fidelity. The approach achieves a 42.9% average reduction in forecasting error and outperforms Walrus on 8/10 datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard auto-regressive ML emulators for PDE solving suffer from two critical limitations: error accumulation over long time horizons and inability to capture the stochasticity inherent in complex physical systems. While physics foundation models exist, adapting them into efficient generative surrogates that are both accurate and stable remains an open challenge.

Method: The paper introduces three components: (1) A two-stage inference scheme combining a large-stride causal auto-regressive model with a non-causal temporal super-resolution network to reduce error accumulation and computational cost. (2) Mean Prediction Regularization (MPR), a training objective that constrains the generative model to predict the deterministic distribution mean under null noise conditioning, improving stability for both Functional Generative Networks (FGN) and diffusion-based emulators. (3) Spatial gradient matching to enhance physical fidelity, evaluated via power spectrum density.

Result: On The Well benchmark, Kastor achieves a 42.9% average reduction in forecasting error compared to the Walrus finetuning methodology baseline, and outperforms Walrus on 8 out of 10 datasets measured by variance-normalized RMSE (VRMSE). Additional gains are demonstrated in spectral consistency and computational efficiency.

Conclusion: The proposed Kastor methodology effectively transforms deterministic physics foundation models into highly efficient and accurate generative surrogates. The combination of two-stage inference, MPR, and spatial gradient matching yields significant improvements in long-horizon forecasting, physical consistency, and stability across diverse simulation datasets.

Abstract: Machine learning offers a promising avenue to accelerate physical simulations by replacing computationally expensive traditional Partial Differential Equation (PDE) solvers with fast, differentiable surrogate models. However, standard auto-regressive ML emulators often suffer from error accumulation over long horizons and struggle to capture the stochasticity of complex physical systems. In this paper, we propose Kastor, a comprehensive methodology to adapt a deterministic physics foundation model into a highly efficient and accurate generative surrogate. First, we introduce a two-stage inference scheme that combines a large-stride causal auto-regressive model with a non-causal temporal super-resolution network, significantly reducing error accumulation while minimizing computational cost. Second, we present Mean prediction regularization (MPR), a novel training objective that constrains the generative model to predict the deterministic distribution mean under null noise conditioning. This regularization dramatically improves the performance and stability of both Functional Generative Networks (FGN) and diffusion-based emulators. Finally, we demonstrate that incorporating spatial gradient matching improves the accuracy and physical fidelity of the simulations as measured by power spectrum density. Extensive evaluations on diverse simulation datasets of the benchmark The Well show that with these components, our model outperforms competing methods in forecasting accuracy, spectral consistency, and computational efficiency. Our model achieves a 42.9% average reduction in forecasting compared to our reference based on the Walrus finetuning methodology, and outperforms Walrus for 8 out of 10 datasets on variance-normalized RMSE (VRMSE).

</details>


### [299] [Is Self-Pretraining really useful to improve diagnosis in medical Time Series?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06122)
*Omar Coser,Antonio Orvieto,Paolo Soda,Loredana Zollo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Self-PreTraining (SPT) with masking-based objectives consistently improves transformer accuracy on medical time-series tasks by 0–6 percentage points, especially for deeper models and under limited data, across multivariate and univariate settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivated by SPT's success on long-context benchmarks, the authors investigate whether SPT benefits transfer to medical time-series domains—particularly multimodal, multivariate, and univariate tasks—where data scarcity is common and transformer performance gains could improve clinical outcomes.

Method: Transformer architectures are trained from scratch vs. SPT using four masking-based objectives (promoting temporal and cross-modal representation learning) on three medical time-series datasets: Camargo (rehabilitation robotics), Non-EEG Stress (stress detection), and Gait Parkinson's (PD detection). Model depth is systematically varied to assess capacity–pretraining interactions.

Result: SPT consistently improves classification accuracy by 0–6 pp across datasets and configurations. Gains persist in univariate settings, not just multivariate. Deeper models benefit more, as they better exploit enriched temporal representations from pre-training.

Conclusion: SPT is a simple, general, architecture-agnostic strategy that boosts transformer performance and robustness on medical time-series tasks, particularly in data-limited clinical scenarios, without requiring task-specific architectural modifications.

Abstract: Inspired by recent evidence that transformer architectures benefit from Self-PreTraining (SPT) on long-context benchmarks, we investigate whether similar gains extend to multimodal, multivariate, and even simple univariate medical time series. Our objective is to assess the impact of SPT on the performance and scalability of transformer-based models across diverse medical applications, particularly under limited data conditions. We evaluate transformer architectures on three representative medical time-series tasks: rehabilitation robotics (Camargo dataset), stress detection (Non-EEG Stress), and Parkinson's disease detection (Gait Parkinson's Disease). Models are trained either from scratch or through SPT using four masking-based objectives designed to promote temporal and cross-modal representation learning, and we systematically vary model depth to examine how capacity interacts with pre-training benefits. Across datasets and configurations, SPT consistently improves classification accuracy by 0-6 percentage points depending on masking strategy, dataset and architecture, with gains observed not only in multivariate settings but also when models are restricted to simple univariate inputs. The improvements increase for deeper models that can better exploit the enriched temporal representations learned during pre-training. These findings indicate that SPT is a simple and general strategy that enhances transformer performance on medical time-series tasks without requiring task-specific architectural changes, supporting its potential to improve robustness and accuracy in data-limited clinical settings.

</details>


### [300] [LLM Inference Under Bursty Workload Distribution: Modifying the WAIT Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06135)
*Anjali Gangadhar Katageria,Shobha Rani,Raghu Nandan Sengupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a lightweight extension to the WAIT scheduling algorithm that adapts to time-varying, bursty traffic by performing online estimation of request arrival rates using observed interarrival times, outperforming Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, and vLLM in throughput under low arrival-rate shift scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM scheduling algorithms (Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, vLLM) assume Poisson request arrivals with constant rates, which fails to capture the bursty and dynamic nature of real-world traffic. This mismatch motivates the need for an adaptive scheduling approach.

Method: The authors extend the state-of-the-art WAIT algorithm with a lightweight online estimation module that infers request intensity from observed interarrival times. Evaluation uses Markov Modulated Poisson Process (MMPP)-based synthetic workloads with diverse request types in a simulation-based framework.

Result: The proposed method achieves higher throughput than Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, and vLLM in low arrival-rate shift scenarios while maintaining comparable latency.

Conclusion: Adaptive, online estimation of time-varying arrival rates can improve LLM serving throughput without sacrificing latency, demonstrating the practical benefits of moving beyond constant-rate Poisson assumptions in scheduling algorithms.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Claude are widely used for information retrieval and problem-solving. Recent work has focused on improving scheduling algorithms to boost throughput while maintaining low latency. However, these approaches often assume Poisson request arrivals with constant rates - an assumption that fails to reflect the inherently bursty and dynamic nature of real-world traffic. We propose a lightweight extension to the state-of-the-art WAIT algorithm [1], which adapts to time-varying arrival rates without prior traffic knowledge. The proposed algorithm performs online estimation of request intensity based on observed interarrival times. Using Markov Modulated Poisson Process (MMPP)-based synthetic workloads with diverse request types, we conduct a simulation-based evaluation demonstrating that the proposed method achieves higher throughput than Sarathi-Serve [2], ORCA [3], and vLLM [4] in the evaluated low arrival-rate shift scenarios while maintaining comparable latency.

</details>


### [301] [SkillTFM: Gated Skill Evolution for Training-Free Adaptation of Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06137)
*Yi He,Zhengkang Guan,Anpeng Wu,Peng Cui,Fei Wu,Kun Kuang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SkillTFM introduces a training-free, agentic skill evolution framework that adapts tabular foundation models (TFMs) to new tasks without parameter updates, using a gated skill bank that identifies boundary evidence and retrieves/extend reusable skills, achieving significant AUC gains on both synthetic boundary tasks and real-world electricity-price forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TFMs offer reusable predictors across diverse tabular datasets, but their practical deployment is hindered by distribution shifts, heterogeneous feature semantics, and task-specific patterns. Addressing these issues typically requires costly fine-tuning or additional labeled data, motivating a training-free adaptation approach.

Method: SkillTFM replaces parameter updates with gated evolution of agentic skills via a verifiable and extensible skill bank. The system couples two mechanisms: (1) boundary evidence identification, which characterizes task structure and base-model failure patterns; and (2) gated skill evolution, which retrieves and extends reusable skills subject to explicit validation, ensuring only verified skills are deployed.

Result: Across simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128–0.142, raises nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898, and generalizes effectively across multiple TFM backbones.

Conclusion: SkillTFM demonstrates that training-free, skill-based adaptation is a viable and effective alternative to fine-tuning for tabular foundation models, offering substantial performance gains while maintaining generality across backbones and task types.

Abstract: Tabular data are ubiquitous in real-world applications and are crucial for data-driven prediction and decision-making across science, industry, finance, healthcare, and public services. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose tabular learning, offering reusable predictors across diverse datasets and substantially reducing the need for task-specific training, tuning, and model development. However, their practical deployment remains constrained by distribution shifts, heterogeneous feature semantics, and task-specific patterns that are difficult to capture without costly fine-tuning or additional labeled data.
  To this end, we propose SkillTFM, a training-free system that shifts TFM adaptation from parameter updates to the gated evolution of agentic skills. The core of SkillTFM is a verifiable and extensible skill bank that couples boundary evidence identification with gated skill evolution: the former characterizes task structure and base-model failure patterns, whereas the latter retrieves and extends reusable skills subject to explicit validation. Across simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128--0.142, raises nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898. Furthermore, experiments across TFM backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of SkillTFM.

</details>


### [302] [Threshold-Based Early Stopping of Accumulations in Neural Networks with Binary Activation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06177)
*Quentin Luquet de Saint-Germain,Massil Ait Abdeslam,Jean Pierre David*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a post-training early-stopping mechanism for binary neural networks that skips accumulation terms once the final sign of the running sum becomes confidently predictable, achieving up to 86.6% reduction in accumulation operations in deep convolutional layers with minimal accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In binary neural networks, dot products with binary activations reduce to sign-controlled additions/subtractions, but the number of operations remains unchanged—every output channel still accumulates all inputs even though only the sign is retained. The authors observe that running partial sums frequently drift far from zero, making the final sign highly predictable long before all terms are processed, rendering subsequent accumulations wasteful since they cannot change the output activation.

Method: A post-training early-stopping mechanism that characterizes running accumulation behavior on the training dataset to predict the final sign as early as possible. When the partial sum's magnitude exceeds a confidence threshold, accumulation halts and the final sign is inferred. The approach requires no retraining of model parameters and counts operations under an idealized weight ordering.

Result: On VGG11 with CIFAR-10, the method removes 86.6% of accumulation terms in the deepest convolution layer at a cost of only 0.37-point accuracy drop. When applied simultaneously to the three deepest convolutions, it eliminates 25% of full-network arithmetic with a 1.36-point accuracy drop.

Conclusion: Early stopping of accumulation in binary neural networks is an effective post-training optimization that significantly reduces computational cost with negligible accuracy degradation, demonstrating that many MAC operations in BNNs are redundant for determining the output sign.

Abstract: Binary neural networks are very attractive for constrained deployment, enabling small footprint and low-power inference. For binary activations, the dot products become sign-controlled additions or subtractions, but the number of operations is unchanged. Indeed, every neuron or output channel still accumulates all of its input, even though only the sign will be retained, which is often wasteful. As the accumulation progresses, the running partial sum frequently drifts so far from zero that its final sign becomes highly predictable long before the last term is reached; every contribution evaluated after that point changes the value of the sum but not the final output activation. This paper turns this observation into a post-training early-stopping mechanism. We characterize the behavior of the running accumulations on the training dataset and use this information to predict the final sign as soon as possible. No model parameter is retrained. We count the number of operations under an idealized ordering of weights. On VGG11 applied to the CIFAR-10 dataset, the method removes $86.6\%$ of the accumulation terms of the deepest convolution for a $0.37$-point accuracy drop, and $25\%$ of the full-network arithmetic when used on the three deepest convolutions simultaneously, for a $1.36$-point drop.

</details>


### [303] [SAGA: Score-Weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment for Low-Resource Nordic Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06179)
*Hoda Fakharzadehjahromy,Emil Wiman,Andreas Bueff,Hafsteinn Einarsson,Fredrik Heintz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAGA uses dependency parser supervision instead of human labels for preference optimization, significantly improving grammatical quality in low-resource languages (Danish, Icelandic, Norwegian Bokmål) with gains up to +28 percentage points in parse success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preference optimization for LLMs typically requires costly human preference annotations, which are especially scarce for morphologically rich, low-resource languages. This motivates finding an alternative, automated supervision signal.

Method: SAGA (Score-weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment) is a parser-guided framework that: (1) converts dependency parser judgments into preference pairs for delta-DPO training; (2) combines parser quality with lexical diversity into a composite reward; (3) filters low-information pairs using a reward-gap criterion; and (4) monitors reward hacking to maintain reliable supervision.

Result: Using GPT-SW3-1.3B: Danish parse success rose from 69.0% to 93.8%; Icelandic improved +4.5 pp on Stanza evaluation (three-run mean +3.3 pp) with 80% native-speaker preference; Norwegian Bokmål improved by +28 pp.

Conclusion: Parser-derived supervision is a practical, effective alternative to human preference annotation for grammatical alignment in low-resource languages where high-quality dependency parsers exist.

Abstract: Preference optimisation has proven effective for improving large language models but typically relies on costly human preference annotations. Extending these methods to morphologically rich, low-resource languages remains challenging because such annotations are scarce. We present SAGA (Score-weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment), a parser-guided preference optimisation framework that replaces human labels with dependency-parser supervision. SAGA converts parser judgements into preference pairs for delta-DPO, combines parser quality with lexical diversity in a composite reward, filters low-information pairs using a reward-gap criterion, and monitors reward hacking to maintain reliable supervision. Across Danish, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål using GPT-SW3-1.3B, SAGA consistently improves grammatical quality without requiring human preference labels. Danish parse success increases from 69.0% to 93.8%, Icelandic achieves a +4.5 percentage-point improvement on an independent Stanza evaluation (three-run mean +3.3 percentage points) while native speakers prefer SAGA outputs in 80% of pairwise comparisons, and Norwegian Bokmål improves by +28 percentage points. These results demonstrate that parser-derived supervision is a practical alternative to human preference annotation for grammatical alignment in low-resource languages where high-quality dependency parsers are available.

</details>


### [304] [Continual Learning in Transition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06216)
*Zhiyan Hou,Dan Zhang,Tao Feng,Liyuan Wang,Wei Li,Xiangzhao Hao,Hongyan An,Junfeng Fang,Haokai Ma,Zhaohui Xu,Haiyun Guo,Jinqiao Wang,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This survey reframes continual learning (CL) as a transition from parameter-centric model adaptation to system-level adaptation, organized along three axes: When (pre-training, post-training, inference), How (off-policy, on-policy, beyond-gradient optimization), and Where (internal parameters vs. external structural harnesses).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional CL research has narrowly focused on parameter-centric mechanisms (training strategies, architectures, weight adaptation), but emerging paradigms—on-policy learning, test-time training, external memory, skill libraries, and interaction protocols—have expanded CL beyond this scope. The paper argues that these developments collectively signal a paradigm shift toward system-level adaptation, requiring a new conceptual framework to characterize and survey the field.

Method: The authors propose a tri-axial taxonomy for classifying continual learning methods: (1) When — the temporal stage of learning (pre-training, post-training, inference-time); (2) How — the optimization mechanics (off-policy, on-policy, beyond-gradient); (3) Where — the locus of updates (internal parameters vs. external structural components). Using this framework, they systematically survey representative methods and trace the ongoing transition in CL research.

Result: The survey maps the CL landscape along the three axes, showing how methods have progressively moved from internal, post-training, off-policy parameter updates toward more diverse configurations involving inference-time adaptation, on-policy learning, and external harness components (memory modules, skill libraries, interaction protocols). The framework reveals the field's trajectory toward system-level continual adaptation.

Conclusion: Continual learning is undergoing a fundamental paradigm shift from parameter-centric to system-level adaptation. The proposed When-How-Where framework effectively captures this evolution and provides a structured lens for understanding current methods, identifying key challenges, and charting future research directions in continual learning.

Abstract: Classical continual learning (CL) has primarily focused on enabling models to update and retain knowledge through parameter-centric mechanisms, e.g., training strategies, architectural designs, and weight adaptation. However, emerging paradigms are reshaping the scope of CL beyond this traditional model adaptation view. For instance, on-policy learning broadens the space of update mechanisms; test-time training extends CL from the training phase to inference; and external harness components such as memory, skill libraries, and interaction protocols extend the evolutionary boundaries of model capabilities far beyond the static parameter space. Collectively, these developments indicate a transition from parameter-centric learning toward system-level adaptation. To characterize this transition, we examine the evolution of continual learning through three dimensions: When, How, and Where learning occurs. The How dimension encompasses off-policy, on-policy, and beyond-gradient optimization mechanics. The When dimension captures evolution across pre-training, post-training, and inference-time stages. The Where dimension delineates updates occurring within internal parameters versus external structural constraints. Anchored by this tri-axial framework, we systematically survey representative methods, trace the ongoing transition of continual learning, and discuss the key challenges, broader implications, and future directions arising from this paradigm shift.

</details>


### [305] [Timestep-Conditioned Transformers for Global Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06241)
*Sam Levang,Fran Bartolic,Ty Dickinson,Chase Dwelle,Paulius Rauba,Viktor Cikojevic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GEM-3 is a probabilistic global weather model (~134M parameters) that uses multi-timestep inference to balance the trade-off between short timesteps (fine diurnal resolution, more error accumulation) and long timesteps (less error, limited short-range usability). Mixed-timestep training improves rollout stability, and the model achieves near-SOTA medium-range skill with efficient training/inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ML weather models use fixed autoregressive timesteps, creating a fundamental trade-off: short timesteps (1–6h) resolve diurnal dynamics well but accumulate more errors over long horizons, while long timesteps (24h) reduce error accumulation but degrade short-range forecast utility where sub-daily predictability is high. A flexible solution is needed.

Method: GEM-3 enables explicit multi-timestep inference from a single set of trained weights, allowing the timestep to be configured at inference time. It employs mixed-timestep training to enhance rollout stability over timestep-specialist models. Architecturally, it is a lightweight neighborhood-attention transformer (~134M parameters) on an equirectangular grid, with several advancements over its predecessor GEM-2.

Result: Mixed-timestep training consistently improves rollout stability. The model achieves near-state-of-the-art medium-range probabilistic skill, stable extended-range rollouts, and efficient training and inference, while providing decision-relevant diagnostics.

Conclusion: GEM-3 demonstrates that multi-timestep inference with mixed-timestep training effectively resolves the timestep trade-off in ML weather forecasting, yielding a practical system that couples competitive forecast skill with operational flexibility.

Abstract: Existing machine-learning weather forecasting models rely on predetermined and fixed autoregressive timesteps. The choice of model timestep involves a fundamental trade-off: shorter timesteps (e.g. 1 to 6 hours) finely resolve atmospheric dynamics within the diurnal cycle but increase error accumulation for a given forecast horizon, while longer timesteps (e.g. 24 hours) reduce error accumulation but limit the usability of short-range forecasts where sub-daily predictability is high. In this work, we present GEM-3, a probabilistic global weather model that addresses this trade-off through explicit multi-timestep inference. With a single set of trained weights, the model timestep can be configured at inference time to balance predictability and usability across a broad forecast horizon. Additionally, we find that mixed-timestep training consistently improves rollout stability relative to timestep-specialist models. Under the hood, GEM-3 is a lightweight neighborhood-attention transformer with ~134M parameters on an equirectangular grid with a number of architectural advancements beyond its predecessor GEM-2. The result is a practical forecasting system that couples near-SOTA medium-range probabilistic skill, stable extended-range rollouts, efficient training and inference, and decision-relevant diagnostics.

</details>


### [306] [A Six-Dimensional Taxonomy of Post-Training Adaptation Techniques with Applications in AI Governance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06246)
*Fardin Afdideh,Fernando Seoane,Farhad Abtahi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This survey synthesizes the fragmented post-training adaptation literature by introducing a six-dimensional taxonomy (mechanism, goal, data requirement, persistence, structural scope, model type) that clarifies conflated terms, maps technique relationships, and identifies open challenges in evaluation, unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The post-training adaptation literature is fragmented across technique families (retraining, fine-tuning, PEFT, alignment, RAG, model editing, unlearning, etc.), model classes, and deployment contexts, making it difficult to compare methods or systematically describe how trained models are modified. A unified vocabulary and taxonomy is needed.

Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive literature survey and propose a six-dimensional taxonomy for classifying post-training adaptation techniques: (1) mechanism, (2) goal, (3) data requirement, (4) persistence, (5) structural scope, and (6) model type. They use this taxonomy to distinguish commonly conflated terms (e.g., fine-tuning vs. retrieval augmentation vs. prompting), trace the evolution of adaptation strategies across machine learning paradigms, and map inter-technique relationships including inheritance, supersession, hybridization, and layered deployment stacks.

Result: The taxonomy provides a consistent vocabulary that disambiguates overlapping terminology. It reveals how adaptation strategies have evolved from traditional ML through deep learning, foundation models, LLMs, and multimodal LLMs. The framework supports technical documentation, model-change tracking, and governance analysis.

Conclusion: The survey identifies several open challenges: evaluation and reproducibility of adaptation methods, persistent inference-time adaptation, effective unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance-aware post-training workflows. The proposed taxonomy serves as a foundation for more systematic research and practice in post-training model modification.

Abstract: Post-training adaptation has become central to modern machine learning practice and includes techniques such as retraining, fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation, alignment, retrieval augmentation, model editing, unlearning, calibration, and Multimodal Instruction Tuning. However, the literature remains fragmented across technique families, model classes, and deployment contexts, making it difficult to compare methods or describe how a trained model has been modified. This survey synthesizes the post-training adaptation literature and introduces a six-dimensional taxonomy organized by mechanism, goal, data requirement, persistence, structural scope, and model type. The taxonomy distinguishes commonly conflated terms such as fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, and prompting, and shows how adaptation strategies evolve from traditional machine learning through deep learning, foundation models, large language models, and multimodal large language models. It also maps relationships among techniques, including inheritance, supersession, hybridization, and layered deployment stacks. The resulting vocabulary can support technical documentation, model-change tracking, and governance analysis. The survey concludes by identifying open challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, persistent inference-time adaptation, unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance-aware post-training workflows.

</details>


### [307] [MetaboLLM: a metabolomics-specialized large language model for biochemical knowledge integration and predictive metabolite graph construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06253)
*Dohyun Ku,Min Gu Kwak,Francisco J. Pasquel,Jing Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MetaboLLM adapts large language models to metabolomics via continual pretraining and retrieval, while MetaboLLM-GIN converts outputs into metabolite graphs for patient-level prediction, achieving state-of-the-art AUCs on stress hyperglycemia (0.8616) and hormone regimen classification (0.8123).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Metabolomics knowledge is scattered across heterogeneous, unstructured resources and cannot be readily translated into predictive, structured representations for downstream biomedical tasks.

Method: MetaboLLM combines continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and structured retrieval to create a metabolomics-specialized LLM. MetaboLLM-GIN pairs this with a graph isomorphism network (GIN) that converts LLM-generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs for patient-level prediction.

Result: MetaboLLM outperformed base and medically adapted models across four backbone families on metabolomics knowledge, relational, and description tasks, and transferred to an external benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved the highest AUC for stress hyperglycemia prediction post-CABG (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), surpassing conventional models, alternative graphs, and non-adapted LLM configurations. Interpretations yielded biologically meaningful findings.

Conclusion: Domain-specialized LLMs can effectively organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive, interpretable metabolite graph representations, bridging unstructured metabolomics knowledge and clinically actionable predictions.

Abstract: Metabolomics knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous resources and remains difficult to translate into predictive representations. We developed MetaboLLM, a metabolomics-specialized large language model adapted through continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and structured retrieval, together with MetaboLLM-GIN, which converts generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs for patient-level prediction using a graph isomorphism network. Across four backbone families, MetaboLLM outperformed corresponding base and medically adapted models on metabolomics knowledge, relational, and description tasks, and transferred to an external public benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved the highest AUC for stress hyperglycemia prediction after coronary artery bypass grafting (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), outperforming conventional models, alternative graph constructions, and graphs generated from unadapted or non-retrieval LLM configurations. Model interpretation further produced biologically meaningful findings in both applications. These results show that domain-specialized language models can organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive and interpretable metabolite graph representations.

</details>


### [308] [RxnCLF: Contrastive Transformation-Aware Reaction Foundation Model for Improved Reactivity Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06259)
*Yiting Zheng,Cheng Fang,Anthony Donofrio,Haote Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RxnCLF is a self-supervised contrastive learning framework for reaction representation that uses a condensed reaction graph (CRG) to unify reactants and products into a single graph. Pretrained on 1.7M reactions, it learns a transformation-aware latent space and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple yield prediction benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reaction yield prediction is hampered by scarce labeled data and a combinatorially large, sparsely populated reaction space. Existing string-, fingerprint-, and graph-based encodings capture chemical transformations only partially, especially for reactions with complex substrates. A representation that explicitly encodes the full transformation structure is needed.

Method: The authors propose RxnCLF, a self-supervised contrastive learning framework built on a condensed reaction graph (CRG) that merges reactant and product information into a single unified graph. This CRG captures both reaction-center features and side-chain contexts. The model is pretrained on 1.7 million reactions from the Pistachio database using contrastive objectives, then fine-tuned for yield prediction.

Result: RxnCLF consistently outperformed graph- and sequence-based baselines across multiple yield prediction benchmarks (Buchwald-Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed BH coupling, HTE C-N coupling, and amide formation), achieving the best overall R² scores.

Conclusion: CRG-based RxnCLF demonstrates strong promise as a scalable reaction foundation model. Beyond yield prediction, it has potential for broader reaction informatics tasks such as regioselectivity prediction, enantioselectivity prediction, and reaction condition optimization.

Abstract: Reaction yield prediction remains challenging because labeled data are scarce and reaction space is both combinatorially large and sparsely populated, limiting the generalization of existing reaction representations. String-, fingerprint-, and graph-based reaction encodings only partially capture chemical transformations, making accurate prediction difficult for reactions with complex substrates. We propose reaction contrastive learning foundation (RxnCLF), a self-supervised contrastive framework for reaction representation learning. RxnCLF is built on a condensed reaction graph (CRG) that unifies reactant and product information into a single graph, enabling the model to learn explicit and enriched transformation structure rather than disconnected graphs. Pretrained on 1.7 million Pistachio reactions, RxnCLF learns a compact and continuous latent space that captures both reaction-center features and broader side chain contexts, making it transformation-aware and chemically interpretable. Fine-tuned on multiple yield prediction benchmarks, including Buchwald-Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed BH coupling, and proprietary HTE C-N coupling and amide formation datasets, RxnCLF consistently outperforms graph and sequence-based baselines, improving R2 and achieving the best performance overall. Our results highlight the promise of CRG-based RxnCLF as a scalable reaction foundation model, with the potential to generalize across broader reaction spaces and support diverse downstream reaction informatics tasks, including regioselectivity prediction, enantioselectivity prediction, and reaction condition optimization.

</details>


### [309] [Hypothesis Testing with Conditional Queries: Learnability and the Value of Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06262)
*Zonghuan Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the adaptivity gap in model evaluation, comparing fixed (non-adaptive) vs. adaptive testing strategies. It establishes that adaptive testing offers at most a quadratic reduction in queries (Θ(N²) gap), not exponential, and characterizes when distribution classes are distinguishable via conditional queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model evaluation often involves choosing tests adaptively based on earlier responses versus fixing all tests beforehand. Understanding the power of adaptivity is fundamental: how much does interaction reduce the number of queries needed? The paper seeks to quantify the adaptivity gap and determine whether exponential branching in adaptive testing yields exponential savings.

Method: The authors use a conditional-query model on a finite outcome space of size N. They analyze pairwise conditional probability separation as the condition for learnability. They construct a randomized non-adaptive procedure using O(N²(T + log(1/ρ))) pair queries that simulates any T-query adaptive policy within total variation distance ρ, uniformly over all distributions. A matching lower bound is constructed using a family with constant adaptive complexity but Ω_ε(N²) non-adaptive complexity.

Result: Key results: (1) Distribution classes are distinguishable iff they have positive separation in pairwise conditional probabilities; when separation is zero, worst-case error is exactly 1/2 at any finite budget. (2) The adaptivity gap is Θ_ε(N²) — adaptive testing can reduce queries by at most a quadratic factor. (3) The exponential branching of interactive evaluation does not yield an exponential query advantage.

Conclusion: Interaction provides a quadratic reduction in testing queries at best, not exponential. The adaptivity gap is precisely characterized as Θ(N²), establishing that the apparent exponential branching of adaptive evaluation is ultimately limited in its query efficiency gains.

Abstract: Model evaluations may fix all tests before observing any responses or select later tests using earlier responses. We study this choice in a conditional-query model on a finite outcome space $\mathcal{X}$ with $|\mathcal{X}|=N$. We first ask which pairs of distribution classes can be reliably distinguished. We then ask how many additional queries are required to match an adaptive tester when all queried events must be fixed in advance. We show that learnability holds if and only if the two classes have positive separation in their pairwise conditional probabilities. When this separation is zero, the optimal worst-case error is exactly $1/2$ at every finite query budget. For any $T$-query adaptive policy and any $ρ\in (0,1)$, we construct a randomized non-adaptive procedure using $O(N^2(T + \log(1/ρ)))$ pair queries chosen before any response is observed. Its simulated transcript is within $ρ$ in total variation of the adaptive transcript, uniformly over all distributions in the model. We also construct a matching family with constant adaptive query complexity and $Ω_\varepsilon(N^2)$ non-adaptive query complexity. Consequently, the worst-case fixed-error adaptivity gap is $Θ_\varepsilon(N^2)$. Thus interaction can reduce the required number of tests by a quadratic factor, but the apparent exponential branching of an interactive evaluation does not yield an exponential query advantage.

</details>


### [310] [The Tamed Subgradient Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm beyond Convexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06283)
*Iosif Lytras,Nikolaos Makras,Sotirios Sabanis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SG-TULA introduces a tamed subgradient Langevin algorithm for sampling from non-smooth, non-convex potentials with superlinear gradient growth, providing explicit non-asymptotic Wasserstein-2 convergence bounds and demonstrating competitive LLM pretraining performance against AdamW and Muon.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Langevin-based sampling algorithms struggle with potentials that are simultaneously non-smooth, non-convex, and exhibit superlinear gradient growth. Smoothing approximations (e.g., Moreau-Yosida) are computationally expensive, and standard subgradient methods lack theoretical guarantees in the superlinear regime. The authors aim to develop a provably convergent, computationally efficient algorithm that operates directly on subgradients while handling these challenging conditions.

Method: The authors propose the Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA), a discrete-time Langevin diffusion that uses subgradients directly (no smoothing) combined with taming techniques to stabilize the drift term under superlinear growth. They derive non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance with explicit dimension and inverse temperature dependence, and extend the analysis to excess risk bounds for optimization. A coordinate-wise variant is also developed and applied to LLM pretraining.

Result: SG-TULA achieves improved non-asymptotic convergence rates over existing subgradient Langevin methods, with all constants explicitly tracked. The assumptions are verified for the regularized pretraining potential of GPT-2 lineage models. Empirically, the boosted coordinate-wise variant pretrains an LLM competitively against fine-tuned AdamW and Muon optimizers, which themselves lack comparable non-asymptotic guarantees.

Conclusion: SG-TULA provides a theoretically grounded, practical algorithm for sampling and optimization in challenging non-smooth, non-convex, superlinear settings. The explicit theoretical guarantees and competitive empirical LLM pretraining results suggest it is a viable alternative to popular optimizers like AdamW and Muon, offering the advantage of formal convergence assurances.

Abstract: We study the problem of sampling from target distributions whose potentials are simultaneously non-smooth, subject to superlinear gradient growth, and non-convex. We introduce the Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA), a discretisation of the Langevin diffusion that operates directly on subgradients, without relying on computationally demanding smoothing procedures. To handle the superlinear regime, taming techniques are employed to produce a stable, explicit scheme. We derive non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance, with all constants tracked explicitly in terms of dimension and inverse temperature, improving upon the currently known rates for subgradient-based Langevin algorithms. We further provide excess risk estimates for the associated optimisation problem. We verify the assumptions, with explicit constants, for the regularized pretraining potential of a LLM in the GPT-2 lineage and the boosted coordinate-wise variant of SG-TULA pretrains the former competitively against finetuned AdamW and Muon, for which no comparable non-asymptotic guarantees are presently available.

</details>


### [311] [Surv-IPTB: An Attention-Based Model for Estimating Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit with Survival Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06288)
*Lev V. Utkin,Stanislav K. Kogan,Andrei V. Konstantinov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Surv-IPTB introduces an attention-based framework that reformulates individual treatment benefit estimation in survival analysis as a binary classification problem. It handles right-censoring via interval-valued imprecise probabilities and uses a learnable query-key attention mechanism to aggregate pairwise patient comparisons across treatment/control cohorts, outperforming conventional meta-learners in nonlinear settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
