Motivation: Estimating individualized treatment effects in survival contexts is challenging due to right-censoring and the need to capture complex, nonlinear relationships between covariates and outcomes. Existing meta-learner approaches (T-learner, S-learner) with standard survival models often fail in nonlinear scenarios. A principled, scalable method that directly estimates the probability of treatment benefit while properly accounting for censoring uncertainty is needed.

Method: The Surv-IPTB framework reformulates Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit estimation as a binary classification problem using pairwise patient comparisons across treatment and control cohorts. Right-censored observations are handled through imprecise probability representations, yielding interval-valued probabilities for uncertain cases. An attention mechanism with learnable query-key transformations performs data-driven aggregation of pairwise comparisons and simultaneously learns soft class probabilities for censored instances. The model is evaluated on synthetic datasets with nonlinear structures (spiral, bell-shaped, circular) across varying censoring rates and treatment effect strengths.

Result: Surv-IPTB demonstrated robust performance across diverse synthetic nonlinear scenarios (spiral, bell-shaped, circular feature spaces) and under varying censoring rates and treatment effect magnitudes. The model consistently outperformed T-learner and S-learner baselines equipped with random survival forests, Cox proportional hazards, and Beran estimators, with particularly pronounced advantages in challenging nonlinear settings where conventional methods degraded significantly.

Conclusion: The proposed attention-based framework offers a scalable, statistically principled solution for personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival analysis. Its strong empirical performance, especially in nonlinear settings where conventional methods falter, supports its utility for real-world clinical decision-making applications.

Abstract: This work presents a novel attention-based framework for estimating the Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit (IPTB) in survival analysis contexts. The proposed model, called Surv-IPTB, directly quantifies the probability that a specific patient will experience extended survival time under treatment versus control. We reformulate IPTB estimation as a binary classification problem, leveraging pairwise patient comparisons across treatment and control cohorts. The framework incorporates a principled handling of right-censored observations through imprecise probability representations, where uncertain treatment effects are characterized by interval-valued probabilities. An attention mechanism with learnable query-key transformations enables flexible, data-driven aggregation of pairwise comparisons, while simultaneously learning soft class probabilities for censored cases. Through extensive experiments on synthetic datasets with complex nonlinear structures, including spiral, bell-shaped, and circular feature spaces, we demonstrate that our approach maintains robust performance across varying censoring rates and treatment effect strengths. The model consistently outperforms meta-learner baselines (T-learner and S-learner) equipped with random survival forests, Cox proportional hazards, and Beran estimators, particularly in challenging nonlinear scenarios where conventional methods exhibit significant degradation. The results establish the proposed attention-based framework as a scalable and statistically principled solution for personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival settings. The code implementing the model is publicly available.

</details>


### [312] [BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06291)
*Johann Birnick,Rayan Saab*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BaKron is an efficient solver for two-sided adaptive rounding in neural network quantization that leverages Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations. It reduces computational complexity from O(m²n²) to O(mn(m+n)) using anti-diagonal parallelism and recursive divide-and-conquer, matching GPTQ's cubic scaling while exploiting richer curvature information from both input activations and output correlations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GPTQ-style adaptive rounding uses only one-sided (input activation) information, ignoring correlations across output coordinates. While two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations (as in BoA and YAQA) capture richer curvature, applying GPTQ directly in the vectorized weight domain is computationally prohibitive. The goal is to achieve two-sided rounding with efficiency comparable to one-sided methods.

Method: BaKron combines anti-diagonal parallelism with a recursive divide-and-conquer construction to solve the two-sided adaptive-rounding problem efficiently. For an m×n weight matrix, it uses O(m+n) sequential steps and reduces total work to O(mn(m+n)). The method is modular with respect to both the base quantizer and the Hessian estimator, and the authors also develop efficient techniques for computing the required Kronecker-factored Hessians.

Result: BaKron achieves cubic scaling (matching GPTQ) while exploiting richer two-sided curvature information. The paper provides practical benchmarks across a range of Hessian estimators and validates the approach experimentally.

Conclusion: BaKron demonstrates that two-sided adaptive rounding for neural network quantization can be made computationally practical, offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off by leveraging Kronecker structure in the Hessian. Its modular design allows flexibility in both quantizer and Hessian estimator choices.

Abstract: We accelerate a family of algorithms for neural network quantization whose geometry is informed by any Kronecker-factored approximation of the Hessian. GPTQ-style adaptive rounding typically uses one-sided information derived from input activations. Two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations can additionally capture correlations across output coordinates, but applying GPTQ directly in the vectorized weight domain is computationally expensive. Building on the two-sided adaptive-rounding formulation used by BoA and YAQA, we introduce BaKron, an efficient solver that combines anti-diagonal parallelism with a recursive divide-and-conquer construction. For an $m\times n$ weight matrix, BaKron uses $O(m+n)$ sequential steps while reducing the total work from $O(m^2n^2)$ to $O(mn(m+n))$. Thus, it matches the cubic scaling of GPTQ while exploiting richer curvature information. Moreover, BaKron is modular with respect to both the base quantizer and the Hessian estimator. We also provide practical benchmarks, consider a range of Hessians that BaKron can be called with, find an efficient technique to compute these Hessians, and evaluate the algorithm experimentally.

</details>


### [313] [On-Policy Self-Distillation without Any Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06296)
*Yijiang Li,Bingyang Wang,Yijun Liang,Yunjie Tian,Di Fu,Nuno Vasconcelos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: U-OPSD achieves genuine self-distillation for LLMs without external supervision by using internal consistency: it constructs pseudo-solutions via majority voting, then conditions on the shortest correct answer to distill into the longest incorrect completion, enabling the model to self-correct where confidently wrong. It matches or exceeds supervised methods like OPSD and GRPO across math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy (self-)distillation methods (OPD/OPSD) claim to be "self"-distillation but still depend on external supervision — ground-truth labels, environmental feedback, or larger teacher models. The authors aim to achieve genuine self-distillation using only the model's own generations, eliminating all external signals.

Method: U-OPSD works in three stages: (1) Sample multiple rollouts from the model and construct a pseudo-solution via majority voting, accepting only when a self-consistency threshold is met. (2) Select the shortest pseudo-solution as the teacher distribution. (3) Distill this teacher into the prefixes of the model's longest incorrect completion, targeting the precise locations where the model is confidently wrong, enabling targeted self-correction.

Result: On AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, MATH500, and AMC23: U-OPSD improves over base Qwen3 by 8.5% (4B) and 10.7% (8B) in non-thinking mode, outperforming OPSD by 3.2% and 2.3% on average. In thinking mode, it surpasses OPSD by 0.9% at 4B and matches at 8B, while beating GRPO by 0.7% and 1.1% respectively.

Conclusion: Genuine self-distillation without external supervision is not only feasible but can match or surpass supervised alternatives. U-OPSD's key insight — leveraging internal consistency to identify and correct confident mistakes — provides an effective, fully unsupervised post-training paradigm for LLMs.

Abstract: On-policy (Self-)Distillation (OPD / OPSD) has shown strong potential for post-training large language models (LLMs). However, existing methods still rely heavily on external supervision, including ground-truth signals, environmental feedback, or guidance from larger models, and therefore fall short of genuine "self"-distillation. In this study, we show that on-policy self-distillation can be achieved using only a model's own generations via internal consistency. We propose Unsupervised On-Policy Self-Distillation (U-OPSD). U-OPSD first samples multiple rollouts and constructs a pseudo-solution by majority vote under a self-consistency threshold. It then conditions a teacher distribution on the shortest pseudo-solution and distills it into prefixes of the model's longest incorrect completion, allowing the model to correct itself precisely where it is confidently wrong. Across diverse benchmarks, base models, and training settings, U-OPSD consistently improves over the base models and matches or surpasses supervised methods with ground truth (GT), such as OPSD and GRPO. On AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, MATH500, and AMC23, U-OPSD improves over the base model by 8.5% and 10.7% on Qwen3 non-thinking mode at the 4B and 8B scales, respectively, and outperforms OPSD by an average of 3.2% and 2.3%. In thinking mode, U-OPSD remains on par with OPSD, outperforming it by 0.9% at 4B and matching it at 8B, while surpassing GRPO by 0.7% and 1.1%, respectively.

</details>


### [314] [RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06310)
*Chenglong Wang,Ziming Zhu,Yifu Huo,Bei Li,Qiaozhi He,Yan Ding,Xiaoyang Hao,Yuxin Gao,Tianhua Zhou,Xiaojia Chang,Tongran Liu,Jingbo Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Generative reward models excel at ranking but fail in RL due to a scalar-vs-comparative mismatch. The proposed RRC method bridges this gap by constructing rewards from relative rankings via self-competitive and anchor-guided strategies, achieving consistent RL improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative reward models show strong response ranking capabilities but underperform in reinforcement learning (RL). The authors identify a fundamental mismatch: generative reward models produce comparative outputs, while existing RL algorithms require scalar reward signals. This gap prevents generative reward models from realizing their full potential in RL-based policy optimization.

Method: The authors propose Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC), which converts relative preference rankings into effective RL reward signals. RRC employs two complementary strategies: (1) self-competitive ranking, which leverages pairwise comparisons among multiple sampled responses from the policy itself; (2) anchor-guided ranking, which constructs scalable ranking-based rewards using a small, fixed set of reference responses.

Result: Experiments on open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks show that RRC substantially improves RL training with generative reward models, yielding consistent performance gains over existing reward construction approaches.

Conclusion: RRC effectively bridges the gap between generative reward models and RL algorithms by transforming comparative ranking signals into scalar rewards, enabling generative reward models to serve as effective RL training signals.

Abstract: Recent advances in reward modeling show a paradigm shift from discriminative reward models to generative reward models. However, despite their strong capabilities in response ranking, generative reward models have not realized their potential in reinforcement learning (RL). Our analysis reveals that this limitation arises from a mismatch between the comparative nature of generative reward modeling and the scalar scoring paradigm adopted by existing RL algorithms. To bridge this gap, we propose a Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC) approach, which enables generative reward models to provide more effective RL learning signals by deriving rewards from relative preference rankings. RRC introduces two complementary strategies: self-competitive ranking, which exploits comparisons among sampled responses, and anchor-guided ranking, which enables scalable ranking-based reward construction with a small set of reference responses. Experiments across open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RRC substantially improves RL training with generative reward models, achieving consistent gains over existing reward construction approaches. Our code can be found at https://github.com/wangclnlp/RRC.

</details>


### [315] [CalibForge: Adversarial Solver Calibration for Scaling Learnable Terminal Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06352)
*Fanzhe Meng,Guoxin Chen,Jiale Zhao,Shuang Sun,Zhiyu Lin,Wayne Xin Zhao,Ruihua Song,Ji-Rong Wen,Kai Jia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CalibForge is an autonomous terminal-task synthesis system that uses adversarial solver calibration—leveraging disagreement among heterogeneous solvers and targeted strong-pass/weak-fail relations—to generate tasks within a solver-relative learnable zone. The system produced 5,431 calibrated tasks, yielding models with significant gains on Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Pro, and Doc2Repo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training terminal agents requires tasks that are not just executable and verifiable, but appropriately challenging for learning. Existing executable validation confirms feasibility but does not reveal how a task behaves relative to a given solver, leaving a gap in identifying tasks that fall within a productive "learnable zone" for agent training.

Method: CalibForge synthesizes terminal tasks using two adversarial solver calibration strategies: (1) multi-solver calibration, which targets disagreement within a heterogeneous solver pool, and (2) contrastive solver calibration, which targets a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation between solvers. Both strategies operationalize a solver-relative learnable zone anchored in demonstrated solvability. Candidate tasks are revised iteratively based on verified solver behavior.

Result: CalibForge constructed 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks. Ablations show both calibration strategies yield more effective supervision than authoring with validation alone or ordinary single-solver feedback. Models trained on the full collection achieve 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, with improvements over the base model reaching 24.71 pp on Terminal-Bench 2.0, 27.68 pp on SWE-bench Pro, and 30.04 pp on Doc2Repo.

Conclusion: Solver-relative learnability is a practical and effective target for constructing agent training data, as demonstrated by the transferable improvements across multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: Training terminal agents requires executable and verifiable tasks that are not merely solvable, but appropriately challenging for learning. Executable validation establishes feasibility, yet does not reveal how a task behaves relative to a given solver setting. In this paper, we present CalibForge, an autonomous terminal-task synthesis system that uses verified solver behavior to revise candidate tasks through adversarial solver calibration. Multi-solver calibration targets disagreement within a heterogeneous solver pool, whereas contrastive solver calibration targets a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation; both operationalize a solver-relative learnable zone anchored in demonstrated solvability. Using CalibForge, we construct 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks. Our ablations show that both strategies yield more effective supervision than authoring and validation alone or ordinary single-solver feedback. Models trained on the full collection achieve 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0. The largest improvements over the corresponding base model reach 24.71 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.0, 27.68 points on SWE-bench Pro, and 30.04 points on Doc2Repo. Together, these results support solver-relative learnability as a practical target for constructing effective and transferable agent training data.

</details>


### [316] [An Optimal Agnostic PAC Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06363)
*Markus Engelund Mathiasen,Jian Qian,Nikita Zhivotovskiy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A learner is constructed that achieves a statistically optimal risk bound for agnostic PAC learning with finite VC dimension, matching known lower bounds up to universal constants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To settle the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning by closing the gap between achievable risk bounds and the lower bounds established by Devroye, Györfi, and Lugosi (1996), providing a learner whose excess risk matches the optimal rate at every fixed noise level L*.

Method: The authors construct a learning algorithm over a hypothesis class H of finite VC dimension d≥1 and analyze its performance on an i.i.d. sample of size n. The analysis yields a high-probability risk bound decomposing excess risk into a variance term (scaling as √(L*(d+log(1/δ))/n)) and a complexity term (scaling as (d+log(1/δ))/n), with explicit universal constants.

Result: The constructed learner achieves, with probability at least 1-δ, the bound L(ĥ) ≤ L* + 7×10⁸ [√(L*(d+log(1/δ))/n) + (d+log(1/δ))/n], which matches the lower bounds from Devroye et al. (1996) at every fixed L*, thereby settling the sample complexity up to universal constants.

Conclusion: The paper definitively resolves the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning for VC classes, demonstrating that the classic lower bounds are tight and achievable by an explicit learner with the derived risk bound.

Abstract: Let $H\subseteq\{-1,+1\}^X$ be a class of finite VC dimension $d\ge1$. Writing $L$ for the binary risk and $L^*=\min_{h\in H}L(h)$, we construct a learner achieving the statistically optimal risk bound: from an i.i.d.\ sample of size $n$, for every $0<δ\le 1/2$, with probability at least $1-δ$, \[
  L(\widehat h)
  \le L^*+ 7\cdot10^8\left(
  \sqrt{\frac{L^*(d+\log(1/δ))}{n}}
  +\frac{d+\log(1/δ)}{n}
  \right). \] This settles the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning up to universal constants at every fixed $L^*$, matching the lower bounds of Devroye, Györfi, and Lugosi [A Probabilistic Theory of Pattern Recognition, Springer, 1996].

</details>

### [317] [F$^2$Agent: Financial Fusion of Agentic Intelligence for Multimodal Trading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05668)
*Changshuo Liu,Yanzheng Jin,Shangfeng Cai,Peng Fang,Xiaokui Xiao,Beng Chin Ooi*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: F²Agent is a multimodal agentic framework for financial trading that uses specialized agents for signal extraction and a noise-robust adaptive fusion mechanism to capture cross-modal dependencies, outperforming 16 baselines with over 20% relative improvement in annualized returns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based trading agents struggle with (1) limited multimodal modeling that fails to capture nuanced cross-modal dependencies, (2) ineffective fusion mechanisms, and (3) inadequate robustness to market noise. With increasingly diverse and heterogeneous information sources, these limitations prevent effective leveraging of multimodal data for high-quality financial trading.

Method: F²Agent introduces two key innovations: (1) a hierarchy of specialized agents that comprehensively extract modality-specific signals from diverse data sources, and (2) a modality-aware adaptive fusion mechanism with noise-robust consistency regularization that dynamically captures fine-grained inter-modality dependencies while generating noise-resilient trading signals.

Result: Extensive experiments on six stocks and cryptocurrency assets show F²Agent consistently outperforms 16 competitive baselines across multiple trading metrics. It achieves over 20% relative improvement in annualized return on average, with notable returns of 120.48% on GOOG and 148.41% on TSLA.

Conclusion: F²Agent demonstrates strong efficacy and robustness across varying market dynamics, validating that hierarchical specialized agents combined with modality-aware adaptive fusion and noise-robust regularization can significantly advance multimodal financial trading performance.

Abstract: With increasingly diverse and heterogeneous information sources, effectively leveraging multimodal data is becoming pivotal for high-quality financial trading. Although recent advancements in Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have enabled the ingestion of multimodal inputs, existing methods fail to capture nuanced cross-modal dependencies and remain vulnerable to market noise, due to limited multimodal modeling, ineffective fusion mechanisms, and inadequate robustness. To address these challenges, we propose F$^2$Agent, a novel multimodal agentic paradigm driven by the Financial Fusion of Agentic Intelligence. F$^2$Agent first deploys a hierarchy of specialized agents to comprehensively extract modality-specific signals. It further introduces a modality-aware adaptive fusion mechanism coupled with noise-robust consistency regularization to dynamically capture fine-grained inter-modality dependencies and generate noise-resilient trading signals. Extensive experiments on six stocks and cryptocurrency assets demonstrate that F$^2$Agent consistently outperforms 16 competitive baselines across multiple trading metrics, with over 20% relative improvement in annualized return on average. Notably, F$^2$Agent delivers returns of 120.48% on GOOG and 148.41% on TSLA, demonstrating its efficacy and robustness in varying market dynamics.

</details>


### [318] [A Two-Tier Perspective on Inference-Time Parallelism in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05791)
*Zihan Xu,Haolin Tian,Hai Jiang*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: TIPEX is a unified execution framework for LLM-driven multi-agent systems that models two levels of inference-time parallelism—Replica Parallelism (exploring multiple complete solution paths) and Structural Parallelism (concurrent execution within a single path via task decomposition)—and demonstrates their complementary effects on accuracy, latency, and token cost on the GAIA benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-driven multi-agent systems require multiple model invocations and complex coordination, and their execution strategies directly impact accuracy, latency, and cost. While parallel execution can improve efficiency, the roles and interrelationships of different forms of parallelism (replica-level vs. structural-level) lack systematic study regarding unified organization and coordination.

Method: The authors propose TIPEX, a controllable execution framework that unifies Replica Parallelism and Structural Parallelism under a single execution semantics. It supports systematic combinations and analyses of different parallel strategies and parameter configurations, enabling coordinated inference-time parallelism across both task-level exploration and within-path task decomposition.

Result: Experiments on the GAIA benchmark show that inference-time parallelism significantly improves accuracy and reduces end-to-end latency at the cost of increased token consumption. Replica and Structural Parallelism exhibit complementary effects across task complexities, with tasks of intermediate difficulty benefiting most from their coordination, while overly aggressive parallel strategies do not necessarily yield better performance.

Conclusion: The two levels of parallelism are complementary rather than redundant: intermediate-difficulty tasks benefit most from their coordination. TIPEX provides a unified semantics for organizing parallelism in multi-agent LLM inference, and the authors caution that aggressive parallelism yields diminishing returns, pointing toward adaptive, complexity-aware parallel strategies as a promising direction.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven multi-agent systems typically require multiple model invocations and complex coordination during inference, and their execution strategies directly affect system accuracy, latency, and computational cost. Parallel execution provides a means to improve inference-time efficiency. From the perspective of inference-time execution, this paper models parallelism in multi-agent systems as two distinct levels of decision processes: Replica Parallelism, which explores multiple complete solution paths at the task level, and Structural Parallelism, which enables concurrent execution within a single solution path through task decomposition. However, the roles of different forms of parallelism and their interrelationships still lack systematic study in terms of unified organization and coordination. We therefore propose TIPEX, a controllable execution framework that unifies these two levels of parallelism and coordinates their roles within the inference process under a unified execution semantics while supporting systematic combinations and analyses of different parallel strategies and parameter configurations. Systematic experiments on the GAIA benchmark demonstrate that inference-time parallelism can significantly improve accuracy and reduce end-to-end latency at the cost of increased token consumption. Further analysis shows that Replica and Structural Parallelism exhibit complementary effects across task complexities, with tasks of intermediate difficulty benefiting most from their coordination, while overly aggressive parallel strategies do not necessarily yield better performance.

</details>


### [319] [Certifying Collective Reasoning in Multi-Agent Systems via Koopman Spectral Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05956)
*Nuzhat Khan,Indrakshi Dey*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Koopman operator theory framework for analyzing LLM agent collectives that debate and vote. It provides machine-checkable certificates for convergence deadlines, faction attribution, and compressed decision representations, achieving 0.93 log-log correlation on convergence tracking and 99.7% fidelity with just 8 of 32 spectral coordinates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agent collectives that debate and vote improve task accuracy, but remain black boxes at the system level: there is no principled test of convergence, no bound on debate rounds needed, and no faithful account of what drove a collective decision.

Method: The authors treat the multi-agent collective as a single nonlinear dynamical system on a communication graph and apply Koopman operator theory. The Koopman transfer operator provides an exact linear representation of the nonlinear dynamics, estimated from interaction traces. The spectrum yields three certificates: (1) the sub-dominant eigenvalue λ₂ determines the convergence timescale and deadline, (2) its eigenvector identifies coherent factions, and (3) leading spectral coordinates form a compressed, auditable message basis.

Result: On an attention-consensus model, the convergence deadline tracks observed convergence with log-log correlation 0.93 and bounds it in 96% of 24 configurations. Attribution is exact when the spectrum certifies metastability. Eight of 32 coordinates preserve decisions at 99.7% fidelity. A certificate learned from 15 debates held on 60/60 held-out debates. The method runs in minutes on a CPU.

Conclusion: Spectral certification via Koopman operator theory provides a practical, computationally efficient layer for trustworthy collective reasoning, offering convergence guarantees, interpretable faction analysis, and compressed auditing—all computable before debates run.

Abstract: Orchestrated collectives of large language model (LLM) agents that debate and vote are an emerging form of computational intelligence: the intelligent behaviour resides in the \emph{interaction}, not in any single agent. They improve task accuracy, yet remain black boxes at the system level: there is no principled test of convergence, no bound on the rounds needed, and no faithful account of what drove a decision. This paper develops a novel framework based on Koopman operator theory and validates its theoretical guarantees on multi-agent consensus dynamics. Treating the collective as one nonlinear dynamical system on a communication graph, we read its essential behaviour off the spectrum of its Koopman transfer operator, an exact linear representation of the nonlinear dynamics estimated from interaction traces. The spectrum yields three machine-checkable certificates: the sub-dominant eigenvalue $λ_2$ fixes the intrinsic timescale of reasoning and yields a convergence deadline computable \emph{before} the debate runs; its eigenvector names the coherent factions the collective reasons in, and $|λ_2|$ certifies when that explanation is valid; and the leading spectral coordinates form a compressed, auditable message basis. On an attention-consensus model, the deadline tracks observed convergence with log--log correlation $0.93$ and bounds it in 96\% of 24 configurations; attribution is exact whenever the spectrum certifies metastability; eight of 32 coordinates preserve the decision at 99.7\% fidelity; and a certificate learned from 15 debates held on 60/60 held-out debates. The study runs in minutes on a CPU, making spectral certification a practical layer for trustworthy collective reasoning.

</details>


### [320] [ASGE-RR: Agentic Service Graph Embedding with Revisable Reservations for Dynamic AI-Agent Calls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06033)
*Trond Vatten,Yuming Jiang*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: AI-agent workflows generate runtime-revealed dependency calls forming an Agentic Service Graph (ASG). The paper formulates ASG Embedding (ASGE) as an online network-control problem and proposes ASGE-RR, a controller with revisable reservations that protects capacity for likely future calls. Evaluated on OpenHands and GPT Researcher workflows, ASGE-RR completes up to 10% more workflow value than baseline controllers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-agent workflows involve distributed calls to models, memory stores, and tools, many of which are revealed only at runtime. This creates a resource allocation challenge: committing resources to currently visible calls may starve higher-value future calls that have not yet been revealed. Traditional service graph embedding assumes full prior knowledge of the graph, making it inadequate for this setting.

Method: The authors formulate the problem as Agentic Service Graph Embedding (ASGE), an online network-control problem with capacity, cost, and deadline constraints. They propose ASGE-RR, an online controller employing revisable reservations. ASGE-RR evaluates candidate replica-and-path mappings against predicted workflow continuations and dynamically updates reservations as new execution information arrives. It exploits a key control point: runtime-revealed dependency calls can be steered before connection establishment.

Result: Evaluated using OpenHands and GPT Researcher workflows with gpt-5.6-luna on a Docker testbed and a WAN testbed, ASGE-RR completes up to 10% more workflow value than a same-information rolling-horizon controller and a current-call steering controller on the WAN testbed. All evaluated AI-agent tasks exposed at least one runtime-revealed dependency call steerable before connection establishment.

Conclusion: Runtime-revealed workflow structure creates a new network control opportunity: proactively protecting resources for likely future calls enables more AI-agent workflows to meet their deadlines, yielding measurable improvements in completed workflow value.

Abstract: AI-agent workflows often involve remote calls to models, memory stores, and tools distributed across a network. As execution progresses, these dependency calls collectively form an agentic service graph (ASG). Unlike traditional service requests, many dependency calls are revealed only at runtime. Consequently, allocating resources to a currently visible call may consume capacity later needed by a call from a higher-value workflow. We formulate this challenge as Agentic Service Graph Embedding (ASGE), an online network-control problem that maps runtime-revealed workflow calls to service replicas and network paths under capacity, cost and deadline constraints. We present ASGE-RR, an online ASGE controller with revisable reservations. ASGE-RR protects capacity for likely future calls while enforcing the constraints. ASGE-RR evaluates candidate replica-and-path mappings against predicted workflow continuations and updates reservations as new execution information becomes available.
  We evaluate ASGE-RR using OpenHands and GPT Researcher workflows executed with gpt-5.6-luna and replayed over in two complementary experimental environments, a controlled Docker testbed and a WAN testbed. The investigation shows that all the evaluated AI-agent tasks expose at least one runtime-revealed dependency call that can be steered before connection establishment. Exploiting this control point, even though the experimental environments are small-scale, ASGE-RR already demonstrates noticeable potential: It completes (up to) 10% more workflow value than a same-information rolling-horizon controller and a current-call steering controller on the WAN testbed. The results suggest that runtime-revealed workflow structure creates a new network control opportunity: protecting resources for likely future calls allows more AI-agent workflows to finish in time.

</details>
